campaign.title: SlimTea 14-day detox — influencer push
campaign.text: Instagram and TikTok posts by fitness influencer @LenaFitLife (280k followers, paid 4,000 EUR per post, contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'). Copy: 'Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE. The SlimTea 14-day detox flushes out toxins, melts belly fat while you sleep and cures bloating for good — I lost 6kg without changing anything else! Use my code LENA20.' No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere. Landing page repeats the fat-melting and cure claims with before/after photos.

detected_practices: undisclosed paid influencer endorsement (no #ad / paid-partnership label)
contractual requirement to hide advertising nature ('authentic tone, no ad markers')
unsubstantiated health claims (detox, flushes toxins, melts belly fat, cures bloating)
weight-loss efficacy claim ('lost 6kg without changing anything else')
before/after photos supporting efficacy claims
discount/referral code (LENA20)
triage.summary: Paid influencer campaign on Instagram/TikTok promoting a 'SlimTea 14-day detox' to women 18-35 in the EU, using undisclosed paid endorsement and aggressive, unsubstantiated health/weight-loss claims (detoxing, fat-melting, curing bloating) with before/after photos. The absence of any #ad or paid-partnership label, combined with a contract requiring hidden advertising, raises serious hidden-advertising and misleading-claim concerns. Health and cure claims for an ingestible product also implicate consumer-protection standards.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The posts are paid advertisements (4,000 EUR per post) presented on online platforms (Instagram, TikTok). DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients be able to identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that the content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The complete absence of any ad/paid-partnership identifier means recipients cannot recognise the commercial nature of the content, breaching the advertising-transparency requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Apply a clear, real-time advertising label to every post (e.g. platform 'Paid partnership' tag plus visible '#ad'/'Werbung') identifying that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf (SlimTea) it is presented. Ensure the label is displayed before the persuasive content, not buried in hashtags.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The advertiser's contract contractually prohibits the very ad identifiers that DSA Art. 26(1) transparency depends on. This turns a potential omission into a deliberate suppression of the ad's identifiability on the platform, aggravating the Art. 26(1) breach and undermining any platform ad-disclosure mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'no ad markers' clause from influencer contracts and instead contractually mandate use of the platform's paid-partnership tools and explicit ad disclosure. Audit all live posts to add the missing labels retroactively.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is a paid influencer push on Instagram and TikTok (online platforms within DSA scope). Under DSA Art. 26(1), recipients must be able to identify, clearly and in real time, that content presented on the platform is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is shown. Here the paid posts carry no #ad or paid-partnership label, and the contract actively requires hiding the advertising nature ('authentic tone, no ad markers'), making the transparency failure deliberate. Art. 28 (profiling-based ads to minors) and Art. 25 (dark patterns) are not clearly engaged, as the campaign declares no personalisation/profiling; the disclosure duties under the platforms' own ad tools (and the advertiser's obligation to declare commercial nature) remain the DSA focus.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: The influencer is paid €4,000 per post to promote SlimTea, yet the posts are presented as her genuine, independent personal experience with no disclosure of the paid relationship. Using editorial-style content to promote a product where the trader has paid, without making that clear, is an undisclosed advertorial — blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances. The contractual clause requiring 'no ad markers' is direct evidence of intent to conceal the paid nature.
findings.evidence_quote: paid 4,000 EUR per post, contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers' ... No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent and unambiguous disclosure of the commercial relationship in every post (e.g. '#ad' / 'paid partnership' at the start of the caption and via the platform's paid-partnership tool). Remove the contractual clause prohibiting ad markers, as it mandates an unlawful practice.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice, where it is not apparent from context, is a misleading omission. The average follower would perceive '@LenaFitLife' recommending a tea that 'CHANGED MY LIFE' as a genuine personal endorsement, not paid advertising. The undisclosed material connection (payment) is information the consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, and it is deliberately hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'
findings.recommendation: Disclose the material connection (payment/sponsorship) clearly and up front in each post and on the landing page, so the commercial intent is immediately apparent to the average consumer before they engage with the content or use code LENA20.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Claiming that the tea 'cures bloating for good' asserts a curative effect over a physical dysfunction. Falsely claiming a product can cure illnesses, dysfunction or malformations is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances; there is no basis to support that an ingestible tea permanently cures bloating. Health/food claims of this kind also engage the Health Claims Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.
findings.evidence_quote: cures bloating for good
findings.recommendation: Remove all cure/treatment claims ('cures bloating for good') entirely. Do not substitute with softened medical claims; any permitted claim about a food/supplement must be authorised under the Health Claims Regulation and be substantiated.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: These are unsubstantiated claims about the product's main characteristics and results ('flushes out toxins', 'melts belly fat while you sleep', specific 6kg weight loss with no other changes). Such physiologically implausible and unproven efficacy claims deceive the average consumer about the benefits and results of the product and are likely to cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The before/after photos amplify the misleading efficacy impression.
findings.evidence_quote: flushes out toxins, melts belly fat while you sleep ... I lost 6kg without changing anything else!
findings.recommendation: Remove or substantiate every efficacy claim with robust, verifiable evidence and authorised health claims. Delete unqualified quantified results ('lost 6kg without changing anything else') and remove before/after photos unless they can be evidenced and are not misleading; add any legally required context.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort economic behaviour, particularly given the campaign runs on TikTok/Instagram addressing 'Girls' where younger and body-image-vulnerable audiences may be reached and are more credulous toward aspirational weight-loss endorsements. This reinforces the specific breaches above where any element falls outside them.
findings.evidence_quote: Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE ... target audience: women 18-35
findings.recommendation: Treat this as an overarching fairness obligation: bringing the campaign into line with the specific fixes above (disclosure, removal of cure/efficacy claims) will address the general unfairness. Avoid targeting/tone that exploits body-image vulnerability in younger audiences.

verdicts.notes: This paid influencer campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, several of them blacklisted (prohibited in all circumstances). The €4,000/post paid promotion is presented as authentic personal experience with no #ad or paid-partnership label — indeed the contract expressly requires hiding the advertising nature — which is an undisclosed advertorial (Annex I point 11) and misleading omission of commercial intent (Art. 7). The product claims that the tea "cures bloating for good" and "melts belly fat" / "flushes out toxins" constitute a blacklisted false cure claim (Annex I point 17) and unsubstantiated misleading actions about the product's main characteristics (Art. 6), reinforced by an unverifiable "lost 6kg without changing anything else" testimonial and before/after photos. Overall this is a high-risk campaign requiring substantial rework before publication.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a paid fitness influencer (€4,000/post) on Instagram and TikTok to promote a "SlimTea 14-day detox" to young women, with no advertising disclosure and with health/weight-loss claims that cannot be substantiated. It carries critical legal risk on two fronts. First, disclosure: the posts hide their commercial nature, and the contract actively forbids ad markers — this is a blacklisted undisclosed advertorial under the UCPD (prohibited in all circumstances) and also breaches DSA advertising-transparency rules. Second, the claims: saying the tea "cures bloating for good" is a blacklisted false cure claim, and "flushes out toxins", "melts belly fat while you sleep" and "lost 6kg without changing anything else" (plus before/after photos) are misleading, unsubstantiated efficacy claims. Because several breaches are blacklisted practices banned outright, the campaign cannot go live in its current form. The AI Act and GDPR were assessed as not applicable. Bottom line: do not publish — the copy, the disclosure approach and the influencer contract all need rework.
recommendations: Do not publish (or immediately pause any live posts) until the campaign is reworked — several issues are blacklisted practices banned in all circumstances.
Delete the cure claim 'cures bloating for good' entirely; do not replace it with a softened medical claim.

Remove or fully substantiate all efficacy claims — 'flushes out toxins', 'melts belly fat while you sleep', and the '6kg without changing anything else' testimonial — and remove the before/after photos unless independently evidenced. Any surviving health claim must be authorised under the EU Health Claims Regulation.

Add clear, prominent advertising disclosure to every post before the persuasive content — use the platform 'Paid partnership' tool plus a visible '#ad'/'Werbung' at the start of the caption — and apply the same disclosure on the landing page.

Remove the 'authentic tone, no ad markers' clause from the influencer contract and instead contractually require use of platform paid-partnership tools and explicit ad disclosure; audit all existing @LenaFitLife posts and retroactively add labels.
Review targeting and tone that address 'Girls' and body-image-sensitive audiences to avoid exploiting the credulity of younger consumers.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Instagram and TikTok are online platforms presenting advertisements; this paid post (4,000 EUR) is an advertisement. Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'. ... No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Require the influencer to use the platform's native paid-partnership/branded-content disclosure tool for every post and story, plus a clear in-copy label (e.g. #ad / 'Paid partnership with SlimTea'). findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Instagram and TikTok are very large online platforms subject to Art. 39, which requires paid advertisements to be logged in a public ad repository with advertiser, payer and targeting details. An influencer post deliberately not flagged as paid/branded content is unlikely to be captured in the platform's advertising system, so the campaign risks circumventing the ad-repository transparency the platform must maintain. The campaign must be structured so it can withstand public archiving.
findings.evidence_quote: No #ad or paid-partnership label anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Declare the paid partnership through the platform's branded-content/ad tools so it is correctly registered; assume the ad content, payer (SlimTea), and any targeting parameters will appear in the public VLOP ad repository, and ensure the creative and claims can withstand that public scrutiny.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Body-image/weight-loss content by a large fitness influencer is foreseeably accessible to minors on Instagram/TikTok, engaging the Art. 28 duty on platforms to ensure a high level of safety for minors. However, Art. 28(2) specifically bans advertisements based on profiling to minors, and the campaign declares no personalisation or profiling-based targeting; on the facts described the specific profiling-ad prohibition is not clearly triggered. Flagged as context: if any behavioural/profiling-based amplification is used on audiences that may include under-18s, the Art. 28(2) ban would be engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: fitness influencer @LenaFitLife (280k followers ... 'Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE.'
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy any profiling- or interest-based paid amplification for this diet/weight-loss creative on audiences that may reasonably include minors, as that would breach the Art. 28(2) ban on profiling-based ads to minors. Confirm no such targeting is used and document that decision.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as paid advertising on Instagram and TikTok (both designated VLOPs), engaging the DSA's platform advertising-transparency regime. The most significant DSA concern is the deliberate suppression of ad identification: a 4,000 EUR/post paid partnership with a contractual requirement of "no ad markers" undermines the recipient's Art. 26(1) right to identify content as an advertisement in real time and risks the ad never being properly registered/labelled through the platform's ad tools (and thus its ad repository under Art. 39). The DSA's minor-protection ban in Art. 28 targets profiling-based ads, and no profiling/personalised targeting is declared, so that specific prohibition is not clearly triggered by the described creative, though minors' foreseeable reach warrants attention. Note that the undisclosed-advertising conduct is primarily a UCPD matter (covered by another agent); here it is assessed only through the DSA platform-transparency lens.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims

findings.evidence_quote: cures bloating for good
findings.recommendation: Remove all cure/treatment claims ('cures bloating for good', 'flushes out toxins'). Do not make any claim that the product cures, treats or prevents a condition; food/health claims must comply with Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and be authorised and substantiated.

findings.title: Misleading actions

findings.evidence_quote: flushes out toxins, melts belly fat while you sleep ... I lost 6kg without changing anything else
findings.recommendation: Remove unsubstantiated efficacy and weight-loss claims and before/after imagery unless supported by robust, verifiable scientific evidence and compliant authorised health claims; avoid implying results with no diet/exercise change.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice, where not apparent from context, is a misleading omission. findings.evidence_quote: contract requires 'authentic tone, no ad markers'
findings.recommendation: Clearly disclose the material connection (paid partnership) in the content itself at the point of first exposure; ensure the disclosure is clear, prominent and not dependent on clicking through or reading captions.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The content is body-image/weight-loss messaging delivered by a 280k-follower fitness influencer on Instagram/TikTok, foreseeably reaching under-18s and body-image-vulnerable young women. Under the Art. 5(3) safety-net, practices likely to distort the economic behaviour of an identifiable vulnerable group are assessed from that group's perspective, heightening unfairness where aggressive/misleading diet claims are used.
findings.evidence_quote: Girls, this little tea has CHANGED MY LIFE
findings.recommendation: Apply audience-restriction and age-gating measures, avoid weight-loss/body-image messaging that exploits the credulity of minors and vulnerable users, and ensure claims meet the professional-diligence standard for the actual (not merely declared) audience.

The copy makes an explicit false cure claim ("cures bloating for good") that is blacklisted, alongside unsubstantiated toxin-flush/fat-melting/weight-loss claims that are misleading actions. Because the content readily reaches minors and body-image-vulnerable young women, the general fairness safety-net is also engaged.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a paid fitness influencer (@LenaFitLife, 4,000 EUR/post) to promote SlimTea on Instagram and TikTok, deliberately styled as authentic personal content with no ad disclosure and making strong weight-loss and health claims. Two practices are on the EU "blacklist" — prohibited outright regardless of consumer impact: the undisclosed paid advertorial (no #ad, a contract clause requiring "no ad markers"), and the false cure claim ("cures bloating for good"). On top of that, the "melts belly fat while you sleep" and "lost 6kg without changing anything else" claims plus before/after photos are misleading and almost certainly unsubstantiated. The missing disclosure also breaches DSA platform advertising-transparency rules on Instagram/TikTok. Because a fitness/body-image message aimed at "girls" foreseeably reaches minors and vulnerable young women, the fairness risk is heightened. The campaign cannot run in its current form and needs substantial rework before launch.

Remove the unsubstantiated efficacy and weight-loss claims ('melts belly fat while you sleep', 'lost 6kg without changing anything else') and the before/after photos unless backed by robust scientific evidence and authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.

Apply age-gating/audience-restriction and avoid body-image messaging targeting 'girls'; do not use any profiling- or interest-based paid amplification on audiences that may include minors (DSA Art. 28(2) ban).

campaign.title: FlashSale mattress countdown
campaign.text: Own-brand webshop promotion for the CloudRest mattress. Every product page shows a red banner: 'HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' with a live countdown, and 'Only 3 left in stock!'. The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, and stock is not actually limited (fulfilment is made-to-order with 2,000+ units weekly capacity). Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.

detected_practices: countdown timer (fake urgency)
resetting countdown that never truly expires
false scarcity claim ('Only 3 left in stock!')
recurring 'last chance / tonight only' email messaging despite ongoing availability
misleading limited-time offer
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult EU consumers; no targeting declared. However, the weekly email blast implies a marketing contact list, so GDPR should verify lawful basis/consent for email marketing. The countdown-reset and false-scarcity tactics are classic misleading commercial practices under the UCPD (potentially blacklisted/aggressive practices).
triage.summary: Own-brand webshop and weekly email promotion for the CloudRest mattress that uses a resetting countdown timer and a false 'Only 3 left in stock!' scarcity message despite made-to-order fulfilment with ample capacity, plus recurring 'last chance/tonight only' emails. The urgency and scarcity claims appear materially false, and email marketing involves processing recipient personal data.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The weekly email blast is unsolicited direct marketing that processes recipients' personal data (email addresses). Under Art. 6(1) read with ePrivacy, email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (or a narrow soft opt-in for existing customers of similar products). The submission does not identify any lawful basis or consent for the marketing list, so lawfulness of the processing cannot be established as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for the email list. Ensure recipients either gave prior opt-in consent or qualify for the ePrivacy soft opt-in (existing customers, own similar products, opt-out offered at collection and in every message). Maintain records demonstrating this basis for every recipient.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: If consent is the basis for the email list, Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate consent, and to make withdrawal as easy as giving it. The recurring blast implies a standing list, but no consent-capture or easy-withdrawal mechanism is described.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Keep auditable consent records (who, when, what wording). Provide a one-click, no-friction unsubscribe in every email that is as easy to use as the original sign-up, and process withdrawals promptly.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct marketing message must inform recipients of their absolute right to object and facilitate opt-out; continued weekly sends must respect any objection. The campaign describes a repeated weekly send with no reference to an objection/opt-out mechanism or suppression list.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Include a clear right-to-object/unsubscribe notice in each email, honour objections immediately by adding addresses to a suppression list, and ensure the Thursday blast excludes anyone who has objected.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (e.g. email addresses) is collected for marketing on the webshop, Art. 13 requires transparency information at the point of collection: controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention and data-subject rights. No sign-up notice or privacy information is described.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email
findings.recommendation: At any point where email addresses are collected on the webshop, present a concise privacy notice (or link) covering controller identity, marketing purpose, legal basis, retention period and data-subject rights, before or at the moment of collection.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged only through the recurring email marketing channel, which necessarily processes recipients' personal data (email addresses). The campaign is not personalised and involves no profiling, special-category data, or minors, so the higher-risk provisions do not apply. However, the submission is silent on lawful basis/consent, transparency at collection, and opt-out handling for the weekly email blast, so several core obligations are engaged but unverified. No prohibited practice is evident under GDPR; findings are precautionary and easily satisfied with proper documentation.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 blacklists falsely stating that a product will only be available for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. The countdown deadline is fictitious — it resets whenever it hits zero or the visitor returns — and the offer is in fact continuously available. This is a per se prohibited practice; no assessment of average-consumer effect is required. The campaign text itself confirms the falsity.
findings.evidence_quote: 'HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' with a live countdown ... The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, and stock is not actually limited
findings.recommendation: Remove the resetting countdown timer entirely, or only display a countdown tied to a genuine, single, non-recurring expiry after which the offer is actually withdrawn. Do not reset the timer per visitor or per session.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 also covers false 'only X left' stock claims used to create artificial scarcity. The campaign admits stock is not limited (made-to-order, 2,000+ units weekly), so the 'Only 3 left' message is false and blacklisted in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Only 3 left in stock!'. ... stock is not actually limited (fulfilment is made-to-order with 2,000+ units weekly capacity)
findings.recommendation: Delete the 'Only 3 left in stock!' message. Only display genuine stock counts reflecting real, verifiable inventory constraints; for made-to-order products with ample capacity, do not display scarcity messaging at all.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The urgency and scarcity claims contain false information about the availability and terms of the product and the existence of a limited-time price advantage, deceiving the average consumer and likely causing a transactional decision (immediate purchase) they would not otherwise have taken. This constitutes a misleading action under Art. 6, running in parallel with the Annex I point 7 breach.
findings.evidence_quote: 'HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' ... 'Only 3 left in stock!'
findings.recommendation: Ensure all availability, deadline and price-advantage statements are truthful and substantiated before publication; align on-page claims with actual fulfilment capacity and offer duration.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of a perpetual countdown and repeated weekly 'last chance / tonight only' emails applies sustained, persistent time-pressure through undue influence, potentially impairing the average consumer's freedom of choice. The recurring false-deadline messaging strengthens the case that the practice is aggressive as well as misleading, though the primary breach remains the blacklisted Annex I point 7 conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Stop sending recurring 'last chance / tonight only' messaging for an offer that is in fact ongoing; reserve genuine-deadline messaging for real, non-repeating campaign end dates and avoid manufactured time pressure.

verdicts.notes: The CloudRest campaign uses a resetting countdown timer and a "Only 3 left in stock!" message despite the campaign's own admission that the deadline never truly expires and stock is not limited (made-to-order, 2,000+ units/week). This is a textbook blacklisted false-urgency/false-scarcity practice under UCPD Annex I point 7 — prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer effect. The same falsehoods also amount to misleading actions under Art. 6, and the recurring weekly "last chance / tonight only" emails add a persistent high-pressure dimension relevant to Arts. 8-9.

report.executive_summary: The FlashSale campaign promotes the CloudRest mattress using a countdown timer ("sale ends in 02:59:41") and a "Only 3 left in stock!" banner, backed up by weekly "last chance, tonight only" emails. The problem is that none of this is true: the timer resets every three hours or whenever a visitor returns, and stock is effectively unlimited because the product is made-to-order with 2,000+ units of weekly capacity. Under EU consumer law this is a per se prohibited practice — false urgency and false scarcity are blacklisted outright (UCPD Annex I point 7), meaning regulators do not even need to prove consumer harm to act. The same claims are also misleading actions, and the repeated weekly "tonight only" emails add an aggressive, high-pressure dimension. Separately, the weekly email blast raises GDPR/ePrivacy questions because the submission does not show any consent or lawful basis for the marketing list, or any opt-out handling. Bottom line: the campaign cannot run in its current form — the fake countdown and stock claims must be removed before launch, and the email list needs a documented lawful basis and unsubscribe mechanism.
recommendations: Remove the resetting countdown timer immediately. Only show a countdown tied to a single, genuine expiry date after which the offer is actually withdrawn — never reset it per visitor, per session, or when it hits zero.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The posts are paid advertising (EUR 4,000 per post) presented on Instagram and TikTok, which are online platforms within the meaning of the DSA. Art. 26(1) requires recipients to be able to identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The complete absence of any ad / paid-partnership label — reinforced by a contractual requirement of 'authentic tone, no ad markers' — means recipients cannot identify the content as advertising, defeating the platform ad-transparency regime the DSA establishes and which platform branded-content tools are designed to satisfy.

Concealing the commercial and promotional nature of the content manipulates the audience's perception of the endorsement's independence. (Primary Art. 25 obligation rests on the platform, but the campaign's design intent squarely engages the concept.)

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The claim that the offer is 'last chance, tonight only' is false because the identical offer is repeated every week. This deceives the average consumer as to the existence and duration of a specific price advantage and the availability of the product on those terms, and is likely to cause a transactional decision (immediate purchase) they would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6. (This overlaps with the per se prohibition in Annex I point 7 for the underlying false-urgency claim.)
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Stop describing a recurring weekly promotion as 'last chance' or 'tonight only'. Advertise the sale accurately (e.g. an ongoing or clearly time-bound offer) so the stated urgency reflects reality.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of a perpetually resetting timer, false scarcity, and weekly-recurring artificial deadlines constitutes persistent high-pressure messaging. Under Arts. 8-9, timing and persistence are factors in assessing whether undue influence significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. The relentless manufactured time pressure may amount to an aggressive practice, above and beyond the misleading dimension.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the manufactured pressure elements (resetting timer, false scarcity, recurring false deadlines) so purchasing decisions are not driven by artificial coercion; give consumers a genuine, pressure-free opportunity to make an informed choice.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a fake countdown timer that resets on return/expiry and an "Only 3 left in stock!" message despite made-to-order capacity of 2,000+ units/week, plus a weekly-recurring "last chance, tonight only" email. These are textbook false urgency and false scarcity tactics, which are blacklisted per se under UCPD Annex I point 7 (prohibited in all circumstances, no case-by-case assessment needed). The same conduct constitutes misleading actions under Art. 6, and the persistent recycled deadline pressure engages the aggressive-practices provisions (Arts. 8-9).

report.executive_summary: Your "FlashSale mattress countdown" campaign promotes the CloudRest mattress on your webshop and by weekly email, using a red countdown timer, an "Only 3 left in stock!" message, and a "last chance, tonight only" email every Thursday. The problem is that none of this urgency is real: the timer resets to three hours whenever it hits zero or a visitor returns, stock is effectively unlimited (made-to-order, 2,000+ units/week), and the "tonight only" offer runs every single week. Under EU consumer law (UCPD) these are textbook fake countdowns and false "only X left" claims — they are on the blacklist of practices banned in all circumstances, meaning regulators do not even need to show consumer harm to act. That makes this a critical compliance risk, not a grey area, and it exposes you to enforcement action and fines across EU markets. Separately, the recurring Thursday emails raise medium-level GDPR/ePrivacy issues: your submission does not show a lawful basis, proper consent, or a working unsubscribe/objection mechanism. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. Bottom line: the core creative concept must be reworked before this campaign can run in the EU.
report.recommendations: ["Immediately remove or disable the resetting countdown timer. Only ever show a countdown that reflects a genuine, fixed, one-time deadline after which the offer truly ends and is not re-offered — the timer must never restart on page revisit or when it reaches zero.

campaign.title: CryptoMasterclass — guaranteed returns funnel
campaign.text: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course: 'Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed. Join 50,000 students.' Landing page shows testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course. Fine print says results may vary.

detected_practices: guaranteed returns / 'risk-free' investment claim
unrealistic profit projections (250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days)
fabricated testimonials with stock photos and invented names
fake celebrity endorsement (fabricated quote from TV economist)
inflated social proof ('Join 50,000 students')
AI trading signals claim
disclaimer contradicting main claim ('results may vary' vs 'guaranteed')
high-price course upsell (499 EUR)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults interested in investing, but broad open channels (search, YouTube pre-roll) with no age gating mean minors can plausibly be reached. Financial 'get-rich-quick' framing raises heightened consumer-protection concern.
triage.summary: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll campaign for a 499 EUR crypto trading course promising guaranteed, risk-free returns via 'AI signals'. It relies on fabricated testimonials, invented names/stock photos, a fake celebrity (TV economist) endorsement, and inflated student counts, with a contradictory fine-print disclaimer. Multiple hallmarks of misleading and aggressive commercial practices targeting consumers.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: If the fabricated endorsement of a real, identifiable public figure is realised as an AI-generated or AI-manipulated image, audio or video (a deep fake) — or the testimonial faces are AI-generated portraits rather than genuine stock photos — Art. 50(4) requires the deployer to clearly disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign declares no generative AI, but a synthetic likeness of a named TV economist is a classic deep-fake scenario, so the AI provenance of these assets must be confirmed. Note: separately from AI-provenance, the fabrication itself is a misleading/false-endorsement matter under UCPD (handled by another agent).
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether the economist endorsement and testimonial visuals/audio/video were produced or altered with generative AI. If so, either remove them or apply a clear, prominent deep-fake/AI-generated disclosure at the point the consumer sees them (Art. 50(4)). Retain provenance records for each asset. Irrespective of AI, do not use fabricated endorsements or invented testimonials.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: If any campaign visuals, video or copy (including the pre-roll video) are outputs of a generative AI system, the provider must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated. This obligation is engaged only if generative AI actually produced the assets; the submission declares it did not, so this is a verification/hygiene point rather than a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented
findings.recommendation: Audit the creative pipeline for any generative-AI-produced assets. Where present, ensure machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) is applied and preserved through publishing to search and YouTube pre-roll.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from a specific economic situation to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm. The get-rich-quick, guaranteed-returns framing targets people in or seeking to escape financial hardship, and the product is promoted as AI-driven. However, the prohibition bites on an AI system that does the exploiting; the campaign as described uses human-written copy and provides no evidence that an AI system performs the targeting or persuasion. Flagged for awareness: if the funnel later uses AI to identify or micro-target financially vulnerable users, this prohibition would be directly engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy any AI system that detects or targets users based on financial distress to drive them into this high-risk, guaranteed-returns funnel. If AI is used anywhere in the acquisition/targeting chain, document that it does not exploit economic vulnerability, and drop the 'risk-free/guaranteed' framing that materially distorts financial decisions.

verdicts.notes: The AI Act attaches obligations to the actual deployment of AI systems. As described, the campaign's AI touchpoints are (a) a product claim that the course provides "AI signals" and (b) a fabricated celebrity endorsement plus invented testimonials. The manipulative/deceptive content here is human-authored marketing copy, not an AI system deploying subliminal or exploitative techniques on consumers, so the Art. 5 prohibitions are not squarely triggered by the campaign as written. The main AI Act exposure is conditional: Art. 50(4)/50(2) disclosure duties would apply if the "well-known TV economist" endorsement or the testimonial imagery is in fact realised as AI-generated/deep-fake media — the submission declares "no" generative AI, so this must be verified. Most of the deception (guaranteed returns, fake endorsement, fake testimonials) falls to UCPD/DSA rather than the AI Act.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: YouTube/Google Search are online platforms subject to Art. 26(1), which requires each ad to be clearly identifiable as an advertisement with the advertiser's identity, the payer, and main targeting parameters disclosed in real time. The advertiser must provide accurate 'on whose behalf' and 'who paid' information for these paid placements, and the ad's heavily testimonial/editorial framing (invented students, a purported economist quote) must not obscure that it is a paid advertisement.
findings.evidence_quote: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ad account registers a truthful advertiser/payer identity with the platform so it can render the mandatory ad label and 'paid by' disclosure; do not design ad creative to appear as organic editorial or genuine third-party endorsement in a way that undermines the platform's ad-identifiability obligation.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to protect them and bans profiling-based ads served to users known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign declares an adult audience and no personalisation/targeting, so a profiling-based-ad breach is not asserted; however, the triage notes broad open channels (search, YouTube pre-roll) with no age gating for a high-risk 'get-rich-quick' financial product, which raises the minor-protection concern the platform must manage.
findings.evidence_quote: adults interested in investing
findings.recommendation: Apply available audience age controls/exclusions and age signals for this financial product, and refrain from any behavioural/profiling-based delivery that could reach minors; document the adults-only targeting configuration to support the platform's Art. 28 obligations.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's operative obligations here fall on the online platforms carrying the ads (Google Search / YouTube), not directly on this advertiser. The advertiser nonetheless engages two provisions: Art. 26(1) ad-transparency (it must supply accurate payer/advertiser identity so the platform can label the ad, and the ad's testimonial/endorsement content must remain clearly identifiable as advertising) and, contextually, Art. 28 protection of minors (open, un-age-gated search/pre-roll for a high-risk get-rich-quick financial product may reach minors). The core deception (fake testimonials, fabricated celebrity endorsement, guaranteed-returns claims) is primarily a UCPD matter and is left to that agent. No sensitive-data targeting, recommender ownership, or VLOP ad-repository obligations are engaged by the advertiser as described.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Presenting invented customer testimonials with stock photos and fabricated names, plus a fabricated endorsement quote attributed to a real TV economist, is submitting/misrepresenting false consumer reviews and endorsements to promote the product. This is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c — no unfairness balancing is required.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove all fabricated testimonials, invented names and stock-photo customers entirely. Only display genuine, verifiable reviews from real students who actually took the course, and remove the fabricated economist endorsement completely (a real endorsement would need documented, truthful authorisation).

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Claiming the course is recommended/endorsed by a well-known economist when no such endorsement exists is a false claim of endorsement, prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 4 (which covers unfounded 'recommended by' claims).
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Delete the fabricated economist recommendation. Do not attribute any recommendation, approval or endorsement to a person or body without documented, verifiable authorisation from that person/body.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The claims that returns are 'guaranteed' and the product is 'RISK-FREE', together with the specific 40x profit projection, are false and unsubstantiated statements about the product's main characteristics and results. Crypto trading is inherently high-risk; such claims deceive the average consumer about benefits/results and are likely to cause a transactional decision (buying the 499 EUR course) that would not otherwise be taken — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Remove 'guaranteed', 'risk-free' and the specific profit projection. Do not promise or imply any specific or guaranteed return; include a truthful, prominent risk warning that trading crypto can result in loss of capital, and only make performance claims that are fully substantiated and typical.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: A near-invisible 'results may vary' disclaimer directly contradicts the headline 'guaranteed' / 'risk-free' claim. Material qualifying information provided in an unclear, ambiguous and untimely (buried fine-print) manner does not cure a headline false claim; this is a misleading omission/obscuring of material information under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: Fine print says results may vary.
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on fine print to contradict the main message. Ensure the headline itself is truthful; risk and no-guarantee information must be presented clearly, prominently and at the same time as the performance claim, not hidden in the fine print.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The '50,000 students' figure functions as social proof about the trader/product's popularity and track record. Given the surrounding fabricated evidence, this number appears unsubstantiated and, if inflated or invented, is a misleading action about the product's characteristics and reach under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Join 50,000 students.
findings.recommendation: Only state student/enrolment figures that are accurate and can be substantiated with records; otherwise remove the claim.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall get-rich-quick funnel — combining guaranteed-return promises, fabricated proof and a high-price upsell delivered through broad open channels — is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of consumers, including the credulous/financially hopeful segment attracted by 'get-rich-quick' framing (Art. 5, incl. Art. 5(3) vulnerable-group perspective).
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Redesign the campaign to meet professional diligence: truthful, balanced claims, clear risk disclosures, no fabricated proof, and no exploitation of consumers' financial hopes/credulity.

verdicts.notes: This crypto course campaign is riddled with core UCPD violations. The "guaranteed" / "RISK-FREE" returns and the "250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days" projection are false/unsubstantiated main-characteristic claims (Art. 6), aggravated by a contradictory "results may vary" fine print (Art. 7 misleading omission). Most seriously, the invented testimonials with stock photos and the fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist are per-se prohibited blacklist practices (Annex I points 23c and 4) — unfair in all circumstances, no case-by-case assessment needed. The inflated "50,000 students" social proof and get-rich-quick framing engage the general fairness prohibition (Art. 5), especially given the financially vulnerable audience.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes a 499 EUR crypto trading course through paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads, using "guaranteed" and "risk-free" return promises, a specific "250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days" projection, invented student testimonials with stock photos, and a fabricated endorsement from a real TV economist. As written, it contains multiple serious and outright-prohibited consumer protection breaches under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. Two of these — the fake testimonials/endorsements and the false claim of endorsement by a named public figure — are blacklisted practices that are illegal in all circumstances, with no room for justification. The "guaranteed/risk-free" claims are classic misleading actions, and burying "results may vary" in fine print does not fix them. There are also conditional AI Act transparency risks: if the celebrity endorsement or testimonial imagery was in fact AI-generated (a likely deep-fake scenario despite the "no AI" declaration), disclosure obligations apply — and the "no AI" declaration must be verified. DSA ad-transparency and minor-protection points require truthful advertiser/payer identity and adults-only delivery controls. Bottom line: this campaign cannot run in its current form and must be substantially rebuilt.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as written. Immediately remove all fabricated testimonials, invented student names and stock-photo 'customers' — these are blacklisted (illegal in all circumstances) under UCPD Annex I point 23c.
Delete the fabricated economist endorsement entirely. Never attribute a recommendation or endorsement to any real person without documented, verifiable authorisation (UCPD Annex I point 4).

Remove the words 'guaranteed' and 'risk-free' and the specific '250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days' profit projection. These are misleading actions under UCPD Art. 6; crypto trading is high-risk and cannot be sold as risk-free.

Add a clear, prominent capital-loss risk warning presented at the same time as any performance claim — do not rely on fine print. A buried 'results may vary' does not cure a false headline (UCPD Art. 7).
Only state a student/enrolment figure (e.g. '50,000 students') if it is accurate and can be substantiated with records; otherwise remove it.

Verify the 'no generative AI' declaration. Confirm in writing whether the economist endorsement and testimonial visuals/audio/video were AI-generated or manipulated. If so, they must be removed (they are already prohibited as fabricated) and, more broadly, any AI-generated assets require AI Act Art. 50(2)/50(4) disclosure and provenance marking.
Do not deploy any AI system that targets users based on financial distress to feed this funnel (AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) risk).

Register a truthful advertiser/payer identity with Google/YouTube so the mandatory ad label and 'paid by' disclosure render correctly, and ensure the creative is clearly identifiable as advertising, not organic editorial (DSA Art. 26).
Apply adults-only audience controls and age signals and avoid profiling-based delivery for this high-risk financial product to prevent reaching minors (DSA Art. 28).

Rebuild the entire funnel to meet professional diligence: truthful, balanced, substantiated claims with no exploitation of consumers' financial hopes (UCPD Art. 5). Given the volume and severity of breaches, obtain legal sign-off before any relaunch.

campaign.title: CryptoMasterclass — guaranteed returns funnel
campaign.text: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads for a 499 EUR crypto trading course: 'Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days — our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed. Join 50,000 students.' Landing page shows testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course. Fine print says results may vary.

detected_practices: guaranteed returns claim
risk-free investment claim
unrealistic profit/earnings claim ('250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days')
AI trading signals claim
fabricated testimonials with stock photos and invented names
fabricated celebrity endorsement (TV economist)
inflated social proof ('50,000 students')
misleading fine print disclaimer ('results may vary')
paid search and video pre-roll advertising
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'adults interested in investing', but open YouTube pre-roll and paid search on financial/crypto topics cannot reliably exclude minors, so minor reach cannot be ruled out. Note declaration mismatch: the campaign declares no generative AI and no personalisation/targeting, yet promotes 'AI signals' and runs on ad platforms that inherently involve targeting and personal data processing — both warrant specialist verification.
triage.summary: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll campaign for a 499 EUR crypto trading course promising guaranteed, risk-free returns via 'AI signals', supported by fabricated testimonials and a fabricated celebrity endorsement. Despite declaring no AI use and no personalisation, the ad markets an AI-based trading tool and contains multiple clearly misleading and deceptive claims targeting EU consumers/investors.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: A fabricated statement attributed to a real, identifiable public figure is exactly the risk profile Art. 50(4) addresses. If this endorsement was created or realistically depicted using AI (a synthetic/deep-fake likeness, voice, or image of the economist), the deployer must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign declares 'no' generative AI, but simultaneously promotes 'AI signals', creating a declaration mismatch that must be verified before the fabricated endorsement can be cleared of Art. 50(4) obligations. If the fabrication is purely textual and non-AI, Art. 50(4) is not triggered (and the issue is a UCPD/false-endorsement matter handled elsewhere).
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Confirm how the economist endorsement was produced. If any AI-generated or AI-manipulated image/audio/video of the person is used, either remove it or add a clear, prominent disclosure that the depiction is artificially generated/manipulated. In practice, a fabricated endorsement of a real person should be removed outright regardless, as no disclosure cures a false endorsement.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Art. 50(2) requires providers of generative AI systems to mark synthetic audio/image/video/text outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format. The campaign declares no generative AI, but uses fabricated testimonial personas; if any testimonial imagery, video or copy was AI-generated (rather than stock/manual fabrication), those assets must carry machine-readable provenance marking. This is contingent on the same unresolved AI-use declaration mismatch.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented
findings.recommendation: Verify the provenance of all testimonial and creative assets. Any AI-generated visual, audio, video or text must carry machine-readable AI-provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermark). Correct the campaign's AI-use declaration to match reality.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The product is an AI-based trading tool marketed as 'RISK-FREE' with 'guaranteed' returns in an inherently high-risk financial domain. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that use deceptive techniques to materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm. If the marketed 'AI signals' system is itself designed to deceive users about risk/returns and drive financial decisions likely to cause significant financial harm, it could engage this prohibition. On the campaign text alone the AI system's actual operation is not described, so this is flagged as a risk requiring verification rather than a confirmed prohibited practice; the misleading nature of the advertising claim itself is primarily a UCPD matter.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Obtain and review technical documentation of the 'AI signals' system. Remove absolute 'RISK-FREE'/'guaranteed' claims. Ensure the AI tool does not deploy deceptive outputs that materially distort users' investment decisions; if it does, it cannot be placed on the EU market.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a set of misleading commercial claims that fall under other regulations (UCPD in particular). Under the AI Act specifically, exposure hinges on an unresolved declaration mismatch: the ad markets "AI signals" and includes a fabricated celebrity endorsement, yet declares no generative AI use. If any of the endorsement/testimonial assets were in fact AI-generated or manipulated (deep fake likeness/voice/image or synthetic content), Art. 50(4) and 50(2) transparency obligations would be triggered and are unmet. The AI trading tool's "RISK-FREE / guaranteed" framing also raises an Art. 5(1)(a) deceptive-AI concern. On the text as declared (no generative AI) no AI Act obligation is definitively breached, so findings are calibrated to the verification needed rather than confirmed violations.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The campaign runs as paid search and YouTube pre-roll targeted to 'adults interested in investing'. Serving ads to an interest-based audience on these platforms relies on automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (economic situation, interests, behaviour), which meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling. The 'no personalisation/targeting' declaration therefore mischaracterises the processing actually taking place through the ad platforms.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no
findings.recommendation: Correct the declaration: acknowledge that interest/behaviour-based ad delivery on search and video platforms constitutes profiling, and document the audience-segmentation and targeting parameters actually used so the lawful basis and transparency obligations can be assessed.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Interest-based targeting on paid search and YouTube pre-roll involves processing of personal data (audience segments, behavioural signals) that requires a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1). No lawful basis (consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment) is identified for the targeting, nor for any lead capture in the 499 EUR course funnel ('Join 50,000 students').
findings.evidence_quote: adults interested in investing
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6(1) basis for the ad-targeting and for any sign-up/lead data collected on the landing page (typically consent for tracking-based targeting per ePrivacy, plus consent or legitimate interest for the funnel), and ensure it is recorded before processing begins.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Attributing an invented endorsement to a named, identifiable real person (the TV economist) is processing of that individual's personal data — their name and reputation — done without their knowledge, without a lawful basis, and in a way that is neither fair nor transparent, breaching the Art. 5(1)(a) lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle. The broader undeclared ad-platform processing (targeting declared as 'no') also sits uneasily with the transparency limb of this principle.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated endorsement entirely; do not process any identifiable person's name/likeness in marketing without their informed consent and a lawful basis. Ensure all personal-data processing tied to the campaign is transparent and accurately declared.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The funnel structure of a paid course landing page strongly implies collection of personal data (email/lead sign-up, payment for the 499 EUR course). Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller provide identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and any profiling. The campaign material describes no such privacy information, only commercial fine print ('results may vary').
findings.evidence_quote: Join 50,000 students.
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, layered Art. 13 privacy notice at every data-collection point in the funnel (lead forms, checkout), covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients, and data-subject rights including the right to object to marketing.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Open YouTube pre-roll and paid search on crypto/finance topics cannot reliably exclude minors, so the funnel may collect data from users under 16. If consent is the basis for any data collection (e.g. tracking/marketing sign-up) from a child under the applicable age threshold, Art. 8 requires parental consent and reasonable age-verification efforts, which the campaign does not provide for.
findings.evidence_quote: adults interested in investing
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance/verification in the sign-up flow and configure platform targeting to exclude minors; where consent-based processing of children's data cannot be excluded, obtain and verify parental consent in line with the applicable national age threshold.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares "no personalisation/targeting" and does not describe any data-collection flow, but it runs on paid search and YouTube pre-roll (which inherently profile audiences) and is a lead-funnel for a 499 EUR course ("Join 50,000 students"), so personal-data processing is almost certainly involved. The declaration mismatch and absence of any stated lawful basis or transparency information engage GDPR Arts. 6(1), 5(1)(a), 13, 4(4) and — given non-excludable minor reach on open channels — Art. 8. A distinct GDPR concern is the fabricated quote attributed to a named, identifiable real TV economist, which is unlawful/unfair processing of that individual's personal data. Several findings rest on inference because the sign-up mechanics are not spelled out; these should be verified against the actual landing-page data flow.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign runs open YouTube pre-roll and paid search on financial/crypto topics on very large online platforms. As the triage notes, minor reach cannot be ruled out. DSA Art. 28(2) bans presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients the platform is aware with reasonable certainty are minors, and requires appropriate measures for a high level of minor protection. A high-risk 'guaranteed returns' crypto investment ad delivered via profiled placement on channels accessible to minors engages this prohibition, notwithstanding the advertiser's 'no targeting' declaration, because VLOP ad delivery inherently involves profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Paid search and YouTube pre-roll ads
findings.recommendation: Configure the campaigns to exclude minors and disable profiling-based delivery to any audience that may include under-18s (use age-gating / contextual-only delivery on YouTube and Search). Confirm with the platforms that no profiling-based ad delivery reaches recipients identifiable as minors, and document age-assurance controls.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, in a clear and unambiguous manner, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. While the platform bears the labelling obligation, the advertiser must supply truthful advertiser/payer information and must not undermine the 'on whose behalf' transparency by dressing paid promotion as an independent endorsement from a TV economist. The fabricated endorsement obscures the true commercial source of the message.
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated celebrity endorsement and ensure all placements carry accurate advertiser and payer identity so the platform's Art. 26(1) ad-transparency labelling reflects the true commercial source. Do not present paid advertising as independent third-party recommendation.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Google Search and YouTube are designated VLOPs subject to DSA Art. 39, which requires a public ad repository capturing ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. This campaign's 'guaranteed / risk-free' claims and fabricated endorsement will therefore be publicly archived and open to regulator, journalist and complainant scrutiny, amplifying legal exposure under other regimes.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Assume every creative and targeting parameter will be permanently public in the VLOP ad repository; ensure all claims are substantiated and lawful before launch so they can withstand public and regulatory scrutiny.

verdicts.notes: The DSA primarily binds providers of online platforms (Google Search, YouTube) rather than the advertiser directly, so most exposure here is indirect. The strongest DSA-relevant risk is Art. 28: open YouTube pre-roll and paid crypto search cannot reliably exclude minors, and profiling-based ads that would reach minors are banned — the "no targeting" declaration does not eliminate this because VLOP ad delivery inherently involves profiling. Art. 26(1) transparency and Art. 39 ad-repository archiving are engaged as context: the campaign's deceptive claims and fabricated endorsement will be publicly archived and must withstand scrutiny. The deceptive-design substance (fabricated testimonials/celebrity endorsement) is better addressed under UCPD; under DSA Art. 25 it is a weaker fit because the trader's own landing page is not a platform interface.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Annex I point 23c prohibits in all circumstances submitting/commissioning false consumer reviews or endorsements, or misrepresenting endorsements, to promote a product. The invented testimonials with stock photos and fabricated names are false consumer endorsements, and the fabricated quote from a TV economist is a false endorsement — both are per-se blacklisted, with no need to prove consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: testimonials with stock photos and names we invented ('Marta from Sevilla made 14,000 EUR in her first month') and a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove all invented testimonials and the fabricated celebrity/economist quote entirely. Only use genuine, attributable endorsements from real, consenting people who actually used the product, and never fabricate names, images or quotes.

findings.title: Blacklist: unverified consumer reviews
findings.rationale: Annex I point 23b prohibits presenting reviews/testimonials as coming from consumers who actually used the product without reasonable steps to verify this. Here the testimonials are presented as real customer results ('made 14,000 EUR in her first month') but are admittedly invented, so no verification exists and the practice is per-se prohibited.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows testimonials with stock photos and names we invented
findings.recommendation: Do not present any testimonial as a real customer result unless you have verified the reviewer genuinely used the course; disclose your verification method.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits false information deceiving the average consumer about a product's main characteristics and results that causes a transactional decision. Crypto trading is inherently high-risk and returns can never be guaranteed; 'RISK-FREE' and 'guaranteed returns' are objectively false claims about performance and are central to inducing the 499 EUR purchase.
findings.evidence_quote: our AI signals are RISK-FREE and returns are guaranteed
findings.recommendation: Delete the 'risk-free' and 'guaranteed returns' claims. Any performance statement must be truthful, substantiated and accompanied by a prominent risk warning that capital is at risk and returns are not guaranteed.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers exaggerated/unsubstantiated claims about results and benefits. A 40x return in 90 days is an unrealistic, unsubstantiated earnings claim likely to deceive the average consumer about the course's likely outcomes and to distort their purchasing decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Turn 250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days
findings.recommendation: Remove the specific unrealistic profit projection. Do not quantify potential returns unless backed by verifiable, representative evidence, and include a prominent risk disclaimer.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers deception about the trader's endorsements and qualifications. Attributing a recommendation to a well-known economist who never gave it falsely lends authority and credibility to the product, deceiving consumers and distorting their decision (also reinforcing the Annex I point 23c breach).
findings.evidence_quote: a fabricated quote from a well-known TV economist recommending the course
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated economist quote. Only cite endorsements that were genuinely given, with documented consent and accurate wording.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers false claims about the product/trader. An inflated or unsubstantiated social-proof figure ('50,000 students') deceives consumers about the product's popularity and track record if it cannot be substantiated, influencing the transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Join 50,000 students
findings.recommendation: Only state student numbers if they are accurate and can be substantiated; otherwise remove the figure.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 covers misleading omissions and information provided in an unclear or untimely manner. A buried 'results may vary' disclaimer cannot cure headline claims of 'guaranteed' and 'risk-free' returns; the material qualification is hidden while the false headline dominates, leaving the consumer unable to make an informed decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Fine print says results may vary
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on fine-print disclaimers to offset false headline claims. Correct the headline claims themselves and give material risk information equal prominence at the point of the claim.

verdicts.notes: This crypto-course campaign contains multiple clear UCPD breaches, including two per-se blacklisted practices (fabricated testimonials/endorsements under Annex I point 23c and undisclosed unverified reviews under 23b), alongside serious misleading actions under Art. 6 (guaranteed/risk-free returns, unrealistic earnings, fabricated celebrity recommendation) and a misleading omission under Art. 7 (contradictory 'results may vary' fine print). The 'RISK-FREE' and 'guaranteed' investment claims are objectively false for crypto trading and central to inducing a 499 EUR purchase. Overall risk is critical and the campaign should not run in its current form.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises a 499 EUR crypto trading course using promises of "risk-free" and "guaranteed" returns, an unrealistic "250 EUR into 10,000 EUR in 90 days" claim, invented customer testimonials with stock photos, and a fabricated endorsement attributed to a real TV economist. These are not borderline issues — several are outright illegal under EU consumer law. Fabricating testimonials and endorsements is on the UCPD "blacklist" of practices banned in all circumstances, and the "risk-free/guaranteed" language is objectively false for crypto and is the core hook driving the sale. On top of that, the campaign's declarations are inaccurate: it says "no targeting" and "no generative AI," but paid search and YouTube ads inherently profile audiences (GDPR/DSA exposure, including a ban on profiling-based ads reaching minors), and the "AI signals" plus fabricated endorsement raise AI Act transparency questions that need verification. Using a real person's name and reputation without consent is also unlawful data processing under GDPR, and the funnel appears to collect personal data with no visible privacy notice or lawful basis. The verdict: the campaign must not run in its current form and requires substantial rework, not cosmetic fixes. A buried "results may vary" disclaimer does not cure any of this.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as-is. Immediately remove all invented testimonials (e.g. 'Marta from Sevilla') and the fabricated TV economist quote — fabricated reviews and endorsements are banned outright under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I 23b/23c) with no defence available.

Stop relying on the 'results may vary' fine print — it cannot offset false headline claims. Fix the headline claims themselves.
Remove or substantiate the '50,000 students' figure; only state numbers you can prove.

Correct the campaign declarations: paid search and YouTube ad delivery constitutes profiling/targeting, so the 'no personalisation/targeting' declaration is inaccurate. Document the actual targeting and a valid GDPR Art. 6 lawful basis, and configure campaigns to exclude minors and disable profiling-based delivery to any audience that may include under-18s (DSA Art. 28).
Never use a real, identifiable person's name or likeness in marketing without their informed consent — the fabricated economist endorsement is also unlawful processing of personal data under GDPR.
Add a complete privacy notice (GDPR Art. 13) at every data-collection point in the funnel (lead forms, checkout), and implement age assurance in the sign-up flow.

Resolve the AI-use declaration mismatch: the ad promotes 'AI signals' yet declares no generative AI. Verify how the endorsement and testimonial assets were produced — any AI-generated or AI-manipulated content triggers AI Act transparency/marking obligations (Art. 50), and a deceptive AI trading tool could engage the Art. 5 prohibition.

Assume all creatives and targeting parameters will be permanently public in the VLOP ad repositories (DSA Art. 39) and open to regulator scrutiny, so every claim must be lawful and substantiated before launch.
