triage.audience_notes: Explicitly directed at children 6-11 — a vulnerable audience under EU consumer law. UCPD Annex I No. 28 prohibits direct exhortations to children to buy or to persuade their parents to buy advertised products; both the YouTube script and Roblox pop-ups appear to breach this blacklisted practice. DSA duties on protection of minors and prohibition on advertising to minors on platforms are engaged (Roblox/YouTube as intermediaries). Although personalisation is declared 'no', online platforms serving children inevitably process personal data (age assurance, account data, in-game identifiers), so GDPR — especially children's data protections (Art. 8) — should be reviewed. Declared 'no AI', so AI Act is not flagged, but the influencer/animator voice authenticity and any generative content should be verified during specialist review.
triage.summary: Toy-line launch campaign for RoboPets directly targeting children aged 6-11 via YouTube Kids videos and a Roblox branded world, using influencer voicing and repeated in-game pop-ups. The messaging directly exhorts children to buy and to pressure their parents into purchasing, with virtual-currency rewards tied to spending. This raises significant child-directed marketing and vulnerable-audience concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The entire audience (6-11) is below the GDPR digital-consent threshold, which is 16 and at most lowered to 13 by Member States. Delivering a branded Roblox world and repeated daily per-player pop-ups is an information society service offered directly to children that processes their personal data (account/in-game identifiers, engagement/session data enabling 'daily' delivery). Where consent is the legal basis, processing children under the age threshold is lawful only with verified parental consent, and the controller must make reasonable efforts to verify it. The campaign gives no indication that parental consent is sought or age/parental-consent verification is performed.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: children 6-11 ... The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Before launch, map exactly what personal data of child players is processed to run the branded world and pop-ups. If any processing relies on consent, implement a robust parental-consent mechanism with reasonable age-and-consent verification appropriate to a 6-11 audience; otherwise identify and document an alternative lawful basis and minimise data to what is strictly necessary.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Serving recurring, per-player prompts within a branded world requires processing personal data (identifiers, engagement/frequency-capping data). The submission declares no personalisation and discloses no lawful basis, yet a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis (consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment) is required for this processing. Legitimate interests is difficult to rely on for marketing directed at young children given the strong weighting of their interests.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Document a specific Art. 6(1) lawful basis for all data processing supporting the campaign in the branded world and complete a legitimate-interest balancing test if that basis is used, explicitly weighting the reasonable expectations and vulnerability of children aged 6-11. Prefer parental consent where processing is not strictly necessary.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle is engaged. A campaign that declares 'no personalisation/targeting' while running a branded world that sends 'daily pop-ups to child players' raises a fairness/transparency tension: recurring per-player delivery implies some form of identification or engagement tracking. Processing children's data for commercial pressure without clear, honest disclosure risks breaching the fairness limb, which is applied strictly where children are involved.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: no
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the 'no personalisation' declaration with the actual delivery mechanics of the daily pop-ups. Ensure any data-driven delivery is honestly and clearly described, avoid covert tracking, and ensure the processing is fair to a child audience (e.g. frequency limits, no exploitation of children's inability to appreciate commercial intent).

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected from children in these services, information under Arts. 12-13 must be provided in a concise form and in clear, plain language specifically adapted to a child audience. A campaign aimed at 6-11 year olds must present any privacy information in a way this age group can understand, and there is no indication such child-appropriate transparency is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for the RoboPets collectible toy line on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world
findings.recommendation: Provide any required privacy information in child-friendly language and format at the point of collection (and to parents), tailored to a 6-11 audience, covering controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, retention and children's rights.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is explicitly directed at children aged 6-11 and is delivered through information society services (YouTube Kids channels and a branded Roblox world) that inevitably process children's personal data — account/in-game identifiers and session data needed to serve "daily pop-ups" to individual child players. Because all targets (6-11) are below the GDPR digital-consent age (16, or as low as 13 in some Member States), no child in the audience can validly consent, so any consent-based processing requires verified parental consent (Art. 8), a documented lawful basis (Art. 6), and child-intelligible transparency (Art. 12). The "no personalisation/targeting" declaration is inconsistent with recurring, per-player in-game prompts and should be verified. No detailed data-collection flow is disclosed, so these obligations are engaged and, as described, unlikely to be satisfied — but not yet confirmed breaches.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: YouTube Kids and the Roblox branded world are online platforms accessible to and here explicitly directed at minors. Art. 28(1) requires providers to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors, including age-appropriate design. A campaign built on purchase pressure, pester-power exhortations and repeated nagging aimed at 6-11 year-olds is inconsistent with the age-appropriate, protective environment the DSA requires for minors, exposing both the platforms and the advertiser driving that content to compliance risk.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for the RoboPets collectible toy line on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world ... Declared target audience: children 6-11
findings.recommendation: Redesign the creative to meet age-appropriate-design expectations for a child audience: remove purchase-pressure and pester-power messaging, remove urgency/scarcity cues, and confirm with the platforms that the placement fits their minor-protection measures. Avoid any placement relying on profiling of users known to be minors (Art. 28(2)).

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits online-interface design that deceives, manipulates or materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, and expressly names repeatedly requesting a choice (nagging). Daily repeated pop-ups pressuring child players, combined with a virtual-currency reward ('500 RoboCoins') contingent on a real-money purchase, constitute a manipulative/nagging pattern that distorts decision-making — an effect amplified because the recipients are young children.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'
findings.recommendation: Stop the daily repeated purchase pop-ups and remove the virtual-currency incentive tied to spending real money. Any in-world promotional message should be a single, clearly identifiable, non-repeating notice with no pressure or reward-for-purchase mechanic.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that platform advertisements be identifiable as ads in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time. Advertising embedded in a Roblox branded world and delivered through a trusted kids'-animator voice risks not being recognisable as advertising, particularly to a 6-11 audience, amounting to disguised advertising. In-world branded content and influencer-voiced promotion must be transparently marked as advertising on whose behalf it is presented.
findings.evidence_quote: on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world ... voiced by a popular kids' animator
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad touchpoint (branded world content, videos, pop-ups) carries a clear, child-comprehensible 'advertisement/paid promotion' label identifying RoboPets as the advertiser, presented in real time and in a form intelligible to the target age group; coordinate labelling requirements with YouTube and Roblox.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on YouTube Kids and a Roblox branded world — both online platforms subject to the DSA — and is explicitly directed at children aged 6-11. This engages the DSA minor-protection duty (Art. 28), the prohibition of manipulative interface design/dark patterns via repeated nagging pop-ups and purchase incentives (Art. 25), and ad-identifiability/disguised-advertising concerns (Art. 26(1)). The Art. 28(2) profiling-ad ban is not clearly triggered because no personalisation is declared, but the age-appropriate-design duty and the dark-pattern prohibition are squarely in play. Platform operators bear primary DSA duties, but the advertiser's own creative directly drives the non-compliant experiences and should be remediated.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits, in all circumstances, including in an advertisement a direct exhortation to children to buy or to persuade their parents/adults to buy the advertised product for them. The video script, aimed at YouTube Kids and voiced for a 6-11 audience, does exactly this: it both directly tells the child to buy ('buy you one RIGHT NOW') and explicitly instructs the child to nag their parents ('tell your mum and dad to buy you one', 'Ask them today'). This is a per se blacklisted practice — no case-by-case assessment or exemption is available.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Remove all imperatives directing children to buy or to ask/tell/persuade parents to buy. Reframe messaging to be information-only and, for purchase decisions, address the parent/adult (not the child), e.g. product information directed at parents rather than 'ask your mum and dad to buy you one'.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: The Roblox pop-up is a second, distinct instance of a blacklisted direct exhortation: it tells child players to get their parents to purchase ('Get your parents to order'), tying the purchase to an in-game virtual-currency reward that further incentivises children to pressure parents. Being an in-game purchase prompt aimed at children is expressly within the marketing relevance of point 28. Prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!
findings.recommendation: Remove the pop-up prompt entirely, or eliminate any call for children to get parents to purchase and remove the purchase-linked RoboCoins reward. In-game currency should not be granted contingent on a real-money purchase solicited through the child.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, by harassment, coercion or undue influence — with persistence and timing as express factors — it significantly impairs freedom of choice and prompts a transactional decision. Daily, repeated purchase prompts inside a game played by 6-11 year-olds, reinforced by urgency ('tonight', 'RIGHT NOW') and social pressure ('before your friends get theirs'), amount to persistent undue influence on a credulous audience whose freedom of choice is readily impaired (assessed per Art. 5(3) from the perspective of the average child).
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Cease the daily repeated pop-ups. Any in-game brand presence should be non-transactional, capped in frequency, and free of urgency or social-pressure framing directed at children.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5, with Art. 5(3), provides that practices likely to distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (here children, due to age and credulity) are assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. The combination of social-pressure/FOMO framing ('before your friends get theirs'), urgency ('RIGHT NOW', 'tonight'), influencer voicing and purchase-linked rewards, all aimed at 6-11 year-olds, is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the behaviour of that vulnerable group, breaching the general fairness standard even beyond the specific blacklist entries.
findings.evidence_quote: before your friends get theirs
findings.recommendation: Redesign the campaign to meet professional-diligence standards for child audiences: remove FOMO/social-pressure and urgency cues, avoid influencer purchase-driving of children, and address purchase messaging to parents rather than children.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that the commercial (advertising) intent be clearly identifiable, and paid/incentivised influencer content presented as normal creator content risks a misleading omission — especially for a child audience less able to distinguish advertising from entertainment. Using a popular kids' animator to voice branded video scripts must be clearly and age-appropriately identified as advertising; if the commercial nature is not apparent to child viewers, the practice omits material information about its commercial intent.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Ensure prominent, child-comprehensible ad labelling on all videos and in-game content (clear 'advert'/'ad' identification), and disclose any material connection or payment involving the animator so the commercial intent is unmistakable.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is explicitly directed at children aged 6-11 and contains multiple direct exhortations to children to buy and to pressure their parents to buy — a practice blacklisted in all circumstances under UCPD Annex I point 28. The urgency/social-pressure framing and the reward-linked, daily-repeated in-game purchase prompts compound the unfairness, engaging the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9) and the general fairness safety-net applied to a vulnerable audience (Art. 5(3)). At least one blacklisted (per se prohibited) practice is clearly present.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes RoboPets toys to children aged 6-11 on YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world, using scripts and pop-ups that directly tell kids to buy and to nag their parents to buy. As drafted, it is very likely unlawful. The most serious problem is a hard, no-exceptions rule: EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 28) bans advertising that directly urges children to buy a product or to pressure their parents into buying it — and your video script ("tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW") and Roblox pop-up ("Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight") do exactly that. On top of this, the daily repeated pop-ups and the RoboCoins reward-for-purchase amount to aggressive/manipulative practices (UCPD Arts 5, 8-9) and prohibited "nagging" dark patterns under the DSA, while running these ads to children raises age-appropriate-design and ad-labelling duties (DSA Arts 25, 26, 28). Separately, because the entire audience is below the EU digital-consent age, any personal data used to serve per-player daily pop-ups needs a proper lawful basis and verified parental consent (GDPR Arts 6, 8), and the "no personalisation" declaration looks inconsistent with per-player daily delivery. This campaign should not launch in its current form; the child-directed purchase exhortations must be removed before any relaunch.
recommendations: Do not launch the campaign as written. Remove every instruction that tells children to buy or to ask/tell/persuade their parents to buy — both the video script line ('tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW') and the Roblox pop-up ('Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight'). This is a per se banned practice with no exemption (UCPD Annex I, point 28).
Eliminate the RoboCoins-for-purchase mechanic. Do not grant in-game currency contingent on a real-money purchase solicited through a child.

Stop the daily repeated purchase pop-ups. Any in-world brand presence should be a single, non-repeating, non-transactional, clearly labelled notice with no urgency, scarcity, or social-pressure framing (removes DSA dark-pattern and UCPD aggressive-practice risk).
Remove all urgency and FOMO cues ('RIGHT NOW', 'tonight', 'before your friends get theirs') and reframe purchase messaging to address parents/adults, not children.

Add clear, child-comprehensible 'advertisement/paid promotion' labelling to all videos, in-world content, and pop-ups, and disclose the paid relationship with the kids' animator (DSA Art 26; UCPD Art 7).
Reconcile the 'no personalisation/targeting' declaration with the reality of per-player daily pop-ups; if data-driven delivery is used, describe it honestly and confirm it to the platforms.

Before any data-processing goes live, map what child data is used, document a valid GDPR Art 6 lawful basis, and implement verified parental consent (Art 8) with child-friendly transparency (Art 12) given the 6-11 audience is below the EU consent age.
Coordinate placement and minor-protection measures with YouTube and Roblox to meet age-appropriate design expectations, and re-submit the revised creative for compliance review before launch.

campaign.title: RoboPets launch — kids YouTube push

They're SO cool — tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!' The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'

direct exhortation to children to pester parents to purchase ('tell your mum and dad', 'ask them today')
influencer/creator endorsement (popular kids' animator voicing scripts)
urgency/pressure tactics ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'tonight', 'before your friends get theirs')

triage.audience_notes: Explicitly directed at children 6-11. UCPD Annex I(28) blacklists direct exhortations to children to buy or to persuade adults to buy; both video scripts and Roblox pop-ups appear to breach this per se. DSA is engaged as advertising is delivered on very large online platforms (YouTube/Google, Roblox) with heightened protections for minors and a ban on profiling-based ads to minors. Although personalisation is declared 'no', targeting children as an audience segment and in-game/platform ad delivery almost certainly involves processing children's personal data, so GDPR (esp. Art. 8 child consent, and profiling protections) should be reviewed. No generative AI declared or evident, so AI Act not currently engaged, but re-triage if AI content is added.
triage.summary: A toy-line campaign targeting children aged 6-11 across YouTube Kids and a branded Roblox world, using a popular kids' animator and in-game pop-ups. The messaging directly urges children to buy and to pressure their parents into purchasing, using urgency, social-pressure and virtual-currency incentives. This raises serious concerns around unfair commercial practices aimed at minors, platform/online-advertising obligations, and processing of children's data.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The campaign targets children 6-11 and is delivered via information society services (YouTube Kids, Roblox branded world). Delivering daily pop-ups to identified 'child players' requires processing their personal data. Where consent is the legal basis, GDPR Art. 8 makes processing lawful only where the child is at least 16 (or 13 where a Member State has lowered the threshold) — all far above the 6-11 declared audience. Below that age, verified parental consent is required, and the controller must make reasonable verification efforts. No such mechanism is described, so any consent-based processing of these children's data is presumptively unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on consent obtained from the children themselves. Map all data flows in the Roblox world and any YouTube Kids ad delivery, and implement a robust, age-appropriate parental-consent and age-verification mechanism before collecting or using any personal data of users known/likely to be under the applicable age threshold. If verified parental consent cannot be obtained, remove data-driven pop-up delivery to child players.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing of children's personal data in connection with in-game pop-up delivery and the branded world requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Consent from a 6-11 year old is not valid (see Art. 8/Art. 4(11)), and legitimate interests will rarely override the interests of children in a marketing context. The submission declares no personalisation but does not identify any lawful basis for the platform/in-game data processing that pop-up delivery entails.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: children 6-11
findings.recommendation: Document the specific lawful basis for every processing operation involved in delivering the campaign to children (with the platforms as joint/independent controllers where relevant). Conduct a DPIA given the vulnerable audience, and confirm that legitimate interests do not override children's rights before relying on it; otherwise obtain valid parental consent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle applies with heightened force to children. Data processing that underpins pressure-based marketing to 6-11 year olds who cannot understand how their data is used, and where no age-appropriate privacy information is provided, risks breaching the fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a). Fairness under GDPR is closely linked to whether the processing is exploitative of a vulnerable audience.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs!
findings.recommendation: Ensure any processing supporting the campaign is demonstrably fair to child data subjects: avoid data-driven delivery that exploits children's inability to assess commercial intent, and align processing with the best-interests-of-the-child standard expected for services reaching minors.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires that information provided to data subjects be concise, transparent and intelligible using clear and plain language, 'in particular for information addressed to a child'. A campaign environment delivering promotional pop-ups to 6-11 year olds must provide any privacy/data-collection information in a child-comprehensible form; none is evidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: If any personal data is collected or used in the Roblox world or ad delivery, provide age-appropriate, plain-language transparency information (and route substantive consent/notice to parents), tested for comprehension by the 6-11 age group.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is explicitly directed at children aged 6-11 and is delivered through information society services (YouTube Kids channels and a branded Roblox world with in-game pop-ups targeted at "child players"). Delivering ads/pop-ups to identified child players and operating a branded gaming world almost certainly involves processing children's personal data, so GDPR is engaged despite the "no personalisation" declaration. The core exposure is under Art. 8 (child consent) reinforced by Art. 6(1) lawful basis and the fairness/transparency principle in Art. 5(1)(a) / Art. 12, since children this young cannot give valid consent and the marketer has not evidenced any verified parental-consent mechanism. Findings are framed as risks requiring verification, as the campaign text does not fully describe the data flows.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces that deceive, manipulate or materially distort recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions. The in-game daily pop-ups combine nagging (repeated daily prompts), urgency/deadline pressure ('tonight'), social pressure ('before your friends get theirs') and a virtual-currency reward tied to purchase, all directed at children aged 6-11 who are especially susceptible. This is textbook manipulative interface design that impairs free/informed decision-making, engaged via the connected urgency/scarcity and dark-patterns concepts.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'
findings.recommendation: Remove the daily nagging pop-ups, the purchase-contingent RoboCoin incentive, and all urgency/social-pressure framing from the Roblox experience. Any in-world commercial messaging aimed at children must avoid repeated prompting, deadlines, peer-pressure and reward-for-purchase mechanics. Coordinate with the platform to ensure the branded world's interface does not constitute a prohibited manipulative design.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors and bans profiling-based ads to recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign is explicitly directed at children 6-11 on YouTube Kids and a Roblox children's world. Delivering commercially aggressive advertising into environments the platforms treat as minor-directed conflicts with the age-appropriate, high-protection standard; and any audience delivery that relies on knowing the recipients are children risks the profiling-ad ban. Personalisation is declared 'no', but audience selection targeting children as a segment must be verified not to rely on profiling of minors.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: children 6-11
findings.recommendation: Confirm in writing that no profiling of minors is used to select or deliver these ads. Redesign the creative to meet an age-appropriate, high-protection standard (no pressure tactics, no exhortations to purchase). Obtain and document the platform's confirmation that the placement complies with its minor-protection measures; treat kids' environments as no-go for purchase-pressure advertising.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that platform advertisements be identifiable in a clear, concise, unambiguous, real-time manner as ads, with the advertiser identity disclosed. Creator-voiced video content and an immersive branded Roblox world blur the line between entertainment and advertising, particularly for young children who cannot readily recognise commercial intent. As described there is no indication these units are clearly labelled as advertising or that the advertiser (RoboPets) is disclosed at point of exposure.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator) ... The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups
findings.recommendation: Ensure every video and in-game promotional unit is clearly and prominently labelled as an advertisement in real time, with the advertiser's identity, using child-comprehensible labelling. Do not rely on advergaming immersion; the commercial nature must be unmistakable to the audience it reaches.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is delivered on online platforms accessible to minors (YouTube Kids / Roblox) and explicitly targets children 6-11, squarely engaging DSA minor-protection and platform advertising rules. The most serious DSA exposure is the manipulative, high-pressure interface design directed at children (Art. 25 dark patterns) and the age-appropriate-design/profiling-ad obligations for minors (Art. 28). Advertising transparency (Art. 26(1)) is also engaged because the creator-voiced videos and immersive branded Roblox world blur commercial intent. Art. 26(3) is not engaged on the current facts (no special-category data). Note that the platforms bear primary DSA obligations, but the advertiser's design/placement choices create direct compliance risk and can force removal.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits, in all circumstances, including in an advertisement a direct exhortation to children to buy or to persuade their parents/adults to buy the product for them. The campaign is explicitly directed at children 6-11 and the video script directly tells children to buy ('buy you one RIGHT NOW') and, more pointedly, to persuade their parents ('tell your mum and dad to buy you one', 'Ask them today'). This is a per se blacklisted practice — no case-by-case unfairness assessment is needed.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Remove all direct calls to action addressed to the child audience. Do not instruct children to buy or to ask/tell their parents to buy. Reframe any purchase messaging as information addressed to parents/adults, in adult-facing placements, with no pester-power prompt.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: The Roblox in-game pop-ups repeat the blacklisted practice: they directly exhort child players to persuade their parents to purchase ('Get your parents to order the Mega Pack'), and add a virtual-currency incentive (500 RoboCoins) to intensify the pester pressure. In-game purchase prompts aimed at children are expressly identified as within scope of Annex I point 28.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!
findings.recommendation: Remove the purchase-exhortation pop-ups from the child-facing Roblox world entirely. Do not tie reward/virtual currency to a child persuading a parent to purchase. Any commercial offer must be directed to and evaluated by adults outside the child gameplay environment.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: The campaign uses a popular kids' animator to voice promotional scripts. Where a trader has paid for such promotion and the commercial nature is not made clear, using content that appears editorial/entertainment to promote a product is blacklisted as an undisclosed advertorial. On YouTube Kids, child viewers are especially unlikely to recognise paid endorsement, so the commercial intent must be unmistakably clear.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose the paid/commercial nature of the animator's involvement in a way an average child viewer would understand (e.g. explicit 'Advertisement' framing suitable for the audience). Ensure the content is unambiguously identifiable as advertising, not independent editorial or entertainment.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 treats failure to identify the commercial intent of a practice (where not apparent from context) as a misleading omission. Using a trusted kids' creator to voice the ad blurs the line between content and advertising for a young audience that cannot reliably identify commercial intent, so the material connection and advertising nature must be disclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: voiced by a popular kids' animator
findings.recommendation: Make the commercial intent apparent from context: label the creator content as advertising and disclose the material connection between the creator and RoboPets in a form appropriate to a child audience.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that, by undue influence, significantly impair freedom of choice and prompt a transactional decision otherwise not taken. The messaging combines urgency ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'tonight') with social-pressure/FOMO ('before your friends get theirs') and, in Roblox, daily persistent pop-ups — all aimed at children, whose vulnerability makes undue influence markedly more likely. The persistent, repeated daily solicitation compounds the pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Remove urgency and social-pressure cues ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'before your friends get theirs') from child-facing copy and stop daily repeated purchase pop-ups. Avoid any high-pressure or coercive framing in communications reaching minors.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is explicitly directed at children aged 6-11 and contains textbook per se breaches of UCPD Annex I. Both the video scripts and the Roblox pop-ups directly exhort children to buy and to pester their parents to buy, which is blacklisted in all circumstances (Annex I point 28). The campaign also aggravates matters through undisclosed influencer commercial intent (Art. 7 / Annex I point 11) and high-pressure, socially-coercive, persistent messaging aimed at a vulnerable audience (Arts. 8-9). These are among the most serious UCPD infringements and require the offending copy to be removed before launch.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes the RoboPets toy line to children aged 6-11 via YouTube Kids videos (voiced by a popular kids' animator) and daily pop-ups in a branded Roblox world. As written, it cannot launch: both the video scripts and the in-game pop-ups directly tell children to buy the toy and to nag their parents to buy it — a practice that is banned outright in all circumstances under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I point 28). This is a per se illegal "pester power" violation, not a grey area. The campaign layers on further serious problems: aggressive urgency and social-pressure tactics aimed at young children, an undisclosed paid influencer endorsement, manipulative "dark pattern" pop-up design and profiling/minor-protection concerns under the DSA, and unlawful processing of children's personal data with no parental-consent or age-verification mechanism under the GDPR. The "no personalisation" and "no data use" declarations do not hold up, because delivering targeted daily pop-ups to identified child players necessarily processes their data. The verdict is critical: the core purchase-exhortation content must be removed and the campaign fundamentally redesigned before any launch in the EU.
recommendations: STOP — do not launch as designed. Remove every direct call to action addressed to children, including all instructions to buy or to ask/tell parents to buy ('tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW', 'Ask them today', 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack'). These are per se illegal under UCPD Annex I point 28 and cannot be fixed with disclaimers.

Delete the daily Roblox purchase pop-ups entirely and remove the RoboCoin reward tied to a child persuading a parent to buy. Repeated daily prompting, deadlines, peer-pressure and reward-for-purchase mechanics aimed at children are both a blacklisted exhortation and a prohibited manipulative interface (DSA Art. 25).

Strip all urgency and social-pressure language from child-facing copy ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'tonight', 'before your friends get theirs') — these constitute aggressive practices under UCPD Arts. 8-9 given the vulnerable audience.

Redirect any purchase messaging to parents/adults in adult-facing placements outside the child gameplay environment. Treat kids' environments (YouTube Kids, Roblox children's worlds) as no-go zones for purchase-pressure advertising.

Clearly and prominently label the animator's videos and all in-game units as advertising in a form a young child would understand, and disclose the RoboPets/creator material connection (UCPD Annex I point 11, Art. 7; DSA Art. 26). Undisclosed influencer promotion to children is blacklisted.
Confirm in writing that no profiling of minors is used to select or deliver these ads, and obtain the platforms' confirmation that placement meets their minor-protection measures (DSA Art. 28).

Correct the compliance declarations: 'no personalisation/data use' is inconsistent with delivering targeted daily pop-ups to identified child players. Map all data flows, document a valid lawful basis for each, and conduct a DPIA (GDPR Arts. 6, 8, 5(1)(a), 12).

Implement a robust parental-consent and age-verification mechanism before processing any personal data of users known/likely to be under the applicable age threshold; if verified parental consent is not obtainable, remove data-driven pop-up delivery to child players.
Have legal/compliance re-review the fully redesigned campaign before resubmission — the current version contains multiple independent breaches across UCPD, DSA and GDPR.

triage.audience_notes: Declared target is children 6-11, an especially vulnerable and protected audience. The direct exhortation to children to purchase (and to pester parents) is a blacklisted unfair practice under UCPD Annex I (No. 28). Although personalisation/AI are declared as 'not used', both YouTube Kids and Roblox routinely process children's personal data, so GDPR (child data, Art. 8) and the DSA (protection of minors, ban on profiling minors for ads, dark-pattern-like pop-ups) should be verified rather than assumed absent. AI Act is included for completeness given the platforms' potential use of AI-driven recommender/ad systems, though the declared use is none — flag for confirmation.
triage.summary: A toy-line campaign explicitly targeting children aged 6-11 across YouTube Kids and a Roblox branded world, using an influencer voice and in-game pop-ups. The messaging directly exhorts children to buy or to pressure their parents into buying, adds urgency/peer pressure, and ties a purchase to in-game reward currency. This raises serious concerns around advertising directed at minors.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit age-related vulnerabilities of a group (here, children 6-11) so as to materially distort their behaviour in a way likely to cause harm. The messaging is exactly the kind of vulnerability-exploiting, behaviour-distorting content the prohibition targets — but the prohibition is triggered only by an AI system. The campaign declares no AI and no personalisation, so on the stated facts Art. 5(1)(b) is not engaged (the practice is instead handled under UCPD/DSA). This is flagged because IF an AI-driven recommender/ad-delivery or targeting system is in fact used to serve these exhortations to a child audience, Art. 5(1)(b) would likely be breached at critical severity.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs!
findings.recommendation: Confirm in writing that no AI system (including platform AI recommender, ad-targeting, or optimisation systems used to place or personalise these messages toward children) is involved in delivering the campaign. If any AI targeting/optimisation is used to direct these child-directed exhortations, do not deploy — this risks the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on exploiting age-related vulnerability, which carries no cure other than removing the AI-driven exploitation.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires deployers to disclose AI-generated or manipulated audio/video constituting a deep fake, including synthetic or cloned voices presented as a real person. The campaign presents a real, named human creator's voice, so on its face no synthetic content is used and Art. 50(4) is not engaged. Flagged only to rule out use of an AI voice clone of the animator.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Confirm the animator's voice is a genuine human recording, not an AI-cloned/synthesised voice. If any AI voice generation or manipulation is used, add a clear disclosure that the audio is artificially generated/manipulated (and ensure machine-readable marking per Art. 50(2)).

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: Art. 50(1) requires disclosure when an AI system interacts directly with natural persons (e.g., a conversational agent). The described pop-ups are scripted broadcast prompts, not a conversational AI, so Art. 50(1) is not engaged as described. Flagged only to confirm no AI chatbot/agent interacts with the child players.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Confirm the in-game pop-ups are static/scripted and not delivered by an AI conversational agent. If an AI chatbot interacts with players, disclose its AI nature in a manner comprehensible to children (bearing in mind that AI persuasion aimed at children may separately raise Art. 5(1)(b) concerns).

verdicts.notes: On the declared facts, the AI Act is not engaged: the campaign declares no generative AI and no personalisation/targeting, and all operative AI Act provisions require an actual AI system. The serious harms here (exhorting children to buy, pester power, urgency and peer pressure, purchase-linked rewards) are delivered via human-written video scripts and static in-game pop-ups, and fall under UCPD/DSA rather than the AI Act. However, three factual assumptions should be confirmed, because if any AI were in fact used the assessment would change materially — most importantly, an AI recommender/targeting system placing these vulnerability-exploiting messages to 6–11-year-olds could trigger the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The entire declared audience (6-11) falls below the GDPR Art. 8 digital-consent age threshold (13-16 depending on Member State). YouTube Kids and a Roblox branded world are information society services offered directly to children that routinely process personal data (identifiers, engagement/behaviour, in-game 'RoboCoins' activity). Where consent is the legal basis for that processing, it is only valid if given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility, and the controller must make reasonable efforts to verify parental consent. A child-directed campaign built to prompt in-game interaction cannot rely on the children's own consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: children 6-11
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the platforms/agency exactly what child personal data the campaign causes to be processed. For any consent-based processing of the 6-11 audience, ensure verifiable parental consent is obtained and that reasonable age-verification/parental-verification measures are in place before campaign delivery; if this cannot be assured, restructure delivery to avoid processing minors' data.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Delivering daily pop-ups to identified child players and operating a branded in-game world with a reward-currency mechanic implies processing of players' personal data (identifiers, session/engagement data) to trigger and target the prompts. Any such processing requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Consent from children 6-11 is not valid without parental authorisation, and a legitimate-interest basis is very difficult to sustain for commercial prompting of young children given their vulnerability and the balancing test.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for every processing operation the campaign relies on. Do not rely on children's own consent; if relying on legitimate interests, complete and record an LIA that specifically weighs children's rights and vulnerability, and be prepared to conclude that commercial prompting of 6-11 year olds is not justified.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness principle requires processing of personal data to be fair, with heightened protection for children who may be less aware of the risks and consequences. Using children's engagement/in-game data to serve repeated purchase-pressure and reward-linked pop-ups to a 6-11 audience exploits their vulnerability and is difficult to reconcile with fair processing, even absent overt profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!
findings.recommendation: Redesign the in-game and video mechanics so that any data-driven delivery to children is limited, transparent and non-manipulative; remove purchase-pressure and reward-for-purchase prompts targeted at minors, and treat children's data with the elevated fairness standard the GDPR expects.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires that information about data processing be concise, transparent and intelligible using clear and plain language, in particular where addressed to a child. A campaign directed at 6-11 year olds that processes their data must provide age-appropriate transparency; the submission shows no child-friendly privacy information at the point of collection/interaction.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for the RoboPets collectible toy line on YouTube Kids channels and a Roblox branded world
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, child-appropriate (and parent-facing) privacy information at the point where any data is collected or the branded world is entered, explaining what data is processed, by whom and why, in language a child of this age can understand.

verdicts.notes: The campaign targets children aged 6-11 across YouTube Kids and a Roblox branded world — both information society services that routinely process children's personal data (device IDs, in-game identifiers/behaviour, engagement analytics). Although the submission declares no personalisation or AI, personal-data processing of minors is highly likely on these platforms, engaging GDPR Art. 8 (child's consent/parental consent below the age threshold), Art. 6(1) (valid lawful basis), Art. 5(1)(a) (fairness) and Art. 12 (child-appropriate transparency). The pester-power messaging and reward-linked pop-ups amplify the fairness concern where any behavioural/engagement data of children underpins delivery. These points should be verified rather than assumed absent; a data-flow confirmation from the platforms/agency is recommended.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign is knowingly directed at children 6-11 on online platforms accessible to minors. Art. 28(1) requires appropriate, age-appropriate measures ensuring a high level of safety and security for minors. Daily commercial pop-ups nagging child players to trigger a parental purchase, combined with a purchase-linked reward incentive, are the opposite of age-appropriate design and exploit the vulnerability of the target audience. Art. 28(2) additionally bans presenting ads based on profiling to recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors; although personalisation is declared 'no', delivering these ads on platforms that process children's data on an audience declared as minors requires confirmation that no profiling-based targeting is used.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the in-game experience to remove persistent commercial pop-ups directed at child players and any purchase-linked reward mechanics; adopt an age-appropriate design that does not pressure minors. Obtain written confirmation from Roblox/YouTube that no profiling-based ad delivery is applied to this minor audience, and document age-assurance and safety measures for the campaign.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives, manipulates or materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including repeatedly requesting/nagging. Daily pop-ups repeatedly prompting children toward a purchase, tying it to an in-game currency reward ('unlock 500 RoboCoins') and a same-day deadline ('tonight'), constitute nagging plus urgency manipulation targeting an especially vulnerable audience whose ability to make free decisions is impaired.
findings.evidence_quote: pushes daily pop-ups to child players: 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!'
findings.recommendation: Eliminate repeated/daily purchase prompts and any confirm-shaming or urgency framing in the interface; do not condition in-game rewards on real-money purchases prompted through the child-facing interface. Ensure any commercial message is a single, clearly labelled, non-manipulative placement.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. Advertising embedded in YouTube Kids content voiced by a trusted kids' animator, and within a Roblox 'branded world', risks the commercial nature not being clearly and unambiguously identifiable to a child audience, blurring editorial/entertainment content and advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator): 'The new RoboPets are here! ...'
findings.recommendation: Ensure prominent, child-comprehensible ad labelling for the video placements and clear identification of the advertiser (RoboPets) in real time; make the commercial nature of the Roblox branded world unmistakable to child players and confirm the platform surfaces the required 'this is an advertisement / on whose behalf' disclosures.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is explicitly directed at children aged 6-11 on YouTube Kids and a Roblox branded world, both online platforms accessible to minors within the DSA's scope. The DSA engages primarily through Art. 28 (protection of minors / age-appropriate design and the ban on profiling-based ads to minors) and Art. 25 (dark patterns), given the persistent daily in-game pop-ups nagging children to trigger a purchase, plus a purchase-linked reward and urgency messaging aimed at a highly vulnerable audience. Ad-transparency (Art. 26(1)) is also engaged because advertising is embedded in children's content via a trusted influencer voice and an in-game branded world where the commercial nature may not be clearly identifiable. Note: the platform-level obligations largely bind the platforms (YouTube/Roblox), but the marketer's campaign design directly creates these risks and should be remediated.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: This is a direct exhortation to children to persuade their parents to buy the advertised product, delivered in advertising aimed at a declared audience of children 6-11. The Roblox pop-up 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight' is a second, equally direct instance. Annex I point 28 prohibits such exhortations in all circumstances — no balancing or materiality test applies; presence alone constitutes an unfair practice.
findings.evidence_quote: tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW before your friends get theirs! Ask them today, don't wait!
findings.recommendation: Remove all copy that instructs children to buy or to ask/tell/get their parents to buy (e.g. 'tell your mum and dad to buy you one', 'Ask them today', 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack'). Reframe any child-facing creative so it neither urges the child to purchase nor to solicit an adult purchase; direct any call-to-action to the parent/adult audience through channels not aimed at children.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: In-game pop-ups aimed at child players that tell children to get their parents to order the product are precisely the 'in-game purchase prompts aimed at children' identified as blacklisted under Annex I point 28. Adding a purchase-linked reward (500 RoboCoins) to induce the child to pester the parent aggravates the exhortation.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight and unlock 500 RoboCoins!
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the in-game daily pop-ups directing child players to obtain a parental purchase, and remove the reward incentive tied to that purchase. Any commercial messaging inside the Roblox world must not exhort children to buy or to procure a parental purchase.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Persistent, repeated (daily) pressure prompts combined with urgency framing ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'tonight'), peer pressure ('before your friends get theirs') and a purchase-linked reward, directed at children, amount to undue influence/harassment that significantly impairs the freedom of choice of an especially credulous audience and pushes them toward a transactional decision (getting a parent to buy). Under Art. 5(3) fairness is assessed from the perspective of the average child in this group, for whom this pressure is materially distorting.
findings.evidence_quote: The Roblox world pushes daily pop-ups to child players
findings.recommendation: Stop the recurring/daily pressure prompts and remove urgency and peer-pressure devices ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'before your friends get theirs') and the purchase-linked reward from all child-facing placements. Apply frequency capping and age-appropriate, non-pressuring messaging design.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Using a trusted kids' animator/influencer voice to deliver promotional content embedded in children's entertainment (YouTube Kids videos, a Roblox branded world) risks failing to make the commercial intent apparent to an audience that, given their age, cannot readily distinguish advertising from content. Art. 7 treats failure to identify commercial intent, where not apparent from context, as a misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: Video scripts (voiced by a popular kids' animator)
findings.recommendation: Ensure clear, prominent, child-comprehensible ad identification (e.g. explicit 'Advertisement'/'Ad' labelling and disclosure of the material connection with the animator) on all placements, and confirm the branded Roblox world is unambiguously identifiable as advertising.

verdicts.notes: The campaign explicitly targets children aged 6-11 and contains textbook direct exhortations to children to buy the product and to pressure their parents into buying it — a practice blacklisted in all circumstances under UCPD Annex I point 28. Combined urgency, peer-pressure, daily in-game nagging pop-ups and a purchase-linked reward directed at a credulous, protected audience also engage the prohibition on aggressive practices (Arts. 8-9, read with the vulnerable-group standard in Art. 5(3)). The influencer/animator delivery embedded in children's content without evident ad identification raises a hidden-commercial-intent concern under Art. 7. This is a high-risk, likely-unlawful campaign as drafted.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes RoboPets toys to children aged 6-11 on YouTube Kids and a Roblox branded world, using scripts and pop-ups that directly tell kids to get their parents to buy the product. As drafted, it is very likely unlawful. The single biggest problem: EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 28) bans, in all circumstances, any advertising that directly tells children to buy a product or to nag their parents to buy it — and your copy does exactly that twice ("tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW", "Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight"). There is no fix other than removing this messaging entirely; there is no balancing test. On top of that, the daily pressure pop-ups, urgency language, peer-pressure ("before your friends get theirs") and a purchase-linked reward (500 RoboCoins) amount to aggressive/dark-pattern practices banned under the UCPD and the DSA (Arts. 25 and 28). Because both platforms process children's data, GDPR duties around parental consent, lawful basis, fairness and child-friendly transparency also apply. The AI Act is not triggered on the facts you declared, but if any AI targeting, recommender, or voice-cloning is actually used, the risk escalates sharply — so this needs written confirmation. Bottom line: do not run this campaign in its current form.
recommendations: STOP: Do not deploy in current form. Remove every line that tells children to buy or to ask/tell/get their parents to buy — 'tell your mum and dad to buy you one RIGHT NOW', 'Ask them today', 'Get your parents to order the Mega Pack tonight'. These are outright banned (UCPD Annex I, point 28) with no cure other than removal.

Remove the purchase-linked reward mechanic (500 RoboCoins for a parental purchase) and all urgency/peer-pressure framing ('RIGHT NOW', 'don't wait', 'tonight', 'before your friends get theirs') from all child-facing placements.

Eliminate the daily/recurring in-game pop-ups. Persistent nagging of child players is a prohibited dark pattern (DSA Art. 25) and an aggressive practice (UCPD Arts. 8-9); redesign the Roblox experience to be age-appropriate under DSA Art. 28.
Redirect any purchase call-to-action to adults/parents through channels not aimed at children; keep child-facing creative free of any buy/pester messaging.

Ensure clear, child-comprehensible ad labelling on all placements and disclose the material connection with the animator/influencer, so the commercial nature is unmistakable (UCPD Art. 7; DSA Art. 26).
Obtain written confirmation from Roblox/YouTube that no profiling-based ad targeting is applied to this minor audience (DSA Art. 28(2)).

Confirm in writing that NO AI system (recommender, ad-targeting/optimisation, chatbot, or voice-cloning of the animator) is used. If any AI is used to place these messages to children, do not deploy — this risks the AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition, which has no cure short of removing the AI-driven exploitation.

Map the child personal data the campaign causes to be processed and secure a valid GDPR lawful basis: obtain verifiable parental consent for the 6-11 audience (GDPR Art. 8); do not rely on children's own consent; document any legitimate-interest assessment (Arts. 6, 5(1)(a)).
Provide age-appropriate, plain-language privacy information for children and parents at the point of data collection / entry to the branded world (GDPR Art. 12).

campaign.title: FitCoach FREE trial funnel
campaign.text: Display and social ads: 'Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.' Checkout requires full card details; page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled. Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing. 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.

detected_practices: 'FREE' offer with hidden subscription (negative-option / subscription trap)
drip pricing (1.95 EUR shipping hides 49.99 EUR/month charge)
material information buried in footer/terms (page 3)
short 5-day trial auto-converting to paid subscription
obstructed cancellation (phone-only, business hours)
forced retention with three counter-offers before cancellation
collection of full card details at checkout
'personalised' plan claim despite declaring no personalisation
repetition of 'FREE' (11 times) to create misleading impression
triage.summary: A "free trial" funnel that advertises a 100% FREE personalised FitCoach plan for only 1.95 EUR shipping, while burying in footer terms an automatic 49.99 EUR/month subscription starting after 5 days. Cancellation is deliberately obstructed (phone-only, business hours, mandatory retention counter-offers), and full card details are collected at checkout. The campaign shows hallmarks of a misleading/aggressive subscription trap.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Full card details are collected at checkout to enable recurring billing, but the genuine purpose of the data collection (setting up an ongoing 49.99 EUR/month payment mandate) is deliberately obscured behind a '100% FREE' framing and buried in footer/page-3 terms. Processing personal/financial data under a materially misleading pretext breaches the fairness and transparency principle — the data subject cannot reasonably foresee how their data will be used.
findings.evidence_quote: the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link
findings.recommendation: Present the recurring-billing purpose and the 49.99 EUR/month charge prominently and truthfully at the point where card details are collected, so the data subject understands what their financial data will be used for before submitting it.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting personal data (including card/financial data) at checkout triggers the Art. 13 duty to provide, at the point of collection, the controller identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing (including that the card data will be used for recurring subscription billing), recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The campaign describes no such notice at the collection point; the only reference is a footer terms link, which is not information provided 'at the time when personal data are obtained' in an accessible way.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout requires full card details
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at the checkout/collection point covering identity, all processing purposes (including recurring payment processing), legal basis, retention and rights — not solely via a footer terms link.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Even where information exists, Art. 12 requires it to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Placing material data/billing information on 'page 3 of the terms' and 'only in the footer terms link' while repeating 'FREE' 11 times makes the relevant information neither easily accessible nor intelligible, undermining transparent communication with the data subject.
findings.evidence_quote: page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription
findings.recommendation: Surface the key processing and billing information in plain language on the main landing/checkout view with equal prominence to the 'FREE' messaging, rather than concealing it in deep terms pages.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Advertising a 'personalised' fitness plan implies automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (fitness, health, performance, preferences), which meets the definition of profiling. The submission declares 'use of personalisation/targeting: no' and 'use of generative AI: no', so either profiling is occurring undisclosed (a data-protection gap) or the 'personalised' claim is unsubstantiated. Both are problematic: undisclosed profiling requires a lawful basis and Art. 13 information about it.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the claim with actual processing: if the plan is genuinely personalised, disclose the profiling, its lawful basis and logic per Arts. 6/13; if not, remove the word 'personalised' to avoid an inaccurate representation of processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: If the 'personalised' plan involves profiling of the user's data, that processing needs a valid lawful basis (consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment). No lawful basis is indicated in the campaign, and processing that may extend to health/fitness attributes cannot rely on an unexamined basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a lawful basis for any personalisation/profiling and for the payment-data processing, and ensure any consent relied upon is freely given, specific and informed rather than bundled into the 'free trial' sign-up.

verdicts.notes: The funnel collects personal and financial data (full card details) within a deliberately misleading "FREE" framing where the true processing purpose — setting up a recurring 49.99 EUR/month charge — is buried in page 3/footer terms. This engages the GDPR fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), the Art. 12 requirement for accessible/intelligible information, and the Art. 13 obligation to disclose purposes and legal basis at the point of collection. The advertised "personalised" plan additionally implies profiling (Art. 4(4)) with no disclosed lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) or Art. 13 information, despite the submission declaring no personalisation — meaning either an undisclosed processing operation or a misleading claim. Findings are risk-level because the underlying privacy notice text was not provided for review.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 expressly prohibits designing/operating online interfaces so as to make cancellation of a service harder than subscribing to it. Users subscribe frictionlessly online at checkout, but can only cancel via a restricted phone channel during business hours and must overcome three mandatory retention counter-offers. This is a textbook obstruction-of-cancellation / forced-continuity dark pattern that materially impairs users' ability to make a free and informed decision to exit.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide a cancellation mechanism that is at least as easy as sign-up — e.g. a one-click online cancellation available at all times in the account interface. Remove mandatory retention counter-offer scripts as a precondition to cancelling.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits giving disproportionate prominence to certain messages/choices and designing interfaces that deceive or materially distort informed decision-making. Repeating 'FREE' 11 times while confining the 49.99 EUR/month recurring charge and 5-day auto-conversion to a footer/page-3 terms link creates a deceptive visual hierarchy that hides the material cost from the point of decision.
findings.evidence_quote: 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the recurring 49.99 EUR/month charge, the 5-day trial length and the auto-renewal with equal prominence to the 'FREE' claim, adjacent to the call-to-action and before card details are entered; obtain express informed confirmation of the paid subscription terms.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign runs on social platforms, engaging Art. 26(1), which requires each ad to be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, in a clear and unambiguous manner in real time. Nothing in the campaign text shows these disclosures are provided; this is primarily the platform's obligation but the advertiser must supply the necessary declarations.
findings.evidence_quote: Display and social ads: 'Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.'
findings.recommendation: Ensure the social/display placements carry clear 'ad/sponsored' labelling and correct advertiser/payer identity declarations to the platform so the platform's Art. 26(1) transparency requirements are satisfied.

verdicts.notes: The funnel exhibits several practices that map directly onto the DSA Art. 25 prohibition of dark patterns: forced-continuity design where cancellation is made materially harder than subscription (phone-only, business hours, mandatory retention counter-offers), and false visual hierarchy where "FREE" (11 repetitions) is given overwhelming prominence while the 49.99 EUR/month auto-conversion is hidden in footer/page-3 terms. Applicability of Art. 25 depends on whether the interface is operated by a "provider of an online platform"; the identical conduct is in any event caught by the UCPD for all traders (covered by another agent). Art. 26(1) ad-transparency applies to the social-platform placements. Note the "personalised" claim while personalisation is declared as "no" is chiefly a UCPD/GDPR issue.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 blacklists describing a product as 'free' or '100% FREE' where the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of delivery. Here the offer is presented as '100% FREE' but enrolls the consumer into a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that begins automatically after 5 days. A recurring 49.99 EUR charge is plainly a payment beyond delivery cost, so the 'FREE' claim is misleading per se and prohibited in all circumstances. The problem is aggravated by 'FREE' appearing 11 times on the landing page while the subscription is mentioned only in a footer terms link, reinforcing the false impression of a genuinely free offer.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan 100% FREE — just cover 1.95 EUR shipping for your welcome kit.
findings.recommendation: Stop describing the plan as '100% FREE'. Present it accurately as a 5-day paid trial that converts to a 49.99 EUR/month subscription, with the price, billing frequency and start date shown up-front with equal prominence to any promotional language. Remove the repeated 'FREE' claims unless the product is genuinely free of charges beyond delivery.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision, or providing it in an unclear, unintelligible or untimely manner. The existence, price (49.99 EUR/month), billing trigger (auto-start after 5 days) and negative-option nature of the subscription are all material to the transactional decision, yet they are buried on 'page 3' of the terms and in a footer link rather than disclosed at the point of the offer and before card entry. This is a textbook drip-pricing / hidden-cost misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: page 3 of the terms states enrolment in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription that starts after 5 days unless cancelled ... the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full price, recurring nature, trial length and auto-renewal trigger clearly and prominently on the ad and on the checkout screen before card details are collected — not in linked terms. Obtain express, informed acknowledgement of the recurring charge before enrolment.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive any practice that, through undue influence or by imposing onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights, impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Restricting cancellation to phone during business hours only (while sign-up is instant and online) and forcing consumers through three mandatory retention counter-offers before a cancellation is processed are onerous barriers designed to obstruct the exercise of the right to cancel and pressure the consumer into staying subscribed.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Provide a cancellation route at least as easy as sign-up (e.g. one-click online cancellation available 24/7). Remove the mandatory three counter-offer retention gate; process cancellation requests immediately without conditioning them on hearing sales offers.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits false information or deception about the main characteristics of a product. The ad promises a 'personalised' plan, yet the campaign declares no use of personalisation/targeting. If no genuine personalisation is delivered, the 'personalised' claim deceives the consumer about a main characteristic of the product and may cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Severity is medium because it depends on whether any real personalisation is actually provided post-enrolment.
findings.evidence_quote: Get your personalised FitCoach plan
findings.recommendation: Only use the word 'personalised' if the plan is genuinely tailored to the individual based on their inputs; otherwise remove the claim. Be able to substantiate what personalisation actually occurs.

verdicts.notes: This "free trial" funnel shows classic subscription-trap hallmarks that engage multiple UCPD provisions, including a blacklisted practice. The "100% FREE" framing conceals an auto-converting 49.99 EUR/month subscription (Annex I point 20 and Art. 7 misleading omission), the "personalised" claim appears unsupported (Art. 6), and cancellation is deliberately obstructed through phone-only, business-hours-only access plus mandatory retention counter-offers (Arts. 8-9 aggressive practice). Overall high likelihood of unfairness under UCPD.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a "free trial" funnel that advertises a FitCoach plan as "100% FREE" (asking only for €1.95 shipping) but actually enrols customers into a €49.99/month subscription that auto-starts after 5 days, with the paid terms hidden on page 3 of the terms and in a footer link. This is a serious problem: describing an offer as "free" when the consumer must pay ongoing charges is a blacklisted practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 20) — banned outright, no case-by-case assessment needed. On top of that, cancellation is deliberately obstructed (phone-only, business hours only, three mandatory retention offers), which is both an aggressive commercial practice and a prohibited dark pattern under the Digital Services Act. Collecting full card details behind this misleading "free" framing also breaches GDPR fairness and transparency rules, and the "personalised" claim contradicts your declaration of no personalisation — meaning either an undisclosed data operation or an unsubstantiated marketing claim. The AI Act is not engaged. The overall verdict is critical: this funnel is very likely unlawful in the EU in its current form and should not run until fundamentally redesigned.
recommendations: Stop describing the plan as '100% FREE'. Present it accurately and up-front as a 5-day trial that auto-converts to a €49.99/month subscription, showing the price, billing frequency and start date with equal prominence to any promotional language. (Fixes the blacklisted 'free' claim — the single most serious, per-se-illegal issue.)

Disclose the recurring €49.99/month charge, 5-day trial length and auto-renewal clearly on the ad and on the checkout screen before card details are entered — not in linked/footer/page-3 terms — and obtain express informed acknowledgement of the paid subscription before enrolment.

Make cancellation at least as easy as sign-up: provide one-click online cancellation available 24/7, and remove the mandatory three-counter-offer retention gate. This addresses both the DSA dark-pattern prohibition and the UCPD aggressive-practice rules.

Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at the point card details are collected, covering controller identity, all processing purposes (including recurring payment billing), legal basis, retention and data-subject rights, in plain accessible language.

Reconcile the 'personalised' claim with reality: if the plan is genuinely tailored, disclose the profiling and its lawful basis and update the campaign's declaration; if not, remove the word 'personalised' entirely, as the current declaration says no personalisation is used.
Ensure the social/display placements carry correct 'ad/sponsored' labelling and accurate advertiser/payer identity declarations to satisfy DSA advertising-transparency requirements.

Do not launch this funnel in the EU until the above changes are implemented and reviewed; the combination of a blacklisted 'free' claim, hidden pricing and obstructed cancellation carries high enforcement and penalty exposure.
