findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 expressly prohibits interface design that makes cancellation harder than subscription and that repeatedly requests a choice already made. Here subscribing takes a few clicks and full card entry online, while cancellation is confined to phone lines in business hours and is deliberately obstructed by a mandated three-counter-offer retention script — a textbook forced-continuity dark pattern and obstruction of a contractual right. Note: Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms; on the trader's own landing page this conduct is primarily caught by the UCPD, but it is a live DSA risk to the extent the funnel operates within social-platform interfaces.
findings.evidence_quote: Cancellation is only possible by phone during business hours, and the retention script requires agents to offer three counter-offers before processing.
findings.recommendation: Make cancellation at least as easy as sign-up — provide an online self-service cancel button reachable in the same number of steps as enrolment. Remove the mandatory multi-offer retention gate; process cancellation on first request. Ensure choices already made are honoured without repeated prompts.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Repeating 'FREE' 11 times while hiding the 49.99 EUR/month auto-enrolment in a footer terms link and on page 3 gives disproportionate prominence to one choice and materially distorts the recipient's ability to make a free and informed decision — a deceptive interface design of the type Art. 25 targets (false hierarchy / obscured material terms).
findings.evidence_quote: 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page; the subscription is mentioned only in the footer terms link.
findings.recommendation: Give the recurring 49.99 EUR/month charge, the 5-day trigger and auto-renewal equal visual prominence to the 'FREE' claim at the point of decision (before card entry), not buried in linked terms.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Ads presented on social/display online platforms must let recipients identify, clearly and in real time, that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. The submission contains no indication that the ads carry the required advertisement labelling and advertiser identification, so this transparency obligation is engaged and not evidenced as met.

findings.recommendation: Ensure every social and display placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement and identifies the advertiser (FitCoach) and payer, using the platform's ad-disclosure tools, in a clear, concise and unambiguous manner in real time.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social/display channels and its funnel design engages the DSA in two ways. Most significantly, the cancellation and enrolment design mirrors the exact conduct named in Art. 25 (making cancellation harder than subscription; nagging/repeated requests) — a dark-pattern risk, though Art. 25 binds "providers of online platforms," so this conduct is primarily actionable under the UCPD for a trader's own landing page (covered by another agent) and is a DSA risk chiefly where it occurs within platform interfaces. Ad-transparency obligations under Art. 26(1) are engaged by the social/display ads and there is no indication they are met. findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'

Here the consumer must in fact provide full card details and, unless they cancel within 5 days, is enrolled in a 49.99 EUR/month subscription. This recurring charge is not the unavoidable cost of responding/delivery, so the 'free' claim is a blacklisted misuse of 'free' — a per se unfair practice requiring no case-by-case assessment.

Describe the offer accurately as a 'paid subscription with a 5-day introductory period' and state the 49.99 EUR/month recurring price with equal prominence to any promotional wording, at the point the consumer makes the decision (not only in footer terms).

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent

Providing this only on page 3 of the terms / a footer link — while 'FREE' appears 11 times on the landing page — hides material information and presents it in an unclear and untimely manner, constituting a misleading omission. findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making cancellation onerous — restricting it to phone during business hours and forcing consumers through three mandatory counter-offers before their cancellation is processed — creates disproportionate, non-contractual barriers to exercising a right. Under Arts. 8-9 undue influence and onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights that impair the consumer's freedom of choice can render a practice aggressive, especially combined with the earlier deceptive 'free' hook.

findings.title: Misleading actions

If the plan is not in fact personalised, this is false information about the product's main characteristics that could cause the average consumer to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6.

Deliberately obstructive, phone-only cancellation with a mandatory three-counter-offer retention script is a strong candidate aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9). findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible using clear and plain language. Placing the key information affecting data processing (recurring enrolment tied to stored card data) on 'page 3 of the terms' and a footer link, while the headline messaging repeatedly says 'FREE', is neither easily accessible nor intelligibly presented, undermining transparent communication about the processing.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Email direct marketing and the subsequent phone follow-ups require a valid lawful basis. For unsolicited electronic direct marketing to purchased contacts this generally requires prior consent, and no consent records exist. Legitimate interest cannot rescue processing of data acquired from a broker with no verifiable, documented basis. Every downstream operation (emailing, list upload, calling) is therefore unlawful at its root.
findings.evidence_quote: sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Cease using the purchased list immediately. Do not send email/phone marketing without a demonstrable lawful basis — for cold electronic marketing this means documented, valid prior consent captured by the controller (or a properly assessed and disclosed legitimate-interest basis where lawful). Rebuild the audience from first-party opt-ins.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: The controller must be able to demonstrate that consent was given. Here there are no consent records at all, so the accountability requirement in Art. 7(1) cannot be met. A vague broker assertion of an opt-in 'somewhere in 2019' with no proof, scope, or wording does not satisfy the conditions for consent.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Only process data where you hold auditable proof of valid consent (who, when, what wording, what purposes). Discard any records lacking such evidence rather than relying on broker assurances.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent relied on must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A generic broker opt-in of unknown scope, later resold for a home-alarm campaign and platform ad targeting, is neither specific nor informed for these purposes and cannot be shown to be unambiguous.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Collect purpose-specific, informed opt-ins directly from data subjects for each processing purpose (email marketing, phone marketing, ad-platform targeting) rather than reusing repurposed broker consents.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and controllers must facilitate that right. Emails with no unsubscribe mechanism — relying on manual reply handling — do not provide an easy, effective means to object, and non-opener follow-up calls compound the failure to respect opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out in every marketing email and an easy opt-out in phone contact, honour objections across all channels (email, phone, ad platforms) immediately, and maintain a suppression list.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is obtained (including indirectly via a broker), the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and profiling information. No privacy notice is provided and the policy is not referenced, so none of this mandatory information reaches data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete privacy notice at first contact: controller identity, purposes and legal basis, the fact that data was obtained from a broker and which one, recipients (Meta/Google), retention, and rights including the right to object. Reference/link it in every communication.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information owed to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. With no privacy notice referenced anywhere in the campaign, the transparency-communication obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Make the privacy information easily accessible and clearly linked in emails and disclosed at the start of calls, using clear and plain language.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached across the campaign: processing has no lawful basis, data is repurposed and shared with ad platforms without the individuals' knowledge, and no information is given — the essence of covert, unfair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Establish a lawful basis, be transparent about all recipients and purposes, and stop covert repurposing/sharing of the data with third-party platforms.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading personal data to build lookalike audiences and targeting individuals based on email open/non-open behaviour constitutes profiling (automated processing to evaluate personal preferences/behaviour). This profiling is carried out without a lawful basis, without transparency, and without offering an objection route.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Do not upload personal data for lookalike/behavioural targeting without a valid lawful basis and prior information; where consent is required for such ad-platform processing, obtain it, and enable objection to profiling for marketing.

verdicts.notes: This campaign relies almost entirely on unlawfully sourced personal data and breaches multiple core GDPR obligations. There is no valid lawful basis for the email marketing, profiling and phone follow-ups (Art. 6(1)); the purported "consent" fails every element of a valid consent (Arts. 4(11), 7); there is no transparency notice provided to data subjects (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13); the emails offer no way to object to direct marketing (Art. 21); and uploading the list to build lookalike audiences and targeting non-openers constitutes profiling without a basis (Arts. 4(4), 6(1)). Severity is critical/high across the board.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Uploading a broker-sourced list of 400,000 individuals to Meta and Google to generate lookalike audiences is platform advertising based on profiling. DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits platform ads based on profiling that uses GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including where such attributes are inferred via proxies. Lookalike expansion from an opaque broker list with no known provenance carries a material risk that the seed data or the modelled expansion encodes sensitive proxies (e.g., health/vulnerability signals), which the advertiser cannot verify or exclude. While home-alarm marketing does not target sensitive categories on its face, the uncontrolled provenance of the seed data means compliance with the Art. 26(3) prohibition cannot be demonstrated.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Do not build lookalike/custom audiences from the purchased broker list. Only seed audiences from data with a verified lawful basis, exclude any sensitive or proxy attributes from targeting parameters, and document that no GDPR Art. 9 categories inform the audience. If provenance cannot be verified, abandon the platform-targeting component entirely.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: By running ads on Meta and Google, the campaign is subject to platform ad-transparency obligations under DSA Art. 26(1): each ad must clearly identify that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid for it, and expose the main targeting parameters. As advertiser, HomeSecure must supply accurate 'paid for by / on behalf of' information and must not obscure its identity; the described covert use of a purchased list to expand reach sits uneasily with meaningful parameter transparency to recipients.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the advertiser's true identity and payer information are correctly declared in the platforms' ad-transparency fields, use only auditable targeting parameters, and align the on-platform ad disclosures with the campaign's actual targeting so recipients can understand why they see the ad.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's advertising provisions (Arts 25-28) are addressed primarily to providers of online platforms (here Meta and Google), not directly to HomeSecure as advertiser. The campaign nonetheless engages the DSA regime by uploading a purchased list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences, which triggers platform ad-transparency (Art. 26(1)) and the ban on sensitive-data-based ad targeting (Art. 26(3)). No dark-pattern (Art. 25), minor-targeting (Art. 28) or recommender (Art. 27) issue is supported on the facts. The core unlawfulness (no consent, no opt-out, no privacy notice) sits under GDPR/ePrivacy rather than the DSA; DSA exposure is indirect but real via the platform-targeting activity.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media. Here recipients never solicited or consented to contact (a purchased list with no consent records), the emails deliberately provide no opt-out mechanism, and the trader then escalates across a second channel by cold-calling non-openers. Re-contacting people who ignored the email, via broker-appended phone numbers and with no means to refuse, is exactly the pattern of unwanted, persistent solicitation the blacklist targets. As a blacklisted practice it is unfair per se, with no need to prove consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') ... Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Only market to individuals with a verifiable opt-in for that channel; include a functional one-click unsubscribe in every email and honour it immediately; suppress non-openers rather than escalating to phone; screen phone numbers against national do-not-call/opt-out registers and never re-contact people who have not consented or who have objected.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, through harassment, coercion or undue influence — assessed by factors including timing and persistence — it impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Systematically escalating from unsolicited email to scripted follow-up phone calls of people who did not engage, using numbers they never provided and with no opt-out offered, applies persistent pressure characteristic of an aggressive practice and compounds the Annex I point 26 breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the non-opener phone follow-up entirely absent prior consent; cap contact frequency; provide a clear, low-friction way to decline further contact on first touch and permanently suppress those who do not respond.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, or providing it in an unclear or untimely manner. The emails give no reference to how data was obtained, no identity/contact transparency and no means to object, omitting information material to whether the recipient engages with the offer. (Note: the privacy-notice obligation itself is principally a GDPR matter assessed separately; the UCPD angle is the material omission in the commercial communication.)
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Include clear trader identity, a link to the privacy policy, and a visible opt-out in every marketing message so the consumer has the material information needed to make an informed decision.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD chiefly through its solicitation tactics rather than product claims. Sending unsolicited marketing email with no unsubscribe mechanism and then placing scripted follow-up phone calls to non-openers is a persistent/unwanted solicitation blacklisted per se under Annex I point 26, and reinforces the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9). The lack of any opt-out or identity/transparency information in the emails also raises a misleading-omission concern under Art. 7. The underlying consent and privacy-notice failures are primarily GDPR/ePrivacy matters handled elsewhere.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems by email, social ads and phone to 400,000 contacts bought from a data broker, with no consent records ("opted-in somewhere in 2019"). The emails have no unsubscribe link, no privacy policy is referenced, the same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences, and non-openers are cold-called using broker-appended phone numbers. This is high-risk on every front and should not run in its current form. Under GDPR there is no valid lawful basis for any of the processing, the claimed consent fails every legal test, no privacy information is given, and there is no way to object to marketing — multiple critical breaches. Under the UCPD, the no-opt-out emails plus follow-up calls to non-openers are a per-se prohibited "persistent and unwanted solicitation" and an aggressive practice. The lookalike-audience uploads also create DSA exposure via the ad platforms because the data's provenance cannot be verified against the ban on sensitive-data targeting. The overall verdict is critical: stop the campaign as designed and rebuild from lawfully collected, first-party consent.
recommendations: Stop the campaign immediately and cease all use of the purchased broker list — email sends, phone calls, and platform uploads. It has no verifiable lawful basis and cannot be salvaged.
Delete the broker list rather than relying on the '2019 opt-in' assurance; you have no auditable proof of who consented, when, or to what, so it cannot be used lawfully.

Rebuild the marketing audience from first-party, purpose-specific opt-ins that you collect and document yourself (email marketing, phone marketing, and ad-platform targeting each need their own clear consent).

Remove the list from Meta and Google and do not build lookalike/custom audiences from broker data of unknown provenance; this also creates DSA sensitive-data-targeting exposure you cannot verify away.
Eliminate the phone follow-up to non-openers entirely — cold-calling people who ignored an email, using numbers they never gave you, is a per-se prohibited aggressive practice under the UCPD.
Add a clear one-click unsubscribe to every marketing email and an easy opt-out on every call; honour objections instantly across all channels and maintain a suppression list.

Provide a complete, easily accessible privacy notice at first contact: controller identity, purposes and legal basis, that data came from a broker, recipients (including Meta/Google), retention, and the right to object; link it in every message.
When you do advertise on platforms, declare accurate 'paid for by / on behalf of' information and use only auditable targeting parameters that exclude any sensitive attributes.
Have legal/DPO sign-off on the rebuilt process before any further sends, given the critical GDPR exposure across 400,000 EU data subjects.

Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

no privacy policy referenced in emails
uploading purchased list to Meta/Google to build lookalike audiences

triage.summary: A multi-channel (email, social, phone) marketing campaign for home alarm systems targeting EU homeowners aged 30-65, built on a purchased broker list of 400,000 addresses with no consent records. Practices raise serious GDPR concerns (no valid consent, no unsubscribe, no privacy policy, list uploaded for lookalike audiences, broker-appended phone numbers for cold calls) and UCPD/ePrivacy issues around unsolicited communications. DSA is included due to the use of platform-based ad targeting/lookalike audiences on Meta and Google.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Direct email marketing and cold calling to individuals generally require a valid lawful basis; under the ePrivacy framework prior consent is normally required for unsolicited email/phone marketing. A purchased list with no verifiable consent and vague broker assurances provides no valid lawful basis (neither valid consent nor a sustainable legitimate-interest balancing given the intrusive multi-channel use). Processing 400,000 records this way is unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Do not send to this list. Only market to individuals for whom you can evidence a valid, specific and current lawful basis (e.g. GDPR/ePrivacy-compliant opt-in). Discard broker data lacking consent provenance and rebuild permission-based lists.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that the data subject consented. There are no consent records at all, so consent cannot be demonstrated. A 2019 opt-in to an unknown third party is also not specific to HomeSecure's marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Obtain and retain proper consent records tied to your specific processing; never rely on a broker's unevidenced assertion. Where consent cannot be demonstrated, treat the data as having no consent basis.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Valid consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A generic historic opt-in 'somewhere' to a broker is not specific or informed as to HomeSecure's alarm marketing across email, social and phone, and so does not meet the Art. 4(11) standard.
findings.evidence_quote: purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019'
findings.recommendation: Collect consent through a clear affirmative opt-in that names HomeSecure and the specific channels/purposes, at the point of data collection.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) gives data subjects an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and controllers must facilitate that opt-out. Sending direct marketing with no unsubscribe mechanism (and 'manual' reply handling) fails to provide an easy, effective means to object and stop processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out in every marketing email and a suppression mechanism for phone contact; honour objections immediately and maintain a do-not-contact list.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is obtained (including from a data broker rather than directly), controllers must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, rights and profiling information. No privacy information is given to recipients, and none appears to have been provided when data was obtained from the broker (Art. 14 concerns mirror this). This defeats the transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a full privacy notice (or a prominent link) in every communication and proactively notify individuals whose data was obtained from a third party, covering the required Art. 13/14 information items.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires transparent information to be concise, easily accessible and communicated to data subjects. Failing to reference or make accessible any privacy information in the campaign breaches the accessibility requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Make privacy information easily accessible in all channels (email footer link, verbal notice/reference on calls) in clear, plain language.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached across the board: processing is unlawful (no basis), unfair (individuals had no reasonable expectation their broker data would be used for HomeSecure alarm marketing, lookalike modelling and cold calls) and non-transparent (no privacy notice).
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Re-engineer the campaign around a lawful, fair and transparent data flow: permission-based data, clear notices, and processing consistent with individuals' reasonable expectations.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading the list to build lookalike audiences is automated processing to evaluate/predict personal preferences and behaviour, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4). Doing so with data that has no valid basis compounds the unlawfulness and expands processing to new individuals.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Do not upload non-consented broker data to advertising platforms. Only use audience-matching/lookalike features with data that has a valid lawful basis and where individuals were informed of this specific sharing/profiling purpose.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Broker-appended phone numbers used for cold marketing calls are additional personal data processed without any lawful basis or consent, and unsolicited marketing calls engage ePrivacy consent requirements. This is a further unlawful processing operation distinct from the email send.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker
findings.recommendation: Cease cold calls on broker-appended numbers; only call individuals who have given valid consent to phone marketing and screen against national do-not-call registers.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is built on a purchased broker list of 400,000 addresses with no consent records, used for email, phone and platform lookalike-audience targeting. It engages multiple core GDPR obligations and likely breaches them: no valid lawful basis/consent, no demonstrable consent, no transparency/privacy notice, no opt-out mechanism for direct marketing, and unlawful re-purposing of personal data (including broker-appended phone numbers) for profiling. Multiple high-severity findings across Arts. 4(11), 5(1)(a), 6(1), 7, 12/13, 21 and 4(4)/22.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Running lookalike-audience ads on Meta and Google means these platforms will present advertisements on HomeSecure's behalf. DSA Art. 26(1) requires that, for each ad, recipients can identify in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The advertiser must supply accurate advertiser/payer identity and be transparent about the targeting parameters used (a custom/lookalike audience derived from a broker list). Because the underlying list has no verifiable consent and is being used to seed targeting, the parameter transparency the platform must surface will expose a targeting basis that cannot be legitimately explained, and the campaign gives no indication that compliant advertiser-identity/parameter information is being provided.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the Meta/Google ad account provides accurate advertiser and payer identity so the platform can render the mandatory 'why am I seeing this ad' and 'paid for by' disclosures. Do not use audiences seeded from a list without a lawful, documented basis, since the DSA targeting-parameter disclosure will make the targeting logic visible; rebuild audiences from consented first-party data or platform interest categories that can be transparently and lawfully explained.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Meta and Google's ad services are designated VLOPs, so under DSA Art. 39 the ads and their targeting parameters and reach will be entered into a public ad repository. This is an obligation on the platform, but it means HomeSecure's targeting choices (including audiences derived from an unconsented broker list) will be publicly archived and subject to scrutiny by regulators, journalists and competitors.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Treat all platform targeting as if it will be published: only run audiences and creative that can withstand public inspection and demonstrate a lawful basis, and document the provenance/consent status of any audience uploaded to a VLOP before campaign launch.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The declared audience excludes minors and there is no indication the platform providers would be aware with reasonable certainty that recipients are minors, so the DSA Art. 28 ban on profiling-based ads to minors is not triggered as described. However, the supervisor notes the broker list quality is unverified and lookalike audiences may reach beyond the declared 30-65 segment, so reach control should be confirmed rather than assumed.
findings.evidence_quote: homeowners 30-65
findings.recommendation: Apply platform age-gating/exclusion settings (18+ minimum) on the lookalike campaigns and confirm no under-18 recipients can be reached, so that no profiling-based advertising is served to minors.

verdicts.notes: The DSA primarily binds providers of online platforms rather than advertisers directly, but the campaign's use of Meta and Google lookalike audiences squarely engages the DSA advertising-transparency regime. The dominant compliance problems here (unconsented purchased list, no unsubscribe, no privacy policy, cold calls) are GDPR/ePrivacy/UCPD matters outside this regulation. Within the DSA, the main relevant obligation is ad transparency (Art. 26(1)); the sensitive-data and minor-targeting bans are not triggered on the facts as described, and VLOP ad-repository publication is a contextual flag.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Recipients on a purchased list never solicited contact, and the campaign design specifically escalates to unsolicited phone calls to those who did not open the email — combined with emails that carry no opt-out, this is scripted, multi-channel re-contact of people who have not consented and cannot easily refuse. Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances 'making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, fax, e-mail or other remote media' outside enforcement of a contractual obligation; no contractual relationship exists here, and the email-then-call sequencing supplies the 'persistent' element.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Do not cold-call non-openers from broker-appended numbers. Only contact individuals who have given verifiable, specific consent to marketing by that channel; screen phone numbers against opt-out/do-not-call registers; and immediately suppress any recipient who does not engage or who objects, rather than escalating to another channel.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive a practice that impairs the consumer's freedom of choice through persistence or by imposing onerous barriers to exercising their rights. Sending marketing with no functioning opt-out and then pursuing recipients by phone removes any easy means to refuse further contact and pressures recipients across channels, an aggressive-practice factor (timing, persistence, burdensome exit) reinforcing the Annex I point 26 concern.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, one-click, no-cost opt-out in every marketing message and honour it across all channels immediately. Avoid re-contacting or switching channels to reach people who have not opted in, and never use non-engagement as a trigger for more intrusive outreach.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD chiefly through its solicitation model, not through misleading content. A purchased list with no consent is emailed with no unsubscribe mechanism, and non-openers are then cold-called on broker-appended numbers — a scripted, cross-channel re-contact of people who never asked to be contacted and have no easy way to stop it. This pattern risks the Annex I point 26 blacklist prohibition on persistent and unwanted solicitations, and the removal of any opt-out route supports an aggressive-practice reading under Arts. 8-9. Consent/privacy-notice deficiencies themselves are primarily GDPR/ePrivacy matters handled by other agents.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems to 400,000 people on a purchased broker list, across email, social lookalike ads, and follow-up phone calls. The core problem is that none of these contacts have valid consent — the broker's vague "opted-in somewhere in 2019" claim with no consent records provides no lawful basis under GDPR/ePrivacy for emailing, calling, or uploading the list to Meta and Google. On top of that, the emails have no unsubscribe link and no privacy notice, and non-openers are escalated to cold calls, which regulators would treat as persistent and unwanted solicitation (blacklisted under consumer-protection law) and an aggressive practice. The lookalike-audience uploads add unlawful profiling and will be publicly archived in platform ad repositories, exposing the illegitimate targeting to scrutiny. In short, the campaign as designed is unlawful on multiple independent grounds and cannot be fixed with minor tweaks. Do not launch it — the purchased list must be discarded and the campaign rebuilt on consented, permission-based data. Financial and reputational exposure here is severe (GDPR fines, DPA enforcement, consumer-protection sanctions).
recommendations: Do not send, call, or upload this list. Halt the campaign entirely and discard the broker data — a 400,000-record purchased list with no consent records has no valid lawful basis for any channel.

Rebuild your audience from permission-based, first-party data where you can evidence a specific, current, GDPR/ePrivacy-compliant opt-in naming HomeSecure and each channel (email, phone, ad targeting).
Add a clear one-click unsubscribe to every marketing email and a working opt-out for phone contact; maintain a suppression/do-not-contact list and honour objections immediately.

Stop the email-then-cold-call escalation of non-openers on broker-appended numbers — this is a blacklisted persistent/unwanted solicitation and an aggressive practice; screen any future calls against national do-not-call registers.
Include a full privacy notice (or prominent link) in every communication, covering identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights (GDPR Arts. 12/13/14).

Do not upload non-consented broker data to Meta or Google for lookalike audiences — this is unlawful profiling; only use audience-matching with consented data, and note these ads are publicly archived in VLOP ad repositories.
If any campaign proceeds, ensure the ad account carries accurate advertiser/payer identity for DSA transparency disclosures and apply 18+ age exclusions on the platform audiences.
Document consent provenance for every future data source and never rely on a broker's unevidenced assurance of opt-in.

Do not process data where the source cannot evidence a lawful basis.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that consent was obtained. With no consent records and only a broker's unverifiable claim, consent cannot be demonstrated. Consent must also be as easy to withdraw as to give, which the absence of any opt-out mechanism further breaches.
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on consent that cannot be evidenced. Retain granular, auditable proof of consent (timestamp, scope, method) for every contact, and provide an equally easy withdrawal mechanism before any send.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent under Art. 4(11) must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A vague 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' for an unspecified purpose cannot constitute specific and informed consent for HomeSecure's marketing, list upload to Meta/Google, or follow-up phone calls. Consent is not transferable across unrelated controllers/purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker
findings.recommendation: Obtain fresh, purpose-specific, informed opt-in consent naming HomeSecure and each processing purpose (email, phone, ad-platform matching) rather than relying on stale, generic broker consent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached: data subjects were never informed that HomeSecure would market to them, that their data was bought from a broker, or that phone numbers were appended and the list uploaded to Meta/Google. This is covert, unfair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Ensure all processing is lawful, fair and transparent — inform individuals of the source and purposes of processing before marketing to them, and never process data covertly acquired without their knowledge.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Although data was obtained indirectly (Art. 14 territory), no privacy information at all is provided: no controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (Meta/Google), retention, or data subject rights. Marketing recipients receive no transparency information, breaching the information obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, accessible privacy notice in every communication: controller identity, purposes and legal basis, that data was sourced from a broker, recipients including ad platforms, retention period, and how to exercise data subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute and must be facilitated. Emails with no unsubscribe link, plus follow-up phone calls, deny recipients an easy means to object. 'Replies handled manually' is not an adequate, clearly signposted opt-out and creates friction that obstructs the right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe link in every email and an easy opt-out on calls; honour objections immediately and suppress objecting contacts across all channels (email, phone, and ad-platform audiences).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading the list to build lookalike audiences and behavioural targeting constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4) (automated evaluation of personal preferences/behaviour). This profiling is carried out on data with no lawful basis and no transparency, compounding the Art. 6 and Art. 13 breaches and triggering the right to object to profiling for direct marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Do not upload personal data to ad platforms without a valid lawful basis and disclosure. If profiling for marketing continues, inform data subjects and provide an effective means to object to profiling under Art. 21.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages GDPR at almost every level and is very likely non-compliant. It relies on a 400,000-address list bought from a data broker with no verifiable consent, uses it for email/phone direct marketing, uploads it to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences (profiling), provides no privacy information and no opt-out. There is no demonstrable lawful basis, no valid consent, no transparency, and no mechanism to exercise the right to object — multiple high/critical GDPR breaches.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Running lookalike/behaviourally-targeted ads on Meta and Google means those platform ads must let recipients identify, in real time, that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf and by whom it is paid, and the main targeting parameters. While the transparency obligation formally binds the platform, the advertiser must supply accurate advertiser/payer identity and cannot rely on obscure or misdescribed targeting. A campaign built on an untraceable purchased list and giving no attention to transparency risks feeding inaccurate or non-disclosable targeting parameters into the platform's Art. 26(1) disclosures.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the advertiser and paying entity are correctly declared in the Meta/Google ad account so platform ad-transparency labels are accurate, and use only targeting parameters that can be lawfully and honestly disclosed. Do not target audiences whose data provenance you cannot substantiate.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Meta and Google are designated very large online platforms and must maintain public ad repositories containing the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. Ads from this campaign will therefore be publicly archived and open to regulator, journalist and researcher scrutiny, including the fact that targeting is based on custom/lookalike audiences derived from a purchased broker list with no consent records — materially increasing exposure of the underlying GDPR/UCPD deficiencies.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Assume all Meta/Google ad creative, targeting basis and reach will be permanently public; only run targeting whose data sourcing and consent basis would withstand public and regulatory examination. Remediate the list-provenance/consent issues before activating any platform advertising.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's core obligations bind online platforms (here Meta and Google), not the advertiser directly, so the campaign's most serious defects (no consent, no opt-out, no privacy notice) sit under GDPR/UCPD rather than the DSA. The DSA is nonetheless engaged because the list is uploaded to Meta and Google to run lookalike, behaviourally-targeted advertising: those platform ads must satisfy Art. 26(1) transparency and, as VLOPs, will be publicly archived under Art. 39. No special-category (Art. 26(3)) targeting and no minor-targeting (Art. 28) is evident, so those prohibitions are not engaged.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: The list is cold and unsolicited (purchased, no verifiable consent), emails provide no working opt-out mechanism, and non-openers are then actively re-contacted by telephone across a second channel. This matches the blacklisted practice of making persistent and unwanted solicitations by e-mail and telephone: the solicitations are unwanted (recipients never asked to be contacted) and effectively persistent/unstoppable because no opt-out is offered and refusal-by-non-engagement is met with escalation to phone calls. This is prohibited in all circumstances, with no need to prove consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') ... Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Do not market to purchased/broker lists without a verifiable opt-in and a clear, functioning one-click unsubscribe in every email plus honoured suppression across all channels. Remove the follow-up-call-to-non-openers sequence entirely; non-engagement is not consent to be phoned. Maintain and respect a global suppression/do-not-contact list before any send or call.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Escalating from unsolicited email to phone calls targeting people who did not open, using numbers they never provided, exhibits the persistence and channel-stacking that can amount to an aggressive practice through harassment/undue influence, impairing the average consumer's freedom of choice. The absence of any easy way to stop contact compounds the onerous-barrier factor listed in Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Cease multi-channel re-contact of individuals who have not engaged and who have no relationship with the advertiser. Frequency-cap contacts, provide a clear and cost-free way to refuse further contact on first touch, and stop immediately on any objection.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information the consumer needs — notably a clear identity of the sender and an accessible means to object to further contact — is omitted from the communications. While the commercial intent of an alarm-system marketing email is itself apparent (so the hidden-commercial-intent limb is weak), the failure to surface opt-out and sender/transparency information can constitute a misleading omission that impairs an informed decision to keep receiving or stop the communications.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Include clear sender identity, a transparent statement of how the consumer's data was obtained, and a prominent, easily actionable opt-out in every communication. (Detailed data-processing transparency obligations sit under GDPR/ePrivacy and should be addressed there as well.)

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD chiefly through its solicitation practices rather than through misleading product claims. Sending unsolicited marketing to a cold purchased list with no opt-out mechanism, then re-contacting non-openers by phone across channels, matches the Annex I point 26 blacklist prohibition on persistent and unwanted solicitations and also carries an aggressive-practices dimension (Arts. 8-9). Data-consent/transparency defects are primarily GDPR/ePrivacy issues and are left to the other agents; the UCPD angle is the harassment-by-repeated-contact and lack of any means to stop it.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems by email, phone and social ads to a 400,000-person list bought from a data broker with no consent records — just a vague claim people "opted in somewhere in 2019." The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. As designed, the campaign is unlawful at its foundation: there is no valid legal basis to contact these people, no privacy information is given, and there is no way to unsubscribe (emails have no opt-out link and non-openers are then phoned on numbers they never provided). This triggers multiple critical and high-severity GDPR breaches (lawful basis, consent, transparency, right to object) and matches an EU blacklisted unfair practice — persistent, unwanted email-and-phone solicitations — under the UCPD, which is prohibited outright regardless of harm. The ad-platform uploads add DSA exposure because Meta and Google publicly archive all ads and their targeting, putting the untraceable list provenance on display to regulators. The AI Act is not engaged. Bottom line: do not launch this campaign in its current form; the purchased list cannot be lawfully used and the core mechanics need to be rebuilt around documented consent and easy opt-out.
report.recommendations: Do not send to, call, or upload the purchased broker list — it has no verifiable consent and cannot be used lawfully; suspend the campaign now.

campaign.title: You've WON — iPhone giveaway retargeting
campaign.text: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.' Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked. Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page. A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.

detected_practices: false 'you have won' prize claim
fake prize giveaway (no draw, no phones stocked)
false scarcity / 15-minute countdown urgency
hidden subscription trap (39 EUR/month VIP club buried on separate terms page)
small upfront 'verification shipping' fee (4.99 EUR)
fake progress bar / simulated verification
behavioural retargeting
SMS blasts
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is "general consumers" with no age gating, so minors could plausibly be reached, especially via untargeted SMS blasts and display popups. Targeting a general audience with a high-pressure scam raises heightened vulnerability concerns.
triage.summary: A deceptive prize-giveaway campaign using retargeting popups and SMS blasts that falsely tells every visitor they have "won" an iPhone, demanding a 4.99 EUR fee within 15 minutes and covertly enrolling them into a 39 EUR/month subscription. It relies on false claims, a fake progress bar, false urgency, and a hidden subscription trap. Behavioural retargeting and SMS distribution imply processing of personal data.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data processed via retargeting and SMS is collected and used in a demonstrably deceptive context (a fake prize, a simulated verification, a concealed subscription). Processing personal data as part of a manipulative, misleading flow breaches the requirement that data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Fairness under Art. 5(1)(a) is violated where the data subject is deceived about what is happening to them and their money.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visitor 'wins'; there is no draw and no phones are stocked. A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.
findings.recommendation: Cease the deceptive framing entirely. Personal data may only be processed for genuine, clearly disclosed purposes; abandon the fake-win/fake-verification mechanics that make any associated data processing inherently unfair.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting and SMS direct marketing both require a valid lawful basis; SMS marketing to consumers generally requires prior consent (ePrivacy/Art. 6(1)). The description gives no indication of any lawful basis or prior consent for the SMS blasts or the retargeting, and a deceptive scam context cannot support a legitimate-interest balancing test.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before any processing: obtain valid prior opt-in consent for SMS marketing and for behavioural retargeting cookies/identifiers, and do not send marketing to recipients who have not consented.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent for SMS marketing and behavioural targeting must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. 'SMS blasts' to a general audience embedded in a deceptive prize scam show no evidence of any freely given, informed opt-in; consent cannot be validly obtained through a misleading flow.
findings.evidence_quote: SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Collect genuine, unbundled opt-in consent through a clear, non-deceptive interface, keep records of it, and only message consenting recipients.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be clearly distinguishable, in plain language, and not bundled or hidden. Burying material terms and any data-processing/marketing consent on a separate terms page while the user is pressured to pay a fee is a consent dark pattern that fails Art. 7's conditions, and there is no indication consent is as easy to withdraw as to give.
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Present any consent request separately and prominently in plain language at the point of collection, unbundled from payment, and provide an equally easy withdrawal/unsubscribe mechanism.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data (phone numbers for SMS, retargeting identifiers), the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients and data-subject rights at the point of collection. The campaign provides none of this; instead it presents a fake prize claim, so the mandatory Art. 13 information is absent.
findings.evidence_quote: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro!
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, accessible privacy notice at the point of data collection covering controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, retention, recipients, profiling and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and related profiling, and every marketing communication must facilitate opt-out. The described SMS blasts and retargeting show no opt-out/unsubscribe mechanism, so the right to object is not respected or facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning opt-out in every SMS and marketing touchpoint (e.g. STOP keyword), honour objections immediately, and stop profiling for marketing on objection.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The behavioural retargeting constitutes profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4) (automated processing of personal data to analyse/predict behaviour and interests), which is what brings the lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations into play.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Treat the retargeting as profiling and ensure all associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection) are met.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: With no age gating, untargeted SMS blasts and display popups can reach minors. Where consent is the basis for data processing in services offered to children, processing is lawful only with parental consent below the applicable age (13-16), with reasonable verification efforts. No age verification is described, so children's data may be processed unlawfully.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general consumers
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance measures and, where minors may be reached, obtain and verify parental consent before processing their data, or reliably exclude minors from the campaign.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data through behavioural retargeting (profiling) and SMS direct marketing to a general EU audience. Nothing in the description evidences a lawful basis, valid consent, transparency at point of collection, or an opt-out mechanism, and the whole flow is built on deception (fake win, fake progress bar, hidden subscription) which independently breaches the fairness/transparency principle. Given untargeted SMS blasts that can reach minors with no age gating, child-consent obligations are also engaged. Multiple GDPR obligations are likely breached.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: A simulated verification/progress bar that fabricates a 'verified' outcome deceives and manipulates recipients into believing a genuine prize-claim process is occurring, materially distorting their ability to make a free and informed decision. Combined with the artificial 15-minute countdown and the 39 EUR/month subscription concealed on a separate terms page (forced continuity / obscured cancellation terms), this is core dark-pattern conduct prohibited by DSA Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fake progress bar and simulated 'verified' messaging entirely; eliminate the artificial countdown; and surface all recurring charges (the 39 EUR/month VIP club) and cancellation terms with equal prominence to the offer before any payment or enrolment, so no deceptive or manipulative interface design steers the decision.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Enrolling users into an ongoing paid subscription whose terms are hidden on a separate page — while the interface presents only a 4.99 EUR one-off 'verification shipping' fee — is a forced-continuity dark pattern that gives disproportionate prominence to the cheap upfront choice and obscures the material recurring commitment, impairing free and informed decision-making under DSA Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Present the recurring 39 EUR/month charge clearly and unambiguously on the same screen as the payment step, obtain explicit informed agreement to the subscription, and make cancellation at least as easy as sign-up.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting means these communications are advertisements presented on the basis of profiling. Where delivered through an online platform interface, Art. 26(1) requires recipients to be able to identify in real time that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters with a way to change them. The described disguised 'you've WON' popups give no such disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Clearly label the retargeting content as advertising, disclose the advertiser identity and who paid for the ad, and provide meaningful information about the targeting parameters and an accessible means to change them.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The declared audience is 'general consumers' with no age gating, and untargeted SMS blasts and display popups can plausibly reach minors. DSA Art. 28 bans presenting profiling-based (behaviourally retargeted) advertisements to recipients who are, with reasonable certainty, minors, and requires appropriate protective measures where interfaces are accessible to minors. The profiling-driven retargeting here provides no age assurance or safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Implement age-assurance / exclusion measures to ensure profiling-based retargeting ads are not served to minors, and avoid distributing behaviourally targeted, high-pressure promotions through channels (SMS blasts, display) that lack any age gating.

verdicts.notes: The campaign relies on textbook deceptive-design / dark-pattern techniques (fake "verified" progress bar, artificial 15-minute deadline, and a hidden 39 EUR/month subscription trap buried on a separate terms page) that DSA Art. 25 prohibits in online interfaces. Behavioural retargeting engages the ad-transparency duties of Art. 26(1), which the described popups/SMS do not appear to satisfy, and the lack of any age gating on untargeted SMS/display retargeting raises Art. 28 concerns about profiling-based ads reaching minors. Note: DSA Arts. 25/26/28 formally bind providers of online platforms; applicability depends on whether the campaign runs on/through such a platform or the marketer qualifies as a provider — the underlying conduct is nonetheless the exact target of these provisions.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 31 prohibits in all circumstances creating the false impression that the consumer has won a prize when there is in fact no prize, or when claiming it is subject to paying money. Here every visitor 'wins', there is no draw and no phones are stocked, and claiming the 'prize' requires paying a 4.99 EUR fee. This is the textbook blacklisted false prize practice — a per se violation requiring no assessment of consumer effect.
findings.evidence_quote: CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected — you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.
findings.recommendation: Do not run the campaign. A 'you have won' claim is only lawful where a genuine prize exists, has actually been awarded to the specific recipient, and can be claimed at no cost beyond unavoidable delivery. This campaign cannot be made compliant.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits in all circumstances falsely stating that a product is available only for a very limited time to force an immediate decision and deprive consumers of a chance to make an informed choice. The 15-minute deadline is artificial (there is no genuine prize or draw) and is designed purely to pressure payment before the consumer reflects — a per se blacklisted false-urgency practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Claim within 15 minutes
findings.recommendation: Remove the artificial 15-minute countdown/deadline. Any time limit must reflect a genuine constraint; a fabricated deadline attached to a non-existent prize is prohibited.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices containing false information or otherwise deceiving the average consumer about the nature of the product/offer and causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The simulated 'checking/verified' progress bar is a fabricated verification that misrepresents that a real prize is being confirmed, deceiving the consumer into paying. The whole offer misrepresents its existence and nature.
findings.evidence_quote: A fake progress bar shows 'checking your prize... verified!'.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fake verification/progress bar and all false representations. Interfaces must not simulate a verification process that does not occur.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the consumer needs, or providing it in an unclear or untimely manner. The recurring 39 EUR/month subscription is the true financial commitment yet is hidden on a separate terms page and not disclosed at the point the consumer decides to pay the 4.99 EUR. Price and the existence of an ongoing contractual obligation are material information; burying them is a misleading omission (a subscription trap).
findings.evidence_quote: Paying enrols the user in a 39 EUR/month 'VIP club' described on a separate terms page.
findings.recommendation: Any recurring charge must be disclosed clearly, prominently and before the consumer commits, adjacent to the price and the call to action — not on a separate terms page. Given the other blacklist violations, however, the campaign should not run at all.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits describing a product as won/free where the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of collection/delivery. The offer is framed as a free prize but requires a 4.99 EUR 'verification shipping' fee and, crucially, subsequent enrolment in a 39 EUR/month subscription — costs far exceeding unavoidable delivery. This is a misuse of the 'free/won' framing.
findings.evidence_quote: you've WON an iPhone 16 Pro! Claim within 15 minutes: just pay 4.99 EUR verification shipping.
findings.recommendation: Do not present the item as a free prize. Costs beyond genuine unavoidable delivery cannot be attached to something described as won or free.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that impair the consumer's freedom of choice through undue influence, timing and persistence. The combination of relentless retargeting popups, SMS blasts, a high-pressure 15-minute deadline and a simulated verification is calculated to pressure an immediate payment, materially distorting the average consumer's transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your number was selected
findings.recommendation: Cease the high-pressure retargeting/SMS pressure sequence. Legitimate marketing must not use coercive urgency and persistence to force immediate payment.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits persistent and unwanted solicitations by SMS/other remote media (outside enforcing a contractual obligation). Untargeted SMS blasts and repeated retargeting popups pushing a fabricated prize to a general audience are likely to constitute persistent unwanted solicitations, especially where recipients have not consented or wish no further contact.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting popups and SMS blasts
findings.recommendation: Only send SMS to recipients who have given valid prior consent, honour opt-outs immediately, and cap repeated retargeting. Do not re-contact users who have not opted in.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is a deceptive prize-giveaway scam that engages multiple UCPD blacklist ("in all circumstances") prohibitions as well as the general misleading and aggressive-practice provisions. The core claim — every visitor "wins" an iPhone but there is no draw, no stock, and claiming requires a 4.99 EUR payment plus covert enrolment in a 39 EUR/month subscription — is a per se prohibited practice under Annex I point 31. Multiple independent critical violations are present; the campaign as described is unlawful and cannot be salvaged by disclosure edits — it should not run.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a deceptive prize scam and cannot be made compliant — it must not run. It tells every visitor they have "won" an iPhone when there is no draw and no phones exist, pressures them with a fake 15-minute deadline and a simulated "verified" progress bar, charges a 4.99 EUR "shipping" fee, and secretly enrols them into a 39 EUR/month subscription buried on a separate terms page. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive this hits several outright-banned ("in all circumstances") practices: false prize claims, false urgency, misuse of "free/won", and hidden subscription costs — no amount of editing fixes a per se prohibited practice. Under the Digital Services Act, the fake progress bar, artificial countdown and concealed recurring charge are textbook prohibited dark patterns. Under the GDPR, the SMS blasts and behavioural retargeting have no lawful basis, no valid consent, no privacy notice, no opt-out, and no age gating to protect minors. The bottom line: this is an unlawful scam, not a marketing campaign, and running it would expose the business to enforcement action, fines and likely liability for consumer losses.
report.recommendations: ["Do not launch this campaign in any form. The false-prize mechanic (UCPD Annex I point 31) is banned outright and cannot be fixed with disclosures — abandon the fake-win concept entirely.
