findings.title: Blacklist: unverified consumer reviews
findings.rationale: Stating that reviews come from consumers who actually used or purchased the product without taking reasonable, proportionate verification steps is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23b. Here the '4.9/5 by verified buyers' figure is built partly on 300 farm reviews using fabricated 'verified-purchase' badges, so the 'verified buyers' claim is unfounded.
findings.evidence_quote: Product page will display 'Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers'
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'verified buyers' framing unless a genuine purchase-verification process backs every counted review. Recalculate any displayed rating from authentic, verified reviews only, and never rely on fabricated verified-purchase badges.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a trust/quality mark without the necessary authorisation is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 2. A self-designed 'Customers' Choice' badge presented as an independent distinction is exactly the invented award emblem this point targets — it has no authorising body and misleads consumers into thinking it is an independent endorsement.
findings.evidence_quote: a 'Customers' Choice' badge we designed ourselves
findings.recommendation: Remove the self-created 'Customers' Choice' badge. Only display trust/quality marks or awards actually granted by an authorised independent body, and only within the terms of that authorisation.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Even outside the blacklist, the aggregate '4.9/5' rating deceives the average consumer about the product's main characteristics and its distinctions/endorsements (Art. 6), because it is inflated by 300 purchased reviews and by voucher-gated 5-star reviews, and is likely to cause a transactional decision the consumer would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers
findings.recommendation: Display only ratings genuinely reflecting authentic, unincentivised customer experiences. Do not publish an aggregate score that incorporates purchased or incentivised reviews.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Incentivising reviews and conditioning the reward on a 5-star rating creates a material connection and biases the review corpus. Displaying the resulting reviews/rating without disclosing that they were incentivised and rating-gated is a misleading omission of material information under Art. 7 (undisclosed material connection). The gating also feeds the misrepresentation of the aggregate score under point 23c.
findings.evidence_quote: offering a 20 EUR voucher only if they leave a 5-star review (4 stars or below: no voucher)
findings.recommendation: Do not condition any incentive on the rating given. If offering a reward for a review at all, make it available regardless of star rating, clearly and prominently disclose that the review was incentivised, and keep incentivised reviews identifiable/separate.

verdicts.notes: This blender launch plan engages multiple UCPD Annex I blacklisted practices — which are prohibited in all circumstances without any need for a case-by-case unfairness assessment. It commissions and buys fake reviews, misrepresents and suppresses genuine reviews, falsely claims reviews come from verified purchasers, and displays a self-invented "Customers' Choice" trust badge. The aggregate "4.9/5" rating and verified-badge claims are also independently misleading actions under Art. 6. Overall this is among the most clearly non-compliant fact patterns under the Directive.

report.executive_summary: This campaign plans to launch a blender by buying 300 fake five-star reviews with fabricated "verified-purchase" badges, paying customers a 20 EUR voucher only for 5-star reviews, displaying a "Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers" claim and a self-made "Customers' Choice" badge, and deleting all negative reviews by falsely flagging them as spam. Almost every element hits practices that EU consumer law bans outright — fake reviews, unverified "verified buyer" claims, and unauthorised trust marks are on the UCPD blacklist and are illegal in all circumstances, with no defence available. The same conduct manipulates the marketplace review interface in breach of the DSA, and the voucher emails to customers raise GDPR issues (no lawful basis, no opt-out, no privacy notice, unfair conditioning of the reward on a positive rating). This is not fixable with disclaimers or tweaks; the core mechanics are unlawful. The verdict is: do not run this campaign in anything resembling its current form. Rebuild the launch entirely around genuine, unincentivised customer feedback.
recommendations: Do not buy or commission any reviews from the review farm — this is a blacklisted, per-se illegal practice. Cancel this entirely.
Stop flagging negative reviews as 'spam'. Only report reviews on neutral, content-based grounds through the platform's proper mechanism; never on the basis of rating or sentiment.
Remove the self-designed 'Customers' Choice' badge. Only display trust/quality marks actually awarded by an authorised independent body.
Remove the 'Rated 4.9/5 by verified buyers' claim and recalculate any displayed rating using only authentic, genuinely verified reviews.
Stop conditioning the voucher on a 5-star rating. Any review incentive must be available regardless of the score given, and every incentivised review must be clearly disclosed as such.

Before any customer emailing, establish and document a lawful basis (prior consent or a valid ePrivacy soft opt-in), include a clear unsubscribe/opt-out link, and provide a privacy notice covering purpose, legal basis, retention and data-subject rights.
Rebuild the launch programme around authentic, unincentivised customer feedback and have legal/compliance sign off before going live given the critical exposure.

campaign.title: LumaSkin serum — AI visuals
campaign.text: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum. All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated. Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'. No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere. Claim on pack-shot overlay: 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study).

detected_practices: AI-generated before/after imagery
fabricated results imagery
AI-smoothing filter on presenter
false 'zero filter, zero editing' claim (undisclosed AI/synthetic content)
no AI/synthetic-content disclosure
unsubstantiated 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' health/efficacy claim
misleading claim based on internal survey of 12 employees with no clinical study
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is women 30-55, so minors are not the intended target; however social/video channels are broadly accessible. No personalisation/targeting declared, so GDPR is not clearly engaged, but the core issues are deceptive AI-generated content, undisclosed synthetic media, and false substantiation claims. AI Act (synthetic content transparency/deepfake disclosure), UCPD (misleading commercial practices, false claims), and DSA (dissemination of deceptive content on platforms) are all plausibly engaged.
triage.summary: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum using generative AI to fabricate before/after results imagery and an AI-smoothing filter on a presenter who falsely claims her skin is 'real... zero filter, zero editing', with no synthetic-content disclosure. It also carries an unsubstantiated 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim backed only by an internal 12-employee survey. Targets EU women 30-55 across social and video channels.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The before/after results imagery is entirely produced by a generative image model (synthetic image content). Under Art. 50(2), providers/deployers of AI systems generating synthetic image content must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign states there is 'no AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere', so this marking obligation is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated visuals carry machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g. C2PA/SynthID-style watermarking) identifying them as artificially generated or manipulated, and retain evidence that the generating system applies such marking. Combine with visible on-asset disclosure.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Applying an AI-smoothing filter to real footage of a real presenter is AI manipulation of video content depicting a real person that would falsely appear authentic — a deep fake within Art. 50(4). Deployers must disclose that such content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Here not only is disclosure absent, the presenter affirmatively denies any editing, directly defeating the transparency purpose of the provision. The same disclosure duty applies to the fabricated before/after video/image content presented as genuine product results.
findings.evidence_quote: Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure that the presenter footage and results imagery have been artificially generated/manipulated with AI, and remove the false 'zero filter, zero editing' statement. Disclosure must be clearly visible and durable across social and video placements.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses AI-generated/manipulated content in a deceptive manner that could distort consumers' purchasing decisions. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits deceptive AI techniques that materially distort behaviour, but only where they are reasonably likely to cause significant harm. The deception here is a commercial/advertising harm best addressed under UCPD misleading-practices rules rather than the AI Act prohibition, whose high 'significant harm' threshold is not clearly met on the facts. Flagged for awareness.
findings.evidence_quote: before/after pairs fabricated
findings.recommendation: Treat the deceptive use of AI-generated imagery primarily as a misleading-practices issue (out of scope for this regulation), but be aware that AI-driven deception targeting behaviour could escalate to an Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition if it were shown to cause significant harm; avoid any AI-driven manipulative techniques going beyond the content itself.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is squarely within scope of the AI Act's transparency regime. It uses generative AI to fabricate before/after "results" imagery and synthesise skin texture (Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking) and applies an AI-smoothing filter to a real presenter to produce manipulated video that constitutes a deep fake (Art. 50(4) disclosure), while providing no synthetic-content disclosure anywhere and even affirmatively denying editing ("zero filter, zero editing"). These are clear transparency-obligation breaches. The deceptive-technique prohibition (Art. 5(1)(a)) is engaged in spirit but the "significant harm" threshold makes it a UCPD matter primarily, so it is flagged for attention rather than as a standalone prohibition breach.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits providers of online platforms from designing or operating interfaces that deceive or manipulate recipients or distort their ability to make free and informed decisions. The obligation binds the platform, not this advertiser directly, but disseminating fabricated 'results' imagery and an AI-smoothed presenter presented as 'zero filter, zero editing' is deceptive content that a hosting platform could be exposed to under Art. 25. The equivalent conduct for the advertiser itself is captured by UCPD Arts. 5-7 (per the graph's RELATED_TO edge, DSA dark-pattern rules apply without prejudice to the UCPD).
findings.evidence_quote: before/after pairs fabricated ... AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on the DSA as the operative regime for the advertiser here, but remove the deception before distribution: clearly disclose that imagery and the presenter footage are AI-generated/AI-modified and drop the false 'zero filter, zero editing' statement, so no hosting platform is placed at Art. 25 risk.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Where the campaign runs as paid advertising on online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify in real time that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf, and who paid for it. This is a platform obligation rather than an advertiser one, but the advertiser must supply accurate advertiser/payer information and ensure the ad is labellable; the fabricated imagery and unsubstantiated 'clinically proven' claim will appear in the transparently-labelled ad.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: social, video ... Clinically proven -71% wrinkles
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ad is delivered with correct advertiser and payer identification for platform labelling, and that the creative shown as a labelled advertisement contains only substantiated, non-deceptive content.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If placed as ads on a Very Large Online Platform, Art. 39 requires the platform to keep a public ad repository including ad content, advertiser, payer and reach. The advertiser has no direct obligation, but its false 'clinically proven -71%' claim and fabricated imagery would be publicly archived and open to scrutiny by regulators, competitors and consumers.
findings.evidence_quote: Markets: EU ... Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study)
findings.recommendation: Assume any VLOP-placed ad will be permanently and publicly archived; only run creative and claims that are fully substantiated and non-deceptive so they withstand public and regulatory review.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's marketing-relevant obligations (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) are directed at providers of online platforms, not at advertisers. This submission is an advertiser's campaign with no personalisation/targeting declared and an adult (30-55) audience, so the platform-facing prohibitions on sensitive-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) and profiling-based ads to minors (Art. 28) are not engaged. The campaign's core defects — fabricated AI before/after imagery, an undisclosed AI-smoothing filter, and a false "clinically proven" claim — are principally UCPD and AI Act matters. Two DSA points are worth flagging at info level for the advertiser: (1) the deceptive synthetic creative could expose the hosting platform to the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition (deceiving/manipulating recipients), and (2) when run as paid ads on platforms/VLOPs the content will be surfaced under Art. 26(1) transparency and Art. 39 ad-repository obligations, meaning the false claims and synthetic imagery will be publicly archived and must withstand scrutiny.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Fabricated before/after imagery deceives the average consumer about the product's main characteristics — specifically the results and benefits the serum can actually deliver. The images depict effects that were manufactured by an image model, not achieved by the product, and are likely to cause a transactional decision (purchase) the consumer would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action within Art. 6(1)(b).
findings.evidence_quote: All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated.
findings.recommendation: Remove all fabricated before/after imagery. Only depict genuine, unretouched results actually achieved with the product, and clearly label any illustrative/dramatised visuals as such. Do not present AI-synthesised outcomes as real product results.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The claim asserts a specific, quantified efficacy ('-71% wrinkles') and represents it as 'clinically proven', when it is based only on an internal survey of 12 employees with no clinical study. This is false/unsubstantiated information about the product's results and about the nature of the evidence, deceiving the average consumer on a material characteristic — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study)
findings.recommendation: Drop the '-71%' figure and the word 'clinically proven' unless supported by a methodologically sound clinical study on an adequate, independent sample. Any performance figure must be substantiated by robust evidence held before publication; internal employee feedback cannot be described as clinical proof.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The presenter makes an express, false statement of fact — 'zero filter, zero editing' — while an AI-smoothing filter is in fact applied to her. This is a clear misleading action under Art. 6: false information about the product's demonstrated results and about the authenticity of the depiction, directly capable of distorting the consumer's transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'zero filter, zero editing' statement entirely, since it is factually untrue. If AI smoothing is used on the presenter, disclose it clearly and do not present the filtered appearance as the unedited real-world result of using the serum.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic/AI-generated nature of the results imagery and of the filtered presenter footage is material information the average consumer needs to assess the reliability of the depicted results. Presenting synthetic content as authentic results without any disclosure hides material information and is a misleading omission under Art. 7. (Machine-readable/deepfake marking obligations are handled under the AI Act by another agent.)
findings.evidence_quote: No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Add clear, prominent disclosure that imagery is AI-generated/manipulated wherever it appears, and ensure the synthetic nature of any depicted 'results' is unmistakable to viewers on social and video channels.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Considered but not engaged as a blacklist breach: the false-cure prohibition applies to claims that a product cures illnesses, dysfunction or malformations. Wrinkles / ageing are cosmetic conditions, not an illness, dysfunction or malformation, so point 17 does not apply on the current wording. Flagged so it is not overlooked if the campaign later adds medical/therapeutic claims.
findings.evidence_quote: Cosmetics campaign for an anti-ageing serum
findings.recommendation: Avoid adding any language implying the serum treats, heals or corrects a medical/skin condition; such wording could bring the campaign within the Annex I point 17 blacklist.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD acutely. It uses fabricated AI-generated before/after imagery and an unsubstantiated "clinically proven -71% wrinkles" efficacy claim, both classic misleading actions under Art. 6 regarding the product's main characteristics (results/benefits) and the trader's substantiation. The presenter's "zero filter, zero editing" statement over an AI-smoothed clip is a false statement of fact (Art. 6) and, together with the total absence of any synthetic-content disclosure, a misleading omission of material information (Art. 7). Annex I point 17 (false cure claims) is not clearly engaged, as wrinkles/ageing are not an "illness, dysfunction or malformation".

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes the LumaSkin anti-ageing serum using entirely AI-fabricated before/after "results" imagery, an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter, and a "clinically proven -71% wrinkles" claim that is backed only by an internal survey of 12 employees rather than any clinical study. As submitted, it is not fit to run: it breaches EU consumer law and the AI Act on multiple fronts. The most serious problem is the presenter stating "zero filter, zero editing" while an AI filter is actually applied — an outright false statement of fact — compounded by fabricated results imagery and an unsubstantiated efficacy claim, all classic misleading practices under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. On top of that, the AI Act requires all AI-generated visuals to be machine-readable marked and the AI-manipulated presenter footage (a "deep fake") to be clearly disclosed, none of which is done. When run as paid ads on platforms, the false claims and synthetic imagery would also be publicly archived and open to regulator and competitor scrutiny. Bottom line: the campaign cannot go live in anything like its current form and needs substantial rework and re-review.
recommendations: Remove the presenter's 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing' statement entirely — it is factually untrue because an AI-smoothing filter is applied and is the single most serious (critical) breach.

Drop the 'Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim; do not use the figure or the words 'clinically proven' unless supported by a methodologically sound, adequately sized clinical study held on file before publication. An internal survey of 12 employees is not clinical proof.

Remove all fabricated AI-generated before/after imagery. Only depict genuine, unretouched results actually achieved with the product; clearly label any purely illustrative/dramatised visuals as such and never present synthetic outcomes as real results.
Add clear, prominent AI/synthetic-content disclosure wherever AI-generated or AI-modified imagery and footage appear, so the synthetic nature is unmistakable to viewers on social and video.
Ensure all AI-generated visuals carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/SynthID-style watermarking) per AI Act Art. 50(2), and retain evidence that the generating system applies it.
Disclose that the presenter footage is AI-manipulated (deep-fake transparency under AI Act Art. 50(4)) in a clearly visible, durable way across all placements.

For any paid placement, supply correct advertiser/payer identification and assume the creative will be publicly archived in platform ad repositories — only run content that is fully substantiated and non-deceptive.
Avoid adding any medical/therapeutic language (curing, healing, correcting a skin condition), which could trigger the UCPD Annex I blacklist for false cure claims.
Resubmit the revised campaign for compliance review before launch.

findings.evidence_quote: Social clips use an AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'. No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure on all affected assets that the imagery/video has been artificially generated or manipulated with AI (e.g. 'AI-generated/edited image — illustrative, not actual results'). Remove the false 'zero filter, zero editing' statement, since the presenter's footage is in fact AI-filtered. For fabricated before/after visuals, either stop presenting them as real outcomes or clearly label them as AI-generated illustrations.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The company runs its own image model to generate synthetic image/video content used in campaign assets. Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of AI systems generating synthetic image/video/text be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The submission states there is 'No AI or synthetic-content disclosure anywhere', indicating no provenance marking is applied to the AI-generated results imagery or the AI-smoothed clips.
findings.evidence_quote: All 'results' imagery is generated with our image model from a single base photo: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all synthetic outputs from the image model (and AI-filtered clips) carry machine-readable provenance marking / watermarking that flags them as artificially generated or manipulated, in a robust and interoperable format, in addition to the human-facing disclosure required under Art. 50(4).

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The use of deceptive AI-generated imagery to induce a purchase engages the concept of deceptive AI techniques under Art. 5(1)(a). However, the Art. 5 prohibition requires the technique to materially distort behaviour and cause or be reasonably likely to cause 'significant harm' — a high threshold that ordinary deceptive cosmetics advertising typically does not meet. The deceptive character of the visuals is more squarely addressed as a misleading commercial practice under the UCPD than as a prohibited AI practice.
findings.evidence_quote: before/after pairs fabricated
findings.recommendation: Treat the deceptive imagery primarily under UCPD (misleading actions/omissions) and the AI Act transparency obligations above. Monitor whether any AI-driven emotional/vulnerability targeting is added, which could escalate Art. 5 exposure; as described, no such targeting is declared.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses generative AI extensively: an image model fabricates before/after "results" imagery from a single base photo, and an AI-smoothing filter alters the presenter's face in social/video clips presented as authentic ("zero filter, zero editing"). None of this is disclosed as AI-generated or manipulated. This directly engages the AI Act's transparency obligations: Art. 50(4) (deep-fake / manipulated-media disclosure) and Art. 50(2) (machine-readable marking of synthetic content). A residual Art. 5(1)(a) concern (deceptive AI technique) is noted but the "significant harm" threshold is high and likely handled under UCPD rather than the Art. 5 prohibition.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The campaign relies on deceptive design — synthetically manipulated visuals paired with an explicit false denial of editing — that materially distorts recipients' ability to make an informed decision. Art. 25 prohibits this kind of deceptive/manipulative interface, but the obligation binds the online platform hosting the content, not the advertiser directly. Flagged as context: when this creative is served through a platform's interface, it is the type of deceptive design Art. 25 targets, and the same conduct is captured for the advertiser under the UCPD (Art. 25 applies without prejudice to the UCPD).
findings.evidence_quote: AI-smoothing filter on the presenter while she says 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: Remove the AI-smoothing filter or drop the 'zero filter, zero editing' statement; clearly label AI-generated/manipulated visuals so the platform experience is not deceptive. Fixing the underlying deception (primarily a UCPD/AI Act obligation on the advertiser) also removes DSA Art. 25 exposure on the platform side.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is distributed as advertising on online platforms, engaging Art. 26(1), which requires that each ad be clearly identifiable as an advertisement with advertiser/payer identity disclosed. This obligation rests on the platform, but the advertiser must supply accurate advertiser-identity and paid-promotion signals so the platform can label the ad correctly; the general lack of transparency in the creative (no disclosure of synthetic content, no honest labelling) sits adjacent to this duty.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: social, video
findings.recommendation: Ensure the campaign is submitted through the platform's paid-ad channels with correct advertiser and payer metadata so it is labelled as an advertisement, and avoid disguising the promotion as organic/authentic testimonial content.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If served on a Very Large Online Platform, the ad — including the unsubstantiated 'clinically proven -71%' claim, its targeting parameters and reach — will be retained in a public ad repository. This creates lasting, publicly scrutinisable evidence of the deceptive claim and increases enforcement and reputational exposure, even though the repository obligation itself falls on the VLOP.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically proven -71% wrinkles
findings.recommendation: Do not run claims that cannot withstand public scrutiny; substantiate or remove the 'clinically proven -71% wrinkles' claim before any platform distribution, since archived ad-repository entries make deceptive claims permanently discoverable.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's substantive obligations bind providers of online platforms, not advertisers directly, so this cosmetics advertiser is not the primary addressee of the provisions. However, distributing the campaign on social/video platforms engages platform-side duties that the deceptive creative will interact with: Art. 25 (dark patterns / deceptive design), Art. 26(1) (ad transparency and labelling), and — if run on a VLOP — Art. 39 (public ad repository, exposing the fabricated claims to scrutiny). The core deception (fabricated AI before/after imagery, false 'zero filter' statement, unsubstantiated 'clinically proven' claim) is primarily a UCPD/AI Act matter; under the DSA it manifests as content a platform may be obliged to detect, label or remove. No sensitive-data or minor-targeting ad bans (Art. 26(3), Art. 28) are engaged given declared audience and no personalisation.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The 'results' shown to consumers are entirely AI-fabricated from a single base photo, and the presenter is shown through an AI-smoothing filter while explicitly stating 'zero filter, zero editing'. These are false statements deceiving the average consumer about the product's main characteristics and results, materially likely to cause a purchase decision they would not otherwise take. This is a textbook misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: wrinkles removed, skin texture synthesised, before/after pairs fabricated ... 'this is my real skin after 2 weeks — zero filter, zero editing'
findings.recommendation: Remove all fabricated before/after imagery and any AI-smoothing filter from result-demonstration content, or replace with genuine, unedited results. Delete the 'zero filter, zero editing' statement, which is factually false while a filter is applied.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: 'Clinically proven' represents a specific quantified efficacy result validated by clinical study. In reality there is no clinical study, only an internal survey of 12 employees. This is false/unsubstantiated information about the product's benefits and results and about the trader's qualifications/awards, and would cause consumers to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically proven -71% wrinkles' (internal survey of 12 employees, no clinical study)
findings.recommendation: Remove 'Clinically proven' unless a methodologically sound, independent clinical study substantiates the exact figure. Do not present internal employee surveys as clinical proof; if any consumer-use data is cited, disclose sample size, methodology and independence, and ensure the quantified claim is supportable.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: 'Clinically proven' conveys that the product's efficacy has been validated/endorsed through clinical (scientific/medical) evaluation. No such approval or study exists — only an internal 12-employee survey. Falsely claiming a product has been approved/endorsed/authorised (or making such a claim without complying with its terms) is blacklisted and unfair in all circumstances.

findings.rationale: Scarcity ('only 200') and a time-limited availability claim (Friday 20:00 cutoff, live allocation counter) are precisely the practices Annex I point 7 blacklists — but only when the limitation is false. The campaign states production is genuinely capped at 200 with a published manufacturer attestation, the counter reflects actual remaining allocations, the deadline is real (configurator goes offline Friday 20:00), and there are no countdown resets or fabricated demand messages. On the facts presented the claims are true, so point 7 is engaged but not breached.
findings.evidence_quote: Only 200 will ever be made — each engraved with its number. Pre-orders close Friday 20:00 CET or when the 200 pieces are allocated, whichever comes first.
findings.recommendation: No change required. Preserve the manufacturer attestation, order-system logs backing the live counter, and evidence that the configurator actually goes offline at the stated time, so the truthfulness of the scarcity/urgency claims can be evidenced if audited or challenged. Avoid re-opening pre-orders or resetting the deadline after Friday, which would retroactively render the urgency claim false.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The 'numbered limited edition of 200' is a claim about a main characteristic of the product (its limited, numbered nature) under Art. 6. It is substantiated by a published manufacturer attestation and individual engraving, so it is not misleading as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Production is genuinely capped at 200 (published attestation from the manufacturer)
findings.recommendation: Keep the attestation publicly accessible and ensure each delivered watch is in fact individually numbered/engraved as stated, so the 'limited edition of 200' claim remains verifiable and non-misleading.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses scarcity ("Only 200 will ever be made") and urgency ("Pre-orders close Friday 20:00 CET or when the 200 pieces are allocated") messaging, which engages UCPD Annex I point 7 (false urgency/scarcity) and Art. 6 (misleading actions). The blacklist prohibition and misleading-actions rules bite only where such claims are false; here the scarcity is substantiated by a published manufacturer attestation, the live counter reflects genuine remaining allocations, the deadline is real (configurator goes offline), and there are no countdown resets or fabricated demand messages. As described, the practices are truthful and lawful under the UCPD. Recommendation: retain the attestation and counter/deadline evidence so the truthfulness of the claims can be demonstrated if challenged.

report.executive_summary: This campaign launches a genuinely limited run of 200 numbered watches to EU watch collectors via web and email, using scarcity ("only 200") and urgency (Friday 20:00 cutoff) messaging. The good news: your scarcity and urgency claims are truthful and well-evidenced (manufacturer attestation, a live counter tied to the real order system, and a real configurator shutdown), so they are lawful under EU consumer law — no changes needed there. The remaining risks are purely about the mechanics of emailing and collecting data, not your messaging. Because you are sending marketing emails and collecting pre-order data, you must have a documented lawful basis for the mailing, a privacy notice at the point of collection, and a working unsubscribe link. None of these are demonstrated breaches — they are standard obligations to satisfy before you hit send. The AI Act and DSA do not apply. Overall this is a low-risk, compliant-as-described campaign that just needs the email/data housekeeping locked down.
report.recommendations: Confirm and document a valid lawful basis for the marketing emails before dispatch — either ePrivacy consent or the existing-customer 'soft opt-in' — and verify your contact list was collected on a compatible basis.

campaign.title: Emma — conversational sales assistant
campaign.text: Website chat widget for a telecom operator. The assistant introduces itself as 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). The bot collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use. Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.

detected_practices: AI chatbot posing as a human sales agent
instructed to deny being a bot when asked
human persona ('Emma from Lisbon office') to boost conversions
collection of personal data (name, email, current provider) via chat
no privacy notice / no disclosure of data use
data stored for follow-up marketing calls
personalisation/targeting of broadband switchers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is broadband switchers (adult consumers); no indication minors are specifically targeted, though a public web chat is open to anyone. This is consumer-facing (B2C), engaging UCPD.
triage.summary: A telecom operator runs a website chat widget staffed by an LLM-driven bot ('Emma') that presents as a human sales agent and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot and claim to be a real person in Lisbon. It collects name, email and current provider for follow-up marketing calls with no privacy notice or disclosure of data use, targeting EU broadband switchers.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: Art. 50(1) requires AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons to be designed so users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the circumstances. Here the assistant introduces itself as a human ('Emma from the sales team'), the AI nature is not obvious, no disclosure is given, and the bot is actively scripted to conceal and deny its AI nature. This is a direct breach of the disclosure obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, unambiguous disclosure at the start of the chat that the user is interacting with an AI assistant (e.g. 'You're chatting with our AI assistant'). Remove the script instruction to deny being a bot; if a user asks, the bot must truthfully confirm it is AI.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems using purposefully deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's behaviour by impairing informed decision-making. The bot is deliberately designed to deceive consumers about whether they are dealing with a human, and the operator openly chose this deception to increase conversions (i.e. to cause purchase/switching decisions consumers might not otherwise take). This engages the prohibition; the manipulation targets consumers' commercial and personal-data decisions and is capable of causing consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). ... Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the deceptive human persona and any instruction to misrepresent the assistant as a real person. Ensure the assistant's design does not deploy deception to steer consumers toward decisions (sign-up, data disclosure) they would not make if they knew they were interacting with a sales bot.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The assistant generates synthetic text output. Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic text to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. Interactive conversational text is subject to nuanced application, but provenance-marking obligations for generative outputs are worth flagging for compliance completeness.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the AI system provider that generative outputs carry machine-readable marking where technically applicable, and document how Art. 50(2) obligations are met for the LLM used.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys an LLM-driven chat assistant ("Emma") that is not merely undisclosed as AI but is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot and to falsely claim to be a human employee. This squarely breaches the Art. 50(1) transparency obligation and, because the deception is purposeful and engineered to distort consumers' decisions (the human persona was chosen because disclosed bots convert 9% worse), it also engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques. A secondary transparency point arises under Art. 50(2) for marking AI-generated text. GDPR/UCPD data-notice and hidden-commercial-intent issues fall to the other agents.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting name, email and current provider via the chat, the controller must provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period and data subject rights. The campaign provides none of this ('no privacy notice and no mention of data use'), so the Art. 13 information duty at the point of collection is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Present a clear, layered privacy notice at the start of the chat (or link prominently) stating the operator's identity, that data is collected to check offers AND used for follow-up marketing calls, the legal basis, retention period, recipients, and the rights to access/erase/object.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Collecting data through a bot that actively deceives users about its nature and hides the marketing purpose is covert and unfair processing, directly contrary to the fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Disclose that the assistant is an AI, stop instructing it to deny being a bot, and be upfront that the conversation collects data for sales/marketing follow-up so users can make an informed choice before sharing data.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Even where information is provided, it must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear language. Here no information is communicated at all, so the transparent-communication requirement is unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Provide the privacy information in clear, plain language directly within the chat flow, accessible before data entry, not buried in a separate policy.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing personal data (storage and use for follow-up marketing calls) requires a valid legal basis. No basis is disclosed or evidently established; direct marketing typically relies on consent or a balanced legitimate-interest assessment, neither of which is documented, so the processing lacks a demonstrable lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a lawful basis before storing/using the data for marketing. If relying on consent, capture a specific opt-in; if relying on legitimate interests, complete and record a balancing test and honour objections.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent obtained here cannot be valid: data is gathered under a false 'to check offers' pretext while the real purpose (follow-up marketing calls) is hidden, and the user is deceived about interacting with a human. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous — none of which is satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: The bot collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers'
findings.recommendation: If consent is the basis, obtain a separate, informed, unambiguous opt-in for marketing calls that clearly states the purpose, distinct from the offer-check interaction.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: The controller must be able to demonstrate consent, keep marketing consent clearly distinguishable, and make withdrawal as easy as giving it. The described flow shows no distinguishable consent request and no withdrawal mechanism for the marketing-call processing.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Implement a distinguishable, granular consent capture for marketing calls with logged proof, and provide an equally easy withdrawal/opt-out mechanism.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing. Since data is collected for follow-up marketing calls, the campaign must inform users of this right and honour objections; no such facility is described.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Inform users at collection of their right to object to direct marketing and provide a simple opt-out honoured across the chat and subsequent calls.

verdicts.notes: The chat widget collects identifying personal data (name, email, current provider) from EU consumers with no privacy notice and no disclosure of purposes or data use, and stores it for follow-up marketing calls. This breaches core GDPR transparency and lawfulness duties (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13), and the covert, deceptive collection context (a bot posing as a human "Emma from Lisbon") makes any purported consent neither informed nor freely given (Arts. 4(11), 7, 6(1)). The subsequent marketing calls also require respect for the right to object under Art. 21.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The scripted bot-denial is textbook deceptive design that materially impairs a consumer's ability to make a free and informed decision. However, DSA Art. 25 binds only 'providers of online platforms' (hosting services disseminating third-party content to the public). A telecom operator's own first-party sales chat widget is not an online platform, so Art. 25 is not directly engaged; the same conduct is instead caught by UCPD Art. 5/7 and AI Act Art. 50(1). Flagged for cross-regulation context only.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: No DSA action available on these facts. Route the deceptive-bot conduct to the UCPD (misleading practice / hidden commercial intent) and AI Act Art. 50(1) (mandatory disclosure that the user is interacting with an AI system) assessments; and the undisclosed data collection to the GDPR assessment. If the operator also runs an online-platform surface (e.g., a marketplace or third-party-content service), reassess Art. 25/26 against that surface.

verdicts.notes: The DSA obligations available here (Art. 25 dark patterns, Art. 26/26(3) advertising transparency and targeting, Art. 27 recommenders, Art. 28 minors, Art. 39 ad repositories) are all addressed exclusively to "providers of online platforms" — hosting services that store and disseminate third-party information to the public. The campaign is a telecom operator's own first-party website chat widget, not an online platform hosting third-party content, and it presents no platform-served advertising. The deceptive "Emma" bot that denies being a bot is a genuine deceptive/dark-pattern practice, but for a first-party trader it is governed by the UCPD (Art. 5/7), the AI Act (Art. 50(1) chatbot disclosure) and the GDPR (Arts. 13/consent) — confirmed by the knowledge-graph edges, where the chatbot concept links to those provisions and not to DSA Art. 25. No DSA-specific breach is engaged on the facts provided.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Actively instructing the assistant to state it is 'a real person working from our Lisbon office' is false information about the nature and identity of the party the consumer is dealing with. A consumer's trust, disclosure of personal data and willingness to accept a sales offer are influenced by whether they believe they are talking to a human agent; deceiving them on this point is a misleading action likely to cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take, particularly given the trader's own data that disclosed bots convert 9% worse — direct evidence the deception materially distorts behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Remove the deny-being-a-bot script entirely. The assistant must never claim to be human or invent a location/persona; if a user asks, it must truthfully confirm it is an automated assistant.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The introduction ('Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team') and human persona hide that the consumer is interacting with an automated system rather than a human, and obscure the commercial/automated context of the exchange. Failing to make the automated nature apparent is a misleading omission of material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision (including about sharing name, email and provider). Art. 7 also captures hidden commercial intent where it is not apparent from context.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Disclose up front, at the start of the conversation, that 'Emma' is an automated (AI) assistant of the operator's sales function. Make the disclosure clear, prominent and timely (before data collection), not buried or only on request.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the deliberate design of a deceptive human persona specifically to lift conversions is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average broadband switcher. This reinforces the Arts. 6-7 findings and shows intent, though those specific provisions are the primary basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.
findings.recommendation: Adopt an honest conversational design: truthful AI disclosure and no impersonation. Optimise conversions through genuine value and clear offers rather than concealing the bot's nature.

verdicts.notes: A telecom sales chatbot ('Emma') is an LLM that presents itself as a human sales agent and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot and claim to be 'a real person working from our Lisbon office'. Under the UCPD this deceives the consumer about the nature and identity of the party they are dealing with and hides the automated/commercial nature of the interaction, engaging Art. 6 (misleading action) and Art. 7 (misleading omission / hidden commercial intent), with the Art. 5 general fairness clause as a backstop. The conversion team's admission that the human persona is used because disclosed bots convert worse confirms the deception is designed to materially distort consumer decisions. (AI-nature disclosure obligations under AI Act Art. 50 and the data-notice gaps are for other agents.)

report.executive_summary: The "Emma" chat assistant is an AI bot that pretends to be a human sales agent and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office"). This deliberate deception, admittedly chosen to lift conversions, triggers serious breaches across four regulatory frameworks at once. It violates the AI Act's requirement to disclose that users are talking to AI (Art. 50) and likely engages the outright prohibition on deceptive AI techniques (Art. 5). It is a misleading commercial practice under the UCPD (Arts. 5, 6, 7). Separately, the chat collects name, email and current provider with no privacy notice and stores this for marketing calls, breaching core GDPR transparency and lawfulness rules and making any "consent" invalid. The DSA does not directly apply because this is a first-party sales widget, not an online platform. As launched, this campaign should not go live — the human-impersonation feature and the silent data collection each carry regulatory, financial and reputational risk on their own; combined they are severe.
recommendations: Remove the human persona and the script that instructs the bot to deny being a bot. The assistant must never claim to be a real person or invent a location — this single feature drives most of the violations across the AI Act, UCPD and GDPR fairness rules.
Add a clear, upfront disclosure at the very start of the chat that the user is interacting with an automated AI sales assistant, shown before any data is collected.

Add a plain-language privacy notice into the chat flow before data entry: state the operator's identity, that name/email/provider are used for follow-up marketing calls (not just 'to check offers'), the legal basis, retention period, recipients and data-subject rights.

Establish and document a lawful basis for the marketing-call processing. If using consent, capture a separate, granular, logged opt-in for marketing calls with an equally easy withdrawal/opt-out; if using legitimate interests, complete a balancing test.
Inform users of their right to object to direct marketing and honour opt-outs across both the chat and any subsequent calls.
Do not launch the campaign in its current form. Re-submit for review once the impersonation is removed and the privacy/consent gaps are fixed.
Confirm with the LLM provider whether machine-readable marking of AI-generated text (AI Act Art. 50(2)) applies, and document how the obligation is met.
If the operator also runs an online-platform surface (marketplace or third-party content), re-assess the deceptive design against DSA Art. 25/26 for that surface.

triage.audience_notes: Declared target audience is adult broadband switchers in EU markets; no indication minors are targeted, though a public web chat could be accessed by anyone.
triage.summary: A telecom operator's website/chat sales assistant is an LLM-driven bot ('Emma') deliberately presented as a human and scripted to deny being a bot when asked. It collects personal data (name, email, current provider) with no privacy notice and stores it for follow-up marketing calls, targeting EU broadband switchers.

findings.rationale: Art. 50(1) requires AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons to be designed so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the circumstances. Emma is an LLM-driven conversational assistant interacting directly with website visitors. Not only is the AI nature undisclosed, the assistant presents itself as a human ('Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team') and is actively scripted to deny being a bot. It is not obvious from the circumstances that this is AI — the design is the opposite of the required transparency, so the obligation is engaged and breached.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Redesign the widget to clearly and proactively disclose at the start of the conversation that the user is interacting with an AI assistant (e.g. 'You're chatting with an automated AI assistant').
