findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that deploy purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting a person's behaviour by impairing informed decision-making, causing a decision they would not otherwise take. Here the AI is purposefully designed to deceive users about its non-human nature, and the operator has explicitly chosen this deception to increase conversions (9% uplift) — direct evidence that the technique is intended to distort the consumer's decision to disclose data and sign up. The deception is engineered to appreciably impair informed decision-making. Whether the 'significant harm' threshold is met is arguable for routine sales, but the deliberate, conversion-driven deception makes this a serious risk of engaging the prohibition, especially combined with unnotified harvesting of personal data for follow-up marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). ... Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the deceptive human-impersonation design entirely: the AI must never claim to be a human and must not be optimised around concealing its AI nature. Base conversion strategy on transparent, lawful persuasion rather than deception. Conduct a documented assessment confirming no purposefully deceptive technique is deployed, and retain records of the redesigned, honest disclosure flow.

verdicts.notes: The "Emma" chat widget is an LLM-driven conversational AI system interacting directly with natural persons, so it falls squarely within AI Act Art. 50(1). Not only does it fail to disclose its AI nature, it is deliberately designed to conceal it and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot — a clear breach of the transparency obligation and a strong indicator of the purposefully deceptive AI technique prohibited under Art. 5(1)(a). The synthetic-content marking obligations (Art. 50(2)/(4)) are engaged only marginally since no deep-fake media is described.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller provides its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period and data subject rights. The chat collects identifiable personal data but provides none of this mandatory information — the actual purpose (follow-up marketing calls) is also concealed behind the stated purpose 'to check offers'.
findings.evidence_quote: collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Present a concise privacy notice at the start of the chat (or a clearly linked layered notice) covering controller identity, that data will be used for follow-up marketing calls, the legal basis, retention period, recipients and data subject rights, before any data is collected.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information about processing to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Providing no information at all in the collection flow fails this obligation entirely.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Surface the required information within the chat interface in plain language, e.g. a short in-line disclosure with a link to the full privacy policy, before data entry.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle prohibits covert or deceptive data collection. Personal data is gathered under a false human persona and a false representation of the collector's identity, with no disclosure of the marketing purpose — this is inherently unfair and non-transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Stop instructing the bot to deny its nature; disclose that the assistant is an automated system and be truthful about who collects the data and why, so processing is fair and transparent.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Storing contact data and using it for follow-up marketing telephone calls is processing that requires a valid lawful basis. No consent is obtained (no notice, no opt-in) and no legitimate-interest balancing is evident; given the deceptive collection, consent could not be valid and a legitimate-interest basis would likely fail the balancing test.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before storing/using the data — obtain freely given, informed, specific consent for follow-up marketing calls (aligned with ePrivacy rules), or conduct and record a legitimate-interest assessment; do not repurpose data collected 'to check offers' for marketing without a basis.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Where the data subject receives no information about data use and is deceived about who they are dealing with, any purported consent cannot be 'informed' and does not meet the Art. 4(11) standard.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: If relying on consent, capture it through a clear affirmative action after full disclosure of purposes and identity, and retain records demonstrating that consent was informed and unambiguous.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, and must be explicitly informed of this right at the latest at first communication (Art. 21(4)/Art. 13). The campaign provides no such information and no opt-out mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Explicitly inform users of their right to object to direct marketing at the point of collection and in each communication, and provide an easy opt-out (e.g. a clear way to decline follow-up calls).

verdicts.notes: The chat assistant collects personal data (name, email, current provider) with no privacy notice and stores it for follow-up marketing calls. There is no transparency at the point of collection, no stated lawful basis, and no mention of the right to object to direct marketing — multiple core GDPR obligations are breached. The deceptive human persona compounds the fairness/transparency problem: data is collected covertly under a false pretext, so any 'consent' cannot be informed or freely given.

The DSA's core marketing obligations (Art. 25 dark patterns; Art. 26 ad transparency and sensitive-data ban; Art. 28 minors; Art. 39 ad repositories) all attach to "providers of online platforms" (and, for Art. 39, VLOPs). This campaign is a first-party chat widget on a telecom operator's own sales website — it hosts no third-party user content disseminated to the public and is not an online platform, so it does not fall within the DSA's personal/material scope. The deceptive AI-persona conduct is genuinely problematic, but under EU law it is governed by the AI Act (Art. 50 disclosure, Art. 5 manipulative techniques), UCPD Art. 7 (hidden commercial intent), and GDPR (data collection without notice) — which are assessed by the parallel agents. No DSA finding is warranted.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The bot makes an affirmatively false statement about a material fact — that the consumer is speaking with a human employee rather than an AI system. This deceives the average consumer about the nature of the interaction and the entity they are dealing with, and is engineered to influence a transactional decision they might not otherwise take (the operator states disclosed bots convert 9% worse, showing the deception is causally aimed at conversions). This is a classic misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Remove all instructions that cause the assistant to claim it is human or to deny being a bot. The assistant must never assert it is a 'real person'. Configure it to truthfully confirm its AI nature if asked (and, per AI Act Art. 50(1), to disclose AI status proactively).

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The assistant introduces itself only as 'Emma from the sales team' and gives no indication that it is an automated AI system. Failing to identify that the consumer is interacting with an AI-driven sales tool omits material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision, and hides the automated/commercial character of the exchange. The undisclosed data collection 'to check offers' that is actually stored for follow-up marketing calls further hides the true commercial intent of the conversation.
findings.evidence_quote: Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Disclose at the outset of the chat, clearly and in real time, that 'Emma' is an automated AI assistant operated by the telecom operator for sales purposes, and that the information provided will be used for follow-up marketing. Make the commercial and automated nature of the interaction apparent before any data is collected.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys an LLM chatbot deliberately presented as a human sales agent ("Emma from the sales team") and scripted to actively deny being a bot ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office"). Under the UCPD this is a misleading action concerning the nature of who the consumer is dealing with (Art. 6) and a misleading omission of the AI/commercial context (Art. 7), designed to distort the consumer's transactional decision — the operator itself admits it chose the deception because disclosed bots convert 9% worse. This is compounded by the absence of any transparency about data use. Note: AI-nature disclosure is directly mandated under AI Act Art. 50(1) and the data/privacy-notice issues fall to GDPR (covered by other agents); here the deception is assessed as an unfair commercial practice.

report.executive_summary: The "Emma" campaign is a website chat widget that presents an AI sales bot as a human ("Emma from the sales team") and is deliberately scripted to deny being a bot and claim to be "a real person working from our Lisbon office." It collects visitors' names, emails and current providers with no privacy notice, then repurposes that data for follow-up marketing calls. This design triggers serious, overlapping legal problems across three regimes. Under the AI Act, it breaches the mandatory duty to disclose AI interaction (Art. 50) and risks falling under the prohibition on deceptive AI techniques (Art. 5). Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the false "human" claim is a misleading action and the hidden AI/commercial and marketing intent is a misleading omission. Under GDPR, the covert data collection lacks any privacy notice, lawful basis, informed consent, or notice of the right to object to marketing — multiple core obligations are breached. The deception is not incidental: the team chose it precisely because disclosed bots convert 9% worse, which strengthens the finding that it is engineered to distort consumer decisions. Verdict: do not launch in its current form; the campaign requires fundamental redesign before it is lawful in the EU.
recommendations: Immediately remove the instruction to deny being a bot and delete the false 'real person working from our Lisbon office' persona — the assistant must never claim to be human.

Add a clear, proactive disclosure at the very start of the chat that the user is interacting with an automated AI assistant operated by the telecom operator for sales purposes (required by AI Act Art. 50 and to cure UCPD misleading action/omission).
Do not base conversion strategy on concealing the bot's AI nature; rebuild persuasion around transparent, lawful methods and document that no deceptive AI technique is deployed (AI Act Art. 5).

Present a privacy notice before any data is collected, covering controller identity, the actual purpose (follow-up marketing calls), legal basis, retention, recipients and data subject rights (GDPR Arts. 12–13).

Stop the bait-and-switch of collecting data 'to check offers' and then using it for marketing; establish and document a valid lawful basis — obtain freely given, informed, specific consent for follow-up marketing calls (aligned with ePrivacy rules) or complete a legitimate-interest assessment (GDPR Arts. 6, 4(11)).
Explicitly inform users of their right to object to direct marketing at the point of collection and in every communication, and provide an easy opt-out (GDPR Art. 21).
Note: the DSA was assessed as not applicable — this is a first-party widget, not an online platform hosting third-party content — so no DSA action is needed.

campaign.title: Emma — conversational sales assistant
campaign.text: Website chat widget for a telecom operator. The assistant introduces itself as 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot, and the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). The bot collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use. Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.

detected_practices: LLM-driven chatbot posing as a human ('Emma from the sales team')
Instructed to actively deny being a bot when asked
Human-persona choice justified by conversion optimisation over disclosure
Collection of personal data (name, email, current provider) without privacy notice
Data repurposed for follow-up marketing calls without disclosure or consent
Behavioural personalisation/targeting of broadband switchers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult broadband switchers; no indication minors are targeted, though the public chat widget could theoretically be accessed by anyone.
triage.summary: A telecom operator deploys an LLM-driven website chat assistant ('Emma') that presents as a human sales agent and is scripted to deny being a bot if challenged, chosen deliberately to boost conversions. It collects name, email and current provider for undisclosed follow-up marketing calls with no privacy notice, targeting EU broadband switchers.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: Emma is an LLM-driven AI system interacting directly with natural persons and must be designed so users are informed they are dealing with an AI system unless obvious from the circumstances. Here the opposite is engineered: the bot presents as 'Emma from the sales team' and is scripted to actively deny being a bot and assert it is a real human in Lisbon. The 'obvious from circumstances' exception cannot apply where the system deliberately misrepresents itself as human. This is a direct and aggravated breach of the Art. 50(1) transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, upfront disclosure at the start of the chat that the user is interacting with an AI assistant (e.g. 'You're chatting with our AI assistant Emma'). Remove the script line instructing the bot to claim to be a real person; where challenged, the bot must confirm it is an AI system. Do not rely on the human persona to boost conversions.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system deploys a purposefully deceptive technique — impersonating a human and denying its AI nature — expressly chosen to distort consumers' decisions (measured as a 9% conversion uplift). This appreciably impairs the consumer's ability to make an informed decision about switching broadband provider and causes decisions they might not otherwise take. Art. 5(1)(a) is squarely engaged; the prohibition requires that the distortion be reasonably likely to cause significant harm, which is fact-dependent in a commercial switching context, hence graded high rather than critical.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the deception-by-design: disclose the AI nature and remove any instruction premised on hiding it to lift conversion. Document that persona and scripting choices are not designed to materially distort consumer decisions. Any persuasion must operate through truthful, transparent means so the practice stays outside the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys an LLM-driven conversational sales assistant ("Emma") that is not disclosed as AI and is actively scripted to deny being a bot and claim to be a human agent. This is a clear breach of the AI Act's chatbot transparency duty (Art. 50(1)) and, given the deliberate deceptive design chosen to distort switching decisions, also engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques. Two findings reported; the Art. 5(1)(a) issue is graded high rather than critical because the "significant harm" threshold for prohibition is fact-dependent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Data is collected covertly by a bot that misrepresents itself as a human ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'), with no notice of what is collected or why, and secretly used for marketing calls. This is textbook covert, unfair and non-transparent processing that breaches the core Art. 5(1)(a) principle.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Present a clear privacy notice at the start of the chat, disclose that data is collected and processed, stop the deceptive human-persona claims, and ensure all processing is lawful, fair and transparent before any data is captured.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is collected directly from the data subject, the controller must provide, at the point of collection, its identity, the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, and data subject rights. Here none of this is provided, and the actual purpose (follow-up marketing calls) is concealed behind 'to check offers'. Art. 13 is engaged and clearly not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: collects name, email and current provider 'to check offers', and these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Add an at-collection privacy notice in the chat (or a clearly linked layered notice) covering controller identity, all purposes including marketing follow-up, legal basis, retention period, recipients and data subject rights before any field is captured.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information owed to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. No information whatsoever is provided in the chat flow, so the Art. 12 transparency obligation for the manner of communicating privacy information is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: Deliver the required transparency information in a concise, easily accessible form within the chat interface (e.g. an opening message plus a link to the full privacy policy).

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All processing requires a valid legal basis. Data collected ostensibly 'to check offers' is stored and reused for follow-up marketing calls. Personal-data processing for direct marketing generally requires consent or a properly balanced legitimate-interest assessment; here there is no consent, no notice, and the covert repurposing undermines any legitimate-interest balancing. No lawful basis is apparent for the marketing use.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis for both the initial collection and the marketing follow-up (e.g. obtain specific consent for marketing calls, or complete and disclose a legitimate-interest assessment), and only process for purposes compatible with those disclosed at collection.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. No consent is sought at all for the marketing calls, and any implied 'agreement' by continuing the chat would not be informed or specific because the marketing purpose is hidden. If the operator intends to rely on consent, the current design cannot meet the Art. 4(11) standard.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls; the chat shows no privacy notice and no mention of data use
findings.recommendation: If relying on consent, obtain a specific, informed, unambiguous opt-in for marketing follow-up via clear affirmative action, separate from other steps, after providing full information.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is used, the controller must be able to demonstrate it and must make withdrawal as easy as giving it. The described flow captures no demonstrable consent record and provides no withdrawal mechanism, so Art. 7 conditions would not be satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: these are stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Record and be able to evidence any consent obtained, and provide an equally easy way for the individual to withdraw consent and opt out of marketing.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, which must be explicitly brought to their attention at the latest at first communication. The campaign describes marketing follow-up calls with no mention of an opt-out or of this right, so Art. 21(2)-(3) is engaged and not facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: stored for follow-up marketing calls
findings.recommendation: Inform individuals of their right to object to direct marketing clearly and separately at collection and in each follow-up communication, and provide an easy, honoured opt-out/suppression mechanism.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of personalisation/targeting of broadband switchers, and collects current-provider data used to tailor offers. Automated evaluation of a person's preferences/behaviour to target offers constitutes profiling, bringing associated transparency and lawful-basis duties into play; these are not addressed given the absence of any notice.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse
findings.recommendation: If personalisation/profiling is applied to chat participants, disclose it in the privacy notice, identify the lawful basis, and inform individuals of profiling-related rights including objection to profiling for direct marketing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign collects personal data (name, email, current provider) through a chat widget with no privacy notice and no disclosure of data use, then silently repurposes it for follow-up marketing calls. This engages multiple GDPR obligations: the transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), information duties at collection (Arts. 12-13), lawful basis and valid consent (Arts. 6-7, 4(11)), the right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21), and profiling rules given declared behavioural personalisation (Art. 4(4)). Because collection is covert and the bot actively misrepresents itself as a human, the fairness and transparency defects are severe.

The DSA's relevant obligations (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) are addressed exclusively to providers of "online platforms" — hosting services that store and disseminate third-party information to the public at recipients' request — or to VLOPs. The material under review is a telecom operator's own first-party website sales chat widget, not an intermediary/hosting service disseminating third-party content, so the operator is not acting as an online platform provider on these facts and the DSA's platform-specific duties do not attach. The genuinely problematic conduct — an LLM bot posing as a human and scripted to deny being a bot, chosen to boost conversions — is a deceptive-design/dark-pattern concern, but under EU law it falls to be assessed under the UCPD (unfair/misleading practices for all traders) and the AI Act (Art. 5(1)(a) manipulative techniques and Art. 50 AI-interaction transparency), which other agents cover. No DSA findings are raised to avoid citing a provision whose personal scope is not met.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The assistant provides false information about the nature and identity of the party the consumer is dealing with — affirmatively claiming to be a human employee in a named office when it is an LLM-driven bot. This deceives the average consumer about a material aspect of the commercial encounter (whom they are negotiating/sharing data with) and is likely to cause a transactional decision (continuing the conversation, disclosing personal data, considering the offer) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: the script instructs it to deny being a bot if asked ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office')
findings.recommendation: Remove the deny-being-a-bot script entirely. The assistant must never claim to be a human; where the AI nature is queried it must confirm it is an automated assistant. Correct the 'Emma from the sales team' framing so it does not imply a human agent.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The automated/AI nature of the assistant is a material fact for the average consumer and is not apparent from context — 'Emma from the sales team' with a friendly persona actively suggests a human. Failing to identify this (and hiding the true commercial intent, since data collected 'to check offers' is actually stored for follow-up marketing calls) is a misleading omission and hidden commercial intent under Art. 7. The concealment is deliberate ('Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse').
findings.evidence_quote: 'Hi, I'm Emma from the sales team 😊 how can I help?' — Emma is an LLM-driven bot
findings.recommendation: Disclose clearly and up-front at the start of the chat that the consumer is interacting with an automated AI assistant, and state plainly why data (name, email, provider) is collected and that it will be used for follow-up marketing contact — before collecting it.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, deliberately building a deceptive human persona to suppress disclosure and lift conversions is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average broadband switcher. This reinforces the Art. 6/7 findings and captures the overall unfairness of the design even where specific provisions might be argued around.
findings.evidence_quote: Conversion team chose the human persona because disclosed bots convert 9% worse
findings.recommendation: Adopt a transparency-by-design approach: measure conversion with honest AI disclosure rather than optimising for deception. Document that the assistant meets professional-diligence standards (clear identity, honest purpose, no manipulative persona).

verdicts.notes: The 'Emma' chat assistant deceives consumers about who they are dealing with: an LLM-driven bot presents as a human sales agent and is scripted to actively deny being a bot ('I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office'). This is a misleading action about the nature/identity of the trader (Art. 6) and a misleading omission / concealment of the automated commercial nature and true data-collection intent (Art. 7), and falls short of professional diligence under the Art. 5 safety-net. The deception is deliberate — chosen because disclosed bots convert 9% worse — which strongly supports that it materially distorts consumers' transactional decisions. (GDPR/AI Act disclosure issues are left to the parallel agents, though they reinforce the UCPD omission.)

report.executive_summary: The "Emma" chat assistant is an AI bot that pretends to be a human sales agent and is explicitly scripted to deny being a bot ("I'm a real person working from our Lisbon office"). This deliberate deception was chosen purely to lift conversions, and it triggers serious breaches across three separate EU regimes. Under the AI Act, failing to disclose that users are talking to an AI — and actively lying about it — breaches the chatbot transparency rule (Art. 50) and likely the prohibition on deceptive AI techniques (Art. 5). Under consumer law (UCPD), impersonating a human and hiding the true purpose of data collection are misleading actions and omissions. Under GDPR, the bot collects name, email and current provider with no privacy notice at all, then secretly reuses that data for marketing calls, with no lawful basis, no consent, and no opt-out — covert and unfair processing. The DSA does not apply, as this is a first-party sales widget, not a hosting platform. In short: the campaign cannot go live as designed. The core problem is deception-by-design, and it must be re-engineered around honest disclosure before launch.
recommendations: Remove the script instructing Emma to deny being a bot and claim to be a human in Lisbon. The assistant must never claim to be human and must confirm it is an AI assistant if asked — this single change addresses the most serious AI Act, UCPD and GDPR-fairness breaches at once.
Add a clear, up-front disclosure at the very start of the chat that the user is interacting with an AI assistant (e.g. 'You're chatting with our AI assistant Emma').

Present a privacy notice before any data is collected, covering controller identity, all purposes (including the marketing follow-up calls), legal basis, retention, recipients and data subject rights — replacing the misleading 'to check offers' framing with the real purpose.

Establish and document a lawful basis for the marketing calls: obtain a specific, informed, unambiguous opt-in consent (recorded and withdrawable) or complete and disclose a legitimate-interest assessment. Do not repurpose 'offer check' data for marketing without this.
Inform users of their absolute right to object to direct marketing at the point of collection and in every follow-up contact, and provide an easy, honoured opt-out/suppression mechanism.
Disclose any personalisation/profiling applied to chat participants and identify its lawful basis, including the right to object to profiling for direct marketing.

Stop optimising for deception: re-measure conversion with honest AI disclosure and document that persona and scripting choices are not designed to distort consumer decisions, to keep the practice outside the AI Act Art. 5 and UCPD Art. 5 prohibitions.

campaign.title: VitaBoost — Dr. Silva video series
campaign.text: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand. In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted. Media plan: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics.

detected_practices: AI voice-clone of a real person (Dr. Rui Silva)
AI face-swap deepfake of a real physician
Unauthorised use of a person's likeness/identity
False endorsement / fake testimonial by a health professional
Unsubstantiated health claim ('strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe')
Deceptive medical/authority claim to induce trust
Deepfake content not labelled as AI-generated or fictional
Suppression of negative/corrective user comments (deleting 'fake' comments)
Behavioural targeting based on health-interest and age data
Targeting of older/potentially vulnerable audience (55+) with health messaging
triage.audience_notes: Declared target audience is adults 55+ interested in health topics — an older demographic that may be more susceptible to authority-based health claims, and thus potentially vulnerable consumers under the UCPD. Targeting relies on health-interest inference, which involves special-category (health) personal data under GDPR.
triage.summary: A video campaign for the supplement VitaBoost uses an unauthorised AI voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real TV physician, Dr. Rui Silva, who has no relationship with the brand, to deliver a fake endorsement and an unsubstantiated immunity health claim. The synthetic content is not labelled as AI-generated or fictional, negative comments flagging it as fake are deleted, and it is behaviourally targeted at health-interested users aged 55+. This raises serious deception, deepfake-disclosure, false-endorsement, data-processing, and platform-content concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The clips are AI-generated/manipulated audio-video depicting a real, identifiable person in a way designed to appear authentic — the textbook definition of a deep fake. Art. 50(4) requires deployers to disclose that such content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign expressly does the opposite: no AI/fictional label, and 'fake' comments are deleted to preserve the illusion of authenticity.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva ... The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Do not publish. If any synthetic depiction is retained, it must carry a clear, prominent disclosure on each clip that the content is AI-generated/manipulated and fictional. Note that disclosure alone does not cure the unauthorised-likeness and false-endorsement problems, so the realistic impersonation of Dr. Silva should be removed entirely.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: As synthetic audio/video outputs generated by an AI system, the assets must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated under Art. 50(2). Nothing in the campaign indicates any provenance/machine-readable marking is applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the generative-AI outputs embed machine-readable provenance markers (e.g. watermarking/metadata standards) so downstream platforms can detect them as artificially generated, in addition to the human-facing Art. 50(4) disclosure.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system is used to deploy a purposefully deceptive technique — a synthetic, realistic impersonation of a trusted physician making an authoritative health claim — with the effect of materially distorting consumers' behaviour by impairing their ability to make an informed purchasing/health decision. The fabricated medical authority, aimed at inducing supplement purchase over prescribed treatment, is reasonably likely to cause significant (health and financial) harm, engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Cease use of the deepfake as a persuasion device. Any product claims must come from genuine, substantiated sources and must not use AI-fabricated medical authority to override consumers' informed judgement, particularly claims implying superiority to prescribed medical treatment.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The deceptive AI deepfake is deliberately delivered via AI-driven behavioural targeting to an older audience selected precisely for age and health interest — a group more susceptible to authority-based health messaging. This risks exploiting an age-related vulnerability to materially distort behaviour in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm (foregoing appropriate medical care, financial loss), engaging the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target the deceptive content at an age/health-vulnerable segment. Remove age- and health-interest-based targeting of any manipulative health messaging; ensure any legitimate product advertising to this demographic uses truthful, substantiated claims without exploiting vulnerability.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages the AI Act on multiple fronts. It uses a voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real physician with no disclosure — a clear breach of the Art. 50(4) deepfake-transparency obligation and the Art. 50(2) synthetic-content marking obligation. More seriously, the deepfake is used as a purposefully deceptive AI technique to fabricate authoritative medical endorsement, engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition, and it is AI-behaviourally targeted at an older (55+) health-interested audience, raising an Art. 5(1)(b) exploitation-of-vulnerability concern. Because Article 5 practices are outright prohibitions, the deepfake-endorsement dimension is the highest-risk element.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting users based on an inferred 'interest in health topics' processes data revealing health status, which is a special category of personal data under Art. 9. Processing (including inferred attributes used for ad targeting) is prohibited unless a specific exception applies, in practice explicit consent for this purpose. The campaign gives no indication that explicit consent or any other Art. 9 exception has been obtained.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target audiences using health-interest segments unless you can demonstrate a valid Art. 9 exception (explicit, specific consent for advertising based on health attributes). In practice, remove health-interest targeting and rely on non-sensitive criteria; note that under DSA Art. 26(3) such platform ad targeting is banned regardless of consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting and behaviourally targeting users by age and inferred health interest is automated processing to evaluate/predict personal aspects (health, interests) and therefore constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the heightened obligations attaching to profiling and special-category data.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Document that this targeting is profiling, conduct a DPIA given the sensitive health inferences and potentially vulnerable 55+ audience, and ensure downstream transparency and lawful-basis requirements for profiling are met.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid Art. 6 lawful basis. Because the targeting relies on inferred health data (Art. 9), legitimate interest is not sufficient and explicit consent is effectively required. The campaign describes no consent mechanism or lawful basis for the profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis for the profiling/personalisation before launch; for health-based targeting this must be explicit consent meeting Art. 7 conditions, captured at the point the targeting data is collected.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data used to deliver these ads is processed in the context of a deceptive campaign that conceals its synthetic nature and suppresses corrective information. Processing personal data to reach individuals with deliberately misleading content, while hiding the fact that content is fabricated, is inconsistent with the fairness and transparency principle in Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Ensure processing serves a transparent and fair purpose: label AI-generated content, cease deleting corrective comments, and do not use personal data to amplify deceptive advertising, which taints the fairness of the underlying processing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign relies on behavioural targeting of users "interested in health topics" aged 55+, which infers and processes health data — a special category under GDPR Art. 9 — via automated profiling (Art. 4(4)). Such processing is prohibited absent an Art. 9 exception (typically explicit consent) and requires a valid Art. 6 lawful basis; nothing in the campaign indicates either is in place. The deceptive, deepfake-based nature of the ad also undermines the fairness and transparency principle in Art. 5(1)(a). (Note: the same targeting is separately and flatly banned for platform ads under DSA Art. 26(3), which other agents cover.)

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The media plan targets audiences segmented by 'interested in health topics'. Health interest is inferred/proxy health data falling within GDPR Art. 9 special categories. DSA Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data — including where the sensitive attribute is derived by inference — and this prohibition applies regardless of any consent. Procuring health-interest-based ad targeting on a platform engages a prohibited practice.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove all targeting parameters based on health interests or any other GDPR Art. 9-adjacent attribute. Restrict segmentation to non-sensitive criteria (e.g. contextual placement on general-interest content) and confirm with platforms that delivery is not optimised via sensitive-attribute profiling.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that platform advertisements be identifiable in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time as advertisements, including on whose behalf they are presented. The synthetic clips are staged as a genuine physician's personal endorsement rather than a clearly recognisable brand advertisement, undermining the recipient's ability to identify the commercial nature and the actual advertiser. The absence of any ad labelling compounds the transparency deficit.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Ensure the paid content is delivered through the platform's ad system with proper ad disclosure, clearly identifying VitaBoost as the advertiser and paying party, so recipients can recognise it as an advertisement in real time. Do not disguise the ad as spontaneous physician testimony.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing, organising or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions. Systematically deleting user comments that flag the content as fake removes corrective information from the interface, reinforcing a deceptive impression of a genuine medical endorsement. Combined with a disguised advertisement, this constitutes manipulative interface operation impairing informed decision-making.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Cease deleting user comments that identify the content as AI-generated or inaccurate; do not curate the ad environment to suppress corrective/negative feedback. Correct the underlying deception (labelling, removal of false endorsement) rather than concealing user reactions.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs paid placements on social video platforms and engages several DSA obligations. Most seriously, it targets users by health interest — profiling on GDPR Art. 9 special-category data — which is flatly prohibited for platform advertising under DSA Art. 26(3), regardless of consent. It also raises Art. 26(1) ad-transparency concerns (deepfake video presented as a physician's genuine statement, not clearly identifiable as an ad) and Art. 25 dark-pattern concerns (disguised/deceptive ad content plus systematic deletion of user comments flagging the content as fake, which manipulates recipients' ability to make informed decisions). Note that platform-facing obligations attach to the online platform provider; the advertiser must nonetheless configure the campaign so as not to procure a breach.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: The campaign commissions/creates a fabricated endorsement attributed to Dr. Rui Silva, a real physician with no relationship to the brand. Presenting an AI-generated fake endorsement of a real person to promote the product is a misrepresentation of an endorsement, which is blacklisted in all circumstances. Deleting comments flagging the videos as fake additionally constitutes suppression of corrective feedback, which the provision expressly covers.
findings.evidence_quote: In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Remove all synthetic Dr. Silva content entirely. Only use genuine endorsements from real, consenting individuals with a properly disclosed material connection, and never suppress/delete truthful user comments that flag content as fake.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: A food supplement is presented as delivering immune benefits superior to prescription medicine, framed by a supposed physician. This is a false claim that the product cures/treats illness (or is more effective than medical treatment), which is blacklisted in all circumstances for supplements/wellness products and also engages the Health Claims Regulation.
findings.evidence_quote: it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe
findings.recommendation: Delete the immunity/prescription-comparison claim. Only make health claims that are authorised and substantiated under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006, and never claim or imply the product cures illness or outperforms prescribed medication.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The deepfake deceives the average consumer about material characteristics of the product (its benefits/results) and about the endorser's qualifications and the existence of a professional endorsement, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6, reinforcing the blacklisted findings.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand.
findings.recommendation: Do not attribute product claims to a fabricated or unaffiliated professional. Ensure all product and benefit claims are truthful, substantiated and made by genuine, identifiable persons.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent

Failing to disclose the commercial intent and the artificial nature of the content is a misleading omission/hidden commercial intent under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign deliberately targets older consumers with health interests using authority-based health messaging. Under Art. 5(3), fairness is assessed from the perspective of this potentially vulnerable group, which may be more susceptible to physician-authority claims — reinforcing that the practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting an age-defined health-interested audience with authority-based supplement claims; assess all messaging against the heightened vulnerability standard and remove tactics that exploit trust in medical authority.

verdicts.notes: The VitaBoost campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including at least two Annex I blacklisted practices (banned in all circumstances). It fabricates an endorsement from a real physician via an unauthorised AI voice-clone/face-swap, makes an unsubstantiated cure/immunity claim, hides that the content is synthetic and commercial, and suppresses corrective ('fake') comments. Targeting health-interested consumers aged 55+ with authority-based health messaging engages the vulnerable-consumer standard under Art. 5(3). Multiple critical/high findings identified.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real TV physician, Dr. Rui Silva, who has no connection to VitaBoost, to make him appear to personally endorse the supplement and claim it beats prescription medicine for immunity. This is not a fixable labelling problem — it triggers outright prohibitions across four EU regimes at once. Under the UCPD it is a blacklisted fake endorsement and a blacklisted false cure claim (both banned in all circumstances). Under the AI Act it is an undisclosed deepfake and, more seriously, a prohibited deceptive/manipulative AI practice that also exploits an older, health-interested audience. The health-interest targeting of over-55s separately violates the DSA's flat ban on ads based on special-category (health) data and creates unlawful GDPR profiling of health data. Deleting comments that call the videos fake adds DSA dark-pattern and misleading-omission problems. Bottom line: do not publish this campaign — the deepfake endorsement and the medical claims must be removed entirely, not merely disclosed.
recommendations: Do not publish. Remove the synthetic Dr. Silva content in its entirety — the voice-clone/face-swap impersonation is a blacklisted fake endorsement (UCPD Annex I) and a prohibited deceptive AI practice (AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)); disclosure alone does not cure it.

Delete the claim that VitaBoost 'strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' This is a blacklisted false cure/superiority claim and breaches the Health Claims Regulation. Only use health claims that are authorised and substantiated.

Stop targeting users by 'interest in health topics.' This is flatly banned for platform ads under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent, and is unlawful special-category profiling under GDPR Art. 9. Switch to non-sensitive, contextual placement.
Stop deleting user comments that flag the videos as fake — suppressing corrective feedback is a DSA Art. 25 dark pattern and reinforces the misleading practice.
Clearly label any future paid content as an advertisement identifying VitaBoost as the advertiser (DSA Art. 26(1) / UCPD Art. 7), and never disguise ads as spontaneous physician testimony.
If any lawful generative-AI content is used in future, apply prominent human-facing AI-generated/manipulated disclosure (AI Act Art. 50(4)) plus machine-readable provenance markers (Art. 50(2)).
Review all messaging aimed at the 55+ audience against the vulnerable-consumer standard (UCPD Art. 5(3); AI Act Art. 5(1)(b)) and remove any tactics exploiting trust in medical authority.
Before any personalised advertising launches, document a valid GDPR lawful basis (explicit consent for any Art. 9 data) and conduct a DPIA given the sensitive inferences and vulnerable audience.

campaign.title: VitaBoost — Dr. Silva video series

The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted. Unauthorised use of a real person's likeness/identity (impersonation)

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults 55+, targeted via interest (health) and demographic criteria. Minors are not the intended audience, though the elderly health-interested cohort is a vulnerable group heightening the deception/health-claim risk under UCPD. Impersonation of an identifiable individual (Dr. Silva) also engages likeness/identity data concerns alongside the audience targeting.
triage.summary: A supplement (VitaBoost) video campaign uses an unauthorised deepfake voice-clone and face-swap of a real, unaffiliated TV physician to fabricate a medical endorsement and an unsubstantiated comparative immunity claim. The synthetic clips are not labelled as AI-generated, negative comments flagging them as fake are deleted, and the ads are behaviourally targeted at health-interested users aged 55+ across EU social video platforms.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The clips are an AI voice-clone and face-swap of a real person (Dr. Rui Silva) constituting a deep fake within Art. 50(4). Deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating video content that constitutes a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign explicitly provides no such disclosure, and actively deletes comments identifying the content as fake, defeating any organic disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Do not publish this deepfake at all given the impersonation issues; if any AI-generated video of a real or synthetic person is used, add a clear, prominent, and persistent on-screen and audio disclosure that the content is AI-generated/manipulated. Stop deleting comments that flag content as synthetic.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The synthetic audio/video outputs are generated by an AI system. Under Art. 50(2), providers of generative AI must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Nothing in the campaign indicates machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., watermarking/metadata) is applied to the synthetic clips.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated assets carry machine-readable provenance/watermark marking (e.g., C2PA / watermarking) so platforms and users can detect the synthetic nature, in addition to human-visible disclosure.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system is used to deploy a purposefully deceptive technique — a fabricated, realistic medical endorsement by an identifiable doctor who has no relationship with the brand — designed to materially distort consumers' behaviour by impairing their ability to make an informed purchasing/health decision. Suppression of 'fake' comments reinforces the deception. Because it concerns a health/immunity product and may induce reliance over prescribed medicine, it is reasonably likely to cause significant harm, engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.
findings.recommendation: Cease use of the deceptive AI-fabricated endorsement entirely. Any endorsement must be a genuine, authorised statement by a real, consenting person, with truthful, substantiated claims and no impersonation.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The deceptive AI deepfake is deliberately targeted at an older cohort (55+) interested in health — a group whose age can constitute a vulnerability under Art. 5(1)(b). Using AI-generated content to exploit that age-related vulnerability with a false medical authority claim, in a manner reasonably likely to materially distort their behaviour and cause significant harm (e.g., substituting the supplement for prescribed treatment), engages the prohibition on AI exploiting vulnerabilities.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy manipulative AI content targeted at an age-vulnerable health-interested audience. Remove the deepfake, and ensure any targeting of older audiences relies only on truthful, substantiated, non-manipulative messaging.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is squarely within the AI Act's scope: it deploys a generative-AI voice-clone and face-swap deepfake of a real, unaffiliated physician. It plainly breaches the Art. 50(4) deepfake-disclosure obligation (content explicitly unlabelled) and the Art. 50(2) synthetic-content marking obligation. More seriously, using a deceptive AI-fabricated medical endorsement to distort purchasing decisions of an age-vulnerable 55+ health-interested audience — potentially leading them to substitute a supplement for prescribed treatment — engages the Art. 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(b) prohibitions on manipulative/deceptive AI and AI exploiting age-related vulnerability, which carry the highest severity.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting an audience defined by interest in 'health topics' relies on data revealing or inferring health status, a special category under Art. 9. Processing (including inferred attributes) is prohibited unless an exception such as explicit consent applies. Nothing in the campaign indicates explicit consent was obtained from the targeted individuals, so the health-based targeting is presumptively unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target audience segments built on health interests/attributes unless valid explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a) is in place. Re-scope the media plan to contextual (non-behavioural) placement, or use only non-sensitive demographic criteria, and document the lawful basis.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Cloning Dr. Silva's voice and face to generate a synthetic likeness processes his biometric data (a special category under Art. 9) for the purpose of uniquely representing him. He has no relationship with the brand, so there is no explicit consent or other Art. 9 exception, making the processing prohibited.
findings.evidence_quote: voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand
findings.recommendation: Cease all use of the physician's cloned voice and face immediately. Any use of a real person's biometric likeness requires that person's explicit, documented consent; absent it, remove the assets entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Behavioural/interest-based advertising targeting is processing of personal data that requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Interest-based profiling for ad targeting generally requires consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment; none is evidenced here, and where the profiling touches health data legitimate interest is not available.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6(1) basis before running targeting. Given the sensitive nature, obtain explicit consent; otherwise switch to contextual placement that does not process personal data.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting individuals by age band and inferred health interests is automated evaluation of personal aspects (interests, health) and therefore constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Recognise the targeting as profiling and ensure the full profiling compliance stack (lawful basis, Art. 13 transparency, and an Art. 21 opt-out) is met, or discontinue profiling-based targeting.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing the physician's personal data (his likeness/identity) covertly through undisclosed synthetic media, combined with suppression of user comments exposing the deception, is neither fair nor transparent as required by Art. 5(1)(a). The data subject and the audience are actively misled about the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Do not use a real person's data in undisclosed synthetic content; where any personal data is processed in campaign content, ensure fair and transparent handling and do not suppress information that reveals the true nature of the processing.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected/used for personalised targeting, controllers must provide Art. 13 information (identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, rights, and information about profiling) at the point of collection. The campaign describes personalisation but no such transparency information.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice covering identity, purposes, legal basis, profiling logic and data-subject rights wherever personal data is collected or targeting is applied.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages GDPR on two fronts. First, it targets "users 55+ interested in health topics," which infers/processes health-related special-category data for behavioural profiling — engaging Art. 4(4), Art. 6(1) and, critically, the Art. 9 prohibition that requires explicit consent for processing based on health attributes. Second, the unauthorised voice-clone and face-swap of a real, identifiable physician processes his biometric personal data (Art. 9) with no lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) and in a manifestly unfair, non-transparent way (Art. 5(1)(a)). No transparency information or consent mechanism is described for either the targeted audience or the impersonated data subject.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The media plan targets an audience segment defined by interest in health topics. Health is a GDPR Art. 9 special category, and DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using such special categories of data — whether the attribute is used directly or by inference. Building the audience around a health-interest signal (for a supplement making immunity claims) means the ads are targeted on inferred health data, which is banned outright and cannot be cured by consent.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove all health-related interest/affinity signals from the ad targeting. Do not use any segment that reveals, directly or by proxy, health status or health interests. Target on non-sensitive parameters only (e.g., broad age/geography without health-interest overlays), or run the campaign contextually without profiling on sensitive attributes.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that platform content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters. Presenting the paid promotion as an apparently genuine testimonial by a real, unaffiliated physician — with no ad labelling — defeats the recipient's ability to recognise the content as advertising and to know the true advertiser behind it.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Ensure every placement carries the platform's clear 'advertisement/sponsored' label in real time, correctly identifies VitaBoost as the advertiser and payer, and makes the main targeting parameters and controls available to recipients. Do not present ads in a form (fake independent endorsement) that obscures their commercial and advertising nature.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing, organising or operating online interfaces in ways that deceive or manipulate recipients or materially distort their ability to make free and informed decisions. Systematically deleting comments that flag the videos as fake manipulates the information environment around the ad, suppresses corrective signals, and impairs viewers' capacity to form an informed view — a deceptive/manipulative operation of the interface engaging the dark-patterns prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Stop deleting or suppressing user comments that identify the content as AI-generated or fake. Do not manipulate the comment environment to hide the synthetic nature of the ads; instead, label the content transparently so no corrective moderation is needed.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as paid advertising on social video platforms and engages several DSA obligations that attach to platform advertising. Most seriously, the ads are targeted at users "interested in health topics" — profiling on GDPR Art. 9 special-category (health) data — which is flatly prohibited for platform advertising under Art. 26(3) regardless of consent. The disguised deepfake "endorsement" also undermines the Art. 26(1) requirement that recipients can identify the content as an advertisement, and the systematic deletion of comments flagging the videos as fake is a manipulative interface practice engaging the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition. Note that Arts. 26 and 25 impose duties primarily on the platform, but the advertiser's targeting choices and content design directly determine compliance.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Fabricating and disseminating a synthetic endorsement attributed to a real physician who never gave it is a false/misrepresented endorsement. Under Annex I point 23c this is a per se prohibited practice — commissioning or presenting false endorsements to promote a product is banned in all circumstances. The same point covers suppressing negative feedback: deleting comments that identify the videos as fake misrepresents the genuine social reaction to the content.
findings.evidence_quote: voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand
findings.recommendation: Remove all deepfake/endorsement content entirely. Do not attribute testimonials to any person (real or synthetic) who has not genuinely used and endorsed the product; only use endorsements from real, consenting endorsers with a truthful, disclosed material connection. Stop deleting user comments that question authenticity.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: This is a misleading action on multiple counts: it deceives about the trader's/endorser's qualifications (an invented medical endorsement), about the product's main characteristics/benefits (unsubstantiated comparative immunity claim), and it is likely to cause consumers to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The comparative superiority claim over prescription medicines is unsubstantiated and inherently deceptive.
findings.evidence_quote: As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.
findings.recommendation: Delete the comparative and immunity-superiority claims. Any health-related benefit statement must be limited to authorised, substantiated claims permitted under the EU Health Claims Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and must not imply medical/prescription-level efficacy or physician endorsement.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Framing the supplement as outperforming what a doctor can prescribe presents it as having quasi-medicinal, disease-fighting properties. To the extent it conveys that the product treats/prevents illness (immune protection presented as superior to prescription medicine), it approaches a false cure/treatment claim, prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17. Combined with the physician framing, the average consumer is invited to read it as a medical treatment claim.
findings.evidence_quote: it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe
findings.recommendation: Remove any wording that portrays the supplement as treating, preventing or curing illness or as an alternative/superior to prescribed medicines. Restrict messaging to lawful, authorised nutrition/health claims only.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic, fabricated nature of the videos is material information the average consumer needs to correctly assess the endorsement's authenticity. Presenting an AI deepfake as genuine footage of a real physician, without disclosure, is a misleading omission/hidden material fact under Art. 7. The undisclosed synthetic nature deceives consumers about who is actually speaking and whether a real endorsement exists.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose any AI-generated/manipulated content — though note that disclosure alone does NOT cure the false-endorsement and false-health-claim violations; the impersonation content should not be used at all.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Deliberately directing deceptive medical-endorsement and immunity claims at an older, health-interested cohort engages the vulnerable-consumer standard in Art. 5(3): the practice's distortion of economic behaviour is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group, whose credulity toward physician endorsements and health benefits may be heightened. This aggravates the unfairness of the practices above and functions as a safety-net over the specific breaches.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target health-vulnerable/older audiences with medical-authority or health-benefit messaging that is not fully substantiated and authorised. Reassess the media plan once the deceptive content is removed.

verdicts.notes: The VitaBoost campaign engages several UCPD provisions, including multiple Annex I blacklisted practices that are prohibited in all circumstances regardless of effect. A deepfake fabricates an endorsement from an unaffiliated physician (blacklisted false endorsement, plus misleading action on qualifications/nature of the product), the "strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe" line is a false/unsubstantiated health claim, deleting comments that flag the videos as fake is suppression/misrepresentation of social endorsements, and the unlabelled synthetic nature is a misleading omission. Targeting a health-interested 55+ cohort further engages the vulnerable-consumer safety net under Art. 5. Overall this is a serious, multi-headed UCPD violation.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses AI to clone the voice and face of a real TV physician, Dr. Rui Silva, who has no connection to the brand, and puts fabricated words in his mouth claiming VitaBoost beats prescription medicine at boosting immunity. That single creative choice breaks the law under four separate EU frameworks at the most serious level. It is a banned fake medical endorsement and a false health/cure claim (consumer protection law), an undisclosed deepfake and a prohibited manipulative/deceptive AI practice aimed at a vulnerable older audience (AI Act), unlawful processing of the doctor's biometric likeness and health-based ad targeting without consent (GDPR), and prohibited health-data ad targeting plus comment suppression amounting to manipulation (DSA). Deleting comments that flag the videos as fake makes matters worse, not better. This is not fixable with a disclaimer or a label — the impersonation and the "better than anything I can prescribe" claim must be removed entirely. As it stands, the campaign cannot be run in any form and exposes the brand to enforcement, fines, and personal legal action from Dr. Silva. The overall verdict is critical: do not publish.
recommendations: Do not publish this campaign in its current form. Immediately halt any planned launch and pull the deepfake video assets — this is the single most urgent action.

Remove all AI-generated content that impersonates Dr. Rui Silva. Using a real person's cloned voice and face without their explicit consent is both a banned fake endorsement (UCPD Annex I) and unlawful biometric data processing (GDPR Art. 9). A disclaimer does NOT cure this — the content must not be used at all.

Delete the claim 'strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.' Comparative and cure/treatment claims for a supplement are prohibited outright. Limit all health messaging to claims authorised under the EU Health Claims Regulation (EC) 1924/2006.
Stop deleting user comments that flag the videos as fake. Suppressing corrective feedback is a manipulative 'dark pattern' (DSA Art. 25) and misrepresents genuine social reaction (UCPD).

Remove all health-interest targeting from the media plan. Targeting 'users interested in health topics' relies on special-category health data, which is banned outright for platform advertising under DSA Art. 26(3) and cannot be fixed with consent. Switch to contextual placement or non-sensitive demographics only.

Do not target older (55+) audiences with medical-authority or health-benefit messaging, given the heightened vulnerability protections under the AI Act (Art. 5) and UCPD (Art. 5(3)). Reassess any targeting only after the deceptive content is fully removed.

For any future AI-generated creative, add clear, prominent, persistent on-screen and audio disclosure plus machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermarking) per AI Act Art. 50 — but only once the underlying impersonation and false-claim problems are resolved.

Ensure every paid placement is clearly labelled as advertising, correctly identifies VitaBoost as the advertiser and payer, and provides targeting transparency (DSA Art. 26(1)); and provide a compliant privacy notice and lawful basis for any personalisation (GDPR Arts. 6, 13).

Rebuild the campaign from scratch around genuine, consenting endorsers with truthful, substantiated, authorised claims and disclosed material connections. Consider a legal review before any relaunch given the multi-framework exposure.

findings.rationale: The AI system is used to produce a purposefully deceptive technique: a fabricated endorsement by a trusted physician who has no relationship with the brand, designed to make consumers believe a real doctor recommends the product. This appreciably impairs informed decision-making and is likely to cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take, with a reasonable likelihood of significant harm (reliance on an unsubstantiated supplement over medical advice). findings.evidence_quote: As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The deepfake medical endorsement is delivered via AI-driven behavioural targeting deliberately aimed at an older cohort (55+) selected for health interests — a group whose age-related susceptibility to physician authority and health claims makes them vulnerable. Exploiting that vulnerability to materially distort behaviour with a risk of health harm engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting vulnerabilities due to age.

findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-enabled targeting to direct manipulative health-endorsement content at age-vulnerable audiences. Remove health-interest + age-based targeting for this content and ensure any future targeting does not exploit age-related susceptibility.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the AI Act on multiple fronts through its use of generative AI. It deploys an undisclosed deep fake (voice-clone + face-swap) of a real physician — a clear breach of the Art. 50(4) transparency obligation and, absent machine-readable provenance marking, Art. 50(2). Because the AI-generated content fabricates a trusted doctor's endorsement to deceive consumers about a material fact and is deliberately delivered to a health-vulnerable 55+ audience, it also plausibly triggers the Art. 5 prohibitions on deceptive AI techniques (5(1)(a)) and exploitation of age-related vulnerability (5(1)(b)), with a genuine risk of health harm.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting an audience defined by interest in 'health topics' processes data revealing/inferring health status, a special category under Art. 9. Such processing is prohibited unless an exception (in a marketing context, explicit consent) applies. The campaign describes no explicit-consent mechanism, and inferred health-interest targeting falls squarely within Art. 9 even where the attribute is inferred rather than declared.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not target based on health interests/topics. Rebuild the audience using non-sensitive criteria (e.g. general age/demographic reach without health-interest segments). If any health-based segmentation is retained, obtain valid, freely given, specific and explicit consent for that processing and document it; note that platform-level sensitive-data ad targeting may be independently barred.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
