findings.rationale: Behavioural/interest-based ad targeting and audience segmentation is automated processing to evaluate personal aspects (interests, health, age cohort) and therefore constitutes profiling. This triggers the associated GDPR obligations on lawful basis, transparency and the right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Map the profiling logic used to build the audience, document the categories of data and inferences involved, and ensure downstream lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations are satisfied before running the placements.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis. Interest-based targeting on an ad platform generally relies on consent, and because the segmentation involves health-related inferences a legitimate-interest basis is unlikely to be adequate. The campaign material identifies no lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6 lawful basis for the targeting; given the health dimension, rely on explicit consent (which also satisfies the Art. 9 exception) rather than legitimate interests, and record a supporting assessment.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that individuals whose data is used for targeting are not deceived about the processing and its context. Presenting synthetic, unlabelled content while suppressing signals that reveal its true nature to a targeted, health-interested 55+ audience undermines the fairness of processing personal data used to reach and influence those individuals.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional; comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Ensure targeting is accompanied by fair, non-deceptive delivery: label the advertising nature of the content, stop deleting comments that flag authenticity, and provide clear information to targeted users about who is processing their data and why.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is processed to target individuals, controllers must provide transparency information including purposes, lawful basis and the existence of profiling. The campaign as described provides no privacy information at the point of targeting/collection.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide an accessible privacy notice covering controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, retention, data-subject rights and the existence of profiling, linked from the ad creative and landing destinations.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct-marketing profiling triggers an absolute right to object. The campaign describes no opt-out or objection mechanism for the profiling-based targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Implement and clearly signpost an easy, effective opt-out from direct-marketing profiling, and ensure objections immediately stop further targeting of the individual.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses paid social placements that behaviourally target users "interested in health topics" and aged 55+. Under GDPR this is profiling (Art. 4(4)) that processes health information — a special category under Art. 9 — because it segments people by inferred health interest. Art. 9 prohibits such processing absent explicit consent, and any personalised advertising also needs a lawful basis (Art. 6) and satisfies fairness/transparency and profiling-information duties (Arts. 5(1)(a), 13). The campaign as described shows no consent capture, privacy notice or opt-out, so these obligations are engaged and very likely unmet. (Note: the deepfake/likeness and health-claim issues are primarily for the AI Act/UCPD/DSA agents; the platform-level ban on sensitive-data ad targeting sits in DSA Art. 26(3).)

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The media plan targets users based on their interest in health topics. Health is a special category of personal data under GDPR Art. 9, referenced by DSA Art. 26(3). Presenting advertisements based on profiling that uses — directly or by inference — such sensitive attributes is flatly prohibited for platform advertising, regardless of user consent. Targeting a 'health topics' interest segment infers health-related sensitive attributes and falls squarely within this ban.
findings.evidence_quote: paid placement on social video platforms targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Remove all health-interest / health-topic targeting parameters from the media plan. Rely only on non-sensitive targeting (e.g., broad contextual placement not derived from profiling on health, or general age/geographic parameters that do not proxy for health status). Confirm with the platform that no sensitive-data-derived segments are used.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Systematically deleting user comments that correctly flag the videos as fake manipulates the online interface so that recipients cannot see accurate information exposing the deception. This deceives and materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions about the product, engaging the DSA Art. 25 prohibition on deceptive/manipulative interface design (and, without prejudice, UCPD Art. 5). It compounds the disguised, synthetic nature of the ads.
findings.evidence_quote: comments calling them fake are deleted
findings.recommendation: Cease deleting or suppressing comments that identify the content as AI-generated or fictional. Do not curate the ad environment to hide truthful information about the content's synthetic and promotional nature; instead label the content accurately so such corrective comments are unnecessary.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As paid placements on social video platforms, these ads must allow recipients to identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it (Art. 26(1)). Presenting a synthetic 'physician endorsement' with no ad labelling and no disclosed advertiser identity means the commercial and paid nature is concealed, so the Art. 26(1) transparency requirement is not met as described.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: Ensure every placement carries a clear, real-time 'advertisement' label identifying the VitaBoost brand as the advertiser and the payer, using the platform's disclosure tools. Do not disguise paid promotional content as organic or editorial physician commentary.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages multiple DSA provisions. Most seriously, paid social-video placements behaviourally target users "55+ interested in health topics" — profiling on a GDPR Art. 9 special category (health), which is flatly prohibited for platform advertising under Art. 26(3) regardless of consent. The deletion of comments identifying the videos as fake is a manipulative interface practice engaging the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition, and the unlabelled synthetic/paid placements raise Art. 26(1) ad-transparency concerns. Note DSA obligations bind the platform providers, but the advertiser's targeting instructions and content directly cause these breaches and cannot lawfully be executed.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: An entirely fabricated endorsement is attributed to a real physician who has no relationship with the brand. Submitting/commissioning false endorsements and misrepresenting social endorsements to promote a product is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances. The deletion of comments calling the videos fake is textbook suppression of negative feedback, expressly named in this provision's marketing relevance.
findings.evidence_quote: Video ads built with a voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva, a well-known TV physician who has no relationship with the brand. In the synthetic clips 'he' says: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily...'
findings.recommendation: Cease the campaign entirely. Do not create or publish any endorsement attributed to a person who has not genuinely and verifiably endorsed the product. Stop deleting comments that flag the content as fake; any moderation must not suppress truthful consumer statements about authenticity.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Presented by a purported doctor as superior to prescription medicine, the claim conveys that the supplement has curative/therapeutic power against illness. Falsely claiming a product can cure or treat illness is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances; there is no substantiation for such a medicinal effect for a food supplement.
findings.evidence_quote: it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe
findings.recommendation: Remove any claim that the product cures, treats, prevents illness or is superior to prescription medicine. Health/nutrition claims for food supplements must be limited to those authorised under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and be properly substantiated.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The ad contains false information about the product's main characteristics (immunity benefits, results) and about a professional's qualifications/endorsement, deceiving the average consumer and likely to cause a transactional decision (purchase) they would not otherwise take. The physician's authority is fabricated and the immunity/comparative claim is unsubstantiated.
findings.evidence_quote: 'As a doctor, I take VitaBoost daily — it strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe.'
findings.recommendation: Substantiate every product benefit claim with evidence before publication and remove the fabricated physician endorsement. Comparative superiority claims ('better than anything I can prescribe') must be objectively verifiable or dropped.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic, fictional nature of the footage is material information that the average consumer needs to assess the credibility of the 'doctor's' statements. Hiding that the endorsement is an AI fabrication—and not disclosing the commercial/manipulated nature of the content—is a misleading omission that distorts the consumer's ability to make an informed decision.
findings.evidence_quote: The videos are not labelled as AI-generated or as fictional
findings.recommendation: If any legitimate synthetic content were ever used, clearly and prominently disclose that it is AI-generated and fictional, and disclose the commercial intent. In this case the underlying practice is impermissible regardless of labelling.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice is contrary to professional diligence and is deliberately directed at an age cohort that may include consumers particularly susceptible to physician-authority and health claims. Under Art. 5(3) fairness is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group, which aggravates the distortion of economic behaviour caused by the fake medical endorsement.
findings.evidence_quote: targeting users 55+ interested in health topics
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy physician-authority or health-benefit persuasion tactics toward audiences selected for age and health interest. Any legitimate campaign should avoid exploiting the susceptibility of older consumers to medical claims.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including several Annex I blacklisted practices that are unfair in all circumstances (no case-by-case assessment needed). A synthetic deepfake of a real physician falsely endorsing the product is a fabricated endorsement (point 23c); the accompanying "strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe" is a false/unsubstantiated health-benefit claim, with a false-cure dimension (point 17) and a misleading action on product benefits and on a professional's qualifications (Art. 6). Deletion of comments exposing the content as fake is suppression of negative reviews and reinforces the deception. Targeting a potentially vulnerable 55+ cohort with physician-authority claims aggravates the fairness assessment under Art. 5(3). Overall risk is severe.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses AI to create fake video "endorsements" from Dr. Rui Silva, a real TV physician who has never worked with the brand, showing him claiming VitaBoost "strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe." As designed, it breaks multiple EU laws at once and cannot be fixed with a disclaimer — it must be stopped. The fabricated doctor endorsement and the "better than prescription medicine" claim are outright blacklisted practices under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (banned in all circumstances), while deleting comments that flag the videos as fake is illegal suppression of truthful feedback. Under the AI Act, the undisclosed deepfake of an identifiable person breaches transparency rules and likely triggers the prohibitions on deceptive AI and on exploiting age-related vulnerability. Targeting people "interested in health topics" processes sensitive health data, which is flatly banned for platform advertising under the DSA (regardless of consent) and lacks any GDPR lawful basis, notice, or opt-out. There is also serious legal exposure to Dr. Silva personally (personality/image rights and likely defamation) entirely separate from these regulatory findings. Verdict: do not launch — this campaign must be abandoned in its current form.
recommendations: Do not publish this campaign. Halt production and pull any assets already created — the core concept (a fabricated physician endorsement) is prohibited in all circumstances and cannot be made compliant.

Permanently drop the AI voice-clone and face-swap of Dr. Rui Silva. Never attribute any endorsement to a person who has not genuinely and verifiably agreed to endorse the product; expect potential legal action from Dr. Silva over his image and reputation.
Stop deleting comments that call the videos fake. Suppressing truthful authenticity feedback is itself an illegal manipulative practice under both the UCPD and the DSA.

Remove the claim 'strengthens immunity better than anything I can prescribe' and any wording implying the supplement cures, treats, or beats prescription medicine. Limit health claims to those authorised under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and hold evidence for every claim before use.

Eliminate all health-interest / 'health topics' targeting. Targeting on inferred health status is banned for platform ads under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent, and lacks a GDPR basis. Rebuild reach on non-sensitive criteria only.

For any future compliant campaign: put in place a GDPR lawful basis and privacy notice, an easy direct-marketing opt-out, clear real-time 'advertisement' labelling identifying VitaBoost as advertiser, and — if any AI-generated content is ever used — prominent human-facing disclosure plus machine-readable provenance marking.
Do not deploy physician-authority or health-scare persuasion tactics aimed at the 55+ audience; this aggravates the fairness assessment and engages the AI Act's vulnerability prohibition.
Have legal/compliance sign off on any replacement concept before spend, given the breadth of exposure across the AI Act, UCPD, DSA and GDPR.

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.

detected_practices: engagement quiz collecting personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests)
custom audience creation from quiz completions
behavioural targeting on 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
profiling of minors
always-on behavioural retargeting loop
late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00) targeting teens
health/energy claim ('energy type', energy drink to minors)
targeting minors with energy drink advertising
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is minors aged 13-17, explicitly targeted. DSA Art. 28 prohibits targeted advertising to minors based on profiling; GDPR imposes heightened protections for children's data and consent. The quiz collects mood and behavioural data that may qualify as special-category or highly sensitive profiling of minors.
triage.summary: A short-video energy-drink campaign uses a branded quiz to collect sensitive data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) from teens, building custom audiences that feed behavioural ad targeting and an always-on retargeting loop. It deliberately targets 13-17 year-olds profiled as 'gamers' and 'late-night scrollers' with late-night creatives (22:00-01:00). Despite the 'no' declaration on generative AI, the platform's behavioural profiling and audience-matching systems likely constitute AI-driven targeting warranting review.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The platform's ad system is an AI system that profiles and targets a group defined by age (minors 13-17) — a vulnerability the AI Act expressly protects. Combining behavioural profiling ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') with late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) and an always-on retargeting loop is designed to materially distort the behaviour of minors, exploiting their reduced impulse control and age-related susceptibility. Directing an energy-drink (a caffeinated stimulant) at teens late at night is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (sleep disruption, over-consumption, dependency), satisfying the Art. 5(1)(b) elements. This is a prohibited practice, not merely a regulated one.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-driven behavioural profiling to target minors. Disable age-based (13-17) targeting entirely, remove the 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' custom audiences, and stop late-night scheduling for any audience that may contain minors. Restrict energy-drink advertising to a verified 18+ audience with no profiling of under-18s.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The quiz collects 'mood' data that feeds a custom audience, and the AI system then times and repeats ad delivery (late-night window plus a persistent 2-second-trigger retargeting loop) in a way that operates below conscious awareness and is calibrated to nudge impulsive consumption. Emotion/mood-based timing combined with covert, relentless behavioural nudging by an AI system to appreciably impair minors' informed decision-making, causing consumption decisions they would not otherwise take, engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative AI techniques (see emotion-based AI targeting concept).
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Remove mood data from the profiling/targeting pipeline and cease using it to time ad delivery. Eliminate the always-on 2-second-trigger retargeting loop directed at minors and impose frequency caps and transparent, non-manipulative delivery. Ensure no AI-driven emotional or temporal nudging is used to influence consumption decisions.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses the platform's AI-driven behavioural profiling and audience-matching system to deliberately target minors (13-17) profiled as 'gamers' and 'late-night scrollers' with an always-on retargeting loop and late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling. Although generative AI is declared 'no', the ad-serving/profiling system is an AI system for AI Act purposes. This engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting age-related vulnerability and, given mood-data collection and late-night timing designed to erode teens' decision-making, the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative AI techniques. Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition) is not engaged as it is confined to workplace/education contexts.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The quiz is an information society service offered directly to a declared audience of teens 13-17 and collects their personal data. Where consent is the legal basis, Art. 8 requires the child to be at least 16 (or the Member-State floor down to 13), and below that age requires parental consent with reasonable verification efforts. The campaign targets an EU-wide 13-17 band, so it will reach children below the applicable digital-consent age in many Member States, yet nothing indicates parental consent or verification. Collecting birthdate could confirm age but no age-gating or parental consent mechanism is described.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Determine the applicable digital-consent age per Member State (13-16). For users below that age, obtain verifiable parental consent before any data collection or profiling, and implement reasonable age-verification. Where verification is not feasible, exclude under-age users from data collection entirely.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: 'Mood' data, combined with inferred behavioural profiles ('late-night scroller'), can reveal or be used to infer information about a person's mental/health state. Processing data revealing health (including inferred emotional/mental states) of minors engages the Art. 9 prohibition and requires explicit consent or another Art. 9(2) exception, which is not present. Emotion/mood inference used to time and tailor marketing to teens is precisely the risk Art. 9 guards against.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Cease collecting and processing 'mood' data for targeting minors. If any emotional/wellbeing signal is genuinely needed, do not use it for ad targeting; otherwise establish a valid Art. 9(2) basis (explicit consent, here parental) and document a necessity/proportionality assessment.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting individuals based on automated analysis of watch behaviour, interests and mood to build 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' profiles and custom audiences is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). Profiling of children for marketing is discouraged and requires a valid lawful basis and heightened safeguards, none of which are evidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling activity, its lawful basis and a DPIA. For minors, avoid behavioural profiling for advertising altogether; rely on contextual (non-profiling) advertising instead.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Building a custom audience from quiz completions and using it for behavioural ad targeting and retargeting requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Personalised advertising/profiling generally requires consent; legitimate interest is very hard to justify for profiling minors. No valid basis is described, and for children the balancing test under legitimate interest is unlikely to succeed.
findings.evidence_quote: completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Identify and record a valid lawful basis. For profiling-based advertising to minors, consent (parental where required) is effectively necessary; do not rely on legitimate interest for this audience.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: If consent is relied upon, Art. 7 requires it to be demonstrable, granular, in clear plain language and as easy to withdraw as to give, and not bundled or conditional. A gamified quiz that harvests data and silently feeds a custom audience for retargeting suggests bundled, non-transparent consent and no described withdrawal mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Separate consent for (a) quiz participation and (b) advertising/profiling; use clear child-friendly language; provide an equally easy withdrawal path; and keep records demonstrating valid consent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Collecting data via a fun 'energy type' quiz while the real purpose is building targeting audiences and an always-on retargeting loop risks breaching the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — the processing purpose (behavioural ad targeting of minors) is not evident to the teen at the point of collection. Fairness is especially demanding where children are concerned.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Make the true advertising/profiling purpose clear and prominent at the quiz entry point in age-appropriate language; do not disguise data-harvesting as entertainment.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Where information is addressed to a child, Art. 12 requires it to be concise, transparent, intelligible and in especially clear, plain, age-appropriate language. There is no indication of any child-appropriate privacy information in the quiz flow.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered, child-friendly privacy notice at the point of collection, using simple language and visuals suited to 13-17 year-olds.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must disclose its identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients (e.g. the ad platform / custom audience), retention, data-subject rights, and the existence of profiling/automated decision-making. None of this is described in a quiz that immediately feeds a custom audience and retargeting loop.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Add a complete Art. 13 notice before data is submitted, expressly covering the custom-audience/profiling purpose, recipients, retention period, and rights including objection to direct marketing.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct marketing (including profiling-based retargeting) triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3); data subjects must be informed of this right explicitly and at the latest at first communication. The always-on loop offers no described objection/opt-out mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Explicitly present the right to object to direct marketing, provide an easy opt-out, and immediately stop retargeting any user who objects.

verdicts.notes: This campaign collects personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) directly from minors aged 13-17 via a branded quiz, builds custom audiences and drives behavioural profiling and always-on retargeting. It engages multiple GDPR obligations that are highly unlikely to be satisfied as described: valid child consent (Art. 8), lawful basis and consent conditions (Art. 6/7/4-11), profiling of minors (Art. 4(4)/Art. 22), transparency at collection (Arts. 5(1)(a),12,13), and processing of inferred sensitive data — 'mood' (Art. 9). Given the explicit minor audience and behavioural profiling, the data-processing design is likely non-compliant absent verified parental consent and full transparency.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients they are aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Here the declared and explicitly targeted audience is minors aged 13-17, the quiz captures birthdate and school year (so age is known with reasonable certainty), and ads are served on the basis of behavioural profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') plus an always-on retargeting loop. This is exactly the profiling-based advertising to minors the provision bans, and consent cannot cure it.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Cease all profiling-, behaviour- and retargeting-based ad delivery to the 13-17 audience. Any ads reaching users known to be minors must be contextual only (no profiling of personal data). Remove birthdate/school-year-driven custom audiences and behavioural retargeting for this cohort.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) bans presenting ads based on profiling that uses GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including by inference. The quiz collects 'mood' and derives energy-type/behavioural profiles ('late-night scroller') that can infer mental-health or well-being states; feeding these into a custom audience used for ad delivery risks sensitive-attribute targeting, which is prohibited regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Do not use mood data or any inferred health/well-being attribute as a targeting or audience-building parameter for platform advertising. Exclude mood and derived psychological signals from the custom-audience pipeline entirely.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement recipients can identify in real time that it is an ad, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign describes custom-audience and behavioural retargeting delivery but shows no ad labelling or disclosure of targeting parameters to recipients.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Ensure every VoltZ placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement with advertiser identity and payer, and expose the main targeting parameters and controls to recipients as required by Art. 26(1).

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives, manipulates or materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions. An 'always-on' engagement loop that re-serves ads after a 2-second view, combined with late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) aimed at teens profiled as 'late-night scrollers', is an interface/delivery design that exploits and nags a vulnerable minor audience rather than supporting free, informed choices.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on re-serving loop and late-night scheduling directed at minors; frequency-cap and time-restrict delivery, and avoid delivery patterns that exploit vulnerability or repeatedly nag the same users.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deliberately targets minors (13-17) on a short-video platform with ads served on the basis of behavioural profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') and an always-on retargeting loop. This directly engages the DSA's core prohibition on profiling-based advertising to minors (Art. 28) and, through the quiz's collection of 'mood' data, the ban on sensitive-data ad targeting (Art. 26(3)). Advertising transparency (Art. 26(1)) and the anti-manipulation rule (Art. 25) are also engaged. The Art. 28 breach is a hard prohibition and the most serious issue.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Under Art. 5(3), practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (here minors, by reason of age and credulity) are assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. Deliberately targeting 13-17 year-olds with an energy drink, using inferred mood and 'late-night scroller' profiling and scheduling creatives at 22:00-01:00, is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of teenagers who are less able to resist tailored, well-timed commercial pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not target the campaign to under-18s. Remove age brackets 13-17 from targeting, drop mood- and behaviour-based profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller'), and apply an age-gate/exclusion so energy-drink creatives are not delivered to minors. Restrict scheduling to non-nocturnal hours and apply age-appropriate professional-diligence standards.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat persistence, timing and undue influence as key factors in identifying an aggressive practice. An always-on loop that repeatedly re-serves ads to minors triggered by only 2 seconds of viewing, concentrated in late-night hours (22:00-01:00) and informed by inferred mood data, applies sustained pressure that can significantly impair the freedom of choice of a young, vulnerable audience and push a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on retargeting loop for minors entirely; if retained for adults, apply strict frequency caps, minimum meaningful engagement thresholds (not 2 seconds), quiet hours excluding late-night delivery, and easy opt-out. Do not use inferred mood/emotional state to time or intensify ad delivery.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the commercial intent of a practice to be identified where not apparent from context. A 'What's your energy type?' quiz is presented as playful engagement, but its material purpose is to harvest personal data (including mood) to build a custom advertising audience for targeted marketing. If that commercial/data-collection intent is not clearly and timely disclosed — particularly to minors — it is a misleading omission of material information.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose, before participation, that the quiz is advertising and that responses are used to build a marketing audience and target ads. Given the audience are minors, reconsider running such a data-collecting quiz at all; at minimum make the commercial intent unmistakable and remove sensitive fields (mood, school year, birthdate).

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits, in all circumstances, including in an advertisement a direct exhortation to children to buy the product or to persuade adults to buy it for them. The submitted material describes targeting and mechanics but does not quote the creative copy, so no direct 'buy now'-style exhortation can be confirmed. Given the child-directed nature of the campaign this is a high-risk area to verify.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform ... target audience: teens 13-17
findings.recommendation: Review all creative copy and calls-to-action to ensure no direct exhortation to children to buy VoltZ (or to ask adults to buy it). Because the audience is minors, avoid any imperative purchase language; this blacklisted practice is prohibited without exception.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign engages several UCPD concerns because it deliberately targets a clearly identifiable vulnerable group — minors aged 13-17 — with an energy-drink product, using inferred mood/behaviour data, late-night scheduling and an always-on retargeting loop. The strongest UCPD issues are the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-group fairness test, aggressive-practice factors under Arts. 8-9 (persistence, timing, undue influence), and possible hidden commercial intent under Art. 7 in the branded quiz. No blacklisted direct exhortation to children (Annex I point 28) is quotable from the supplied text, so that remains a risk to verify against the actual creative copy rather than a confirmed violation. GDPR/DSA/AI Act dimensions are handled by other agents.

report.executive_summary: The VoltZ "teen engagement loop" campaign deliberately targets minors aged 13-17 with an energy drink, using a data-harvesting quiz to build behavioural profiles ("gamer", "late-night scroller"), late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00), and an always-on retargeting loop triggered by just 2 seconds of viewing. As designed, this campaign is not merely risky — it runs headlong into several outright legal prohibitions. The DSA (Art. 28) flatly bans profiling-based advertising to minors, and this cannot be fixed with consent. The AI Act (Art. 5) prohibits AI systems that exploit the vulnerabilities of minors, which the profiling-plus-late-night-timing design does. The GDPR is breached on multiple fronts: no valid basis for processing children's data, no parental consent where required, and unlawful use of "mood" (sensitive/health-inferring) data. On top of this, targeting a vulnerable young audience with persistent, well-timed pressure raises serious unfair and aggressive commercial practice concerns under the UCPD. The verdict is clear: as submitted, the campaign is unlawful in the EU and must not run in its current form.
recommendations: STOP: Do not launch this campaign as designed. Multiple hard prohibitions (DSA Art. 28 profiling ads to minors, AI Act Art. 5 exploitation of minors' vulnerability) apply and cannot be cured by adding consent or disclosures.

Remove all age-based targeting of 13-17 year-olds. Restrict energy-drink advertising to a verified 18+ audience with reliable age assurance — this single change resolves the majority of the critical findings.

Eliminate all behavioural profiling and retargeting for any audience that may contain minors: drop the 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' custom audiences, disable the always-on 2-second retargeting loop, and use contextual (non-profiling) advertising only.

Stop collecting and using 'mood' data entirely. It infers sensitive health/emotional states, is banned as an ad-targeting parameter (DSA Art. 26(3), GDPR Art. 9), and must be removed from the quiz and the custom-audience pipeline.

Remove late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) directed at any potentially under-18 audience and apply frequency caps and quiet hours; late-night delivery of a caffeinated stimulant to teens is a key aggravating factor across the AI Act, DSA and UCPD.

Reconsider running the 'What's your energy type?' quiz at all. If retained for adults, disclose clearly and up front that it is advertising and that responses build a marketing audience; separate and document consent, provide a child-friendly Art. 12/13 privacy notice, a lawful basis, a DPIA, and an easy opt-out/right to object.
Review all creative copy for any direct 'buy now' exhortation to children — a UCPD Annex I blacklisted practice prohibited without exception — before any version of the campaign proceeds.
Given the breadth of critical issues, redesign the campaign concept from scratch around a verified adult audience and contextual advertising, and obtain legal/DPO sign-off before relaunch.

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.

detected_practices: branded quiz collecting personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests)
custom audience creation from quiz completions
behavioural targeting on 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
behavioural retargeting loop (re-serving to 2-second viewers)
dayparting/late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00)
targeting of minors
profiling based on watch behaviour and mood
energy drink marketing to teens
triage.audience_notes: Declared and actual target is minors (13-17). DSA Art. 28 prohibits targeted advertising to minors based on profiling; GDPR requires special protection for children's data and Art. 22 concerns for automated profiling; UCPD prohibits aggressive/unfair practices exploiting vulnerable audiences (late-night scheduling to teens, always-on retargeting loop). AI Act flagged because the platform's automated profiling/audience system may constitute an AI system despite the 'no generative AI' declaration.
triage.summary: A short-video energy drink campaign that uses a branded quiz to collect sensitive-adjacent data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) from teens aged 13-17, then builds custom audiences and behaviourally targets/retargets minors matching 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles with late-night (22:00-01:00) creatives. Although generative AI is not declared, the platform's ad system performs automated profiling and audience optimisation, and the campaign heavily relies on personalisation and profiling of minors.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The platform's automated profiling/audience-optimisation system is an AI system (the 'no generative AI' declaration is irrelevant — Art. 5 covers any AI system). VoltZ deploys it to target a group vulnerable due to age (declared minors 13-17), matching them on behavioural profiles and timing energy-drink ads to a late-night window (22:00-01:00) when self-control is lower. This exploits age-related vulnerability with the objective/effect of materially distorting behaviour (driving energy-drink consumption by minors, at night) in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm to their health and sleep. This falls squarely within the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-driven profiling/audience systems to target minors. Exclude the 13-17 cohort from all behavioural targeting and custom audiences, remove the late-night (22:00-01:00) dayparting aimed at teens, and drop mood/behaviour-based optimisation for this age group. If minors may be reached incidentally, disable profiling-based delivery entirely for them.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The quiz harvests a mood signal that feeds an AI-optimised custom audience, and an always-on retargeting loop repeatedly re-serves ads on the basis of minimal (2-second) engagement. Used against minors, this emotion-informed, high-frequency AI nudging is a purposefully manipulative technique that appreciably impairs the target's ability to make an informed decision and pushes consumption they would not otherwise choose, with reasonably likely significant harm — engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative AI techniques (see also the emotion-based AI targeting concept).
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience... An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Remove 'mood' from the quiz and from any signal fed to audience optimisation; do not use inferred emotional state to time or tailor ads. Cap frequency and remove the always-on 2-second retargeting loop, especially for minors. Ensure the quiz is clearly identified as advertising and not a covert data-collection/nudging mechanism.

verdicts.notes: Although the campaign declares "no generative AI", the AI Act's prohibitions in Art. 5 apply to any AI system, not only generative ones. The short-video platform's automated ad-optimisation and audience-matching system (custom audiences, behavioural profile matching on 'gamer'/'late-night scroller', always-on retargeting) is such an AI system, and the deployer (VoltZ) is using it. The campaign deliberately directs this system at declared minors (13-17) and incorporates a mood signal and late-night scheduling, engaging the prohibitions on exploiting age-related vulnerabilities (Art. 5(1)(b)) and on manipulative AI techniques (Art. 5(1)(a)). These are outright prohibitions with the highest exposure. AI-system status of the platform tooling should be confirmed, but on the described facts a breach is likely.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The quiz is an information society service directed at children aged 13-17 and collects their personal data. Where consent is the lawful basis, Art. 8 requires that the child be at least 16 (or the Member State's lowered floor down to 13), and below that age parental consent with reasonable verification is mandatory. The campaign describes no age-gating, no parental-consent flow and no verification effort, so processing of the data of 13-15 year olds (and likely all minors, depending on Member State) is unlawful as described. This spans EU markets with differing age thresholds, compounding the risk.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Implement robust age verification at quiz entry. For users below the applicable national digital-consent age, obtain and verify parental/guardian consent before any data collection, or exclude them entirely. Map the digital-consent age per EU Member State and apply the highest applicable safeguard by default.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Behavioural profiling and personalised advertising require a valid lawful basis. Consent is effectively the only viable basis for this kind of profiling of minors, and legitimate interests cannot easily be balanced against children's interests. The campaign describes no lawful basis for the profiling and audience-building, indicating processing without a demonstrable legal ground.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Document a lawful basis for each processing operation (quiz data, audience creation, profiling, retargeting). Given the audience is minors, rely on properly obtained (parental) consent and do not rely on legitimate interests for profiling children for advertising.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: If consent is relied upon, Art. 7 (with Art. 4(11)) requires it to be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, clearly distinguishable and as easy to withdraw as to give. A gamified quiz that silently repurposes collected data to 'feed a custom audience' does not describe a distinct, informed opt-in for advertising/profiling and looks like bundled/implied consent, which is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Separate the fun-quiz purpose from any marketing/profiling purpose. Present a granular, unbundled consent request in clear language, with a genuine choice not to be profiled, and an equally easy withdrawal mechanism. Keep records demonstrating consent.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting and processing 'mood' data — and using late-night 'late-night scroller' behavioural inferences to time advertising — risks revealing or being used to infer emotional/mental-health-adjacent states of children. Where such data reveal health or are processed to infer psychological state, Art. 9's prohibition applies and requires explicit consent or another specific exception, which is not described. Inferred attributes are covered.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Do not collect 'mood' or use emotional-state signals for targeting minors. If any special-category data are genuinely necessary, obtain explicit consent and apply an Art. 9 exception; otherwise remove mood collection and mood/emotion-based targeting from the campaign entirely.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing watch behaviour to build 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' segments and to re-serve ads is automated processing to evaluate and predict personal preferences, interests and behaviour — profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This framing confirms the activity is profiling of minors and triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Treat the audience-optimisation and retargeting as profiling and apply all attaching obligations; given the subjects are children, minimise or cease behavioural profiling for advertising purposes.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Fairness and transparency require that data subjects understand how their data are used. Repurposing quiz answers to silently build advertising audiences and drive an always-on retargeting loop, without any described notice, is a covert secondary use that breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — especially heightened for children.
findings.evidence_quote: completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Make all downstream uses (audience creation, profiling, retargeting) transparent up front in child-friendly language; avoid using playful quiz framing to obscure a data-collection-for-advertising purpose.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Where information is addressed to a child, Art. 12 requires it to be concise, intelligible and in especially clear and plain language. Nothing in the campaign indicates any child-appropriate privacy communication at the quiz, so the transparency-to-children standard is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Provide a concise, age-appropriate privacy notice at the point of quiz entry, written for a 13-17 audience, explaining what is collected and why in plain language.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of data collection the controller must provide identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention and information about profiling/automated decision-making. The quiz collects personal data but the campaign describes none of this mandatory information being given, and profiling for advertising is a key purpose that must be disclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Add a compliant Art. 13 notice at the quiz collection point covering controller identity, all purposes (including profiling and retargeting), legal basis, recipients (the ad platform/custom audience), retention periods and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct marketing, including profiling for such marketing, triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21. The always-on retargeting loop must provide a clear, easily exercised opt-out that stops processing for direct marketing; none is described.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Provide a prominent, easy opt-out from direct-marketing profiling/retargeting, honour it immediately and suppress objecting users from the custom audience and retargeting loop.

verdicts.notes: This campaign collects personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) from minors aged 13-17 via a branded quiz, then builds custom audiences and profiles/retargets those minors — engaging multiple GDPR obligations with no described safeguards. The most serious concern is processing children's data without any indication of valid lawful basis or age-appropriate consent/parental-consent mechanism (Art. 8, Art. 6, Art. 7). The collection of "mood" and the intensive behavioural profiling of children, with no transparency described at the point of collection, further engage Arts. 4(4), 9, 5(1)(a), 12/13 and 21. Overall this is likely non-compliant as described.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients they know with reasonable certainty are minors. Here the declared and actual audience is 13-17 (known minors via collected birthdate/school year), and ads are served precisely because their watch behaviour matches profiled segments ('gamer', 'late-night scroller'). This is textbook profiling-based advertising to minors — a flat prohibition, not curable by consent.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Do not serve any profiling- or behaviour-based advertising to the 13-17 audience. If VoltZ wishes to reach this age group at all, restrict to contextual (non-profiled) placements only, and disable the custom-audience and behavioural-profile targeting entirely for minors. Given the audience is known to be minors, the compliant path is to remove profiling-based delivery altogether.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting ads based on profiling that uses special categories of GDPR Art. 9 data, including directly or by inference. Collecting and using 'mood' to build the custom audience risks profiling on emotional/mental-health state — a sensitive-attribute proxy — as a targeting parameter, which is prohibited for platform advertising regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Remove 'mood' (and any other emotional/health-adjacent signal) from the quiz and from audience-building and targeting logic. Ensure no targeting parameter can act as a proxy for Art. 9 special-category data.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces that manipulate or materially distort recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, including repeated nagging. An always-on loop that re-serves ads to teens after only 2 seconds of incidental viewing, reinforced by 22:00-01:00 late-night scheduling to a minor audience, is manipulative persistence design aimed at an audience with reduced capacity to resist — engaging the dark-patterns prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Cap retargeting frequency, remove the 'always-on' loop, raise the qualifying engagement threshold above an incidental 2-second view, and eliminate late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling to minors. Design the experience so viewers can genuinely disengage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires each ad served on the platform to be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, disclose on whose behalf and who paid for it, and provide meaningful information on the main targeting parameters. The branded quiz and native short-video format risk blurring commercial intent, and the campaign must ensure ad labelling and targeting-parameter disclosure are in place.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all VoltZ creatives and the branded quiz are clearly labelled as advertising with advertiser identity, and that the platform surfaces meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how users can change them.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core mechanics violate the DSA. It deliberately serves profiling-based advertising to a declared audience of minors aged 13-17 — the exact practice prohibited by Art. 28. Targeting profiles are built on inferred emotional/mood and behavioural data (Art. 26(3) risk), and the always-on retargeting loop combined with late-night dayparting to teens raises Art. 25 dark-pattern/manipulative-design concerns. Advertising transparency (Art. 26(1)) is also engaged. These are among the most serious DSA breaches and the campaign should not run as described.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: An always-on, relentless retargeting loop triggered by a mere 2-second view, combined with late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) and profiling on 'late-night scroller' and 'gamer' and 'mood' signals, directed at minors, amounts to undue influence and persistent pressure. Arts. 8-9 expressly treat 'timing' and 'persistence' as aggravating factors and cite 'relentless retargeting' as a marketing example. Because the audience is minors (a group whose freedom of choice is more easily impaired), the practice is likely to significantly impair their freedom of choice and distort their transactional decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the always-on retargeting loop and the mood/behaviour-based late-night targeting of minors. Set frequency caps, remove late-night (22:00-01:00) dayparting aimed at teens, and stop triggering re-serving on trivial 2-second engagement. Do not exploit inferred emotional state ('mood') to time ads.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Under Art. 5(3) a practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where it is likely to distort that group's economic behaviour due to age or credulity. Deliberately profiling 13-17-year-olds by watch behaviour and mood and pushing energy-drink ads to them late at night is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of this vulnerable group. This is the general fairness safety-net capturing the overall design even where no single blacklist item applies.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Redesign the campaign so it is not built around profiling and targeting minors. Exclude the 13-17 age segment from behavioural targeting, apply age-appropriate safeguards, and document a professional-diligence assessment showing the campaign does not exploit the credulity or age of minors.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice where it is not apparent from context. The quiz is presented as a fun personality game ('What's your energy type?') but its actual purpose is to harvest personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) to build a marketing custom audience. The commercial and data-collection intent is not made apparent to the (minor) user, constituting a misleading omission / hidden commercial intent, especially serious given the audience's age and credulity.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose, before participation and in age-appropriate language, that the quiz is advertising by VoltZ and that answers will be used to build advertising audiences and target the user. Ensure the commercial intent is obvious from the outset rather than framed purely as entertainment.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 bans, in all circumstances, direct exhortations to children to buy or to pester adults to buy. The submitted material does not contain verbatim creative copy, so no direct exhortation can be confirmed. This is flagged so the marketer ensures the child-directed creatives contain no 'buy now' / 'ask your parents' style calls to action, which would be a per-se blacklisted violation.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform ... serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Review all final creatives served to the 13-17 audience and remove any direct purchase exhortation or 'get your parents to buy it' messaging; keep evidence that none is present.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign targets a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (minors 13-17) using a data-harvesting quiz, mood/behaviour profiling, late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) and an always-on retargeting loop. Under the UCPD this engages the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9) through undue influence and persistence, the general unfairness safety-net assessed from the perspective of the vulnerable group (Art. 5(3)), and the misleading-omission rule on hidden commercial intent (Art. 7) because the 'What's your energy type?' quiz functions as an undisclosed data-collection/ad-targeting mechanism. No blacklisted direct exhortation text (Annex I point 28) is present in the material, so it is flagged only as a risk.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets VoltZ energy drink to a declared audience of minors (13-17) using a "What's your energy type?" quiz that harvests birthdate, school year, mood and interests, then builds custom audiences and serves behaviourally profiled ads to teens matched as "gamers" and "late-night scrollers", scheduled 22:00-01:00, with an always-on loop that re-serves ads after just 2 seconds of viewing. As designed, it breaches four separate EU regimes at the most serious level. The DSA flatly prohibits profiling-based advertising to known minors (Art. 28) — this cannot be fixed with consent. The AI Act's outright prohibitions on exploiting age-related vulnerability and on manipulative techniques (Art. 5) are engaged, regardless of the "no generative AI" declaration, because the platform's ad-optimisation system is itself an AI system. Under the GDPR, there is no valid lawful basis or age/parental-consent mechanism for processing children's data, and "mood" likely constitutes special-category data. The UCPD captures the relentless retargeting, late-night timing and the quiz's hidden commercial intent as aggressive and unfair practices targeting a vulnerable group. The bottom line: this campaign should not run in its current form — the core mechanics (profiling minors, mood targeting, late-night dayparting, always-on retargeting) are illegal, not merely risky.
recommendations: STOP: Do not launch this campaign as designed. The profiling-based targeting of known 13-17 minors is prohibited outright under DSA Art. 28 and cannot be cured by obtaining consent.

Disable all behavioural/profiling-based delivery to the 13-17 audience. If reaching this age group at all, restrict strictly to contextual (non-profiled) placements and remove custom-audience and 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' targeting entirely.

Remove 'mood' from the quiz and from all audience-building and targeting logic. Mood/emotional-state data is a special-category (Art. 9 GDPR) proxy and its use in ad targeting is separately banned under DSA Art. 26(3); its use to time ads also triggers the AI Act manipulation prohibition.
Eliminate the late-night 22:00-01:00 dayparting aimed at teens — this is central to the AI Act vulnerability-exploitation and UCPD aggressive-practices findings.

Discontinue the always-on retargeting loop; raise the qualifying threshold well above a trivial 2-second view and apply strict frequency caps to avoid dark-pattern (DSA Art. 25) and aggressive-practice (UCPD Arts. 8-9) exposure.

If any data collection from minors remains, implement robust age verification and, below each Member State's digital-consent age (13-16, mapped per market), verified parental consent — and establish a documented lawful basis for every processing operation.

Make the quiz's commercial and data-collection intent unmistakable and provide an age-appropriate, Art. 12/13-compliant privacy notice at the point of collection; separate any marketing/profiling purpose into a granular, unbundled, easily withdrawable opt-in.

Provide a prominent, immediately honoured opt-out from direct-marketing profiling/retargeting (GDPR Art. 21) and ensure all creatives are clearly labelled as VoltZ advertising with required targeting-parameter transparency (DSA Art. 26(1)).
Review all final teen-facing creatives to confirm no direct purchase exhortation or 'ask your parents to buy' messaging, which would be a per-se blacklisted UCPD violation.
Confirm the AI-system status of the platform's ad-optimisation tooling and document a professional-diligence/compliance assessment; treat VoltZ as a deployer with obligations under the AI Act.

campaign.title: VoltZ energy drink — teen engagement loop
campaign.text: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform. A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience. The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00. An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.

detected_practices: branded quiz collecting personal and sensitive-ish data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests)
custom audience creation from quiz completions
behavioural targeting based on watch behaviour ('gamer', 'late-night scroller' profiles)
profiling of minors
always-on retargeting loop (re-serving to viewers of 2+ seconds)
late-night ad scheduling (22:00-01:00) targeting teens
targeting of children/minors with energy drink (high-caffeine) advertising
triage.audience_notes: Audience is explicitly declared and designed as minors aged 13-17. DSA prohibits targeted advertising based on profiling to minors, and the quiz plus behavioural profiling (gamer/late-night scroller) directly implicates that ban. GDPR concerns include lawful basis and special protection for children's data, plus collection of birthdate/school year/mood/interests. UCPD relevance stems from exploiting minors' credulity and manipulative retargeting; late-night scheduling of a caffeinated product to teens heightens vulnerability concerns. AI Act flagged because the platform's algorithmic profiling/ad-targeting system is used despite the 'no generative AI' declaration — automated profiling engine should be reviewed for prohibited manipulative/exploitative practices.
triage.summary: VoltZ energy drink runs a short-video campaign explicitly targeting teens 13-17, using a branded quiz to harvest birthdate, school year, mood and interests, then building a custom audience for behavioural targeting and an always-on retargeting loop with late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling. Although generative AI is declared as not used, the campaign relies on the platform's algorithmic ad-serving/profiling system, and it involves extensive personal data processing and profiling of minors. This raises significant concerns across advertising to children, data protection, platform targeting rules, and unfair/manipulative commercial practices.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The platform's AI ad-targeting system is deliberately deployed to reach a group whose vulnerability arises from their age (minors 13-17). It profiles them ('gamer', 'late-night scroller'), times delivery to late-night hours when impulse control and adult supervision are lowest, and does so to drive consumption of a high-caffeine energy drink. That is an AI system exploiting an age-based vulnerability with the objective/effect of materially distorting the minors' behaviour, in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm (excess caffeine intake, sleep disruption). This matches the Article 5(1)(b) prohibition, which is not curable by consent.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles, with creatives scheduled 22:00-01:00
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-driven profiling/targeting to serve this campaign to minors. Exclude the 13-17 age segment entirely from any algorithmic audience-building, custom-audience or retargeting logic, remove the late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling aimed at teens, and restrict any energy-drink advertising to age-gated adult audiences with no vulnerability-exploiting timing or profiling.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The quiz harvests 'mood' and interests, which the AI ad system combines with behavioural signals and an unrelenting always-on retargeting loop triggered by a 2-second view. Coupling inferred emotional/mood state with repetitive covert nudging engineered to keep re-serving ads to minors constitutes purposefully manipulative techniques deployed via an AI system, aimed at materially distorting behaviour by impairing informed decision-making. Given the audience (minors) and product (high-caffeine drink), it is reasonably likely to cause significant harm, engaging the Article 5(1)(a) prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Disable the mood-based and always-on retargeting loop for minors, and do not use inferred emotional/mood data collected via the quiz to time or tailor ad delivery. Frequency-cap and remove the 2-second retrigger; ensure any remaining targeting to adults is transparent and does not rely on emotional-state exploitation or covert repetitive nudging.

verdicts.notes: Although generative AI is declared "no", the campaign is built entirely on the platform's algorithmic profiling/ad-serving system — an AI system in scope of the AI Act. As deployed here it is designed to target minors (13-17) using age-, mood- and behaviour-based profiles ("gamer", "late-night scroller"), with late-night scheduling (22:00-01:00) and an always-on retargeting loop that re-serves ads to anyone watching ≥2 seconds. This configuration engages the Article 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting age-related vulnerability and the Article 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative techniques, given the objective/effect of materially distorting the behaviour of children toward consuming a high-caffeine product in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant (health/sleep) harm. Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition in workplace/education) is not applicable to this consumer-marketing context.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The quiz is offered directly to children (teens 13-17) on an information society service and collects their personal data to feed a custom audience. Where consent is the basis, processing of data of children below the applicable age (16, or 13-15 where a Member State lowered the threshold) requires verifiable parental consent. The campaign spans the EU with a 13-17 audience but shows no age-verification or parental-consent mechanism, and in Member States retaining the age 16 threshold, most of this audience cannot lawfully consent alone.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience ... users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Implement age gating and, for users below the applicable national digital-consent age, obtain and verify parental/guardian consent before collecting quiz data or building audiences. Map the age threshold per EU market (13-16) and block processing where valid consent cannot be obtained.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of watch behaviour to classify users into 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles and evaluate their interests/behaviour is profiling within Art. 4(4). This confirms profiling is occurring and triggers the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations, here applied to minors who merit specific protection.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Document that behavioural segmentation constitutes profiling, and cease profiling-based targeting of minors; profiling of children for marketing should be avoided given EDPB guidance on the special protection children merit.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling and personalised advertising require a valid lawful basis. For behavioural targeting the realistic basis is consent, and legitimate interests will rarely override the rights of child data subjects for profiling-based marketing. The campaign describes an always-on retargeting engine with no indication of a valid legal basis for processing minors' behavioural data.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 ... An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6 basis before any profiling/retargeting; for minors, rely on properly obtained consent (with parental verification where required) rather than legitimate interests, and disable retargeting where no valid basis exists.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: The quiz appears to harvest data and feed a marketing custom audience without a clearly distinguishable, freely given, specific and informed consent request, and without a demonstrable consent record or easy withdrawal mechanism. Bundling audience-building into a fun quiz for minors risks non-compliant consent under Art. 7 conditions.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Separate any consent for audience-building/marketing from quiz participation, present it in clear plain language suited to minors, keep records of consent, and provide an equally easy withdrawal path.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent used as basis must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Feeding quiz completions into a custom audience by default does not evidence a specific, informed, affirmative opt-in for profiling/advertising — especially problematic with a minor audience.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Obtain explicit affirmative opt-in specifically for building marketing audiences and profiling, distinct from taking the quiz, and ensure it meets the Art. 4(11) standard.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information addressed to a child must be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear, plain language. A gamified quiz aimed at teens with no described child-friendly privacy information likely fails this heightened Art. 12 standard.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered, child-appropriate privacy notice at the quiz entry point using plain language explaining what data is collected and why.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must disclose its identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights, and the existence of profiling. The quiz collects personal data and feeds profiling/audience-building, but no such information is described as being provided.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Add an Art. 13 notice at collection covering controller identity, purposes (including profiling and ad targeting), legal basis, recipients (the ad platform), retention, and rights including objection.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, including profiling related to it. An always-on retargeting loop implies persistent marketing profiling with no described opt-out, failing to respect and facilitate the Art. 21 objection right.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy, always-available opt-out from marketing/retargeting profiling, honour it immediately, and inform users of this right at first contact.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
