findings.rationale: Collecting 'mood' can reveal or allow inference of a person's emotional or mental state; combined with targeting late-night scrollers (22:00-01:00) this risks processing that touches on health/psychological state, which is a special category requiring explicit consent and, for minors, is especially sensitive. If mood is used to time/tailor ads to emotional vulnerability, Art. 9 is engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests
findings.recommendation: Do not collect 'mood' or use it for targeting; if any emotional/health-adjacent inference is unavoidable, obtain explicit consent and conduct a DPIA, though targeting minors on mood should be abandoned outright.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Fairness and transparency require that data subjects are not misled about processing. Presenting audience-building and behavioural profiling of minors as an entertainment quiz, with late-night ad scheduling, is unfair and non-transparent processing contrary to Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Redesign the flow so data collection purposes are transparent and fair, avoid exploiting the quiz format to obscure profiling of children, and conduct a DPIA given the high risk of processing minors' data.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign processes children's personal data (birthdate, school year, mood, interests) via a branded quiz and builds behavioural profiles of teens 13-17 for targeted retargeting. This engages GDPR on multiple fronts: children's consent for information society services (Art. 8), conditions and validity of consent (Arts. 4(11), 7), lawful basis and the transparency/fairness principle for profiling minors (Arts. 6(1), 5(1)(a), 4(4)), transparency at collection (Arts. 12-13), and the right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). "Mood" data risks revealing emotional/mental state, potentially engaging special-category concerns (Art. 9). As described, the campaign provides no evidence of valid legal basis, parental-consent verification, transparency notices, or opt-out mechanisms.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients they are aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Here the audience is explicitly declared and constructed as 13-17 year olds, and the ads are served based on profiling: a quiz collecting birthdate/school year/mood/interests, a custom audience built from those completions, and behavioural profiles ('gamer', 'late-night scroller') derived from watch behaviour. The birthdate and school-year collection means the platform has reasonable certainty the recipients are minors, so this is a prohibited practice, not a mere risk.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Do not present profiling- or behaviour-based advertisements to the 13-17 audience. Remove the custom-audience/behavioural targeting entirely for minors; if reaching this age group at all, use only contextual (non-profiled) placement and age-appropriate design. Disable the retargeting loop for any user known or reasonably likely to be a minor.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that manipulates or materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, including nagging/repeated re-serving. An 'always-on' loop that re-serves ads on the basis of a 2-second view — combined with a mood-harvesting quiz and 22:00-01:00 scheduling of a high-caffeine product to teens — is an engagement/persistence design that exploits the reduced resistance of a vulnerable audience and pressures continued interaction, engaging the dark-patterns prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on re-serving loop and any frequency design that repeatedly pushes the ad after minimal engagement. Apply reasonable frequency caps, avoid late-night scheduling to teen audiences, and ensure the quiz and ad interfaces do not manipulate or nag recipients into further engagement.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) bans presenting advertisements based on profiling that uses special categories of personal data under GDPR Art. 9, including directly or by inference. Collecting 'mood' and feeding quiz completions into a custom audience risks profiling that infers or relies on health/emotional-state data. If the mood signal contributes to the targeting/custom audience used to serve VoltZ ads, this engages the prohibition regardless of any consent obtained.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience.
findings.recommendation: Exclude 'mood' and any emotional/health-adjacent signal from the custom-audience and ad-targeting logic. Confirm that no targeting parameter (direct or inferred) draws on Art. 9 special categories; if it does, cease that targeting entirely.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement presented on an online platform, recipients can identify in real time that it is an ad, on whose behalf, who paid, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign description specifies profiled ad-serving but says nothing about ad labelling, advertiser identity disclosure, or exposure of the (behavioural/custom-audience) targeting parameters, so this obligation appears unaddressed.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every VoltZ placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement, discloses VoltZ as advertiser/payer, and surfaces meaningful information about the main targeting parameters plus a means for recipients to change them, in real time.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If the short-video platform is a designated VLOP, DSA Art. 39 requires a public ad repository containing the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. This campaign's targeting of minors via behavioural/custom-audience parameters would be publicly archived and thus exposed to regulator and researcher scrutiny.
findings.evidence_quote: The platform's ad system then serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Assume all creative, advertiser identity and targeting parameters will be publicly archived if the platform is a VLOP. Ensure the campaign's targeting can withstand public scrutiny — which, given the minor-profiling issues, reinforces the need to redesign the targeting before launch.

verdicts.notes: The campaign explicitly and by design targets minors aged 13-17 on a short-video platform using behavioural profiling (quiz-derived custom audience plus 'gamer'/'late-night scroller' watch-behaviour profiles) and an always-on retargeting loop. This is a clear engagement of the DSA Art. 28 ban on profiling-based advertising to persons known with reasonable certainty to be minors, and the retargeting loop plus mood-based inputs raise dark-pattern (Art. 25) and sensitive-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) concerns. Ad transparency obligations under Art. 26(1) also apply to every ad served.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is deliberately designed to reach a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (teenagers 13-17) whose behaviour is assessed under Art. 5(3) from the perspective of the average member of that group. Engineering an engagement loop that profiles and re-targets minors with a high-caffeine energy drink is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of an audience that lacks adult critical distance, making the practice unfair under the Art. 5 safety-net.
findings.evidence_quote: serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17 whose watch behaviour matches 'gamer' and 'late-night scroller' profiles
findings.recommendation: Do not target under-18s with behaviourally profiled advertising for a high-caffeine product. Age-gate the campaign to 18+ and remove teens from the custom audience; if any lawful reach of minors remains, adopt age-appropriate, non-profiled, non-manipulative creative aligned with professional-diligence standards.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat timing and persistence as key factors in whether a practice amounts to undue influence that impairs freedom of choice. An 'always-on' loop that re-serves ads to minors after only a 2-second view, combined with 22:00-01:00 scheduling of a caffeinated product and mood-based targeting, exploits the reduced resistance of a vulnerable, late-night teen audience and applies relentless pressure characteristic of an aggressive commercial practice.
findings.evidence_quote: An always-on retargeting loop re-serves ads to teens who watched at least 2 seconds
findings.recommendation: Remove the always-on/2-second retargeting loop for this audience, impose frequency caps and quiet-hours, and drop late-night (22:00-01:00) scheduling to minors. Do not use inferred mood to time or intensify delivery.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits hiding the commercial intent of a practice where it is not apparent from context. The quiz is presented as playful self-discovery ('What's your energy type?') but its actual purpose is to harvest personal data to build a marketing custom audience and drive targeted advertising. Minors are unlikely to grasp that completing the quiz enrols them into a profiling/retargeting system, which is a misleading omission of material information about the commercial purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: A branded 'What's your energy type?' quiz collects birthdate, school year, mood and interests; completions feed a custom audience
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose at the point of the quiz that it is advertising by VoltZ and that responses will be used to target them with ads; state what data is collected and why in child-comprehensible language, and make participation and profiling genuinely optional.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 bans, in all circumstances, any direct exhortation to children to buy the advertised product. This child-directed campaign is squarely in the risk zone, but the submitted text does not quote any actual creative wording, so a blacklist breach cannot be confirmed from the material provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Campaign for VoltZ energy drink on a short-video platform ... serves VoltZ ads to users aged 13-17
findings.recommendation: Review the actual ad creatives for any 'buy now', 'get yours', 'ask a parent' style calls to action directed at minors; remove any such direct purchase exhortation to avoid a per-se prohibited practice.

verdicts.notes: The VoltZ campaign is explicitly built around minors aged 13-17 — a group protected under UCPD Art. 5(3) due to age and credulity — and combines mood/behavioural profiling, a disguised data-harvesting quiz, always-on retargeting and late-night scheduling of a high-caffeine product. Under UCPD this engages the general unfairness/vulnerable-group standard (Art. 5), the aggressive-practices rules on timing and persistence (Arts. 8-9) and hidden commercial intent (Art. 7). The blacklist point 28 (direct exhortation to children) is not confirmed because no purchase-exhortation wording is quoted, but should be checked in the actual creatives. Overall the design is likely to materially distort the transactional behaviour of an average teenager and requires substantial redesign.

report.executive_summary: This VoltZ campaign targets 13-17 year-olds with a high-caffeine energy drink using a quiz that harvests birthdate, school year, mood and interests, then builds behavioural profiles ("gamer", "late-night scroller") to serve profiled ads late at night (22:00-01:00) via an always-on retargeting loop. As designed, it breaks multiple EU laws simultaneously — this is not fixable with tweaks or consent boxes. The single biggest problem is that presenting profiling-based ads to users you know are minors is outright banned under the DSA (Art. 28), and the AI-driven targeting that exploits the age and late-night vulnerability of teens hits the AI Act's prohibited-practices list (Art. 5) — the most serious tier of both regimes. On top of that, the campaign has no lawful basis, age-verification, parental consent, or transparency for processing children's data (GDPR), the "mood" data likely counts as sensitive data whose use for targeting is separately banned, and the disguised quiz plus relentless late-night re-serving amount to dark patterns and aggressive/unfair practices under the DSA and UCPD. The verdict is do-not-launch as configured; the concept requires fundamental redesign, not remediation at the margins. Targeting minors with profiled advertising for this product is the core defect and cannot be salvaged.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign in its current form. Stop building or serving any profiling-, behaviour- or custom-audience-based advertising to the 13-17 age group — this is a per-se prohibition under DSA Art. 28, not a curable risk.
Age-gate the entire campaign to 18+ and exclude all minors from audience-building and retargeting. If you cannot reliably verify adult age, do not run profiled ads at all.

Remove the 'mood' data collection entirely and exclude it (and any emotional/health inference) from all targeting — using such special-category data for ad targeting is separately banned under DSA Art. 26(3) and GDPR Art. 9.

Kill the always-on / 2-second retargeting loop and the 22:00-01:00 late-night scheduling; these constitute dark patterns (DSA Art. 25), aggressive practices (UCPD Arts. 8-9) and prohibited AI manipulation (AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)). Apply reasonable frequency caps at most.

For any lawful adult audience, establish and document a valid GDPR Art. 6 lawful basis (consent), provide a clear child/adult-appropriate privacy notice at collection (Arts. 12-13), separate marketing consent from quiz participation (Arts. 4(11), 7), and offer an easy, always-available opt-out from marketing profiling (Art. 21).
Redesign the quiz so its commercial intent is unmistakable up front — clearly label it as VoltZ advertising and disclose that responses feed ad targeting (UCPD Art. 7).

Ensure every ad placement is clearly labelled as advertising, discloses VoltZ as advertiser/payer, and exposes main targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26(1)); assume all creatives and targeting will be publicly archived if the platform is a VLOP (Art. 39).
Review the actual ad creatives for any direct 'buy now' exhortation to children, which is a per-se prohibited practice (UCPD Annex I, point 28).
Conduct a DPIA and obtain legal sign-off before any relaunch, mapping the national digital-consent age (13-16) per EU market.

campaign.title: FlexiPure joint supplement
campaign.text: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules: 'Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days — or your money back. Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers. Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently. Order today and end your arthritis forever.' Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference. Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.

detected_practices: health claim (disease cure/treatment)
unsubstantiated efficacy claim ('Clinically PROVEN', '97% cure rate' with no study reference)
misleading before/after X-ray imagery
'doctors don't want you to know' conspiracy framing
encouraging discontinuation of prescribed medication
money-back guarantee claim
permanence/absolute claims ('reverses joint damage permanently', 'end your arthritis forever')
checkout upsell / cross-sell ('diabetes reversal' bundle)
AI-generated marketing content
personalised targeting
targeting vulnerable audience (older adults with chronic illness)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults 50+ with chronic joint pain — a vulnerable consumer group (health condition, age) warranting heightened UCPD scrutiny for aggressive/misleading practices. Health-related personal data may be processed for personalisation (GDPR special category). Social/web distribution engages DSA (online platform advertising transparency, targeting rules). No indication minors are targeted, though supplement/health ads on social should confirm audience gating.
triage.summary: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure joint supplement making aggressive, unsubstantiated medical cure claims (arthritis cure in 30 days, '97% cure rate', misleading before/after X-rays) aimed at a vulnerable audience of adults 50+ with chronic joint pain. It uses generative AI content and personalised targeting, encourages discontinuation of prescription medication, and cross-sells an unsubstantiated 'diabetes reversal' bundle at checkout.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign is declared to use AI-driven personalised targeting directed at a specifically vulnerable group — adults 50+ with chronic joint pain (vulnerability due to age and health condition/disability). Combined with deceptive cure claims and encouragement to discontinue prescribed medication, an AI system used to target and tailor this messaging to that group has the objective or effect of materially distorting their behaviour in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm (health harm from stopping prescribed treatment). This engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting vulnerabilities of a group due to age or disability.
findings.evidence_quote: Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers... Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI targeting/personalisation to direct these claims at older adults or chronically ill consumers. Remove all encouragement to discontinue prescription medication and all curative claims. If any AI-based audience selection is used, ensure it cannot be configured to exploit age- or health-related vulnerability, and document a conformity/exploitation review before deployment.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign combines declared generative-AI content and AI personalisation with objectively false and deceptive claims (unsubstantiated '97% cure rate', fabricated proof, absolute permanence claims, conspiracy framing). Where an AI system deploys or delivers such purposefully deceptive/manipulative techniques to distort consumers' ability to make an informed decision and induce a purchase (and discontinuation of medication) they would not otherwise make, causing significant harm, the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative/deceptive AI techniques is engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days... reverses joint damage permanently... end your arthritis forever
findings.recommendation: Withdraw the deceptive claims and ensure any AI-generated or AI-optimised persuasion does not impair informed decision-making. Substantiate every efficacy claim with a cited study or remove it. Confirm that AI content-generation and optimisation tools are not being used to amplify deceptive messaging to consumers.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of generative AI ('Declared use of generative AI: yes'). AI-generated synthetic image and text content used in the campaign assets (including the before/after X-ray visuals and marketing copy if AI-generated) must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated under Art. 50(2). Nothing indicates this marking is applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure
findings.recommendation: Apply machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA/watermarking) to all AI-generated images and text used in the campaign, and confirm with the AI tool provider that outputs carry the required detectable marking.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: If the before/after X-ray images are AI-generated or AI-manipulated to appear as authentic medical evidence of a real outcome, they are realistic manipulated content of the deep-fake type. Under Art. 50(4) deployers must clearly disclose that such image content has been artificially generated or manipulated. No disclosure is indicated, and presenting synthetic medical imagery as genuine proof compounds the deception.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently disclose any AI generation/manipulation of the X-ray imagery. Better: do not use synthetic or manipulated medical imagery as evidence at all, as it cannot substantiate a genuine clinical outcome.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI for content and AI-driven personalised targeting of a vulnerable audience (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain), which engages three AI Act provisions. The most serious concern is that AI-based targeting/persuasion is combined with deceptive health claims and an exhortation to discontinue prescribed medication, potentially triggering the Art. 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(b) prohibitions (manipulation and exploitation of vulnerability causing significant harm). The AI-generated visuals (before/after X-rays) and copy also engage the Art. 50 transparency/marking obligations. Whether the Art. 5 prohibitions are actually breached depends on the extent to which the AI system itself drives the manipulative distortion — this needs verification, but the risk is high given the health-harm potential.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Targeting individuals selected/segmented by a chronic health condition (arthritis/joint pain) processes health data, a special category under Art. 9. Such data — whether collected directly or inferred to build the audience — is prohibited from processing unless a specific exception (e.g. explicit consent) applies. Nothing in the campaign indicates explicit consent for health-based marketing was obtained, so the health-based personalisation is likely unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Do not build or use audiences based on health status without a valid Art. 9 exception, in practice explicit, specific opt-in consent for health-based marketing profiling. If explicit consent cannot be reliably obtained and demonstrated, target on non-sensitive criteria only and remove health-condition segmentation.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Personalised targeting and audience segmentation is automated processing to evaluate/predict personal aspects (here, health, interests, behaviour) and therefore constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This brings the campaign within the GDPR profiling regime and triggers the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document the personalisation as profiling, map what data and inferences feed it, and ensure each downstream obligation (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) is met before launch.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising/profiling requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — generally consent, or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign identifies no lawful basis for the personalisation, and where health data is involved consent must additionally satisfy Art. 9.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for the personalisation before processing. For health-based targeting this must be explicit consent; carry out and retain the assessment.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where the personalisation relies on consent (mandatory for health-data targeting), Art. 7 requires that consent be freely given, specific, demonstrable, in clear language, and as easy to withdraw as to give. The campaign describes no consent mechanism, so these conditions are not shown to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Implement a granular, unbundled opt-in for health-based marketing profiling with an equally easy withdrawal mechanism, and retain records demonstrating valid consent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The landing page collects orders and (per declared personalisation) personal data, but no transparency information is described. Art. 13 requires, at the point of collection, the controller's identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data subject rights and information about profiling/automated decision-making.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at every data-collection point (landing page, checkout) covering all Art. 13 items, expressly including the health-based profiling and its legal basis.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is undermined where individuals are profiled by sensitive health status without a disclosed lawful basis or privacy information. Exploiting inferred health vulnerability for targeted marketing without transparency conflicts with the fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the processing is lawful (valid Art. 9/6 basis), transparent (Art. 13 notice) and fair — avoid covert inference of health status and do not exploit the audience's health vulnerability in the targeting logic.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalised targeting to an audience defined by health status ("adults 50+ with chronic joint pain"), which processes special category (health) data and constitutes profiling. This engages GDPR Art. 9 (requiring explicit consent, largely unmet as described), Art. 6(1) (lawful basis), Art. 4(4) (profiling), plus transparency/consent obligations under Arts. 5(1)(a), 7 and 13. No privacy notice, lawful basis, or consent mechanism is described, so the personalisation as framed is likely unlawful without substantial changes.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign is distributed on online platforms (web, social) with declared personalised targeting explicitly directed at people with a chronic health condition (joint pain/arthritis). Health status is a special category of personal data under GDPR Art. 9, referenced directly by DSA Art. 26(3). Presenting platform advertisements based on profiling that uses such data — whether declared directly or inferred via proxies — is prohibited outright, regardless of any consent obtained.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Do not target platform advertisements using health status or any proxy for it (e.g. arthritis/joint-pain interest segments, medical-condition lookalikes). Deliver ads via contextual placement (e.g. general 50+ wellness content) rather than health-based profiling, and document that no Art. 9 attribute — direct or inferred — feeds the targeting parameters.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As a personalised advertising campaign presented on online platforms, each ad must let recipients identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid for it, plus meaningful information on the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submitted material contains no ad label, advertiser/payer identity, or targeting-parameter disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: Web, Social ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure every platform placement carries a clear 'ad'/'sponsored' label, names the advertiser and the payer, and surfaces meaningful information about the main targeting parameters with a link to adjust them, consistent with the platform's DSA ad-transparency tooling.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Injecting an unrelated, unsubstantiated 'diabetes reversal' add-on into the checkout flow of a vulnerable, health-motivated audience can materially distort free and informed decision-making and, depending on how it is presented (pre-selection, prominence, steering), amount to a prohibited dark pattern in the platform interface under DSA Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.
findings.recommendation: Present any cross-sell neutrally: no pre-ticked/pre-added items, no false button hierarchy or confirm-shaming, and ensure the add-on carries its own truthful, substantiated claims. Review the checkout interface to confirm it does not steer or pressure the purchase decision.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on web and social platforms with declared personalised targeting explicitly aimed at "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain" — i.e. ad targeting based on health status, a GDPR Art. 9 special category. Presenting platform advertisements based on profiling using special-category data is flatly prohibited under DSA Art. 26(3), so this is the central and most serious DSA issue. The campaign also engages Art. 26(1) ad-transparency obligations (labelling, advertiser/payer identity, targeting-parameter disclosure), none of which are evidenced, and the checkout upsell raises a lower-level Art. 25 dark-pattern flag. Note that DSA advertising duties formally bind the online platform presenting the ad; the advertiser cannot lawfully procure such targeting.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 17 prohibits in all circumstances falsely claiming a product can cure illnesses. FlexiPure is a supplement and cannot cure arthritis; explicit claims to 'CURE arthritis', 'reverses joint damage permanently' and 'end your arthritis forever', plus the checkout 'diabetes reversal' bundle, are blacklisted false cure claims requiring no case-by-case unfairness test. The '97% cure rate' figure and before/after X-ray images reinforce the same prohibited curative representation.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days
findings.recommendation: Remove all curative, reversal and permanence claims entirely. A food supplement may not claim to cure, treat, reverse or prevent arthritis or diabetes. Any permitted health claim must be limited to authorised claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 and be scientifically substantiated.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 catches false or deceptive claims about a product's main characteristics (benefits, results) that cause a transactional decision. 'Clinically PROVEN', the '97% cure rate' with no study reference, and before/after X-ray images all create a false impression of proven medical efficacy that cannot be substantiated, deceiving the average consumer into purchasing.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Delete unsubstantiated efficacy claims and statistics. Only make claims that are backed by verifiable, referenced evidence and comply with the Health Claims Regulation; remove misleading before/after X-ray imagery unless it depicts genuine, representative, referenced clinical results.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 (with Art. 5(3)) treats as unfair practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group due to age, credulity or physical infirmity, assessed from that group's perspective. The declared audience is adults 50+ with chronic joint pain — a vulnerable group. The conspiracy framing ('Doctors don't want you to know') combined with personalised targeting exploits their condition and credulity, contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough
findings.recommendation: Remove conspiratorial 'doctors don't want you to know' framing and any messaging that exploits the health vulnerability of the target audience. Ensure claims meet professional-diligence standards appropriate for marketing to older, chronically ill consumers.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices using undue influence that significantly impair the consumer's freedom of choice, including exploitation of misfortune (here, chronic illness). Encouraging vulnerable, ill consumers to discontinue prescribed medication ('thrown away their prescription painkillers') and end their treatment applies undue influence exploiting their health situation and poses significant harm, distorting their transactional and health decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers
findings.recommendation: Remove all content encouraging or implying consumers should stop or replace prescribed medication or treatment. Include a clear statement that the product is not a substitute for medical treatment and that consumers should consult a healthcare professional.

verdicts.notes: This FlexiPure campaign contains multiple clear UCPD violations, most seriously a per se blacklisted false cure claim (Annex I point 17) for both arthritis and diabetes. It also makes exaggerated/unsubstantiated efficacy claims and misleading imagery/statistics (Art. 6), constitutes an unfair practice targeting a clearly vulnerable group of ill older adults (Art. 5), and applies aggressive undue-influence pressure by urging discontinuation of prescribed medication (Arts. 8-9). Immediate withdrawal or substantial rework is required before this campaign can run in the EU.

report.executive_summary: The FlexiPure campaign promotes a food supplement with claims that it is "clinically proven to cure arthritis," reverses joint damage permanently, and encourages people to throw away their prescription painkillers — plus a checkout upsell claiming to "reverse diabetes." These are outright illegal claims in the EU. A food supplement may never claim to cure disease, and doing so is an automatic, no-exceptions violation (UCPD blacklist). The campaign compounds this by targeting a vulnerable group (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain) using their health status, which breaks GDPR rules on sensitive data and is flatly banned for platform ad targeting under the DSA. The declared use of generative AI (including unlabelled before/after X-ray images) triggers further AI Act problems, from transparency-marking failures up to the prohibited-practice zone because AI-driven persuasion is aimed at a vulnerable audience and encourages stopping medication. Urging ill consumers to discontinue prescribed treatment also creates real health-harm risk and qualifies as an aggressive practice. This campaign cannot run in its current form and requires withdrawal, not tweaks. A substantial rebuild is needed before anything goes live.
recommendations: Do not launch. Remove every curative, reversal and permanence claim ('CURE arthritis', 'reverses joint damage permanently', 'end your arthritis forever') and delete the 'diabetes reversal' upsell entirely — these are per se illegal false cure claims for a supplement (UCPD Annex I point 17).

Delete the '97% cure rate' statistic, the 'Clinically PROVEN' wording and the before/after X-ray images. Only use health claims that are authorised under the EU Health Claims Regulation and backed by referenced evidence.

Remove all content telling consumers to stop or replace prescription medication ('thrown away their prescription painkillers') and add a clear statement that the product is not a substitute for medical treatment and users should consult a healthcare professional.

Stop targeting ads by health status. Health-condition targeting is banned outright for platform ads (DSA Art. 26(3)) and unlawful without explicit consent under GDPR Art. 9. Switch to contextual placement (e.g. general 50+ wellness content) and confirm no health attribute or proxy feeds the targeting.

Remove the conspiratorial 'Doctors don't want you to know' framing and any messaging that exploits the audience's age or illness (UCPD Arts. 5 and 8-9; AI Act Art. 5 prohibitions on manipulative/vulnerability-exploiting AI).

If personalisation is retained on non-sensitive criteria, implement a compliant data setup: a lawful basis, a granular opt-in consent mechanism, an easy withdrawal option, and a full privacy notice at every collection point (GDPR Arts. 5, 6, 7, 13).

For any AI-generated images or copy, apply machine-readable provenance marking and clearly disclose AI generation/manipulation (AI Act Art. 50). Do not use synthetic or manipulated medical imagery as evidence at all.

Ensure every platform ad carries a clear 'ad/sponsored' label, names the advertiser and payer, and discloses main targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26(1)); present any cross-sell neutrally with no pre-ticked items or steering (DSA Art. 25).

campaign.text: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules: 'Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days — or your money back. Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers. Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference. Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.

triage.audience_notes: Explicitly targets a vulnerable group — older adults (50+) suffering chronic joint pain — heightening UCPD aggressive/misleading-practice concerns; claims to reverse serious diseases (arthritis, diabetes) are prohibited unfair commercial practices and likely breach EU health/nutrition claim rules. No indication minors are targeted.
triage.summary: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure joint supplement using generative AI content and personalised targeting, aimed at adults 50+ with chronic joint pain. It makes prohibited/unsubstantiated medical claims (curing arthritis, '97% cure rate', reversing joint damage, before/after X-rays) plus an upsell claiming to reverse diabetes. The messaging pressures and exploits vulnerable, chronically ill consumers.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign uses AI-driven personalisation/targeting explicitly directed at a group vulnerable by reason of age (older adults) and a health-related situation (chronic joint pain / chronic illness). Coupled with claims urging them to 'throw away their prescription painkillers' and 'end your arthritis forever', the targeting has the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of that vulnerable group in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm — abandonment of medically necessary treatment and financial loss to consumers with limited means. This is the exact scenario Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI-based targeting or personalisation that keys on age or chronic-illness vulnerability to promote unproven health products. Remove exhortations to abandon prescribed medication, and gate any health-product targeting so it cannot exploit vulnerability. If personalisation is retained, ensure it cannot distort decisions in a way that risks health or financial harm.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign is declared as AI-generated and deploys purposefully deceptive/manipulative techniques — conspiracy framing ('Doctors don't want you to know'), a fabricated '97% cure rate', unreferenced 'clinically PROVEN' claims and before/after X-ray 'proof'. When such deceptive content is produced and delivered via an AI system, it appreciably impairs the target's ability to make an informed decision and causes them to take decisions (stopping medication, purchasing) they would not otherwise take, in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant health and financial harm — engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative/deceptive AI techniques.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently
findings.recommendation: Remove the deceptive and manipulative messaging (conspiracy appeals, unsubstantiated cure/percentage claims, fabricated imagery). Ensure any AI system used to generate or target marketing does not employ deceptive techniques that distort informed decision-making. Substantiate every efficacy claim with verifiable evidence before publication.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign confirms generative AI is used to create marketing assets (copy and likely the '97% cure rate' figure and possibly the before/after X-ray images). Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic image/text content must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. Nothing in the submission indicates the AI-generated assets carry any provenance marking. If the before/after X-ray images are AI-generated or AI-manipulated realistic imagery, this obligation is especially acute.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Apply machine-readable synthetic-content marking (e.g. C2PA/provenance metadata) to all AI-generated copy and visuals. Confirm whether the before/after X-ray images are AI-generated or manipulated; if so, mark them accordingly (and note undisclosed manipulated realistic imagery may also engage Art. 50(4) deep-fake disclosure). Maintain records of which assets are AI-generated.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI content and AI-driven behavioural personalisation, both of which squarely engage the AI Act. Two Article 5 prohibitions are likely triggered: AI-driven targeting explicitly aimed at a group vulnerable by age and health status (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain), combined with deceptive persuasion designed to make them abandon prescription treatment and buy the product, is reasonably likely to cause significant health and financial harm (Art. 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(a)). Separately, AI-generated campaign assets — including potentially fabricated before/after X-ray images — must carry machine-readable synthetic-content marking under Art. 50(2), with nothing in the submission indicating this is done. Other laws (UCPD health-cure blacklist, GDPR Art. 9 health data, DSA) are handled by parallel agents.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Personalisation/targeting is declared 'yes' and the audience is defined by a health condition (chronic joint pain / arthritis). Segmenting or reaching people because they have a particular medical condition — whether from data they provide, inference, or proxy signals — means processing data revealing health status, a special category under Art. 9. Such processing is prohibited unless a specific exception applies, and the only realistic marketing basis is the data subject's explicit consent, which is not evidenced anywhere in the submission.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Do not target or segment audiences on the basis of joint pain, arthritis, diabetes or any inferred health status without freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous explicit consent obtained before processing. If explicit consent cannot be reliably secured, remove health-condition targeting and rely on non-sensitive, contextual criteria instead. Document the Art. 9 exception relied upon.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/targeting to a defined health-condition audience is automated processing used to evaluate/predict personal aspects (health, interests, behaviour) of individuals, and therefore constitutes profiling within Art. 4(4). This triggers the associated GDPR obligations on lawful basis, transparency and the right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Map and document the profiling logic used to build and reach this audience, and ensure each stage has a lawful basis, transparency information and an easy objection route. Where the profiling analyses health, treat it as Art. 9 processing requiring explicit consent.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising/profiling requires a valid legal basis. Behavioural personalisation generally needs consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment; where the processing touches health data, legitimate interest is not available and explicit consent is required. The submission identifies no lawful basis for the targeting and profiling described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and record the Art. 6(1) lawful basis for the personalisation before launch. For the health-related targeting, use explicit consent (Art. 9(2)(a)); for any e-mail/SMS follow-up, secure prior opt-in consent. Keep a documented assessment on file.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that individuals are not deceived about data processing. A campaign built on knowingly false medical claims ('97% cure rate', 'clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis') that simultaneously profiles and targets vulnerable chronically ill consumers cannot be considered fair processing, and no transparent information about the data handling is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure capsules
findings.recommendation: Ensure any personal data collected or used for this campaign is processed on a fair, non-deceptive basis with clear, accurate privacy information; misleading efficacy claims taint the fairness of associated processing and should be corrected before any data is used.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The landing page and checkout collect personal data (order/lead data, and targeting signals). Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller provide its identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and information about profiling. Nothing in the submission indicates a privacy notice is presented at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, layered privacy notice at every point of data collection (landing page, checkout, any sign-up), including purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients, data-subject rights and details of any profiling used for targeting.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Because the campaign involves direct marketing and profiling related to it, data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time, and the controller must inform them of this right explicitly and facilitate opt-out. The submission describes no opt-out or objection mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide an explicit, prominent notice of the right to object to direct marketing and profiling, and implement an easy opt-out (e.g. one-click unsubscribe and suppression list) that is honoured immediately.

verdicts.notes: The campaign combines declared personalisation/targeting with an explicit health-based audience — "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain." Targeting on the basis of a health condition means processing special-category data under GDPR Art. 9, which is prohibited absent explicit consent, and the segmentation constitutes profiling requiring a valid lawful basis (Art. 4(4), 6(1)). The submission discloses no consent flow, transparency notice, or opt-out mechanism, so the fairness/transparency and objection obligations are also engaged and appear unmet. GDPR risk is substantial; the exact severity depends on data flows not fully described, so most findings are graded medium/high.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign explicitly uses personalised/behavioural targeting on social platforms, and the declared audience is defined by a health condition (chronic joint pain / arthritis). Presenting platform advertisements based on profiling that uses special categories of personal data under GDPR Art. 9 — including health status, whether captured directly or by inference — is prohibited under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of any consent. A joint-pain/arthritis product deliberately targeted to chronically ill older adults falls squarely within this ban.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Do not target the social/platform ads using any health-related segments, inferences or proxies (e.g. arthritis interest, joint-pain audiences, chronic-illness lookalikes). Restrict delivery to non-sensitive, contextual criteria only (e.g. general age/interest categories not derived from health status), and document that no Art. 9 attribute is used directly or by inference.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The online interface uses manipulative urgency and pressure framing ('Order today', 'end your arthritis forever') and steers users at checkout into an unrelated 'diabetes reversal' bundle. This kind of pressure and steering toward additional purchases can materially distort recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, engaging the DSA Art. 25 prohibition on dark patterns in online interface design.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever ... Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.
findings.recommendation: Remove artificial urgency and 'forever/end' pressure language from the interface; present any cross-sell of the additional bundle as a neutral, non-preselected, clearly optional choice with truthful information, and ensure no confirm-shaming, preselected add-ons or obstruction of declining.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is delivered as advertisements on social platforms with declared paid personalisation/targeting. DSA Art. 26(1) requires that each ad be identifiable in real time as an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submission gives no indication that these transparency elements are in place.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: Web, Social
findings.recommendation: Ensure each social placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement, discloses the advertiser (FlexiPure) and payer, and surfaces the main targeting parameters with a means to change them, in line with the platform's Art. 26(1) tooling.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social platforms with declared personalisation/targeting of a health-defined audience (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain). Targeting platform ads on the basis of health status is flatly prohibited under DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent — the most serious DSA issue. The landing-page/checkout design also engages the dark-patterns prohibition (Art. 25) through manipulative urgency and an unrelated health upsell, and the ads must meet Art. 26(1) transparency (ad labelling, advertiser identity, targeting parameters), which nothing in the submission satisfies. DSA obligations bind the platform provider, but the advertiser's targeting choices and interface design are what trigger them.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 17 prohibits in all circumstances falsely claiming that a product can cure illnesses. FlexiPure is a food supplement marketed as curing arthritis 'in 30 days', reversing joint damage 'permanently' and ending arthritis 'forever'. The checkout upsell adds a 'diabetes reversal' bundle — a second disease-cure claim. Both are blacklisted per se; no substantiation can lawfully support a supplement curing these conditions, and none is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days
findings.recommendation: Remove all curative/disease-reversal claims entirely (arthritis and diabetes). Supplement marketing may only use authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 (e.g. limited joint-comfort wording if authorised); it cannot claim to cure, reverse or eliminate any disease.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 makes it a misleading action to give false or unsubstantiated information about a product's main characteristics, benefits and results that causes consumers to transact. The '97% cure rate', 'Clinically PROVEN', 'reverses joint damage permanently' and the before/after X-ray imagery present unverifiable efficacy as established scientific fact with no cited study, deceiving the average consumer.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Delete unsubstantiated efficacy figures and 'clinically proven' language, or replace only with claims backed by properly referenced, methodologically sound evidence and authorised under the Health Claims Regulation. Remove before/after X-ray images used as proof of efficacy.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (by age or infirmity) to be assessed from that group's perspective. The campaign explicitly targets older adults suffering chronic joint pain and exploits their condition with cure promises, contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour. This acts as the fairness safety-net over the specific breaches.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Do not design messaging that exploits the health vulnerability of the targeted group; ensure all claims meet professional-diligence standards and are truthful and substantiated for the average member of that vulnerable audience.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices using undue influence that impair freedom of choice, with express regard to exploitation of consumers' misfortune (here, chronic illness). Combining time pressure ('Order today') with an emotive promise to 'end your arthritis forever' aimed at chronically ill older adults exerts undue influence exploiting their condition and health anxiety.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever
findings.recommendation: Remove pressure-and-fear framing that leverages the consumers' medical condition; present the product neutrally without urgency tied to health outcomes.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The conspiracy/appeal-to-authority framing invokes the medical profession to lend credibility. If any medical or scientific approval/endorsement is implied ('clinically proven', doctor-related messaging) without a genuine endorsing body, Annex I point 4 prohibits falsely claiming approval or endorsement. At minimum this reinforces the misleading-action finding by suggesting suppressed authoritative validation.
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough
findings.recommendation: Remove any implied medical/institutional endorsement. Only reference an approval or endorsement where a named, genuine body has actually granted it and the terms are complied with.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or obscuring material information consumers need. The 'money-back guarantee' is stated without any conditions, timeframe or process, and the upsell of a 'diabetes reversal' bundle at checkout risks obscuring material terms. Undisclosed conditions of a guarantee are material information whose omission can mislead.
findings.evidence_quote: or your money back
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full, clear conditions of the money-back guarantee (eligibility, deadline, refund process) prominently, and present any bundle upsell with transparent pricing and terms rather than at the point of checkout pressure.

verdicts.notes: The FlexiPure campaign makes explicit, unqualified disease-cure claims for a supplement — a practice blacklisted outright under UCPD Annex I point 17 (arthritis and, via the upsell, diabetes). It compounds this with unsubstantiated "clinically PROVEN" / "97% cure rate" efficacy claims backed by uncited "studies" and before/after X-rays (misleading actions, Art. 6), false urgency framing, and high-pressure tactics deliberately aimed at a vulnerable audience (older adults with chronic illness), engaging Arts. 5 and 8-9. Several findings are critical because they concern per se prohibited practices requiring no case-by-case unfairness test.

report.executive_summary: This campaign for FlexiPure joint capsules cannot run in anything close to its current form — it breaches multiple EU laws at once, several of them in ways that are banned outright with no possibility of justification. The core problem is that it claims a food supplement can "CURE arthritis in 30 days," "reverse joint damage permanently," and (via the checkout upsell) reverse diabetes. Disease-cure claims for supplements are flatly prohibited under EU consumer law, and the "97% cure rate," "clinically PROVEN" wording, before/after X-rays, and "doctors don't want you to know" framing are all deceptive and unsubstantiated. On top of the content problems, you are targeting a health-defined, vulnerable audience (adults 50+ with chronic joint pain) using personalisation — this triggers a hard ban on health-based ad targeting on social platforms, requires explicit consent under data-protection rules that isn't in place, and engages the AI Act's prohibitions because AI is used to generate and target manipulative content aimed at a vulnerable group. The checkout's urgency tactics and unrelated diabetes upsell add dark-pattern and aggressive-practice risks, and encouraging people to abandon prescription painkillers creates real health-harm exposure. In short: this is not a matter of tweaking wording — the campaign needs to be rebuilt from the ground up before any launch. Do not deploy it as submitted.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign in its current form. The disease-cure claims and health-based targeting are outright prohibited, not merely risky.

Remove ALL curative and disease-reversal claims — for both arthritis and diabetes. Never state or imply the supplement cures, reverses, or ends any disease. Only use health claims authorised under the EU Health Claims Regulation (e.g. limited joint-comfort wording, if authorised).
Delete the diabetes-reversal upsell bundle entirely; it is a second banned disease-cure claim.

Remove all deceptive 'proof': the '97% cure rate' figure, 'clinically PROVEN' language, and the before/after X-ray images. Any retained efficacy statement must be backed by properly referenced, authorised evidence.

Remove the 'Doctors don't want you to know' conspiracy framing and any implied medical endorsement, and delete the exhortation to throw away prescription painkillers — this creates serious health-harm liability.

Stop targeting the ads by health status. Health-based ad targeting on social platforms is banned under the DSA regardless of consent — do not use arthritis/joint-pain/chronic-illness segments, inferences, or lookalikes. Use only non-sensitive, contextual criteria.

If any personalisation is retained, secure explicit GDPR consent before processing health-related data, add clear privacy notices at every collection point, document a lawful basis and the profiling logic, and provide an easy opt-out from direct marketing.
Remove artificial urgency ('Order today', 'end your arthritis forever') and the pressured checkout upsell; present any cross-sell as a neutral, non-preselected, clearly optional choice.
Disclose full money-back guarantee terms (eligibility, deadline, refund process) prominently.
Apply machine-readable provenance marking to all AI-generated copy and images, and confirm whether the X-ray images are AI-generated/manipulated — if so, disclose them accordingly.

Ensure the AI system is not used to generate or target manipulative content aimed at vulnerable groups, and label social placements as advertisements with advertiser identity and targeting-parameter transparency.
