personalisation/behavioural targeting
triage.audience_notes: Declared target audience is adults 50+ with chronic joint pain — a vulnerable group due to age and health condition, heightening UCPD scrutiny of misleading/aggressive practices. No indication minors are targeted, but health and inferred medical-condition data used for targeting is special-category data under GDPR.
triage.summary: Web and social campaign for FlexiPure joint supplement making aggressive, unsubstantiated medical claims (curing/reversing arthritis, '97% cure rate', 'clinically proven') with before/after X-rays, conspiracy framing, and a checkout upsell for 'diabetes reversal'. Uses generative AI content and personalisation/targeting aimed at older adults with chronic pain. Multiple potentially misleading and health-related claims raise serious consumer-protection concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares that generative AI produced marketing content, so AI-generated audio/image/video/text outputs are used in campaign assets. Art. 50(2) requires such synthetic outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. The submission gives no indication that any AI-generated copy or imagery carries provenance marking, so the obligation is engaged and apparently unmet as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets (copy, images, video) embed machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA/watermarking) indicating they are artificially generated, and confirm the AI provider supplies compliant marking. Document which assets are AI-generated.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The before/after X-ray images are realistic images presented as authentic medical evidence. Combined with the declared use of generative AI, if these visuals are AI-generated or AI-manipulated they constitute artificially generated/manipulated realistic content that appears authentic (deep-fake-type content) and must be disclosed as AI-generated under Art. 50(4). Presenting synthetic X-rays as genuine clinical proof without disclosure would breach this transparency duty (and independently mislead consumers).
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether the X-ray images and other realistic visuals are AI-generated or AI-manipulated. If so, clearly disclose that they are artificially generated/manipulated; ideally remove synthetic medical imagery presented as real clinical evidence entirely, as it cannot substantiate the efficacy claims.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: AI-driven personalisation/targeting is declared and directed at a group vulnerable due to age (50+) and a health condition (chronic joint pain). The messaging materially distorts behaviour by urging consumers to 'throw away their prescription painkillers' and 'end your arthritis forever', which is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (discontinuing necessary medication). Where an AI system exploits such age/health/situational vulnerability to distort behaviour and cause significant harm, Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits the practice. This is engaged to the extent AI targeting selects or tailors delivery to this vulnerable group.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI targeting/personalisation to select or tailor this campaign to people inferred to be older or in chronic pain. Remove content encouraging discontinuation of prescribed medication. Have the AI targeting logic reviewed to ensure it does not exploit age- or health-based vulnerability; restrict inputs used for audience selection accordingly.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign combines declared AI-generated persuasive content and AI personalisation with deceptive framing (conspiracy narrative, false 'cure'/'clinically proven'/'97% cure rate' claims) designed to impair informed decision-making and cause purchases and harmful medical decisions. To the extent the AI system deploys these deceptive/manipulative techniques with the effect of materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm, Art. 5(1)(a) may be engaged. Flagged as a risk pending confirmation of how far AI drives the persuasion mechanism (the underlying deception is primarily a UCPD matter).
findings.evidence_quote: Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough that reverses joint damage permanently.
findings.recommendation: Ensure AI-generated copy does not deploy deceptive or manipulative techniques; remove the false 'cure'/'clinically proven'/'97%' claims and conspiracy framing. Establish human review and guardrails so the AI system cannot generate or amplify manipulative health claims that could distort consumers' decisions.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI for marketing content and AI-driven personalisation/targeting, which brings it within the AI Act's transparency regime (Art. 50) and potentially the prohibited-practice regime (Art. 5). The most concrete engagement is the absence of any AI-generation marking/disclosure on AI-produced assets, notably the realistic before/after X-ray images (Arts. 50(2) and 50(4)). Because AI is used to target a group vulnerable by age and health condition with content likely to cause significant harm (urging discontinuation of prescription painkillers), the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition is also plausibly engaged and warrants scrutiny. Note that the substance of the deceptive medical claims falls primarily under UCPD; the AI Act findings concern the AI-specific dimensions.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Segmenting and targeting an audience defined by a chronic health condition (arthritis/joint pain) constitutes processing of data concerning health — a special category under Art. 9 — whether the attribute is collected directly or inferred from behaviour. Such processing is prohibited unless a specific exception applies, and the only realistic marketing exception is the data subject's explicit consent. The campaign describes no explicit-consent mechanism, so the Art. 9 prohibition is engaged and likely breached.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Do not target or segment audiences on health status/arthritis unless you have collected valid, freely given, specific and explicit consent (GDPR Art. 9(2)(a)) for that specific purpose, and document it. If explicit consent cannot be obtained, remove health-condition targeting entirely and rely on non-sensitive, contextual signals. Note that for platform-served ads, targeting on Art. 9 categories is separately banned regardless of consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/behavioural targeting to evaluate and predict audience health interests is automated processing to evaluate personal aspects of individuals and therefore constitutes profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This characterisation is what brings the campaign within the GDPR obligations on lawful basis, transparency, and the right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Recognise the targeting as profiling and apply the full GDPR profiling regime: identify a lawful basis, provide profiling information under Art. 13, and honour objection rights under Art. 21.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising / profiling requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Because the targeting relies on health data, legitimate interests is not an adequate basis and explicit consent is effectively required (aligning Art. 6 with Art. 9). The campaign text discloses no lawful basis or consent flow, so lawfulness of the profiling is not established as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6(1) basis for the profiling — in practice explicit consent given the health dimension — before running personalised targeting. Do not fall back on legitimate interests for health-based segmentation.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that individuals are not subjected to covert or unfair processing. Targeting a vulnerable group (older adults in pain) using inferred health data, with no visible privacy information or explanation of targeting parameters, is neither transparent nor fair as described, compounding the Art. 9/Art. 6 issues.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the processing is transparent and fair: clearly disclose that health-related targeting occurs, avoid exploiting the audience's vulnerability, and provide accessible privacy information at every collection point.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The landing page collects/processes personal data (checkout, targeting) but the campaign describes no privacy notice. Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller provide identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data subject rights, and information about profiling. None of this is present as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Landing page shows before/after X-ray images and a '97% cure rate' figure
findings.recommendation: Add a layered Art. 13 privacy notice at every data-collection point (landing page, checkout, any sign-up), including the identity of the controller, purposes and legal basis, retention periods, recipients, data subject rights, and the existence and logic of any profiling.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Where personal data is processed for direct marketing, including related profiling, data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time. The campaign shows no opt-out or objection mechanism for the marketing/profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy-to-use objection/opt-out mechanism in every marketing communication and on the landing page, and suppress objecting individuals from further marketing and profiling immediately.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation/behavioural targeting aimed specifically at "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain," which means the audience is segmented on health status — a special category of personal data. Under GDPR this triggers the Art. 9 prohibition (processing of health data is banned absent an exception such as explicit consent), and the profiling requires a valid Art. 6 lawful basis plus transparency (Arts. 4(4), 5(1)(a), 13) and respect for the right to object (Art. 21). The campaign text discloses no consent mechanism, lawful basis, privacy information, or opt-out, so the health-based targeting is likely unlawful as described. Findings below assume the controller is the advertiser processing/segmenting on health condition; some points are cross-linked to DSA Art. 26(3) which is another agent's remit.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The campaign is delivered on social platforms with declared personalisation/targeting to an audience defined by a health condition ('chronic joint pain'). Health status is a special category of personal data under GDPR Art. 9. DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of data — directly or by inference — regardless of any consent obtained. Targeting people by their arthritis/joint-pain condition therefore falls squarely within the prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Stop all platform ad targeting that segments audiences by health condition or proxies for it (joint pain, arthritis interest, painkiller-related behaviour). Reach audiences only through contextual (non-profiled) placements or broad demographics that do not rely on health-related attributes. Document that no Art. 9 data or inferred health attributes are used in targeting parameters.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The landing page and checkout combine high-pressure urgency ('Order today', 'end your arthritis forever'), conspiracy framing ('Doctors don't want you to know') and a checkout upsell of a second unproven health product ('diabetes reversal' bundle) aimed at a vulnerable older, health-anxious audience. Such interface and communication design may deceive or manipulate recipients and materially impair their ability to make a free and informed transactional decision, which DSA Art. 25 prohibits for online-platform interfaces.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever ... Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle.
findings.recommendation: Remove manipulative and pressure-based interface elements, present the upsell neutrally (no exploitation of health fears, clear opt-in, no prominence bias), and ensure the checkout flow does not steer users through deceptive framing. Align the interface with Art. 25's requirement not to distort free/informed decision-making.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: As a paid social-platform advertising campaign, DSA Art. 26(1) requires that each ad be clearly identifiable as an advertisement in real time, disclose on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submission gives no indication these disclosures are in place.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: Web, Social
findings.recommendation: Ensure every social placement carries the platform's ad label, the advertiser/payer identity, and accessible information on the main targeting parameters and how users can adjust them, as required by Art. 26(1).

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social platforms with declared personalisation/targeting aimed at "adults 50+ with chronic joint pain" — i.e. profiling using health data, a GDPR Art. 9 special category. Presenting platform advertisements based on such profiling is flatly prohibited by DSA Art. 26(3) regardless of consent, making this the central DSA violation. The interface design (pressure/urgency messaging plus a checkout upsell exploiting health anxiety of a vulnerable group) also raises a dark-patterns concern under Art. 25, and standard ad-transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)) apply. The underlying false-cure and misleading-claim conduct is primarily a UCPD matter handled by another agent.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 17 prohibits, in all circumstances, falsely claiming that a product can cure illnesses. FlexiPure is a food supplement, not an authorised medicine; arthritis is a chronic condition with no supplement cure. The claims to 'CURE arthritis', 'reverses joint damage permanently' and 'end your arthritis forever' are per-se blacklisted regardless of any qualifiers, requiring no proof of consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: Clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis in 30 days
findings.recommendation: Remove all curative/reversal claims entirely. Supplements may only carry authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006; do not state or imply cure, reversal or permanent elimination of arthritis or any disease.

findings.title: Blacklist: false cure claims
findings.rationale: The upsell of a 'diabetes reversal' product is a second false cure claim, also caught in all circumstances by Annex I point 17. Claiming to reverse diabetes via a bundle product is a curative claim for a serious chronic condition.
findings.evidence_quote: Checkout upsells a 'diabetes reversal' bundle
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'diabetes reversal' bundle claim; no supplement may be marketed as reversing diabetes. Any cross-sell must be free of disease cure/reversal messaging.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits false or deceptive claims about a product's main characteristics, benefits and results that cause consumers to transact. The '97% cure rate', 'Clinically PROVEN', and before/after X-ray images present specific, quantified and medical-grade efficacy claims with no substantiation or study reference, deceiving the average consumer (especially the vulnerable target group) about the product's actual effects.
findings.evidence_quote: a '97% cure rate' figure with no study reference
findings.recommendation: Delete the unsubstantiated '97% cure rate', 'clinically proven' wording and the before/after X-ray imagery. Only make efficacy claims that are authorised and backed by robust, referenced scientific evidence held on file.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or obscuring material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision. The conspiracy framing and encouragement to abandon prescription medication omits the material fact that FlexiPure is an unproven supplement and that discontinuing prescribed treatment carries health risks; it provides medically material information in a misleading, one-sided manner.
findings.evidence_quote: Thousands have thrown away their prescription painkillers. Doctors don't want you to know about this natural breakthrough
findings.recommendation: Remove conspiracy framing and any message encouraging discontinuation of prescription medication. Provide balanced, non-misleading information and, given the health context, advise consumers to consult a healthcare professional.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive practices those that use undue influence to impair the average consumer's freedom of choice, with exploitation of misfortune and pressure as key factors. Directing high-pressure, fear-and-hope messaging at older adults suffering chronic pain — exploiting their misfortune and combining urgency ('order today') with false cure promises — significantly impairs informed choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Order today and end your arthritis forever.
findings.recommendation: Remove high-pressure urgency combined with health promises. Do not exploit the target audience's pain/condition to force immediate purchase decisions.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net; Art. 5(3) requires the practice to be assessed from the perspective of the average member of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where one is targeted. The campaign explicitly targets older adults with a chronic health condition — vulnerable by age and physical infirmity — so the aggregate of false cure claims, conspiracy framing and pressure is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: adults 50+ with chronic joint pain
findings.recommendation: Given the vulnerable target audience, apply heightened diligence: eliminate the misleading/aggressive elements above and ensure all remaining messaging would not distort the decision of an average older adult with joint pain.

verdicts.notes: The FlexiPure campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including at least one per-se blacklisted practice. The core claim that a supplement is "clinically PROVEN to CURE arthritis" and "reverses joint damage permanently" is a false cure claim prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 17, and is compounded by unsubstantiated efficacy claims, conspiracy framing and before/after imagery that constitute misleading actions (Art. 6). Because the campaign explicitly targets a vulnerable group (adults 50+ with chronic pain) with high-pressure, medically dangerous messaging, the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer standard and the aggressive-practice rules (Arts. 8-9) apply with heightened scrutiny. Overall this is a high-risk campaign requiring substantial rework before it can be lawful.

report.executive_summary: This campaign for FlexiPure cannot run in anything close to its current form. Its central claims — that the supplement is "clinically proven to cure arthritis," "reverses joint damage permanently," and delivers a "97% cure rate," plus the checkout "diabetes reversal" upsell — are outright banned false cure claims for a food supplement and are illegal in all circumstances under EU consumer law, no matter what disclaimers you add. On top of that, the campaign deliberately targets a vulnerable group (adults 50+ in chronic pain), urges them to throw away prescription medication, and uses fear and high-pressure tactics, which compounds the unlawfulness and creates real safety risk. Targeting people by their health condition ("chronic joint pain") on social platforms is separately and flatly prohibited by the DSA regardless of consent, and processing that health data breaches GDPR, which requires explicit consent, a privacy notice and an opt-out that the campaign lacks. Because generative AI is used, any AI-generated assets — especially the before/after X-ray images presented as real medical evidence — must be marked and disclosed, and the AI-driven targeting of a vulnerable audience may itself be a prohibited AI practice. In short: multiple critical violations across four regulations. This is not a fixable-with-tweaks campaign; the core proposition and targeting model must be rebuilt.
recommendations: Remove ALL cure/reversal claims immediately — both the arthritis 'cure/reverses joint damage/end arthritis forever' messaging and the 'diabetes reversal' upsell bundle. These are per-se illegal false cure claims (UCPD Annex I point 17) and must go entirely, not be softened.

Delete the unsubstantiated efficacy claims ('clinically proven', '97% cure rate') and the before/after X-ray images. Only use authorised health claims backed by referenced evidence you hold on file (Regulation 1924/2006).

Remove any content urging consumers to stop prescription medication and all conspiracy framing ('Doctors don't want you to know'); this is a serious safety and misleading-omission issue. Add advice to consult a healthcare professional.

Stop targeting or segmenting the audience by health condition (joint pain/arthritis) on any platform. DSA Art. 26(3) bans this outright even with consent — switch to contextual or broad, non-health-based placements only.

For any remaining personal-data processing, establish a GDPR lawful basis (explicit consent given the health context), add a layered privacy notice at the landing page and checkout, and provide a clear opt-out/objection mechanism.
Strip out dark patterns and pressure tactics from the landing page and checkout ('order today', fear-based urgency, exploitative upsell); present any cross-sell neutrally with clear opt-in.

Mark all AI-generated assets as artificially generated (machine-readable provenance) and disclose AI-generated realistic imagery. Confirm whether the X-ray images are AI-generated — if so, disclose and, given they cannot substantiate anything, remove them.
Ensure all social placements carry proper ad labelling, advertiser/payer identity, and targeting-parameter transparency (DSA Art. 26(1)).

Have the AI targeting/personalisation logic reviewed so it does not select or exploit users inferred to be older or in chronic pain (potential prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5), and put human review/guardrails on AI-generated health copy.
Given the number of critical issues, pause the campaign and rebuild the core proposition and targeting model before any relaunch, with legal sign-off.

campaign.title: ScanGenius 'free' PDF app
campaign.text: App-install ads: 'ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!' After install, the app requires account creation and starts a 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled; the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen. App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title. Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.

detected_practices: 'Free' claim contradicted by recurring subscription (drip pricing / hidden costs)
Free trial auto-converting to €11.99/week subscription
Material price information buried in small grey text on fourth onboarding screen
'No hidden costs' claim that is misleading
Omission of recurring charge and cancellation method in confirmation email
Subscription trap / obstacles to cancellation
Mandatory account creation to access 'free' app
triage.summary: An app-install and display campaign for 'ScanGenius', advertised as a '100% FREE' PDF scanner with 'no hidden costs', that in fact triggers a 3-day trial auto-converting to an €11.99/week subscription, with the price hidden in small grey text and no mention of the recurring charge or cancellation in the confirmation email. This presents classic misleading/omission and subscription-trap patterns. Mandatory account creation means personal data is processed.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Mandatory account creation collects personal data (at minimum account/email data) at the point of sign-up. Art. 13 requires that, at the moment of collection, the controller provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention periods and data-subject rights. The campaign describes a forced onboarding/registration flow but shows no privacy information being surfaced at that point, so the Art. 13 information obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Present a concise, layered privacy notice at the account-creation screen covering controller identity, processing purposes and legal basis, retention, recipients and data-subject rights, before the user submits registration data.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information addressed to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible, in clear and plain language. The onboarding flow's demonstrated design habit of hiding material terms in small grey text signals that any data-processing/privacy information is likely presented in the same non-transparent, hard-to-access manner, contrary to Art. 12.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Ensure privacy/data-processing information is displayed in clear, legible, plain language with adequate contrast and prominence — not buried, greyed-out, or deferred — and is easily accessible throughout the onboarding flow.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle governs how personal data is processed. Inducing users to create accounts and hand over personal data through a materially misleading premise ('100% FREE / no hidden costs' that in fact conceals a recurring charge and buries terms) makes the data collection unfair and non-transparent, engaging Art. 5(1)(a) — data obtained via deception is not fairly processed.
findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: Align the acquisition journey with the fairness principle: only collect account data after truthful, upfront disclosure of price and terms, so consumers understand what they are signing up to before providing personal data.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing account data requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis (likely contract for delivering the service, or consent). The campaign discloses no basis. If any data processing goes beyond what is necessary to provide the scanner (e.g. marketing), a separate valid basis is needed and cannot be bundled into mandatory registration.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Document and disclose the Art. 6(1) legal basis for each processing purpose; keep processing strictly necessary for service delivery under the contract basis and obtain separate, freely given consent for any non-essential processing such as marketing.

verdicts.notes: The GDPR footprint here is real but secondary to the misleading-pricing issues handled under UCPD/DSA. Mandatory account creation to use a "free" app means personal data is collected, triggering transparency and lawful-basis obligations. The campaign as described shows no privacy information at the point of sign-up, and the surrounding deception (a "100% FREE / no hidden costs" claim that is false, terms buried in grey text) undermines the fairness and transparency principle that also governs how personal data is processed. No profiling, personalisation, special-category data, or targeting of minors is present, so those provisions are not engaged.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The onboarding flow embodies the deceptive/manipulative design DSA Art. 25 prohibits: forced continuity (a trial silently converting to a recurring charge), obscuring material price information (small grey text on the fourth screen), and providing no way to cancel (the confirmation email omits the recurring charge and cancellation method) — i.e. making cancellation harder than subscription. This materially impairs the consumer's ability to make a free and informed decision. The provision applies to providers of online platforms designing their online interfaces; whether ScanGenius's own app onboarding qualifies as an 'online platform' interface is doubtful, so this is flagged as medium/attention rather than a clear breach. The same conduct is squarely caught by the UCPD for all traders regardless of platform status.
findings.evidence_quote: 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled; the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Redesign the onboarding so the recurring price (€11.99/week) and the auto-renewal after the 3-day trial are disclosed clearly and prominently before the consumer commits, on the same screen as the trial acceptance and with equal visual prominence. Provide an obvious, symmetrical cancellation path (cancellation no harder than subscription) and include the recurring charge amount, renewal date and step-by-step cancellation instructions in the confirmation email. If the app or its distribution surface is or becomes an online platform under the DSA, this is mandatory; in all cases it removes the dark-pattern risk.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The install and display ads are disseminated on online platforms (app store, display networks) that are subject to DSA Art. 26(1) ad-transparency duties (identifiable as advertising, advertiser identity, who paid, targeting parameters). The obligation rests principally on the platform, and the campaign text gives no indication the ads are disguised as non-advertising content, so no advertiser breach is evident. Flagged only so the marketer ensures cooperation with platform ad-labelling requirements. (Note: the misleading 'FREE'/'no hidden costs' claim is a UCPD matter handled by another agent, not an Art. 26(1) issue.)
findings.evidence_quote: App-install ads: 'ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!'
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ads carry the platform's advertising labels and that accurate advertiser/paid-by information is supplied to the platform. No specific DSA action required beyond standard platform ad-transparency cooperation.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core wrongdoing — the "100% FREE"/"no hidden costs" claim contradicted by a trial auto-converting to €11.99/week, price buried in small grey text, and no cancellation information — is classic forced-continuity/subscription-trap dark-pattern conduct that DSA Art. 25 expressly targets ("making cancellation harder than subscription", forced continuity). However, DSA Art. 25 binds "providers of online platforms" in the design of their own online interfaces; a PDF scanner app's onboarding is not obviously an "online platform" interface, so the primary legal home for this conduct is the UCPD (covered by another agent). The DSA is flagged for attention rather than a clear breach. The declared absence of personalisation/targeting and general adult audience mean Art. 26(3) (sensitive-data ad targeting) and Art. 28 (ads to minors) are not engaged; Art. 26(1) ad-transparency obligations rest chiefly on the platform, and nothing indicates the ads are disguised.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits, in all circumstances, describing a product as 'free' or 'without charge' where the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of responding/delivery. Here the app is marketed as '100% FREE' and the app-store title repeats 'Free', yet after a 3-day trial it auto-converts to €11.99/week — a substantial recurring charge unrelated to any delivery cost. This is a blacklisted practice requiring no case-by-case assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!
findings.recommendation: Remove the '100% FREE' / 'Free' claims from the ad copy and the app-store title, or restrict them to genuinely free functionality. If a paid subscription follows a trial, describe the offer accurately (e.g. '3-day free trial, then €11.99/week' with equal prominence).

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices containing false information deceiving the average consumer as to price or manner of price calculation and causing a transactional decision (installing/creating an account) they would not otherwise take. The explicit 'No hidden costs' claim is directly false: the €11.99/week recurring charge is a hidden cost, concealed on the fourth onboarding screen. This false price claim is a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: No hidden costs. Download now!
findings.recommendation: Delete the 'No hidden costs' statement. State the full price and recurring nature clearly and prominently before the consumer commits (before install/account creation), so the price representation is truthful.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting material information the average consumer needs, or providing it in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely manner. The price, recurring frequency and auto-conversion of the trial are material information, yet they are hidden in small grey text on the fourth screen (untimely and unclear) and the confirmation email omits the recurring charge and how to cancel entirely. This is a misleading omission of key pricing and contract-continuity information.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Disclose the recurring price, billing frequency, trial-to-paid conversion date and cancellation method clearly, legibly and up front — on the first relevant screen and in the confirmation email — with prominence at least equal to the 'free' messaging.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The overall design — a headline 'free' claim, mandatory account creation to use the app, price concealment, silent auto-conversion, and a confirmation email that omits the charge and cancellation route — is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour. Art. 5 acts as a safety-net capturing the cumulative unfairness of this subscription-trap design even beyond the specific breaches above.
findings.evidence_quote: starts a 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled
findings.recommendation: Redesign the onboarding and post-purchase flow so consumers give informed consent to the paid subscription: obtain explicit acknowledgement of the price before charging, send a pre-billing reminder, and provide an easy, clearly signposted cancellation mechanism.

verdicts.notes: The ScanGenius campaign presents a classic "free" subscription trap that engages several UCPD prohibitions. Advertising the app as "100% FREE" with "No hidden costs" when it in fact requires payment of €11.99/week after a 3-day trial is a per se breach of the Annex I point 20 blacklist (misuse of 'free') and a misleading action under Art. 6. Burying the price in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and omitting the recurring charge and cancellation method from the confirmation email are misleading omissions under Art. 7. These practices are strongly likely to be found unfair.

report.executive_summary: The ScanGenius campaign advertises a "100% FREE" PDF scanner "with no hidden costs," but the app actually forces account creation and starts a 3-day trial that silently converts to €11.99/week, with the price buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and no mention of the charge or how to cancel in the confirmation email. This is a textbook "free" subscription trap. The most serious problem is that calling the product "free" when a recurring charge follows is a per se banned practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I) — it is illegal in all circumstances with no defence available, which is why the overall risk is rated critical. The "no hidden costs" claim and the buried, untimely price disclosure add further misleading-action and misleading-omission breaches, and the whole design (silent auto-renewal, no clear cancellation route) is a dark pattern also relevant under the DSA. Separately, forcing users to create accounts to use the "free" app triggers GDPR transparency and lawful-basis duties that the current flow does not meet. The AI Act is not engaged. Bottom line: this campaign cannot run as described and needs substantial rework before launch.
report.recommendations: Remove the "100% FREE" and "Free" claims from the ad copy and the app-store title, and delete "No hidden costs" — this is the top priority because using "free" here is a banned practice regardless of any disclaimers.

campaign.title: ScanGenius 'free' PDF app
campaign.text: App-install ads: 'ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!' After install, the app requires account creation and starts a 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled; the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen. App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title. Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.

detected_practices: 'Free' claim contradicted by recurring paid subscription
hidden/obscured pricing (small grey text on fourth onboarding screen)
free trial converting to auto-renewing subscription (subscription trap)
misleading app store title repeating 'Free'
omission of material information on recurring charge and cancellation in confirmation email
forced account creation post-install
triage.summary: An app-install campaign promotes ScanGenius as a "100% FREE" PDF scanner while in fact it forces account creation and enrols users in a €11.99/week auto-renewing subscription after a 3-day trial, with the price buried in small grey text and no mention of the recurring charge or cancellation in the confirmation email. This presents classic misleading advertising and subscription-trap concerns, plus personal-data collection via mandatory account creation. No generative AI or declared targeting is involved.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Mandatory account creation collects personal data (at minimum an email address, given the confirmation email) directly from the data subject. Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller provide identity, purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period, and data-subject rights. The submission describes an onboarding flow engineered to conceal material information (price buried in small grey text, silent confirmation email) and gives no indication that any privacy notice is presented at sign-up, so the Art. 13 obligation is engaged and likely not satisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Present a concise, layered privacy notice at the account-creation screen (or immediately before) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention and data-subject rights, with a link to the full privacy policy. Confirm it is displayed before data is submitted, not buried after.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear, plain language. The onboarding flow demonstrably uses obscuring design (small grey text, deferred disclosure) for commercial terms; if the same design approach is applied to privacy information, the transparency of data-processing information fails the Art. 12 accessibility and intelligibility standard.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Ensure privacy/data-processing information is presented with equal or greater prominence than other onboarding content — clear typography, plain language, and easy accessibility — and not obscured or deferred behind multiple screens.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing of the personal data collected at account creation requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). The campaign discloses no lawful basis. Basic account/service data may rest on contract necessity, but any marketing use of the collected email would require a separate basis (consent or a balanced legitimate interest). The obligation is engaged and the basis is undeclared.
findings.evidence_quote: the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Document and disclose the lawful basis for each processing purpose. Limit contract-based processing to data strictly necessary to provide the service, and obtain separate consent (or perform a legitimate-interest assessment) before using account data for marketing.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(4) requires that performance of a contract/service not be made conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for that service. Forcing account creation to use a PDF scanner risks bundling non-necessary data collection into access to the service; if consent is relied upon and access is conditioned on it, the consent would not be 'freely given'.
findings.evidence_quote: After install, the app requires account creation
findings.recommendation: Assess whether account creation (and each data field) is genuinely necessary to deliver the scanning function. Where not necessary, offer the core service without mandatory sign-up, and keep any marketing consent separate, granular and non-conditional, with withdrawal as easy as giving it.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a misleading-advertising/subscription-trap matter (UCPD/DSA territory), but GDPR is engaged because the app forces mandatory account creation, which entails collection of personal data. Nothing in the submission indicates that the required transparency information (identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, data-subject rights) is provided at the point of collection, and the flow's overall lack of transparency (hidden pricing, silent confirmation email) suggests the privacy layer likely mirrors these deficiencies. Findings below flag the transparency and lawful-basis/consent obligations that must be verified; they are medium/low because the campaign text does not positively confirm a breach, only that the obligations are engaged and probably unmet as described.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: Annex I point 20 prohibits in all circumstances describing a product as 'free' where the consumer must pay anything beyond the unavoidable cost of responding/delivery. Here the app is marketed as '100% FREE' with 'No hidden costs', yet it converts a 3-day trial into an €11.99/week recurring subscription. This is exactly the blacklisted scenario of a 'free' trial auto-converting to a paid subscription without clarity, and it is a per se violation requiring no case-by-case assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs. Download now!
findings.recommendation: Remove the '100% FREE' and 'No hidden costs' claims from the install ads and the app-store title. Describe the offer accurately, e.g. '3-day free trial, then €11.99/week — cancel anytime', with the recurring price and billing frequency shown up front and with equal prominence to the word 'free'.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers practices that deceive the average consumer about the price or the existence of a specific price advantage and thereby cause a transactional decision (installing/creating an account) they would not otherwise take. Repeating 'Free' in the store title and ads, when the real cost is €11.99/week, gives a false overall impression of the price and is a misleading action driving the install decision.
findings.evidence_quote: App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title
findings.recommendation: Ensure all headline claims (ad creatives and store title/subtitle) reflect the true pricing model. Do not use 'Free' as the dominant price signal when a paid recurring subscription is the effective outcome of ordinary use.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or obscuring material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision. Price, the recurring nature of the charge, the trial-to-paid conversion, and the cancellation method are all material. Presenting the price only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen provides it in an unclear and untimely manner, and the confirmation email omits the recurring charge and cancellation route entirely.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen. App store listing repeats 'Free' in the title. Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the full price, billing frequency, renewal date and cancellation method clearly and prominently before the consumer commits (ideally on the first relevant screen), and repeat these details in the confirmation email, including a direct link or clear instructions to cancel.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall design — a 'free' hook, forced account creation, buried pricing and a silent auto-conversion to a weekly charge — is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer, causing enrolment into paid billing they did not knowingly accept. This reinforces the specific breaches under Annex I(20), Art. 6 and Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: requires account creation and starts a 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled
findings.recommendation: Redesign the onboarding so consumers give informed, active consent to the paid subscription with clear pre-contractual disclosure, and avoid forcing account creation as a precondition to the advertised 'free' functionality.

verdicts.notes: This campaign presents a clear UCPD violation. Describing the app as "100% FREE" while it in fact enrols users in a €11.99/week auto-renewing subscription after a 3-day trial is a per se prohibited misuse of "free" under Annex I, point 20 (a blacklisted practice unfair in all circumstances). The same conduct independently constitutes a misleading action on price (Art. 6) and a misleading omission (Art. 7), since the price is buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and the recurring charge and cancellation method are omitted entirely from the confirmation email. The general fairness prohibition (Art. 5) applies as a safety net.

report.executive_summary: Your ScanGenius campaign advertises a "100% FREE" PDF scanner "with no hidden costs," but in reality forces account creation and enrols users in a 3-day trial that silently converts to a €11.99/week subscription, with the price hidden in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and no mention of the charge or cancellation route in the confirmation email. This is a textbook "subscription trap" and carries critical legal risk. Under EU consumer law (UCPD), calling the app "free" when it leads to a recurring paid subscription is a blacklisted practice that is banned outright — no case-by-case defence is available. The same conduct also amounts to misleading price claims and misleading omissions of material information (price, renewal, cancellation). Separately, because the app forces account creation and collects personal data (email), GDPR transparency and consent obligations are engaged and appear unmet as described. The AI Act and DSA were assessed as not applicable to this campaign. Bottom line: the campaign cannot run in its current form and needs substantive rework, not just cosmetic tweaks.
recommendations: Immediately stop using '100% FREE' and 'No hidden costs' in the app-store title, subtitle and all display/install ads — this is a per se prohibited misuse of 'free' (UCPD Annex I, point 20) and is the single most serious issue.

Rewrite the headline offer to state the true pricing up front, e.g. '3-day free trial, then €11.99/week — cancel anytime', giving the recurring price and billing frequency at least equal prominence to any mention of 'free'.

Move full pricing disclosure (price, billing frequency, renewal date, how to cancel) to the first relevant onboarding screen in clear, legible text — not small grey text buried on screen four — and require an active, informed opt-in before any billing starts.
Fix the confirmation email so it clearly states the recurring charge, the renewal date, and a direct link or plain instructions to cancel.

Reassess whether mandatory account creation is genuinely necessary to deliver the scanning function; if not, offer the core service without forced sign-up and keep any marketing consent separate, granular and non-conditional (GDPR Art. 7).

Present a concise, layered privacy notice at (or before) the account-creation screen covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention and data-subject rights, with equal prominence to other onboarding content (GDPR Arts. 12-13).

Document and disclose the lawful basis for each processing purpose, limiting contract-based processing to necessary data and obtaining separate consent for any marketing use of the email (GDPR Art. 6).

campaign.title: GrandDraw 'You have won' mailer
campaign.text: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up.' The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.

detected_practices: false 'guaranteed winner' prize claim
advance-fee scam (processing/insurance fee to release prize)
false urgency/deadline (7-day forfeiture)
unverifiable/absent draw terms and conditions
misleading prize value (fee exceeds actual voucher value)
creating false impression consumer has won a prize
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers but explicitly skews elderly, a vulnerable group heightening the aggressive/misleading concern; no indication minors are targeted.
triage.summary: A prize-draw mailer that falsely tells recipients they are a "guaranteed winner" of €2,500 and demands a €29.90 advance fee to release winnings that amount only to a low-value voucher, using a 7-day forfeiture deadline and no verifiable draw terms. This is a textbook misleading/aggressive practice (arguably a blacklisted "false prize" practice under the UCPD) targeting elderly consumers. Personal data (names/addresses) is processed to select and contact recipients.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (names/addresses) is processed to select and contact recipients, but the communication is built on a deception (a non-existent 'guaranteed win' and a fee exceeding the actual voucher value). Processing personal data as the vehicle for a misleading solicitation breaches the requirement that data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently — recipients are given a false account of why they are being contacted and their data is used to their detriment.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Cease using recipient data to deliver deceptive prize solicitations. Any legitimate marketing must be based on honest, accurate messaging and processing must be fair to the data subject; align the message with the true nature of the offer before any further mailing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing of personal data for direct marketing requires a valid lawful basis. Email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (per ePrivacy), and postal marketing requires at minimum a properly balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign discloses no lawful basis and shows no indication of consent or an LIA; the sourcing of the elderly-skewing address list is unexplained, casting doubt on any valid basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Email and postal mailer
findings.recommendation: Document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis before sending: obtain prior consent for email marketing, and for postal marketing conduct and record a legitimate-interest assessment. Verify that the recipient list was lawfully sourced with an appropriate basis and honour any suppression preferences.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The mailer collects/uses personal data and even solicits identity confirmation, yet provides none of the Art. 13 information: the controller's identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period, data subject rights, or the source of the address data. Data subjects cannot understand or control how their data is used.
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice with each communication covering controller identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and the source of the data (Art. 14 also relevant where data was not obtained directly).

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: This is direct marketing sent to individuals, so each recipient has an absolute right to object to processing for direct-marketing purposes. The mailer contains no opt-out/objection mechanism and instead pressures recipients to act (pay a fee) within 7 days, frustrating rather than facilitating the right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy opt-out/objection mechanism (e.g. unsubscribe link for email, and a stated method for postal mail) in every direct-marketing communication, and suppress objecting recipients immediately and permanently.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data (names, postal addresses and email addresses) to select and contact recipients for direct marketing. Although the underlying prize deception is primarily a UCPD matter, the same conduct engages GDPR: the processing is neither fair nor transparent, no lawful basis is disclosed (email direct marketing generally requires prior consent), the Art. 13 information required at collection/first contact is absent, and no means of objecting to direct marketing is offered. The elderly skew heightens the fairness concern. These are risks/likely breaches on the data-protection dimension, distinct from the UCPD deception itself.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: This is a per-se prohibited practice under Annex I point 31: creating the false impression that the consumer has won a prize while making claiming it subject to paying money or incurring a cost. Here recipients are told they are a 'GUARANTEED WINNER' but must pay a €29.90 fee to 'release' the prize, and the draw has no verifiable terms while the actual 'prize' (a voucher) is worth less than the fee. This is prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer effect.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days
findings.recommendation: Do not run this campaign. A prize promotion may never require payment of any fee to claim, and 'winner' claims must reflect a genuine, verifiable draw with published terms. Remove the fee entirely and only communicate wins that are real and unconditional.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 7-day forfeiture deadline is an artificial, false time limit designed to elicit an immediate payment decision and deprive the consumer of opportunity to reflect or verify. Because the underlying prize claim is fabricated, the deadline is a false urgency claim prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 7.
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Remove the countdown/forfeiture pressure. Any genuine promotional deadline must be truthful and not used to rush consumers into paying money.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The mailer contains false information on the main characteristics and value of the 'prize' and the price/benefit balance: recipients are led to believe they have won €2,500 when in fact they receive a low-value voucher worth less than the €29.90 they pay. This deceives the average consumer as to the existence and nature of the benefit and the price advantage, causing a transactional decision (paying the fee) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent
findings.recommendation: Never represent a low-value voucher as a €2,500 prize. Prize values, odds and terms must be accurate and substantiated; the net value of any benefit must be clearly and truthfully stated.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The mailer omits material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision: verifiable draw terms and conditions, the true nature and value of what is actually sent, the identity/odds of the promotion, and the fact that the fee exceeds the item's value. Hiding these facts constitutes a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, complete and timely terms: promoter identity, full rules, actual prize value, odds, and any conditions — before any payment is requested (and, per Annex I point 31, no payment may be required at all).

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Coupled with the declared audience that 'skews elderly', the coercive forfeiture threat and immediate-payment pressure exploit a vulnerable group and may significantly impair freedom of choice through undue influence, engaging the aggressive-practice prohibition in Arts. 8-9. Timing pressure and exploitation of credulity are recognised aggravating factors.
findings.evidence_quote: or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Eliminate coercive loss-framing and payment deadlines. Do not design prize communications that pressure vulnerable recipients into paying; assess the practice from the perspective of the elderly average member of the targeted group.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a general safety-net, Art. 5 (and Art. 5(3)) applies because the practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (elderly, credulous consumers). Even beyond the specific blacklist entries, the overall scheme is an unfair commercial practice assessed from the vulnerable group's perspective.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general adult consumers, skews elderly
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the practice. Any consumer promotion should meet professional-diligence standards and be tested against the perspective of the vulnerable audience it foreseeably reaches.

verdicts.notes: This mailer is a textbook advance-fee false-prize scam and squarely engages a per-se prohibited (blacklisted) practice under UCPD Annex I. It falsely tells recipients they are a "guaranteed winner" of a €2,500 prize while conditioning release on a €29.90 fee, with no verifiable draw terms and an actual "prize" worth less than the fee. It also uses a false forfeiture deadline and misleads on price/value, and its high-pressure, deadline-driven design aimed at an elderly-skewing audience raises aggressive-practice and general-fairness concerns. Findings are critical.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a "you have won" mailer telling recipients they are a guaranteed winner of a €2,500 prize, then demanding a €29.90 "processing and insurance fee" within 7 days to release winnings that turn out to be a low-value voucher worth less than the fee. In plain terms, this is a textbook false-prize / advance-fee scam and cannot be run. It hits an outright banned practice under EU consumer law (Annex I of the UCPD): you may never require a payment to claim a prize, and "winner" claims must reflect a real, verifiable draw. It compounds this with a fake forfeiture deadline, misleading value claims, and high-pressure tactics aimed at an elderly-skewing audience — all serious violations. Separately, it also breaches data-protection rules: personal data is being used unfairly and deceptively, with no lawful basis, no privacy information, and no way to opt out. The verdict is that this campaign must not be sent in any form; it is not fixable with wording tweaks because the core mechanic (pay to claim a win) is illegal.
recommendations: Do not send this campaign in any form. Requiring any payment to claim a prize is a per-se prohibited practice under UCPD Annex I point 31 and cannot be remedied by rewording.
Remove the €29.90 fee entirely. A genuine prize must be released unconditionally, with no processing, insurance, or any other charge.
Only communicate a win if it is real, unconditional, and backed by a genuine, verifiable draw with published terms, promoter identity, actual prize value, and odds.
Delete the '7 days or forfeited to the runner-up' countdown and all loss-framing/urgency; false deadlines are a banned practice, especially when aimed at an elderly audience.
Do not represent a low-value voucher as a €2,500 prize; any stated prize value must be accurate and substantiated.
Given the elderly-skewing audience, discontinue the coercive, pressure-based design entirely; it foreseeably exploits vulnerable consumers.

Before any legitimate future marketing: establish and document a lawful basis (prior consent for email, a recorded legitimate-interest assessment for post), verify the address list was lawfully sourced, include a clear privacy notice and an easy opt-out, and honour objections immediately.
Treat this submission as a compliance red flag and route it for internal legal/anti-fraud review rather than campaign revision.

findings.evidence_quote: Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.

findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen
findings.recommendation: Present privacy information (and material terms) in clearly legible, adequately sized and contrasted text at an accessible point in the flow, avoiding low-contrast 'grey on grey' or deferred placement that impairs comprehension.

findings.title: Conditions for consent

findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: If relying on consent, obtain it separately from acceptance of the (accurately disclosed) subscription, in clear language, with a genuine free choice and equally easy withdrawal; do not bundle marketing/other consent into mandatory account creation.

No profiling/personalisation, minors or special-category data are declared, so those GDPR provisions are not engaged on the current facts. Findings below are limited to the data-collection touchpoints that are evident from the text; a full DPIA of the onboarding flow and privacy notice is recommended.
