findings.evidence_quote: ScanGenius — 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: Remove all 'FREE' / '100% FREE' / 'No hidden costs' claims from the app-install ads and store title. Describe the offer accurately, e.g. '3-day free trial, then €11.99/week — cancel anytime', with the recurring price disclosed up front and with equal prominence.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The claim contains false information regarding the price and manner of price calculation: the app is presented as costless when it in fact triggers a recurring €11.99/week charge. This deceives the average consumer about the price and is likely to cause a transactional decision (install, create account, start trial) they would not otherwise take. 'No hidden costs' is directly contradicted by the concealed recurring charge.
findings.evidence_quote: 100% FREE PDF scanner. No hidden costs.
findings.recommendation: State the full price and billing frequency truthfully in the ad and store listing before the consumer commits (installs/creates an account), so no material price information is false or contradicted.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information (the recurring €11.99/week price, the trial auto-conversion, and how to cancel) is hidden or provided in an unclear, untimely manner — buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and omitted entirely from the confirmation email. This is a misleading omission: the average consumer needs the price and cancellation terms before/at the point of decision, not obscured after install.
findings.evidence_quote: the price appears only in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen. ... Confirmation email does not mention the recurring charge or how to cancel.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the recurring price, trial-conversion date and cancellation method clearly and prominently at the point of sign-up (not the fourth screen), and include the recurring charge, renewal date and cancellation steps in the confirmation email.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a fallback safety-net, the overall design — 'free' hook, mandatory account creation, silent auto-conversion, obscured price and absent cancellation info — is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the average consumer's economic behaviour (a subscription-trap pattern). This reinforces the specific breaches above.
findings.evidence_quote: starts a 3-day trial that converts to €11.99/week unless cancelled
findings.recommendation: Redesign the trial-to-paid flow so the consumer gives informed, explicit consent to the recurring charge with clear price and cancellation information, and send a reminder before the trial converts.

verdicts.notes: The ScanGenius campaign describes a PDF app as "100% FREE" with "no hidden costs" while in fact requiring account creation and a 3-day trial that auto-converts to a mandatory €11.99/week subscription. This is a blacklisted misuse of 'free' (Annex I point 20) and a clear misleading action on price (Art. 6), compounded by misleading omission of material cost and cancellation information (Art. 7). Multiple critical/high UCPD breaches are present.

report.executive_summary: The ScanGenius campaign advertises a PDF scanner app as "100% FREE" with "no hidden costs," but the app actually forces account creation and starts a 3-day trial that silently converts to a mandatory €11.99/week subscription — with the price buried in small grey text on the fourth onboarding screen and omitted entirely from the confirmation email. This is a textbook "subscription trap." The most serious problem is that calling the app "free" when consumers must pay is a per se prohibited practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I, point 20) — banned in all circumstances, no consumer-harm test needed. It is compounded by misleading claims about price (Art. 6) and by hiding the price, trial conversion and cancellation terms (Art. 7). Because using the app also requires handing over personal data through this deceptive flow, it additionally breaches GDPR's fairness/transparency principles and raises questions about the lawful basis for the data collection. The overall verdict is critical: the campaign cannot run in its current form and requires substantive redesign, not just tweaks. AI Act and DSA were assessed as not applicable.
recommendations: Immediately remove every 'FREE', '100% FREE' and 'No hidden costs' claim from the app-install ads and the app store title — this is a blacklisted practice banned in all circumstances and is the single most urgent fix.</br>

Rewrite the offer to state the truth up front and prominently, e.g. '3-day free trial, then €11.99/week — cancel anytime', with the recurring price and billing frequency shown before the consumer installs or creates an account.
Move the price, trial-conversion date and cancellation method to a clear, legible, high-contrast disclosure at the point of sign-up — not the fourth onboarding screen in small grey text.

Fix the confirmation email so it clearly states the recurring €11.99/week charge, the renewal/conversion date, and step-by-step cancellation instructions; send a reminder before the trial converts to paid.
Obtain informed, explicit consent to the recurring charge at sign-up, and redesign the trial-to-paid flow so the consumer knowingly agrees to the subscription.

Provide a complete GDPR Art. 13 privacy notice at the moment of account creation (controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights) and reference it in the confirmation email.
Document the lawful basis for the mandatory account data, limit collection to what is strictly necessary, and do not bundle marketing or unnecessary consent into account creation.
Conduct a full review/DPIA of the onboarding flow before relaunch to confirm the corrected flow is both UCPD-compliant and GDPR-fair.

campaign.title: GrandDraw 'You have won' mailer
campaign.text: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up.' The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.

detected_practices: false 'guaranteed winner' prize claim
advance-fee scam pattern (pay to release prize)
fake urgency / deadline pressure (7 days or forfeit)
misleading prize draw with no verifiable terms
fee exceeding actual value of prize received
targeting/skewing toward elderly / vulnerable consumers
triage.summary: A prize-draw mailer (email and postal) telling recipients they are a 'guaranteed winner' of €2,500 but requiring an upfront €29.90 fee to release winnings within 7 days, where the draw has no verifiable terms and the fee exceeds the value of the voucher actually sent. This is a textbook misleading/aggressive advance-fee prize scam skewing toward elderly consumers. It processes personal data (names/addresses, requests for identity confirmation) and exploits vulnerable audiences.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (names, postal addresses, emails) is processed, and further identity data is solicited, on the basis of a demonstrably false 'guaranteed winner' premise where the 'draw has no verifiable terms' and the fee exceeds the value of the voucher actually sent. Collecting and processing personal data under a deceptive pretext to extract a fee is neither fair nor transparent, breaching the lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not process or solicit personal data under a false prize pretext. Any legitimate promotion must describe the actual offer truthfully, identify the controller, and process data fairly and transparently; abandon the deceptive framing entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The mailer is unsolicited direct marketing sent to recipients' postal addresses and email addresses, yet nothing in the campaign indicates any lawful basis (consent or a valid legitimate-interest assessment) for processing these addresses for marketing. E-mail direct marketing in particular generally requires prior consent; none is evidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis before sending: obtain prior opt-in consent for email marketing, or complete and record a legitimate-interests assessment for postal marketing, using only lawfully sourced contact data.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign collects personal data (existing contact data used for the mailer, plus identity data it asks recipients to 'confirm') but provides none of the mandatory Art. 13 information at the point of collection: controller identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, or data-subject rights. Indeed no verifiable identity of the sender is given ('the draw has no verifiable terms').
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of any data collection: clearly identify the controller, the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights, in an accessible location referenced in the mailer.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: As a direct-marketing communication, recipients have an absolute right to object to further processing of their data for direct marketing, which must be facilitated in every such communication. The mailer contains no opt-out or objection mechanism and instead uses forfeiture pressure to compel a response.
findings.evidence_quote: or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy-to-use opt-out/objection mechanism (e.g. unsubscribe link and a postal opt-out address) in every marketing communication, and suppress objecting recipients from future mailings.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Any information about the processing must be concise, transparent, intelligible and provided in clear and plain language. The mailer's misleading, unverifiable framing (particularly toward an audience that skews elderly) is the opposite of transparent, intelligible communication about how recipients' data is used.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms
findings.recommendation: Communicate any data-processing information in clear, plain, verifiable language appropriate to the audience, avoiding deceptive framing and pressure tactics.

verdicts.notes: This is a postal/email direct-marketing mailer that processes personal data (names, addresses, email addresses) and actively solicits further personal data by asking recipients to "confirm your identity." Because the entire premise (a "guaranteed winner" prize draw with no verifiable terms, used to extract an advance fee) is deceptive, the processing engages the GDPR lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle, lacks any evident lawful basis or transparency information, and provides no means to object to direct marketing. Profiling/Art. 22 and children's-consent provisions are not engaged on the facts (no personalisation or minors declared).
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 31 prohibits in all circumstances creating the false impression that the consumer has won a prize where claiming it is subject to paying money or incurring a cost. This mailer does exactly that: a 'guaranteed winner' claim conditioned on paying a €29.90 fee to 'release' winnings, where the actual item sent (a voucher) is worth less than the fee and the draw has no verifiable terms. This is a per se blacklisted practice with no need to assess consumer effect.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not run this campaign in any form. A prize/sweepstake may never require any payment to claim it. Remove the fee entirely, or discontinue the promotion. If a genuine draw exists, publish full verifiable terms and provide the prize at no cost beyond unavoidable delivery.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices containing false information likely to deceive the average consumer about the nature of the product, its main characteristics and price, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Representing a paid-for, below-value voucher as a €2,500 'GrandDraw prize' with a 'GUARANTEED WINNER' status is materially false and induces payment of the €29.90 fee.
findings.evidence_quote: the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent
findings.recommendation: Eliminate false and exaggerated prize representations. Any promotional communication must accurately describe what the recipient actually receives and its true value, with no invented 'win' framing.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or obscuring material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision. The mailer omits verifiable draw terms, the identity/qualifications of the trader, the true nature and value of what is 'won', and the fact the fee exceeds that value — all material to whether to pay. Providing pressure while withholding these facts is a misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms
findings.recommendation: Disclose full draw terms, the trader's identity, the true nature and value of the item, and any conditions, clearly and before any payment is requested.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices using coercion or undue influence that impair the consumer's freedom of choice. The artificial 7-day deadline coupled with the threat of forfeiture to a 'runner-up' applies high-pressure timing to force an immediate payment decision, significantly impairing informed choice.
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Remove deadline-and-forfeiture pressure tactics. Do not use manufactured time limits or loss framing to compel payment. (Independently, no fee should be demanded at all — see point 31.)

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5, with the vulnerable-consumer standard in Art. 5(3), requires assessing practices likely to distort the behaviour of an identifiable vulnerable group (by age or credulity) from that group's perspective. A prize-scam mailer knowingly skewing toward elderly recipients is contrary to professional diligence and is especially likely to materially distort their economic behaviour, reinforcing the unfairness even beyond the blacklist.
findings.evidence_quote: general adult consumers, skews elderly
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting/skewing toward elderly recipients with prize-draw solicitations. Any legitimate promotion should meet professional-diligence standards and not exploit age-related credulity.

verdicts.notes: This is a textbook advance-fee prize scam and engages the UCPD at multiple levels. Most seriously, it falls squarely within the Annex I blacklist point 31 (false prize claims), which is prohibited in all circumstances: the consumer is told they are a "GUARANTEED WINNER" but must pay a fee to release the prize, and the "prize" is worth less than the fee. It also constitutes misleading actions (Art. 6), a misleading omission of prize terms (Art. 7), an aggressive practice via undue pressure (Arts. 8-9), and — given the elderly skew — falls foul of the vulnerable-consumer standard in Art. 5(3). Enforcement recommendation: do not run this campaign.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a "you have won" prize mailer that tells recipients they are a guaranteed winner of a €2,500 prize, then demands a €29.90 fee to release winnings within 7 days or lose them to a "runner-up." The specialists assess this as a textbook advance-fee prize scam. It falls squarely within an EU consumer-law practice that is banned outright in all circumstances (UCPD Annex I, point 31): you may never require any payment to claim a prize, and here the item actually sent (a voucher) is worth less than the fee. On top of that it involves false claims, hidden terms, high-pressure forfeiture tactics, and it deliberately skews toward elderly recipients, who are legally treated as vulnerable. It also breaches GDPR: personal data is processed and further identity data solicited under a deceptive pretext, with no lawful basis, no privacy notice, and no way to opt out. This campaign cannot be fixed with edits — it must not run.
report.recommendations: Do not run this campaign in any form — it is a per se prohibited practice (banned prize scam) under UCPD Annex I point 31, not a fixable one.

campaign.title: GrandDraw 'You have won' mailer
campaign.text: Email and postal mailer: 'CONGRATULATIONS! Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up.' The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent.

detected_practices: false 'you have won' prize claim
guaranteed winner deception
advance-fee / pay-to-claim scheme (processing and insurance fee)
false urgency deadline (7-day forfeiture)
no verifiable prize draw terms
fee exceeds actual value of prize delivered
misleading action - creating false impression consumer has won
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers but skews elderly, a vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3) — the deceptive prize/advance-fee tactics are especially harmful to older recipients. Assess whether the average member of this vulnerable group is materially misled.
triage.summary: A postal and email mailer falsely tells recipients they are the guaranteed winner of a €2,500 prize and demands a €29.90 fee within 7 days to release winnings, though the 'draw' has no verifiable terms and the fee exceeds the value actually delivered. This is a classic advance-fee prize deception targeting elderly consumers. The campaign uses named recipients' addresses (personal data) and no AI or minor targeting is indicated.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires personal data (the recipient's name/address, and the identity data solicited) to be processed fairly and transparently. Using recipients' personal data to send a knowingly false 'you have won' communication designed to extract a fee is a paradigmatic example of unfair, deceptive processing: data subjects cannot reasonably expect their data to be used to mislead them into paying money. The misleading framing directly infects the lawfulness/fairness of the underlying processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Cease using personal data for this deceptive prize communication. Any legitimate direct-marketing use of the address/email must be truthful, non-misleading, and consistent with the data subject's reasonable expectations at the point the data was obtained.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending direct-marketing email requires a valid lawful basis, and under GDPR/ePrivacy email direct marketing generally requires prior consent. The campaign discloses no consent and no legitimate-interest assessment; given the deceptive nature, a legitimate-interest basis could not survive the balancing test. There is therefore no demonstrable lawful basis for processing the personal data used to send these communications, nor for collecting the identity/fee-payment data it solicits.
findings.evidence_quote: Email and postal mailer
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any marketing send: obtain prior opt-in consent for email marketing (ePrivacy), and for postal marketing conduct and record a legitimate-interest assessment. Deceptive campaigns cannot meet this requirement and should not be sent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The mailer collects personal data (identity confirmation and payment/insurance details) but provides none of the mandatory Art. 13 information: the controller's identity and contact details, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention period, data subject rights, or the source of the recipient's address. This information must be given at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days
findings.recommendation: Provide a compliant privacy notice at the point any data is collected, stating the controller's real identity and contact details, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients, the source of the address, and how to exercise data subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: As a direct-marketing communication, recipients have an absolute right to object to processing of their personal data for direct marketing, and the controller must inform them of this right and facilitate opt-out. The mailer contains no opt-out/unsubscribe mechanism and no notice of the right to object, so this obligation is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: To release your prize, confirm your identity
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy-to-use opt-out in every marketing communication (unsubscribe link for email; opt-out address/instructions for post), explicitly inform recipients of their right to object, and honour objections by suppressing the individual from further marketing.

verdicts.notes: The mailer processes personal data (names/postal addresses of selected recipients, plus email addresses and the identity/payment data solicited to "confirm your identity") for direct marketing. Although the deception is primarily a UCPD matter, the same conduct engages several GDPR obligations: there is no evident lawful basis (email direct marketing generally requires prior consent), the deceptive "guaranteed winner" framing means the processing is not fair or transparent, no Art. 13 information (controller identity, purpose, legal basis, source of the address) is provided, and no right-to-object/opt-out mechanism is described. No profiling/AI is declared, so Arts. 4(4)/22 are not central.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false prize claims
findings.rationale: This is the archetypal practice prohibited in all circumstances by Annex I point 31: creating the false impression the consumer has already won a prize, where claiming it is subject to paying money or incurring a cost. The 'draw' has no verifiable terms and the €29.90 fee is a required cost to 'release' the supposed winnings. No case-by-case unfairness assessment is needed — it is per se prohibited.
findings.evidence_quote: Your address has been selected as the GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize. To release your prize, confirm your identity and pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee
findings.recommendation: Do not run this campaign. A prize promotion may never state or imply the consumer has won while requiring any payment or cost to claim it. Remove all 'guaranteed winner' / 'you have won' language and any fee to release winnings entirely.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Misleading action: the message contains false information about the existence and nature of the product/benefit (a €2,500 prize that does not exist) and its value — the fee exceeds the worth of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually delivered. This deceives the average consumer about the main characteristics and price advantage and causes a transactional decision (paying €29.90) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED WINNER of our €2,500 GrandDraw prize
findings.recommendation: Eliminate all false claims of winning and of a €2,500 prize. Any promotion must accurately describe what is actually provided (the voucher) and its real value, with genuine, verifiable draw terms.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: False urgency/scarcity blacklisted under Annex I point 7: an artificial 7-day forfeiture deadline is used to elicit an immediate decision and deprive the consumer of sufficient opportunity to reflect. As there is no genuine prize, the deadline is entirely fabricated pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited to the runner-up
findings.recommendation: Remove the artificial forfeiture deadline. Any genuine promotional time limit must be true and not designed to rush a payment decision.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Aggressive practice by undue influence and pressure: the combination of a fabricated windfall, a countdown/forfeiture threat and a demand for payment significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. The exploitation is aggravated because the audience skews elderly, a vulnerable group whose credulity the tactic exploits (Art. 5(3)).
findings.evidence_quote: pay the €29.90 processing and insurance fee within 7 days, or your winnings will be forfeited
findings.recommendation: Cease the high-pressure payment-to-claim mechanic. Do not exploit deadlines and loss-aversion framing, particularly toward elderly recipients.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: General fairness safety-net and Art. 5(3): the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of the vulnerable group (elderly consumers, more susceptible to prize deceptions). The practice is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of that group, reinforcing the unfairness beyond the specific blacklist entries.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: general adult consumers, skews elderly
findings.recommendation: Abandon the deceptive prize model. Any marketing directed at an audience skewing elderly must meet heightened diligence standards and avoid credulity-exploiting tactics.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Misleading omission: material information — the absence of any genuine draw, the true nature/value of what is delivered (a voucher worth less than the fee), and the real cost/benefit — is hidden or provided in an unclear manner, preventing an informed decision.
findings.evidence_quote: The 'draw' has no verifiable terms; the fee exceeds the cost of the 'prize catalogue voucher' actually sent
findings.recommendation: If any legitimate promotion is run, disclose full, verifiable draw terms, odds, the identity of the promoter, and the true nature and value of what recipients actually receive, clearly and up front.

verdicts.notes: This mailer is a classic advance-fee "you have won" prize deception, squarely caught by the UCPD blacklist. It falsely tells recipients they are the guaranteed winner of a €2,500 prize and conditions release of "winnings" on paying a €29.90 fee — the exact conduct prohibited in all circumstances by Annex I point 31. It also compounds several general prohibitions: misleading action (false prize, false value), false urgency (7-day forfeiture), and aggressive high-pressure tactics targeting an elderly, vulnerable audience under Art. 5(3). No lawful cure exists other than withdrawing the campaign.

report.executive_summary: This campaign is a "you have won" prize mailer telling recipients they are the guaranteed winner of a €2,500 GrandDraw and demanding a €29.90 "processing and insurance" fee within 7 days to release winnings that don't actually exist (the real deliverable is a voucher worth less than the fee). This is a textbook advance-fee prize scam and is prohibited outright under EU consumer law — no wording changes can make it lawful. It breaches the UCPD blacklist (which bans false prize claims and fake urgency in all circumstances), the general bans on misleading and aggressive practices, and is aggravated by deliberately targeting an elderly, vulnerable audience. It also triggers multiple GDPR failures: no lawful basis, unfair/deceptive processing, no privacy notice, and no opt-out. This is not a compliance-tuning exercise — the campaign must be withdrawn, not amended. Running it exposes the business to enforcement action, fines, and potential fraud liability.
report.recommendations: Do not run this campaign in any form — withdraw it entirely. The core mechanic (false claim of winning + payment to release a prize) is banned outright under EU law and cannot be fixed by editing the wording.

campaign.title: RugPalace closing down sale
campaign.text: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots: 'CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever.' The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged. Radio spot adds 'last weekend, we mean it this time'.

detected_practices: Persistent closing-down sale claim (14 months continuous with no actual cessation of trade)
False 'final days'/'last weekend' urgency claim
Fake reference prices (pre-sale prices never actually charged) — misleading discount / 70% off claim
Countdown/urgency pressure ('EVERYTHING MUST GO', 'before we shut our doors forever')
AI-generated marketing content
Personalisation/targeting of ads
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general adult consumers; no indication of minor targeting, though outdoor/radio channels are broadcast and could incidentally reach minors. Core concern is aggressive/misleading practices toward the general consumer public.
triage.summary: RugPalace runs a continuous 'closing down — everything must go' sale across web, radio and outdoor that has persisted for 14 months despite no cessation of trade, monthly restocking, and reference prices that were never charged. The campaign uses generative AI and personalised targeting while making false urgency and misleading discount claims aimed at general adult consumers in the EU.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares that its assets (web homepage copy, storefront banners and radio spots) are produced with generative AI. Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The campaign gives no indication that any AI-generated audio (radio spots) or text/image assets carry provenance marking, so the obligation is engaged and not evidently satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all generative-AI outputs used in the campaign carry machine-readable provenance/watermark marking (e.g. C2PA metadata for images/copy, detectable markers for AI-generated audio) as required by Art. 50(2), and obtain confirmation from the AI provider/tool that outputs are so marked. Document which assets were AI-generated.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign is manifestly deceptive and manipulative (false 'closing down', fake urgency, fabricated reference prices) and uses declared personalised targeting. Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that deploy manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm. However, on the facts the deception is a human-devised marketing strategy merely rendered/distributed via AI; there is no evidence the AI system itself deploys subliminal or manipulative techniques or that personalisation exploits users to cause significant harm. Flagged for awareness — the deceptive substance is squarely addressed under UCPD by the parallel review.
findings.evidence_quote: before we shut our doors forever
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-driven personalisation to time or tailor these false-urgency messages to individuals in ways that exploit inferred emotional or financial vulnerability, which could cross into the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition. Correcting the underlying misleading claims (a UCPD matter) removes the deceptive-technique risk. If personalisation logic infers emotional states, reassess against Art. 5(1)(a).

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce marketing assets (web copy, banners, radio spots), which engages the AI Act transparency regime — specifically Art. 50(2)'s obligation to mark synthetic content in a machine-readable format. The obvious deception and false urgency in the campaign are serious, but on the facts described they are human-authored marketing tactics merely rendered via generative AI; there is no evidence that an AI system itself deploys subliminal/manipulative techniques or exploitative personalisation, so the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition is not clearly met (this deception is primarily a UCPD matter). No chatbot (Art. 50(1)), deep fake, or public-interest text (Art. 50(4)) is present. The core AI Act obligation genuinely triggered is synthetic-content marking.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The campaign expressly relies on personalisation/targeting of ads. Audience segmentation and behavioural targeting of consumers is 'profiling' within Art. 4(4) (automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal preferences, interests and behaviour), which brings the campaign within the scope of the GDPR obligations that govern profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document that the targeting activity is profiling, map exactly what personal data (e.g. behavioural, location, interest signals) feeds it, and treat the operation as subject to the full set of profiling/direct-marketing obligations below.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising/profiling requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — in practice consent or a properly documented legitimate-interests assessment, and for any tracking cookies/identifiers prior consent under ePrivacy. The submitted material identifies no lawful basis for the targeting, so the obligation is engaged but not shown to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for the personalised advertising before running it: obtain valid opt-in consent for cookie/tracker-based targeting, or complete and record a legitimate-interests balancing test if relying on Art. 6(1)(f), and retain evidence of that basis.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is the basis for the targeting (typically required for web tracking), Art. 7 demands a freely given, unbundled, clearly-distinguishable consent that is as easy to withdraw as to give and demonstrable by the controller. Nothing in the campaign shows a compliant consent flow exists.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Implement a granular, unbundled consent mechanism for personalised advertising on the web homepage, with a withdrawal path as easy as opt-in, and keep records demonstrating each consent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected for targeting (e.g. via the web homepage), Art. 13 requires transparent information at the point of collection: controller identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights, and the existence of profiling. The campaign material describes no such privacy information.
findings.evidence_quote: web homepage
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered, accessible privacy notice at the point of data collection on the website covering all Art. 13 items, expressly disclosing the personalisation/profiling purpose and how to object.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Consumers have an absolute right under Art. 21(2)-(3) to object at any time to processing (including profiling) for direct-marketing purposes, and the right must be brought to their attention explicitly and clearly. No opt-out/objection facility is described for the personalised advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Offer and clearly signpost an easy, always-available opt-out from personalised/direct-marketing profiling; on objection, stop processing that data for marketing immediately.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) requires processing to be lawful, fair and transparent. Fairness also considers the wider context in which data is used: here the personal data is used to deliver advertising that is itself materially misleading (false closing-down and reference-price claims), which raises a fairness/transparency concern about the processing purpose. With no privacy information disclosed, transparency is also unevidenced.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the targeting is not used to amplify misleading marketing; align the underlying ad claims with the UCPD and disclose the processing clearly so the use of personal data is fair and transparent to consumers.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's headline problems (persistent fake closing-down sale, false urgency, invented reference prices) are misleading-practice issues under the UCPD, not GDPR. GDPR is engaged only through the declared use of personalisation/targeting, which constitutes profiling of consumers for direct marketing. The submitted material describes no lawful basis, privacy notice, consent flow, or opt-out mechanism, so the relevant GDPR obligations are engaged but cannot be verified as satisfied. Findings below flag the obligations the marketer must be able to demonstrate; severities are moderate because the compliance artefacts normally sit outside the ad copy and no covert or sensitive-data processing is evidenced in the text.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign declares personalised/targeted advertising and runs on the web. Insofar as any of these ads are served through an online platform, that platform must ensure recipients can identify in real time that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters. The advertiser (RugPalace) must supply this information for the platform to comply. There is no indication in the campaign text that this transparency data is provided, but placement on an in-scope online platform is not confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Where these ads are delivered via third-party online platforms, ensure the advertiser identity, clear 'advertisement' labelling and meaningful targeting-parameter information are supplied so the hosting platform can meet DSA Art. 26(1). Retain records of the targeting parameters used for each ad set.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The false-urgency and perpetual closing-down messaging is exactly the type of manipulative design that DSA Art. 25 prohibits on online-platform interfaces (deceiving/materially distorting recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions). However, Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms, and RugPalace is the advertiser operating its own storefront/website rather than an online-platform provider. The graph expressly notes Art. 25 applies 'without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers the same conduct for all traders' — so the substantive breach here falls under the UCPD blacklist (assessed by another agent), not DSA obligations binding RugPalace.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! ... before we shut our doors forever.
findings.recommendation: No DSA action required of RugPalace as an advertiser; remediate the deceptive urgency and closing-down claims under the UCPD. If RugPalace operates its own in-scope online-platform interface (e.g. a marketplace hosting third parties), ensure that interface does not deploy false-urgency dark patterns contrary to Art. 25.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's operative obligations here (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 39) bind "providers of online platforms," not advertisers/traders. RugPalace's declared channels are its own storefront, web homepage, radio and outdoor — it is acting as an advertiser, not as an online-platform provider, so the DSA does not directly bind RugPalace for most of the conduct. The manipulative/deceptive practices (perpetual "closing down", false "final days" urgency, fake reference prices) are the platform-side mirror of DSA Art. 25 but are properly assessed under the UCPD (Annex I points 7 and 15), covered by another agent. The one DSA-relevant residual point is that the declared personalised/targeted advertising, if delivered through any online platform, must carry Art. 26(1) transparency information (ad labelling, advertiser identity, targeting parameters) — flagged for attention as it depends on placement channel.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claim of ceasing trade
findings.rationale: Claiming the trader is about to cease trading when this is not the case is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances. A 'closing down / shut our doors forever' sale that has run continuously for 14 months with no cessation of trade and monthly restocking is precisely the perpetual closing-down sale this point targets. No materiality assessment is needed — it is unfair per se.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! ... before we shut our doors forever. The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly
findings.recommendation: Cease all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging immediately, since the business is not ceasing trade. If a genuine closure is later planned, such claims may only be used with a real, verifiable end date and actual cessation of trading.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Falsely stating that a product/offer is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances. 'Final days' and 'last weekend, we mean it this time' repeated over a 14-month continuous campaign is a false time-limit designed to pressure consumers, with the 'we mean it this time' wording confirming prior deadlines were untrue.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Remove all 'final days' and 'last weekend' deadline claims unless there is a genuine, fixed and honoured end date. Do not reset or repeat expired deadlines.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: A practice is misleading where it deceives the consumer about the existence of a specific price advantage and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Advertising '70% off' against reference prices that were never actually charged fabricates a price advantage, making the discount claim false. (Price-reduction announcements must also reference the genuine lowest prior price under the Price Indication Directive.)
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs ... the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged
findings.recommendation: Only advertise discounts against a genuine prior selling price, and reference the lowest price applied in the 30 days before the reduction. Remove the '70% off' claim unless it can be substantiated against actually-charged prices.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of false permanent-closure pressure and relentless, repeated false deadlines over 14 months across web, radio and outdoor amounts to undue influence and high-pressure timing/persistence that can significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice, engaging the aggressive-practices prohibition alongside the blacklisted findings.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... before we shut our doors forever ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the manufactured urgency and closure pressure entirely; base any promotional messaging on truthful, non-coercive information rather than artificial deadlines.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The overall campaign is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort consumer economic behaviour, functioning as the general-fairness safety net that reinforces the specific blacklist and Art. 6 findings above.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO!
findings.recommendation: Redesign the campaign around accurate representations of the business's ongoing operation, genuine prices and truthful offer terms.

verdicts.notes: The RugPalace campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including two Annex I blacklisted practices that are unfair in all circumstances (per se prohibited, no case-by-case materiality test needed). The "closing down / everything must go / before we shut our doors forever" message run continuously for 14 months with no cessation of trade and monthly restocking is a textbook false cessation-of-trade claim (Annex I point 15). The recurring "final days / last weekend, we mean it this time" is a false urgency claim (Annex I point 7). Separately, the "70% off" against pre-sale reference prices that were never charged is a misleading action on price advantage (Art. 6). The general aggressive/misleading safety-net provisions are also engaged.

report.executive_summary: This "RugPalace closing down sale" campaign runs continuously across web, radio and outdoor telling consumers the shop is shutting "forever" with "70% off" and "final days" deadlines. The problem is that none of it is true: the sale has run for 14 months, the business is not closing, new stock arrives monthly, and the "pre-sale" prices used to justify the 70% discount were never actually charged. This triggers the most serious category of consumer-protection breach — two practices that are banned outright under EU law in all circumstances: falsely claiming you are ceasing trade, and falsely claiming a limited-time offer to pressure buyers. The false "70% off" also constitutes a misleading price claim. Separately, because you use personalisation/targeting and generative AI, you have unmet GDPR obligations (lawful basis, consent, privacy notice, opt-out) and an AI Act obligation to mark AI-generated content. The core issue is not paperwork — it is that the entire campaign message is false and must stop. Overall verdict: critical, requiring immediate action before the campaign continues.
recommendations: STOP immediately: remove all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor — the business is not closing, so this is a per-se banned practice (UCPD Annex I, point 15).</br>
Remove all 'final days' and 'last weekend, we mean it this time' deadline claims — repeated fake deadlines are also banned outright (UCPD Annex I, point 7). Never reset or repeat an expired deadline.

Drop the '70% off' claim unless you can substantiate it against genuine prices actually charged, referencing the lowest price applied in the 30 days before the reduction (UCPD Art. 6 / Price Indication Directive).
Rebuild the campaign around truthful messaging: the business is trading normally, real prices, and any promotion tied to a genuine, honoured end date only.

For the personalised/targeted advertising, establish and document a GDPR lawful basis (opt-in consent for web trackers, or a recorded legitimate-interests assessment), a compliant granular consent flow, a layered privacy notice at point of collection, and an easy, signposted opt-out from marketing profiling.

For generative-AI assets (web copy, banners, radio audio), ensure outputs carry machine-readable provenance/watermark marking per AI Act Art. 50(2) and get confirmation from your AI tool/provider; keep a record of which assets were AI-generated.

If any ads are served through third-party online platforms, supply advertiser identity, clear 'advertisement' labelling and targeting-parameter information so the platform can meet DSA Art. 26(1); retain targeting records.
Do not use AI personalisation to time or tailor urgency messaging to individuals' inferred emotional or financial vulnerability, which could raise AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) concerns.

campaign.title: RugPalace closing down sale
campaign.text: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots: 'CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever.' The campaign has run continuously for 14 months; company filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged. Radio spot adds 'last weekend, we mean it this time'.

detected_practices: closing down / going out of business sale claim
persistent urgency ('final days', 'last weekend, we mean it this time')
false liquidation claim (14 months continuous, no cessation of trade, new stock monthly)
false reference / fictitious 'pre-sale' prices (70% off never-charged prices)
generative AI use in campaign content
personalisation / behavioural targeting
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers; no indication of minor-directed content, so minor reach is unlikely but not tightly age-gated. Key concern is the misleading nature of the claims: a permanent "closing down" sale that never ends and blacklisted practices under UCPD Annex I (going-out-of-business misrepresentation, false urgency, fictitious former prices). GDPR is engaged by declared personalisation/targeting; AI Act by declared generative AI use (transparency/labelling); DSA potentially engaged for the web/online advertising component and its advertising transparency obligations.
triage.summary: A multi-channel (web, radio, outdoor) retail campaign for handmade rugs promoting a "closing down — everything must go" 70%-off sale with heavy urgency messaging. Company filings show no cessation of trade after 14 months of continuous running, stock is replenished monthly, and the reference prices were never actually charged, strongly indicating misleading liquidation and false-discount practices. Declared use of generative AI and personalisation/targeting adds further compliance dimensions.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared as used to produce campaign content deployed as web homepage copy/visuals, radio audio spots and outdoor banners. Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The submission gives no indication that any AI-generated asset (radio audio, banner imagery or web copy) carries such machine-readable provenance marking, so the obligation is engaged and not evidently satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm which specific assets are AI-generated and ensure each carries machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA content credentials / watermarking) as generated by the AI provider; require the generative-AI tool vendor to attest that Art. 50(2) marking is applied, and retain documentation of the marking for each channel (web, radio, outdoor).

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign is manifestly deceptive (perpetual fake liquidation, false urgency, fictitious reference prices). Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems that deploy manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm. Here, however, the deception is human-authored marketing messaging rather than a deceptive technique deployed by the AI system itself, and the 'significant harm' threshold is not evidenced. Flagged for context only; the deceptive-claims issues fall under UCPD, not the AI Act prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: No AI Act Art. 5 action required on the current facts. If generative AI is later used to individually tailor manipulative nudges (e.g., timing pressure to inferred vulnerable/emotional states), reassess against Art. 5(1)(a)-(b). Resolve the deceptive-claims problems under the UCPD assessment.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce content deployed across web (text/image), radio (audio) and outdoor (text/image). This engages the AI Act's transparency/marking obligation in Art. 50(2): AI-generated audio, image and text outputs should be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated, and nothing in the submission indicates this is done. The deep-fake/public-interest disclosure duty (Art. 50(4)) is not engaged as there is no synthetic likeness of a real person, synthetic influencer, or public-interest text. The campaign is clearly deceptive, but that deception is human-authored marketing copy governed by UCPD; the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition requires the AI system itself to deploy the manipulative/deceptive technique causing significant harm, which is not evidenced here — noted only as context.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural targeting and personalisation of advertising typically involve automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal preferences, interests and behaviour, which meets the definition of profiling in Art. 4(4). This brings the campaign's targeting activities within the scope of the GDPR's profiling regime.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document and map the personalisation/targeting pipeline (data sources, segments, inferences drawn) so that the profiling can be assessed and appropriate GDPR safeguards applied.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis — generally consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign material contains no indication of any lawful basis for the declared targeting, so the Art. 6(1) obligation is engaged but not demonstrably satisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and record the lawful basis for the targeting/profiling. If relying on consent, ensure it is validly obtained before tracking/personalisation; if relying on legitimate interests, complete and retain a legitimate-interests balancing assessment (noting consent may be required for tracking technologies under ePrivacy).

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Targeting consumers with claims that are demonstrably false (a 'closing down' sale running 14 months with no cessation of trade and never-charged reference prices) uses their personal data to deliver deceptive messaging, undermining the fairness of any profiling-based processing and the transparency owed about how their data drives the ads they see.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days!
findings.recommendation: Ensure targeted communications are truthful and that data subjects receive clear, accurate information about how their data is used to personalise ads; correct the misleading sale claims so profiling is not used to amplify deceptive content.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected and used for personalised advertising, controllers must provide at the point of collection their identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and information about any profiling. The web homepage/campaign shows no such information, so the Art. 13 transparency obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at the point of data collection (e.g. web homepage/landing page) covering controller identity, purposes and legal basis of the targeting, recipients, retention periods, data-subject rights and existence of profiling.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Any privacy information provided in the campaign's web sign-up or data-collection flows must be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear and plain language. The campaign as described gives no indication that transparent privacy information is presented, so the Art. 12 modalities obligation is engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: Storefront banners, web homepage and weekly radio spots
findings.recommendation: Present privacy information in clear, plain, easily accessible language within the campaign's online journey, distinct from the marketing copy.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time to processing for direct marketing, including related profiling. The campaign material shows no opt-out or objection mechanism for the personalised/targeted marketing, so the Art. 21(2)-(3) obligation to facilitate and honour objection appears unaddressed.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Offer a clear, easy-to-use opt-out from direct marketing and profiling in every relevant channel/touchpoint, and ensure objections immediately stop the targeting for that individual.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged by the declared use of personalisation/behavioural targeting, which constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). The campaign text itself does not evidence a lawful basis, privacy notice, opt-out mechanism or the transparency required for such processing, so the associated obligations (Arts. 6, 5(1)(a), 13/12, 21) appear engaged but unaddressed as described. No special-category (Art. 9) targeting or minor-directed processing is indicated, and there is no evidence of solely-automated significant decisions triggering Art. 22. Findings are risk-level pending confirmation of the actual data-processing practices behind the targeting.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: RugPalace declares personalised/behavioural targeting for its web advertising. Where these personalised ads are disseminated through third-party online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires that each ad be identifiable in real time as an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters. RugPalace is the advertiser rather than the platform, but it must provide accurate advertiser-identity/payer declarations so the hosting platform can meet these obligations; the deceptive 'closing down' framing also increases the importance of clear ad identification.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: For any personalised web ads delivered via third-party online platforms, ensure RugPalace supplies complete and truthful advertiser-identity and 'paid for by' information and that ads are clearly labelled as advertising. Document the targeting parameters provided to the platform so the platform's Art. 26(1) parameter-disclosure requirement can be satisfied. Confirm whether RugPalace's own web homepage qualifies as an online platform (it likely does not); if it does, implement the Art. 26(1) real-time disclosures directly.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The campaign uses persistent false-urgency and deceptive 'closing down' messaging in an online interface (web homepage), which is the type of deceptive/manipulative design Art. 25 targets. However, Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms, and RugPalace's own storefront website is not a platform hosting third-party content, so the prohibition does not directly apply here. Flagged for awareness because the same conduct is squarely a blacklisted/unfair practice under the UCPD (assessed separately) and would engage Art. 25 if delivered through, or on, an online platform interface RugPalace controls.
findings.evidence_quote: web homepage ... 'CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! Final days!'
findings.recommendation: Treat the deceptive urgency and perpetual liquidation framing as the primary (UCPD) compliance defect and remove it. If any part of the campaign is delivered through an online-platform interface, ensure the interface design does not deceive or manipulate consumers' decision-making, consistent with Art. 25.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is only marginally engaged. Its core marketing obligations (Arts. 25, 26, 28, 39) bind providers of online platforms, whereas RugPalace is an advertiser/retailer running a campaign on its own web homepage, radio and outdoor — there is no evidence it operates an online platform hosting third-party content or is a VLOP. The substantive misleading-liquidation, false-urgency and fictitious-price issues are UCPD matters handled by another agent. The one genuine DSA-facing point is that RugPalace's declared personalised/targeted web advertising, when served through third-party online platforms, triggers the platforms' Art. 26(1) transparency duties, for which RugPalace as advertiser must supply accurate advertiser-identity and payer declarations. No special-category targeting or minor-directed content is indicated, so Arts. 26(3)/28 are not engaged.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claim of ceasing trade
findings.rationale: Annex I point 15 prohibits, in all circumstances, claiming the trader is about to cease trading when this is not the case. The campaign has run continuously for 14 months, company filings show no cessation of trade, and new stock arrives monthly — so the 'closing down / shut our doors forever' claim is demonstrably false. This is a per se violation requiring no proof of consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! ... before we shut our doors forever
findings.recommendation: Immediately cease all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor. Do not use liquidation/cessation-of-trade framing unless the business is genuinely and imminently ceasing to trade, with documentary evidence.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits falsely stating that a product will only be available for a very limited time (or on particular terms for a limited time) to elicit an immediate decision. A '70% off, final days / last weekend' offer that has in fact run continuously for 14 months is an artificial, false deadline designed to pressure immediate purchase. The self-aware 'we mean it this time' underscores that prior deadlines were false. Prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Remove all false time-limited framing ('Final days', 'last weekend', 'we mean it this time'). Only use deadline messaging where the offer genuinely expires on the stated date and is not immediately renewed on identical terms.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 makes a practice misleading where it deceives as to the existence of a specific price advantage. The campaign advertises a 70% discount against 'pre-sale' reference prices that 'were never charged', so the price advantage is fictitious and likely to cause consumers to buy on the belief they are receiving a genuine reduction. (This also engages the lowest-prior-price rule under the Price Indication Directive Art. 6a.)
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs
findings.recommendation: Base any advertised discount on the genuine lowest price actually charged in the 30 days before the reduction, and hold documentary evidence of prior prices. Withdraw the '70% off' claim unless it can be substantiated against real former prices.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Beyond the specific blacklist entries, the sustained, high-pressure and persistent urgency messaging across storefront banners, homepage and weekly radio spots over 14 months may constitute an aggressive practice through undue influence and persistence that impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. This operates as a fairness safety-net alongside the Annex I findings.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Eliminate high-pressure, relentless deadline-based messaging; ensure promotional communications allow consumers genuine time and information to make an informed, unpressured transactional decision.

verdicts.notes: The RugPalace campaign engages multiple UCPD Annex I blacklisted practices that are prohibited in all circumstances, regardless of consumer impact. It runs a perpetual "closing down" liquidation sale despite 14 months of continuous trading, no cessation filing and monthly restocking (Annex I point 15); it deploys false and persistent urgency ("Final days!", "last weekend, we mean it this time") for a sale that never ends (Annex I point 7); and it advertises "70% off" against reference prices that were never actually charged, a false price-advantage claim (Art. 6). These are strong, per se violations warranting critical/high severity.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises a "closing down — everything must go" sale with "70% off," "final days," and "last weekend, we mean it this time" across web, radio and outdoor. The problem is that it isn't true: the sale has run continuously for 14 months, company filings show the business is not ceasing trade, new stock arrives monthly, and the "before" prices used to calculate the 70% discount were never actually charged. This triggers the most serious category of EU consumer law breach — practices that are banned outright regardless of whether any consumer was harmed (falsely claiming you are about to stop trading, and using fake time-limited/urgency deadlines), plus a misleading fake-discount claim. Separately, your declared use of personalisation/targeting engages GDPR obligations (lawful basis, privacy notice, opt-out from marketing) that are not evidenced, and your declared use of generative AI engages an AI Act requirement to mark AI-generated audio, image and text as artificially generated. The DSA is only lightly relevant — mainly ensuring accurate advertiser/payer info if you run these ads through third-party platforms. Bottom line: the core messaging is unlawful and must be pulled immediately; the data and AI issues are fixable with proper documentation and disclosures. This campaign cannot run in its current form.
recommendations: STOP RUNNING THE CAMPAIGN IN ITS CURRENT FORM. Immediately remove all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging from web, radio and outdoor — falsely claiming you are ceasing trade is banned outright (UCPD Annex I point 15) and needs no proof of harm.

Remove all false urgency and deadline language ('Final days!', 'last weekend', 'we mean it this time'). A perpetual 14-month 'final days' offer is a prohibited false scarcity practice (UCPD Annex I point 7). Only use a deadline if the offer genuinely ends on that date and is not immediately renewed.

Withdraw or substantiate the '70% off' claim. Discounts must be calculated against the genuine lowest price actually charged in the 30 days before the reduction (Price Indication Directive / UCPD Art. 6). Since the reference prices were never charged, this claim is a misleading fake discount — do not use it without documentary evidence of real prior prices.

For the personalisation/targeting: identify and document a valid GDPR lawful basis (consent or a documented legitimate-interests assessment), and note tracking technologies likely require consent under ePrivacy.

Add a clear, plain-language privacy notice at the point of data collection (web) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and the existence of profiling (GDPR Arts. 12-13).
Provide an easy, effective opt-out from direct marketing and profiling on every channel/touchpoint, and ensure objections immediately stop targeting for that individual (GDPR Art. 21).

For AI-generated assets (radio audio, banner imagery, web copy), confirm which are AI-generated and ensure each carries machine-readable provenance marking as artificially generated; obtain vendor attestation and retain documentation (AI Act Art. 50(2)).

If personalised web ads are delivered via third-party platforms, supply complete and truthful advertiser-identity and 'paid for by' information and clearly label ads as advertising, and document targeting parameters so the platform can meet its DSA Art. 26 duties.
Re-submit the revised creative and a corrected pricing/discount methodology for compliance review before relaunch.

false reference price ('70% off' from prices never actually charged)
false scarcity / countdown urgency ('last weekend, we mean it this time')
