personalisation/targeting of consumers
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is general adult consumers; no indication of intent to reach minors, but broad web/radio/outdoor reach means incidental exposure to minors is possible. Personalisation/targeting on web channel implies processing of personal data for the general adult consumer base.
triage.summary: RugPalace runs a multi-channel (web, radio, outdoor) "closing down / everything must go / final days" sale that has continued for 14 months despite no actual cessation of trade, with ongoing new stock and reference prices that were never charged. The campaign combines classic misleading commercial practices (false going-out-of-business claim, false scarcity/urgency, deceptive reference pricing) with declared use of generative AI and consumer personalisation/targeting.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares that generative AI produces campaign content across web, radio and outdoor assets. AI Act Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The submission gives no indication that AI-generated assets (e.g. imagery, radio-spot audio, ad copy) carry any provenance marking, so the transparency obligation is engaged and, as described, likely unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm which campaign assets are AI-generated/manipulated and ensure the underlying generative-AI system applies machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. watermark/metadata) to all synthetic outputs, and document that the provider's tool satisfies Art. 50(2). Where the deployer controls output publishing, add clear provenance/labelling on synthetic visuals and audio.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign combines objectively deceptive messaging (false going-out-of-business claim, false 'final days'/'last weekend' scarcity, and reference prices never charged) with declared generative-AI content and declared personalisation/targeting. If an AI system is used to generate and adaptively deliver this deceptive, urgency-driven messaging in a way that materially distorts consumers' economic decisions, it could engage the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive/manipulative AI techniques. On the facts stated, however, the deception stems from the ad copy content rather than a demonstrated AI-driven behavioural-distortion technique, so this is flagged as a watch-point rather than an established breach.
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs before we shut our doors forever
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the generative-AI/personalisation stack is being used to time, tailor or optimise the delivery of the false urgency/closing-down messaging to individual consumers. If so, disable AI-driven optimisation of deceptive urgency claims; the underlying claims must first be made truthful (see UCPD assessment). Retain records of how AI selects and targets recipients to demonstrate no manipulative technique that impairs informed decision-making is deployed.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core problems (false closing-down claim, perpetual "final days" urgency, deceptive reference pricing) are misleading-practice issues primarily governed by the UCPD, not the AI Act. Under the AI Act specifically, the campaign declares use of generative AI, which engages the Art. 50(2) transparency/marking obligation for synthetic content. There is no evidence of deep fakes, synthetic personas or public-interest text (Art. 50(4) not engaged), and no indication that an AI *system* itself deploys the manipulative techniques or targets vulnerable groups, so the Art. 5 prohibitions are only a contextual watch-point rather than a demonstrated breach.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation/targeting of web-channel consumers is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal preferences and interests, which is 'profiling' under Art. 4(4). This is the definitional gateway that brings the campaign's targeting activity within GDPR scope.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document precisely what data is used to segment/target consumers and confirm whether audience building, lookalike or behavioural targeting is in use, so the profiling operation can be mapped to a lawful basis and covered by the required disclosures.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising / profiling requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis — in practice consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interests assessment. The campaign material discloses targeting but gives no indication of any identified lawful basis, consent flow, or LIA, so lawfulness of the processing is not demonstrated.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and record the lawful basis for the targeting before go-live: obtain valid consent (and any ePrivacy consent for tracking technologies) or complete and retain a legitimate-interests balancing assessment. Do not run personalised targeting until a defensible basis is documented.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. The campaign performs web-based personalisation but the material provides no privacy information; combined with the fact that the underlying offer is itself misleading, there is a heightened risk that data collection/tracking is neither transparent nor fair to data subjects.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web ... Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at the point of any web data collection/tracking and ensure the personalisation is not built on covert tracking; align the consumer-facing messaging with transparent processing.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected on the web (e.g. sign-ups, tracking for targeting), Art. 13 requires controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and information about profiling to be given at the point of collection. The submitted material shows no such information.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, radio, outdoor
findings.recommendation: Ensure every web data-collection touchpoint (forms, cookie/tracking consent, sign-ups feeding the targeting) presents the full Art. 13 information set at the point of collection, including that profiling is carried out and its logic and consequences.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing purposes triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3). The campaign describes targeting but presents no opt-out/objection mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, clearly signposted way for consumers to object to marketing profiling at any time (e.g. preference centre / opt-out), and stop processing their data for targeting on objection.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of personalisation/targeting of consumers on its web channel, which under GDPR necessarily involves processing of personal data and constitutes profiling (Art. 4(4)). This engages a lawful-basis requirement (Art. 6(1)), transparency/information duties (Art. 5(1)(a), Art. 13) and the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). The submitted material contains only advertising copy and provides no privacy notice, lawful-basis statement, or opt-out mechanism, so these obligations appear engaged but unaddressed. No special-category (Art. 9) processing or targeting of minors is indicated, and the deceptive pricing/"closing-down" claims are matters for other regulations, not GDPR.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The campaign uses false urgency/scarcity ('Final days', a 14-month 'closing down' claim, 'last weekend, we mean it this time') which is exactly the kind of manipulative, choice-distorting design DSA Art. 25 prohibits. However, Art. 25 only binds providers of online platforms in the design of their online interfaces. RugPalace's own storefront/homepage/radio/outdoor presence is not shown to be an 'online platform' under the DSA, and the ads are not shown to run on a third-party platform. The prohibition is therefore only conditionally engaged; the same conduct is primarily addressed under the UCPD (covered by another agent).
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... 'last weekend, we mean it this time'
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether RugPalace's web presence constitutes an online platform (e.g. hosts user-generated listings/interaction). If it does, remove the perpetual false-urgency/false-deadline design elements from the online interface, since manipulative deadline design would breach Art. 25. If it is a plain owned website, the deceptive-design exposure sits under the UCPD rather than the DSA — but the underlying false-urgency messaging should be corrected either way.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's marketing-relevant obligations (Arts. 25–28, 39) attach to providers of online platforms and to advertising presented on online platforms. RugPalace's campaign runs on its own storefront banners, its own web homepage, radio and outdoor — none of which are, on the facts given, "online platform" services within the meaning of the DSA, and there is no indication the ads are served on a third-party platform. The deceptive false-urgency and false-scarcity conduct is genuine but is squarely a UCPD matter for all traders; it engages DSA Art. 25 only if RugPalace's web interface qualifies as an online-platform interface. No sensitive-data or minor-targeted profiling, recommender system, or VLOP ad-repository issue is evidenced. Net: the DSA is largely not engaged on the facts; one conditional flag is worth noting.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claim of ceasing trade
findings.rationale: Annex I point 15 prohibits in all circumstances claiming the trader is about to cease trading when this is not the case. The campaign has run continuously for 14 months, company filings show no cessation of trade, and new stock arrives monthly — confirming the closing-down claim is false. This is a blacklisted per se prohibition requiring no proof of consumer detriment.
findings.evidence_quote: CLOSING DOWN — EVERYTHING MUST GO! ... before we shut our doors forever.
findings.recommendation: Cease all 'closing down', 'everything must go' and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor channels immediately. Only use such language if a genuine, documented cessation of trade is imminent, and remove it once trading continues.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits in all circumstances falsely stating a product is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. A 'final days'/'last weekend' deadline repeated across a 14-month continuous campaign is demonstrably false; the added 'we mean it this time' underscores that prior deadlines were fictitious. Blacklisted per se prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Remove all 'final days', 'last weekend' and equivalent artificial deadline claims unless the sale genuinely ends on a fixed, honoured date. Do not renew or repeat expired deadlines.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers misleading actions regarding price, the manner of price calculation, and the existence of a specific price advantage that cause the average consumer to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Advertising '70% off' against reference prices that were never actually charged deceives consumers as to the existence and size of the price advantage.
findings.evidence_quote: 70% off all handmade rugs ... the 'pre-sale' reference prices were never charged
findings.recommendation: Base any '% off' claim on a genuine, previously charged price (align with the lowest price applied in the prior 30 days per the Price Indication Directive Art. 6a). Remove reference prices that were never charged and substantiate all discount claims with records.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, by undue influence including persistent pressure and exploitation of urgency, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Sustained artificial time-pressure ('final days', 'last weekend, we mean it this time') maintained over 14 months applies undue influence to force premature decisions, compounding the false-urgency issue.
findings.evidence_quote: Final days! ... last weekend, we mean it this time
findings.recommendation: Eliminate high-pressure, repeated urgency messaging; allow consumers adequate time and accurate information to make an informed, unpressured purchasing decision.

verdicts.notes: The RugPalace campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions with strong supporting evidence. Two blacklisted (per se prohibited) practices are clearly present: a false ceasing-trade claim (Annex I point 15) and a false limited-availability/urgency claim (Annex I point 7), both prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer impact. The deceptive '70% off' reference price from prices never actually charged is a misleading action on price advantage under Art. 6. These are among the clearest possible UCPD violations, corroborated by company filings showing no cessation of trade, monthly new stock, and 14 months of continuous running.

report.executive_summary: The RugPalace "closing down sale" campaign advertises a permanent going-out-of-business event with 70% discounts and "final days"/"last weekend" urgency across web, radio and outdoor. The problem is that none of it is true: the sale has run continuously for 14 months, the business is not closing (filings show no cessation of trade, new stock arrives monthly), and the "70% off" reference prices were never actually charged. This puts the campaign squarely into two of the EU's outright-banned advertising practices — falsely claiming you are about to stop trading, and falsely claiming a deadline/limited availability — which are illegal in all circumstances with no need to prove consumer harm. On top of that, the discount claims are misleading on price, and the relentless fake urgency amounts to an aggressive practice. Separately, the declared use of generative AI triggers a duty to mark AI-generated content, and the declared personalisation/targeting triggers GDPR obligations (lawful basis, privacy notice, opt-out) that are not currently addressed. The DSA is largely not engaged unless your website is actually an online platform. Bottom line: this campaign cannot run as written — the core claims must be corrected or removed before anything goes live.
recommendations: Immediately stop all 'closing down', 'everything must go', and 'shut our doors forever' messaging across web, radio and outdoor — this is a per se prohibited practice (UCPD Annex I point 15) and is the single most serious exposure. Only use such language if a genuine, documented cessation of trade is imminent.

Remove all 'final days', 'last weekend' and 'we mean it this time' artificial deadline claims (UCPD Annex I point 7). Do not renew or repeat expired deadlines; only state a deadline if the sale truly ends on a fixed, honoured date.

Rebase every '70% off' or discount claim on a genuine previously charged price, in line with the Price Indication Directive (lowest price in the prior 30 days). Delete reference prices that were never charged and keep records substantiating all discount claims.
Eliminate the sustained high-pressure urgency messaging that, over 14 months, amounts to an aggressive practice (UCPD Arts. 8-9); give consumers accurate information and time to decide.

Before running any personalised/targeted web activity, identify and document a GDPR lawful basis (consent or a documented legitimate-interests assessment), provide a full Art. 13 privacy notice at every data-collection point, and give consumers an easy opt-out from marketing profiling (Art. 21).

Confirm which assets are AI-generated and ensure the generative-AI tool applies machine-readable provenance marking (watermark/metadata) to synthetic images, audio and copy, per AI Act Art. 50(2); document that the tool meets this requirement.

Do not use AI or personalisation to time, tailor or optimise delivery of urgency/closing-down messaging — fix the underlying claims first, then keep records showing no manipulative optimisation is deployed (AI Act Art. 5 watch-point).

Clarify whether the RugPalace website qualifies as an 'online platform' (e.g. hosts user listings/interaction); if so, remove manipulative deadline design elements to avoid a DSA Art. 25 dark-patterns breach.

campaign.title: FitBoost win-back blitz
campaign.text: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS ('Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'). Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'. The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly.

detected_practices: repeated win-back emails after unsubscribe (days 1,3,5,7,10)
SMS after unsubscribe
emotionally manipulative/shaming copy ('Reply STOP to give up on yourself')
unsolicited phone calls to unsubscribed users
delayed unsubscribe processing (up to 30 days) while sends continue
objection/opt-out requests routed to a mailbox reviewed only monthly
behavioural personalisation/targeting
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is former subscribers and adults; no indication minors are targeted. However, personal contact data (email, phone, SMS) of unsubscribed users is processed, and marketing continues despite withdrawal of consent — key ePrivacy/GDPR direct-marketing and right-to-object issues. The shaming SMS copy ('give up on yourself') and repeated persistent contact after opt-out may constitute aggressive/unfair commercial practices under the UCPD.
triage.summary: A win-back campaign targeting lapsed adult gym-app subscribers across email, SMS and phone, using personalisation and emotionally manipulative copy. It continues contacting users after they unsubscribe, delays opt-out processing for up to 30 days, and handles objection requests slowly (monthly mailbox review), raising significant consent/right-to-object and unfair/aggressive practice concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing under Art. 21(2)-(3) is absolute: once a data subject objects (an unsubscribe is such an objection), their personal data must no longer be processed for direct marketing. Continuing to send five emails, two SMS and two phone calls after unsubscribe processes personal data for exactly the purpose the user refused, breaching the absolute objection right.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS
findings.recommendation: Treat every unsubscribe as an immediate, irreversible objection to all direct marketing across all channels. Suppress the contact from email, SMS and phone win-back sequences at once and add them to a permanent suppression list; remove the days 1/3/5/7/10 email cadence, the SMS and the 'churn' phone calls for unsubscribed users.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Phone contact to unsubscribed users is further processing of personal data for a purpose connected to marketing/retention after the objection was made. Even reframed as a 'churn' survey, contacting people who have opted out of communications continues processing that must cease under Art. 21.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'
findings.recommendation: Do not phone unsubscribed users. If genuine churn research is needed, use a separate, clearly non-marketing channel that people can decline, and exclude anyone who has objected; document a distinct lawful basis and purpose that is not marketing.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires controllers to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights and act without undue delay. A 30-day processing lag during which marketing continues, and objection requests handled only via a monthly-reviewed mailbox, means requests are neither actioned promptly nor facilitated; the objection right (Art. 21) should take effect essentially immediately, not after continued sends.
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly
findings.recommendation: Implement objection/unsubscribe handling that takes effect immediately (near real-time suppression). Remove the '30 days' language for opt-outs; monitor the objection mailbox continuously (or automate suppression) so no further marketing is sent after a request is received.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where the marketing relies on consent, Art. 7(3) requires withdrawal of consent to be as easy as giving it and to take effect promptly. A 30-day delay with continued sends and a slow objection channel makes withdrawal materially harder than opt-in and effectively ineffective for weeks.
findings.evidence_quote: processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue
findings.recommendation: Ensure withdrawal/unsubscribe is one-step and effective immediately, mirroring the ease of opt-in. Stop all sends the moment consent is withdrawn rather than after a processing window.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Continued email/SMS/phone marketing to users who have unsubscribed lacks a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1): consent has been withdrawn, and legitimate interests cannot override the data subject's clearly expressed objection to direct marketing (which Art. 21 makes absolute). Processing therefore proceeds without a lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers
findings.recommendation: Cease processing former subscribers' contact data for marketing once they unsubscribe. Only re-contact if the individual later provides fresh, specific consent; document the lawful basis for any residual processing (e.g. retaining minimal data on a suppression list) separately.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural personalisation/targeting of former subscribers constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4) (automated evaluation of preferences, behaviour, churn risk). Under Art. 21, the objection right extends to profiling related to direct marketing, so profiling of unsubscribed users must also stop.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Exclude unsubscribed users from all marketing profiling and segmentation. Ensure the personalisation engine reads the suppression/objection flag and halts profiling for direct-marketing purposes for those individuals.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a) requires processing not to be manipulative or exploitative. Using shaming, emotionally coercive copy to process a lapsed subscriber's contact data for retention, combined with an opt-out framed as 'giving up on yourself', is unfair processing of personal data and inconsistent with the fairness/transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself
findings.recommendation: Remove manipulative, shaming language from any communications. Present unsubscribe/opt-out neutrally and honestly; ensure the overall processing (persistent re-contact, emotive pressure) can be justified as fair to the data subject.

verdicts.notes: This win-back campaign continues direct marketing (email, SMS and phone) to individuals who have unsubscribed, which directly engages and likely breaches the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21). Withdrawal/objection must be effective immediately, yet processing is delayed up to 30 days while sends continue and objection mailboxes are only reviewed monthly, undermining both Art. 21 and the "as easy to withdraw as to give" standard in Art. 7 and the undue-delay/transparency requirements of Art. 12. The unsubscribe was a clear signal to stop, so there is no valid lawful basis (Art. 6) for continued sends, and behavioural personalisation of former subscribers constitutes profiling that must also respect the objection.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 blacklists persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media, prohibited in all circumstances unless justified to enforce a contractual obligation. Here the solicitations begin precisely because the user unsubscribed (a refusal), across three channels — five emails, two SMS and two phone calls — none of which enforces any contractual obligation. This is a per-se prohibited practice; no proof of consumer harm is required.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS
findings.recommendation: Cease all win-back contact once a user unsubscribes. Honour the opt-out immediately across email, SMS and phone, suppress the contact across all channels, and remove the day-1/3/5/7/10 re-contact cadence and the two SMS entirely. A single confirmation of unsubscription is permissible; repeated 'Are you sure?' nagging is not.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Framing marketing re-contact as churn research does not change its character: two scripted phone calls to users who have already refused are persistent, unwanted solicitations by telephone, prohibited outright under Annex I point 26. The 'to understand churn' label is a pretext that still results in unsolicited marketing calls to people who opted out.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'
findings.recommendation: Remove the instruction to phone unsubscribed users. If genuine churn research is desired, obtain separate, freely given consent to be contacted for research and keep it strictly separate from any marketing content; do not call anyone who has unsubscribed.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, by harassment or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. The relentless timing and persistence across channels, combined with confirm-shaming copy that frames exercising the opt-out ('Reply STOP') as 'giving up on yourself', apply psychological pressure and stigmatise the consumer's legitimate choice to leave, pushing them toward re-subscription they would not otherwise choose.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'
findings.recommendation: Remove all confirm-shaming and guilt-inducing language. Any single retention message must be neutral, must not frame opting out as a personal failing, and must present the STOP/unsubscribe option plainly without emotional penalty.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat onerous barriers to exercising rights and the persistence of contact as indicators of an aggressive practice. Deliberately delaying opt-out processing for up to 30 days while continuing to send, and routing objections to a mailbox reviewed only monthly, make it disproportionately burdensome and slow for consumers to escape the marketing, amounting to undue influence through obstruction of cancellation (a recognised dark pattern).
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly
findings.recommendation: Process unsubscribes and objections immediately (and stop all sends the moment the request is made, not after 30 days). Replace the monthly-review mailbox with an automated, instant suppression mechanism and remove the '30 days' delay language.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 provides a general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the average consumer's economic behaviour. The overall design of this sequence — ignoring refusals, obstructing exit, and shaming users into re-subscribing — is contrary to professional diligence even where individual elements are addressed under the more specific provisions above.
findings.evidence_quote: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers
findings.recommendation: Redesign the win-back programme around respect for the consumer's refusal: a single, optional, neutral win-back message before permanent suppression, immediate opt-out handling, and no cross-channel escalation. Document a professional-diligence review of the retention flow.

verdicts.notes: This win-back campaign engages the UCPD strongly. The scripted re-contact of users who have already unsubscribed — five 'Are you sure?' emails, two SMS and two phone calls after the consumer's clear refusal — squarely matches the blacklisted per-se prohibition on persistent and unwanted solicitations (Annex I, point 26), which is unfair in all circumstances without any need to prove consumer harm. The confirm-shaming copy ('give up on yourself'), the sheer persistence/timing, and the deliberately onerous barriers to exiting (30-day 'processing' with sends continuing, objections reviewed only monthly) also constitute an aggressive commercial practice by harassment and undue influence (Arts. 8-9), with Art. 5 available as a fairness safety-net. These are treated as UCPD issues here; parallel GDPR/ePrivacy right-to-object concerns are for the GDPR agent.

report.executive_summary: The "FitBoost win-back blitz" bombards people who have already unsubscribed with five emails, two SMS and two phone calls — plus guilt-tripping copy telling them that stopping means "giving up on yourself." This is a serious problem. Under EU consumer law (UCPD), repeatedly soliciting someone who has already refused is a blacklisted practice that is banned outright, no exceptions — and the shaming language plus a deliberately slow, obstructive opt-out process count as aggressive, manipulative tactics on top of that. Under GDPR, an unsubscribe is a legally absolute objection to marketing: once someone opts out you must stop contacting them immediately, so continuing to send for "up to 30 days" while reviewing objections only monthly is unlawful, as is phoning opted-out users under the guise of "churn research." There is no valid basis to keep marketing to these people. This campaign cannot go live in its current form and must be substantially redesigned. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged.
report.recommendations: ["STOP all win-back contact the moment a user unsubscribes — remove the day 1/3/5/7/10 email cadence and both SMS entirely. At most, send a single neutral confirmation that they have been unsubscribed.

The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly.

No generative AI is used, but personal data of former subscribers is processed for personalisation and continued contact despite withdrawal of consent.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute: once a data subject objects (unsubscribing is such an objection), personal data must no longer be processed for that purpose. Here the system continues five emails, two SMS and two phone calls after the user has unsubscribed, and the objection right applies equally to the profiling/personalisation used to tailor these messages. Continuing to process and contact the individual after opt-out is a direct breach of Art. 21(2)-(3).
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS
findings.recommendation: Treat every unsubscribe/opt-out as an immediate, absolute objection: suppress the individual across all channels (email, SMS, phone) the moment the request is received, and permanently exclude them from win-back and profiling for marketing. Remove the day 1/3/5/7/10 sequence and the SMS/call re-contact for anyone who has unsubscribed.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent to marketing must be as easy to withdraw as it was to give (Art. 7(3)). Imposing a 30-day delay during which marketing continues makes withdrawal materially harder than the (typically one-click) opt-in, rendering the withdrawal ineffective. Withdrawal must take effect without undue delay and stop further processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue
findings.recommendation: Make unsubscribe effective immediately with a single action, confirm it in real time, and stop all sends at once. Remove the '30 days' processing language for the act of stopping marketing; any residual deletion timeline must not permit continued marketing in the interim.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Objections to direct marketing must be acted on at any time and without delay; batching them into a monthly review means the controller keeps processing data for marketing for up to a month after a valid objection, defeating the absolute nature of the Art. 21 right.
findings.evidence_quote: objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly
findings.recommendation: Implement immediate, automated processing of objection requests (or at minimum same-day handling) with prompt suppression across all channels; do not queue opt-out/objection requests for monthly manual review.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing (including phoning) requires a valid lawful basis. After a subscriber has unsubscribed, consent no longer exists and there is no contractual necessity, so continued marketing/re-contact lacks a lawful basis; legitimate interest cannot override the individual's explicit objection to marketing. Framing marketing calls as 'churn understanding' does not create a lawful basis for contacting people who have opted out.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'
findings.recommendation: Do not contact unsubscribed users for marketing or win-back under any label. If genuine, non-marketing service/research contact is ever needed, base it on a documented lawful basis, keep it strictly non-promotional, and still honour any objection; otherwise cease the calls entirely.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural personalisation/targeting of the win-back messages is automated processing to evaluate/predict personal aspects (behaviour, preferences) and therefore constitutes profiling. Profiling related to direct marketing is expressly within the scope of the Art. 21 objection right, so it must cease on opt-out and requires a valid lawful basis; as described it continues post-unsubscribe.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document the personalisation logic as profiling, ensure a valid lawful basis (consent) while active, and stop all marketing profiling for any individual immediately upon their objection/unsubscribe.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: A gym/fitness app processes data (activity levels, fitness goals, workout history) capable of revealing health data, a special category under Art. 9. If the personalisation or 'churn' targeting uses or infers such health-related attributes, processing is prohibited absent an Art. 9 exception such as explicit consent — which is unlikely to survive after the subscriber has withdrawn.
findings.evidence_quote: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers
findings.recommendation: Assess whether targeting relies on health/fitness-derived attributes. If so, either stop using such data for marketing or obtain valid explicit consent; never infer or target on health status for win-back messaging, and exclude special-category data from any post-cancellation processing.

verdicts.notes: This win-back campaign processes personal data of former subscribers for direct marketing after they have unsubscribed, and materially fails to honour the GDPR right to object and the equivalence between withdrawing and giving consent. The unsubscribe itself is an objection to/withdrawal of consent for direct marketing under Art. 21 and Art. 7, yet the system continues emailing, texting and phoning for up to 30 days, routes objections to a mailbox reviewed only monthly, and lacks any demonstrable lawful basis for continued contact. Behavioural personalisation of these communications is profiling that compounds the Art. 21 breach. A fitness/gym context also risks Art. 9 exposure if health-related attributes are used to target.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances 'making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, fax, e-mail or other remote media', except to enforce a contractual obligation. Here the user has unsubscribed (withdrawn any interest), yet the trader launches a scripted multi-channel re-contact sequence — five emails, two SMS and two phone calls — precisely the 'repeated win-back sequences ignoring the consumer's refusal' and 'scripted re-contact of unsubscribed users' captured by this blacklist item. There is no contractual-enforcement justification for marketing win-back. This is a per se prohibited practice requiring no case-by-case unfairness test.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS ... call unsubscribed users twice
findings.recommendation: Stop all marketing contact immediately upon unsubscribe. Remove the post-unsubscribe email/SMS/phone win-back sequence entirely, or restrict any single win-back message to lawful pre-unsubscribe contexts only. Do not instruct support to phone unsubscribed users under a 'churn research' pretext.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, by harassment, coercion or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Relevant factors expressly include timing, persistence, and onerous barriers to exercising contractual/opt-out rights. The copy here uses confirm-shaming/guilt manipulation (framing opting out as 'giving up on yourself'), combined with relentless multi-channel persistence and a deliberately obstructive opt-out. Together these exert undue influence and pressure the consumer to reverse a decision they freely made.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'
findings.recommendation: Remove shaming/guilt-inducing language that frames unsubscribing as a personal failing. Ensure opt-out is frictionless and honoured immediately, so timing/persistence factors do not weigh against the trader.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making the exercise of an opt-out right burdensome and slow — continuing to send for up to 30 days and reviewing objections only monthly — is an 'onerous barrier to exercising contractual rights' expressly listed as an aggressive-practice factor under Arts. 8-9. Obstruction of cancellation/opt-out is a recognised dark pattern regulated by UCPD Arts. 5-9. The delay ensures the consumer keeps receiving unwanted solicitations after clearly refusing.
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly.
findings.recommendation: Process unsubscribe requests immediately (near-real-time) and cease all sends at once. Handle objection requests without undue delay through an automated, promptly-monitored channel rather than a mailbox reviewed only monthly.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general prohibition of unfair commercial practices and acts as a safety net. Even if any element narrowly escaped the blacklist or the aggressive-practice test, the overall design — contacting people who have refused, shaming them, and obstructing their opt-out — is contrary to the requirements of professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer, and is therefore unfair under Art. 5.
findings.evidence_quote: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers
findings.recommendation: Redesign the win-back programme so it only targets users who have not opted out and who can lawfully be contacted, using neutral, non-manipulative messaging and immediate opt-out compliance.

verdicts.notes: This win-back campaign directly engages the UCPD blacklist. It continues to email, text and phone users after they have explicitly unsubscribed, using scripted repeated re-contact — a textbook "persistent and unwanted solicitation" (Annex I point 26), prohibited in all circumstances. The guilt-tripping copy and the deliberately obstructive opt-out (30-day processing while sends continue, monthly objection review) also amount to an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9 (undue influence, persistence, onerous barriers to exercising rights). These are high-confidence violations under UCPD.

report.executive_summary: The "FitBoost win-back blitz" bombards people who have already unsubscribed with five emails, two SMS and two phone calls, wrapped in guilt-tripping copy ("Reply STOP to give up on yourself") and backed by an opt-out that "may take up to 30 days" while messages keep flowing. This design breaks the law on two fronts. Under GDPR, an unsubscribe is an absolute objection to direct marketing — you must stop immediately across all channels — yet the campaign keeps contacting people, has no lawful basis for the post-unsubscribe calls, and lets objection emails sit in a mailbox reviewed only monthly. Under the UCPD, continuing to contact people who have refused is a per se banned practice (persistent and unwanted solicitations, Annex I point 26), and the shaming language plus the obstructive opt-out add up to an aggressive commercial practice. In a fitness/health context there is also a risk of processing special-category health data without valid grounds. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. Bottom line: this campaign as described is not launchable — the core mechanic (contacting people after they opt out) is unlawful and must be removed, not merely tweaked.
recommendations: Stop the entire post-unsubscribe sequence now: the moment someone unsubscribes, suppress them immediately across email, SMS and phone. Delete the day 1/3/5/7/10 emails, the two SMS and the two 'churn' calls — this is the single most important fix, as continuing to contact opted-out users is both a GDPR breach (Art. 21) and a per se banned UCPD practice (Annex I point 26).

Make unsubscribe take effect instantly with one action and confirm it in real time. Remove the 'processing may take up to 30 days' language for stopping marketing — withdrawal must be as easy as opt-in and act without delay (GDPR Art. 7).
Replace the monthly-review objection mailbox with automated, same-day processing that suppresses the person across all channels immediately (GDPR Art. 21).

Do not phone unsubscribed users under any label, including 'to understand churn' — there is no lawful basis for it post-opt-out (GDPR Art. 6). If genuine non-marketing research is ever needed, it must be strictly non-promotional, separately justified, and still honour objections.
Remove all guilt/shaming copy such as 'Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself' — this is manipulative and contributes to an aggressive-practice finding (UCPD Arts. 8-9).

Confirm whether personalisation/targeting uses health or fitness-derived data. If it does, treat it as special-category data (GDPR Art. 9) requiring explicit consent, and exclude it entirely from any post-cancellation processing.
Document your personalisation as profiling, secure a valid lawful basis while active, and ensure it stops on any opt-out (GDPR Arts. 4(4), 21).
Redesign win-back so it only targets users who have NOT opted out, using neutral messaging, a single lawful contact where permitted, and immediate opt-out compliance (UCPD Art. 5).

campaign.title: FitBoost win-back blitz
campaign.text: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS ('Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'). Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice 'to understand churn'. The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly.

detected_practices: persistent 'Are you sure?' win-back email sequence after unsubscribe (days 1,3,5,7,10)
SMS with guilt/shaming/manipulative copy ('Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself')
unsolicited phone calls to unsubscribed users ('to understand churn')
continued sends during a 30-day unsubscribe processing delay (ignoring/delaying opt-out)
objection/opt-out requests routed to a mailbox reviewed only monthly
behavioural personalisation/targeting of former subscribers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults (former subscribers) in the EU; no indication minors are targeted or likely reached. Key concerns: ignoring/delaying withdrawal of consent and objection requests (GDPR Art. 7(3), 21, and ePrivacy direct-marketing rules — continued messaging after unsubscribe/'STOP'), unsolicited marketing calls/SMS, and aggressive/manipulative commercial practices under UCPD (undue pressure, disparaging 'give up on yourself' framing). GDPR flagged given personalisation and processing of contact data despite opt-out.
triage.summary: A win-back campaign targeting lapsed gym-app subscribers via email, SMS and phone, continuing to contact users after they unsubscribe and delaying opt-out processing by up to 30 days with objection requests reviewed only monthly. Uses guilt/shaming and pressure tactics, plus personalisation/targeting of former subscribers. No generative AI declared or apparent.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing under Art. 21(2)-(3) is absolute and takes effect at the moment the data subject objects — from that point the data must no longer be processed for direct marketing. Continuing to send emails/SMS/calls during a 30-day 'processing' window, and reviewing objection mailboxes only monthly, means the controller keeps marketing to people who have exercised an absolute right to stop. The persistent day 1/3/5/7/10 'Are you sure?' sequence and phone calls 'to understand churn' to unsubscribed users are direct marketing continuing after the objection.
findings.evidence_quote: processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly
findings.recommendation: Suppress the contact immediately (in near real time) upon any unsubscribe/objection across all channels (email, SMS, phone). Remove the 30-day continuation window; stop all further win-back sends the moment a user unsubscribes. Monitor the objection mailbox continuously (or route to an automated suppression flow) rather than monthly, and honour STOP replies instantly.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it and that withdrawal take effect without undue hindrance. A 30-day delay during which messaging continues, plus objection requests only reviewed monthly, makes withdrawal materially harder and slower than opt-in, obstructing the withdrawal right. The 'Are you sure?' nag sequence is a confirm-shaming/obstruction pattern that impedes effective withdrawal.
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue
findings.recommendation: Make opt-out effective immediately and as frictionless as opt-in: one-click unsubscribe that stops all messaging at once, no nagging re-confirmation loops, and no artificial processing delay. Confirm the withdrawal promptly to the user.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Once a user has unsubscribed/objected, any lawful basis for direct-marketing processing (consent or legitimate interest) falls away — consent is withdrawn and the Art. 21 objection overrides legitimate interest for direct marketing. Continued sends and calls therefore lack a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1) and constitute unlawful processing.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS
findings.recommendation: Cease all marketing processing of a user's personal data (email address, phone number) for direct marketing the moment they unsubscribe/object; retain the identifier only on a suppression list for the purpose of not contacting them. Do not rely on legitimate interest to continue after an objection.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness element of Art. 5(1)(a) requires that data not be processed in ways that are unfair, manipulative or contrary to the reasonable expectations of the data subject. Guilt/shaming copy that frames unsubscribing as 'giving up on yourself', combined with obstructed opt-out and continued contact after refusal, is manipulative processing of personal data inconsistent with the fairness principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself
findings.recommendation: Remove confirm-shaming and coercive framing from win-back messaging. Ensure marketing communications and opt-out flows are fair, neutral and respect the user's expressed choice, and that the volume/cadence of contact does not amount to pressure.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Personalising and targeting former subscribers based on their behaviour (e.g. churn/lapse status, engagement) is profiling within Art. 4(4). This is not itself a violation, but it brings the campaign squarely within the direct-marketing profiling that Art. 21 objection covers and reinforces the need to stop profiling for marketing once a user objects.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling/personalisation logic and its lawful basis, and ensure that upon objection you also stop profiling related to direct marketing, not just the message sends. Provide clear Art. 13-style information about profiling at the point of data collection.

verdicts.notes: The campaign continues to contact users after they unsubscribe and delays/obstructs opt-out and objection handling, which directly conflicts with the GDPR right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21(2)-(3), an absolute right) and with the requirement that consent be as easy to withdraw as to give (Art. 7(3)). Continued sends during a 30-day "processing" window and objection requests reviewed only monthly mean processing continues without a valid lawful basis after the objection/withdrawal (Art. 6(1)), and the confirm-shaming design plus obstructed unsubscribe breach the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)). Personalisation of former subscribers is profiling (Art. 4(4)) that must respect these rights. Overall: multiple likely violations of GDPR data-subject-rights and lawfulness obligations.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media, except where justified to enforce a contractual obligation. Contacting users who have already unsubscribed — five emails, two SMS and two phone calls across a scheduled sequence — is precisely the blacklisted conduct: repeated win-back sequences and scripted re-contact of unsubscribed users that ignore the consumer's refusal. These are pure marketing/retention messages, not enforcement of any contractual obligation, so the exception does not apply. A blacklisted practice requires no case-by-case fairness test.
findings.evidence_quote: after a user unsubscribes, the system sends 'Are you sure?' emails on days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, plus two SMS ... Internal playbook instructs support to call unsubscribed users twice
findings.recommendation: Cease all further email, SMS and phone contact immediately once a user unsubscribes. Remove win-back re-contact of unsubscribed users from the automation entirely; if any post-cancellation message is genuinely needed (e.g. confirming account closure), send a single transactional, non-marketing message only.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, by harassment, coercion or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice — with express factors including persistence and onerous barriers to exercising rights. Deliberately delaying opt-out for up to 30 days while continuing to send, and routing objections to a mailbox reviewed only monthly, creates onerous barriers to the consumer's right to stop contact and, combined with the relentless day-1/3/5/7/10 cadence, constitutes harassment/undue influence.
findings.evidence_quote: The unsubscribe page states 'processing may take up to 30 days' while sends continue; objection requests via email are routed to a mailbox reviewed monthly.
findings.recommendation: Make opt-out immediate and effective on receipt (suppress across all channels at once). Provide a one-click unsubscribe and honour STOP instantly; process objections in real time rather than monthly. Remove the '30 days' processing language for marketing suppression.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: This confirm-shaming copy uses guilt and disparagement (framing continued unsubscribing as 'giving up on yourself') to pressure the consumer into reversing a decision. As undue influence exploiting emotional vulnerability, it is capable of significantly impairing the average consumer's freedom of choice and pushing a transactional decision (re-subscribing) they would not otherwise take — an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9 and a manipulative dark-pattern communication.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'
findings.recommendation: Remove all guilt/shaming and disparaging framing from opt-out and win-back messaging. Present the STOP/unsubscribe option in neutral, non-judgemental language with no emotional pressure.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour. The overall design — ignoring refusals, obstructing opt-out and applying emotional pressure — is contrary to professional diligence and reinforces the specific breaches above, catching any residual conduct not covered by the blacklist or Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: Win-back sequence for lapsed gym-app subscribers
findings.recommendation: Redesign the win-back programme around genuine consent and easy opt-out: only re-engage users who have not withdrawn consent, cap frequency, and adopt honest, pressure-free messaging aligned with professional diligence.

verdicts.notes: This win-back campaign engages the UCPD strongly. The multi-channel re-contact of users who have unsubscribed — five "Are you sure?" emails on days 1/3/5/7/10, two SMS, and two scripted phone calls — is a textbook persistent and unwanted solicitation that is blacklisted in all circumstances (Annex I point 7... i.e. point 26). The guilt/shaming SMS copy and the deliberate obstruction of opt-out (30-day "processing" delay with continued sends, objections reviewed only monthly) additionally amount to aggressive practice by undue influence/harassment under Arts. 8-9, with the general safety-net of Art. 5 also engaged. None of the messaging is justified to enforce a contractual obligation.

report.executive_summary: This "FitBoost win-back blitz" chases people who have already unsubscribed with five "Are you sure?" emails (days 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10), two guilt-tripping SMS messages, and two phone calls — and it delays actually honouring the opt-out for up to 30 days while continuing to send, with objections only checked monthly. That combination triggers serious problems under two EU regimes. Under GDPR, the right to object to marketing is absolute and takes effect immediately, so continuing to contact people during a 30-day window and reviewing opt-outs only monthly means you are marketing without a lawful basis and obstructing withdrawal of consent. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, repeatedly contacting people who have refused is a blacklisted practice banned in all circumstances, and the deliberate opt-out obstruction plus the "give up on yourself" shaming copy amount to aggressive, manipulative practices. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. The core fix is simple in principle: stop contacting anyone the moment they unsubscribe, across every channel. As written, this campaign should not go live — it carries critical regulatory and enforcement risk.
recommendations: Stop the campaign as designed — do not launch until the post-unsubscribe re-contact is removed. Contacting people who have already unsubscribed via email, SMS and phone is a practice banned in all circumstances under the UCPD blacklist and has no case-by-case defence.

Suppress every contact immediately (in near real time) upon any unsubscribe/STOP/objection, across all three channels at once. Remove the 'processing may take up to 30 days' window entirely for marketing suppression.
Stop reviewing objection requests only monthly — route them to an automated suppression flow or continuous monitoring, and honour SMS STOP replies instantly.

Delete the guilt/shaming copy ('Your body misses you. Reply STOP to give up on yourself'). Present opt-out in neutral, pressure-free language. This is both a GDPR fairness breach and an aggressive/manipulative practice under UCPD.

Remove the 'Are you sure?' nag sequence and the two 'understand churn' phone calls to unsubscribed users. If a single account-closure confirmation is genuinely needed, send one transactional, non-marketing message only.

Confirm you have a valid lawful basis (consent or legitimate interest) for win-back messaging to users who have NOT opted out, and ensure profiling/personalisation of former subscribers also stops on objection — not just the message sends.

Redesign the programme around easy, one-click opt-out that is as simple as opting in, with frequency caps and honest messaging, and document the personalisation logic with clear Art. 13 information at data collection.

campaign.title: SleepWell mattress radio spot
campaign.text: A 30-second radio and podcast spot uses an AI-cloned voice of a nationally famous talk-show host: 'Hi, it's me — you know I only recommend what I use, and I sleep on a SleepWell every night.' The host has no relationship with the brand and never consented. No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears in the spot or the podcast description. The media plan notes the clone 'tested 40% better than an actor'.

detected_practices: AI voice cloning of a real person
fake celebrity endorsement / false testimonial
impersonation without consent
undisclosed synthetic voice (no AI disclosure)
misleading claim of personal use ('I sleep on a SleepWell every night')
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers on radio and podcast; no personalisation or targeting declared. DSA not clearly engaged as this is broadcast/podcast audio rather than an intermediary/online platform service. The host's voice and identity constitute personal data used without consent (GDPR), the AI-generated deepfake triggers AI Act transparency obligations, and the unauthorised fake endorsement/false personal-use claim is a misleading and likely aggressive commercial practice under the UCPD.
triage.summary: A 30-second radio/podcast ad uses an AI-cloned voice of a famous talk-show host who never consented, falsely implying a personal endorsement of the SleepWell mattress, with no disclosure that the voice is synthetic. The spot involves generative AI impersonating an identifiable real person and fabricating a testimonial, raising deepfake transparency, personal-data/likeness, and misleading-endorsement concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The AI-cloned voice of a real, nationally recognisable person, presented as an authentic recommendation, is audio content constituting a deep fake within the meaning of Art. 50(4). Deployers of such AI-generated/manipulated audio must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. Here there is explicitly no disclosure in either the radio spot or the podcast description, so the mandatory transparency obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: uses an AI-cloned voice of a nationally famous talk-show host ... No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears in the spot or the podcast description.
findings.recommendation: Do not run the ad without a clear, contemporaneous disclosure that the voice is AI-generated (e.g. an unambiguous spoken statement in the spot and a note in the podcast description). Note that disclosure alone does not cure the underlying lack of consent/false-endorsement problem — the safest fix is to stop using the cloned voice of a non-consenting real person.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The synthetic audio is generated by an AI system, so under Art. 50(2) the provider of that generative AI system must ensure the output is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. As described, the asset carries no provenance marking, so this obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: A 30-second radio and podcast spot uses an AI-cloned voice
findings.recommendation: Ensure the AI-generated audio output carries machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g. watermarking or metadata identifying it as artificially generated) as produced by the generative-AI provider, and verify the tool used supports Art. 50(2)-compliant marking.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses a deceptive AI technique — a cloned voice falsely implying a genuine personal endorsement, deliberately optimised because it 'tested 40% better than an actor' — which is capable of distorting consumer decisions. However, Art. 5(1)(a) requires that the technique be reasonably likely to cause significant harm; for a consumer mattress endorsement this high threshold is unlikely to be met, so this is flagged for awareness rather than as a probable breach. The misleading-endorsement wrong is more squarely addressed under the UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: the clone 'tested 40% better than an actor'
findings.recommendation: Be aware that deploying AI specifically because it deceives consumers more effectively edges toward the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition; avoid framing or scaling the technique in ways that could materially distort decisions or cause harm, and address the deception through truthful, consented advertising.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses an AI-cloned voice of a real, identifiable talk-show host presented as an authentic personal endorsement — an audio deep fake under the AI Act. No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears anywhere in the spot or podcast description, breaching the Art. 50(4) deep-fake transparency obligation. The Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking obligation is also engaged for the generative audio. Deceptive-technique concerns under Art. 5(1)(a) exist but the "significant harm" threshold is unlikely met for a mattress ad, so it is flagged as informational; the core misleading-endorsement wrong sits with the UCPD.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Cloning and broadcasting the host's voice is processing of the personal data of an identifiable natural person. Processing is lawful only with a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. There is no consent, no contract, and no legitimate interest could plausibly override the fundamental rights of a person whose voice is used to fabricate a false commercial endorsement. There is therefore no lawful basis for the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The host has no relationship with the brand and never consented.
findings.recommendation: Cease using the cloned voice. Only process an identifiable person's voice/likeness in advertising with a documented lawful basis — in practice a signed licence/consent from the individual — and retain evidence of that authorisation before broadcast.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: To the extent the brand would rely on consent as its Art. 6 basis, GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous by clear affirmative action. The host gave no indication whatsoever, so no valid consent exists. This confirms the absence of a consent-based lawful basis for cloning the voice.
findings.evidence_quote: never consented
findings.recommendation: Obtain freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous written consent (a talent/likeness release) from any real individual before their voice or identity is used, and document it.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: An AI voice clone reproduces the unique vocal/physiological characteristics of a specific identifiable individual for the purpose of recognisably reproducing that person. This engages the special-category/biometric regime, for which processing is prohibited absent a specific exception such as explicit consent. No exception applies, so the heightened prohibition is likely breached in addition to the general lawful-basis failure.
findings.evidence_quote: uses an AI-cloned voice of a nationally famous talk-show host
findings.recommendation: Treat cloning of a named individual's voice as processing that can involve biometric/special-category data; do not proceed without an applicable Art. 9 exception (explicit consent) and a documented Art. 6 basis. Where no authorisation exists, do not create or use the clone at all.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires personal data to be processed lawfully and fairly. Covertly cloning a real person's voice and attributing statements ('I sleep on a SleepWell every night') they never made is fundamentally unfair processing and gives the data subject no transparency or opportunity to exercise their rights. The processing breaches Art. 5(1)(a) on all three limbs.
findings.evidence_quote: No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears in the spot or the podcast description.
findings.recommendation: Do not process a person's voice to make false attributed statements. Ensure any use of a real individual's data in campaigns is lawful, fair to that individual, and transparent to them, with authorisation obtained in advance.

verdicts.notes: The GDPR concern here is not the audience (no personalisation/targeting/data collection from listeners is declared) but the talk-show host, an identifiable natural person whose voice and identity are personal data. The brand cloned and processed that voice to fabricate an endorsement without any lawful basis and without consent, in breach of the lawfulness and fairness principle. A voice clone that reproduces a specific person's unique vocal characteristics also engages the special-category/biometric regime. Findings relate solely to the host as data subject.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: The brand has commissioned the creation of a fabricated endorsement attributed to a real, identifiable person who never gave one. Presenting an AI-synthesised, non-existent endorsement as a genuine personal recommendation is a false endorsement / misrepresented social endorsement, which is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c. No consumer-detriment or averaging test applies — it is blacklisted per se.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises payday-style loans to "adults in financial difficulty" using guaranteed-approval claims, a hidden 312% APR, emotional pressure, and a fake countdown timer, and it cannot run as written. Separately, the fake timer is also a prohibited "dark pattern" under the Digital Services Act, and the personalised targeting raises unmet GDPR obligations (no evident lawful basis, consent, privacy notice, or opt-out, plus a real risk of profiling on sensitive proxies). The AI Act does not apply. Verdict: do not launch — this needs a fundamental rework, not minor edits, and given the product and audience some elements may not be salvageable at all.

findings.rationale: As the safety-net provision, Art. 5 (with Art. 5(3)) requires the practice to be assessed from the perspective of the clearly identifiable vulnerable group being targeted — here, financially distressed consumers. verdicts.notes: This payday-lender campaign engages multiple UCPD provisions, including at least one per se blacklisted practice (Annex I point 7 — false urgency). The "15 minutes to expire" countdown for an application that was never started is a false limited-time claim prohibited in all circumstances. The campaign also contains misleading actions ("GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks; everyone qualifies"), a serious misleading omission (312% representative APR hidden behind a "rates" link), and aggressive/undue-influence tactics that exploit the misfortune of a vulnerable audience explicitly defined as "adults in financial difficulty."
