report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises payday-style loans to "adults in financial difficulty" using headline claims of "guaranteed approval," "no credit checks," and "everyone qualifies," while hiding the 312% representative APR behind a "rates" link and pushing a fake "your application expires in 15 minutes" countdown for applications that were never started. As currently designed, it should not run — it contains an outright banned practice (false urgency/scarcity), which is prohibited in all circumstances under EU consumer law regardless of any harm test. On top of that, the "guaranteed approval / no credit checks" claims are almost certainly false for a regulated credit product, the buried APR is a serious omission of the single most important cost figure, and the fear-based "don't let your family go without" messaging aimed at people in financial distress is likely an aggressive practice exploiting a vulnerable audience. Separately, the behavioural retargeting is profiling under data protection law with no evidence of a lawful basis, privacy notice, or opt-out, and it lacks the required platform ad-transparency and anti-dark-pattern safeguards. The vulnerability of the target audience aggravates every one of these issues and invites regulator and platform enforcement. Verdict: do not launch; the campaign needs fundamental redesign, not minor edits.
recommendations: Do not launch the campaign in its current form. Immediately remove the fake 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' countdown — this is a blacklisted false-urgency practice banned outright, and also an illegal dark pattern; never fabricate deadlines or reference applications the user never started.

Delete the absolute claims 'guaranteed approval', 'everyone qualifies' and 'no credit checks / no questions / no paperwork'. Replace with truthful statements that lending is subject to eligibility and affordability/creditworthiness checks required by law.
Show the representative APR (312%) and total cost of credit clearly and prominently at the same level as the headline offer — not hidden behind a 'rates' link.

Remove the fear/pressure framing ('Don't let your family go without this weekend') and any escalating retargeting sequences; these amount to aggressive tactics exploiting a financially vulnerable audience.
Reconsider deliberately targeting 'adults in financial difficulty' with high-cost credit at all — the vulnerability of this group raises the legal bar and makes the whole approach hard to defend.

Before any retargeting runs, establish and document a lawful basis (valid prior consent for tracking cookies/audiences, or a documented legitimate-interest assessment), provide a layered privacy notice at every collection point, and offer a clear, easy opt-out from marketing profiling.

Ensure every social/display placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement, names the advertiser and payer, and discloses the main targeting parameters with a means to change them, using the platforms' ad-transparency tools.
Verify audience-building does not use or infer sensitive/special-category data (e.g. health or debt-illness proxies) and document the segmentation criteria.

campaign.title: QuickCash 'guaranteed approval' loans
campaign.text: Search and social ads for a payday-style lender: '€1,000 in your account in 10 minutes. GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks, no questions, no paperwork. Bad credit? Perfect credit? Everyone qualifies. Don't let your family go without this weekend.' The representative APR (312%) appears only behind a 'rates' link. Retargeting creatives escalate: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started.

detected_practices: 'guaranteed approval' claim
'no credit checks' claim
hidden/obscured APR (312% behind a link)
false urgency ('application expires in 15 minutes' for a non-existent application)
false countdown/expiry pressure
emotional pressure targeting ('don't let your family go without')
targeting financially vulnerable consumers
behavioural retargeting
personalised targeting
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is adults in financial difficulty — a vulnerable audience under UCPD, which heightens scrutiny of misleading and aggressive practices. Financially distressed consumers are more susceptible to false urgency and 'guaranteed approval' claims. No indication of minors being targeted, though social/display channels could incidentally reach them.
triage.summary: A payday-style lender campaign across search, social and display promising instant 'guaranteed approval' loans with no credit checks, while burying the 312% representative APR behind a link and using false-urgency retargeting ('application expires in 15 minutes' when none was started). It explicitly targets financially vulnerable adults with emotional pressure and behavioural personalisation. Multiple aggressive/misleading practices and consumer-credit disclosure concerns are present.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting and declared personalised targeting of a segment defined by 'financial difficulty' is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict a person's economic situation and behaviour — the textbook definition of profiling in Art. 4(4). This engages the downstream GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection).
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes'
findings.recommendation: Document that retargeting/personalisation is profiling, map the personal data and inferences used, and ensure each downstream GDPR obligation (Arts. 6, 13, 21) is satisfied before running the campaign.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and behavioural retargeting require a valid legal basis — in practice consent (typically via ePrivacy for tracking cookies/pixels) or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The submission identifies no lawful basis and no consent capture; a legitimate-interest basis is very hard to sustain for retargeting a financially vulnerable audience with a payday-loan product, where the data subject's interests weigh heavily.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before targeting: obtain valid consent for the tracking/retargeting, and if relying on legitimate interests conduct and record an LIA that specifically accounts for the vulnerability of the audience. Do not deploy retargeting pixels without a compliant consent layer.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be fair and transparent. Retargeting an individual with a fabricated 'application expires' message based on tracking that the individual is unaware of — combined with buried pricing (APR hidden behind a link) — reflects processing that is neither transparent nor fair to the data subject. False personalised urgency built on collected behavioural data undermines the fairness principle.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove fabricated personalised claims (no 'application expires' where no application exists), disclose tracking clearly, and ensure retargeting messages are truthful and transparent about the data-driven basis on which they are served.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected (e.g. via tracking pixels, lead forms, or the loan application flow) the controller must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, data-subject rights and information about any profiling at the point of collection. The campaign describes collection-driven retargeting with no indication that this transparency information is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at every data-collection point (ad landing pages, tracking consent banner, application form) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, profiling/retargeting and the rights in Arts. 21/22.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct-marketing processing, including profiling for retargeting, must respect an absolute right to object, and the data subject must be informed of that right explicitly and separately at the latest at first communication. Nothing in the campaign indicates an opt-out/objection mechanism for the retargeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes'
findings.recommendation: Present a clear, easy opt-out from direct-marketing profiling/retargeting, honour it immediately by suppressing the individual, and inform recipients of this absolute right explicitly and separately in the first communication.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Financial distress is not itself an Art. 9 special category, but audiences built around debt/hardship are frequently assembled using or correlating with proxies that reveal health, or other sensitive attributes. If the targeting relies on such inferred sensitive attributes, Art. 9's prohibition (explicit consent required) is engaged, and platform ad targeting on such data is separately banned. Flagged as a risk to verify against the actual targeting parameters.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Audit the audience-build parameters and data broker segments used; ensure no Art. 9 attributes (including proxies/inferences for health, etc.) drive targeting. If any are present, either cease that targeting or secure explicit consent (noting platform bans may still prohibit it).

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses behavioural retargeting and declared personalised targeting of "adults in financial difficulty," which constitutes profiling of personal data under GDPR (economic situation/behaviour are named in Art. 4(4)). The submission describes no lawful basis, no consent mechanism, no Art. 13 transparency information, and no facilitation of the right to object — and the covert/manipulative framing (false "application expires" retargeting, hidden APR) undermines the fairness and transparency principle. Targeting on inferred financial distress also risks shading into special-category inferences. Findings are grounded in Arts. 4(4), 6(1), 5(1)(a), 13, 21 and 9.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Retargeting creatives display a false countdown/expiry ('your application expires in 15 minutes') for an application the consumer never started. This is a deceptive/manipulative design element delivered through platform online interfaces that materially distorts recipients' ability to make a free and informed decision — the paradigm of a false-urgency dark pattern prohibited by Art. 25. It is aggravated by the declared targeting of financially distressed adults, who are especially susceptible to fabricated deadlines.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove all fabricated countdowns and expiry claims. Do not present time-limited pressure referring to an application or offer that does not genuinely exist or has no real deadline. Any deadline shown must be true, verifiable and applied consistently, with no manufactured urgency in retargeting creatives.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is delivered on social and display platforms using personalised/behavioural targeting and retargeting. Art. 26(1) requires that, for each ad, recipients can identify in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is shown, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. Nothing in the submission indicates the advertiser identity and targeting-parameter information are surfaced, and obscuring the offer's key terms (APR behind a link) sits uneasily with the clear/unambiguous standard.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad is clearly labelled as an advertisement with the QuickCash advertiser/payer identity, and that the platform-provided 'why am I seeing this ad' targeting-parameter disclosure is complete and accurate for the personalised segments used. Coordinate with the hosting platforms to confirm Art. 26 transparency elements are populated for all creatives.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The declared audience is defined by financial distress. Financial hardship is not, in itself, a GDPR Art. 9 special category, so the Art. 26(3) ban on profiling with special-category data is not directly triggered. However, if the targeting relies on proxies that infer Art. 9 attributes (e.g. health/medical debt, or over-indebtedness datasets correlated with health), the prohibition would apply regardless of consent. Flagged for monitoring rather than as a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Audit the targeting data sources and lookalike/interest segments to confirm no special-category data (health, etc.) is used directly or as an inferred proxy to reach 'adults in financial difficulty'. Document the parameters used so the segmentation can withstand scrutiny under Art. 26(3).

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social and display platforms with personalised behavioural targeting, engaging the DSA's platform-advertising rules. The most serious DSA concern is the false-urgency retargeting ("application expires in 15 minutes" for an application that was never started), which is a deceptive/manipulative interface design captured by the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition. Ad-transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)) are also engaged given the personalised targeting. The Art. 26(3) sensitive-data ban is not clearly triggered because financial difficulty is not itself a GDPR Art. 9 category, though proxy-inference risk warrants monitoring; the minors provision (Art. 28) is not applicable per the triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits, in all circumstances, falsely stating that terms are available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. Here a 15-minute expiry countdown is asserted for an application that was never started — the deadline is fabricated. This is a blacklisted false-urgency practice requiring no case-by-case unfairness assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove all countdown/expiry messaging that does not correspond to a genuine, verifiable time-limited offer tied to an actual application. Never state that a non-existent application is 'expiring'.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The representative APR is the single most material price term of a credit product. Hiding it behind a 'rates' link while headlining '€1,000 in your account in 10 minutes' provides material information in an unclear and untimely manner, and omits it from the point where the consumer forms their transactional decision — a misleading omission under Art. 7. Vulnerability of the audience heightens the materiality.
findings.evidence_quote: The representative APR (312%) appears only behind a 'rates' link
findings.recommendation: Display the representative APR (312%) and total cost of credit with equal prominence to the headline offer, at the first point of promotion, not behind a click. Meet consumer-credit disclosure standards inline in every creative.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits false information on the main characteristics of the product. 'Guaranteed approval' and 'Everyone qualifies' with 'no credit checks' are almost certainly untrue for a regulated lender (which must conduct affordability/creditworthiness assessment), and deceive consumers about a key characteristic of the credit, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks, no questions, no paperwork. Bad credit? Perfect credit? Everyone qualifies.
findings.recommendation: Drop absolute claims of 'guaranteed approval' / 'everyone qualifies' / 'no credit checks' unless literally and lawfully true. State that approval is subject to eligibility and affordability assessment.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive practices that use undue influence — including exploitation of misfortune, timing pressure and persistence — to impair the consumer's freedom of choice. Combining emotional coercion aimed at people in financial distress with escalating retargeting and a fake expiry countdown exploits misfortune to force an immediate transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Don't let your family go without this weekend.
findings.recommendation: Remove emotionally coercive framing that exploits family/financial hardship and stop escalating high-pressure retargeting. Advertising to financially distressed consumers must avoid urgency and guilt-based pressure.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group to be assessed from that group's perspective. Deliberately targeting financially distressed consumers — who are especially susceptible to 'guaranteed approval' and false-urgency claims — means the misleading and aggressive elements above are judged against a heightened standard and are likely to materially distort their economic behaviour, contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Reassess the entire campaign against the average vulnerable (financially distressed) consumer standard; strip out claims and pressure tactics that exploit that vulnerability, and ensure professional-diligence safeguards (clear costs, no false promises) throughout.

verdicts.notes: This payday-lender campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including at least one blacklisted (per se prohibited) practice. The retargeting "application expires in 15 minutes" message — where no application was even started — is a false urgency claim blacklisted under Annex I point 7. The buried 312% APR is a misleading omission of material price information (Art. 7). "GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks... Everyone qualifies" is a misleading action (Art. 6). Emotional pressure ("Don't let your family go without") aimed at a clearly vulnerable group (adults in financial difficulty) via escalating retargeting engages the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9) and the Art. 5 vulnerable-consumer standard. Multiple serious breaches are likely.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises payday-style loans to "adults in financial difficulty" using guaranteed-approval claims, a hidden 312% APR, emotional pressure, and retargeting ads with a fake 15-minute countdown for an application the person never started. As written, it breaks EU consumer law in multiple serious ways. The fake countdown is a blacklisted false-urgency practice that is banned outright — no case-by-case defence is possible — and it also counts as a prohibited "dark pattern" on the platforms. Burying the APR behind a "rates" link, promising "guaranteed approval / no credit checks / everyone qualifies," and using guilt-based pressure ("don't let your family go without") on a vulnerable audience add up to misleading and aggressive practices. On the data side, your behavioural retargeting is profiling under GDPR with no stated lawful basis, no consent layer, no privacy notice, and no opt-out, and the "financial difficulty" audience risks pulling in sensitive-data proxies. This campaign should not run in its current form; it needs a fundamental rework, not tweaks.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as-is. It contains a blacklisted per-se-illegal practice and multiple likely serious breaches; a full rework is required before any deployment.

Remove all fabricated countdown/expiry messaging immediately. Never state that an 'application expires' when no application was started; any deadline shown must be genuine, verifiable, and consistently applied. (Blacklisted false urgency + prohibited dark pattern.)

Drop the absolute claims: no 'guaranteed approval', 'everyone qualifies', or 'no credit checks'. As a regulated lender you must assess affordability/creditworthiness — state that approval is subject to eligibility and affordability checks.
Display the representative APR (312%) and total cost of credit inline, with equal prominence to the headline offer, in every creative — not hidden behind a 'rates' link.
Remove emotionally coercive, guilt-based framing ('don't let your family go without') and stop the escalating high-pressure retargeting aimed at financially distressed consumers.

Establish and document a GDPR lawful basis before any retargeting: capture valid consent for tracking pixels, or complete a legitimate-interest assessment that specifically weighs the audience's vulnerability (which will be hard to sustain here).

Provide a layered privacy notice at every data-collection point (landing pages, consent banner, application form) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, profiling/retargeting, and an explicit, easy right to object to direct-marketing profiling that is honoured immediately.

Ensure DSA ad-transparency elements are populated on every social/display creative: clear 'advertisement' label, QuickCash payer identity, and accurate 'why am I seeing this ad' targeting-parameter disclosure.

Audit the audience-build and data-broker/lookalike segments to confirm no special-category attributes (e.g. health, medical debt) are used directly or as inferred proxies to target 'financial difficulty'; document the parameters used.

Re-evaluate the whole campaign against the vulnerable-consumer standard and, given this is regulated consumer credit, confirm compliance with sector-specific credit-advertising disclosure rules alongside these fixes.

campaign.title: PharmaPlus loyalty-driven baby campaign
campaign.text: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience and receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products ('Week by week, we're with you'). Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'. Household members sharing the account also see the campaign.

detected_practices: behavioural retargeting from loyalty-card purchase history
automatic silent enrolment into inferred audience segment
inference of health/pregnancy status from purchase data
personalised email and app-push marketing
profiling of special-category (health) data without clear consent
vague privacy notice ('personalised offers') failing to disclose actual processing
targeting based on inferred life-stage / medical condition
triage.audience_notes: Target is loyalty-card holders algorithmically inferred as pregnant — this involves special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9. Silent enrolment means no valid consent basis is evident, and the inference of pregnancy is disclosed to household members sharing the account, creating a further confidentiality/data-protection risk. Although no minors are directly targeted, the inference concerns reproductive/pregnancy status, a highly sensitive domain. The vague 'personalised offers' notice may also constitute a misleading omission under the UCPD.
triage.summary: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories to silently enrol customers inferred to be pregnant into a 'Growing Family' audience, then sends personalised prenatal and baby-product marketing via email and app-push. It infers highly sensitive health/pregnancy status from purchase data without transparent consent, relying on a vague privacy notice, and exposes the inference to other household members sharing the account.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring pregnancy/reproductive status from purchase data and using it to target marketing constitutes processing of special-category health data. Art. 9 prohibits such processing absent an exception; the only realistic marketing exception is explicit consent, which is absent here (enrolment is silent). Inferred attributes are expressly covered.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Do not derive or use pregnancy/health inferences for marketing without prior explicit, granular opt-in consent specifically covering the inference and use of health data. If explicit consent cannot be obtained, cease the Growing Family segmentation entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised marketing and profiling require a valid lawful basis. Silent enrolment provides no consent and, for special-category health inferences, legitimate interests is not available. No valid Art. 6 basis (nor Art. 9 condition) is evident for the processing described.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before processing — for this sensitive use, prior explicit consent under Art. 6(1)(a) + Art. 9(2)(a). Suspend the audience until this is in place.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent purportedly relied on fails the Art. 4(11) standard: silent/automatic enrolment is not a freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous affirmative action. Inactivity and bundling do not qualify.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent
findings.recommendation: Implement a clear affirmative opt-in (unticked, unbundled) that specifically describes the health-based profiling and marketing before any enrolment.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to demonstrate consent, present requests distinctly in plain language, and make withdrawal as easy as giving. With silent enrolment there is no demonstrable, distinguishable consent and no described withdrawal mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products
findings.recommendation: Provide a distinguishable consent request in plain language and an equally easy withdrawal/opt-out; retain records demonstrating each individual's consent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Covert inference of a sensitive attribute and a privacy notice that conceals the true processing breach the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. The processing is neither transparent nor fair, and disclosing the inference to household members further undermines fairness.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the notice to disclose the actual processing (health inference, profiling, purpose) and process only in ways the data subject would reasonably expect.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires disclosure at collection of the purposes, legal basis, and the existence of profiling. Describing processing merely as 'personalised offers' omits that health data is inferred and used for profiling-based marketing, failing the information obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy information to specify that purchase data is used to infer health/life-stage status, the legal basis (explicit consent), the profiling logic, retention and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of purchase histories to predict health/life-stage and segment individuals is profiling within Art. 4(4), which triggers the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories
findings.recommendation: Treat the segmentation as profiling: ensure a lawful basis, disclose the profiling, and support objection rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and related profiling. The campaign describes no opt-out/objection mechanism, and silent enrolment means individuals cannot readily exercise this right.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy opt-out in every message and honour objections immediately by ceasing all direct-marketing profiling for that individual.

verdicts.notes: The campaign infers pregnancy — a health/reproductive status protected as special-category data — from loyalty-card purchase histories and uses it to target marketing, with silent enrolment, no explicit consent, and a misleading privacy notice. This engages GDPR Art. 9 (special-category processing), Art. 6/4(11)/7 (no valid lawful basis/consent), Arts. 5(1)(a)/12/13 (transparency), Art. 4(4) (profiling), and Art. 21 (right to object). Sharing the inference with household members compounds the fairness/confidentiality breach. Multiple likely violations centred on unlawful processing of inferred health data.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The average consumer is not told that their loyalty-card purchase history is being analysed to infer pregnancy and to auto-enrol them in a 'Growing Family' marketing audience. Presenting this as generic 'personalised offers' provides material information in an unclear, ambiguous manner and hides the true nature and commercial intent of the practice, which a consumer would need to make an informed decision about whether to remain in the loyalty programme or engage with the marketing. This is a misleading omission within Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: Replace the vague 'personalised offers' wording with a clear, prominent, timely disclosure at or before enrolment: state that purchase history is analysed to infer life-stage/health interests (e.g. pregnancy) and used to send targeted prenatal/baby marketing, identify it explicitly as advertising, and offer an easy, upfront opt-in/opt-out. Do not rely on silent enrolment.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Silently inferring a sensitive and emotionally charged condition (pregnancy or attempts to conceive) and marketing on that basis may be contrary to professional diligence and liable to materially distort the transactional behaviour of consumers who are in a vulnerable life-stage, especially as inferences can be wrong or unwanted (e.g. after pregnancy loss). Art. 5 operates as the fairness safety-net where no specific rule fully captures the conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Adopt a heightened-diligence approach for sensitive inferences: require explicit, informed opt-in before any pregnancy/baby targeting, provide a one-click way to leave the 'Growing Family' audience in every message, and suppress the segment where the inference is uncertain or potentially distressing.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Emotionally framed, week-by-week messaging tied to an inferred pregnancy could edge toward undue influence exploiting a sensitive circumstance, which Arts. 8-9 treat as an aggressive-practice factor. On the facts given there is no evidence of harassment, coercion or high-pressure persistence, so the risk is limited rather than a clear breach.
findings.evidence_quote: personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products ('Week by week, we're with you')
findings.recommendation: Keep messaging frequency modest and non-pressurising, avoid deadline/urgency framing around the pregnancy life-stage, and honour opt-outs immediately to prevent the campaign from becoming persistent or coercive.

verdicts.notes: The UCPD is engaged principally through the vague, uninformative privacy notice. Describing the practice merely as "personalised offers" while in reality mining loyalty data, inferring pregnancy status and silently enrolling customers into a marketing audience is a likely misleading omission under Art. 7: it hides material information and the true nature/commercial intent of the processing behind an ambiguous term. The exploitation of a sensitive life-stage (inferred pregnancy) also raises a professional-diligence/vulnerable-consumer concern under Art. 5. No blacklisted (Annex I) practice is clearly present, and no misleading product claims (Art. 6) appear. The core health-data/consent problems fall to the GDPR assessment.

report.executive_summary: This campaign mines loyalty-card purchase data to infer that customers are pregnant (or trying to conceive) and silently enrols them into a "Growing Family" audience that receives prenatal and baby marketing via email and app push. The central problem is that inferred pregnancy is special-category health data under GDPR, and using it for marketing requires prior explicit opt-in consent — which the silent enrolment does not provide. The privacy notice, which describes the practice only as "personalised offers", fails GDPR transparency duties and is also a likely misleading omission under consumer-protection law, because it hides what is really being done. Additional concerns include the lack of a valid lawful basis, no clear opt-out, and the fact that household members sharing an account can see the inference, which risks exposing a sensitive condition to third parties. There is also a real-world harm dimension: inferences can be wrong or distressing (e.g. after pregnancy loss), touching on fair-practice and vulnerable-consumer rules. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. Overall this is a high-exposure campaign that should not go live in its current form.
recommendations: Suspend the 'Growing Family' segmentation immediately — do not run the campaign until a lawful footing is in place, as it currently processes inferred health data without any valid basis.

Obtain prior explicit, granular, unbundled opt-in consent that specifically describes the health/pregnancy inference and its use for targeted marketing; use an unticked affirmative action and keep records demonstrating each person's consent.

Rewrite the privacy notice and enrolment disclosure to state plainly that purchase history is analysed to infer life-stage/health status and used for profiling-based marketing, including the legal basis, profiling logic, retention, and data-subject rights — replace the vague 'personalised offers' wording.
Add a clear, one-click opt-out/objection mechanism in every email and app push, and honour objections immediately by ceasing all marketing profiling for that individual.
Prevent exposure of the pregnancy inference to household members sharing an account, and suppress the segment where the inference is uncertain or potentially distressing (e.g. after pregnancy loss).
Keep messaging frequency modest and avoid urgency or emotionally pressuring framing around the pregnancy life-stage to avoid straying into aggressive-practice territory.
If explicit consent cannot realistically be obtained at the point of loyalty sign-up, abandon the pregnancy/baby inference model entirely and use only non-sensitive, consented targeting.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring that a customer is pregnant/expecting from purchase history is processing of data concerning health — a special category under Art. 9. Such processing is prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) exception applies; for marketing the only realistic basis is explicit consent, which is absent given the silent enrolment and vague notice.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Do not infer or target on pregnancy/health status without prior explicit, granular opt-in consent specifically covering the use of purchase data to infer pregnancy for baby-product marketing. Absent that, exclude health-derived inferences from the audience entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Behavioural profiling and personalised email/app-push marketing require a valid Art. 6 basis. Silent enrolment means no consent was obtained, and legitimate interests cannot lawfully cover Art. 9 health inferences or override the reasonable expectations of customers who were not told their purchases would be mined.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before processing. For this sensitive personalisation, rely on freely given, specific, informed consent obtained up front, and run a documented balancing/assessment for any non-sensitive elements.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous affirmative action. Silent automatic enrolment is the opposite of an affirmative indication, so no valid consent exists — critically fatal where Art. 9 requires explicit consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent
findings.recommendation: Replace silent enrolment with an explicit, unbundled opt-in (clear affirmative action) that specifically names the pregnancy/family inference and the channels used, and keep records demonstrating each consent.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that consent be demonstrable, clearly distinguishable, and as easy to withdraw as to give. With silent enrolment there is nothing to demonstrate, and no withdrawal mechanism is described for the audience/profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products
findings.recommendation: Implement a consent record and a one-click withdrawal that removes the person from the 'Growing Family' audience and stops the profiling, mirroring the ease of the (currently non-existent) opt-in.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached on two fronts: covert profiling based on purchase data the customer did not expect to be used this way, and unfair/unlawful disclosure of a highly sensitive inferred pregnancy to other household members who share the account.
findings.evidence_quote: Household members sharing the account also see the campaign.
findings.recommendation: Make the processing transparent and expected, and suppress sensitive family/pregnancy messaging on shared or household accounts (or verify the intended recipient) to avoid revealing a person's pregnancy to third parties.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At collection the controller must disclose the purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and the existence of profiling. A notice referencing only 'personalised offers' fails to disclose the mining of purchase histories, the pregnancy/health inference and the automated audience enrolment.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice at the point of loyalty-card sign-up and in the campaign to specifically disclose profiling of purchase data, the health/pregnancy inference, the lawful basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. A euphemistic single phrase ('personalised offers') that masks sensitive health profiling is neither transparent nor intelligible about what actually happens.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the disclosure in clear, plain language that a customer would understand as covering pregnancy inference and targeted baby-product marketing, presented prominently rather than buried.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of purchase data to predict health status and personal circumstances and segment customers squarely meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling, which triggers the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories ... automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Recognise the operation as profiling and ensure the full profiling compliance stack (lawful basis, Art. 13 profiling disclosure, right to object) is in place before running it.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and to profiling related to it, which must be facilitated. No opt-out from the marketing or the 'Growing Family' profiling is described.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easily exercisable opt-out in every email and app-push, and at first contact explicitly inform recipients of their right to object to the direct marketing and related profiling; honour objections immediately.

verdicts.notes: This campaign processes inferred pregnancy status — special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9 — without the explicit consent that provision requires, and without any valid Art. 6 lawful basis given the silent enrolment. The processing is neither transparent nor fair (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12–13): the privacy notice mentions only vague 'personalised offers' and never discloses the profiling, the health inference, or the automated audience enrolment. Automated segmentation into the 'Growing Family' audience is profiling (Art. 4(4)), yet no lawful basis, right to object (Art. 21) or valid consent (Arts. 4(11), 7) is evidenced, and sharing the campaign to household members risks unlawful disclosure of a person's pregnancy. Multiple high/critical GDPR breaches are likely.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Consumers are silently profiled by mining loyalty-card purchase histories (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) to infer pregnancy and enrol them in a 'Growing Family' audience, yet the only disclosure is a vague reference to 'personalised offers'. This omits and obscures material information the average consumer needs to understand the true nature and basis of the commercial practice — namely that intimate health/pregnancy status has been inferred and is being used to drive the marketing. Providing this in an unclear, ambiguous manner (or not at all) is a misleading omission under Art. 7, which also covers failure to make the commercial nature and its underlying logic apparent.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: Replace the vague 'personalised offers' wording with a clear, specific and timely disclosure explaining that purchase-history data is used to infer life-stage/health status and to enrol customers in targeted audiences; make enrolment transparent (and ideally opt-in) with an easy, prominent opt-out presented before or at first contact.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Under Art. 5(3), a practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of a clearly identifiable group that is particularly vulnerable due to their specific situation. Consumers inferred as pregnant are a clearly identifiable group in a sensitive, emotionally heightened situation. Deliberately building this audience and directing tailored, affect-laden marketing at it heightens the risk that the practice materially distorts their economic behaviour and falls short of professional diligence, especially combined with the opaque enrolment.
findings.evidence_quote: loyalty-card holders inferred as pregnant
findings.recommendation: Assess the campaign against the average pregnant consumer's susceptibility; avoid exploiting the sensitivity of the inferred condition, ensure marketing is proportionate and non-manipulative, and obtain informed, transparent agreement before targeting this group.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The emotionally framed, empathetic messaging delivered as personalised email and repeated app-push during pregnancy leverages the consumer's emotional situation. Where such persistent, affect-driven contact exploits the consumer's circumstances and undue influence significantly impairs their freedom of choice, it can constitute an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. On the current facts this is a risk rather than a clear breach (frequency and pressure are not fully described), but the emotional exploitation of a sensitive life event should be monitored.
findings.evidence_quote: Week by week, we're with you
findings.recommendation: Cap contact frequency, avoid emotionally manipulative framing that exploits the pregnancy situation, and ensure recipients can easily and immediately stop the messaging without onerous barriers.

verdicts.notes: The campaign does not contain false product claims or a clearly blacklisted practice, so no critical Annex I finding applies. However, two UCPD concerns are engaged: (1) the silent enrolment combined with a vague "personalised offers" privacy notice omits/hides material information about the true nature of the practice (health-status profiling to build a pregnancy audience), engaging Art. 7 misleading omission; and (2) the campaign deliberately targets a vulnerable/emotionally susceptible group (consumers inferred as pregnant) with affectively framed, personalised repeat messaging, engaging the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer standard and, at the margin, the Arts. 8-9 undue-influence assessment. These are transparency and fairness risks rather than confirmed breaches. (The data-protection lawfulness of the pregnancy inference and household-account disclosure is for the GDPR agent.)

report.executive_summary: This campaign silently mines loyalty-card purchase histories (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) to infer that customers are pregnant, then auto-enrols them into a 'Growing Family' audience for personalised baby-product emails and app pushes. The core problem is that inferring pregnancy is processing of sensitive health data, which under GDPR is prohibited unless you have the customer's explicit, up-front opt-in consent — and you have none, since enrolment is silent and the privacy notice only mentions vague 'personalised offers'. This makes the campaign a likely serious GDPR breach on multiple fronts (no lawful basis, no valid consent, no transparency, no easy opt-out, and no disclosed right to object). It gets worse: because household members sharing the account also see the messages, you risk revealing someone's pregnancy to their family — a highly damaging unlawful disclosure. On top of the data-protection failures, the silent profiling and vague notice also breach consumer-protection rules on hidden commercial intent, and emotionally framed messaging aimed at a vulnerable, pregnant audience raises fairness concerns. In its current form the campaign should not launch.
recommendations: Do not launch the campaign as designed. Stop any silent enrolment into the 'Growing Family' audience immediately.</br>

Do not infer or target on pregnancy/health status without prior, explicit, granular opt-in consent that specifically names the pregnancy/life-stage inference from purchase data and the email/app-push channels. Absent that consent, remove health-derived inferences from the audience entirely.

Replace silent enrolment with a clear affirmative opt-in (unbundled, plain-language) and keep records demonstrating each consent, with one-click withdrawal that removes the person from the audience and stops the profiling.
Suppress sensitive pregnancy/family messaging on shared or household accounts, or verify the intended individual recipient, to avoid disclosing someone's pregnancy to third parties.

Rewrite the privacy notice and campaign disclosures (at loyalty sign-up and at first contact) to clearly explain that purchase data is profiled to infer life-stage/health status, plus the lawful basis, recipients, retention, and data-subject rights — no more euphemistic 'personalised offers'.
Include a prominent, easy opt-out in every email and app-push and explicitly inform recipients of their right to object to direct marketing and related profiling; honour objections immediately.
Avoid emotionally manipulative framing ('Week by week, we're with you') aimed at pregnant consumers, cap contact frequency, and ensure messaging is proportionate and non-manipulative.
Given the sensitive, large-scale profiling involved, conduct and document a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before any relaunch and consult your DPO/legal team.

campaign.title: PharmaPlus loyalty-driven baby campaign
campaign.text: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience and receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products ('Week by week, we're with you'). Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'. Household members sharing the account also see the campaign.

detected_practices: behavioural profiling from loyalty-card purchase history
inference of health/pregnancy status
automatic silent enrolment into a marketing audience
personalised email and app-push targeting
emotive relationship-building messaging ('Week by week, we're with you')
inadequate/vague privacy notice ('personalised offers' only)
triage.summary: A pharmacy chain profiles loyalty-card purchase histories to infer pregnancy and silently enrols customers into a 'Growing Family' audience receiving personalised prenatal/baby marketing via email and app-push. The privacy notice only vaguely mentions 'personalised offers', and household members sharing the account may also receive the messaging. This engages GDPR (inferred special-category health data, transparency/consent, silent profiling) and UCPD (misleading omission and potential exploitation of a vulnerable life-stage).

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring pregnancy/reproductive status from purchase patterns produces data concerning health (and arguably sex life) — a special category under Art. 9. Art. 9 expressly covers inferred attributes and prohibits processing unless an exception (notably explicit consent) applies. Here enrolment is silent with no explicit consent, so the processing falls squarely within the prohibition with no visible exemption.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Do not infer or process pregnancy/health status for marketing without prior, explicit, freely given consent specific to health-based targeting. Provide a genuine opt-in that separately and explicitly explains that purchase data will be used to infer pregnancy; absent that, cease the inference and targeting entirely.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of purchase histories to predict a life-stage (pregnancy) and personal preferences is profiling within the Art. 4(4) definition, triggering the associated lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: A pharmacy chain mines loyalty-card purchase histories ... are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, complete a DPIA (high-risk profiling of health data at scale), and ensure every downstream GDPR obligation (lawful basis, transparency, objection) is met before running it.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised marketing profiling requires a valid lawful basis; because special-category (health) data is involved, consent must additionally be explicit under Art. 9. Silent enrolment means neither consent nor a defensible legitimate-interest basis is established, so the processing is unlawful under Art. 6(1). Email/app-push direct marketing also generally requires prior consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before processing. For health-based profiling and marketing this must be explicit opt-in consent; a legitimate-interest basis cannot lawfully cover Art. 9 data. Suspend the campaign for any individual without such consent.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent purportedly relied on is not freely given, specific, informed or unambiguous. Silent/automatic enrolment is exactly the inactivity/pre-ticked scenario that does not qualify as consent, and it cannot amount to the explicit consent Art. 9 demands.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent
findings.recommendation: Replace silent enrolment with a clear affirmative opt-in action, worded specifically for pregnancy/health-based profiling and prenatal marketing, and keep records demonstrating the consent.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Covertly mining purchase data to infer pregnancy while disclosing only 'personalised offers' is neither transparent nor fair — data subjects have no way to understand that their health status is being inferred and exploited.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Ensure processing is fair and transparent: clearly disclose the inference of pregnancy/health status, the purpose, and the profiling logic in plain terms up-front, not buried behind a euphemism.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and in clear, plain language. Describing the practice merely as 'personalised offers' fails this standard by obscuring the health-data inference and profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the privacy information in clear, plain language that a customer can actually understand, specifically naming pregnancy inference and the purposes for which purchase data is used.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting/using the data, Art. 13 requires disclosure of purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights and the existence of profiling/automated decision-making. A notice limited to 'personalised offers' omits these mandatory elements, particularly the profiling and health-inference purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete Art. 13 notice covering purposes, legal basis (explicit consent), the profiling logic, retention, recipients (including that household members may see it), and how to object/withdraw.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time to direct marketing and related profiling. The campaign describes no opt-out mechanism, and silent enrolment makes it unlikely the absolute objection right is being facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: receive personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy-to-use opt-out in every email and app-push and honour objections immediately by ceasing all direct-marketing profiling for that individual.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Sensitive prenatal marketing reaches household members who are not the profiled data subject and have given no consent, and who may not know the pregnancy — a serious breach of the fairness and lawfulness principle and a real risk of unlawful disclosure of a person's inferred health status to third parties.
findings.evidence_quote: Household members sharing the account also see the campaign
findings.recommendation: Restrict sensitive health-based messaging to the identified, consenting individual and avoid delivery through shared accounts; assess and mitigate the risk of revealing a pregnancy to other household members.

verdicts.notes: This campaign processes inferred pregnancy/health status — a special category under GDPR Art. 9 — derived from loyalty-card purchase histories, with silent enrolment, no explicit consent, and only a vague 'personalised offers' privacy notice. It engages the Art. 9 prohibition, lacks a valid lawful basis (Arts. 6, 4(11), 7), and breaches the transparency principle and information duties (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13). The automated inference is profiling (Art. 4(4)) and the direct-marketing right to object (Art. 21) must be facilitated. Household members sharing the account receive processing they never consented to, compounding the lawfulness and fairness failures.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting material information the average consumer needs for an informed decision or providing it in an unclear/ambiguous manner, including failing to make the commercial intent apparent. Consumers are not told that their loyalty-card purchase histories (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) are being mined to infer pregnancy and silently enrol them into a 'Growing Family' marketing audience. Describing this only as 'personalised offers' hides the material nature and basis of the targeting, so the average consumer cannot understand or contest how and why they are being commercially targeted at a sensitive life-stage.
findings.evidence_quote: Enrolment is silent; the privacy notice mentions only 'personalised offers'.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the commercial practice transparently before/at enrolment: explain in clear, prominent terms that purchase histories are analysed to build health/life-stage marketing audiences, name the 'Growing Family' programme, and offer a genuine, easy opt-in and one-click opt-out. Replace the vague 'personalised offers' wording with specific, intelligible information.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if it is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer, assessed from the perspective of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where relevant (Art. 5(3)). Pregnancy / trying-to-conceive is an emotionally charged and sensitive life-stage; silently profiling health status and deploying emotive, trust-building marketing ('Week by week, we're with you') to this group falls short of professional diligence and can distort purchasing decisions. The risk is aggravated where the pregnancy inference is wrong (e.g. a lost pregnancy, fertility difficulties) or where household members sharing the account receive the messaging, causing distress and exposing sensitive inferences.
findings.evidence_quote: customers who bought pregnancy tests, folic acid or ovulation kits are automatically enrolled in a 'Growing Family' audience
findings.recommendation: Do not build or target marketing audiences on inferred health/pregnancy status without a lawful, transparent and consent-based approach; apply heightened diligence for sensitive life-stages, suppress emotive prenatal messaging absent affirmative opt-in, and ensure targeting is individual-level (not account-shared) so household members are not exposed to sensitive inferences.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that impair freedom of choice by undue influence, with exploitation of the consumer's circumstances and timing as relevant factors. Emotive relationship-building messaging that leverages an inferred pregnancy and follows the consumer 'week by week' can shade into undue influence exploiting a vulnerable life-stage, particularly via persistent app-push notifications. As described this is a marketing sequence rather than clear harassment or coercion, so the risk is lower, but it should be monitored for frequency and pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: personalised emails and app pushes for prenatal vitamins and baby products ('Week by week, we're with you')
findings.recommendation: Cap message frequency, avoid escalating emotional-pressure tactics, provide easy unsubscribe on every email and push, and review push cadence to ensure the campaign does not become persistent or exploit the emotional sensitivity of the inferred pregnancy.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD primarily through misleading omission / hidden commercial intent (Art. 7) and the general fairness safety-net (Art. 5). Consumers are silently profiled from loyalty purchase data to infer pregnancy and enrolled into a marketing audience without adequate disclosure — the privacy notice only vaguely references 'personalised offers', omitting the material fact that health-related inferences drive the targeting. The emotive, relationship-building messaging aimed at pregnant consumers (an emotionally sensitive life-stage) raises fairness and undue-influence concerns, aggravated where messages reach household members who are not the profiled individual. No blacklisted (Annex I) practice is clearly present, so this is a risk rather than a clear violation.

report.executive_summary: This campaign silently mines loyalty-card purchase histories (pregnancy tests, folic acid, ovulation kits) to infer that customers are pregnant, then enrols them without their knowledge into a "Growing Family" audience for prenatal and baby marketing. The core problem is that inferred pregnancy is health data — a special category under GDPR — and you are processing it with no explicit consent, no meaningful transparency (the notice just says "personalised offers"), and no opt-out. This is a likely serious GDPR breach across multiple provisions, with the Article 9 issue being critical. It also breaches consumer-protection law (UCPD): the hidden commercial intent and emotive targeting of people at a sensitive life-stage are misleading and unfair. Delivering these messages through shared household accounts makes it worse, because it can reveal someone's pregnancy to family members who never consented and may not know. As designed, this campaign cannot run lawfully — do not launch it in its current form. The AI Act and DSA do not apply here.
report.recommendations: ["Stop the campaign in its current form: do not infer or process pregnancy/health status for marketing without prior, explicit opt-in consent that specifically explains purchase data will be used to infer pregnancy. Absent that consent, cease the inference and targeting entirely.

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

detected_practices: impersonation of a government/official authority (fake coat-of-arms emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE')
misleading commercial practice — charging €49 for a publicly free application
false/misleading urgency ('before the deadline')
hidden disclaimer ('not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey)
failure to identify the trader (undisclosed commercial intent) in ads
generative AI used in ad creation
targeting of vulnerable audience (low-income households)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is low-income households — a financially vulnerable group, heightening the aggressiveness/misleadingness assessment under UCPD (Art. 5(3) vulnerable consumers). Although personalisation is declared as 'no', the subsidy portal likely collects personal and eligibility data at €49 checkout (GDPR). Search/display ad targeting to a demographic segment may still implicate GDPR/DSA. No indication minors are specifically targeted.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') to funnel users to a private site charging €49 for an application that is publicly free. The trader is not identified in the ads, the non-affiliation disclaimer is buried in 7pt grey text, and the campaign deliberately targets low-income households while using generative AI in its creation.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared as used in creating the display and search ad assets (the government-bulletin styling, coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours and copy). Art. 50(2) requires AI-generated synthetic image and text outputs to be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format. Nothing in the campaign indicates the AI-generated visuals or copy carry such provenance marking. While the marking duty falls primarily on the provider of the generative system, the deployer must ensure marketing assets it publishes are marked accordingly.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure any AI-generated images and copy used in the ads carry machine-readable provenance/watermark markings (e.g., C2PA/SynthID-style metadata) and use only generative tools that apply Art. 50(2)-compliant marking; retain documentation of AI provenance for the campaign assets.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The ads are AI-assisted text presented as an official public-information notice about a government energy-subsidy scheme — i.e. text published to inform the public on a matter of public interest. Art. 50(4) requires deployers who generate or manipulate such text (and image content constituting a deep fake) to disclose that it is artificially generated. The fabricated coat-of-arms emblem and government-bulletin imagery, if AI-generated to appear as authentic official material, further engage the deep-fake disclosure limb. No AI-generation disclosure is present.
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, non-hidden disclosure that the notice content and imagery are artificially generated where Art. 50(4) applies; more fundamentally, do not use AI to fabricate official-authority text/imagery — the underlying impersonation is unlawful regardless of disclosure.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses purposefully deceptive material with the effect of distorting consumers' decisions (paying €49 for a publicly free application), which mirrors the harm Art. 5(1)(a) targets. However, the prohibition applies to an AI system that itself deploys manipulative/deceptive techniques to distort behaviour; here the deception appears human-designed with generative AI used merely as a content-production tool, so the prohibition is engaged only conceptually rather than clearly breached on the stated facts.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Verify no AI system is used to autonomously optimise or personalise deceptive nudging; regardless, remove the deceptive official-authority framing, as it drives the very behavioural distortion and consumer harm the provision is designed to prevent.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign deliberately targets a group vulnerable due to their economic situation and is reasonably likely to cause them significant (financial) harm — a €49 charge for a free service. This matches the concern of Art. 5(1)(b). But the prohibition requires an AI system that exploits the vulnerability; targeting is declared as 'no' and no AI-driven targeting/exploitation system is described (AI is used only for content creation), so a clear AI Act breach is not established on the facts. The vulnerability exploitation is primarily a UCPD matter.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Confirm that no generative or targeting AI system is used to identify or exploit financially vulnerable users; if any AI-based audience optimisation toward low-income users is in fact deployed, discontinue it, as it would risk the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI in ad creation, which engages the AI Act's transparency obligations (Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking; Art. 50(4) disclosure of AI-generated text on matters of public interest). Because the AI-generated assets are used to fabricate a fake official government bulletin about energy subsidies, the transparency obligations are of heightened importance here. The Art. 5 prohibitions on deceptive/manipulative AI and exploitation of economic vulnerability are contextually relevant given the deceptive impersonation and targeting of low-income households, but on the facts the deception and targeting appear human-designed with AI used only as a content-creation tool (no AI-driven manipulation or targeting system described), so those prohibitions are flagged as attention/low rather than clear breaches. The core, aggressive misleadingness/impersonation issues fall primarily under UCPD/DSA and are handled by those agents.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The controller collects personal data at a paid checkout while deliberately misleading data subjects about its identity and nature (posing as an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' from a government body). Personal data obtained through deception is not processed fairly or transparently, breaching the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. Covert/misleading data collection is precisely what Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Cease impersonating a government authority; collect data only under a truthful presentation of the trader's identity and the commercial (non-official) nature of the service, so that data subjects understand who is processing their data and why before they provide it.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is collected at the €49 application checkout, Art. 13 requires the controller to provide, at the point of collection, its identity and contact details, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients and retention, and data-subject rights. The campaign conceals the trader's identity entirely in the ads and only buries a non-affiliation note in 7pt grey text, indicating the mandatory Art. 13 information is not clearly provided at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, prominent privacy notice at the point of data collection stating the actual controller's legal identity and contact details, the purposes and lawful basis for processing subsidy-eligibility data, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Hiding the material clarification about the controller's true (non-governmental, commercial) identity in 7pt grey footer text is the opposite of accessible and intelligible communication and undermines any transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present controller identity and any material clarifications (including non-affiliation and the fee) in legible, prominent text at the point of collection, not buried in tiny grey footer text.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing of the applicants' personal and eligibility data requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Where the basis relied upon is consent or contract, consent/agreement obtained on the false understanding that the service is an official government portal is not freely given or validly informed, casting serious doubt on the validity of the lawful basis for the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a genuine lawful basis for the processing based on an accurate representation of the service; ensure any consent is informed and freely given without the deceptive 'official notice' framing.

verdicts.notes: Although personalisation is declared "no," the campaign funnels users to a checkout that collects personal data (identity, contact and energy-subsidy eligibility/financial details) to submit an application. The core GDPR problem is that this data is collected under a deceptive premise: the ads and site impersonate an official government body and conceal the identity of the actual private trader, defeating the fairness and transparency requirements. The €49 site therefore likely breaches the Art. 5(1)(a) fairness/transparency principle and the Art. 12/13 duty to identify the controller and processing purposes at the point of collection. Special-category data risk (Art. 9) is possible but not established from the text.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients of ads on online platforms can identify, clearly and in real time, that the content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. These display/search ads are styled as a government 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' with national colours and a coat-of-arms-like emblem and do not identify the commercial trader — so recipients can neither recognise the content as a commercial advertisement nor learn on whose behalf it is presented. Running ads engineered to conceal advertiser identity and disguise their advertising nature undermines the platform's ability to meet, and the advertiser's duty to enable, this transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad clearly and unambiguously identifies itself as a commercial advertisement and names the trader on whose behalf it is presented; remove the government-bulletin styling (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') and provide the platform with accurate advertiser-identity information so the mandated 'ad' label and 'paid for by' disclosure display in real time.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating platform online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions, and disguised advertisements are a recognised dark pattern. Where these ads appear within online-platform interfaces, presenting a commercial €49 offer as an official government notice — reinforced by a non-affiliation disclaimer buried in 7pt grey text so it is effectively hidden — is deceptive interface design that materially distorts users' decision-making.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'
findings.recommendation: Do not disguise commercial ads as official/government communications; present the non-affiliation and pricing information with equal prominence to the headline (legible size and contrast), so the ad and landing experience do not deceive or manipulate recipients.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern regimes to the extent the display/search ads are presented on online platforms. Ads disguised as an "OFFICIAL NOTICE" government bulletin that do not identify the trader defeat the DSA Art. 26(1) requirement that recipients can identify, in real time, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented; the advertiser must supply truthful identity/labelling data to the platform. The disguised-ad format plus the 7pt buried non-affiliation disclaimer are deceptive design engaging Art. 25 where the ad interface is a platform. The sensitive-data-targeting ban (Art. 26(3)), minor-profiling ban (Art. 28) and VLOP ad-repository obligation (Art. 39) are not substantively engaged as described (no profiling/targeting declared, no minors targeted).

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads deliberately present the private trader as an official government body (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'), falsely conveying that the service is approved/authorised by a public authority. Falsely claiming approval, endorsement or authorisation by a public body is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 4 — no averaging or materiality test applies.
