findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all official/governmental signals: no national colours, no coat-of-arms-like emblem, no 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing, and no wording implying government affiliation or authorisation. Present the ad unambiguously as a private commercial service.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Using a coat-of-arms-like emblem that mimics an official/authoritative seal is the display of a quality/authority mark or equivalent without authorisation, which is prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 2. The invented official-looking emblem lends false institutional legitimacy to a private trader.
findings.evidence_quote: a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Delete the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any invented official seal. Only use marks the trader is genuinely authorised to display.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Charging €49 for what is a publicly free application, while presenting the service as an official eligibility check, deceives the average consumer as to the nature of the service, its price, and whether any charge is genuinely necessary, causing a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6 as to price and the trader's status.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently state that the underlying subsidy application is free from the government, that this is an optional paid intermediary service, and what the €49 actually buys, before any payment step. Consider whether charging for a free process is defensible at all.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads omit the identity of the trader and the commercial intent of the practice, which is not apparent from context given the official-notice styling. Under Art. 7 (misleading omissions / hidden commercial intent), material information the consumer needs — the trader's identity and that this is a paid commercial offering — must be given clearly and timely. Burying 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey in the site footer does not cure the omission; it is unclear, untimely and effectively hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Identify the trader clearly in the ads themselves and disclose the commercial nature and the €49 cost up front. Make the non-affiliation statement prominent (adequate size, contrast and placement), not buried in 7pt grey footer text.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures artificial time pressure to elicit an immediate decision (paying €49) and deprive consumers of opportunity to discover the application is free elsewhere. If no genuine, verifiable deadline applies to the private service, this is a false urgency claim prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 7.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove urgency framing unless a genuine, documented deadline exists and applies to this service; if a real government deadline exists, state it accurately and clarify it applies to the free official process, not to the paid service.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Directing an official-looking, urgency-laden paid scheme at low-income households — a financially vulnerable group likely to be seeking energy subsidies — exploits their situation and undue influence to impair informed choice, engaging the aggressive-practices prohibition in Arts. 8-9. The exploitation of financial distress is an aggravating factor.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not exploit the financial vulnerability of low-income households; remove pressure tactics and the official framing, and ensure the offer is transparent so vulnerable consumers can freely decide.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, Art. 5 (with Art. 5(3)) assesses the practice from the perspective of the average member of the targeted vulnerable group (low-income households). The overall scheme — impersonating officialdom, charging for a free service, and concealing the non-affiliation disclaimer in 7pt grey — is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts these consumers' economic behaviour, making it unfair even beyond the specific prohibitions above.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Redesign the entire campaign to meet professional-diligence standards: transparent trader identity, honest pricing, prominent non-affiliation disclosure, and no exploitation of vulnerability.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, several of them blacklisted (unfair in all circumstances). It impersonates an official government notice (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, "OFFICIAL NOTICE") to funnel financially vulnerable low-income households to a private site charging €49 for an application that is publicly free, with the non-affiliation disclaimer buried in 7pt grey and no trader identification in the ads. This constitutes false claims of official endorsement/authorisation and unauthorised trust-mark use (Annex I points 4 and 2), misleading actions and omissions on price and commercial intent (Arts. 6-7), false urgency (Annex I point 7), and an aggressive/unfair practice exploiting a vulnerable group (Arts. 5 and 8-9). Enforcement risk is very high.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up to look like an official government bulletin — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-style emblem and an "OFFICIAL NOTICE" headline — to push people toward a private site that charges €49 for an energy-subsidy application that is actually free from the government. The single "not affiliated with any government" disclaimer is buried in 7pt grey text, and the ads never identify who is really behind them. This is not a borderline case: impersonating a public authority and displaying an unauthorised official-looking emblem are practices banned outright under EU consumer law (UCPD blacklist), and charging for a free service plus the "before the deadline" pressure adds misleading-pricing, false-urgency and aggressive-practice violations. Because the campaign deliberately targets financially vulnerable low-income households, the harm and enforcement exposure are heightened. It also breaches DSA ad-transparency rules (recipients can't tell it's an ad or who paid for it), GDPR fairness/transparency duties (personal data collected under a deceptive premise at the paid checkout), and triggers AI Act transparency obligations because generative AI was used to build the deceptive assets. The overall verdict is that this campaign is unlawful as designed and cannot be fixed with cosmetic tweaks — it needs to be pulled and fundamentally reworked.
recommendations: Do not run this campaign in its current form. The impersonation of a government body and the fake official emblem are blacklisted practices (unfair in all circumstances) — no amount of disclaimer or targeting adjustment makes them lawful.

Remove ALL official/governmental signals immediately: national colours, the coat-of-arms-like emblem, the 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing, and any wording implying government affiliation or authorisation. Present the offer unambiguously as a private commercial service.

State clearly and prominently — before any payment step — that the underlying subsidy application is free from the government and that this is an optional paid intermediary service. Reconsider whether charging €49 for a free process is defensible at all.

Identify the trader by legal name in the ads themselves and label them clearly as advertisements, and supply accurate advertiser-identity data to the platforms so the required DSA 'ad' and 'paid for by' disclosures display in real time.
Move the 'not affiliated with any government' statement out of the 7pt grey footer and give it prominence equal to the headline (legible size, contrast and placement).

Remove the 'before the deadline' urgency framing unless a genuine, documented deadline exists that actually applies to this service; if a real government deadline exists, state it accurately and make clear it applies to the free official process.
Stop exploiting the financial vulnerability of low-income households — drop the pressure tactics and official framing so vulnerable consumers can make a free, informed choice.

At the €49 checkout, provide a proper GDPR privacy notice giving the actual controller's legal identity and contact details, the purposes and lawful basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights — and only collect data under a truthful, non-official presentation.

For AI Act compliance, ensure any AI-generated images and copy carry machine-readable provenance/watermark markings and are disclosed as artificially generated where required; retain documentation of AI provenance. Note this is secondary — the fabrication of official imagery is unlawful regardless of AI disclosure.

Given the severity and the deliberate targeting of a vulnerable group, obtain legal sign-off on a fully redesigned campaign before relaunch; enforcement risk (consumer authorities, DPAs, platform takedown) is very high.

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

detected_practices: impersonation of official/government authority (fake coat-of-arms and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' styling)
false or misleading representation of affiliation (buried 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey)
trader identity not disclosed in ads
charging €49 for an otherwise publicly free service
false urgency / deadline pressure ('before the deadline')
AI-generated ad creative
targeting of vulnerable low-income households
triage.audience_notes: Declared target audience is low-income households — a financially vulnerable group whose vulnerability aggravates the misleading/impersonation practices under the UCPD. Site collects application/payment data (€49 charge), so personal data processing is highly likely despite the 'no personalisation' declaration.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') to funnel low-income households to a private site charging €49 for an application that is publicly free. The ads fail to identify the trader and bury the non-affiliation disclaimer in tiny grey text, using false urgency and official-authority impersonation. Generative AI is used to produce the creative and the audience consists of financially vulnerable consumers.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign creative (styled 'government bulletin', coat-of-arms-like emblem and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' copy) is produced with generative AI. Art. 50(2) requires that synthetic image/text outputs of a generative AI system be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format as artificially generated. Nothing in the submission indicates the AI-generated visuals or ad copy carry any provenance marking, so the obligation is engaged and apparently unmet. This is aggravated by the fact that the synthetic content is designed to look like an authentic official document, where detectability of artificial generation is especially important.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the generative-AI tooling used to create the ad assets embeds machine-readable provenance/watermark marking (e.g. C2PA-style metadata) on all AI-generated images and text, and retain documentation that outputs are marked as artificially generated. Confirm with the AI provider that Art. 50(2) marking is applied to campaign outputs.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Generative AI is used to produce content that deploys a deceptive technique — fabricated official-authority styling combined with false-urgency deadline framing — with the effect of materially distorting consumers' behaviour by impairing their ability to make an informed decision (they believe they are on an official channel) and causing them to take a transactional decision (paying €49 for a publicly free service) they would not otherwise take, in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant (financial) harm. Where the deceptive output is generated and used through an AI system with that objective or effect, Art. 5(1)(a)'s prohibition on manipulative/deceptive AI techniques is engaged. Applicability depends on the extent to which the AI system itself drives the deceptive technique; the submission establishes AI-generated deceptive creative but not the full system design, so this is a strong risk rather than a certain breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'.
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI-generated content that impersonates governmental/official authority or manufactures false urgency. Remove the coat-of-arms emblem, national-colour 'official notice' styling and 'before the deadline' pressure. If any doubt remains about whether the AI deployment constitutes a prohibited deceptive technique, discontinue the campaign pending legal review, as Art. 5 breaches are subject to the highest tier of penalties.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from a specific social or economic situation to materially distort behaviour in a way likely to cause significant harm. The campaign is expressly aimed at low-income households (a financially vulnerable group) and uses AI-generated deceptive official-notice creative to induce them to pay €49 for an application that is publicly free — a direct financial harm falling hardest on those least able to absorb it. The combination of AI-generated persuasive content and deliberate targeting of an economically vulnerable audience engages this prohibition. Confirmation depends on whether the AI system is the operative means of exploitation, so it is flagged as a high-severity risk.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting financially vulnerable low-income households with AI-generated content designed to extract payment for a free public service. Re-scope both the audience and the offer so no exploitation of economic vulnerability occurs; if the paid-intermediary model continues, make the free public alternative and the €49 charge unmistakably clear and drop any vulnerability-based targeting.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires disclosure where AI generates or manipulates text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The AI-generated ad text purports to inform the public about energy-subsidy eligibility — plausibly a matter of public interest — which triggers the disclosure limb of Art. 50(4). It does not appear to be a deep fake of a real person, so the deep-fake limb is not clearly engaged, but the AI-text-on-public-interest limb is arguably in scope.
findings.evidence_quote: 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: If AI-generated text presenting public-interest information is retained, add a clear disclosure that the content is artificially generated. In practice the safer course is to stop presenting the ads as public-interest 'official' information altogether, which removes both the Art. 50(4) trigger and the underlying deception.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce the ad creative, which engages the AI Act. The most concrete, well-founded issue is the Art. 50(2) transparency/marking obligation for synthetic content, which is engaged and not evidenced as satisfied. The Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) prohibitions are potentially engaged because AI-generated content is deployed to deceptively impersonate a government authority and is aimed at financially vulnerable low-income households, causing likely financial harm — but their applicability depends on facts about the AI system's design and intent that are not fully established in the submission, so they are flagged as risks rather than confirmed breaches. The core deception/impersonation harms fall primarily under UCPD/DSA (covered by other agents); here the AI Act adds transparency-marking duties and the possibility that the AI itself constitutes a prohibited manipulative/exploitative technique.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (application details and payment data for the €49 charge) is collected from users who have been deceived into believing they are dealing with an official government energy-subsidy portal. Collecting personal data through impersonation and misleading framing breaches the fairness and transparency principle: the processing is neither fair to the data subject nor transparent about who is really behind the collection. The deception is aggravated by the deliberately targeted financially vulnerable audience.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'
findings.recommendation: Cease the government-impersonation framing entirely. Personal data may only be collected once the identity and true (private, non-governmental) nature of the trader/controller is made clear up front, so that consumers understand who is processing their data and why before they provide any information or payment.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting personal data (the application/payment step), the controller must provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The ads do not identify the trader at all, and the site only carries a buried 7pt grey non-affiliation line rather than a proper controller identity and privacy notice. As described, the Art. 13 information obligation is not satisfied at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, prominent Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of data collection identifying the actual company as controller, the purposes and legal basis, retention period, recipients and data-subject rights, presented before the user submits application or payment data.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible using clear and plain language. Burying material information (here the non-affiliation disclaimer, and by extension any privacy information) in 7pt grey footer text defeats the accessibility and transparency requirement and is characteristic of deceptive design. Any privacy/data-collection information presented in the same manner would fail Art. 12.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present all consumer-facing information — including the non-affiliation statement and the privacy notice — in clear, plain, legible language with adequate contrast and font size, placed where the data subject will actually see it before providing data.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing personal and payment data requires a valid lawful basis. Where the data subject's engagement is procured through impersonation and deception, any purported consent or contract basis is undermined, because the user did not understand who they were contracting with or that the underlying service is publicly free. The lawful basis for the processing is therefore doubtful as the transaction is described.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis for the processing. This requires first removing the deception so that any consent is informed and freely given, or any contract is genuinely understood; a lawful basis cannot be validly relied upon while the data subject is misled about the controller's identity and the nature of the service.

verdicts.notes: Although the campaign declares "no personalisation/targeting", the landing site collects a subsidy application and a €49 payment, so processing of personal (and financial) data is highly likely. The central GDPR problem is fairness and transparency: data is obtained under a deceptive government-impersonation guise, from consumers who believe they are dealing with an official authority, and neither the ads nor (adequately) the site identify the actual trader/controller. This engages Art. 5(1)(a), Art. 13 and Art. 12. Findings are conditional on the confirmed data collection at the €49 application step; no profiling or special-category processing is evidenced from the text.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad presented on an online platform, recipients can identify in a clear, concise and unambiguous manner that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. These ads are styled as an official government bulletin ('OFFICIAL NOTICE', national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem) and expressly do not identify the trader, defeating both the 'this is an advertisement' element and the advertiser-identity element of the transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Redesign the ads to clearly disclose the commercial nature ('Advertisement') and the identity of the private company on whose behalf they are presented, removing any official/government styling. Ensure advertiser and payer identity are supplied to the platform so the Art. 26(1) real-time disclosure is populated correctly.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions, including giving disproportionate prominence to certain information over other. Disguising a commercial ad as an official government notice while relegating the material non-affiliation disclaimer to 7pt grey footer text creates a false hierarchy that obscures the true nature of the offer and manipulates users into paying €49 for a publicly free application.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Remove the government-mimicking design (emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'). Present the non-affiliation statement and the fact that the underlying application is free with equal prominence to the offer, in the same font size and contrast, at the point of decision rather than buried in the footer.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as display and search ads on online platforms, engaging the DSA's advertising-transparency and deceptive-design rules. The ads fail to identify the trader and are disguised as an official government notice, undermining DSA Art. 26(1) ad-transparency requirements; the government-mimicking styling plus a non-affiliation disclaimer buried in 7pt grey constitutes deceptive/manipulative interface design under DSA Art. 25. No evidence of special-category-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) or minor targeting (Art. 28), as personalisation is declared off and the audience is adults.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads create the impression that the trader/service is approved, endorsed or authorised by a public (government) body when it is not — the site is a private company expressly 'not affiliated with any government'. Falsely claiming public-body approval or affiliation is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances, regardless of consumer impact. This is the most serious finding: fake government affiliation via official-looking notices is the paradigm case named in the provision's marketing relevance.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official styling: no 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording, no national colours framing, no official-notice format. Do not imply any government approval, endorsement or authorisation. Clearly present the service as a private, unaffiliated commercial offer from the outset.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a coat-of-arms-like emblem that evokes an official/state mark, without authorisation, is the unauthorised display of a quality/trust mark or equivalent official emblem — prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 2. It manufactures unearned institutional trust.
findings.evidence_quote: a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Remove the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any state-like insignia or seals entirely. Use only the trader's own clearly commercial branding for which it holds rights.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The campaign contains false/deceptive information about the nature of the product and the price: consumers are led to believe they are accessing an official eligibility process, when they are being charged €49 for what is a publicly free application. This deceives the average consumer about the existence of a price/cost and the nature and necessity of the service, causing a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take. A misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State prominently and up-front that the underlying application is available free of charge from the relevant public authority, and disclose exactly what the €49 buys (an optional intermediary service). Do not present the paid service as the official or only route to the subsidy.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Two misleading omissions: (1) the ads fail to identify the trader / commercial intent, which is not apparent from context given the official-notice styling (Art. 7(4)(b) and the commercial-intent requirement); (2) the material non-affiliation fact is provided in an unclear, illegible manner (7pt grey footer) that the average consumer will not perceive in time. Material information is hidden or given untimely/unintelligibly, engaging Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader (company name and commercial nature) within the ads themselves. Move the non-affiliation statement to a prominent, legible position at first point of contact (adequate size/contrast), not a 7pt grey footer, so commercial intent is immediately apparent.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice targets low-income households — a clearly identifiable group vulnerable due to their economic situation/credulity in relation to public subsidies. Under Art. 5(3) the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group, whose susceptibility to an 'official' subsidy notice and reluctance to miss out is heightened. The practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour, engaging the Art. 5 fairness safety-net (aggravating all other findings).
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not exploit the vulnerability of low-income households. Cease the deceptive official framing entirely and ensure any offer to this audience is transparent, non-pressuring, and clearly discloses the free public alternative and the trader's private commercial status.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures time pressure to elicit an immediate decision and payment. Where the referenced deadline is not a genuine, true limitation on the €49 service (and the paid service is unnecessary in any event), this is a false urgency claim, blacklisted under Annex I point 7. Even if a public deadline exists, using it to pressure payment for a free process is misleading.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove artificial deadline/urgency messaging tied to the paid service. If referencing a genuine public-scheme deadline, state it factually alongside the fact that applying is free and does not require this service, without pressure language.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, several of which are per-se blacklisted practices under Annex I and thus unfair "in all circumstances." The ads impersonate an official government notice (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, "OFFICIAL NOTICE") to funnel financially vulnerable low-income households to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free application, while failing to identify the trader and burying the non-affiliation disclaimer in 7pt grey text. The false government affiliation/endorsement (Annex I point 4), unauthorised official emblem (Annex I point 2), misleading action on price/existence of a free service (Art. 6), hidden commercial intent/omission (Art. 7), and exploitation of a vulnerable group (Art. 5(3)) combine into a clear likely violation. The false deadline pressure additionally engages Annex I point 7.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads disguised as an official government energy-subsidy notice — complete with national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" wording — to drive low-income households to a private site that charges €49 for an application that is free from the government. This is not a borderline case: it triggers several practices that EU consumer law bans outright ("in all circumstances"), namely faking government approval/endorsement, displaying an official-looking emblem without authorisation, and hiding the fact that the service is free and privately run behind a 7pt grey disclaimer. On top of that, the campaign fails to identify the advertiser (breaching DSA ad-transparency and dark-pattern rules), collects application and payment data under a deceptive guise without proper controller identity or privacy notice (GDPR), and uses AI-generated official-looking content that is unmarked and potentially falls foul of the AI Act's prohibitions on deceptive and vulnerability-exploiting AI. The deliberate targeting of financially vulnerable people who can least afford the €49 makes every issue worse. In its current form the campaign cannot be run — it must be fundamentally reworked, not merely tweaked. The core problem is the impersonation of a government authority to extract payment for a free service; nothing short of removing that entirely will bring it into compliance.
recommendations: Stop the campaign now. It contains multiple per-se prohibited practices (fake government endorsement, unauthorised official emblem, hiding a free alternative) that are unlawful in all circumstances and carry the highest penalties — these cannot be fixed by minor edits.

Remove all government/official styling entirely: delete the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national-colour framing, and the 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording. Do not imply any government approval, affiliation or authorisation.

State clearly and up front — in the ads and at the top of the landing page — that the application is available free of charge from the relevant public authority, and that your service is an optional, private, paid intermediary. Explain exactly what the €49 buys.

Identify the trader in the ads themselves (company name and clearly commercial nature). Move the 'not affiliated with any government' statement out of the 7pt grey footer to a prominent, legible position at the first point of contact.
Remove the 'before the deadline' urgency messaging tied to the paid service; if a genuine public-scheme deadline exists, state it factually without pressure language.
Stop targeting low-income / financially vulnerable households with this offer; exploiting their vulnerability aggravates every violation.

Fix the data-collection flow: provide a full, prominent GDPR Art. 13 privacy notice identifying the real company as controller, with purpose, legal basis, retention and data-subject rights, before any application or payment data is submitted.
Supply accurate advertiser and payer identity to the ad platforms so the DSA ad-transparency disclosures are populated, and clearly label the content as an advertisement.

For the AI-generated assets, ensure machine-readable provenance/watermark marking is applied (AI Act Art. 50(2)) and retain documentation; but note that once the deceptive official framing is removed, most AI Act exposure falls away.
Obtain legal sign-off before relaunching any version of this campaign, given the AI Act Art. 5 prohibition exposure and the number of blacklisted UCPD practices involved.

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

detected_practices: impersonation of a government/official authority
fake official emblem and national colours (mimicking public authority)
misleading 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing
false urgency ('before the deadline')
charging €49 for a publicly free service
concealed disclaimer in 7pt grey (buried material information)
failure to identify the trader in ads
AI-generated ad content
targeting vulnerable/low-income households
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is low-income households — a vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3), heightening the deceptiveness/aggressiveness assessment. Although personalisation/targeting is declared as 'no', the campaign runs on display/search platforms where audience data and platform ad-transparency obligations (DSA) apply; GDPR review is warranted for any data processing at the €49 payment/application stage.
triage.summary: Display and search ads disguised as an official government bulletin (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') that drive users to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free energy-subsidy application. The ads fail to identify the trader and bury the 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey text, while targeting low-income households. Generative AI is declared as used in producing the campaign.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares generative AI was used and the supervisor identifies 'AI-generated ad content'. Under Art. 50(2), synthetic image/text outputs used as campaign assets must be marked in a machine-readable, detectable format (provenance/watermark). The submission gives no indication that AI-generated visuals or copy carry any such marking, so the obligation is engaged and not evidenced as met.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets (images, emblem-like graphics, ad copy) are produced with machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/SynthID-type watermarking) and retain records that the marking obligation is fulfilled by the generating system's provider.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires deployers who generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest to disclose that it is artificially generated. These AI-produced ads present themselves as an official public notice about a government energy-subsidy scheme — text purporting to inform the public on a matter of public interest. If the ad text is AI-generated, its artificial origin must be disclosed; the campaign discloses nothing and instead disguises the text as an authentic official communication, defeating the transparency purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure that the ad content is artificially generated, and stop presenting AI-generated copy as an official/public-authority communication. Disclosure must be conspicuous, not buried like the 7pt grey footer.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from a specific social or economic situation with the effect of materially distorting behaviour in a way reasonably likely to cause significant harm. The campaign is deliberately directed at low-income households (an economic-situation vulnerability) using AI-produced deceptive 'official notice' content that induces payment of €49 for a publicly free service — a real risk of significant financial harm to those least able to bear it. Whether the prohibition bites depends on whether the AI system is the technique exploiting the vulnerability (rather than only producing content); the declared 'personalisation/targeting: no' leaves this open, so it is flagged as a serious risk pending clarification.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI-generated or AI-driven campaigns that leverage the economic vulnerability of low-income households in a manner likely to cause financial harm. Clarify and document the exact role of AI in audience selection and content generation; if AI participates in targeting/exploiting this group, the practice must be discontinued.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems deploying purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing informed decision-making, causing decisions that cause or are likely to cause significant harm. The AI-generated ads deceptively impersonate a public authority and use a fabricated official emblem to make consumers believe they are dealing with government, causing them to pay €49 for a free service. If the deceptive technique is deployed via an AI system, this prohibition is engaged; the same AI-system-vs-production-tool caveat as Art. 5(1)(b) applies, so this is a risk to resolve, not a confirmed breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Remove all deceptive impersonation of public authorities from the AI-generated assets. Confirm whether an AI system generates/deploys the deceptive framing; if so, cease the practice, as AI-driven deceptive techniques causing consumer harm are prohibited.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce ads that impersonate an official government bulletin (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, "OFFICIAL NOTICE") and target low-income households, driving them to pay €49 for a publicly free service. Under the AI Act this squarely engages the Art. 50 transparency obligations for AI-generated content (including AI-generated text informing the public on a matter of public interest), which are not evidenced as satisfied. The deceptive framing directed at a declared economically vulnerable group also raises the Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) prohibitions, though these turn on whether an AI system is the technique that exploits/distorts behaviour rather than merely a content-production tool — declared "personalisation/targeting: no" leaves that factual question open, so these are flagged as risks requiring clarification of the AI system's role. The core deceptive/impersonation and vulnerable-group issues are primarily for the UCPD/DSA agents.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data collected at the €49 application stage is obtained under a deliberately misleading, government-impersonating pretext. Data subjects believe they are dealing with a public authority, not a private trader. Processing personal data obtained through such deception breaches the principle that personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner; misleading framing undermining the data subject's understanding of who is processing their data and why is a paradigmatic fairness/transparency violation.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin ... 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline' ... a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Cease the government-impersonation framing entirely. Personal data may only be collected once the data subject is clearly and truthfully informed of the trader's private identity and the true (paid, non-official) nature of the service before any data is entered.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data (the application details submitted to obtain the subsidy), the controller must provide its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights at the point of collection. The trader is concealed in the ads and its non-affiliation is buried in 7pt grey text, so the controller's identity is not clearly disclosed to the individual at the point they are induced to hand over personal data.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, prominent Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of data collection stating the private company's legal identity, contact details, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights — not buried in tiny footer text.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information relating to processing must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Presenting the key qualifier that determines who the data subject is actually dealing with in 7pt grey footer text fails the accessibility and intelligibility standard and contaminates the delivery of any privacy information provided in the same manner.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present all transparency information, including controller identity and non-affiliation, in legible, prominent text of adequate size and contrast, positioned before the user submits any personal data.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing requires a valid legal basis. Consent obtained on the back of a deceptive impersonation would not be freely given or informed, and any 'contract' rationale is compromised where the service is misrepresented as official. The described set-up makes it unlikely that a valid, clearly documented lawful basis exists for the application-stage processing.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis for the application data, ensuring any consent or contract basis rests on truthful, transparent information about the trader's identity and the paid nature of the service.

verdicts.notes: The campaign itself declares no personalisation/targeting, so the ad-serving stage raises limited GDPR concerns. However, the landing page 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu' collects personal data to submit an energy-subsidy application and takes a €49 payment — this is personal-data processing by a controller (the private company). Because the whole funnel is built on impersonating a government authority, the data collected at the application stage is obtained under materially misleading pretences, engaging the GDPR fairness and transparency obligations. Findings focus on the collection stage; the deceptive-marketing aspects proper are for the UCPD/DSA agents.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The DSA requires that for each ad on an online platform, recipients can identify in a clear, unambiguous manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. These display and search ads disclose none of this — they are dressed as an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' from a public authority and omit the advertiser's identity entirely, defeating the core transparency obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly label the placements as advertising and identify the actual trader (the private company operating energy-subsidy-portal.eu) and the paying entity within the ad creative itself, in a clear and unambiguous manner, not merely in a footer on the landing page.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits interfaces designed to deceive or manipulate recipients or impair their ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including disguised advertisements and giving misleading prominence. Presenting a private commercial ad as an official government bulletin, combined with concealing the material 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey text, is a deceptive-design pattern that materially distorts users' decision-making — heightened by the low-income target audience.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'
findings.recommendation: Remove all official/government styling (national colours, emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing). Present the commercial nature and non-affiliation prominently and legibly (equal visual weight, not 7pt grey), and make clear up front that the €49 fee is for a service that is otherwise free through official channels.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs paid display and search ads that fail DSA advertising-transparency requirements and use disguised-advertisement design. Under Art. 26(1) the ads must let recipients identify that the content is an ad and on whose behalf/by whom it is paid — but the ads "do not identify the trader" at all. The government-bulletin styling (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, "OFFICIAL NOTICE") plus a disclaimer buried in 7pt grey is a disguised advertisement / deceptive-design pattern within the Art. 25 framework. Art. 26(3), 28 and 39 are not engaged (no special-category or minor profiling; ad-repository duties fall on VLOPs, not the marketer).

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads create the false impression that the trader/service is approved, endorsed or authorised by a public authority. Presenting a private commercial application as an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' with a coat-of-arms-like emblem and national colours is exactly the 'fake government affiliation, official-looking notices' scenario blacklisted under Annex I point 4 and prohibited in all circumstances, regardless of proof of consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all indicia of official/government status: delete the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, the word 'OFFICIAL', and any 'notice'/bulletin styling. The ad must present clearly as a private commercial offer and must not suggest any public authority endorsement or affiliation.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a coat-of-arms-like emblem mimicking an official state/quality mark without authorisation falls within the prohibition on displaying a trust/quality mark or equivalent without the necessary authorisation, prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Remove the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any official-looking seal or badge. Only use marks the trader is genuinely authorised to display.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The overall presentation deceives the average consumer about the nature of the service and its price/price advantage: consumers are led to believe they are dealing with an official channel and paying a necessary fee, when the underlying application is publicly free. This false/deceptive information is likely to cause a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take, constituting a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State prominently and up-front that the underlying application is available free of charge directly from the relevant public authority, and clearly disclose the €49 as the trader's own service/intermediary fee. Do not present the €49 as an official or unavoidable charge.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information is omitted, hidden, or provided in an unclear/untimely manner: the ads fail to identify the trader and the commercial intent, and the only affiliation disclaimer is buried in 7pt grey footer text far from the point of decision. Trader identity and commercial intent are material information the average consumer needs; failing to identify commercial intent where it is not apparent from context is a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader (legal name and contact) in the ads themselves, make the commercial intent obvious, and place the 'not affiliated with any government' statement prominently and legibly at the top of the ad and landing page (adequate size/contrast), not in 7pt grey footer text.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures time pressure to elicit an immediate decision. If there is no genuine, applicable deadline (or the deadline relates only to the free public scheme and is used to pressure payment of the €49 fee), this is a false urgency claim blacklisted under Annex I point 7. The urgency is used to deprive consumers of opportunity to realise the service is free elsewhere.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove deadline/urgency language unless there is a genuine, verifiable and accurately described deadline. Do not use any real public-scheme deadline to pressure consumers into paying the private €49 fee.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is aimed at low-income households — a clearly identifiable group vulnerable due to their economic situation and particular susceptibility to an offer framed around energy subsidies. Under Art. 5(3) the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group, which heightens the deceptiveness of the official-notice impersonation and the €49 charge for a free service, reinforcing that the practice is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: As the campaign targets a vulnerable audience, apply heightened diligence: eliminate all misleading and impersonation elements above and ensure the free public alternative and true trader identity/price are unmistakably clear before any payment step.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages several UCPD prohibitions, including per-se blacklisted practices. The ads impersonate a public authority (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') to falsely imply government affiliation/endorsement — an Annex I(4) and Annex I(2) breach prohibited in all circumstances. They also contain misleading actions (Art. 6) and omissions (Art. 7) about the trader's identity, the nature of the service, and the €49 charge for a publicly free application, plus a false-urgency deadline framing. Targeting low-income households heightens the assessment under Art. 5(3). Overall risk is very high.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up as an official government bulletin — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem and an "OFFICIAL NOTICE" headline — to drive low-income households to a private site that charges €49 for an energy-subsidy application that is actually free through official channels. In plain terms, it impersonates a public authority to get vulnerable people to pay for something they can get for free, which is illegal under EU law regardless of intent or actual harm. Two specialist findings are outright blacklisted practices under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (fake government endorsement and unauthorised use of an official-looking emblem) — these are prohibited in all circumstances and cannot be fixed by tweaking wording. On top of that, the ads fail DSA advertising-transparency rules (they don't identify the trader at all), use prohibited deceptive "dark pattern" design, breach GDPR fairness and transparency because personal data is collected under a false government pretext, and raise serious AI Act concerns (undisclosed AI-generated official-style content, plus possible prohibited exploitation of an economically vulnerable group). The buried 7pt grey "not affiliated with any government" disclaimer does not cure any of this. The verdict is that this campaign must not run in its current form; it needs fundamental redesign, not cosmetic changes.
recommendations: Do not launch or immediately halt this campaign — it contains per-se prohibited practices (UCPD Annex I) that no amount of disclaimer or rewording can make lawful.

Strip all official/government indicia entirely: remove the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, the word 'OFFICIAL', and all 'notice'/bulletin styling. The service must present unmistakably as a private commercial offer with no implied public-authority endorsement.

State clearly and prominently, up front, that the underlying energy-subsidy application is available free of charge directly from the relevant public authority, and that the €49 is solely the trader's own optional service fee.
Identify the trader (legal name and contact details) and label the placements as advertising within the ad creative itself — as required by DSA Art. 26 — not just in a landing-page footer.
Give the 'not affiliated with any government' statement genuine prominence (legible size and contrast, before any decision or payment point); the 7pt grey footer is non-compliant.
Remove the 'before the deadline' urgency framing unless a genuine, verifiable deadline exists and is accurately described; do not use any public-scheme deadline to pressure payment.

Provide a clear GDPR privacy notice (controller's real identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, rights) at the point of data collection, and confirm a valid lawful basis that does not rely on the deceptive framing.

Clarify and document the exact role of generative AI: mark AI-generated assets with machine-readable provenance, disclose AI-generated ad text, and confirm AI is not being used to target or exploit the economic vulnerability of low-income households (potential prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5).
Given the vulnerable low-income audience, apply heightened diligence throughout — assess all messaging from the perspective of that group before any relaunch.
Obtain legal sign-off before any relaunch; consider whether the underlying business model (charging for a free public service via official-looking notices) is viable at all under EU consumer law.

campaign.title: PulseAds sub-audible optimisation pilot
campaign.text: A streaming-audio ad platform pitches advertisers a pilot: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion. Internal deck: 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product'. The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.

detected_practices: subliminal advertising (sub-audible heartbeat acceleration)
sub-perceptual whispered urgency cues ('now', 'running out')
AI-driven per-listener optimisation of subliminal stimuli
manufactured urgency / false scarcity
exploitation of cognitive vulnerability (below conscious perception)
behavioural personalisation/targeting
targeting of relaxation/sleep contexts where listeners are especially susceptible
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'general adult' streaming listeners in the EU, but sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not age-gated and are plausibly reached by minors, so minor exposure cannot be excluded. The sub-perceptual/subliminal technique targeting listeners 'below conscious perception' is a prime candidate for the AI Act Art. 5 prohibition on subliminal and manipulative techniques that distort behaviour and cause harm, and for UCPD unfair/aggressive practice review. Per-listener tuning implies processing of listener data (GDPR), and distribution via a platform implicates DSA advertising-transparency obligations.
triage.summary: An audio-streaming ad platform pilots an AI system that embeds sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration and whispered urgency cues beneath standard spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to drive conversions on sleep/relaxation playlists. The explicit design goal is that listeners cannot perceive why they feel urgency, engaging subliminal and manipulative-technique concerns. Personalisation and generative AI are declared, and the deceptive urgency framing raises serious consumer-protection issues.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: This is an AI system deploying subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness (sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered phrases explicitly 'below conscious perception'), with the objective and effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing the listener's ability to make an informed decision and inducing purchases they would not otherwise make. The internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is direct evidence of intent to bypass conscious reasoning. Covertly engineering purchasing decisions consumers cannot perceive or resist is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (economic loss, loss of autonomy). This falls squarely within the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition — one of the AI Act's absolute bans, not a manageable-risk obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy. The subliminal/sub-perceptual layer must be removed entirely; there is no compliant configuration for a technique whose stated purpose is to influence behaviour below conscious perception. Any urgency messaging must be overt, perceivable and truthful, allowing listeners to recognise and evaluate it. Abandon the 'below conscious perception' design premise.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Deploying the subliminal AI on sleep-and-relaxation contexts targets listeners in a low-vigilance, highly suggestible state, and these playlists are not age-gated so minors cannot be excluded. Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI that exploits vulnerabilities arising from age or a specific situation to materially distort behaviour causing significant harm. Choosing precisely the moments/contexts where listeners are least able to critically assess messaging amounts to exploiting situational (and potentially age-related) vulnerability, compounding the Art. 5(1)(a) breach.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Even setting aside the subliminal layer, do not deliberately target relaxation/sleep contexts or unverified-age audiences with behaviour-distorting persuasion. Apply robust age assurance and exclude vulnerability-heightening contexts from any persuasion optimisation. Given the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition, the safest course is to discontinue the pilot.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The pilot uses a generative AI system to produce synthetic audio content (whispered phrases and heartbeat-acceleration layers embedded in spots). Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio to mark outputs in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated. As described, no such provenance marking is mentioned. Note this transparency obligation does not cure the underlying Art. 5 prohibition — it is a secondary compliance gap that would apply to any lawful generative-audio use.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: If any compliant generative-audio use remains after removing the prohibited subliminal features, ensure all AI-generated audio outputs carry machine-readable marking of artificial generation per Art. 50(2). This does not legitimise the sub-audible technique, which must still be removed.

verdicts.notes: This pilot is a clear candidate for the AI Act's Article 5 prohibitions. An AI system deliberately layering sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases "below conscious perception" is a textbook subliminal/manipulative technique under Art. 5(1)(a), explicitly designed to distort economic decisions in a way consumers cannot detect. Deployment on sleep-and-relaxation playlists (where listeners are in a low-vigilance state and minors are not excluded) additionally engages Art. 5(1)(b) exploitation of vulnerabilities. The declared generative-AI audio also triggers Art. 50(2) synthetic-content marking. These prohibitions are unwaivable and the pilot should not proceed as designed.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Per-listener tuning entails automated processing of listener data, but by explicit design the processing and its effect operate below conscious perception. The stated product goal that 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency' is the antithesis of fair and transparent processing. Covert, deliberately imperceptible processing that steers behaviour breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle of Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Abandon the covert design. Any personalisation must be perceptible and disclosed; processing intended to be undetectable by the data subject cannot be made fair or transparent and should not be deployed.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated per-listener optimisation to raise conversion evaluates and predicts personal aspects (behaviour, susceptibility, preferences) of natural persons and therefore constitutes profiling within Art. 4(4). This triggers the full profiling compliance chain (lawful basis, transparency, objection).
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, its data inputs and logic, and map it against the lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations before any pilot.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The per-listener profiling needs a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Consent cannot be informed or unambiguous where the technique is deliberately imperceptible, and a legitimate-interests basis would fail the balancing test given the covert, manipulative purpose and reasonable expectations of listeners. No lawful basis is apparent.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Establish and evidence a lawful basis before processing; given the manipulative covert design, no lawful basis is realistically available and the profiling should not proceed as described.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: If consent is relied upon, it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Processing engineered so listeners cannot perceive it, let alone understand it, makes informed consent impossible by construction, so any purported consent is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on consent for covert processing; only seek consent for personalisation that is disclosed and comprehensible to the listener.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Tuning stimuli to individual physiological/emotional susceptibility (heartbeat acceleration, urgency response) plausibly involves inferring health/physiological or emotional-state data, which can constitute special-category data under Art. 9. Such processing is prohibited absent explicit consent and a valid exception, which is unavailable here given the covert design.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration ... tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Confirm what listener signals feed the tuning. If physiological or emotional-state data are inferred or used, cease processing unless an Art. 9 exception (e.g. explicit consent) genuinely applies — which the covert design precludes.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected to enable per-listener tuning, listeners must be informed of the controller, purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling/automated processing. A design predicated on imperceptibility provides none of this information.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear Art. 13 notice at the point of data collection identifying the personalisation and profiling; this is incompatible with the current covert approach.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct-marketing purposes triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3), which must be facilitated and communicated. A covert system offers no mechanism for listeners to object.
findings.evidence_quote: AI system layers ... tuned per listener ... to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Implement and clearly signpost an easy opt-out from marketing profiling; ensure objection stops the personalisation immediately.

verdicts.notes: The pilot processes listener data to tune stimuli "per listener," which is profiling under Art. 4(4) and requires a lawful basis and transparent, fair processing. The defining feature — that the technique operates "below conscious perception" and that listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency" — is fundamentally incompatible with the GDPR fairness/transparency principle and makes any valid, informed consent impossible. Because the AI infers/exploits physiological-emotional state (heartbeat, urgency susceptibility) this also risks engaging special-category data under Art. 9. Note: some findings are contingent on whether personal data is actually processed to individualise tuning, which the description strongly implies but does not fully specify.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Providers of online platforms must not design, organise or operate their online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. The audio-ad platform operates its ad-delivery interface to layer sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency cues 'below conscious perception', tuned per listener to raise conversion. Because the manipulation operates beneath awareness, it directly impairs recipients' ability to make a free and informed decision — the design goal is expressly that listeners cannot perceive the influence acting on them. This is a paradigm dark pattern under Art. 25 (and RELATED_TO UCPD Art. 5 for all traders).
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Abandon the sub-audible/sub-perceptual manipulation entirely. Any urgency or persuasion in the ad must be perceptible and honestly presented so listeners retain a genuine, informed choice. Remove per-listener tuning that operates below conscious perception; a covert-by-design mechanism cannot be brought into Art. 25 compliance through disclosure alone.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement and meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that it is shown to them, and how to change them. Here a persuasive advertising layer is deliberately placed beneath conscious perception and individually tuned per listener, so the recipient can neither recognise this element as advertising nor understand or influence the per-listener targeting parameters. The covert layer defeats the transparency the Article requires.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every persuasive element delivered by the platform is perceptible and identifiable as advertising, disclose the advertiser and who paid, and provide clear, real-time information about the main personalisation parameters used to tune the ad to the listener, with an accessible means to change them. A sub-audible layer cannot satisfy this and should be removed.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security and prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. Sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not age-gated and are plausibly reached by minors, yet the pilot applies per-listener tuning (profiling within GDPR Art. 4(4)) to deliver manipulative ads. Where minors are among the recipients, profiling-based ad delivery is banned and the sub-perceptual manipulation is incompatible with a high level of protection for minors.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Implement age assurance appropriate to the risk and exclude any recipient who cannot be established as an adult from the personalised/profiling-based delivery; do not run manipulative or profiled advertising on non-age-gated relaxation/sleep contexts where minors are foreseeably present.

verdicts.notes: The pilot is delivered by an online audio-ad platform and centres on covert AI-driven manipulation, squarely engaging the DSA. Art. 25's prohibition on interfaces that manipulate or materially distort recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions is very likely breached: the whole product is designed so listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency." Advertising-transparency (Art. 26(1)) is undermined because the manipulative layer and per-listener parameters are concealed by design, and non-age-gated sleep/relaxation distribution with per-listener profiling raises an Art. 28 minor-protection risk. Art. 26(3) is not clearly engaged on the facts.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit practices that, by undue influence, significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Delivering persuasive stimuli 'below conscious perception' is the extreme form of undue influence: it removes the consumer's ability to deliberate at all. The stated aim — 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product' — confirms the intent to distort economic behaviour. Deployment on sleep-and-relaxation playlists heightens susceptibility (exploitation of timing/state), and the audience is plausibly not age-gated, so vulnerable and minor listeners cannot be excluded (Art. 5(3)).
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy the sub-audible/sub-perceptual layer at all. Any urgency or persuasion element must be consciously perceptible and disclosed so the listener can evaluate it. Abandon the design objective of concealed influence; the technique is not curable by disclosure because its function depends on being imperceptible.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 blacklists, in all circumstances, falsely stating that a product is available only for a limited time to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of opportunity to make an informed choice. The whispered 'running out' cue asserts scarcity/urgency with no indication that any genuine time or stock limitation exists, and is delivered specifically to trigger immediate conversion without informed deliberation. Delivered sub-audibly it is not only false but wholly unverifiable by the listener.
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'running out'/urgency messaging unless it reflects a genuine, substantiated and clearly stated limitation. Never present scarcity cues in a form the consumer cannot consciously perceive and verify.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits hiding material information and failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice where not apparent from context. The sub-audible layer is deliberately designed so the commercial-persuasion element is imperceptible; consumers cannot recognise that they are being commercially influenced, which is the clearest possible failure to make commercial intent apparent. This deprives the average consumer of information needed to make an informed transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Ensure all persuasive/commercial content in the ad is perceptible and identifiable as advertising. Eliminate any covert layer whose purpose is to influence without the listener's awareness.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, Art. 5 prohibits practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort economic behaviour, assessed from the perspective of a vulnerable group where one is targeted (Art. 5(3)). Targeting listeners in a relaxed/near-sleep state — on playlists that are not age-gated and plausibly reached by minors — exploits reduced critical attention and heightens the distortion of behaviour beyond what Arts. 7-9 already capture.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy sub-perceptual persuasion in low-attention or sleep contexts; apply age-gating/audience controls and assess vulnerable-group impact before any behavioural-influence advertising.

verdicts.notes: The pilot embeds sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration and whispered urgency cues beneath audio spots, tuned per listener "below conscious perception" with the explicit design goal that listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency. Under the UCPD this is a paradigmatic aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9): it uses undue influence to impair the consumer's freedom of choice by bypassing conscious deliberation entirely. The covert whispered "running out" scarcity cue also engages the Annex I point 7 blacklist of false urgency, and the deliberate concealment of commercial persuasion engages Art. 7 (hidden commercial intent), with Art. 5 as an over-arching safety net given the exploitation of sleep/relaxation contexts and potential vulnerable/minor listeners. (AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) issues noted for context but assessed by the AI Act agent.)

report.executive_summary: This campaign proposes layering AI-generated, sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases ("now", "running out") beneath streaming audio ads, tuned to each listener "below conscious perception" and run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists. The entire product concept — that listeners cannot perceive or resist the influence acting on them — is unlawful under four separate EU regimes, and the problem cannot be fixed with disclosures or tweaks.
