The AI Act treats deliberately subliminal, manipulative AI as an outright prohibited practice (Art. 5(1)(a)), with an added exploitation-of-vulnerability breach for targeting relaxed, non-age-gated audiences. The DSA bans this as a dark pattern, and the UCPD treats it as an aggressive practice using undue influence, with the "running out" cue also hitting the blacklist of false urgency. Because the technique is covert by design, it also fails GDPR's fairness and transparency principles and makes valid consent impossible, with additional risk that it processes physiological/emotional (special-category) data. This is not a manageable-risk campaign: it targets absolute, unwaivable prohibitions carrying the AI Act's highest penalty tier. The pilot must not launch as designed and should be abandoned rather than reworked.

campaign.title: PulseAds sub-audible optimisation pilot
campaign.text: A streaming-audio ad platform pitches advertisers a pilot: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion. Internal deck: 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product'. The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.

detected_practices: subliminal/sub-audible manipulation techniques
AI-driven per-listener psychological optimisation
covert urgency cues ('now', 'running out') below conscious perception
artificial scarcity/urgency messaging
exploitation of physiological response (heartbeat acceleration)
behavioural personalisation/targeting
targeting via sleep-and-relaxation playlists (vulnerable/low-alertness state)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 'general adult' streaming listeners in the EU, but streaming platforms lack robust age-gating so minors may be reached. The sleep-and-relaxation playlist context deliberately targets listeners in a low-alertness, suggestible state, heightening vulnerability concerns. The AI Act prohibition on subliminal/manipulative techniques that materially distort behaviour (Art. 5) is squarely implicated; per-listener tuning implies profiling of personal data under GDPR; distribution via an online platform engages DSA advertising/dark-pattern rules; and the covert urgency/scarcity tactics are likely aggressive/misleading practices under the UCPD.
triage.summary: A streaming-audio ad platform pilots an AI system that embeds sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard spots, tuned per listener below conscious perception to drive conversions. The explicit design goal is that listeners cannot perceive why they feel urgency, and it targets low-alertness sleep/relaxation playlists.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market or using an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing the ability to make an informed decision. Here an AI system deploys sub-audible cues and whispered phrases explicitly designed to operate 'below conscious perception'; the stated goal ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') and the aim to 'raise conversion' show intent to impair informed decision-making and cause purchasing decisions consumers would not otherwise take. Every element of the prohibition is present, making this a clear prohibited practice, not a manageable risk.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy. Remove all sub-conscious/sub-audible manipulation entirely: any persuasive audio must be consciously perceptible and disclosed as advertising. A prohibited practice cannot be remedied by disclosure or consent — the covert-by-design mechanism must be abandoned, not relabelled.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities of a person or group (including due to age) to materially distort behaviour causing significant harm. Deliberately scheduling the covert AI urgency system on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets listeners in a low-alertness, suggestible state, and streaming platforms' weak age-gating means minors (an enumerated age-based vulnerability) may be reached and subjected to the same covert manipulation. This compounds the Art. 5(1)(a) breach by exploiting audience vulnerability to amplify the distortion of behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Abandon deployment on low-alertness contexts and remove the covert mechanism (see Art. 5(1)(a) fix). Independently, do not run AI-optimised persuasive advertising in contexts predictably reaching minors without robust age assurance; but note that no targeting safeguard cures the underlying prohibited technique.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Art. 50(2) requires AI-generated/synthetic audio content to be marked as artificially generated. Because the campaign uses generative AI to produce audio, a marking obligation would ordinarily apply. However, the decisive issue here is that the technique is prohibited under Art. 5; transparency marking cannot legitimise it. Flagged for completeness only.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: If any lawful, consciously-perceptible generative-AI audio is used in a redesigned campaign, mark it as AI-generated per Art. 50(2). This obligation is irrelevant while the current prohibited design stands.

verdicts.notes: The pilot deploys an AI system that layers sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath ads "below conscious perception," expressly designed so listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency," in order to raise conversion. This is a paradigmatic prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) (subliminal techniques beyond consciousness that materially distort behaviour and impair informed decision-making). The deliberate targeting of low-alertness sleep/relaxation playlists, combined with weak age-gating exposing minors, additionally engages the Art. 5(1)(b) vulnerability-exploitation prohibition. These are outright prohibitions (not curable by transparency measures), so the pilot cannot proceed in the EU as designed.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The processing of listener data to deliver ad manipulation is expressly designed to operate beneath the data subject's awareness, with the stated product goal that 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency'. Processing personal data covertly, in a way the individual cannot perceive and that is engineered to distort their behaviour, is the paradigm case of unfair and non-transparent processing. Fairness under Art. 5(1)(a) cannot be satisfied by any privacy notice where the processing purpose is deliberate concealment and behavioural manipulation.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy processing whose purpose or effect is to influence data subjects below the threshold of awareness. Any personalisation must be perceivable, explained, and non-manipulative; abandon the sub-audible/covert layer entirely as it cannot be reconciled with the fairness principle.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated per-listener tuning to evaluate and influence personal aspects (behaviour, preferences, physiological/emotional response) is profiling within Art. 4(4). It analyses and predicts aspects of each natural person to optimise conversion, which brings the full profiling regime (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights, automated-decision safeguards) into play.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, its data inputs and logic, and treat it under the full GDPR profiling regime; given the covert manipulative purpose, this profiling should not proceed in its current form.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Per-listener profiling requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. None is described. Consent is impossible because the technique is covert by design (invalidating informed, freely given consent), and legitimate interests cannot succeed a balancing test where the processing is intended to distort listeners' decision-making without their knowledge — the data subjects' interests and fundamental rights clearly override.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before any profiling. For personalised advertising this generally requires valid opt-in consent; since covert manipulation cannot be consented to and fails a legitimate-interest balancing test, the processing lacks any viable lawful basis and must not run.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Tuning content to induce and respond to physiological arousal (heartbeat acceleration) and emotional urgency states involves the inference/processing of health- and emotion-related special-category data. Inferred sensitive attributes fall within Art. 9, whose processing is prohibited absent explicit consent. Explicit consent is unattainable here because the mechanism operates below conscious perception, so no Art. 9 exception can apply.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration
findings.recommendation: Cease any processing that infers or acts upon physiological/emotional states unless valid explicit consent under an Art. 9(2) exception is obtained; a covert design cannot satisfy this, so drop the physiological-response optimisation.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The system makes solely-automated, individualised decisions about how to influence each listener based on profiling. Where such automated behavioural steering significantly affects individuals' economic decisions, Art. 22 restricts it to specific bases (explicit consent, contract, law) with safeguards, none of which are present or feasible given the covert design.
findings.evidence_quote: An AI system layers ... whispered urgency phrases ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Provide human oversight, meaningful information about the logic involved, and one of the Art. 22(2) bases with safeguards — or, given the manipulative purpose, do not deploy solely-automated per-listener influence at all.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information about processing to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. A model whose explicit commercial value is that listeners cannot perceive or understand the influence being exerted on them is structurally incapable of meeting the transparency and intelligibility obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Deliver clear, accessible information about the personalisation logic and its effects to listeners; if doing so would defeat the technique, that confirms the technique is non-compliant and should be withdrawn.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected/used for this profiling, Art. 13 requires disclosure at the point of collection of purposes, legal basis, and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling with meaningful information about the logic. The covert design implies these disclosures are not made.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Ensure Art. 13 information (including the existence and logic of profiling/automated decision-making) is provided to listeners at data collection; note this cannot cure the underlying fairness and lawful-basis defects.

verdicts.notes: The pilot processes personal data to tune audio ads "per listener" beneath conscious perception. This engages GDPR on multiple fronts. Per-listener optimisation is profiling (Art. 4(4)) with no disclosed lawful basis (Art. 6(1)); the explicitly covert design ("below conscious perception", "listeners cannot identify why") is squarely incompatible with the fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and with valid consent/transparency duties (Arts. 7, 12, 13). Tuning to physiological/emotional response (heartbeat acceleration, engineered urgency) likely involves inferred health/biometric-adjacent special-category data (Art. 9), and the solely-automated per-listener behavioural steering engages Art. 22. Overall this is a violation-likely profile driven principally by covert, unfair processing.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits providers of online platforms from designing or operating their online interfaces/experiences in ways that deceive or manipulate recipients or otherwise materially distort or impair their ability to make free and informed decisions. An AI that layers sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases 'below conscious perception', explicitly so recipients cannot perceive why they feel urgency, is manipulation by design and directly impairs free and informed decision-making. Deploying it on sleep-and-relaxation playlists (a low-alertness, suggestible state) heightens the distortion.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Abandon the sub-audible/subliminal layer entirely. Any persuasive audio element must be consciously perceptible and must not be engineered to bypass the listener's awareness. Urgency messaging, if used, must be overt, truthful and resistible.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires online platforms to ensure recipients can identify, in a clear, unambiguous manner and in real time, that a communication is an advertisement, on whose behalf, who paid, and the main targeting parameters. Content deliberately placed beneath conscious perception is inherently unidentifiable as advertising, defeating the ad-transparency obligation for the covert layer.
findings.evidence_quote: beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every advertising element is clearly identifiable as an ad with advertiser identity and meaningful targeting-parameter disclosure. Covert, sub-audible ad content cannot satisfy Art. 26(1) and must be removed.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting ads based on profiling that uses special categories of GDPR Art. 9 data, including by inference. Per-listener tuning that leverages physiological/emotional-state signals (heartbeat, susceptibility on sleep/relaxation playlists) risks constituting profiling on inferred health/emotional-state data, which would prohibit the ad presentation regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration ... tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document that no targeting or per-listener optimisation relies, directly or by inference, on health, emotional-state or other Art. 9 special-category data. If it does, the profiling-based ad presentation must cease.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28 requires online platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of protection and prohibits profiling-based ads to recipients reasonably known to be minors. Audio-streaming platforms typically lack robust age assurance and sleep/relaxation playlists are widely used by minors; per-listener profiled ad optimisation could reach minors, engaging the prohibition and the age-appropriate-design duty.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Implement reliable age-assurance and exclude profiling-based ad delivery for any recipient who cannot be reliably determined to be an adult; do not present profiled ads on content likely to reach minors.

verdicts.notes: The pilot's core mechanism — an AI layering sub-audible urgency cues "below conscious perception" so recipients cannot identify why they feel urgency — is a textbook manipulative design that materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, engaging the DSA Art. 25 prohibition of dark patterns applied to the platform's ad experience. Because the persuasive content is deliberately imperceptible, the ads also cannot be identified as advertisements as required by Art. 26(1). Per-listener tuning on sleep/relaxation playlists that exploits physiological/emotional state raises risks under Art. 26(3) (profiling on inferred sensitive data) and Art. 28 (profiling-based ads on a platform accessible to minors that lacks robust age assurance).

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: A practice is aggressive where, by undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken. Covert, per-listener psychological pressure delivered beneath conscious perception is a paradigm case of undue influence: the consumer cannot resist or even perceive the pressure. The internal deck's stated goal — 'listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product' — is direct evidence that the technique is engineered to bypass rational decision-making, and running it on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets listeners in a low-alertness, maximally suggestible state, heightening the impairment of free choice.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not run this pilot. Any urgency/scarcity messaging must be openly perceivable, honest, and resistible by the listener; remove sub-audible cues, heartbeat-acceleration triggers and any technique operating below conscious perception. Restrict to overt, clearly-audible advertising the listener can recognise and evaluate.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits hiding material information, including failing to make the commercial intent of a practice apparent. Here the persuasive layer (urgency phrases and physiological arousal cues) is delivered entirely below the listener's conscious perception, so the commercial/persuasive intent of that content is not merely unclear but structurally impossible for the consumer to identify. This is a misleading omission/hidden commercial intent of the most extreme kind.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: All persuasive content must be delivered above the threshold of perception and clearly identifiable as advertising. Remove any hidden audio layer; ensure the full commercial message is perceivable so the listener can recognise it as marketing.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 provides that where a practice is likely to distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (e.g. through diminished capacity), fairness is assessed from that group's perspective, and captures unfair practices contrary to professional diligence. Deliberately deploying covert urgency conditioning on listeners in a low-alertness, drowsy or sleeping state exploits diminished ability to make an informed decision and falls below professional diligence, reinforcing the unfairness of the practice.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Exclude sleep/relaxation and other low-alertness listening contexts from any conversion-focused urgency advertising; do not design campaigns that rely on the audience being in a suggestible or diminished-capacity state.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The campaign manufactures urgency and scarcity ('running out') to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of opportunity to choose. Annex I point 7 blacklists falsely stating limited-time availability. The fit is engaged because the urgency appears artificial (a per-listener conversion tactic rather than a genuine availability limit), though point 7 is aimed at explicit false availability statements; the covert delivery here is better captured by Arts. 7-9. Flagged as a risk that these scarcity cues, if not backed by genuine limited availability, are a blacklisted false-urgency practice.
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Only use 'running out'/'now' scarcity language where the underlying limitation is genuine, verifiable and substantiated; drop generic manufactured-urgency cues used purely to lift conversion.

verdicts.notes: The pilot deploys covert sub-audible urgency cues and physiological (heartbeat-acceleration) triggers "below conscious perception," explicitly designed so listeners "cannot identify why they feel urgency." Under the UCPD this is a strongly aggressive commercial practice (Arts. 8-9) operating by undue influence that impairs freedom of choice, compounded by hidden commercial intent (Art. 7) and by targeting listeners in a low-alertness, vulnerable state (Art. 5). The AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) subliminal prohibition is squarely engaged in parallel, but even within the UCPD alone this is a likely serious violation.

report.executive_summary: This pilot uses AI to slip sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases ("now", "running out") underneath your audio ads, tuned to each listener "below conscious perception," and deliberately schedules them on sleep-and-relaxation playlists. Your own deck states the goal is that "listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product." Across all four legal regimes reviewed (AI Act, GDPR, DSA, UCPD), this is a clear, serious violation — not a risk you can manage with disclaimers or consent. It is a prohibited manipulative/subliminal AI practice under AI Act Art. 5, a banned dark pattern under DSA Art. 25, an aggressive/hidden commercial practice under UCPD, and covert unfair processing of (likely sensitive, health-related) personal data under GDPR. Targeting a low-alertness, suggestible audience — and likely reaching minors given weak age-gating on streaming — makes it worse. Critically, the defect is the covert-by-design mechanism itself: adding transparency, consent, or an "AI-generated" label cannot cure it. Verdict: do not deploy this pilot in the EU as designed; it must be fundamentally redesigned around openly perceptible, resistible advertising.
recommendations: Do not launch the pilot. Abandon the sub-audible / sub-conscious layer entirely — the heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases operating 'below conscious perception' are a prohibited practice that cannot be fixed by disclosure or consent.

Stop framing covertness as the product feature. The internal-deck rationale ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is direct evidence of intent to manipulate; remove this design goal, not just the wording.

Redesign any future campaign so all persuasive content is consciously perceptible, clearly identifiable as advertising, honest, and resistible by the listener (satisfying DSA Art. 26 ad-transparency and UCPD hidden-commercial-intent rules).
Only use scarcity/urgency language ('running out', 'now') where the limitation is genuine and verifiable; drop manufactured urgency used purely to lift conversion.

Cease any per-listener optimisation that infers or reacts to physiological or emotional states (heartbeat, arousal), as this likely involves special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9 that cannot be lawfully processed via a covert design.

If you build a lawful redesigned campaign, establish and document a valid GDPR lawful basis and profiling safeguards (Arts. 6, 13, 22) before any personalisation, and mark genuinely AI-generated audio per AI Act Art. 50(2).

Exclude sleep/relaxation and other low-alertness contexts from conversion-focused advertising, and implement reliable age assurance so profiled ads are never served to recipients who cannot be confirmed as adults (DSA Art. 28).

AI-driven per-listener optimisation of subliminal cues
manipulation of consumer decision-making outside conscious awareness
false urgency / scarcity cues ('now', 'running out')
personalised behavioural targeting
exploitation of vulnerable context (sleep-and-relaxation playlists / drowsy listeners)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult streaming listeners, but sleep-and-relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors could plausibly be reached. The context (drowsy, relaxed, reduced-attention listeners) creates situational vulnerability regardless of age. The AI Act's prohibition on subliminal/manipulative techniques (Art. 5) is squarely implicated given the deck admits the covert influence is 'the product'; UCPD is engaged for deception and undue influence; GDPR for per-listener personalisation likely processing personal data / profiling; DSA for advertising delivery and transparency on the streaming platform. Flag as high-severity for specialist review.
triage.summary: A streaming-audio ad platform pilots an AI system that layers sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration cues and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard spots, tuned per listener below conscious perception to drive conversions, explicitly relying on listeners being unable to identify the source of their urgency. It is scheduled on sleep/relaxation playlists targeting drowsy, low-attention listeners. This raises acute concerns around subliminal/manipulative techniques, deception, and personalised targeting.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: This is a prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(a). An AI system deploys subliminal techniques operating beyond the listener's consciousness ('below conscious perception') and purposefully manipulative cues (simulated heartbeat acceleration, whispered urgency) with the explicit objective of materially distorting purchasing behaviour and impairing the listener's ability to make an informed decision. The internal deck ('listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product') is direct evidence of intent to covertly override informed decision-making, and covert commercial pressure that drives unintended purchases is reasonably likely to cause the requisite significant harm.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Do not launch this pilot in the EU. The subliminal/manipulative layer is prohibited outright and cannot be cured by disclosure or consent. Remove all sub-audible cues and covert per-listener 'urgency' manipulation entirely; any urgency messaging must be overt, perceptible and truthful.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities arising from a person's situation. Deliberately scheduling subliminal urgency manipulation on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets listeners in a drowsy, low-attention, reduced-critical-faculty state — a specific situational vulnerability the technique is designed to exploit to distort behaviour. Because such playlists are not reliably age-gated, minors (age-based vulnerability) may also be reached, reinforcing the prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists
findings.recommendation: Independent of the Art. 5(1)(a) breach, do not target reduced-attention or drowsy-listener contexts (sleep/relaxation playlists) with any behaviour-distorting AI technique. If any future campaign uses AI personalisation, exclude vulnerability-heightening contexts and audiences that cannot be reliably age-gated.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The pilot uses generative AI to produce synthetic audio content (whispered phrases and heartbeat cues) inserted into the spots. Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio must mark outputs as artificially generated in a machine-readable format. This obligation is engaged by the AI-generated audio layers, though it is entirely subsidiary to — and does not cure — the outright Art. 5 prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: This transparency obligation cannot legitimise the prohibited technique. For any lawful future use of generative AI audio in campaigns, ensure outputs carry machine-readable provenance/marking as required by Art. 50(2).

verdicts.notes: This pilot is a clear-cut prohibited AI practice under Article 5 of the AI Act. An AI system deliberately deploys sub-audible cues and whispered urgency phrases "below conscious perception" to distort purchasing behaviour, with the deck admitting that listeners' inability to identify the source of their urgency "is the product" — the paradigm case of subliminal/manipulative AI under Art. 5(1)(a). Running the pilot on sleep-and-relaxation playlists targets drowsy, reduced-attention listeners, additionally engaging the vulnerability-exploitation prohibition in Art. 5(1)(b). The AI-generated audio layers also trigger the Art. 50(2) synthetic-content marking obligation, though that is secondary to the outright prohibition. This should not proceed in any form.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: GDPR requires personal data to be processed fairly and transparently. A system whose defining feature is that individuals cannot perceive or understand the influence being applied to them is, by design, the opposite of fair and transparent processing. Covert, non-perceivable manipulation of individuals based on personal data breaches the core fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Abandon the covert-by-design model. Any personalised advertising must be perceivable and explainable to the data subject, with clear disclosure of what data drives the personalisation and how it affects the ad experience. Covert influence that individuals cannot detect cannot be made GDPR-compliant.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Per-listener tuning to optimise conversion is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict personal aspects (behaviour, personal preferences, likely response to urgency cues). This is profiling within Art. 4(4), which triggers the full set of GDPR obligations on lawful basis, transparency and data-subject rights.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, the data inputs used, and conduct a DPIA given the intrusive, opaque nature; ensure downstream obligations (lawful basis, Art. 13 information, Art. 21 objection) are met before any per-listener optimisation runs.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised/targeted advertising and profiling require a valid lawful basis — realistically consent or a defensible legitimate-interest balancing. A covert manipulation technique that individuals cannot detect cannot pass a legitimate-interest balancing test (the data subject's interests and reasonable expectations clearly override), and cannot be based on valid consent because the processing is hidden. No lawful basis is apparent.
findings.evidence_quote: an AI system layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy without a demonstrable, valid lawful basis. Given the covert design, legitimate interests will fail the balancing test and consent cannot be validly obtained; the processing purpose should be reconsidered or dropped.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: If the platform relies on consent for per-listener personalisation, consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Processing that operates below conscious perception cannot be the subject of informed consent — listeners are, by design, unaware of it — so any purported consent is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: below conscious perception
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, specific information about the personalisation and obtain unambiguous opt-in consent before processing; the current covert mechanism is inherently incompatible with informed consent.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. Embedding influence 'beneath' the audible content and below conscious perception ensures no intelligible information reaches the listener about the processing affecting them, breaching the transparency communication obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases beneath standard 20-second spots
findings.recommendation: Surface a clear, accessible explanation of any personalisation applied to the audio experience and how data subjects can access their rights; hidden layering cannot satisfy Art. 12.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is processed for profiling/personalisation, the controller must inform the data subject of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling. A system designed to be imperceptible provides none of this information at or before processing.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Provide Art. 13 information (identity, purposes, lawful basis, profiling logic, rights) to listeners in the streaming environment before any personalised processing occurs.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The AI makes solely-automated, per-individual decisions about which covert cues to apply in order to drive purchasing behaviour. To the extent this significantly affects individuals' economic decisions, Art. 22 is engaged and requires an exception plus safeguards (right to human intervention, to contest). Covert operation makes those safeguards impossible to provide.
findings.evidence_quote: AI system layers ... tuned per listener ... to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Assess Art. 22 applicability; if solely-automated profiling significantly affects individuals, secure a valid exception and implement safeguards (transparency, human intervention, contestation) — none of which are compatible with imperceptible processing as currently designed.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Tuning cues per listener to drive a physiological/emotional (heartbeat, urgency) response strongly suggests inferring or reacting to the listener's emotional/physiological state. Emotion- or health-derived inferences fall within special categories of data under Art. 9, whose processing is prohibited absent a narrow exception such as explicit consent — which cannot be obtained for a covert system.
findings.evidence_quote: sub-audible heartbeat acceleration
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether the system infers or reacts to emotional/physiological state; if so, treat it as Art. 9 processing, which requires explicit consent and cannot proceed covertly. Given the deployment on sleep/relaxation playlists, presume heightened Art. 9 risk and do not deploy without explicit consent.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for direct marketing triggers an absolute right to object. A covert per-listener system provides no mechanism for listeners to know profiling is occurring or to object to it, undermining this right.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easily accessible opt-out from profiling-based advertising and honour objections immediately; ensure listeners are made aware profiling occurs so the right can be exercised.

verdicts.notes: The pilot performs per-listener AI "tuning" of covert cues, which necessarily relies on processing personal data to evaluate/predict individual aspects (profiling, Art. 4(4)). The scheme is engineered to be undetectable — "listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency" — which is fundamentally incompatible with the GDPR fairness and transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and the transparency/information obligations (Arts. 12-13). Because the processing is intentionally covert, no valid lawful basis (Art. 6) or freely-given/informed consent (Arts. 4(11), 7) can realistically be obtained, and Art. 22 safeguards for automated decision-making cannot be satisfied. Reacting to physiological/emotional state per listener also risks engaging special-category (health/emotion-derived) data under Art. 9.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits providers of online platforms from designing, organising or operating their online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or otherwise materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. The platform operates its audio interface to layer sub-audible heartbeat-acceleration and whispered urgency phrases 'below conscious perception', tuned per listener to raise conversion. The internal deck expressly states the manipulation works precisely because listeners cannot identify its source — a direct, admitted material distortion of free and informed decision-making. This is a paradigm case of a manipulative interface operation, aggravated by AI-driven per-listener optimisation.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy the pilot. Any urgency or scarcity signalling must be delivered through perceptible, disclosed ad content that listeners can consciously evaluate. Remove all sub-audible / below-conscious-perception layers and per-listener covert tuning entirely; they cannot be brought into compliance by disclosure alone.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires online platforms presenting advertisements to ensure recipients can identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that content is an advertisement and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. A covert sub-audible advertising layer engineered to operate beneath conscious perception makes it impossible for the recipient to recognise it as advertising or to understand the (per-listener) parameters used to target them, defeating the transparency obligation by design.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots, tuned per listener 'below conscious perception'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every element that influences the listener is presented as clearly identifiable advertising within the audible spot, with advertiser identity and accessible, meaningful information on the main targeting parameters and how to change them. Concealed advertising layers must be abandoned.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28 requires platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy and safety and prohibits ads based on profiling using personal data of recipients reasonably known to be minors. Sleep/relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, so minors may plausibly be reached, and the pilot relies on per-listener profiling/optimisation. If the platform is aware with reasonable certainty that any recipients are minors, this profiling-based delivery would be prohibited, and the manipulative design conflicts with the duty to protect minors.
findings.evidence_quote: The pilot is scheduled to run on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether the platform is accessible to minors and whether age can be established with reasonable certainty; if so, exclude minors from any profiling-based ad delivery and apply age-appropriate protective measures. Given non-age-gated relaxation contexts, treat exposure of minors as likely and suppress profiled delivery accordingly.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting ads based on profiling using special categories of personal data (GDPR Art. 9), including by inference. Per-listener tuning of physiological (heartbeat) cues delivered in a sleep/relaxation context could involve inferring health or emotional/physiological state to target delivery, which if used as a profiling basis would be prohibited regardless of consent. The campaign text does not confirm such inference is used to target, so this is a lower-confidence risk to verify.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Audit the per-listener optimisation to confirm it does not profile or target using inferred health, physiological or other special-category attributes; if it does, cease that targeting entirely, as consent cannot cure an Art. 26(3) breach.

verdicts.notes: The pilot is an ad-platform practice that operates the audio-streaming interface to manipulate listeners below conscious awareness, squarely engaging the DSA. Art. 25 (dark patterns / deceptive design) is very likely breached because the covert sub-audible layer is explicitly engineered to materially distort listeners' free and informed decisions. Art. 26(1) advertising transparency is also engaged and defeated by design, since the covert cues make it impossible for recipients to identify or understand the advertising influencing them. There is additional attention-level risk under Art. 28 (minors) given the sleep/relaxation playlists are not reliably age-gated, and a lower-confidence risk under Art. 26(3) if per-listener tuning infers health/emotional state.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The system uses sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases tuned 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion. This is undue influence: it exploits a covert technique to significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice, causing transactional decisions they would not otherwise take. The trader expressly relies on consumers being unable to perceive or resist the influence, and Art. 9 timing/context factors are aggravated by delivering it to drowsy, low-attention listeners on sleep-and-relaxation playlists.
findings.evidence_quote: listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product
findings.recommendation: Do not launch. Remove all sub-audible/subliminal audio layers and any covert per-listener urgency stimulus. Any urgency messaging must be overt, audible, factually true and perceptible so listeners can consciously evaluate it.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice is contrary to professional diligence and is designed to materially distort economic behaviour by bypassing conscious decision-making. Under Art. 5(3), sleep-and-relaxation listeners are a clearly identifiable situationally vulnerable group (drowsy, reduced attention), so the practice must be assessed from the perspective of that more vulnerable audience, making distortion of their behaviour highly likely.
findings.evidence_quote: tuned per listener 'below conscious perception' to raise conversion
findings.recommendation: Abandon the sub-conscious optimisation approach entirely; adopt only transparent, consciously perceivable advertising, and avoid deployment in low-attention/relaxation contexts that exploit situational vulnerability.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The commercial/persuasive intent of the sub-audible layer is entirely hidden and not identifiable by the listener. Failing to make commercial intent apparent — indeed engineering it to be imperceptible — is a misleading omission and conceals material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision.
findings.evidence_quote: layers sub-audible heartbeat acceleration and whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out') beneath standard 20-second spots
findings.recommendation: Ensure any persuasive audio content is clearly perceptible and identifiable as advertising; eliminate any hidden layer whose influence the listener cannot detect or attribute to an ad.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The campaign manufactures urgency/scarcity ('running out') as a psychological trigger rather than reflecting any genuine limited availability, designed to elicit an immediate decision and deprive consumers of sufficient opportunity to make an informed choice. To the extent it conveys a false limited-availability claim it engages the Annex I point 7 blacklist; even where the wording is imprecise, the fabricated urgency reinforces the aggressive/misleading findings.
findings.evidence_quote: whispered urgency phrases ('now', 'running out')
findings.recommendation: Only use urgency or scarcity claims that are literally true and substantiated by genuine availability limits; remove fabricated 'running out'/'now' urgency cues used purely to pressure conversion.

verdicts.notes: The pilot deliberately deploys covert, sub-conscious influence (sub-audible heartbeat cues + whispered urgency phrases) to drive transactional decisions, with the trader expressly relying on consumers being unable to perceive the manipulation. Under the UCPD this is a serious aggressive practice by undue influence (Arts. 8-9) and breaches the general fairness/professional-diligence standard (Art. 5), aggravated by targeting drowsy, reduced-attention listeners on sleep/relaxation playlists (Art. 5(3) situational vulnerability, and timing under Art. 9). The concealment of the urgency stimulus also engages misleading omissions / hidden commercial intent (Art. 7), and the manufactured "running out" scarcity cue engages false-urgency concerns (Annex I point 7). The parallel AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on subliminal techniques reinforces the assessment but is for the AI Act specialist.

report.executive_summary: This pilot inserts AI-generated sub-audible heartbeat cues and whispered urgency phrases ("now", "running out") beneath normal audio ads, tuned per listener "below conscious perception" to boost conversions, and deliberately targets drowsy listeners on sleep-and-relaxation playlists. Every specialist reached the same conclusion: this is prohibited under EU law and cannot be fixed with disclosures, consent, or tweaks. The AI Act treats it as an outright banned practice (subliminal/manipulative AI, plus exploitation of vulnerable, low-attention listeners). The DSA bans it as a manipulative dark-pattern interface that hides advertising from the people it targets. The UCPD classifies it as an aggressive practice using undue influence with concealed commercial intent and fabricated urgency. The GDPR is breached at its core because covert, per-listener profiling is fundamentally incompatible with fairness, transparency, and any valid lawful basis or consent. The internal deck's own admission — "listeners cannot identify why they feel urgency — that is the product" — is direct evidence of intent to manipulate and is likely to be treated as an aggravating factor. The clear verdict: do not launch this campaign in the EU in any form.
recommendations: Do not launch this pilot in the EU. It is a prohibited practice under multiple regimes and cannot be brought into compliance by disclosure, consent, or adjustments — the covert design is the illegality.</br>

Remove entirely all sub-audible, below-conscious-perception, and covert per-listener 'urgency' layers. Any urgency or scarcity messaging must be fully audible, clearly identifiable as advertising, factually true, and consciously evaluable by the listener.
Do not use urgency/scarcity claims ('running out', 'now') unless they reflect genuine, substantiated limited availability; fabricated scarcity is separately blacklisted.

Stop targeting low-attention, drowsy, or otherwise vulnerable contexts (sleep/relaxation playlists) with any behaviour-influencing AI technique, and exclude audiences that cannot be reliably age-gated to protect minors.

Do not rely on the covert per-listener optimisation: it constitutes profiling with no valid lawful basis, no possibility of informed consent, and no way to honour transparency or objection rights. Redesign any future personalisation to be perceivable, explainable, opt-in, and accompanied by clear Art. 12-13 information and an easy opt-out.

Audit the per-listener system to confirm it does not infer or react to emotional/physiological or other special-category data (heartbeat/emotion); if it does, this is independently prohibited for ad targeting under DSA Art. 26(3) and GDPR Art. 9.

Preserve and review the internal deck language; the stated intent to make manipulation undetectable is direct evidence of prohibited intent and should be treated as a serious governance/reputational risk, not just a legal one.

For any lawful future generative-AI audio, mark outputs as artificially generated in machine-readable form (AI Act Art. 50(2)) — but note this transparency step does not and cannot legitimise the practices above.

campaign.title: AeroFly checkout add-ons
campaign.text: An airline's own booking flow pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking. The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen. Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'. No pressure language is used and all add-ons are genuine services.

detected_practices: pre-ticked/pre-selected optional add-ons (opt-out design)
drip pricing / bundled total hiding add-on costs until final screen
friction in deselecting (accordion unticking required)
headline fare advertising ('Lisbon from €39') excluding mandatory-appearing extras
pre-selected 'carbon contribution' (potential greenwashing / environmental claim)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult EU consumers; minors not a stated target. Note the tension between the UCPD pre-ticked box prohibition (Art. 22 Consumer Rights Directive, additional payments require express consent) and the opt-out add-on design, plus drip pricing as a potential misleading omission.
triage.summary: An airline booking flow pre-selects three paid/optional add-ons (cancellation cover, priority boarding, a €2 carbon contribution) and shows only a bundled total until the final screen, while promo emails advertise the bare fare. This raises drip-pricing, pre-ticked default, and potential environmental-claim concerns under the UCPD; generative AI is declared and the email/web channel involves customer data. Although targeting is declared as 'no', personal data handling via email and checkout warrants a GDPR check.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares generative AI use across web and email channels but does not identify any specific AI-generated asset. If any synthetic image, video, audio or text output is used in these customer-facing assets, the provider/deployer must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated (Art. 50(2)). The obligation is engaged by the declaration but cannot be assessed as satisfied or breached because the description contains no AI-generated content to evaluate.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm exactly where and how generative AI is used in the AeroFly assets. For any AI-generated visuals, audio, video or copy, ensure machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermark) is applied by the generation tool and preserved in the published assets. Document the AI usage in the campaign record.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires deployers to disclose AI-generated or manipulated image/audio/video content that constitutes a deep fake, and AI-generated text on matters of public interest. Nothing in the description indicates deepfakes, synthetic persons/endorsements or public-interest text, so no obligation is currently triggered — but the bare declaration of generative AI use means this should be verified rather than assumed absent.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Verify that no AI-generated realistic depictions of real persons (e.g. synthetic testimonials, staff or influencer likenesses) are used. If any are introduced, add a clear and prominent disclosure that the content is artificially generated or manipulated.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI but provides no detail on how it is used or what AI-generated content (if any) appears in the web/email assets. On the facts described, the AI Act is only weakly engaged: the dark-pattern checkout design (pre-selected add-ons, drip pricing, deselection friction) is a manipulation concern but under UCPD/DSA, not the AI Act, because there is no evidence the steering is AI-driven or that it causes the "significant harm" required by Art. 5(1)(a). The only genuine AI Act touchpoint is the transparency obligation under Art. 50(2)/(4): if any generative-AI output (images, video, audio, copy) is published in these assets, machine-readable marking and — for deepfakes — disclosure are required. No breach can be established from the text; this is flagged for follow-up.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Sending promotional emails is processing of personal data (email addresses) for direct marketing and requires a valid lawful basis. Under GDPR Art. 6(1) (read with ePrivacy Art. 13) this generally means prior consent, or legitimate interest for the airline's own existing customers marketing similar services. The campaign does not state on what basis recipients are emailed, so the obligation is engaged but compliance cannot be confirmed from the text.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the promo email list: rely on prior opt-in consent, or the soft opt-in for existing customers (own similar products, opt-out offered at collection). Retain records demonstrating the basis for each recipient.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct-marketing email must respect the data subject's absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing (Art. 21(2)-(3)), which in practice means a clear, easy, functioning unsubscribe/opt-out in each message. The campaign text does not mention an unsubscribe mechanism, so while no breach is evidenced, the obligation must be satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure each promotional email contains a prominent, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out that is as easy to use as opting in, and that objections are honoured immediately via a suppression list. Also present the right to object explicitly at the point of first communication.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is primarily a consumer-protection (UCPD/Consumer Rights) matter — the pre-selected paid add-ons and drip-pricing concern purchase-decision consent, not GDPR data-processing consent, so GDPR Arts. 4(11)/7 are not directly engaged by the pre-ticked boxes. The genuine GDPR footprint is the promotional email channel, which involves processing of personal data (email addresses) for direct marketing. No profiling, personalisation, special-category data or minors are declared or described, so Arts. 4(4), 8, 9 and 22 are not engaged. The email practice engages Art. 6(1) (lawful basis) and Art. 21 (right to object), but the text gives no evidence of a breach — these are flagged for verification only.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The true price the consumer will pay (fare plus pre-selected Cancellation Cover, Priority Boarding and carbon contribution) is material information. Presenting only a single bundled total and revealing the breakdown of add-on costs only on the final screen provides price information in an unclear and untimely manner, so the consumer cannot easily see what they are being charged for or that the extras are optional. This is a classic drip-pricing misleading omission under Art. 7, likely to cause a transactional decision (proceeding with, or overlooking, paid extras) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen.
findings.recommendation: Itemise every charge (base fare and each optional add-on with its price) transparently from the first pricing screen onwards, and show the fare-only total alongside the total-with-extras so the consumer can see at every step exactly what they are paying and why.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Pre-selecting paid optional add-ons and forcing the consumer to open each accordion and untick to remove them is a 'sneaking items into the basket' dark pattern. It is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour by causing them to pay for extras they did not actively choose. Under UCPD Arts. 5-9 such deceptive-design defaults with asymmetric friction (easy to accept, effortful to decline) fall within the general prohibition on unfair practices, independent of the sector-specific express-consent rule for additional payments.
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Present all optional add-ons unticked by default and require an active, affirmative opt-in for each paid extra. Make selecting and deselecting equally easy (single visible checkbox, no hidden accordions), so the default outcome is the bare fare the consumer searched for.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: 'Carbon contribution' is a vague environmental claim. Charging it by default, without explaining what the money funds, whether it delivers any verified emissions reduction/offset, or who administers it, risks deceiving the average consumer about the nature and environmental benefit of the payment (greenwashing under Art. 6). The risk is heightened because the charge is pre-selected, so consumers pay for an unsubstantiated green claim without actively choosing it.
findings.evidence_quote: a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page
findings.recommendation: Make the carbon contribution opt-in, and substantiate the claim: state precisely what the €2 funds, the standard/certification used, and the verified environmental outcome, with a link to evidence. Avoid implying carbon neutrality or offsetting unless independently verified.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The UCPD lists 'onerous barriers' as a factor in assessing aggressive practices. Requiring the consumer to navigate multiple accordions to remove pre-selected charges creates friction that mildly impairs freedom of choice. On its own, and given the campaign states no pressure language is used, this falls short of harassment/coercion/undue influence, so the aggressive-practice risk is low, but the friction reinforces the unfairness finding above.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Remove the deselection friction: allow add-ons to be declined with a single click at the point they are offered, without opening nested accordions.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Advertising the bare fare with 'from €39' is generally permissible where the extras are genuinely optional and deselectable, as stated here. It is therefore not misleading on its own. It is flagged for context because it interacts with the drip-pricing and pre-selection issues: consumers attracted by €39 encounter a checkout defaulting to a materially higher total.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Keep the 'from' fare accurate and ensure the checkout defaults to the advertised bare-fare price so the promotional claim and the booking experience remain consistent; disclose that optional extras are available but not included.

verdicts.notes: The AeroFly booking flow raises several UCPD concerns even though no pressure language is used and the add-ons are genuine services. The strongest issue is drip pricing: paid add-ons are pre-selected and their cost is folded into a single bundled total that is only broken out on the final screen, which risks a misleading omission of the true price (Art. 7). The pre-ticked/opt-out add-on design with deliberate friction to deselect is a "sneaking into basket" dark pattern engaging the general fairness/professional-diligence safety-net (Art. 5). The pre-selected €2 "carbon contribution" is a vague, unsubstantiated environmental claim consumers pay for by default, engaging misleading-actions rules (Art. 6). The headline "from €39" fare is itself lawful for an optional-extras model but should be assessed alongside the drip-pricing concern.

report.executive_summary: The AeroFly checkout add-ons campaign advertises a low bare fare (e.g. "Lisbon from €39") in emails and on the web, but the booking flow pre-selects three paid extras — Cancellation Cover (€14.99), Priority Boarding (€9.99) and a €2 carbon contribution — and only reveals the itemised breakdown on the final screen. The main compliance problem is consumer protection: this combination of pre-ticked paid add-ons, awkward accordion-based deselection, and a single bundled total until the end amounts to "drip pricing" and "sneaking into basket" dark patterns that are likely unfair and misleading under the UCPD (high risk). The pre-selected "carbon contribution" is also an unsubstantiated green claim that risks greenwashing. Data-protection exposure is limited but real: the promotional email channel needs a documented lawful basis and a working, easy unsubscribe. The declared use of generative AI creates a transparency obligation to mark any AI-generated content, but no specific AI asset was provided to assess. Overall this is a fixable but genuine high-risk campaign — the checkout design is the priority fix before launch.
recommendations: Un-tick all optional add-ons by default: require an active, affirmative opt-in for each paid extra (Cancellation Cover, Priority Boarding, carbon contribution) so the default outcome matches the advertised bare fare.
Remove deselection friction — make declining an add-on a single visible click, no nested accordions — and make declining as easy as accepting.

Itemise every charge from the first pricing screen onward and show the fare-only total alongside the total-with-extras, ending the bundled-until-final-screen presentation (fixes the drip-pricing omission).

Substantiate or make opt-in the €2 'carbon contribution': state exactly what it funds, the certification/standard used and the verified outcome, with a link to evidence; avoid implying offsetting/neutrality unless independently verified.

For promotional emails, confirm and document the lawful basis (opt-in consent or soft opt-in for existing customers), and include a prominent, immediately honoured one-click unsubscribe in every message.

Identify exactly where generative AI is used in the assets; ensure any AI-generated images, video, audio or copy carry machine-readable provenance marking, and add clear disclosure for any realistic depiction of real persons (deepfakes).

The DSA's marketing-relevant obligations (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) all bind "providers of online platforms" — intermediary/hosting services that store and disseminate recipient-provided information to the public — not first-party traders operating their own e-commerce interfaces. cross-site display retargeting for 30 days
personalised email sequence

frequency caps disabled for 'high-intent' users
