triage.summary: ShoeVault runs a cart-abandonment sequence targeting signed-in adult shoppers in the EU across display, email, and app-push, using behavioural retargeting for 30 days plus late-night pushes with surveillance-style messaging. Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users and unsubscribing stops emails but not pushes, raising consent-scope, opt-out consistency, and aggressive/persistent commercial practice concerns. No generative AI is declared or apparent.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute: once a user objects, ALL processing for direct marketing (including profiling and every channel) must stop. Here the opt-out is fragmented — an unsubscribe halts email but push notifications continue — so a user who has clearly indicated they no longer wish to receive marketing keeps being solicited. This fails to give effect to the objection right across the full direct-marketing operation.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Implement a single, channel-agnostic marketing opt-out: any objection (unsubscribe link, preference centre, or app setting) must suppress display retargeting, email AND app-push, and stop associated profiling. Route all channels through one suppression list and honour it in real time.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that consent be demonstrable, specific and as easy to withdraw as to give. A single blanket 'marketing communications' consent at signup is unlikely to validly cover distinct processing operations (cross-site behavioural retargeting for 30 days, personalised email, and late-night app-push). Withdrawal is also not as easy as giving consent, because unsubscribing does not stop pushes, so users cannot cleanly withdraw across all channels.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Collect granular, separately-toggleable consents for (a) email marketing, (b) app push, and (c) cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling. Provide a one-click withdrawal that is at least as easy as the original opt-in and applies to every channel and to the profiling itself. Retain records evidencing the scope of consent given.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A bundled 'marketing communications' opt-in is not 'specific' to the several materially different purposes actually pursued (30-day cross-site retargeting, behavioural profiling, and app-push), so it likely does not constitute valid consent for those purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Separate the purposes and obtain distinct affirmative consent for each; describe each purpose (channels, cross-site retargeting, retention/frequency) in plain terms at the point of collection so consent is genuinely specific and informed.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Cross-site behavioural retargeting is processing of personal data that requires a valid lawful basis. If the only basis is the over-broad signup consent (which is questionable, see Art. 4(11)/7) and a documented legitimate-interests balancing has not been performed, the retargeting and profiling may lack a valid Art. 6(1) basis — especially given the intrusive 30-day cross-site tracking and disabled frequency caps.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the retargeting/profiling. If relying on consent, ensure it is specific per above; if relying on legitimate interests, complete and retain a legitimate-interests assessment weighing the intrusiveness of 30-day cross-site tracking against user expectations, and provide an easy objection route.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Scoring users as 'high-intent' and tailoring targeting/frequency based on their browsing and cart behaviour is automated processing to evaluate personal aspects (preferences, behaviour) and therefore constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, and the objection right) which must be satisfied for the profiling itself, not just the message delivery.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Recognise the 'high-intent' scoring and behavioural retargeting as profiling: ensure a lawful basis and disclosure for it, allow objection to the profiling (not merely to messages), and reconsider disabling frequency caps for scored users as it heightens intrusiveness.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (browsing/cart behaviour) is used to build profiles for retargeting, Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, the controller inform users of the purposes, legal basis, retention (e.g. the 30-day retargeting window), recipients (e.g. third-party ad networks/news sites) and the existence of profiling. There is no indication this information is provided; the surveillance-style messaging suggests tracking that may not have been transparently disclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: three emails ('We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back')
findings.recommendation: Ensure the signup/privacy notice clearly discloses behavioural retargeting purposes, the third-party recipients/ad networks, the 30-day retention window, the existence of profiling and the right to object, in line with Art. 13.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle prohibits processing that misleads users or exploits covert/surveillance-style tracking. Framing that emphasises being watched, combined with cross-site tracking and disabled frequency caps that likely exceed reasonable user expectations from a generic 'marketing communications' opt-in, engages the fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: they're watching you back
findings.recommendation: Align actual processing with what users were transparently told and would reasonably expect; drop surveillance-style framing, and ensure the intensity of tracking (cross-site, uncapped) is proportionate and clearly communicated so processing is fair and transparent.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data of signed-in EU shoppers via behavioural retargeting, personalised email and app-push. The central GDPR problems are (1) reliance on a single, vaguely-scoped "marketing communications" consent to cover cross-site profiling, 30-day retargeting and late-night pushes, which likely fails the specific/informed/granular standard of Arts. 4(11) and 7; and (2) a fragmented opt-out where unsubscribing stops emails but not pushes, undermining the absolute right to object to direct marketing under Art. 21 and the "as easy to withdraw as to give" rule in Art. 7. Behavioural targeting constitutes profiling engaging Art. 4(4) and requiring a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1).

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits online-interface designs that materially distort or impair recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, and expressly covers making withdrawal/cancellation harder than opting in. A fragmented opt-out where the user's unsubscribe action stops one channel (email) but silently leaves late-night app pushes running obstructs the choice already made — the user cannot easily exit the marketing they tried to reject. Combined with disabling frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, the interface is organised to nag and persist rather than honour the user's expressed preference.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make opt-out global and honoured across all channels: a single unsubscribe/objection must stop email, display and push. Provide a clear, equally prominent way in the preference centre and in each push to turn off notifications, and re-enable proportionate frequency caps for all users so the design does not repeatedly solicit users who have not chosen it.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The anthropomorphic/surveillance framing ('they're watching you back', 'Still up? Your cart is too.') deployed via deliberately uncapped, late-night pushes is a pressuring, nagging design pattern that steers the recipient toward a transaction by exploiting attention and timing rather than presenting a neutral choice. This is the type of manipulative operation of an online interface Art. 25 is aimed at.
findings.evidence_quote: an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.')
findings.recommendation: Drop the surveillance-style and late-night 'still up?' framing, avoid off-hours pushes, and present cart reminders as a neutral, non-pressuring notice with an obvious dismiss/opt-out. Ensure messaging does not manipulate or pressure beyond a plain informational reminder.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Cross-site display retargeting places personalised ads on third-party platforms. Where those ads appear on online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires each ad to be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, to disclose on whose behalf it is presented and who paid, and to give meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submission does not describe any of these disclosures being provided, so the obligation is engaged and not evidently satisfied. Note the obligation binds the platform presenting the ad; ShoeVault should ensure its creative and feeds carry the required advertiser-identity and 'why am I seeing this' parameters.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Ensure retargeting creatives are clearly labelled as advertising with ShoeVault identified as the advertiser/payer, and that the ad delivery includes the main parameters used to select the recipient (e.g. 'shown because you viewed items on ShoeVault') plus a link to change them. Coordinate with ad platforms so their Art. 26(1) transparency panels reflect accurate advertiser and targeting information.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages DSA design-integrity and ad-transparency concerns. The strongest DSA angle is Art. 25 (dark patterns): a fragmented opt-out where unsubscribing stops emails but not late-night pushes, combined with deliberately disabled frequency caps and pressuring/surveillance-style messaging, is manipulative interface design that impairs free and informed decisions. The 30-day cross-site display retargeting engages Art. 26(1) ad-transparency obligations on the platforms presenting the ads. Applicability of the DSA to ShoeVault's own app/site depends on whether it qualifies as an 'online platform'; the dark-pattern conduct is in any event squarely covered by the UCPD (assessed by another agent). Art. 26(3) and Art. 28 are not engaged: no special-category data and no minors declared.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances making persistent and unwanted solicitations by remote media, including continued marketing after the consumer has opted out or refused. A user who unsubscribes has signalled refusal, yet the design deliberately continues to deliver marketing pushes through a channel the opt-out does not reach. This is precisely the 'opt-out ignored' / 'continued marketing after opt-out' scenario the blacklist targets, and blacklisted practices are unfair per se with no case-by-case balancing.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the unsubscribe/opt-out global: a single opt-out must stop marketing across all channels (email, display retargeting suppression, and app push). Route all channels through the working preference centre and honour a refusal expressed in any channel across every channel.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, through harassment, persistence or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Disabling frequency caps for targeted 'high-intent' users, combined with 30-day cross-site retargeting and app pushes, produces relentless, uncapped solicitation — the guidance's paradigm of 'relentless retargeting' and pressure through persistence, aimed at consumers precisely because they are more susceptible to pressure.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable frequency caps for all users, including 'high-intent' segments; set a strict per-day/per-week ceiling across the combined display+email+push volume and a defined campaign end (not open-ended 30-day retargeting) so cumulative pressure cannot escalate.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Timing and framing are express factors in the aggressive-practice assessment under Arts. 8-9. A deliberately late-night push using intrusive, personalised 'Still up?' framing exploits a low-resistance moment to pressure a transactional decision. Coupled with the surveillance-style 'they're watching you back' messaging, the tone leans on undue influence rather than informing the consumer.
findings.evidence_quote: an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.')
findings.recommendation: Avoid late-night send windows (e.g. no marketing pushes between 21:00 and 08:00) and drop the surveillance/pressure framing ('they're watching you back', 'Still up?') in favour of neutral, informational reminder copy; ensure push notifications remain within capped frequency and a clear opt-out.

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault cart-abandonment sequence engages the UCPD's rules on aggressive practices. Most seriously, unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night app pushes, and frequency caps are disabled for "high-intent" users — this is a fragmented/ineffective opt-out that continues soliciting consumers who have signalled refusal, squarely within the Annex I point 26 blacklist and the Arts. 8-9 aggressive-practice prohibition (persistence, timing, onerous barriers to exercising opt-out rights). The combination of 30-day cross-site retargeting, uncapped notifications, late-night (21:30) timing and surveillance-style framing compounds the harassment/undue-influence risk. These are consumer-fairness issues distinct from the parallel consent-scope analysis under GDPR.

report.executive_summary: This cart-abandonment campaign hits signed-in EU shoppers who leave a cart with 30 days of cross-site retargeting ads, three emails, and a late-night app push — and deliberately turns off frequency caps for "high-intent" users. The single biggest problem is that unsubscribing only stops the emails, not the pushes: a user who has clearly said "stop" keeps getting solicited. That fragmented opt-out is treated as an outright banned practice under EU consumer law (per se unfair), and it also breaches the absolute right to object to marketing under GDPR. The blanket "marketing communications" consent taken at signup is too vague to validly cover cross-site profiling, retargeting and pushes, so your legal basis for the tracking is shaky. Disabled frequency caps, the 21:30 "Still up?" push and the "they're watching you back" framing add up to aggressive, manipulative design (dark patterns / undue influence). None of this is unfixable, but the campaign should not go live in its current form. Priority fixes are a single global opt-out, restored frequency caps, granular consent, and dropping the surveillance-style copy and late-night sends.
recommendations: Make the opt-out global and immediate: a single unsubscribe or objection (from any channel or the preference centre) must stop email, app-push AND display retargeting, plus the underlying profiling. Continuing pushes after an unsubscribe is a per-se banned practice under UCPD Annex I point 26 — fix this before launch.

Re-enable frequency caps for ALL users, including 'high-intent' segments, with a strict combined per-day/per-week ceiling across display+email+push, and set a defined campaign end rather than open-ended 30-day retargeting.

Replace the blanket signup 'marketing communications' consent with granular, separately-toggleable consents for (a) email, (b) app-push, and (c) cross-site retargeting/profiling; make withdrawal one-click and as easy as opting in, and keep records of what was consented to.

Stop late-night marketing pushes (no sends roughly 21:00–08:00) and drop the surveillance/pressure copy ('they're watching you back', 'Still up?') in favour of neutral, informational reminder wording.

Document your lawful basis for the retargeting/profiling — if consent, ensure it meets the granular standard above; if legitimate interests, complete and retain a documented balancing assessment given the intrusiveness of 30-day cross-site tracking.

Update the signup/privacy notice to disclose the retargeting purposes, third-party ad networks/recipients, the 30-day retention window, the existence of 'high-intent' profiling, and the right to object (GDPR Art. 13).

Ensure retargeting creatives are clearly labelled as ads with ShoeVault named as advertiser/payer, and coordinate with ad platforms so their 'why am I seeing this' transparency panels carry accurate targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26).

campaign.title: ShoeVault 'we saw you looking' sequence
campaign.text: After a signed-in user abandons a cart, ShoeVault triggers: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days, three emails ('We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back'), and an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.'). Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users. The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup; the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes.

detected_practices: behavioural retargeting
cart-abandonment email sequence
app push notifications
late-night timed push (21:30)
disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users
cross-site display retargeting for 30 days
anthropomorphised/persuasive copy ('they're watching you back')
unsubscribe honoured for email but not for push (incomplete opt-out)
broad consent bundling ('marketing communications')
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is signed-in adults; no evidence of intent to reach minors, so minors_potentially_reached set to false. Key concerns for specialists: GDPR (validity/specificity of bundled consent, right to object, behavioural profiling, incomplete opt-out for pushes), DSA (online advertising transparency/profiling-based advertising obligations), and UCPD (aggressive/persuasive practices such as disabled frequency caps, relentless late-night pressure, and potentially manipulative anthropomorphised copy).
triage.summary: ShoeVault runs a cart-abandonment retargeting sequence for signed-in adult shoppers across display, email and app-push in the EU, including 30-day cross-site retargeting, late-night pushes, and disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users. It relies on behavioural personal data and broad 'marketing communications' consent, with unsubscribe stopping emails but not pushes. No generative AI is declared or evident.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing under Art. 21(2)-(3) is absolute: once a data subject objects, personal data must no longer be processed for direct marketing of any kind. A user who unsubscribes has objected to direct marketing, yet app pushes (which are direct marketing) continue. Continuing to send pushes after opt-out is a direct violation of the absolute objection right and means the opt-out is not honoured across all channels/purposes.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out effective for ALL direct marketing channels — email, display retargeting and app push. Route every marketing suppression (unsubscribe, preference-centre objection) to a single global do-not-contact/do-not-profile flag that stops pushes and retargeting audiences, not just email sends, and process objections at the point they are made.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 (read with Art. 4(11)) requires consent to be specific, granular and demonstrable, and as easy to withdraw as to give. A single blanket 'marketing communications' opt-in bundles distinct purposes (email, app push, cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling) into one tick, so it is not specific and likely not a valid basis for the profiling-based retargeting or the multi-channel push. Withdrawal is also not equally easy, since it does not cover pushes.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent into separate, granular opt-ins per purpose/channel (e.g. email marketing, push notifications, cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling). Retain records demonstrating each consent, and ensure a single-action withdrawal that is as easy as giving consent and applies to all channels.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication for defined purposes; bundled consent does not qualify. A broad 'marketing communications' label does not inform the user that they are agreeing to 30-day cross-site tracking, behavioural profiling and late-night app pushes, so the indication is neither specific nor fully informed.
findings.evidence_quote: consented to 'marketing communications'
findings.recommendation: Replace the generic label with clear, purpose-specific consent statements describing each processing operation (behavioural retargeting across third-party news sites, profiling, push timing) in plain language so users can give a genuinely informed, unambiguous choice per purpose.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Cross-site behavioural retargeting and the underlying profiling of a signed-in shopper are processing of personal data that require a valid lawful basis. If the only basis is the invalid bundled 'marketing communications' consent, the retargeting lacks a lawful basis under Art. 6(1); personalised advertising/profiling generally requires consent or a documented, balanced legitimate-interests assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a specific lawful basis for the cross-site profiling/retargeting: obtain granular consent for behavioural retargeting, or if relying on legitimate interests conduct and record a legitimate interests assessment (noting that intrusive cross-site tracking and disabled frequency caps weigh against the balancing test).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Scoring users as 'high-intent' from their cart/browsing behaviour and using that to segment and target them is profiling within Art. 4(4) (automated evaluation of personal preferences, interests and behaviour). This confirms profiling is occurring, which triggers the lawful-basis, transparency and objection obligations above.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Recognise the 'high-intent' scoring as profiling in your records of processing and privacy notice, ensure it rests on a valid basis, and include profiling within the scope of any objection/opt-out the user exercises.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that, at collection, the controller disclose purposes and legal basis, recipients (third-party news/display networks), retention (the 30-day retargeting window), data-subject rights and the existence of profiling. The campaign gives no indication that these specifics are disclosed beyond a generic 'marketing communications' label, so the transparency/information obligation is likely unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at sign-up and in the preference centre disclosing the retargeting purpose, third-party recipients/ad networks, the 30-day retention/targeting window, the existence of behavioural profiling, and the right to object — in clear, accessible terms.

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence relies on broad, bundled "marketing communications" consent to run cross-site behavioural retargeting, an email series and app pushes for signed-in adults. Under GDPR the consent is unlikely to be valid (not specific/granular per purpose), the objection/opt-out mechanism is incomplete (unsubscribe stops emails but not pushes), and the 30-day cross-site profiling needs a proper lawful basis and transparency. The absolute right to object to direct marketing is the most serious breach.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including repeatedly requesting/pressing a choice already made ('nagging'). Removing frequency caps to relentlessly re-serve messages to users classified as 'high-intent', combined with a late-night push ('Still up? Your cart is too.') timed for reduced resistance, is a design/operational choice on ShoeVault's own interface (app) that pressures rather than informs. To the extent ShoeVault operates its own online interface, this engages Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable reasonable frequency caps for all users including 'high-intent' segments, remove the deliberately late-night (21:30) send timing, and ensure messaging does not pressure through repetition; document that the interface/communication design supports rather than distorts free decision-making.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 treats making it harder to stop/cancel a communication than to receive it as a prohibited manipulative interface design. An opt-out mechanism that honours unsubscribe for email but leaves app-push notifications running is an obstruction that impairs the user's ability to withdraw from the sequence, engaging the Art. 25 prohibition on interfaces that impair free choice.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out complete and symmetrical: a single unsubscribe/preference action must stop all channels (email, display retargeting and app push). Provide an equally easy in-app control to turn off push notifications.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, per ad and in real time, that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid, and the main targeting parameters plus how to change them. This obligation falls on the online platform presenting the ad (the news sites/ad networks), not primarily on ShoeVault as advertiser; flagged for context because the cross-site retargeting relies on this ecosystem, and ShoeVault should ensure its advertiser identity and targeting-parameter information are correctly surfaced by its partners.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Confirm with display/retargeting partners that ShoeVault ads carry clear ad labelling, advertiser identity ('paid for by ShoeVault'), and meaningful, changeable targeting-parameter disclosures as required of the presenting platforms under Art. 26(1).

verdicts.notes: The DSA's marketing-relevant provisions are mostly addressed to "providers of online platforms." ShoeVault appears to be an advertiser/trader operating its own site and app rather than a hosting platform presenting third-party ads or a VLOP, so Arts. 26(1), 26(3), 27 and 39 largely fall on the ad networks/publishers or are not engaged (no sensitive-data targeting, no minors, no evidence of VLOP status). The main DSA exposure is Art. 25: to the extent ShoeVault operates its own online interface (website/app), the disabled frequency caps ("nagging"/repeated pressure), the incomplete opt-out for pushes, and the manipulative anthropomorphised copy risk materially distorting users' ability to make free and informed decisions. Note the same conduct is more squarely captured by the UCPD (covered by another specialist).

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 blacklists making persistent and unwanted solicitations by e-mail or other remote media, prohibited in all circumstances, except to enforce a contractual obligation. Once a user unsubscribes, continuing to send marketing app-push solicitations is exactly the continued marketing after opt-out this point targets. App-push falls within 'other remote media', and win-back cart-abandonment messaging is not enforcement of any contractual obligation. This is a per se prohibited practice requiring no case-by-case unfairness assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Wire the unsubscribe / preference centre to suppress ALL marketing channels, including app-push, not just email. Provide a single, effective opt-out that stops every marketing solicitation across display, email and push, and honour it immediately across all systems.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, through harassment or undue influence and having regard to its timing, location and persistence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Disabling frequency caps for targeted 'high-intent' users, combined with 30 days of cross-site retargeting, a three-email sequence and a deliberately timed 21:30 push ('Still up? Your cart is too.'), produces sustained, uncapped pressure engineered around the consumer's vulnerable moments (evening/late-night). The cumulative persistence and timing are hallmarks of an aggressive practice designed to push a transactional decision the consumer might not otherwise make.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Re-enable and enforce reasonable frequency caps for all users including 'high-intent' segments; cap total contacts per user across channels; shorten the 30-day retargeting window; and remove late-night send times (e.g. no pushes after early evening). Ensure overall contact intensity cannot escalate based on inferred purchase intent.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general prohibition on unfair practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort economic behaviour, and it is the UCPD anchor for manipulative/nagging design (dark patterns). The anthropomorphised, surveillance-themed copy ('they're watching you back') and the personalised 'Still up?' push are nagging, pressure-oriented design elements intended to unsettle and prod the consumer rather than inform, contributing to the aggressive character of the sequence and falling short of professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back
findings.recommendation: Drop surveillance/anthropomorphised framing that implies the product or brand is monitoring the user. Use neutral, informative reminder copy and avoid time-of-day 'still up?' framing that leverages the consumer's presence at vulnerable hours.

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence engages UCPD primarily through aggressive commercial practices. The most serious issue is that unsubscribing stops emails but NOT the late-night app pushes, meaning marketing solicitations continue after the consumer has signalled refusal — a practice blacklisted per se under Annex I point 26 and prohibited in all circumstances. In combination, disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, 30-day cross-site retargeting, timed 21:30 pushes, and nagging/anthropomorphised copy amount to relentless pressure likely to constitute an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. The messaging itself is manipulative but not obviously a false product claim, so Art. 6 is only weakly engaged.

report.executive_summary: This campaign triggers a multi-channel cart-abandonment sequence (30 days of cross-site display retargeting, three emails, and a late-night app push) for signed-in EU shoppers, with frequency caps switched off for "high-intent" users. The single most serious problem is that unsubscribing stops the emails but NOT the app pushes — meaning you keep marketing to people after they've said stop. This is a per se prohibited practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I) and also breaches the absolute right to object to direct marketing under GDPR — both very hard to defend. On top of that, the campaign relies on a vague, bundled "marketing communications" consent that almost certainly isn't valid for behavioural profiling, cross-site tracking and push, and it lacks proper transparency about the retargeting, third-party ad networks and 30-day tracking window. The uncapped pressure, deliberate 21:30 timing, and "they're watching you back" / "Still up?" copy also risk being treated as an aggressive/manipulative practice (UCPD and DSA dark-pattern rules). The AI Act is not engaged. Overall verdict: do not launch in its current form — several elements are outright unlawful, not merely risky.
recommendations: Make the opt-out complete and immediate: a single unsubscribe / preference-centre action must stop ALL channels — email, app push AND display retargeting audiences. Route every opt-out to one global do-not-contact/do-not-profile flag. This fixes the two most serious breaches (UCPD Annex I point 26 and GDPR Art. 21) and must be done before any launch.

Re-enable reasonable frequency caps for everyone, including 'high-intent' users, cap total cross-channel contacts per user, and shorten the 30-day retargeting window. Do not let contact intensity escalate based on inferred purchase intent.

Remove the late-night (21:30) push timing and drop the 'Still up?' framing that exploits vulnerable hours; also drop the surveillance/anthropomorphised 'they're watching you back' copy. Use neutral, informative reminder messaging.

Replace the bundled 'marketing communications' consent with separate, granular opt-ins per purpose and channel (email marketing, push notifications, cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling). Keep records demonstrating each consent, and make withdrawal as easy as giving it.

Establish and document a valid lawful basis for the cross-site profiling and retargeting (granular consent, or a documented legitimate interests assessment — noting disabled caps and intrusive tracking weigh against you).

Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at sign-up and in the preference centre disclosing the retargeting purpose, the third-party ad networks/recipients, the 30-day tracking window, the existence of 'high-intent' profiling, and the right to object.

Confirm with your display/retargeting partners that ShoeVault ads carry proper ad labelling, advertiser identity and changeable targeting-parameter disclosures as required of the platforms presenting them (DSA Art. 26).

campaign.title: MegaBasket sponsored search results
campaign.text: MegaBasket, an online marketplace with 40M EU users, sells 'Boosted Placement': paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile. Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.

detected_practices: paid search ranking placement (Boosted Placement)
inadequate/obscured advertising disclosure (6pt grey 'promoted' tag on hover-only desktop, absent on mobile)
misleading ranking explanation ('ordered by relevance' while paid placement drives top positions)
behavioural targeting by inferred price sensitivity
very large online platform / marketplace advertising
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult marketplace shoppers across the EU; no evidence minors are specifically targeted, though a general 40M-user marketplace may incidentally reach some. Given the platform scale, DSA VLOP obligations on advertising transparency and recommender/ranking parameter disclosure are likely engaged. Note the AI Act is not clearly triggered on the declared facts (no generative AI declared and inferred price-sensitivity profiling is not obviously a prohibited/high-risk AI practice), but the accuracy of the 'no AI' declaration for the inference/ranking system may warrant confirmation.
triage.summary: MegaBasket, a large EU online marketplace (40M users), sells paid 'Boosted Placement' that puts advertisers' products in the top four search positions while disclosing them only via a 6pt grey hover-only tag on desktop and no tag at all on mobile, alongside a ranking explanation claiming results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also targets users based on inferred price sensitivity. The campaign raises concerns around undisclosed/misleading advertising, transparency of ranking parameters, and profiling-based targeting.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automatically inferring a user's 'price sensitivity' and using it to target ads is automated processing to analyse/predict aspects of a person's economic situation and behaviour, which is the definition of profiling. This is the gateway fact that triggers the substantive GDPR obligations below.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Recognise price-sensitivity inference as profiling and document it in the RoPA; base all downstream compliance (lawful basis, transparency, objection handling) on that classification.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling for behavioural ad targeting requires a valid lawful basis. The campaign discloses no basis; consent is generally required for such personalised advertising, and legitimate interest would need a documented, defensible balancing test. Targeting on inferred economic vulnerability (price sensitivity) is intrusive and unlikely to pass a legitimate-interest balancing without consent.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before running price-sensitivity targeting — in practice obtain freely given, specific, informed opt-in consent for behavioural ad profiling, or produce a rigorous LIA if relying on legitimate interests; do not enable the targeting by default.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is processed for profiling, the controller must inform users of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling. Nothing in the campaign indicates users are told their price sensitivity is inferred and used to select which ads they see, so the Art. 13 information duty (including meaningful information about the profiling) is likely unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, layered privacy information at the point of data collection and in the ad-settings/privacy policy explaining that price sensitivity is inferred, the purpose (ad targeting), the lawful basis, and users' rights including objection.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that processing not be misleading or covert. Telling users results are 'ordered by relevance' while paid placement drives the top positions, combined with silent inference of price sensitivity, means the actual logic applied to users' data is misrepresented — undermining fair, transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Align user-facing explanations with the true main parameters (paid placement, inferred price sensitivity) so that the processing logic communicated to data subjects is accurate and not misleading.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Users have an absolute right to object at any time to processing for direct marketing, including profiling related to it. The campaign describes no mechanism to object to or opt out of price-sensitivity profiling, so this right is not visibly facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, prominent opt-out from direct-marketing profiling (e.g. an ad-personalisation toggle) and ensure that on objection all price-sensitivity profiling for that user ceases immediately.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Art. 22 applies to solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects. Selecting which ads/rankings a user sees generally does not meet that threshold. However, if inferred price sensitivity were used to drive personalised pricing or to exclude users from offers, Art. 22 would be engaged and require explicit consent/safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Confirm the inference feeds only ad targeting, not automated pricing or offer eligibility. If it influences prices or access to offers, implement Art. 22 safeguards (explicit consent, right to human intervention, contest the decision) and disclose the personalised pricing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data to infer users' price sensitivity and target ads accordingly — this is profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4). The main GDPR exposure is the absence of any stated lawful basis (Art. 6(1)), transparency about the profiling logic (Arts. 13, 5(1)(a)), and an absolute right to object to this direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). Special-category data (Art. 9) is not engaged on the declared facts (price sensitivity is economic, not sensitive), and Art. 22 is unlikely to be met as ad-ranking does not produce legal or similarly significant effects. Overall a real but remediable set of transparency/lawful-basis risks.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, for each ad, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid, and the main targeting parameters. A 6pt light-grey label shown only on hover on desktop — and entirely absent on mobile — does not meet the 'clear, concise, unambiguous and real-time' standard. The advertiser/payer identity and the targeting parameters (inferred price sensitivity) are also not surfaced to recipients.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, high-contrast, adequately sized 'Sponsored/Ad' label on every Boosted Placement result on both desktop and mobile (not hover-dependent), and provide accessible per-ad information on the advertiser, who paid, and the main parameters used to target the recipient (including inferred price sensitivity) with a way to change them.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Making paid ads visually identical to organic results, combined with a hover-only/absent label and an 'ordered by relevance' explanation, is disguised advertising — a deceptive interface design that materially distorts or impairs users' ability to make free and informed decisions, prohibited under Art. 25 (which the graph links to the dark-patterns / disguised-advertisement concept).
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Redesign the search interface so paid placements are visually and structurally distinguishable from organic results (clear labelling, distinct styling/section) and remove any design that conceals commercial intent, so users can tell sponsored from organic listings without interaction.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: Art. 27 requires platforms using recommender/ranking systems to set out in plain language the main parameters used and any options to modify them. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' when paid Boosted Placement in fact drives the top four positions misstates and omits a main ranking parameter (payment), so the ranking-parameter disclosure is inaccurate and incomplete.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Update the ranking explanation to state plainly that paid placement is a main parameter determining the top positions, alongside relevance signals, and disclose the parameters and any user options to influence ranking in plain language.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: At 40M EU users MegaBasket is at very-large-online-platform scale, triggering Art. 39's obligation to maintain a public advertisement repository containing ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach for the Boosted Placement ads. Nothing in the campaign indicates such a repository exists, and the price-sensitivity targeting must withstand public scrutiny.
findings.evidence_quote: an online marketplace with 40M EU users
findings.recommendation: If designated as a VLOP, establish and maintain a compliant public ad repository capturing each Boosted Placement ad's content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters (including inferred price sensitivity) and reach, and ensure targeting practices are defensible under public disclosure.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans platform ad targeting based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories. Inferred price sensitivity is not, on the declared facts, a special category, so this prohibition is not triggered — flagged only so targeting logic is monitored to ensure it does not proxy or infer sensitive attributes (e.g. health, ethnicity).
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Audit the inference model to confirm price-sensitivity segments are not derived from or acting as proxies for GDPR Art. 9 special-category data, which would bring targeting within the Art. 26(3) prohibition.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket is an online marketplace at VLOP scale (40M EU users) selling paid search placement. The disclosure design and misleading ranking explanation engage several DSA advertising and interface-transparency provisions. Most seriously, paid ads are made visually indistinguishable from organic results with a near-invisible hover-only label (absent entirely on mobile) and a false "ordered by relevance" explanation — this fails Art. 26(1) advertising identification and constitutes disguised-advertising dark-pattern design under Art. 25. Art. 27 (ranking parameter transparency) and Art. 39 (VLOP ad repository) obligations are also engaged.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Paid ranking placement is a commercial practice whose commercial (advertising) intent must be identified where not apparent from context. The top four grid positions are advertisements paid for by sellers but are made 'visually identical to organic results'. The only disclosure — a 6pt light-grey label revealed on hover on desktop, and no label at all on mobile — provides the material information about paid placement in an unclear, unintelligible and untimely manner (and omits it entirely on mobile). The average consumer cannot perceive that these are paid results, hiding the commercial intent contrary to Art. 7. Disclosure of paid inclusion in search results is expressly treated as material information under the UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a clear, legible, always-visible 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every boosted result on both desktop and mobile (adequate size, contrast and placement, not hover-dependent), so that the average consumer immediately recognises paid placement without any interaction. Ensure the label is present in the same visual layer as the result, not only on hover.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Stating that results are 'ordered by relevance' when the first four positions are in fact determined by payment (Boosted Placement), not relevance, is false/deceptive information about a main characteristic of the ranking that consumers rely on when choosing products. This is likely to cause the average consumer to take a transactional decision (clicking/buying a top-listed product believing it is the most relevant) they would not otherwise take, satisfying Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking explanation so it truthfully discloses that payment is a main parameter determining placement of the top results (e.g. 'top results include paid placements; remaining results ordered by relevance'). Do not describe paid-driven ordering as purely 'relevance'.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, presenting paid placements as organic search results and describing them as 'relevance' ordering is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average marketplace shopper, who reasonably expects search rankings to reflect merit rather than undisclosed payment. This reinforces the specific Art. 6 and Art. 7 findings.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Adopt transparent ranking practices consistent with professional diligence: clearly separate/label paid results and disclose that payment influences ranking, so consumers are not systematically steered toward paid products under a false impression of neutral relevance ranking.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's 'Boosted Placement' engages the UCPD on two clear grounds. First, the commercial intent of paid top-of-search placement is not adequately identified (Art. 7): the only disclosure is a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag shown on hover on desktop and entirely absent on mobile — the disclosure of paid inclusion/advertising in search rankings is specifically material under UCPD Art. 7. Second, the platform's ranking explanation stating results are 'ordered by relevance' while paid placement in fact drives the top four positions is a misleading action (Art. 6) about a main parameter influencing consumers' transactional decisions. The general fairness safety-net (Art. 5) reinforces both. The price-sensitivity targeting is primarily a GDPR/DSA matter and only marginally relevant here.

report.executive_summary: Your "Boosted Placement" campaign sells the top four search positions to paying sellers while making them look identical to organic results, with only a tiny 6pt grey "promoted" label that appears on hover on desktop and is completely absent on mobile — and you tell shoppers results are "ordered by relevance." Across three regulations (DSA, UCPD, GDPR) this creates serious, overlapping problems: the design hides paid advertising (disguised advertising / dark pattern) and the "relevance" claim is simply untrue, which regulators would treat as misleading. Separately, targeting shoppers by inferred "price sensitivity" is profiling that currently has no stated lawful basis, no transparency, and no opt-out. Because MegaBasket has 40M EU users it likely qualifies as a Very Large Online Platform, triggering additional ad-repository and recommender-transparency duties. None of these issues are fatal to the concept, but the current execution is not compliant and needs meaningful redesign before launch. The AI Act is not engaged. Overall risk is high and remediation should happen before the campaign goes live.
recommendations: Make every Boosted Placement result carry a clear, always-visible, high-contrast 'Sponsored/Ad' label on BOTH desktop and mobile — never hover-dependent and never absent — so shoppers instantly recognise paid placement (fixes UCPD Art. 7 and DSA Art. 26(1)).

Stop describing results as 'ordered by relevance'; state plainly that the top positions are paid placements alongside relevance signals. The current wording is a misleading action (UCPD Art. 6) and misstates ranking parameters (DSA Art. 27).

Redesign the search layout so paid results are visually and structurally distinct from organic results (distinct styling or a separate section), eliminating the disguised-advertising dark pattern (DSA Art. 25).

Establish and document a lawful basis for price-sensitivity profiling before enabling it — in practice obtain opt-in consent (do not enable by default), or produce a rigorous legitimate-interest assessment (GDPR Art. 6).

Give users clear privacy information that their price sensitivity is inferred and used for ad targeting, and provide an easy, prominent opt-out from direct-marketing profiling that takes effect immediately (GDPR Arts. 13, 21).

Provide per-ad transparency (advertiser, who paid, main targeting parameters including inferred price sensitivity) and, if MegaBasket is designated a VLOP, maintain a compliant public ad repository (DSA Arts. 26(1), 39).

Audit the price-sensitivity model to confirm it is not derived from or a proxy for GDPR Art. 9 special-category data (which would trigger the DSA Art. 26(3) targeting ban), and confirm the inference feeds only ad targeting and not personalised pricing or offer eligibility (which would engage GDPR Art. 22).

campaign.title: MegaBasket sponsored search results
campaign.text: MegaBasket, an online marketplace with 40M EU users, sells 'Boosted Placement': paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile. Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.

detected_practices: paid product placement in search results (advertising)
insufficiently disclosed advertising / hidden 'promoted' label (6pt light-grey, hover-only on desktop, absent on mobile)
misleading ranking transparency ('ordered by relevance' while placement is paid)
sponsored/paid ranking without clear disclosure

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult marketplace shoppers across the EU; no specific indication minors are targeted, though a general-audience marketplace could incidentally reach some minors. Inferred price sensitivity implies profiling of individual users.
triage.summary: A large online marketplace (40M EU users) sells 'Boosted Placement', occupying the top four search positions with paid seller products that are visually indistinguishable from organic results, disclosed only via a barely visible 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile, while claiming results are 'ordered by relevance'. The ad system also targets users based on inferred price sensitivity. This engages advertising-disclosure and ranking-transparency obligations, profiling/personal-data rules, and unfair/misleading commercial practice concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Inferring 'price sensitivity' and using it to target users is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict a person's economic situation and personal preferences/behaviour. This falls squarely within the definition of profiling in Art. 4(4), bringing the whole targeting feature within GDPR's profiling regime.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Formally document the price-sensitivity feature as profiling in the RoPA/DPIA, map exactly which personal data (browsing, purchase history, device signals) is used to infer sensitivity, and treat the feature under all GDPR profiling obligations rather than as neutral 'ad tech'.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling users for personalised ad targeting requires a valid lawful basis. For behavioural/inference-based ad targeting this is generally consent, or at best a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment; the campaign describes no consent flow and no LIA. Processing 40M EU users' data for inferred price sensitivity without an identified, valid basis is an unlawful-processing risk.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before running the feature: obtain freely given, specific, informed opt-in consent for price-sensitivity-based ad targeting, or complete and record a legitimate-interest assessment demonstrating the balancing test is passed; provide an easy withdrawal/opt-out path.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Telling users results are 'ordered by relevance' while placement is paid, and profiling users by inferred price sensitivity without disclosing it, means the processing is neither fair nor transparent to the data subjects whose data drives the targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking explanation to accurately reflect paid placement, and give users clear, upfront information that their inferred price sensitivity is used to select which ads they see; ensure processing descriptions match reality.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected and used for profiling/ad targeting, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling. The campaign shows no such information layer accompanying the price-sensitivity inference, so the Art. 13 information duty is likely unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Surface layered privacy information at the point of data collection and in ad settings, explicitly disclosing that price sensitivity is inferred and used for advertising, the legal basis relied on, retention, and the right to object.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Users have an absolute right to object to processing (including profiling) for direct-marketing purposes. The described ad-targeting system provides no visible mechanism to object to or switch off price-sensitivity profiling, so this obligation is engaged and not evidently satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easily accessible control that lets users object to / turn off profiling for ad targeting, honoured at the latest on first request, and signpost this right explicitly (e.g., in ad settings and privacy notice).

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: If inferred price sensitivity were used to drive solely-automated personalised pricing or to exclude individuals from offers, it could produce effects significant enough to engage Art. 22. As described, it selects which ads a user sees rather than making automated decisions with legal/significant effects, so the fit is weaker — but the feature should be monitored so it does not evolve into automated pricing decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Keep the feature restricted to ad selection; if price sensitivity is ever used to set individual prices or eligibility automatically, first ensure an Art. 22 basis (explicit consent/contract) and safeguards including human review and the ability to contest the decision.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages GDPR primarily through its ad system that lets sellers "target users by inferred price sensitivity." Inferring and using price sensitivity to target ads is automated processing evaluating individuals' economic situation and preferences, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4), which requires a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) and transparent information (Arts. 5(1)(a) and 13). None of these safeguards are described, and the "ordered by relevance" claim compounds the transparency concern. Art. 9 (special categories) and Art. 8 (minors' consent) are not engaged on the facts as described.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement recipients can identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. A 6pt light-grey label revealed only on hover on desktop, and completely absent on mobile, does not provide clear, real-time identification of the paid nature of the placement, nor of the advertiser/payer. On mobile the ad is effectively undisclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, high-contrast, always-visible 'Sponsored/Ad' label on every boosted result across desktop AND mobile (no hover requirement), at a legible font size, and surface the seller (on whose behalf) and payer information. Ensure the label meets the 'clear, concise, unambiguous, real-time' standard for each ad.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions; disguised advertisements are a recognised dark pattern. Making paid placements visually indistinguishable from organic search results in the four most prominent positions, combined with a near-invisible/absent label, disguises advertising as neutral organic ranking and manipulates purchase decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Redesign the search interface so paid placements are visually and structurally distinct from organic results (distinct background/shading, clear demarcation, prominent label). Do not present ads in a manner that mimics organic relevance ranking.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: Art. 27 requires platforms using recommender/ranking systems to set out in plain language the main parameters used to determine ranking. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' while the top four positions are in fact determined by payment misrepresents (and omits) a main ranking parameter, i.e., paid consideration. The ranking-parameter explanation is misleading and incomplete.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Update the ranking explanation to plainly disclose that paid placement is a determining parameter for the top positions, distinguish paid from organic ranking criteria, and describe the main organic parameters and any options to modify them.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans platform advertising based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories (health, religion, sexual orientation, political opinion, ethnicity, etc.). 'Inferred price sensitivity' is an economic/behavioural attribute and does not itself constitute a special category, so Art. 26(3) is not engaged on the current facts. Flagged for awareness: if price-sensitivity inference were derived from proxies revealing sensitive attributes, the ban would apply.
findings.evidence_quote: lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Confirm that the price-sensitivity model does not use or act as a proxy for GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. Document the input features to demonstrate no sensitive attributes (directly or by inference) drive ad targeting.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 39 requires very large online platforms (VLOPs) to maintain a public ad repository including ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. VLOP status attaches to platforms with 45M+ average monthly active EU users following Commission designation; at 40M declared users MegaBasket is close to but below the threshold, so the obligation is not clearly triggered on these facts.
findings.evidence_quote: an online marketplace with 40M EU users
findings.recommendation: Monitor monthly active user counts against the 45M VLOP threshold; if designated (or approaching it), stand up a compliant public ad repository capturing the Boosted Placement ads, advertisers, payers, targeting parameters and reach.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's 'Boosted Placement' engages the DSA's core online-platform advertising rules. The paid top-four search slots are visually indistinguishable from organic results and are disclosed only via an inadequate 6pt light-grey, hover-only (desktop) / entirely absent (mobile) 'promoted' tag, breaching Art. 26(1) ad-identification requirements and constituting a disguised-advertising dark pattern under Art. 25. The 'ordered by relevance' explanation misrepresents the main ranking parameters, engaging Art. 27. The 'inferred price sensitivity' targeting is an economic attribute rather than a GDPR Art. 9 special category, so Art. 26(3) is not triggered; VLOP ad-repository duties (Art. 39) depend on formal designation (40M users is near but below the 45M threshold) and are flagged only for awareness.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The paid nature of the top four search positions is material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision. A 6pt light-grey label shown only on hover on desktop, and entirely absent on mobile, fails to identify the commercial intent of the placement clearly, timely and intelligibly. The commercial intent is not apparent from context because the paid results are deliberately made visually indistinguishable from organic results. This is a misleading omission / undisclosed native advertising under Art. 7(2).
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a clearly legible, high-contrast, static 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every paid placement on all devices (including mobile), positioned so it is visible without hover interaction, at a size and contrast comparable to the surrounding result text. Distinguish paid positions visually from organic results (e.g. shading, separator, dedicated section).

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Telling consumers that results are 'ordered by relevance' is false/deceptive about the main parameters determining product ranking when the first four grid positions are in fact allocated to sellers who paid for placement. This deceives the average consumer about the nature of the results and their basis, and is likely to cause a transactional decision (clicking/buying a top-listed product believed to be the most relevant) they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6(1).
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking explanation so it accurately states that top positions are paid placements and describes the actual main ranking parameters. Do not present paid positions as 'relevance'-based ordering. Align disclosures with the ranking-parameter transparency obligations for paid placement in search results.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: The practice is analogous to a blacklisted advertorial: trader-paid promotion presented as if it were neutral/independent content (here, organic search results) without the paid nature being made clear. While search results are not classic 'editorial content in the media', the underlying prohibition — paid promotion disguised as independent content — is engaged and reinforces that undisclosed paid placement is treated as a serious, per se unfair practice. Note the Omnibus-added rule specifically requires disclosure of paid placement/prominence in search results.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Treat undisclosed paid placement as a per se unfair practice: ensure every paid result is unambiguously marked as advertising and that any editorial/independent framing is removed. Comply with the specific obligation to disclose paid rankings/prominence in search results.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Targeting individual users by inferred price sensitivity, combined with disguised paid placements, may fall short of professional diligence and contribute to material distortion of consumer economic behaviour under the Art. 5 general fairness safety-net. Price-sensitivity profiling itself is primarily governed by GDPR/DSA, so this is flagged as a residual concern rather than a standalone UCPD breach, but it aggravates the overall unfairness of the placement design.
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Assess the combined effect of hidden paid placement and price-sensitivity targeting for fairness; at minimum, ensure any personalisation affecting what products or prices users see is transparent to the consumer and does not exploit profiled vulnerabilities. Coordinate with GDPR/DSA compliance for the profiling itself.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket's 'Boosted Placement' presents paid product placements as if they were ordinary organic search results, disclosing the commercial nature only via a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile. This is a hidden-commercial-intent misleading omission under UCPD Art. 7, compounded by an affirmatively false 'ordered by relevance' ranking explanation that is a misleading action under Art. 6. Both are likely breaches. Targeting by inferred price sensitivity is primarily a GDPR/DSA matter but is flagged as a residual fairness concern under Art. 5.

report.executive_summary: MegaBasket's "Boosted Placement" sells the top four search positions to sellers, but shows them as visually identical to organic results with only a tiny 6pt grey "promoted" label that appears on hover on desktop and is completely missing on mobile — while telling users results are "ordered by relevance." This is the campaign's biggest problem: across three separate laws (DSA, consumer protection/UCPD) the disguised paid placement plus the false "relevance" claim are likely violations, because consumers cannot tell what is an ad and are being actively misled about how products are ranked. On top of that, letting sellers target users by "inferred price sensitivity" is profiling under GDPR, and the submission describes no lawful basis, no user disclosure, and no way to opt out — a high-risk data-protection gap affecting 40M EU users. The AI Act was found not applicable, and the DSA VLOP ad-repository duty is not yet triggered because 40M users is just below the 45M threshold (worth monitoring). None of these issues are cosmetic — the ad-labelling and "relevance" claim would need genuine redesign, and the price-sensitivity targeting needs a proper legal foundation before it runs. Overall verdict: high risk; do not launch in its current form.
recommendations: Fix ad labelling immediately: put a clear, high-contrast, always-visible 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every boosted result on BOTH desktop and mobile — no hover required — at a legible font size comparable to surrounding text. This is the single most exposed issue (DSA Art. 26, UCPD Art. 7).

Stop claiming results are 'ordered by relevance'. Update the ranking explanation to state plainly that the top positions are paid placements and describe the real ranking parameters. The current claim is an affirmatively false statement (UCPD Art. 6, DSA Art. 27).

Visually and structurally separate paid placements from organic results (distinct shading, separator, or dedicated section) so they no longer mimic organic ranking — this addresses the disguised-advertising 'dark pattern' finding (DSA Art. 25) and the advertorial-style unfairness (UCPD Annex I).

Before running price-sensitivity targeting, establish and document a lawful basis: obtain freely-given opt-in consent or complete a documented legitimate-interest assessment, and provide an easy opt-out/objection path for direct-marketing profiling (GDPR Arts. 6, 21).

Give users clear upfront privacy information that their inferred price sensitivity is used to select the ads they see, including purposes, legal basis, retention and the right to object; document the feature as profiling in the RoPA/DPIA (GDPR Arts. 5, 13, 4(4)).
Verify the price-sensitivity model does not use or act as a proxy for special-category data (health, ethnicity, etc.); document input features to confirm (DSA Art. 26(3)).

Keep the feature limited to ad selection only — do not use it for automated individual pricing or eligibility decisions without additional GDPR Art. 22 safeguards (explicit consent, human review, right to contest).
Monitor monthly active EU users against the 45M VLOP threshold; if reached or designated, stand up a compliant public ad repository for Boosted Placement (DSA Art. 39).
