findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Inferring 'price sensitivity' from user data is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict a person's economic situation and behaviour, which is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This classification triggers the full set of profiling-related GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: The ad system also lets sellers target users by inferred price sensitivity.
findings.recommendation: Formally document that price-sensitivity targeting constitutes profiling, map the personal data inputs used to derive it, and run a DPIA given the 40M-user scale and behavioural inference involved.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling for advertising requires a valid lawful basis — typically consent or a carefully documented and balanced legitimate-interests assessment. The submission demonstrates no lawful basis for inferring and using price-sensitivity attributes for ad targeting; inference of economic behaviour to serve targeted commercial placements is intrusive and unlikely to be justified without consent or a robust LIA.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before deploying price-sensitivity targeting: obtain freely given, specific consent, or complete and record a legitimate-interests balancing test that weighs the intrusiveness of economic profiling against user expectations, and provide an opt-out.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Using inferred price-sensitivity profiles to influence what users see while telling them results are merely 'ordered by relevance' is a misleading account of how their data drives the experience, breaching the fairness and transparency principle that governs the profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'.
findings.recommendation: Make ranking and targeting logic honest and transparent: disclose that paid placement and profiling (including price-sensitivity inference) affect what users see, and align public explanations with the actual processing.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data are collected, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes and legal basis of processing and provide meaningful information about profiling, including its logic and consequences. The campaign gives no indication that users are told their data is used to infer price sensitivity for ad targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice / point-of-collection information to clearly disclose the price-sensitivity profiling purpose, the lawful basis, and meaningful information about the profiling logic and its consequences for the ads users see.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Users have an absolute right to object at any time to processing for direct marketing, including profiling connected to it. Price-sensitivity targeting is profiling for marketing purposes, yet the submission shows no mechanism to inform users of, or facilitate, this opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easily accessible opt-out from profiling-based targeting, inform users of the right to object explicitly at the point of first communication, and ensure objecting users are excluded from price-sensitivity targeting.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: If price-sensitivity profiling feeds solely-automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects (e.g., automated exclusion from offers or personalised pricing), Art. 22 restrictions and safeguards apply. As described the practice is ad targeting rather than a clearly significant automated decision, so this is engaged only as a risk to monitor.
findings.evidence_quote: target users by inferred price sensitivity
findings.recommendation: Confirm that price-sensitivity profiling is not used to make solely-automated decisions with significant effects (e.g., differential pricing or offer exclusion); if it is, implement Art. 22 safeguards including human review and explicit consent or another valid exception.

verdicts.notes: The campaign enables sellers to target marketplace users by "inferred price sensitivity." Inferring economic/behavioural attributes from user data is automated processing that meets the GDPR definition of profiling (Art. 4(4)) and requires a valid lawful basis, transparent information, and respect for the right to object — none of which the submission evidences. The false "ordered by relevance" explanation also undermines the fairness and transparency principle governing the underlying personal-data processing. No special-category data is indicated, so Art. 9 is not engaged; Art. 22 is engaged only weakly.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each advertisement recipients can identify, in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time, that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. A 6pt light-grey tag that only appears on hover on desktop — and is entirely absent on mobile — fails the clear/unambiguous/real-time standard: on mobile there is no disclosure at all, and on desktop it is neither clear nor available without interaction. Advertiser identity ('on whose behalf'/'who paid') is also not conveyed at the point of presentation.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a persistent, clearly legible 'Sponsored/Advertisement' label on every paid slot on both desktop and mobile (no hover requirement), with sufficient size/contrast to be immediately noticeable, and surface the paying seller's identity and a link to the targeting-parameter information.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including disguised advertisements and giving undue prominence to certain content. Making paid placements visually indistinguishable from organic results, placing them in the top four positions, and pairing this with a false 'ordered by relevance' explanation is a textbook disguised-advertising dark pattern that impairs informed purchasing decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Visually and structurally distinguish sponsored results from organic ones (distinct styling, prominent labelling, and correct explanatory text), and stop presenting paid slots as if they were relevance-ranked organic results.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: Art. 27 requires platforms using recommender systems to set out in plain language the main parameters that determine ranking. Stating results are 'ordered by relevance' when the top four positions are in fact determined by payment misrepresents the main ranking parameter and omits that payment (Boosted Placement) is the decisive factor for those positions, defeating the transparency the provision requires.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Update the ranking explanation to accurately disclose that paid placement is a main parameter determining the top positions, describe the relevance parameters used for the remaining results, and provide options to influence ranking where applicable.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: With 40M EU users MegaBasket exceeds the 45M average-monthly-user VLOP threshold's order of magnitude and is very likely designated (or designatable) as a VLOP; if so, Art. 39 requires a public ad repository containing, for each advertisement, the content, the advertiser/payer, the targeting/main parameters and reach. The Boosted Placement ads — including the inferred-price-sensitivity targeting parameters — must be captured in that repository, and the described set-up does not indicate this is being done.
findings.evidence_quote: MegaBasket, an online marketplace with 40M EU users
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP status against the 45M-user threshold; if applicable, maintain a compliant public ad repository capturing each sponsored placement's content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters (including price-sensitivity segments) and reach for the required retention period.

verdicts.notes: MegaBasket is an online marketplace (an online platform) presenting paid advertising in search results, so the DSA advertising and interface-design rules squarely apply. The near-invisible "promoted" labelling breaches the Art. 26(1) real-time, clear-and-unambiguous ad-identification duty; the visually-identical paid slots combined with a false "ordered by relevance" explanation are a disguised-advertising dark pattern (Art. 25) and a misstatement of recommender-system parameters (Art. 27). At 40M EU users MegaBasket is very likely a designated VLOP, triggering the Art. 39 public ad-repository obligation covering these ads and their targeting parameters.

findings.rationale: Whether payment influences a product's search ranking/placement is material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, and the commercial (paid) intent of the top four slots is not apparent from context because they look identical to organic results. A 6pt light-grey label that only appears on hover on desktop, and is entirely absent on mobile, provides that information in an unclear, ambiguous and effectively hidden manner (and omits it entirely on mobile). This is a misleading omission / failure to identify commercial intent under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: visually identical to organic results except a 6pt light-grey 'promoted' tag visible on hover (desktop) and not at all on mobile
findings.recommendation: Display a clear, legible, always-visible 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label on every paid placement on both desktop and mobile (adequate size and contrast, no hover requirement), positioned so the average consumer immediately understands the placement is paid before interacting with it.

findings.title: Misleading actions

This deceives the average consumer about the nature of the results and the existence of a paid advantage, and is likely to cause a transactional decision (clicking/buying the top items) they would not otherwise take — a misleading action under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: Ranking explanations state results are 'ordered by relevance'
findings.recommendation: Correct the ranking disclosure so it accurately states that top positions are paid placements and that payment is a main parameter determining ranking; do not describe paid slots as ordered solely 'by relevance'. Align the explanation with the actual ranking logic.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: By analogy to the advertorial prohibition, paid promotion presented in the guise of neutral/organic content without making the paid nature clear is prohibited. The Boosted Placement slots are paid promotions dressed as ordinary organic search results with no adequate identifying label, which is the native-advertising / undisclosed-paid-promotion harm this blacklist point targets. (Point 11 is framed around editorial media content, so this reinforces rather than independently establishes a per-se breach; the core anchors are Arts. 6 and 7.)
findings.evidence_quote: paying sellers' products occupy the first four grid positions of every search, visually identical to organic results
findings.recommendation: Ensure any paid promotional placement is clearly identifiable as paid content at the point of display, so it is never presented as if it were independent/organic ranking.

verdicts.notes: The campaign sells paid top-of-search placement ("Boosted Placement") that is visually near-indistinguishable from organic results, with an inadequate disclosure (a 6pt light-grey "promoted" tag visible only on hover on desktop and absent on mobile) and an affirmatively false ranking explanation ("ordered by relevance"). Under the UCPD, whether a product's placement in search results is influenced by payment is material information that must be clearly disclosed (Art. 7 / Annex-I point 11 logic), and describing paid placements as relevance-based is a misleading action (Art. 6). The failure of disclosure on mobile — where no label appears at all — is a clear breach; the "ordered by relevance" claim is likely misleading; and the practice risks the general unfairness prohibition (Art. 5).

report.executive_summary: MegaBasket's "Boosted Placement" campaign sells the top four search positions to paying sellers, presents them as visually identical to organic results, labels them almost invisibly (a 6pt grey "promoted" tag only on hover on desktop, nothing on mobile), tells users results are "ordered by relevance," and lets sellers target shoppers by inferred price sensitivity. This creates serious compliance problems across three regulations. The biggest risks are that the disguised paid placements and the false "ordered by relevance" claim are deceptive to consumers and likely breach EU consumer and platform-transparency law (UCPD Arts. 6 & 7, DSA Arts. 25, 26 & 27). Inferring "price sensitivity" to target users is profiling under GDPR and needs a proper lawful basis, honest disclosure, and an opt-out — none of which is evidenced. At ~40M EU users MegaBasket is likely a Very Large Online Platform, which triggers an additional public ad-repository obligation. The AI Act is not engaged. Overall verdict: high risk — the campaign should not launch in its current form and needs labelling, disclosure, and data-protection fixes before going live.
recommendations: Add a clear, always-visible 'Sponsored'/'Ad' label to every paid placement on BOTH desktop and mobile — adequate size and contrast, no hover required — so shoppers see it before interacting. This fixes the single most severe and clear-cut breach (no disclosure at all on mobile).

Stop describing paid slots as 'ordered by relevance'. Correct the ranking explanation to state honestly that the top positions are paid and that payment is a main ranking parameter (fixes UCPD Art. 6 misleading action and DSA Art. 27 recommender transparency).

Visually and structurally distinguish sponsored results from organic ones so they are not disguised advertising / a dark pattern (DSA Art. 25); surface the paying seller's identity at the point of display (DSA Art. 26).

Establish and document a lawful basis for price-sensitivity profiling before deploying it — obtain consent or complete a robust legitimate-interests balancing test — and provide a clear, easy opt-out plus notice of the right to object to profiling-based marketing (GDPR Arts. 6, 21).

Update the privacy notice / point-of-collection information to disclose the price-sensitivity profiling purpose, its logic and consequences, and run a DPIA given the 40M-user scale (GDPR Arts. 13, 4(4)).

Confirm whether MegaBasket is a designated VLOP against the 45M-user threshold; if so, maintain a compliant public ad repository capturing each sponsored placement's content, advertiser/payer, targeting parameters (including price-sensitivity segments) and reach (DSA Art. 39).

Confirm price-sensitivity inference is not used for solely-automated decisions with significant effects (e.g. differential pricing or offer exclusion); if it is, add Art. 22 safeguards (human review, explicit consent).

campaign.title: HomeFix audience expansion memo
campaign.text: A home-services brand collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'. Marketing now proposes: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list, reasoning 'they are existing customers'. The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email. No sensitive data is involved and an unsubscribe link will be included.

detected_practices: custom audience upload of customer email list to social platforms
lookalike audience creation
weekly promotional email newsletter
reuse of data collected for a different declared purpose (order updates/service info) for advertising
behavioural targeting/personalisation
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult past customers in the EU; lookalike expansion could reach new individuals beyond the original customer base. No minors indicated, but lookalikes reduce control over who is ultimately reached.
triage.summary: A home-services brand plans to repurpose customer emails—collected only for order updates and service information—by uploading them to social platforms for custom and lookalike audiences and by sending a weekly promotional newsletter. The original privacy notice covered neither advertising uploads nor marketing email, raising purpose-limitation, transparency, and consent issues. No generative AI or sensitive data is declared, and audience is adult past customers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Data was collected under a narrow declared purpose ('Receive order updates and service information') and is now being used for advertising uploads and promotional email. Processing personal data for purposes not disclosed and incompatible with the original collection purpose breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. The 'they are existing customers' reasoning does not make the new advertising purposes compatible or transparent.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Do not reuse the checkout email list for advertising or newsletters under the original notice. Either obtain fresh, specific consent for the new purposes or conduct a documented compatibility/legitimate-interests assessment; update the privacy notice to reflect any advertising and marketing-email uses before processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Each new processing operation needs a valid lawful basis. Uploading emails as hashed identifiers to social platforms (custom audiences) and sending promotional email are advertising purposes not covered by the contract-based collection for order/service info. Email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (ePrivacy), and custom/lookalike audience creation typically requires consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment — neither is evidenced here.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before each activity: obtain prior opt-in consent for the promotional newsletter and for platform audience uploads, or complete and record a legitimate-interests balancing test where legally viable. Suspend the uploads and newsletter until a basis is in place.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is relied upon, the controller must be able to demonstrate it and it must be specific and informed. Consent given at checkout for 'order updates and service information' is not consent for advertising uploads or promotional email, so no demonstrable, specific consent exists for the proposed uses.
findings.evidence_quote: reasoning 'they are existing customers'
findings.recommendation: Collect separate, granular, freely given opt-in consent for marketing email and for social-platform audience uploads, keep records to demonstrate it, and ensure withdrawal is as easy as giving consent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collection the controller must disclose all purposes, legal bases and recipients. The notice omitted advertising uploads (disclosing social platforms as recipients) and promotional email, so data subjects were not informed of these purposes/recipients as required.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Provide updated, clear Article 13 information covering the advertising and marketing-email purposes, the social platforms as recipients, retention, and data-subject rights; deliver it to affected individuals before undertaking the new processing.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling. An email unsubscribe link addresses newsletter opt-out but does not by itself provide a means to object to the custom-audience/lookalike profiling processing on social platforms.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsubscribe link will be included
findings.recommendation: Offer an easy, clearly signposted opt-out covering all direct-marketing processing, including audience-upload/lookalike profiling, and honour objections by removing individuals from platform audiences, not just the email list.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Creating lookalike and custom audiences to segment and target individuals constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4), which brings the processing within the profiling-related obligations (lawful basis, transparency, and the right to object) and confirms these are not merely benign list operations.
findings.evidence_quote: build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Treat audience segmentation and lookalike creation as profiling: document it in the privacy notice, ensure a lawful basis, and provide meaningful information about the targeting logic and the right to object.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes customer emails collected solely for "order updates and service information" into advertising (custom/lookalike audiences) and promotional email, with no supporting lawful basis, consent, or transparency. This breaches the transparency/lawfulness principle and lacks a valid Art. 6 basis; the "existing customers" rationale does not cure the purpose mismatch. Multiple obligations (lawful basis, consent conditions, transparency at collection, right to object) are engaged and not satisfied as described.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Running custom-audience and lookalike ads on online platforms brings the campaign within the DSA ad-transparency regime. For each ad, recipients must be able to identify in real time that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. While the primary duty falls on the platform, the advertiser must supply accurate advertiser-identity and payer information and design creative that is clearly identifiable as advertising for these obligations to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all social-platform placements are properly labelled as advertising with correct advertiser/payer identity supplied to the platform, and confirm the platform surfaces the main targeting parameters (custom-audience/lookalike basis) and the 'why am I seeing this' controls to recipients.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The DSA prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients the provider is aware with reasonable certainty are minors. The declared audience is adult past customers, so this is not directly breached; however, lookalike expansion reduces control over who is ultimately reached, so the campaign should confirm minors are not drawn into profiling-based ad delivery.
findings.evidence_quote: build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Apply age constraints to the lookalike/audience configuration so profiling-based ads are not served to individuals who may be minors, and document that targeting is restricted to adults.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged only modestly by this campaign. The core issues (purpose limitation, consent for the ad upload and newsletter) are GDPR matters outside this regulation's scope. Under the DSA, the plan to run custom-audience and lookalike advertising on social platforms triggers the Art. 26(1) ad-transparency framework (ads must be identifiable, disclose the advertiser, and expose meaningful targeting-parameter information), and lookalike expansion is worth flagging because it reduces control over who is ultimately reached. No sensitive-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) or minor targeting (Art. 28) is indicated, and no dark-pattern interface conduct is described.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Data was gathered under a transactional/service framing that did not disclose any commercial marketing intent. Now repurposing that same list for social-platform advertising uploads, lookalike expansion and a weekly promotional newsletter means consumers were not given material information — that their contact data and relationship would be exploited for advertising — and the commercial intent of the collection was not made apparent. Art. 7 treats failing to identify commercial intent and omitting/obscuring material information as a misleading omission. The gap between the declared collection purpose and the actual advertising use is exactly the kind of untimely/unclear disclosure Art. 7 targets.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Do not use the existing list for advertising uploads, lookalikes or promotional email until consumers have been given clear, timely information that their data will be used for marketing and given a genuine choice. For future collection, make the commercial/marketing purpose explicit and separate at the point of sign-up rather than bundling it under 'order updates and service information'.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: A weekly promotional cadence sent to recipients who only ever signed up for order updates/service information risks becoming an unwanted solicitation by email. Annex I point 26 prohibits persistent and unwanted solicitations in all circumstances. The blacklist test is not yet met — an unsubscribe link is offered and no prior refusal is being ignored — but a high-frequency push to a non-opted-in list is on the boundary, and continuing to email anyone who unsubscribes or objects would cross into the prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list
findings.recommendation: Only newsletter recipients who have actually opted into marketing; honour every unsubscribe/objection immediately and permanently (no win-back re-contact of opted-out users); keep frequency proportionate and set expectations at sign-up to avoid the solicitation becoming unwanted.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's central problems (purpose limitation, transparency, consent) sit primarily under GDPR, but there is a genuine UCPD dimension. Collecting emails under an "order updates and service information" framing while planning to use them for advertising uploads and a promotional newsletter engages Art. 7 (misleading omission / undisclosed commercial intent), because the marketing purpose was hidden from consumers at the point of collection. The proposed weekly newsletter to a list that never opted into marketing raises a watch-point under Annex I point 26 (persistent and unwanted solicitations), though the blacklist test is not yet met given an unsubscribe link is offered. No blacklisted practice is clearly present at this stage.

report.executive_summary: This campaign proposes taking a customer email list collected only for "order updates and service information" and reusing it for three marketing purposes: uploading it to social platforms as a custom audience, building lookalike audiences, and sending a weekly promotional newsletter. The core problem is that none of these uses were disclosed or consented to when the emails were collected — being an "existing customer" does not authorise this. This is a likely GDPR violation on multiple fronts (no valid lawful basis, no specific consent, inadequate transparency at collection, and a right-to-object gap because an unsubscribe link only covers email, not the platform audiences). It also creates a consumer-protection (UCPD) risk because the commercial intent was hidden at sign-up, and a weekly cadence to a non-opted-in list edges toward "unwanted solicitation." The DSA adds lighter ad-transparency and adult-only targeting obligations for the social placements. The EU AI Act does not apply. Bottom line: do not proceed as described — the list cannot lawfully be repurposed until fresh consent and updated notices are in place.
recommendations: STOP the plan as described: do not upload the checkout email list to social platforms, build lookalikes, or send the promotional newsletter under the current privacy notice — these purposes were never disclosed or consented to.

Obtain fresh, specific, granular opt-in consent from these customers for (a) the promotional newsletter and (b) social-platform audience uploads/lookalikes, and keep records proving it. Only contact and upload those who actually opt in.

Update the privacy notice to clearly disclose the advertising and marketing-email purposes, name the social platforms as recipients, and cover retention and data-subject rights; deliver this information to affected individuals before any new processing.

Provide an easy opt-out that covers ALL direct marketing — not just email unsubscribe. When someone objects, remove them from the platform custom audiences and lookalikes too, and never re-contact opted-out users.

For future data collection, present the marketing/commercial purpose as a separate, explicit choice at sign-up rather than bundling it under 'order updates and service information', to avoid hidden-commercial-intent (UCPD) issues.
Keep newsletter frequency proportionate and set expectations at sign-up to avoid a weekly cadence becoming an 'unwanted solicitation'.

For the social ads: ensure placements are clearly labelled as advertising with correct advertiser/payer identity, confirm the platform exposes targeting/'why am I seeing this' controls, and apply age constraints so profiling-based ads reach only adults.

campaign.text: A home-services brand collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'. Marketing now proposes: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list, reasoning 'they are existing customers'. The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email. No sensitive data is involved and an unsubscribe link will be included.

detected_practices: custom audience upload to social platforms
lookalike audience creation
email data repurposing beyond original collection consent
promotional newsletter to existing customers
behavioural/interest-based targeting
unsubscribe mechanism included
triage.summary: A home-services brand plans to repurpose customer emails collected only for "order updates and service information" by uploading them to social platforms as custom audiences, building lookalikes, and sending weekly promotional newsletters. The original privacy notice covered neither advertising uploads nor promotional email, creating a clear purpose-limitation and lawful-basis concern despite the "existing customers" justification. No generative AI or sensitive/minor data is involved, and an unsubscribe link is planned.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The emails were collected under 'Receive order updates and service information'. Uploading them to social platforms, building lookalikes, and sending promotional newsletters are new advertising purposes that require their own lawful basis. Consent was never obtained for advertising; contract does not cover marketing uses; and legitimate interest for disclosing a whole customer list to third-party platforms and profiling for lookalikes is unlikely to survive a balancing test absent transparency and objection safeguards. 'Existing customer' status does not itself provide a lawful basis under GDPR.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes, and start a weekly promotional newsletter to the same list, reasoning 'they are existing customers'
findings.recommendation: Do not proceed until a valid legal basis is established for each new purpose. For email marketing and custom-audience uploads, obtain fresh, specific opt-in consent from the list; alternatively conduct and document a legitimate-interest assessment (only viable for limited first-party newsletters, not for disclosing the list to platforms/lookalikes). Suppress any contacts for whom no lawful basis can be established.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — including purpose limitation reflected in it — is breached when data collected for one clearly-stated purpose (order/service updates) is used for incompatible, undisclosed purposes (third-party ad targeting and promotional email). Repurposing data in ways the data subject was not told about and would not reasonably expect is unfair and non-transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Treat the advertising and newsletter uses as new purposes. Assess compatibility with the original purpose (they are unlikely to be compatible), and only process on a fresh lawful basis with updated, clear information provided to data subjects before any new use begins.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Article 13 requires that, at collection, the controller disclose the purposes and legal basis of processing and the recipients of the data. The notice disclosed only order/service information and named neither promotional email nor the disclosure of the list to social media platforms (recipients). Using the data for undisclosed purposes and recipients means the required transparency information was never provided for those uses.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Provide compliant Art. 13/Art. 14 information covering the new purposes (advertising, newsletter), the legal basis, the social-platform recipients, retention, and the right to object, before any processing for those purposes. Where consent is the basis, present this information as part of the consent request.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and informed. The checkout wording relates only to transactional order/service updates and cannot constitute freely given, specific, informed consent for promotional email marketing or for uploading personal data to advertising platforms. Relying on this collection as if it were marketing consent bundles unrelated purposes and fails the Art. 4(11) standard (see also Art. 7 conditions and ePrivacy prior-consent rule for email marketing).
findings.evidence_quote: A home-services brand collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Where consent is used as the basis, run a separate, unbundled opt-in specifically for promotional email and for social-platform advertising, in clear language, as easy to withdraw as to give. Do not treat the transactional sign-up as marketing consent.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Building lookalike audiences and custom-audience targeting is automated processing to analyse and predict personal preferences, interests and behaviour, which meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling. As profiling for direct marketing it engages the lawful-basis requirement (Art. 6) and the absolute right to object (Art. 21), which the campaign does not currently address for the platform processing.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Recognise the custom-audience/lookalike activity as profiling for direct marketing. Ensure a lawful basis, disclose the profiling in the privacy information, and provide a means to object that also stops the platform-side processing (not only email unsubscribe).

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing (including related profiling) is absolute and must be respected across all marketing processing. An email unsubscribe link only covers the newsletter channel; it does not enable data subjects to object to, or stop, the custom-audience upload and lookalike profiling on social platforms. The objection mechanism as described is therefore incomplete.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsubscribe link will be included
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, effective objection mechanism covering all direct-marketing processing: on objection, suppress the individual from the newsletter, remove them from uploaded custom audiences, and exclude their data from lookalike seeding. Maintain a suppression list and propagate opt-outs to the platforms.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes personal data (customer emails) collected solely for "order updates and service information" into three new advertising/marketing uses — social custom-audience uploads, lookalike generation, and a weekly promotional newsletter — none of which were disclosed at collection or supported by a valid legal basis. This breaches the purpose-limitation/lawfulness principle and transparency duties, and the "they are existing customers" justification does not cure the missing lawful basis for these new purposes. The planned email unsubscribe link addresses only part of the Art. 21 objection right and does nothing for the platform-upload processing. Sensitive data and minors are not involved, so those provisions are not engaged.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Running custom-audience and lookalike advertising on social platforms constitutes presenting advertisements to recipients. While the primary Art. 26(1) obligation to display ad-transparency information rests on the online platform, the advertiser must ensure its campaigns can satisfy these requirements: each ad clearly identifiable as an advertisement, disclosure of on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, and meaningful information on the main targeting parameters (here, membership of an uploaded custom audience / lookalike model) with a means for recipients to change them.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all social ads are delivered through platform ad formats that automatically apply the required disclosures: clear 'ad/sponsored' labelling, the brand's correct advertiser/payer identity, and the platform's 'Why am I seeing this ad?' targeting-parameter panel. Do not run these as organic-looking or disguised posts, and confirm the custom-audience/lookalike targeting basis is truthfully reflected in the platform's ad-parameter disclosure.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's substantive advertising prohibitions are largely not engaged here: the campaign involves adults only (so the Art. 28 minors profiling-ad ban does not apply) and explicitly states "No sensitive data is involved" (so the Art. 26(3) special-category targeting ban is not triggered). No online-interface dark patterns (Art. 25) or recommender-system (Art. 27) issues are described, and ad-repository duties (Art. 39) fall on very large platforms, not this advertiser. The one genuine DSA touchpoint is Art. 26(1) ad transparency: by uploading a custom audience and building lookalikes to run social ads, the brand must ensure each ad is clearly identifiable as an advertisement, states on whose behalf it is presented and who paid, and that meaningful targeting-parameter information is available to recipients. The core lawful-basis/purpose-limitation and email-consent problems are GDPR/UCPD matters outside this regulation.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Under Art. 7, failing to identify the commercial intent of a practice when it is not apparent from context is a misleading omission. Consumers gave their email at checkout on the understanding it was for transactional service messages only; the marketing intent (weekly promotional newsletter, upload to social platforms as a custom audience, lookalike expansion) was omitted at the point they made the transactional decision to hand over their data. The 'they are existing customers' justification does not cure the omission, because the consumer was never told this contact channel would be used for advertising. This deprives the average consumer of material information needed to decide whether to share their address.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on service-purpose data for promotional messaging. Before any promotional use, clearly disclose the marketing/ad-platform purpose and obtain a fresh, specific opt-in; going forward, state the marketing intent transparently at the point of collection so commercial intent is apparent, and keep transactional and marketing purposes separate.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is predominantly a data-protection matter (purpose limitation / lawful basis for direct marketing), which falls to the GDPR agent. From the UCPD angle, the one genuine issue is misleading omission / hidden commercial intent: contact data was gathered at checkout under a purely service-framed purpose ("order updates and service information") without disclosing the marketing and ad-platform use now proposed, so the commercial intent was not apparent when the consumer handed over their email. Annex I point 26 (persistent unwanted solicitations) and Arts. 8-9 (aggressive practices) are not engaged: an unsubscribe link is planned and there is no re-contact after refusal or high-pressure tactic described.

report.executive_summary: This campaign takes email addresses that customers gave only for "order updates and service information" and repurposes them for three new marketing uses: a weekly promotional newsletter, uploading the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, and building lookalike audiences. The core problem is that none of these uses were disclosed when the data was collected, and "they are existing customers" is not a lawful basis on its own. Under GDPR this is a likely violation: you have no valid legal basis for the new purposes, you breach the transparency and purpose-limitation principles, and the transactional sign-up does not count as marketing consent. The planned unsubscribe link only covers the newsletter — it does nothing to let people object to the social-platform uploads and lookalike profiling, which is also required. Separately, the UCPD flags a hidden-commercial-intent problem (you gathered the email under a service framing without revealing the marketing purpose), and the DSA requires that any resulting social ads carry proper ad-transparency labelling. Bottom line: do not proceed as planned — you need fresh, specific opt-in consent (or at minimum a documented lawful basis for the limited first-party newsletter) and updated privacy information before any of this can go live.
recommendations: Do not upload the customer list to social platforms or build lookalikes until you have obtained fresh, specific opt-in consent for that purpose — legitimate interest is very unlikely to survive a balancing test for disclosing a whole customer list to third-party platforms.

Run a separate, unbundled opt-in specifically for the promotional newsletter (and a separate one for social-ad use), in clear language and as easy to withdraw as to give. Do not treat the checkout 'order updates and service information' sign-up as marketing consent.
Suppress any contact for whom no valid lawful basis can be established; only market to those who opt in.

Update the privacy notice to provide full Art. 13/14 information for the new purposes: the marketing and ad-platform uses, the social-platform recipients, the profiling/lookalike activity, the legal basis, retention, and the right to object — presented before any new processing begins.

Build an objection/opt-out mechanism that covers ALL marketing processing, not just email: on objection, remove the person from the newsletter, from uploaded custom audiences, and from lookalike seeding, and propagate the opt-out to the platforms. Maintain a suppression list.

Ensure any social ads run through standard platform ad formats so they carry required DSA disclosures: clear 'ad/sponsored' labelling, correct advertiser/payer identity, and the 'Why am I seeing this ad?' targeting panel. Do not run them as organic-looking posts.

Going forward, state marketing intent transparently at the point of data collection and keep transactional and marketing purposes clearly separate to avoid misleading-omission (UCPD) and transparency (GDPR) issues.

findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Collect separate, granular, clearly-worded opt-in consent for (a) promotional newsletters and (b) sharing/matching data with social platforms for advertising, each distinct from the transactional service notice.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, data subjects be told all purposes of processing, the legal basis, and recipients of the data. The notice omitted advertising uploads to social platforms (recipients) and promotional emailing (purpose), so the transparency-at-collection duty is not met for the new processing.
findings.evidence_quote: The privacy notice from collection time mentions neither advertising uploads nor promotional email.
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice to disclose all marketing purposes, the legal basis, and that data may be shared with named social platform recipients; provide this information before undertaking the new processing and, where consent is required, at the consent point.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Custom-audience matching and lookalike modelling are automated processing that evaluates and predicts personal preferences, interests and behaviour, meeting the definition of profiling. This engages the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency and the right to object) and means lookalike expansion also processes the personal data of new individuals who never had a relationship with the brand, for whom no basis or notice exists at all.
findings.evidence_quote: upload the full list to social platforms as a custom audience, build lookalikes
findings.recommendation: Treat custom-audience and lookalike activity as profiling: secure a lawful basis and transparency for it, and avoid lookalike expansion unless a lawful basis and information provision can be assured for the newly-targeted individuals.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling. An email unsubscribe link addresses only the newsletter channel; the right must also be facilitated for the custom-audience/lookalike profiling and honoured by suppressing objecting individuals across all marketing processing, not just email.
findings.evidence_quote: an unsubscribe link will be included
findings.recommendation: Provide an easy, comprehensive opt-out covering both email and platform-based advertising/profiling, inform data subjects of the objection right at first contact, and maintain a suppression list applied across all channels.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes emails collected at checkout under an "order updates and service information" notice for advertising: uploading to social platforms as custom audiences, building lookalikes, and sending a weekly promotional newsletter. None of these purposes was disclosed at collection, and no valid lawful basis (particularly consent) exists for them. This breaches the purpose-limitation/transparency and lawfulness principles, consent conditions, and the transparency-at-collection duty, and lookalike expansion additionally processes data of individuals who never had any relationship with the brand. An unsubscribe link does not cure the missing lawful basis or the notice gap.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The commercial/advertising intent behind the data collection was not identified to consumers: the notice presented the purpose as service/transactional communications, while the brand now intends to use the same contact data for a promotional newsletter and to upload it to social platforms for advertising and lookalike expansion. Under Art. 7, a practice is misleading where it fails to identify commercial intent (where not apparent from context) or omits material information the average consumer needs. A consumer handing over their email for 'order updates and service information' would not reasonably expect advertising use, so the commercial purpose was hidden at the material moment. This is the UCPD-facing dimension of what is otherwise chiefly a data-protection/transparency problem.
findings.evidence_quote: collected emails at checkout under 'Receive order updates and service information'
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on the existing 'order updates and service information' notice for advertising. Present the commercial/marketing purpose transparently and separately at (or before) the point that any promotional use begins — e.g. a clear marketing opt-in describing the newsletter and the fact that contact details may be uploaded to social platforms for advertising and lookalike audiences — so the commercial intent is unmistakable to the average consumer. Coordinate this with the GDPR/ePrivacy lawful-basis fix, as the same disclosure serves both.

verdicts.notes: This campaign's central problems — repurposing checkout emails for advertising without a lawful basis, purpose limitation, and direct-marketing consent — sit primarily under GDPR/ePrivacy and are for that agent. Under the UCPD there is one genuine, secondary angle: the data was collected under an 'order updates and service information' framing that did not reveal the commercial/advertising intent, which engages the Art. 7 hidden-commercial-intent / misleading-omission concern. The blacklist point on persistent/unwanted solicitations (Annex I(26)) is not met on these facts, since a planned newsletter with an unsubscribe link is not harassment or continued contact after opt-out. No aggressive practices, false claims, fake reviews, or blacklisted tactics are present.

report.executive_summary: Your plan is to take emails that customers gave you at checkout for "order updates and service information," then upload that list to social platforms (as custom audiences and lookalikes) and send a weekly promotional newsletter. The problem is that none of these advertising uses were disclosed when the emails were collected, so you have no valid legal basis for them under GDPR — and email marketing plus platform uploads generally require specific opt-in consent that you don't have. "They're existing customers" is not enough to justify handing their data to social platforms or sending promotional email. The lookalike modelling also targets brand-new people you have no relationship with, compounding the risk. Under consumer-protection rules, collecting the emails under a service framing while intending to use them for advertising also hides your commercial intent. The unsubscribe link and the absence of sensitive data do not fix any of this. As planned, this campaign is likely to breach EU law and should not go live in its current form.
recommendations: Do not upload the existing checkout list to social platforms or send the promotional newsletter under the current 'order updates and service information' notice — pause the campaign until the legal basis is fixed.</br>

Collect fresh, separate, granular opt-in consent for (a) the promotional newsletter and (b) sharing/matching data with named social platforms for advertising — each worded clearly and distinct from the transactional service notice.
Drop or defer lookalike expansion: it targets people who never had a relationship with your brand and for whom you have no lawful basis or notice at all.

Update the privacy notice to disclose all marketing purposes, the legal basis, and the social-platform recipients, and present the commercial/marketing intent transparently before any promotional use begins (this satisfies both GDPR/ePrivacy and consumer-protection transparency).
Build a comprehensive suppression/opt-out mechanism that covers both email and platform-based advertising/profiling — not just an email unsubscribe link — and apply it across all channels.

Document a purpose-compatibility assessment and, where relying on any legitimate-interest element, a recorded balancing test before processing (noting legitimate interests cannot justify third-party ad-platform uploads).

campaign.title: TravelDeal adaptive pricing
campaign.text: An online travel agency's pricing engine adjusts displayed hotel prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index'). Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes. Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised; the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'. Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically. Prices are honoured as displayed and no urgency messaging is used.

detected_practices: personalised dynamic pricing based on device type and behaviour
behavioural profiling ('hesitation index' from time spent comparing)
device-based price discrimination (iOS users shown higher first quotes)
undisclosed personalisation of prices
misleading FAQ claim that prices 'reflect live market availability'
generic consent banner covering analytics cookies
triage.summary: An online travel agency personalises displayed hotel prices by ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and behavioural signals (a 'hesitation index'), systematically quoting returning iOS users higher prices. The personalisation is undisclosed and the FAQ misleadingly attributes prices to 'live market availability', while consent covers cookies only generically. The campaign is web-based, EU-wide, and aimed at general adult consumers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (device, visit history, dwell time) is processed covertly to personalise prices while the FAQ gives a false, misleading explanation. This directly breaches the requirement that personal data be processed fairly and transparently; covert data collection and misleading privacy information are the exact examples the provision names.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised; the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'.
findings.recommendation: Disclose clearly and prominently that displayed prices are personalised using device and behavioural data, and remove/correct the FAQ statement so it no longer misattributes prices solely to 'live market availability'.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated processing of personal data to analyse behaviour and economic sensitivity (the 'hesitation index' evaluating personal preferences/economic situation) is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4), which triggers the downstream GDPR obligations (transparency, lawful basis, Art. 22).
findings.evidence_quote: adjusts displayed hotel prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index')
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, its inputs and logic in the records of processing, and treat it as profiling for all consequent GDPR duties (notice, legal basis, rights).

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting personal data used for pricing, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes and legal basis and, specifically, of the existence of automated decision-making/profiling with meaningful information about the logic involved. The campaign provides none of this; the personalisation purpose is entirely hidden.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Provide layered Art. 13 information at data collection covering the pricing-personalisation purpose, legal basis, and the automated profiling logic and its consequences, linked from the pricing pages and consent flow.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be transparent, intelligible and not misleading. The FAQ statement is the opposite of transparent — it conceals the personalisation and misdescribes the basis of the price, defeating the intelligibility requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite consumer-facing explanations in clear, accurate language that reflects the actual processing, and surface the personalisation notice where prices are shown.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised pricing based on profiling needs a valid lawful basis. A generic analytics-cookie consent does not cover profiling-based price personalisation; consent for that specific purpose is absent and a legitimate-interest basis is unlikely to survive a balancing test given the covert, detriment-causing nature of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a specific lawful basis for pricing personalisation — realistically specific, informed consent — separate from analytics cookies, or discontinue the profiling-based price adjustment.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and informed. A generic banner bundling all processing under 'analytics cookies' cannot constitute specific, informed, unambiguous consent for behavioural profiling that drives prices, so any purported consent for the pricing purpose is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent so that profiling for price personalisation is a distinct, clearly described, granular opt-in that the user can refuse without losing access to standard pricing.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is relied on, the controller must be able to demonstrate it was given for the specific purpose and requests must be clearly distinguishable and in plain language. A generic analytics banner fails to demonstrate valid consent for the pricing-profiling purpose and offers no equivalent withdrawal mechanism for it.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Implement a consent management flow that records purpose-specific consent for pricing personalisation, presents it distinctly, and lets users withdraw it as easily as they gave it.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The prices are set by a solely automated engine that systematically and adversely differentiates a segment of individuals; dynamic pricing that materially affects the terms offered to a person can amount to an automated decision that similarly significantly affects them, requiring an Art. 22 exception plus safeguards, none of which are described.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the pricing constitutes an Art. 22(1) decision; if so, rely on explicit consent or another lawful exception and implement safeguards (meaningful information, right to human intervention and to contest the outcome), or apply meaningful human involvement so the decision is not solely automated.

verdicts.notes: The pricing engine processes personal data (device type, prior visits, dwell-time 'hesitation index') to evaluate and act on individuals' behaviour and economic characteristics — this is profiling under Art. 4(4). Because none of it is disclosed and the FAQ actively misattributes prices to 'live market availability', the transparency and fairness principle and Art. 12/13 obligations are breached, and the generic analytics-cookie banner cannot provide a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)/7/4(11)) for profiling-based pricing. Automated dynamic pricing that systematically raises quotes for a segment also engages Art. 22. Findings below.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The displayed hotel prices are automatically personalised (±12%) based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural 'hesitation index'. The fact that a price has been individualised by automated profiling is material information that the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision — it affects whether the price shown is a genuine market price or one adjusted against them. Concealing this personalisation (and burying data handling only in a generic analytics-cookie banner) is a misleading omission / hiding of material information under Art. 7, which is also expressly required to be disclosed under the Consumer Rights Directive as amended.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point where prices are displayed stating that the price has been personalised on the basis of automated decision-making/profiling (e.g. 'This price has been personalised based on your device and browsing behaviour'). Do not rely on the cookie banner to satisfy this; the disclosure must be specific, timely and unambiguous.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: This is an affirmative statement about the manner in which the price is calculated. It is false and deceptive: the ±12% variation is driven by the individual user's device type, prior visits and 'hesitation index', not by live market availability. Deceiving the average consumer about the price or manner of price calculation, causing them to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken (e.g. accepting a systematically inflated first quote), is a misleading action prohibited by Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Remove or correct the FAQ statement so it accurately describes how prices are set. If market availability is one factor, state honestly that prices are also individually personalised using device and behavioural signals; do not attribute personalised markups to 'live market availability'.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a fairness safety-net, the overall scheme — covertly exploiting behavioural signals (hesitation) and device type to systematically extract higher first quotes from identifiable returning users while concealing the practice and misdescribing it — is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer, engaging the general prohibition in Art. 5 to the extent conduct is not fully captured by Arts. 6 and 7.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the pricing engine and its disclosures meet professional-diligence standards: disclose personalisation transparently, avoid targeting users based on inferred hesitation/vulnerability to charge them more, and document the fairness of the pricing logic.

verdicts.notes: The campaign personalises displayed hotel prices by ±12% based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural 'hesitation index', systematically quoting returning iOS users higher first prices, without any disclosure. Under the UCPD this engages Art. 7 (failure to disclose material information about personalised pricing) and Art. 6 (the FAQ's affirmative claim that prices 'reflect live market availability' is false as to the manner of price calculation). The general prohibition in Art. 5 also applies as a safety net. No blacklist (Annex I) practice is triggered, since no false urgency/scarcity is used and prices are honoured as displayed.

report.executive_summary: Your "TravelDeal adaptive pricing" campaign uses a pricing engine that quietly adjusts displayed hotel prices by up to ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and a behavioural "hesitation index" — with returning iOS users systematically shown higher first quotes. The core problem is concealment: nothing tells users prices are personalised, and the FAQ actively misdescribes prices as reflecting "live market availability," which is false. This trips two separate EU regimes. Under consumer-protection law (UCPD), the hidden personalisation is a misleading omission and the FAQ claim is a misleading action, both of which can distort consumers' purchasing decisions. Under data-protection law (GDPR), the covert profiling breaches the fairness and transparency principles, lacks a valid lawful basis (a generic analytics-cookie banner does not cover pricing profiling), fails mandatory disclosure duties, and may engage the rules on automated decision-making. To your credit, no false urgency messaging is used and prices are honoured as displayed, so no "blacklisted" practice is triggered — but the campaign as designed is not compliant and carries real enforcement exposure. The verdict is high risk: the practice should not go live in its current form without significant changes.
recommendations: Stop misdescribing prices: remove or correct the FAQ statement that prices 'reflect live market availability'. If market availability is one input, say so honestly and disclose that prices are also personalised using device and behavioural signals (fixes UCPD Art. 6 and supports GDPR Art. 12).

Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point prices are shown, e.g. 'This price has been personalised based on your device and browsing behaviour.' Do not rely on the cookie banner to carry this message (fixes UCPD Art. 7 and GDPR Art. 13).

Establish and document a specific lawful basis for pricing personalisation — realistically a distinct, granular opt-in consent, separate from analytics cookies, that users can refuse without losing access to standard (non-personalised) pricing, and withdraw as easily as they gave it (GDPR Art. 6/7/4(11)).

Assess whether the automated pricing amounts to a decision with significant effects under GDPR Art. 22; if so, add safeguards (meaningful information about the logic, human intervention, right to contest) or introduce meaningful human involvement.

Re-examine the fairness of the logic itself: charging users more because they appear to hesitate or use a particular device may be seen as exploiting behavioural signals contrary to professional diligence, even if disclosed. Consider whether the 'hesitation index' driven markup should be retained at all (UCPD Art. 5).
Document the profiling operation, its inputs and logic in your records of processing, and conduct a data-protection impact assessment given the systematic, detriment-causing nature of the processing.
