findings.rationale: Personal data (device type, prior visits, hesitation index) is processed to alter the price each user sees, yet this is entirely hidden and the FAQ affirmatively misattributes prices to 'live market availability'. This is covert, unfair and misleading processing that breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised; the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'.
findings.recommendation: Clearly disclose on the site that displayed prices are personalised using automated processing of device and behavioural data, and correct the FAQ so it no longer misrepresents the price-determination logic.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (economic behaviour, preferences, decision hesitancy) squarely meets the definition of profiling, which is the trigger for the transparency and Art. 22 obligations below.
findings.evidence_quote: adjusts displayed hotel prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index')
findings.recommendation: Recognise the pricing engine as profiling and ensure the downstream GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 22 safeguards) are met.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data used for profiling/automated decision-making the controller must inform the data subject of the purposes, lawful basis and, in particular, the existence of automated decision-making including meaningful information about the logic involved. None of this is provided; users are unaware their data drives the price shown.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear privacy notice at the point of data collection covering the personalisation purpose, lawful basis, and the existence and logic of the automated pricing decision, plus the consequences (price variation) for the individual.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The consent obtained is limited to generic analytics cookies and does not cover profiling for price personalisation, so there is no valid consent for that purpose. No other lawful basis is apparent, and legitimate interest would be hard to sustain given the covert, potentially detrimental price manipulation. The processing therefore likely lacks a valid lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis specifically for pricing personalisation; if relying on consent, obtain separate, specific consent for that purpose, or conduct and document a defensible legitimate-interests assessment (unlikely to succeed while covert).

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Any consent purporting to authorise the pricing personalisation is not specific or informed: it is bundled into a generic analytics-cookie banner that does not mention personalised pricing, failing the standard for valid consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Unbundle consent so that pricing personalisation is a distinct, clearly described, opt-in choice separate from analytics cookies, using plain language about what the personalisation does.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information given to users is neither transparent nor intelligible about the actual processing — it is inaccurate and hides the personalisation, contrary to the requirement for concise, transparent, intelligible information in clear and plain language.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite user-facing explanations (FAQ, banner, privacy notice) to describe the personalisation accurately and accessibly.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Prices are set by a solely automated process based on profiling, systematically disadvantaging certain users (e.g. returning iOS users). Adaptive pricing that materially affects the terms offered can constitute an automated decision with similarly significant effects, requiring a valid basis (explicit consent/contract) and safeguards such as the right to human intervention and to contest the outcome — none of which are provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the pricing decision is 'solely automated' with significant effect; if so, secure an Art. 22-compliant basis (explicit consent) and implement safeguards (transparency, human review on request, ability to contest), or introduce meaningful human involvement / remove the significant differential.

verdicts.notes: The adaptive pricing engine processes personal data (device type, prior-visit history, browsing behaviour/"hesitation index") to evaluate individuals' economic behaviour and set the prices they see — this is profiling that feeds an automated pricing decision. The processing is covert: the site gives no indication prices are personalised and the FAQ misattributes prices to "live market availability", while the consent banner only generically covers analytics cookies. This breaches the fairness/transparency principle and the Art. 13 information duty, lacks a demonstrable lawful basis/valid consent for the personalisation, and engages the Art. 22 automated-decision safeguards.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The pricing engine adjusts displayed prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural 'hesitation index', yet this personalisation is not disclosed anywhere. Whether a displayed price is individually personalised through automated profiling is material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision; omitting it (and providing it in no timely manner at all) is a misleading omission. The Consumer Rights Directive (as amended) requires disclosure of personalised pricing based on automated decision-making, reinforcing that this is material.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point where the price is displayed stating that the price shown has been personalised on the basis of automated processing of the user's data (e.g. device, browsing history), and provide accessible information on the main parameters used.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers deception regarding the price or the manner of its calculation. Prices are in fact driven substantially by device type and behavioural profiling (with returning iOS users systematically shown higher quotes), not by 'live market availability'. Affirmatively attributing prices to market availability is false/deceptive about how the price is calculated and is liable to cause consumers to accept a higher personalised quote they would otherwise question or reject — a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Remove or correct the FAQ statement so it accurately describes how prices are set, expressly acknowledging that displayed prices may be adjusted based on automated profiling of the individual user in addition to any market-availability factors.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages two UCPD prohibitions. First, prices are personalised via automated profiling (device type, prior visits, 'hesitation index') with no disclosure — a misleading omission of material information under Art. 7, since consumers need to know displayed prices are individually tailored to make an informed transactional decision. Second, the FAQ statement attributing prices to 'live market availability' is a misleading action under Art. 6, as it actively deceives about the true manner of price calculation (which is behavioural/device-based, not market-driven). No blacklisted practice is clearly present (notably, the campaign expressly uses no urgency messaging, so Annex I point 7 does not apply).

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a pricing engine that quietly adjusts displayed hotel prices by up to ±12% based on each visitor's device type, prior visits and how long they spend comparing (a "hesitation index"), with returning iOS users systematically shown higher first quotes. The core problem is that none of this is disclosed: the site gives no indication prices are personalised, and the FAQ actively tells users prices "reflect live market availability" — which is not the real driver. That combination triggers two sets of EU law problems. Under consumer protection law (UCPD), hiding that prices are individually personalised is a misleading omission, and the "live market availability" claim is a misleading action about how prices are calculated. Under data protection law (GDPR), profiling users to set their price without transparency, without a valid lawful basis (the consent banner only covers generic analytics cookies), and without the safeguards required for automated decisions is likely unlawful. The fact that prices are honoured and no urgency messaging is used helps, but does not cure the transparency and lawful-basis failures. Overall risk is high and the campaign should not go live in its current form. The good news: most issues are fixable primarily through honest, prominent disclosure and proper consent, rather than abandoning personalisation entirely.
recommendations: Correct the FAQ immediately: remove the 'live market availability' claim and accurately state that displayed prices may be adjusted based on automated profiling of the individual user (device, browsing history/behaviour). This false statement is the clearest and most easily remedied violation (misleading action).

Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point the price is shown stating the price has been personalised using automated processing of the user's data, with accessible information on the main parameters used (device type, prior visits, hesitation index).
Obtain separate, specific, opt-in consent for pricing personalisation, unbundled from the generic analytics-cookie banner; do not rely on the existing banner, which does not cover this purpose.

Provide a proper privacy notice at the point of data collection (GDPR Art. 13) covering the personalisation purpose, lawful basis, the existence and logic of the automated pricing decision, and the price-variation consequences for the individual.

Assess whether the pricing decision is 'solely automated' with a significant effect under GDPR Art. 22; if so, secure explicit consent and implement safeguards (human review on request, ability to contest), or introduce meaningful human involvement.

Review the systematic disadvantage to returning iOS users specifically — a persistent higher quote for an identifiable group heightens both fairness and discrimination-type concerns; consider whether this differential can be justified or should be removed.

Document a defensible lawful basis and, if relying on legitimate interests, complete a formal legitimate-interests assessment — but note this is unlikely to succeed while the processing remains covert, so transparency must come first.
Do not launch the campaign in its current covert form; treat honest disclosure and valid consent as go-live prerequisites.

campaign.title: StayFinder availability badges
campaign.text: Hotel listings show red badges: 'Only 1 room left!' and 'In high demand — booked 27 times today'. The room count is technically true for the specific discounted rate class shown, but the hotel has 40+ rooms available at other rates on the same dates; nothing clarifies the count is per rate class. The 'booked 27 times' figure counts all bookings site-wide for the city, not the hotel. Badges are injected by the trader's own site, not a third-party platform.

misleading scarcity framing (count applies only to a specific rate class, not overall availability)
social proof / popularity claim ('booked 27 times today')
misleading popularity metric (figure counts site-wide city bookings, not the specific hotel)
urgency/pressure badges on hotel listings

Badges are first-party (trader's own site), so no third-party platform/DSA intermediary role is engaged; the core issue is misleading/deceptive commercial practices (scarcity and false popularity claims) falling squarely under the UCPD.

The 'Only 1 room left' count is technically true only for a specific discounted rate class (40+ rooms available at other rates) without clarification, and the 'booked 27 times today' figure aggregates all site-wide city bookings rather than the specific hotel — both creating potentially misleading impressions of scarcity and demand. Badges are injected by the trader's own site.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits in all circumstances falsely stating that a product is available only on particular terms for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. The badge presents overall scarcity ('Only 1 room left!') when 40+ rooms are in fact available at other rates on the same dates; the '1 left' figure relates only to a single discounted rate class and nothing discloses this qualification. The badge is engineered to create urgency and pressure an immediate booking, giving consumers a false picture of availability. Because the impression conveyed to the average consumer is false even though the underlying number is technically true for one rate class, this falls within the point 7 blacklist and requires no case-by-case distortion test.
findings.evidence_quote: Only 1 room left!
findings.recommendation: Either remove the scarcity badge or make it accurate and unambiguous: scope the count to overall availability, or clearly state it applies only to the specific rate class shown (e.g. 'Only 1 room left at this discounted rate — other rates available'). Ensure any scarcity claim reflects genuine, verifiable stock for the option the consumer is viewing.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices containing false information or deceiving the average consumer about the main characteristics of the product (including its popularity/demand) that cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken. The '27 times today' figure counts all bookings site-wide for the city, not the specific hotel, yet is displayed on the individual hotel listing so as to represent demand for that hotel. This is materially false and inflates perceived demand to pressure booking, a classic misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: In high demand — booked 27 times today
findings.recommendation: Only display booking/demand counts that are true for the specific hotel and time period stated. If citywide activity is shown, label it explicitly as such and do not attach it to an individual listing in a way that implies hotel-specific demand. Remove the badge unless the metric is accurate and clearly scoped.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 makes a practice misleading where it omits or hides material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision, or provides it in an unclear, ambiguous manner. The material fact that '1 room left' refers only to a discounted rate class (while 40+ rooms remain available at other rates) is omitted, causing the average consumer to overestimate scarcity and act under false pressure. Even if not caught by the point 7 blacklist, the omission independently renders the practice misleading.
findings.evidence_quote: nothing clarifies the count is per rate class
findings.recommendation: Add clear, prominent qualifying information at the point the badge appears, stating that the availability count relates only to the specific rate class and that other rates/rooms may be available, so the consumer is not misled about actual availability.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer. Combining a false-impression scarcity badge with a false demand badge, styled as red urgency alerts, is contrary to the diligent standard expected of a booking platform and is likely to distort booking decisions. This reinforces the more specific findings above and provides a residual basis for unfairness.
findings.evidence_quote: red badges: 'Only 1 room left!' and 'In high demand — booked 27 times today'
findings.recommendation: Adopt an internal substantiation policy ensuring all urgency/scarcity/popularity indicators are accurate, scoped to the specific listing and option shown, and verifiable before display; audit existing badge logic against professional-diligence standards.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys two urgency/social-proof badges on hotel listings that create false or misleading impressions of scarcity and demand. The "Only 1 room left!" badge is literally true only for one discounted rate class while 40+ rooms are available at other rates on the same dates, with nothing clarifying this — engaging the Annex I point 7 scarcity blacklist together with misleading action (Art. 6) and misleading omission (Art. 7). The "booked 27 times today" badge is straightforwardly false as applied to the hotel (it aggregates site-wide city bookings), a misleading action under Art. 6. Both are designed to elicit an immediate transactional decision and should be corrected or removed.

report.executive_summary: Your StayFinder campaign uses two red urgency badges on hotel listings: "Only 1 room left!" and "In high demand — booked 27 times today". Both create false impressions for consumers and carry serious EU consumer-protection risk. The "Only 1 room left!" badge is only true for a single discounted rate class while the hotel actually has 40+ rooms available at other rates on the same dates — and nothing tells the consumer this. That triggers the UCPD Annex I "blacklist" of banned practices, which is prohibited outright with no room for a defence. The "booked 27 times today" figure is worse still: it counts all bookings across the whole city, not this hotel, so it is simply false as displayed. Together these are engineered to pressure an immediate booking and are likely to be treated as unfair, misleading practices by regulators. Data-protection, AI Act and platform (DSA) rules were not engaged. This is a high-severity issue that should be fixed before the campaign runs.
recommendations: Immediately stop displaying the 'booked 27 times today' badge on individual hotel listings — the number is citywide and false as applied to a specific hotel. Only show demand figures that are genuinely true for that hotel and time period, and label the scope clearly.

Fix or remove the 'Only 1 room left!' badge: it must reflect genuine overall availability, or explicitly state it applies only to the specific discounted rate class (e.g. 'Only 1 room left at this rate — other rates available'). As currently framed it falls within the outright-banned scarcity practices under UCPD Annex I point 7.
Add clear, prominent qualifying text wherever availability counts appear, so consumers understand what the number actually covers (rate class vs. whole hotel).
Introduce an internal substantiation policy: every urgency, scarcity and popularity indicator must be accurate, scoped to the exact listing/option shown, and verifiable before it is displayed.

Audit the existing badge-injection logic across all listings against professional-diligence standards, since these badges are generated by your own site and the same flaws likely affect other listings.

campaign.title: DentaBright 'real smiles' video wall
campaign.text: A teeth-whitening brand's landing page features a 'Real customers, real smiles' video wall: twelve testimonial clips ('I tried everything, only DentaBright worked'). All twelve are paid actors reading scripts; two never used the product. On-screen text shows first names and cities. A small footer note says 'individual results may vary'; nothing indicates the testimonials are dramatised. Product claims themselves are within the substantiated range.

detected_practices: fake/undisclosed testimonials (paid actors presented as 'real customers')
false representation that testimonials come from genuine consumers
endorsements from actors who never used the product
dramatised content not disclosed as such
buried/insufficient 'individual results may vary' disclaimer
display of testimonial first names and cities (personal data of depicted individuals)
triage.summary: A teeth-whitening brand runs a 'Real customers, real smiles' testimonial video wall where all twelve endorsers are paid actors reading scripts, two of whom never used the product, presented as genuine customers with first names and cities and no disclosure that the content is dramatised. While the product claims are substantiated, the misrepresentation of paid actors as real users and the missing dramatisation disclosure raise clear misleading-practice concerns. Personal data (names/locations) of depicted individuals is displayed; no generative AI or personalised targeting is declared or apparent.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing

findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices. ... A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed. Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Decouple member pricing from marketing/profiling consent: offer equivalent member benefits regardless of whether the data subject consents to profiling, sharing or targeting. Reinstate a genuine data-minimal membership option and ensure withdrawal of marketing consent does not terminate membership or remove core benefits.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Each processing purpose needs a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Since consent here is invalid (bundled and non-free), there is no lawful basis for the profiling, cross-platform targeting and wide-scale data sharing, rendering that processing unlawful. Legitimate interest is unlikely to support sharing with 60 partners for ad targeting given the intrusiveness and data subject expectations.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid, purpose-specific legal basis for each processing operation. Rely on validly obtained, granular consent for profiling and third-party ad targeting; conduct a documented balancing test if attempting to rely on legitimate interests for any narrow operational purpose.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing purchase history to evaluate personal preferences, behaviour and economic situation and target tailored offers constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This triggers the full set of profiling obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights, Art. 22 safeguards).
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling activity, its logic and consequences; ensure it rests on valid granular consent and that data subjects can object and are informed of the profiling at collection.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: If eligibility for member prices or the specific offers shown is determined solely by automated profiling in a way that produces significant effects (e.g., who gets which price/offer), Art. 22 restrictions and safeguards apply. As described, personalised pricing/offer allocation driven by profiling may amount to automated decision-making without disclosed safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples)
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether pricing/offer eligibility is decided solely by automated means. If so, ensure an Art. 22 exception applies with safeguards (right to human intervention, to contest, meaningful information about the logic), and disclose any personalised pricing to affected individuals.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right under Art. 21(2) to object to direct marketing and related profiling at any time. Because objecting/withdrawing here cancels membership entirely, the right to object is effectively penalised and obstructed rather than facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy, consequence-free mechanism to object to direct marketing and marketing profiling at any time, without loss of membership or core benefits, and honour objections immediately.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is engaged. Quietly removing the privacy-friendly tier and forcing an all-or-nothing consent leverages the data subject's reliance on member pricing to extract consent — an unfair processing design that undermines genuine choice.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Process data fairly: give clear, prominent notice of the change, restore a genuine no-profiling option, and avoid designs that coerce consent through loss of essential benefits.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at the point of collection the controller disclose purposes, legal basis, recipients (or categories), retention and profiling information. A single combined consent with an unnamed set of 60 partners suggests recipients and purposes are not specifically and transparently disclosed at sign-up.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners'
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at enrolment identifying the categories/identities of the 60 partners, each purpose, legal basis, retention periods, profiling logic and data-subject rights in clear, accessible language.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Consent-related information must be concise, transparent, intelligible and use clear, plain language. Framing the consent decision purely as 'Say YES to savings!' emphasises benefit while obscuring the data-processing implications, functioning as a consent dark pattern that undermines transparent, informed choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Present the consent request neutrally and separately from promotional framing, with balanced YES/NO options of equal prominence and a plain-language summary of what data is processed, by whom and why.

verdicts.notes: The relaunch structures consent in a way that almost certainly fails the GDPR standard of freely given, specific, granular and informed consent. A single combined consent covers four distinct processing purposes (profiling, location push, sharing with 60 partners, off-platform ad targeting), and access to member prices — plus continued membership — is conditioned on accepting all of it, with the previous data-free tier removed and consent withdrawal cancelling membership. This engages Art. 4(11), Art. 7, Art. 6(1), Art. 4(4)/Art. 22 profiling, Art. 21 objection, and the fairness/transparency principle. The pressure framing 'Say YES to savings!' compounds the consent-validity problem as a consent dark pattern.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The bundled consent authorises behavioural profiling ('purchase-history profiling') that feeds 'ad targeting on external platforms'. The supervisor triage flags that minors are potentially reached, and grocery-shopper audiences on general-audience platforms will include under-18s. DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients the provider is aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Where the supermarket runs profiled ads across external online platforms without excluding minors, the campaign risks placing profiling-based ads before minors in breach of this prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Exclude minors from all profiling-based ad targeting delivered on external online platforms. Configure platform ad tools to suppress behavioural/profiled ad delivery to any audience reasonably likely to include under-18s, and use only non-profiled contextual placements where minors may be reached. Document the age-exclusion measures applied to each external-platform campaign.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: When the loyalty campaign's offers are delivered as advertisements on online platforms, DSA Art. 26(1) requires that each ad be clearly identifiable as an ad, disclose on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters (here: purchase-history profiling, location) and how to change them. The bundled, opaque consent covering '60 retail media partners' and cross-platform targeting indicates the underlying targeting parameters are not transparently surfaced to recipients as Art. 26(1) requires.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad placed on an online platform is properly labelled as advertising with clear advertiser/payer identity, and that the platform's ad-transparency controls expose the main targeting parameters (profiling of purchase history, location) and an easy route to change them. Keep the targeting logic simple enough to be meaningfully disclosed rather than hidden behind a blanket consent.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Purchase-history profiling shared across 60 retail media partners for cross-platform ad targeting creates a real risk that special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 (e.g. health inferences from purchases of medicines, pregnancy or dietary products, or religious/ethnic dietary items) is used — directly or by inference — to target platform advertisements. DSA Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits presenting platform ads based on profiling using such special-category data, regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners'
findings.recommendation: Contractually and technically prevent any purchase-history-derived segments that could reveal or proxy health, religion, ethnicity or other Art. 9 categories from being used to target advertisements on online platforms. Apply proxy-attribute filtering and audit the retail-media partner segments used for platform ad delivery.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The confirm-shaming framing, single bundled consent, quiet removal of the data-free tier, and 'decline = lose all benefits / withdrawal cancels membership' design are textbook dark-pattern/manipulative-interface tactics. However, DSA Art. 25 only binds providers of online platforms in the design of their platform interfaces; a supermarket's first-party loyalty app and email flows are generally not an 'online platform' under DSA Art. 3(i), so this conduct falls to be assessed primarily under UCPD (unfair/aggressive practice) and GDPR (freely-given, granular consent). Flagged here for context only.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Treat this conduct as the responsibility of the UCPD and GDPR reviewers. If any part of the enrolment flow is presented within an online platform interface the supermarket operates as a platform provider, revisit Art. 25 directly; otherwise no DSA Art. 25 action is required.

verdicts.notes: The DSA governs providers of online platforms and their interfaces; a supermarket's first-party loyalty app and email are generally not "online platforms" under DSA Art. 3(i), so the bundled-consent/confirm-shaming conduct is primarily a UCPD/GDPR matter rather than a direct DSA Art. 25 breach. However, the campaign explicitly extends to "ad targeting on external platforms," which brings the advertiser within the reach of DSA advertising rules on those platforms. The main DSA-relevant risks are profiling-based ad targeting potentially reaching minors (Art. 28(2)) and the transparency/targeting-parameter obligations for platform ads (Art. 26). The dark-pattern flag is noted for context but is not the DSA's primary hook here.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of a take-it-or-leave-it bundled consent, quiet removal of the pre-existing data-free membership tier, membership cancellation on consent withdrawal, and the positively-framed 'Say YES to savings!' signage constitutes a deceptive/manipulative choice architecture (dark pattern). It is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the average grocery shopper's economic decision on whether to join and share data, because the design masks the real trade-off (data for discounts) and penalises the privacy-preserving choice. Under the UCPD, dark patterns are governed by Art. 5.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Reinstate a genuine no-profiling membership option that retains member pricing, present the data-sharing choice neutrally (no confirm-shaming or loss-framing), decouple consent withdrawal from loss of membership, and avoid one-sided 'Say YES' framing that obscures the data cost of the offer.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision — that the advertised 'member prices' are conditioned on extensive profiling and data sharing with 60 partners and off-platform ad targeting, and that declining any element forfeits ALL member prices — is bundled behind a single 'Say YES to savings!' message. Presenting the offer as a straightforward saving while hiding or obscuring its true condition and scope is a misleading omission of material information and of the commercial/data-monetisation intent of the enrolment.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples) now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Disclose clearly and prominently, at the point the offer is presented, that member prices are contingent on data profiling and sharing with named categories/number of third parties for advertising, and provide granular, itemised information before enrolment rather than a single combined 'yes'.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making the exercise of a contractual/legal right (declining or withdrawing data consent) trigger the onerous consequence of losing all member pricing and cancelling membership entirely can amount to undue influence and an onerous barrier to exercising rights, which are aggressive-practice factors under Arts. 8-9. By exploiting the consumer's position (needing everyday grocery savings), the all-or-nothing penalty may significantly impair freedom of choice and push consumers to accept data terms they would otherwise refuse.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices. ... Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Remove the penalty structure: allow consumers to decline individual processing purposes and to withdraw consent without losing membership or member pricing, so that exercising data rights carries no disproportionate detriment.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The 'up to 40% off staples' price-advantage claim must be genuine and substantiated; if the reference/prior prices are not accurate or the '40%' applies only to marginal items, the claim of a specific price advantage could deceive the average consumer as to the existence/extent of the advantage. On the facts provided this cannot be confirmed, so it is flagged as a risk requiring substantiation.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples)
findings.recommendation: Ensure the 'up to 40%' claim is verifiably true, that a representative range of staples achieves meaningful reductions, and that price-reduction references comply with prior-price rules; retain evidence substantiating the advertised discount range.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch does not appear to trigger any Annex I blacklisted per-se prohibitions (no false urgency, false 'free', fake reviews or ceasing-trade claims on the facts given). However, the overall design — conditioning all member pricing on a single, non-negotiable bundled data consent, quietly removing the previous data-free tier, cancelling membership on consent withdrawal, and framing it as 'Say YES to savings!' — engages the UCPD general unfairness and misleading-omission provisions. The consumer is steered by a manipulative choice architecture and is not clearly told that the 'savings' are effectively paid for with far-reaching data sharing (60 partners, off-platform targeting). Note that the freely-given-consent question itself is primarily a GDPR matter; the findings below address only the commercial-practice/deceptive-design and material-information dimensions.

report.executive_summary: This campaign relaunches the SuperSave loyalty club so that member prices (up to 40% off staples) require accepting a single, all-or-nothing consent bundling four very different data uses: purchase-history profiling, location push offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and ad targeting on external platforms. The previous data-free tier was quietly removed, and withdrawing consent cancels membership entirely. This design almost certainly breaks EU consent rules — consent must be freely given, specific, granular and withdrawable without penalty, and bundling plus "decline = lose all savings" fails that standard on multiple counts. Independently, the same design is likely an unfair/misleading commercial practice: the "Say YES to savings!" framing obscures that the discounts are effectively paid for with far-reaching data sharing, and penalising the privacy-preserving choice can amount to an aggressive practice. Because the campaign extends to ad targeting on external platforms, it also picks up DSA obligations — most seriously the ban on profiling-based ads to minors and restrictions on using special-category data — plus ad transparency duties. The AI Act does not apply. Overall this is a high-risk campaign that should not launch in its current form; the core problems (bundled consent, no data-free option, penalty on withdrawal, one-sided framing) are structural and need redesign, not tweaks.
recommendations: Unbundle the consent: give members separate, independently toggleable opt-ins for each purpose (purchase-history profiling, location push, each category/third party of data sharing, off-platform ad targeting) so they can accept some and decline others.

Decouple member pricing and continued membership from marketing/profiling consent — reinstate a genuine data-minimal membership tier that keeps the discounts, and ensure withdrawing consent never cancels membership or removes core benefits.

Replace the 'Say YES to savings!' framing with a neutral, balanced consent screen (equal-prominence YES/NO, no confirm-shaming or loss-framing) and disclose clearly, before enrolment, that discounts involve profiling and sharing with third parties for advertising.

Provide a layered privacy notice at sign-up identifying the 60 partners (or their categories), each purpose, legal basis, retention periods, profiling logic and data-subject rights, and an easy, consequence-free way to object to direct marketing at any time.

For any ads served on external online platforms: exclude minors from all profiling-based targeting, block use of purchase-history segments that could reveal or proxy special-category data (health, religion, ethnicity), and ensure ads carry proper labelling and expose their main targeting parameters.
Confirm whether pricing or offer eligibility is decided solely by automated profiling; if so, put Article 22 safeguards and disclosures in place.
Substantiate the 'up to 40% off staples' claim with accurate prior-price references and a representative range of discounted staples, and retain the evidence.
Do not launch in the current form — treat the bundled consent, removed data-free tier and withdrawal penalty as blocking issues to be redesigned before go-live.

campaign.title: SuperSave club enrolment revamp
campaign.text: A supermarket relaunches its loyalty club: member prices (up to 40% off staples) now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms. Declining any element means losing all member prices. In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'. A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed. Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.

detected_practices: combined/bundled consent for multiple processing purposes
purchase-history profiling
location-based push offers
data sharing with 60 retail media partners
cross-platform ad targeting
conditioning member prices (up to 40% off staples) on consent
loss of all benefits for declining any element
withdrawal of consent cancels membership (detriment/penalty for withdrawal)
quiet removal of prior data-free tier
persuasive in-store signage ('Say YES to savings!')
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult grocery shoppers, but supermarket loyalty programmes and in-store/app/email channels are broadly accessible, so minors could plausibly be reached and enrolled. Key issue is validity of consent (freely given, granular, unbundled) given the take-it-or-leave-it structure and penalty for withdrawal. AI declared as not used; personalisation/targeting confirmed via purchase-history profiling and cross-platform ad targeting.
triage.summary: A supermarket loyalty relaunch that conditions member prices on a single bundled consent covering profiling, location-based offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and external ad targeting, with declining any element or withdrawing consent stripping all benefits/membership. A prior data-free tier was quietly removed. Consent freeness, bundling, and the detriment for withdrawal raise significant GDPR concerns, alongside potentially misleading/aggressive practices under UCPD and cross-platform ad targeting engaging the DSA.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Art. 4(11) requires consent to be specific and granular, and expressly states that bundled consent does not qualify. Forcing four distinct processing purposes into one indivisible 'YES' means data subjects cannot consent separately to each purpose, so no valid consent exists for any of them.
findings.evidence_quote: now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Unbundle the consent into separate, independently toggleable opt-ins for (1) purchase-history profiling, (2) location-based push, (3) sharing with partners, and (4) external ad targeting, each defaulting to off and each refusable without losing others.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that consent not be conditional on unnecessary consent and that it be freely given. Conditioning up to 40% price advantages on accepting marketing/profiling that is unnecessary to provide the loyalty membership creates an imbalance and detriment that makes the consent not freely given, especially given the removal of the prior data-free tier.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices.
findings.recommendation: Decouple core membership pricing benefits from optional data-processing consents; offer members the same essential prices whether or not they accept profiling/sharing, or reinstate a functionally equivalent data-minimal tier.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(3) requires withdrawal of consent to be as easy as giving it and to carry no detriment; consent is not freely given if withdrawal is penalised. Cancelling the entire membership on withdrawal is a clear detriment that renders the original consent invalid and obstructs the withdrawal right.
findings.evidence_quote: Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Ensure withdrawing any data-processing consent stops only that processing and does not terminate membership or strip core benefits; provide a simple, penalty-free withdrawal mechanism in-app and in-store.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Art. 6(1) requires a valid lawful basis. Because the consent relied upon is bundled and coerced (Arts. 4(11)/7), it cannot serve as a valid basis, leaving profiling, partner-sharing and cross-platform ad targeting without any lawful basis for processing.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Re-establish a valid lawful basis: obtain granular freely-given consent per purpose, or document a legitimate-interest assessment where genuinely applicable (noting consent is generally required for third-party sharing and cross-platform ad targeting).

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a) is engaged: quietly removing the only privacy-preserving option and steering members into extensive data processing without prominent explanation is an unfair and non-transparent processing arrangement.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Communicate the tier change transparently, explain the data implications clearly, and avoid leveraging the loss of the data-free option to pressure consent.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that recipients of personal data, purposes, legal basis, retention and profiling information be provided at the point of collection. A generic reference to '60 retail media partners' likely fails to identify recipients (or categories) and the profiling logic with sufficient specificity.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners'
findings.recommendation: Provide at sign-up a clear, accessible privacy notice naming the recipients (or specific categories), each purpose, retention periods, and the profiling logic, with a linked full list of the 60 partners.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing purchase history to evaluate personal preferences and behaviour for targeted offers meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling, which triggers the associated transparency, lawful-basis and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Treat purchase-history analysis as profiling and ensure it is covered by valid consent, transparency and an easy objection route.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) gives data subjects an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling, at any time. The all-or-nothing structure that cancels membership on withdrawal effectively obstructs this right and provides no standalone marketing opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, standalone, penalty-free opt-out from direct-marketing profiling and communications that does not affect membership or pricing, and honour it immediately.

verdicts.notes: This loyalty relaunch presents serious GDPR consent-validity problems. A single combined consent bundling four distinct purposes (profiling, location push, sharing with 60 partners, external ad targeting), conditioning substantial member discounts on acceptance, removal of the prior data-free tier, and cancelling membership on withdrawal, all undermine the "freely given", "specific" and "as easy to withdraw" requirements of Arts. 4(11) and 7. Transparency (Arts. 12/13) around the 60 recipients and profiling, and the right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21) are also engaged. Personal-data processing is central, so GDPR clearly applies.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign runs profiled advertising on third-party external platforms based on purchase-history profiling. Where those ads are presented on online platforms, each ad must be identifiable in real time as an advertisement, disclose on whose behalf and who paid for it, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters used to select the recipient and how to change them. The campaign describes cross-platform ad targeting driven by purchase-history profiling but gives no indication that these transparency elements will be provided.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Ensure every ad delivered on external online platforms is clearly labelled as an advertisement identifying the supermarket as advertiser/payer, and expose the main targeting parameters (e.g. purchase-history-based segmentation) with a link allowing recipients to change them, in line with the platform's DSA Art. 26(1) ad-transparency tooling.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Loyalty enrolment through in-store, app and email channels is broadly accessible, and minors can plausibly be enrolled and reached. DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits presenting profiling-based advertisements to recipients the provider is aware with reasonable certainty are minors. Since the campaign performs purchase-history profiling and cross-platform ad targeting, any such profiled ads reaching enrolled minors would breach this ban, and the platform must maintain a high level of privacy/safety for minors.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: grocery shoppers, general adult
findings.recommendation: Suppress all profiling-based ad delivery for any member who is, or is reasonably likely to be, a minor; implement age assurance at enrolment or exclude under-18 segments from external-platform behavioural targeting, and configure external platform campaigns to disable profiling-based ads to minors.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: If the supermarket's app is treated as an online-platform interface within DSA scope, the combined 'Say YES to savings!' consent design — bundling multiple processing purposes into a single accept, framing declining as loss of all savings, and removing the previous data-free option — gives disproportionate prominence to acceptance and pressures a non-free choice, characteristic of a dark pattern prohibited under Art. 25. Applicability is uncertain because a first-party loyalty app may not qualify as an 'online platform', and the same conduct is primarily caught by UCPD/GDPR.
findings.evidence_quote: Say YES to savings!
findings.recommendation: Redesign the app consent interface so accept/decline options carry equal visual prominence, unbundle the consent purposes into granular toggles, and avoid confirm-shaming framing; confirm whether the app falls within DSA online-platform scope, otherwise rely on the parallel UCPD/GDPR assessment.

verdicts.notes: The DSA binds providers of online platforms; the supermarket here is primarily an advertiser/first-party controller operating in-store, via its own app and email, so most conduct (bundled consent, withdrawal penalty, quiet tier removal) is better addressed under GDPR/UCPD. However, the campaign explicitly extends to "ad targeting on external platforms," which brings the third-party platform ad delivery within scope of DSA advertising-transparency and profiling-restriction rules. The main DSA exposure is: (1) ads delivered on external platforms must meet Art. 26(1) transparency; (2) profiling-based ads must not reach recipients reasonably certain to be minors (Art. 28), which is a live risk given the broadly accessible loyalty channels; and (3) the app's "Say YES to savings!" consent interface could constitute a dark pattern (Art. 25) if the app qualifies as a platform interface. Findings are medium/low because DSA applicability depends on the external platforms and on whether the supermarket's app meets the online-platform definition.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The membership 'savings' are, in reality, conditioned on the consumer surrendering purchase-history profiling, location tracking, data sharing with 60 retail media partners and cross-platform ad targeting. Framing the offer purely as 'savings' while hiding the material nature of the transaction — that broad data commodification is the price of the discount, and that declining any single element forfeits all member prices — omits information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision and obscures the commercial intent of the data collection. That is a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'
findings.recommendation: At the point of enrolment (signage, app screen, email), clearly and prominently disclose the full trade-off in plain language: which data is collected, that it is shared with 60 named categories/partners, that it is used for external ad targeting, and that these are the condition of the discount. Do not present the offer as costless 'savings' when it carries a data cost; separate the price advantage from the data terms.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Making the loss of all member prices (up to 40% off staples — economically significant for everyday grocery essentials) the consequence of declining any single data element, and cancelling membership entirely upon withdrawal, uses the trader's position to apply pressure/undue influence and imposes an onerous, disproportionate barrier to exercising the consumer's choice and withdrawal rights. This can significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and push them into accepting profiling they would not otherwise accept, engaging Arts. 8-9 (aggressive practice / undue influence) and the dark-patterns concept (confirm-shaming, obstruction of withdrawal).
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices ... Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Decouple the core price benefit from optional data purposes so that declining profiling, partner-sharing or external ad targeting does not strip away membership or all savings. Ensure withdrawing consent to a given processing purpose does not cancel membership or unrelated benefits, and make withdrawal as easy and consequence-free as giving consent.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Quietly removing the previously available data-free tier and restructuring the programme so that any refusal forfeits all benefits departs from professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average grocery shopper by leaving no genuine non-data alternative. As a general fairness safety-net, Art. 5 captures this bundled, take-it-or-leave-it design where the specific misleading/aggressive limbs may not fully cover the manipulative overall structure.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Reinstate a genuine equivalent-value membership option that does not require accepting non-essential profiling/partner-sharing, and communicate any material change to the programme's terms transparently rather than removing the data-free tier silently.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch engages UCPD mainly through its design and framing rather than a clear-cut blacklisted practice. The "Say YES to savings!" messaging omits the material nature of the trade-off (data shared with 60 retail media partners and external ad targeting), engaging Art. 7 (misleading omission of commercial intent/nature of the transaction). The take-it-or-leave-it structure — losing all member prices for declining any element, withdrawal cancelling membership, and quiet removal of the prior data-free tier — uses the loss of significant grocery savings as leverage and imposes an onerous detriment on exercising choice, raising undue-influence/aggressive-practice concerns (Arts. 8-9) and engaging the general fairness safety-net (Art. 5) as a consent dark pattern. No Annex I blacklist item is squarely triggered on the facts as described; the consent-validity core is primarily a GDPR matter handled elsewhere.

report.executive_summary: The SuperSave club relaunch ties member discounts (up to 40% off staples) to a single all-or-nothing "YES" that bundles four separate data uses: purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and cross-platform ad targeting. As designed, this almost certainly breaches GDPR because the consent is neither granular, freely given, nor easy to withdraw — declining any element or later withdrawing cancels all member prices, and the old data-free tier was quietly removed. On top of the data-law problems, the "Say YES to savings!" framing hides the real trade-off (your data is the price), which raises misleading-omission and aggressive-practice concerns under EU consumer law (UCPD). The ads placed on external platforms must also meet DSA transparency rules and must not use profiling to target anyone who could be a minor. The core issue is structural: benefits are coerced against consent rather than offered as a genuine choice. This campaign should not launch in its current form; it needs to be re-architected before going live in the EU.
recommendations: Unbundle the single consent into four independent, default-off toggles (profiling, location push, partner-sharing, external ad targeting), each refusable and withdrawable without affecting the others.
Decouple core member pricing from optional data consents: reinstate a genuine data-minimal membership tier that offers the same essential discounts to shoppers who decline profiling/sharing.

Fix withdrawal so that withdrawing any data consent stops only that processing and never cancels membership or strips benefits; make withdrawal as easy and penalty-free as giving consent, in-app and in-store.

Rewrite enrolment messaging so it is not just 'Say YES to savings!': clearly and prominently disclose that data is collected, shared with 60 partners, and used for external ad targeting, and that these are optional — do not present the offer as costless.

Publish a clear Art. 13 privacy notice at sign-up naming the recipients (or specific categories) and linking the full list of 60 partners, with purposes, retention periods and profiling logic; provide a standalone, penalty-free opt-out from direct-marketing profiling.
Redesign the app consent screen so accept and decline carry equal visual prominence and avoid confirm-shaming (removes the dark-pattern risk under UCPD/DSA).
For ads on external platforms, ensure each is labelled as an ad naming the supermarket as advertiser/payer and exposes/enables changing the main targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26).
Implement age assurance and suppress all profiling-based ad delivery to anyone who is or may reasonably be a minor (DSA Art. 28).
Communicate the removal of the previous data-free tier transparently rather than silently, to address the fairness concerns under GDPR Art. 5 and UCPD Art. 5.

campaign.title: NordChair AI-visualised catalogue
campaign.text: Furniture brand campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery. Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue. Copy: 'The Fjord armchair — solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty. Delivery in 2–4 weeks.' All product claims match specification sheets; prices include VAT and delivery is stated. No urgency, no personalisation, standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked).

detected_practices: AI-generated lifestyle imagery
AI disclosure label ('Images created with AI')
product claims (materials, warranty, delivery time)
price transparency (VAT included, delivery stated)
unticked opt-in newsletter box
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers; no indication of targeting minors. Newsletter opt-in implies collection of contact/personal data, engaging GDPR (consent, opt-in must remain genuinely unticked). AI Act transparency obligations for synthetic media are engaged even though disclosure appears present. DSA is plausibly engaged via social/web distribution and advertising transparency obligations. UCPD applies as a general consumer-facing campaign; current claims appear substantiated but should be verified.
triage.summary: Furniture brand catalogue using AI-generated lifestyle imagery, clearly labelled as AI-created both on each visual and beside each web-catalogue image. Product claims match specification sheets, prices include VAT, delivery timing is stated, and there is no urgency or personalisation, with a standard unticked opt-in newsletter box. Targeted at general adult EU consumers across web and social channels.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campuses' AI-generated images engage Art. 50(2), which requires synthetic image outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated (e.g. embedded metadata, watermark or provenance signal such as C2PA). The campaign describes only a visible, human-readable on-image label; it does not confirm any machine-readable marking of the output, so the obligation is engaged but not demonstrably satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the AI provider/tool embeds machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA content credentials / invisible watermark or metadata flag) in each generated image file, in addition to the existing visible label. Confirm with the generative-AI supplier that outputs are marked in a machine-readable, robust and detectable format and retain this marking through the publishing pipeline.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Art. 50(4) requires deployers to disclose AI-generated or manipulated image content that constitutes a deep fake (content that would falsely appear authentic, especially of real persons/places/events). The imagery here is generic furniture lifestyle imagery with no indication of depicting real identifiable persons or real events as authentic, and any deployer disclosure duty is in any case met by the prominent visible 'Images created with AI' label on every asset. This obligation therefore appears satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Furniture brand campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the clear, prominent 'Images created with AI' disclosure on all assets. If future variants depict realistic scenes involving recognisable real persons, places or events, keep the explicit AI-generation disclosure to remain within Art. 50(4).

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses generative-AI lifestyle imagery and therefore engages the AI Act transparency obligations for synthetic content (Art. 50). Human-facing disclosure is well handled: a visible "Images created with AI" label appears on every visual and beside each web-catalogue image, which satisfies the deployer disclosure purpose (Art. 50(4)). The one residual gap is that Art. 50(2) additionally requires machine-readable/embedded provenance marking, which the campaign text does not confirm. No Art. 5 prohibitions are engaged — there is no manipulative, vulnerability-exploiting, social-scoring or emotion-recognition use.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Art. 4(11) requires consent to be a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication given by clear affirmative action; pre-ticked boxes do not qualify. The campaign uses an unticked opt-in box, meaning the subscriber must take an affirmative action to consent. This is the correct design and satisfies the definition of valid consent.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Maintain the unticked box; ensure the newsletter consent is not bundled with any other consent and that the checkbox wording clearly states the marketing purpose.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate consent, present the consent request in clear and plain language, and make withdrawal as easy as giving consent. The unticked box is compliant, but the campaign material does not describe how consent is recorded or how a subscriber can withdraw/unsubscribe.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Ensure the sign-up logs consent (timestamp, wording shown) for accountability, use clear plain-language consent text, and provide a one-click unsubscribe link in every newsletter that is as easy to use as the sign-up.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting an email address via the newsletter box triggers Art. 13, which requires that identity of the controller, purposes and legal basis, retention, recipients and data-subject rights be provided at the point of collection. The campaign text does not mention any privacy notice or link accompanying the sign-up.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Place a concise privacy notice (or a link to it) next to the newsletter box covering controller identity, purpose (marketing), legal basis (consent), retention period, and data-subject rights before the subscriber submits their details.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Since the newsletter is direct marketing, Art. 21(2)-(3) grants an absolute right to object at any time, which must be facilitated in every communication. The campaign does not describe an unsubscribe/opt-out route.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning unsubscribe mechanism in every newsletter and honour objections immediately by suppressing the address from further marketing.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged only through the newsletter opt-in box, which collects contact/personal data. The design choice described — a standard opt-in box that is genuinely unticked — is exactly what GDPR requires for valid consent (freely given, unambiguous, affirmative action), so the consent mechanism itself appears compliant. No personalisation, profiling, automated decision-making, special-category data, or targeting of minors is present, so those provisions are not engaged. The only residual points are transparency-related: the material does not describe a privacy notice at the point of collection or an easy withdrawal/objection route, which are obligations attaching to any newsletter sign-up but may simply be undocumented in this brief.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is distributed on social online platforms. Under DSA Art. 26(1), where the brand's content is a paid/promotional advertisement presented on an online platform, recipients must be able to identify in a clear, concise and unambiguous manner that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The campaign text confirms an AI-content label ('Images created with AI') but does not confirm any advertisement/sponsored identification or advertiser identity on the social placements; the AI label does not satisfy the ad-recognisability requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, social
findings.recommendation: For all paid social placements, ensure the platform's 'Ad'/'Sponsored' labelling is used and that the advertiser (NordChair) is clearly identified as the entity on whose behalf the ad is presented. Provide the platform with the advertiser and payer information it needs to meet Art. 26(1). Keep the AI-content disclosure separate from and additional to the ad-identification label.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is largely benign from a DSA standpoint. There is no personalisation or targeting, general adult audience, no minors, no urgency, and a genuinely unticked opt-in box, so the prohibitions on sensitive-data-based ad targeting (Art. 26(3)), profiling-based ads to minors (Art. 28) and dark patterns (Art. 25) are not engaged on the facts presented. The only live DSA obligation is advertising transparency (Art. 26(1)) where the brand's paid content is distributed on social online platforms: such placements must be clearly identifiable as advertising with advertiser identity, which the campaign text does not confirm. Note that most DSA obligations bind the platform provider rather than the advertiser; the advertiser's role is to supply the transparency information the platform surfaces.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: AI-generated lifestyle imagery falls under UCPD Art. 6 only if it deceives the average consumer about main product characteristics (composition, finish, scale, setting). Here all product claims are stated to match specification sheets and the imagery is expressly labelled as AI-created, so no misleading action is indicated. Flagged for information because the residual UCPD risk with synthetic visuals is that a rendered image could depict a product materially different from the real item.
findings.evidence_quote: Furniture brand campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery ... All product claims match specification sheets
findings.recommendation: Maintain the practice of ensuring AI-generated visuals accurately represent the actual product (true material, colour, proportions and finish); avoid AI renders that imply features the delivered product does not have, and keep the 'Images created with AI' disclosure clearly visible on every asset across web and social.

verdicts.notes: The campaign does not engage any UCPD prohibition on the facts presented. Product claims (materials, warranty, delivery) reportedly match specification sheets, prices include VAT and delivery timing is stated, there is no false urgency, no fake reviews, and no other blacklisted practice. The AI-generated imagery is clearly and consistently disclosed ("Images created with AI"), so its synthetic nature does not deceive consumers about material facts and commercial intent is apparent. One informational point on AI lifestyle imagery is noted so the marketer keeps visuals faithful to the actual product.

report.executive_summary: This is a well-built campaign for NordChair's AI-visualised furniture catalogue on web and social. Product claims match spec sheets, prices include VAT, delivery timing is stated, there's no false urgency, and the newsletter box is genuinely unticked — all of which put you on solid ground for consumer-protection and consent rules. Your visible "Images created with AI" label is good practice and satisfies the human-facing AI disclosure. There are no serious violations, only a handful of minor housekeeping gaps. The main things to close: (1) the AI images likely need machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA/watermark) in addition to the visible label; (2) paid social placements must carry the platform's "Ad/Sponsored" labelling and identify NordChair as advertiser; and (3) the newsletter sign-up should be backed by a privacy notice, consent logging, and an easy unsubscribe route. None of these block the launch, but they should be fixed to be fully compliant.
recommendations: Confirm with your generative-AI supplier that each image embeds machine-readable provenance marking (C2PA content credentials, invisible watermark or metadata flag) and that this survives your publishing pipeline — the visible label alone does not meet AI Act Art. 50(2).

For all paid social placements, use the platform's 'Ad'/'Sponsored' labelling and clearly identify NordChair as the advertiser; supply the platform the advertiser/payer info it needs. Keep this separate from and additional to the AI-content label (DSA Art. 26(1)).
Add a concise privacy notice (or link) next to the newsletter box covering controller identity, purpose, legal basis (consent), retention, and data-subject rights (GDPR Art. 13).
Log newsletter consent (timestamp and wording shown) and include a one-click unsubscribe link in every newsletter that is as easy to use as the sign-up (GDPR Art. 7 & 21).
Keep the unticked opt-in box and ensure the newsletter consent is not bundled with any other consent.

Continue ensuring every AI-generated visual faithfully represents the real product (true material, colour, proportions, finish) and keep the 'Images created with AI' label visible on every asset across web and social (UCPD Art. 6).

campaign.title: SuperSave club enrolment revamp
campaign.text: A supermarket relaunches its loyalty club: member prices (up to 40% off staples) now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms. Declining any element means losing all member prices. In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'. A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed. Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.

detected_practices: combined/bundled consent for multiple distinct processing purposes
consent conditioned on access to core service (loyalty prices)
purchase-history behavioural profiling
location-based push offers
data sharing with 60 retail media partners
cross-platform ad targeting on external platforms
removal of previously available data-free membership tier ('take it or leave it')
withdrawal of consent penalised by full loss of membership
persuasive/pressuring in-store messaging ('Say YES to savings!')
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult grocery shoppers with no minor-specific targeting stated; however cross-platform ad targeting and general in-store/app reach mean incidental exposure to minors is not fully excluded and should be confirmed by GDPR reviewers.
triage.summary: A supermarket loyalty club relaunch conditions member pricing on a single bundled consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and external cross-platform ad targeting, with a previously available data-free tier quietly removed and consent withdrawal cancelling membership entirely. This raises serious GDPR concerns around freely-given, specific, granular consent and 'consent-or-pay'/detriment, alongside potential UCPD issues from pressuring 'Say YES to savings!' messaging and the removed no-data option. DSA is engaged via cross-platform behavioural ad targeting through online platform intermediaries.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and granular for each distinct processing purpose. A single combined consent bundling four materially different purposes (profiling, location offers, third-party sharing, external ad targeting) does not qualify — Art. 4(11) expressly excludes bundled consent. The data subject cannot indicate separate wishes per purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: now require accepting a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Unbundle the consent into separate, independently toggleable opt-ins for (1) purchase-history profiling, (2) location-based push, (3) sharing with named partners, (4) external ad targeting, each defaulting to off, so members can accept some purposes and refuse others.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires consent to be freely given and provides that performance of a contract/service must not be made conditional on consent that is not necessary for that service. Conditioning core loyalty pricing on non-necessary marketing/profiling/sharing consents (with detriment for refusal) means consent is not freely given. The prior existence of a data-free tier that was 'quietly removed' shows the data processing is not necessary to provide member prices, reinforcing invalidity.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices.
findings.recommendation: Decouple member pricing from the marketing/profiling/sharing consents so that refusing them has no effect on access to member prices; restore a genuine equivalent no-/minimal-data membership option so consent is a real, penalty-free choice.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that it be as easy to withdraw consent as to give it, and withdrawal must not entail detriment that renders the original consent not freely given. Making withdrawal trigger total loss of membership imposes a significant penalty that both discourages withdrawal and confirms the initial consent was coerced.
findings.evidence_quote: Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: Ensure withdrawal of any marketing/profiling consent stops only that specific processing while membership and member pricing continue unaffected; provide an easy in-app/one-click withdrawal mechanism.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Purchase-history profiling, location-based offers, third-party sharing and external ad targeting need a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis. If the intended basis is consent that fails Arts. 4(11)/7, there is no lawful basis and the processing is unlawful.
