Legitimate interests is unlikely to cover cross-platform ad targeting and sharing with 60 partners given the intrusiveness.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples) now require accepting a single combined consent
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on the bundled/coerced consent; establish valid per-purpose consent for the marketing and sharing operations, and document a defensible lawful basis (with a balancing test) for any processing genuinely necessary to operate the loyalty scheme.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of purchase history to evaluate personal preferences and behaviour and to target offers/ads constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This triggers the associated GDPR obligations (valid basis, transparency, right to object) which are not satisfied given the consent defects.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operation, ensure a valid lawful basis, and inform members clearly about the profiling logic and its consequences at the point of enrolment.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that recipients (or categories of recipients) of personal data be disclosed at the point of collection, together with purposes, legal basis, retention and rights. A generic reference to '60 retail media partners' plus external-platform targeting is unlikely to meet the transparency standard unless the recipients/categories and purposes are clearly specified.
findings.evidence_quote: sharing with 60 'retail media partners'
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at enrolment identifying the recipients or specific categories (ideally a linked, updated list of the 60 partners), the purposes and legal basis for each transfer, retention periods and how to object/withdraw.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle is undermined where a genuine no-data option is silently withdrawn and members are steered ('Say YES to savings!') into extensive processing without a transparent, balanced choice. Quiet removal of the alternative and pressuring framing point to unfair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Communicate changes transparently, avoid manipulative framing, and offer a fair, clearly-presented choice architecture that does not covertly force members into maximal data sharing.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Members have an absolute right under Art. 21(2)-(3) to object at any time to direct-marketing processing, including related profiling, independent of consent. The design (withdrawal cancels membership) suggests no facilitated, consequence-free objection route for marketing processing specifically.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy, standalone opt-out from direct marketing and marketing-related profiling that stops that processing without affecting membership, and signpost this right in every marketing communication.

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch centres on a single combined consent covering four distinct processing purposes (purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and cross-platform ad targeting), with declining any element causing loss of all member prices and withdrawal cancelling membership. This design fails the core GDPR consent standard: consent is not freely given (conditionality/detriment, removal of the data-free tier), not specific/granular (bundled), and withdrawal is not as easy to give as to receive. Transparency and fairness obligations around the 60 partners and the quietly removed no-data tier are also engaged. Consent as a lawful basis for the profiling/marketing here is very likely invalid.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: To the extent the supermarket operates its own app as an online interface, the consent flow is designed to materially distort recipients' ability to make a free and informed decision: a single non-granular bundled 'Say YES' choice with no equivalent decline option, the quiet removal of the previously available data-free tier (forced/false choice architecture), and penalising withdrawal by cancelling membership entirely all mirror the manipulation, prominence-of-one-choice and obstruction patterns Art. 25 targets. Note the same conduct is primarily governed for all traders by the UCPD and GDPR consent rules, so the DSA angle is limited to the platform/app interface.
findings.evidence_quote: a single combined consent covering purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms. Declining any element means losing all member prices... 'Say YES to savings!'... A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed. Withdrawal of consent cancels membership entirely.
findings.recommendation: In the app, present separate, equally prominent accept/decline controls for each processing purpose, restore a genuine data-free (or non-profiled) membership tier so the choice is not forced, use neutral non-confirm-shaming wording instead of 'Say YES to savings!', and ensure withdrawing consent does not disproportionately cancel core membership.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Grocery purchase-history profiling shared with 60 retail-media partners and used to target ads on external online platforms can readily use proxies that infer GDPR Art. 9 special categories (e.g. health from diabetic/gluten-free/pharmacy items, religion from halal/kosher products). DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits platform advertising based on profiling using special-category data, directly or by inference, regardless of consent — so this targeting setup risks presenting prohibited ads via the platform intermediaries.
findings.evidence_quote: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 'retail media partners', and ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Contractually and technically exclude any special-category attributes and their proxies from the profiles and audience segments shared with retail-media partners and used for external-platform ad targeting; document a filtering/exclusion mechanism to prevent inference-based sensitive targeting before any ads are served on online platforms.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: When these behaviourally targeted ads run on online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires each ad be identifiable as an advertisement in real time, disclose on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign relies on external-platform ad targeting, so it must be built to surface this transparency information.
findings.evidence_quote: ad targeting on external platforms
findings.recommendation: Ensure all external-platform ads are clearly labelled as advertising with the supermarket named as advertiser/payer, and that the targeting-parameter disclosures and opt-out controls the platforms provide are correctly populated for these audiences.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: No minor-specific targeting is declared, but broad in-store/app/cross-platform reach means incidental exposure to minors is not fully excluded. If the supermarket's app or any platform placement is accessible to minors and it becomes aware with reasonable certainty that a recipient is a minor, profiling-based advertising to them is prohibited under Art. 28.
findings.evidence_quote: grocery shoppers, general adult
findings.recommendation: Confirm with GDPR/age-assurance reviewers whether minors can enrol or be reached; if so, suppress all profiling-based advertising to users known with reasonable certainty to be minors and apply age-appropriate design.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged mainly through the campaign's cross-platform behavioural ad targeting (executed via online platform intermediaries) and the manipulative consent design in the supermarket's app. The core DSA prohibitions/obligations bind providers of online platforms, so several duties (Art. 26 transparency, Art. 39 repositories) fall on the platforms carrying the ads rather than the supermarket directly — but the campaign must be designed to comply. The most substantive DSA risks are (1) manipulative interface design in the app consent flow (Art. 25) and (2) profiling-based ad targeting that could rely on proxies for GDPR Art. 9 special-category data, which is flatly prohibited for platform advertising (Art. 26(3)). Detailed consent lawfulness is a GDPR matter and left to those reviewers.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The signage and combined-consent step frame acceptance as being solely about obtaining savings, while omitting or obscuring material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision: that consenting also means purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with 60 'retail media partners' and cross-platform ad targeting. Presenting a broad data bundle as a single 'YES to savings' hides material conditions and provides them in an unclear/ambiguous manner (a confirm-shaming dark pattern), engaging Art. 7 misleading omission.
findings.evidence_quote: In-store signage: 'Say YES to savings!'
findings.recommendation: Replace the single 'Say YES to savings!' framing with a clear, up-front, layered disclosure of each processing purpose and its consequences at the point of enrolment. Do not label a data-sharing consent as merely a 'savings' choice; separate the price benefit from the data purposes so consumers understand what they are agreeing to.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The quiet removal of the no-data tier and the fact that member prices now require accepting the full data bundle are material to a consumer's transactional decision. Not surfacing that alternative options were withdrawn, and burying the 'decline any element means losing all member prices' condition, is likely a misleading omission under Art. 7 (material information hidden or provided untimely).
findings.evidence_quote: A data-free membership tier existed previously and was quietly removed.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently inform members that the data-free tier has been removed and that member pricing is now conditional, at the point of enrolment/renewal. Give consumers a genuine, clearly presented choice rather than an obscured take-it-or-leave-it.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of all-or-nothing bundling, loss of all member prices on any refusal, and cancellation of membership entirely on withdrawal of consent can amount to undue influence and onerous barriers to exercising a contractual right (withdrawing consent / declining processing), significantly impairing the average consumer's freedom of choice and pressuring a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. This engages the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9) and reflects dark-pattern design.
findings.evidence_quote: Declining any element means losing all member prices.
findings.recommendation: Remove the penalty structure that ties core loyalty pricing to acceptance of secondary data purposes and that cancels membership on withdrawal. Allow granular acceptance/refusal and withdrawal without disproportionate detriment, so declining or withdrawing does not coerce the consumer into keeping the data sharing active.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The 'up to 40% off' price-advantage claim must be genuine and, for price-reduction announcements, reference a true prior price. No evidence in the campaign shows the claim is false, but it is a price-advantage claim within Art. 6(1)(d) and should be substantiated.
findings.evidence_quote: member prices (up to 40% off staples)
findings.recommendation: Ensure the 'up to 40% off staples' claim is verifiable, that at least a meaningful range of products reaches that reduction, and that any 'reduction' references genuine prior prices (also relevant under Price Indication Directive 98/6/EC Art. 6a).

verdicts.notes: The loyalty relaunch engages the UCPD principally through the design and framing of the consent step rather than the underlying data lawfulness (a GDPR matter). The upbeat "Say YES to savings!" messaging presents an extensive data bundle (profiling, location push, sharing with 60 partners, cross-platform ad targeting) as a simple saving decision, hiding material conditions from the average consumer — a likely misleading omission and a confirm-shaming/nagging dark pattern. The all-or-nothing structure, the quiet removal of the data-free tier, and cancellation of membership on withdrawal create onerous pressure engaging the aggressive-practices prohibition. The "up to 40% off" claim is flagged for substantiation.

report.executive_summary: The SuperSave loyalty relaunch ties member prices (up to 40% off) to a single "all-or-nothing" consent covering four very different data uses: purchase-history profiling, location-based push offers, sharing with 60 retail media partners, and ad targeting on external platforms. This design has serious legal problems on three fronts. Under GDPR, bundling these purposes into one consent, forcing acceptance to keep member prices, quietly removing the old data-free tier, and cancelling membership if someone withdraws all mean the consent is very likely invalid — it is neither specific/granular nor freely given, so the profiling and marketing would have no lawful basis. Under the UCPD, the upbeat "Say YES to savings!" framing hides what shoppers are really agreeing to (a misleading omission) and the pressure to accept or lose everything can count as an aggressive practice. Under the DSA, the app consent flow shows dark-pattern design, and profiling grocery data for external ad targeting risks unlawfully inferring sensitive categories (e.g. health from pharmacy or dietary items, religion from halal/kosher purchases), which is banned for platform ads. The AI Act does not apply. The core fix is the same across all three regimes: unbundle the consents, stop penalising people for declining or withdrawing, and restore a genuine data-free membership option. As designed, this campaign should not launch.
recommendations: Unbundle the consent: give separate, independently toggleable opt-ins (each defaulting to OFF) for purchase-history profiling, location-based push, sharing with named partners, and external ad targeting — members must be able to accept some and refuse others.

Decouple member pricing from marketing/profiling/sharing consents so that declining or withdrawing has no effect on access to member prices; restore a genuine, penalty-free no-/minimal-data membership tier.
Ensure withdrawing any consent stops only that specific processing and never cancels membership; provide an easy one-click in-app withdrawal that is as simple as giving consent.

Exclude special-category data and its proxies (health from pharmacy/dietary items, religion from halal/kosher, etc.) from any profiles or audience segments shared with retail media partners or used for external-platform targeting; document the filtering mechanism before any ads run.

Replace 'Say YES to savings!' with clear, up-front, layered disclosure at enrolment of each data purpose and its consequences; do not present a data-sharing decision as merely a savings choice (avoid confirm-shaming/dark patterns).

Transparently tell members the data-free tier has been removed and that pricing conditions have changed, at the point of enrolment/renewal — do not bury the 'decline means losing all member prices' condition.

Publish a layered privacy notice identifying the 60 retail media partners (or clear categories), the purpose, legal basis and retention for each transfer, and provide a standalone, consequence-free opt-out from direct marketing and marketing-related profiling.
Establish and document a defensible lawful basis for any processing genuinely necessary to run the loyalty scheme, separate from the marketing consents.
Ensure external-platform ads are clearly labelled with the supermarket named as advertiser/payer and that targeting-parameter disclosures and opt-outs are correctly populated.

Substantiate the 'up to 40% off staples' claim (genuine range of products, true reference prices per PID 98/6/EC), and confirm whether minors can enrol/be reached — if so, suppress profiling-based ads to them.

campaign.title: NordChair AI-visualised catalogue
campaign.text: Furniture brand campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery. Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue. Copy: 'The Fjord armchair — solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty. Delivery in 2–4 weeks.' All product claims match specification sheets; prices include VAT and delivery is stated. No urgency, no personalisation, standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked).

detected_practices: AI-generated lifestyle imagery with visible 'Images created with AI' disclosure
product claims (materials, 10-year warranty) verified against specification sheets
price transparency (VAT-inclusive, delivery stated)
standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked, no pre-ticking)
triage.summary: Furniture brand catalogue campaign on web and social using AI-generated lifestyle imagery, each visual carrying a visible 'Images created with AI' label. Product claims match specification sheets, prices are VAT-inclusive with stated delivery, and there is no urgency or personalisation—only a standard unticked opt-in newsletter box. Aimed at general adult consumers in the EU.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign uses AI-generated synthetic image content. Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of generative AI systems be marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated. The campaign evidences only a visible, human-readable label; there is no indication that the images carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. embedded watermark / C2PA metadata). The visible label satisfies human-facing transparency but does not by itself meet the machine-readable requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the generative-AI provider/tool that outputs embed machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA content credentials or a robust watermark) and preserve that metadata through the publishing/export pipeline so it is not stripped on upload to web and social channels. Keep documentation of the marking as part of the campaign record.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: AI-generated realistic lifestyle imagery can engage the Art. 50(4) obligation to disclose that image content is artificially generated. The campaign already provides clear, prominent human-facing disclosure on every visual and beside each catalogue image, which meets this transparency obligation. Flagged as informational to record that the obligation is engaged and satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner
findings.recommendation: Maintain the current clear disclosure. Ensure the same 'Images created with AI' labelling persists on social-media placements (where crops or thumbnails may hide corner labels) so the disclosure remains visible in every context the imagery is shown.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses generative-AI lifestyle imagery and engages AI Act Art. 50 transparency obligations. The human-facing deep-fake/AI-content disclosure (Art. 50(4)) is handled very well — a visible 'Images created with AI' label appears on every visual and beside each catalogue image. The remaining gap is the machine-readable marking requirement of Art. 50(2): the submission evidences only a human-readable label, with no confirmation of embedded machine-readable provenance marking. This is easily remediable and there are no prohibited-practice concerns.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Collecting an email for a newsletter relies on consent. The described mechanism — a standard, unticked opt-in box — meets the Art. 4(11) standard of a freely given, specific, unambiguous indication by clear affirmative action, and avoids the prohibited pre-ticked/inactivity route. This is a positive/compliant signal rather than a breach.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Maintain the unticked box; ensure the newsletter consent is not bundled with any other purpose and that the request is presented in clear, plain language separate from other terms.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Collecting an email address at sign-up triggers the Art. 13 duty to provide, at the point of collection, the controller's identity, the purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights. The campaign material does not show that this information is presented at or near the newsletter box.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Place a concise privacy notice or a prominent link to the full privacy policy directly beside the newsletter box, covering controller identity, purpose (marketing emails), legal basis (consent), retention and how to exercise data-subject rights.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that consent be demonstrable and as easy to withdraw as to give. The material confirms a clean opt-in but does not evidence a withdrawal mechanism or record-keeping.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Log the consent (timestamp, wording shown) to be able to demonstrate it, and include a one-click unsubscribe link in every newsletter so withdrawal is as easy as sign-up.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The newsletter is direct marketing, so recipients have an absolute right to object at any time. This right must be actively facilitated in each communication; the campaign material does not evidence an opt-out/unsubscribe route.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Provide a clearly signposted, functioning unsubscribe/objection mechanism in every marketing email and honour objections immediately by ceasing marketing processing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's only GDPR-relevant processing is a newsletter sign-up. The consent mechanism as described is compliant with the definition of consent: a standard, unticked opt-in box requires a clear affirmative action and avoids the pre-ticked/inactivity problem prohibited under Art. 4(11). There is no personalisation, profiling, special-category data or targeting of minors, so those provisions are not engaged. Two ancillary obligations are triggered by the act of collecting an email address but are not evidenced in the material: providing Art. 13 information at the point of collection and facilitating the Art. 21 opt-out in each mailing.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Under Art. 6, a practice is misleading only where it contains false information or deceives about main characteristics, price or price advantage. Here every material claim (solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty, 2–4 week delivery) is verified against specification sheets, prices are VAT-inclusive and delivery timing is disclosed. No false price advantage or unsubstantiated claim is present, so Art. 6 is not breached. Recorded as info only.
findings.evidence_quote: All product claims match specification sheets; prices include VAT and delivery is stated.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the practice of substantiating every product claim against specification sheets and continue displaying VAT-inclusive prices with delivery terms; retain the evidence file in case of challenge.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: AI-generated lifestyle imagery could otherwise deceive the average consumer about the synthetic nature of visuals (an Art. 7 misleading-omission / Art. 6 concern under the AI-generated-content concept). The clear, repeated 'Images created with AI' disclosure on every visual — and the fact that the material is plainly a branded product catalogue with obvious commercial intent and disclosed price/delivery — means no material information is omitted or hidden. Art. 7 is satisfied. Note: machine-readable provenance marking is a separate AI Act matter outside UCPD scope.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue.
findings.recommendation: Keep the AI-disclosure label prominent and legible on all channels (including social crops and thumbnails) so it is not lost when images are resized or reshared; ensure it remains present if lifestyle imagery is reused in future assets.

verdicts.notes: The NordChair AI-visualised catalogue does not engage any UCPD prohibition as a violation. Product claims match specification sheets, prices are VAT-inclusive with stated delivery (no misleading action under Art. 6), the commercial intent is obvious and the AI-generated nature of the imagery is prominently and repeatedly disclosed (no misleading omission under Art. 7). There is explicitly no false urgency (Annex I point 7) and no aggressive or high-pressure tactic (Arts. 8-9); the newsletter opt-in is unticked. One informational note is recorded regarding the AI-imagery disclosure being the correct safeguard that keeps the campaign clear of Arts. 6-7.

report.executive_summary: This is a well-built, low-risk campaign. The AI-generated furniture imagery is clearly and repeatedly labelled "Images created with AI," which satisfies human-facing transparency under the AI Act and keeps you clear of misleading-advertising rules. All product claims are backed by specification sheets, prices include VAT, delivery is stated, and there's no false urgency or high-pressure tactics. The newsletter uses a compliant unticked opt-in box. There are no violations — only a few housekeeping items to close out. The main technical gap is that the AI Act also requires machine-readable provenance marking on AI images (not just a visible label), which the submission doesn't confirm. On the data side, you need to make sure a privacy notice sits beside the newsletter box and that every mailing carries a working unsubscribe link. None of these block launch; they are straightforward to fix.
recommendations: Confirm the AI images carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA content credentials or a robust watermark) and that this metadata survives export/upload to web and social — the visible label alone does not meet AI Act Art. 50(2).
Add a concise privacy notice (or prominent link) directly beside the newsletter box covering controller identity, purpose, legal basis (consent), retention and data-subject rights (GDPR Art. 13).
Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe/objection link in every marketing email and honour opt-outs immediately (GDPR Arts. 7 & 21).
Log each newsletter consent (timestamp and the wording shown) so it can be demonstrated on request (GDPR Art. 7).
Ensure the 'Images created with AI' label stays visible on social placements where crops or thumbnails could hide a corner label, and on any future reuse of the imagery.
Keep the unticked box and retain the claim-substantiation evidence file (spec sheets, VAT-inclusive pricing, delivery terms) in case of challenge.

This meets the standard for freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous consent. Flagged as info to confirm the practice is correctly designed, not as a deficiency.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Maintain the unticked opt-in design. Ensure the accompanying text clearly and separately describes the marketing purpose so consent remains specific and unbundled from any other terms.

The campaign text confirms the opt-in mechanism but does not state that controller identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, and data-subject rights are provided at the point of collection. This information must be available at sign-up.
findings.evidence_quote: standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked)
findings.recommendation: Ensure the newsletter form links to or displays a concise privacy notice at the point of collection covering controller identity, purpose (marketing), legal basis (consent), retention period, recipients, and how to withdraw consent / unsubscribe as easily as subscribing (Art. 7(3)).

verdicts.notes: The only GDPR-relevant practice in this campaign is the newsletter sign-up. It uses an opt-in box that is unticked by default, which is the correct standard for valid consent under Arts. 4(11) and 7 (no pre-ticked boxes, no inferred consent). There is no personalisation, profiling, targeting, or special-category data processing declared or evident, so Arts. 9, 21 and 22 are not engaged. The single point worth flagging is a transparency reminder: any personal data collected via the sign-up must be accompanied by Art. 13 information at the point of collection, which the campaign text does not describe either way.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits deceptive/manipulative interface design (confirm-shaming, pre-ticked/prominent choices, obstruction, disguised ads). The campaign's described design is compliant: the newsletter opt-in is unticked by default, there is no urgency pressure, and imagery is clearly labelled rather than disguised. No dark-pattern risk is identified; flagged only to record that the interface was checked against this prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: No urgency, no personalisation, standard opt-in newsletter box (unticked).
findings.recommendation: Maintain the unticked-by-default opt-in and ensure the eventual landing page/checkout keeps the same clean design — no confirm-shaming on unsubscribe, no pre-selected add-ons, and cancellation/unsubscribe as easy as sign-up.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: When ads are served on third-party online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires each ad to be identifiable as an advertisement with the advertiser/payer disclosed. This obligation falls primarily on the platform, but the advertiser should ensure paid social placements are properly labelled as advertising and the advertiser identity is clear. No breach is evident from the campaign text; the copy is factual and the AI label is present.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, social
findings.recommendation: For any paid placements on social platforms, use the platform's native 'paid partnership'/'sponsored' ad-disclosure tools and provide accurate advertiser/payer identity so the platform can meet Art. 26(1).

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA only lightly and shows no violations. The described interface is the opposite of a dark pattern (Art. 25): a genuinely unticked opt-in newsletter box, no urgency, no disguised advertising, no obstruction. There is no personalisation or profiling, so the sensitive-data ad ban (Art. 26(3)) and profiling-based ads to minors (Art. 28) are not triggered. AI-image labelling is an AI Act matter, not a DSA obligation. The only DSA point worth noting is that when the ads run on third-party social platforms, the platform's Art. 26(1) ad-transparency labelling must be respected — an obligation largely on the platform, not the advertiser.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: AI-generated lifestyle imagery can create misleading impressions about a product's actual appearance, composition or main characteristics (Art. 6). Here the risk is mitigated: the synthetic nature is disclosed on every visual and all product claims ('solid oak frame, wool blend, 10-year warranty, Delivery in 2–4 weeks') match specification sheets, so the average consumer is not deceived about material facts. No misleading action is present as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Every visual carries a visible 'Images created with AI' label in the corner and the same statement appears beside each image in the web catalogue.
findings.recommendation: Maintain the practice of ensuring AI-generated visuals do not depict features (materials, dimensions, finishes) that differ from the actual product, and keep the AI disclosure prominent and adjacent to each image so it cannot be overlooked. Retain evidence linking each claim to the specification sheet.

verdicts.notes: Assessed against the UCPD only. The campaign contains factual, specification-matched product claims and transparent pricing (VAT-inclusive, stated delivery), with no urgency, scarcity, fake reviews, false 'free', cure, prize or trust-mark claims — so no blacklist point (Annex I) is engaged. The AI-generated lifestyle imagery is the one practice that could theoretically deceive about product characteristics (Art. 6) or omit material information (Art. 7), but this risk is neutralised by the consistent, visible 'Images created with AI' disclosure on every visual and beside each catalogue image, combined with accurate product claims. No UCPD violation is likely; the only note is informational. (Machine-readable AI marking is an AI Act matter for another agent.)

report.executive_summary: This is a well-constructed, low-risk furniture catalogue campaign using AI-generated lifestyle imagery for EU web and social channels. The compliance posture is strong across the board: every AI image carries a clear, visible "Images created with AI" label, all product claims match specification sheets, prices include VAT, delivery is stated, and there is no urgency, personalisation or profiling. The newsletter uses a correctly designed unticked opt-in box, and the interface shows no dark patterns. Only two small housekeeping items need attention. First, under the AI Act (Art. 50(2)), AI-generated images must be marked in a machine-readable format (e.g. C2PA/Content Credentials metadata or a watermark) in addition to the visible label — this is not confirmed in your submission. Second, the newsletter sign-up must display a short privacy notice at the point of collection (GDPR Art. 13). Neither is a violation as such; they are gaps to close before or at publication. Overall verdict: publishable once these two items are confirmed.
recommendations: Enable machine-readable AI provenance marking on all generated images (e.g. C2PA/Content Credentials metadata or an embedded watermark) in addition to the visible label, as required by AI Act Art. 50(2). If your generation tool does not embed this by default, add it before publication and keep documentation of it.

Add a concise privacy notice at the newsletter sign-up point (GDPR Art. 13) covering controller identity, purpose (marketing), legal basis (consent), retention period, recipients, and how to unsubscribe/withdraw consent as easily as subscribing.

For any paid social placements, use each platform's native 'sponsored'/'paid partnership' ad-disclosure tools and supply accurate advertiser/payer identity so platform ad-transparency (DSA Art. 26(1)) is met.
Retain the evidence linking each product claim to its specification sheet, and ensure AI visuals never depict materials, dimensions or finishes that differ from the actual product.
Keep the unticked-by-default opt-in and clean interface through to the landing page/checkout — no pre-selected add-ons, no confirm-shaming on unsubscribe, and cancellation as easy as sign-up.

campaign.title: BookNook monthly picks
campaign.text: Monthly email to subscribers who ticked 'Send me personalised recommendations' at signup (separate from the account-creation consent). The email explains 'Recommended because you bought Nordic crime fiction', links to a preference centre where profiling can be switched off independently of the newsletter, and includes one-click unsubscribe honoured immediately. Prices are final; claims are factual ('Winner of the 2025 Glass Key award'). No third-party data is used.

behavioural profiling based on purchase history
separate opt-in consent for personalisation
preference centre with granular profiling opt-out
one-click unsubscribe honoured immediately
factual award claim ('Winner of the 2025 Glass Key award')
final/transparent pricing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adults who separately opted in to personalised recommendations; no indication minors are targeted or likely reached. Personal data (purchase history, profiling) requires GDPR review, especially consent granularity, transparency of the 'recommended because' logic, and profiling opt-out. UCPD included for the recommendation and award-claim messaging in a consumer campaign.
triage.summary: Monthly email newsletter to adult, opted-in subscribers offering book recommendations personalised via profiling on the recipient's own purchase history. It uses a separate personalisation consent, a granular preference centre to disable profiling, immediate one-click unsubscribe, factual claims and transparent final pricing, with no third-party data or generative AI.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Generating recommendations by analysing a recipient's purchase history to predict their personal preferences and interests is 'profiling' within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This confirms GDPR applies and triggers the consent, transparency and objection obligations — all of which the campaign appears to satisfy.
findings.evidence_quote: Recommended because you bought Nordic crime fiction
findings.recommendation: No action required. Continue to treat this personalisation as profiling and keep applying the associated consent, transparency and opt-out controls already in place.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent for profiling-based personalisation is collected via a specific, affirmative opt-in that is clearly distinguishable and unbundled from the account-creation consent, and withdrawal is as easy as giving it (preference centre + one-click unsubscribe). This meets the Art. 4(11)/Art. 7 standard for freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous consent that is easy to withdraw.
findings.evidence_quote: subscribers who ticked 'Send me personalised recommendations' at signup (separate from the account-creation consent)
findings.recommendation: Maintain records demonstrating consent (who ticked, when, wording shown) to satisfy the Art. 7(1) accountability requirement to demonstrate consent.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The absolute right to object to direct marketing and associated profiling (Art. 21(2)-(3)) is well facilitated: a granular preference centre allows profiling to be disabled separately, and unsubscribe is one-click and honoured immediately, so processing stops for that purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: links to a preference centre where profiling can be switched off independently of the newsletter, and includes one-click unsubscribe honoured immediately
findings.recommendation: No action required. Ensure the 'honoured immediately' opt-out is also propagated to any downstream systems so profiling genuinely ceases without residual processing.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Art. 22 is not engaged: the recommendations are content suggestions, not a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects the recipient, and prices are final (no personalised/dynamic pricing). Documenting this confirms the higher Art. 22 safeguards are not required here.
findings.evidence_quote: Prices are final
findings.recommendation: No action required. Should personalisation later drive individualised pricing or eligibility decisions, reassess against Art. 22 and add the required safeguards and disclosure.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The campaign explains the recommendation logic in the email and offers a preference centre, which supports transparency (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12). However, the submission does not confirm that a full Art. 13 privacy notice (identity/purposes/legal basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights, and information about the profiling) was provided at the signup point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: ticked 'Send me personalised recommendations' at signup
findings.recommendation: Confirm that the signup flow linked to a layered privacy notice covering the Art. 13 elements — in particular the existence of profiling for personalisation, its purpose and the right to object — so transparency at the point of collection is documented.

verdicts.notes: The campaign involves profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4) (book recommendations derived from the recipient's own purchase history), so GDPR applies. However, the described practices are substantively compliant: a separate, unbundled opt-in consent for personalisation distinct from account creation, a granular preference centre allowing profiling to be disabled independently of the newsletter, immediate one-click unsubscribe, and transparent explanation of the personalisation logic ("Recommended because you bought Nordic crime fiction"). The recommendation is not a solely-automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, so Art. 22 is not engaged. No special-category data, no third-party data, and adults-only audience. Only an informational point remains around ensuring the full Art. 13 notice is available.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Award claims are a 'main characteristic' expressly covered by Art. 6 (false claims about the trader's qualifications and awards are misleading). The campaign declares the claim is factual, so no breach is indicated — but the claim must be genuinely substantiable, accurately attributed to the specific title, and current, or it would become a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: Winner of the 2025 Glass Key award
findings.recommendation: Retain documentary evidence that the referenced title actually won the 2025 Glass Key award and ensure the claim is presented accurately (correct title, correct year); avoid implying the award attaches to the whole catalogue or publisher if it applies only to one book.

verdicts.notes: This is a straightforward commercial email to opted-in adult subscribers. Its UCPD-relevant messaging — a stated-factual award claim and final, transparent pricing — shows no misleading action or omission. The commercial intent of a branded newsletter is apparent from context (Art. 7 satisfied), and the recommendation logic is disclosed ("Recommended because you bought Nordic crime fiction"). No blacklisted practices (no false urgency/scarcity, fake reviews, misuse of 'free', false prizes/awards, or ceasing-trade claims) are present. Only a low-level substantiation reminder applies to the award claim.

report.executive_summary: Your BookNook monthly picks email is well-built and substantively compliant. It sends personalised book recommendations to subscribers who gave a separate, specific opt-in, explains why each recommendation is shown, and offers a granular preference centre plus one-click unsubscribe honoured immediately. The AI Act and DSA don't apply here. Under GDPR, the personalisation counts as profiling, but your consent, transparency and opt-out controls appear to meet the standard, and the automated-decision rules (Art. 22) aren't triggered because prices are final and recommendations don't produce significant effects. The only real GDPR gap is confirming a full privacy notice was shown at signup. Under consumer law (UCPD), your award claim and final pricing are fine as long as the award claim is genuinely substantiated and accurately attributed. Overall: low risk, cleared to proceed with a few housekeeping steps.
recommendations: Confirm the signup flow linked to a full privacy notice covering the required GDPR Art. 13 details — especially the existence of profiling for personalisation, its purpose, and the right to object.

Keep documentary evidence that the referenced title actually won the 2025 Glass Key award, and present the claim accurately (correct title and year); don't imply the award covers the whole catalogue or publisher.
Maintain consent records (who opted in, when, and the exact wording shown) to meet the GDPR accountability requirement to demonstrate consent.

If personalisation ever drives individualised pricing or eligibility decisions in future, reassess against GDPR Art. 22 and add the required safeguards and disclosures.

Here the only disclosure ('virtual personality by StudioNine') sits in the account bio, which most feed and story viewers never open, while the individual posts, stories and first-person captions actively present Mira as a real human. findings.rationale: Although the declared audience is 18-30, the account is open with 2.1M followers, so minors can plausibly interact and disclose personal data. If any consent-based information-society-service data collection is layered onto the account, Art. 8 age/parental-consent rules and child-appropriate transparency would apply. On the current description no consent-based service is offered, so this is a contextual flag rather than an established breach.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Before adding any data-collection or consent-based feature to the account (competitions, sign-ups, DM funnels), assess minor reach and implement age-appropriate transparency and, where relevant, age assurance / parental-consent mechanisms; keep interaction handling child-appropriate given likely minor exposure.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares no personalisation/targeting and describes no sign-up form or lead-capture, so the classic GDPR targeting/profiling provisions (Arts. 4(4), 22, 21) and the point-of-collection notice duty (Art. 13) are only weakly or not engaged on the facts given. The genuine GDPR concern is the fairness/transparency principle: commenters disclose personal data (including questions revealing skincare/health interests) to an AI persona they reasonably believe is a human, with no per-interaction indication that it is automated, and with no controller identity or privacy information surfaced at the point of interaction. Because the open account (2.1M followers) plausibly reaches minors whose data is also processed in interactions, age-appropriate transparency should be considered. No prohibited or clearly-breached obligation is established from the text alone, so status is 'attention' pending verification of the data flows behind the account.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The synthetic influencer is designed and operated to present first-person 'skin-journey' testimonials and to reply to fans reinforcing a human persona, with per-post AI/virtual indication omitted. This operates the on-platform interface content in a way that deceives recipients about the nature of the source and materially affects their ability to make an informed commercial decision — the disguised-advertising/deceptive-design mischief Art. 25 targets. The primary duty-holder under Art. 25 is the platform provider, but the campaign design directly generates the deceptive interface content, so the advertiser should mitigate to avoid facilitating a platform-level breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, per-post and per-story 'AI-generated / virtual persona' indication (not only in the bio) and stop framing the AI account as receiving real human treatments (e.g. dermatologist visits). Ensure the persona's non-human nature is unambiguous at the point each piece of content is viewed, so the presentation is not deceptive.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that ads on platforms be identifiable as ads and disclose on whose behalf they are presented, clearly and in real time. The paid-partnership label satisfies the 'this is an advertisement / advertiser identity' elements, so the core requirement is largely met. However, the clarity and non-ambiguity of the advertisement is undermined by the missing per-post disclosure that the endorsing 'personality' is AI-generated, which weakens recipients' ability to identify the true nature of the promotional content. The obligation formally binds the platform, but the advertiser's content directly determines whether the label is meaningful.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Keep the paid-partnership label and supplement it with a consistent virtual/AI-creator identifier on every ad unit so the advertisement's nature and origin are unambiguous in real time, supporting the platform's Art. 26(1) compliance.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's advertising and dark-pattern provisions (Arts. 25–28) are primarily addressed to providers of online platforms rather than to advertisers/agencies like GlowCosmetics and StudioNine, so direct liability under the DSA sits mainly with the hosting platform. Nonetheless the campaign engages DSA concepts: the paid-partnership label satisfies the core "this is an advertisement / on whose behalf" element of Art. 26(1), but the absence of any per-post AI/virtual indication — combined with first-person testimonials and human-persona replies that commenters demonstrably mistake for a real person — is a disguised-advertising / deceptive-presentation concern that the interface transparency logic of Arts. 25–26 is designed to counter. No profiling-based targeting, sensitive-data targeting, or profiling-based ads to minors are described (campaign declares no personalisation), so Arts. 26(3) and 28 are not engaged on the facts. The synthetic-influencer disclosure gap is chiefly an AI Act Art. 50(4) / UCPD matter, handled by other agents.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Point 23c prohibits, in all circumstances, submitting/commissioning false endorsements or misrepresenting social endorsements to promote products. Mira's first-person testimonial ('my texture has never been this smooth') presents a personal-experience endorsement of the serum by an entity that has no skin and no experience. It is an AI-generated fabricated testimonial presented as a genuine human consumer endorsement — a blacklisted false/misrepresented endorsement, made worse by the fact commenters demonstrably treat it as real.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Stop framing the AI persona as having personally used or benefited from the product. Remove first-person experiential efficacy claims ('my texture...', 'my routine') from a non-human account, or reframe them as brand claims that are clearly not a personal testimonial, and make the virtual/AI nature unmistakable in the endorsing content itself.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers practices that deceive the average consumer about the nature of the product or the trader's/endorser's identity and qualifications, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. A photorealistic AI persona shown 'wearing' the serum and reporting smooth skin conveys a false impression that a real person achieved visible results with the product. The purported results and the human authenticity of the endorser are false, and this is capable of driving purchase decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ... selfies 'wearing' the new serum line
findings.recommendation: Ensure any visual or textual suggestion of real-world product results from Mira is removed or substantiated by genuine evidence, and clearly signal that images are AI-generated and depict no real user outcome.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or obscuring material information the average consumer needs, or providing it in an unclear/untimely manner. The endorser being a synthetic non-human is material information affecting the weight a consumer gives to the endorsement. Placing the 'virtual personality' note only in the account bio — while posts/stories consumed in-feed carry no AI indication — hides that material fact at the decision-relevant moment; the fact that commenters ask which dermatologist she visits is direct evidence the omission actually misleads.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, per-post/per-story disclosure that the influencer is AI-generated/virtual (e.g. a persistent 'AI-generated virtual influencer' label on each post and story), not just in the bio, so the material fact reaches consumers at the point they see the content.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the fairness safety-net and requires assessment from the perspective of a vulnerable group where one is clearly identifiable (age/credulity). On an open social platform with 2.1M followers the persona plausibly reaches younger/more credulous users who are especially unlikely to detect a photorealistic AI persona, and the demonstrated confusion shows the practice materially distorts consumer perception contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30 ... 2.1M followers ... Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: Apply age-appropriate safeguards and heightened, prominent AI-disclosure given the credulity of the reachable audience; verify the declared 'no targeting' and audience composition, and avoid persona interactions (comment replies) that reinforce the belief that Mira is a real human.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is fronted by a photorealistic AI-generated influencer posting first-person testimonials while a material share of the audience demonstrably believes she is a real human. Although paid-partnership is labelled, the non-human nature of the endorser — a material fact — is hidden at the point of consumption, engaging UCPD Arts. 6 and 7 and the Annex I point 23c prohibition on false/misrepresented endorsements. Efficacy claims delivered as a human 'skin journey' compound the misleadingness. The ad-disclosure obligation itself appears met, but the authenticity/AI-persona deception is the core UCPD issue.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses "Mira," a photorealistic AI-generated influencer, to post first-person selfies and "skin-journey" testimonials for GlowCosmetics serums and to reply to fans — and real people demonstrably believe she is human, asking which dermatologist she visits. The paid-partnership label is present, but there is no AI/virtual disclosure on the actual posts and stories; the only hint ("virtual personality by StudioNine") is buried in the account bio that most viewers never see. This creates serious, overlapping compliance problems. The most severe is under EU consumer law (UCPD): a first-person product endorsement from an entity with no skin and no experience is a fabricated/misrepresented testimonial, which is blacklisted outright and cannot be cured by disclaimers alone — the experiential claims must go or be reframed. On top of that, the AI Act requires per-post disclosure that the content is AI-generated (Art. 50), and the same disclosure gap makes the posts misleading omissions under the UCPD and risky under the DSA's deceptive-design rules. A secondary concern: users are handing personal information (skincare/health interests) to an AI persona they think is human, raising GDPR fairness/transparency issues, especially given likely minor exposure on a 2.1M-follower open account. The verdict is high risk and the campaign should not run in its current form.
recommendations: Remove or reframe the first-person experiential endorsements ('my texture has never been this smooth', 'my routine'). A fabricated personal testimonial from a non-human persona is a blacklisted unfair practice (UCPD Annex I 23c) that no label can fix — recast any efficacy statements as clearly non-personal brand claims backed by genuine evidence.

Add a clear, conspicuous 'AI-generated / virtual influencer' disclosure on every post, story and video (persistent on-content label or watermark), not just in the bio, so the AI nature is obvious at the moment each piece of content is viewed. This addresses AI Act Art. 50(4), UCPD Art. 7 (misleading omission) and the DSA deceptive-design concern in one step.

Stop presenting Mira as receiving real human treatments or having real product results (e.g. dermatologist visits, 'wearing' the serum with visible outcomes), which conveys false real-world results (UCPD Art. 6).

Fix the comment-reply behaviour: if replies are AI-generated, disclose that users are interacting with an AI (AI Act Art. 50(1)), and stop reinforcing the human-persona belief. Verify whether replies are automated or human-authored and document it.

Ensure the generative AI provider embeds machine-readable synthetic-content marking (e.g. C2PA/watermark metadata) in all AI images and video, and confirm it survives platform re-encoding (AI Act Art. 50(2)).

Surface controller identity and an accessible privacy notice at the point of interaction, since commenters disclose personal data to the account; make clear the account is an AI persona operated by StudioNine/GlowCosmetics (GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a), 13).

Given a 2.1M-follower open account likely reaches minors and more credulous users, apply age-appropriate safeguards and heightened disclosure, and verify the declared 'no targeting' and actual audience composition (UCPD Art. 5, GDPR Art. 8).

campaign.title: Mira.virtual x GlowCosmetics
campaign.text: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth'), and replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. The account bio states 'virtual personality by StudioNine'; individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.

detected_practices: AI-generated virtual influencer
influencer marketing / paid partnership
endorsement via first-person testimonial ('my texture has never been this smooth')
implied cosmetic efficacy / skincare claims
paid-partnership disclosure present on posts
no per-post AI/virtual disclosure despite consumer confusion
responding to comments to reinforce persona authenticity
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is EU young adults 18-30, but open social channels with a mainstream beauty/skincare influencer realistically reach under-18s; minors cannot be reliably excluded. First-person efficacy testimonials from a non-human persona are particularly likely to mislead where the AI nature is not disclosed on individual posts.
triage.summary: A photorealistic AI-generated influencer ('Mira', 2.1M followers) promotes GlowCosmetics serums via first-person 'skin-journey' testimonials and fan replies. Posts carry paid-partnership labels but no per-post AI/virtual indicator, and commenters clearly mistake Mira for a real human seeking dermatologist advice. Both the undisclosed synthetic nature and the personal efficacy claims raise transparency and misleading-practice concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Mira is a photorealistic AI-generated influencer — a synthetic persona presented as a real human — which Art. 50(4) expressly treats as within scope ('synthetic influencers presented as real'). As deployer, GlowCosmetics/StudioNine must disclose that the image/video content is artificially generated. The paid-partnership label does not discharge this: it discloses commercial intent, not AI generation. The disclosure must be clear at the point of consumption, but individual posts and stories carry no AI/virtual indication, and the ambiguous bio note ('virtual personality by StudioNine') is neither clear nor per-post. The fact that commenters mistake Mira for human and ask which dermatologist she visits confirms the disclosure is ineffective.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent per-asset disclosure that Mira is AI-generated / a virtual (non-human) persona on every post, story and reply — e.g., a visible on-content label such as 'AI-generated virtual character' — not only in the account bio. Ensure disclosure is legible at the moment content is viewed and is not diluted by the separate paid-partnership tag.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic image/video/text to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. The campaign consists of AI-generated images (selfies) and captions produced through a generative system, and there is no indication that machine-readable provenance marking is applied. This obligation is engaged and, as described, not evidently satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ... posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated visuals and copy embed machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g., C2PA content credentials or equivalent watermarking metadata) so the assets are detectable as artificially generated, and confirm the generative-AI provider implements compliant marking.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: If Mira's replies to fan comments are generated by an AI system interacting directly with users, Art. 50(1) requires those users to be informed they are interacting with an AI, unless obvious from the circumstances. Here it is plainly not obvious — commenters believe Mira is human. Whether this provision bites depends on whether the replies are AI-driven or human-authored by StudioNine, which the campaign does not specify.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: Clarify whether interactive replies are AI-generated; if so, disclose the AI nature of the interaction (e.g., a persistent 'automated / AI account' indicator). Avoid replies that reinforce a false impression of a real human's lived experience.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI persona actively deploys deceptive techniques (first-person testimony and interactive replies) that create a false impression of authentic human experience and lead consumers to a decision they might not otherwise take. However, Art. 5(1)(a) requires the deception to materially distort behaviour in a manner causing or likely to cause significant harm — a high threshold not clearly met by ordinary cosmetic marketing on the current facts. Flagged for monitoring; the deception is better addressed via the Art. 50 transparency duties and UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth'), and replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: Treat robust per-post AI disclosure as the primary mitigation; avoid escalating persona-authenticity tactics (e.g., fabricated dermatologist/routine narratives) that could push the deception toward the Art. 5 significant-harm threshold, especially given likely reach to minors.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ("Mira") to promote GlowCosmetics via first-person content, but individual posts and stories carry no indication of the synthetic nature — and consumers demonstrably believe Mira is human. This directly engages the AI Act's transparency regime for synthetic content: Art. 50(4) (deep fake / synthetic-persona disclosure) and Art. 50(2) (machine-readable marking of AI outputs), both of which appear unsatisfied as described. The AI-driven fan replies additionally engage the Art. 50(1) chatbot-interaction disclosure if automated. The Art. 5 prohibitions are not clearly met on the current facts.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The account processes identifiable commenters' personal data (handles, comments, interactions) and actively responds in a way that sustains a false human persona. Personal data must be processed fairly and transparently under Art. 5(1)(a); interacting with data subjects under a concealed synthetic identity, where they demonstrably misapprehend who/what they are engaging with, sits in tension with the fairness limb. (Note: the primary vector for the deception itself is UCPD/DSA/AI Act; the GDPR angle is confined to the fairness of processing the commenters' data.)
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. ... Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.
findings.recommendation: Ensure any handling of commenter data is fair and transparent: add a clear, per-post/persistent indication that 'Mira' is an AI-generated virtual personality, and avoid replies that affirmatively reinforce a false human identity to identifiable users who are being processed as data subjects.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Contingent exposure only. Art. 8 applies where consent is the legal basis for information society services offered to children and data is collected from those under 16 (13 in some Member States). The campaign as described collects no data via forms/sign-ups, so Art. 8 is not currently triggered; however, if any future mechanic (competition, newsletter, DM data capture) collects personal data from this audience, age-verification and parental-consent obligations would apply.
findings.evidence_quote: open social channels with a mainstream beauty/skincare influencer realistically reach under-18s; minors cannot be reliably excluded
findings.recommendation: If any data-collection feature is added (contests, sign-ups, lead capture), implement age assurance and, for users under the applicable digital-consent age, obtain and verify parental consent before processing, with child-appropriate transparency (Art. 12).

verdicts.notes: As described, the campaign does not engage the core GDPR obligations: personalisation/targeting is explicitly declared "no", and the material describes no data-collection mechanism (no sign-ups, lead-gen, competition entries, tracking or cookies). Consequently profiling (Art. 4(4)), lawful basis for targeted ads (Art. 6(1)), point-of-collection notices (Arts. 12/13), automated decisions (Art. 22) and special-category processing (Art. 9) are not triggered by the facts presented. The only genuine GDPR touchpoint is the account's ongoing processing of commenters' personal data (public replies) while concealing the persona's synthetic nature — a fairness question under Art. 5(1)(a) — plus a contingent Art. 8 exposure if any data is in fact collected from an audience that realistically includes under-16s. These are flagged at low/info level; the deceptive-endorser and disclosure issues fall primarily under UCPD/DSA/AI Act.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, for each ad, that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. The paid-partnership label on individual posts satisfies the core commercial-nature and 'on whose behalf' elements, so the DSA ad-transparency obligation is substantially met. The gap is the missing AI/virtual indicator, but that specific disclosure is governed by AI Act Art. 50 and UCPD Art. 7 rather than DSA Art. 26(1). Note also that this obligation binds the platform provider; the advertiser satisfies it by ensuring the label is applied.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Maintain the clear paid-partnership label on every post and story and ensure the advertiser identity (GlowCosmetics) is unambiguous in real time. Add a per-post 'AI/virtual character' indicator to close the transparency gap that arises under adjacent regimes and reinforce the DSA ad-identification purpose.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits online platform providers from designing interfaces that deceive or manipulate users' ability to make free and informed decisions, and captures 'disguised ads'. Here the undisclosed synthetic persona plausibly distorts consumer decision-making, but Art. 25 targets the platform operator's interface design, not the advertiser's creative. As GlowCosmetics/StudioNine are advertisers rather than the platform provider, this is flagged as context only; the deceptive-design substance is addressed under UCPD (misleading practices) by the parallel review.
findings.evidence_quote: Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits
findings.recommendation: Even though Art. 25 binds the platform, avoid conduct that a platform's own dark-pattern controls could flag: disclose the virtual/AI nature at the point of engagement so posts are not experienced as disguised or deceptive, reducing the risk of the platform restricting the campaign.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's advertising and interface obligations fall primarily on online platform providers, not on the advertiser/agency behind this campaign; the marketer's direct DSA exposure is therefore limited. The paid-partnership label satisfies the core "this is an advertisement / on whose behalf" element of Art. 26(1), so ad transparency is largely met. The undisclosed synthetic/AI nature of "Mira" that misleads consumers is chiefly a UCPD misleading-omission and AI Act transparency issue rather than a DSA breach by this advertiser. Because the campaign declares no personalisation/targeting, the profiling-based ad bans (Arts. 26(3) and 28) are not engaged. Findings below are flagged for awareness of the platform-facing obligations the campaign interacts with.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Mira is a commissioned AI-generated persona (by StudioNine) presenting a first-person consumer endorsement of the serum. Presenting a synthetic, non-human persona's fabricated 'experience' as a genuine consumer endorsement misrepresents a social endorsement to promote the product. This is a blacklisted practice prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 23c, independent of any average-consumer/materiality test. Consumer confusion ('ask which dermatologist she visits') confirms the endorsement is being taken as a real human's.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Do not present AI-generated personas as making genuine first-person consumer experience/endorsement claims. Reframe copy so it is not a personal testimonial (e.g. describe product attributes, not 'my texture'), and prominently, per-post, label Mira as a virtual/AI character so no genuine consumer endorsement is implied.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: A first-person efficacy testimonial delivered by a photorealistic entity consumers believe is human deceives the average consumer about the existence and nature of the endorsement and about the product's benefits/results — an AI persona has no skin and no genuine 'results'. This deception is liable to cause a transactional decision (purchasing the serum) that consumers would not otherwise take, satisfying Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: 'my texture has never been this smooth'
findings.recommendation: Remove implied real-world efficacy claims attributed to a synthetic persona, or substantiate product benefit claims independently and clearly disclose that any 'before/after' or experiential imagery is AI-generated and not a real user result.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The synthetic/virtual nature of the influencer is material information the average consumer needs to weigh a testimonial. Placing the disclosure only in the account bio ('virtual personality by StudioNine') provides it in an unclear and untimely manner — it does not travel with the individual posts/stories consumers actually see, and demonstrable consumer confusion proves the omission is misleading in context. Note the commercial-intent element is met via the paid-partnership label; the failure here is the omitted synthetic-nature fact.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, per-post and per-story indicator on every piece of content that Mira is an AI-generated/virtual character (e.g. a persistent 'AI virtual influencer' tag near the caption), not only in the bio, so the disclosure is timely and prominent to every viewer.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a photorealistic AI-generated influencer ('Mira') presenting first-person 'skin-journey' testimonials for GlowCosmetics serums. The paid-partnership label is present (so the pure ad-disclosure/advertorial concern under Annex I point 11 is largely met), but the synthetic/non-human nature of the endorser is not disclosed on individual posts and stories, and commenters demonstrably believe Mira is a real person. This engages a blacklisted practice (Annex I point 23c — false/misrepresented endorsement) and misleading action/omission under Arts. 6 and 7. The first-person efficacy testimonial from a persona that has no skin or real experience is inherently misleading.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses "Mira," a photorealistic AI-generated influencer, to promote GlowCosmetics serums through first-person "skin-journey" testimonials and fan replies. The core problem is that Mira's synthetic, non-human nature is not disclosed on the individual posts and stories people actually see — the only hint sits in the account bio, and commenters demonstrably believe she is a real person and ask which dermatologist she visits. This triggers several serious issues at once. Most seriously, presenting a fabricated AI "consumer experience" as a genuine endorsement is a blacklisted unfair practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I 23c) — prohibited outright, with no defence — and the first-person efficacy claims ("my texture has never been this smooth") are misleading actions and omissions. The AI Act separately requires clear disclosure that this content is AI-generated and machine-readable marking of the synthetic images, neither of which is satisfied. GDPR and DSA exposure is comparatively limited (no data collection or personalisation declared), though the ongoing replies to real commenters under a concealed persona raise a fairness flag. Verdict: the campaign is not launch-ready as described and needs fixing before it runs in the EU.
recommendations: Stop presenting Mira as a real consumer giving a genuine endorsement. Rewrite the first-person testimonial copy ('my texture has never been this smooth', dermatologist/routine narratives) so it describes product attributes rather than a personal lived experience — this addresses the blacklisted-practice risk (UCPD Annex I 23c) that applies regardless of any disclosure.

Add a clear, prominent AI/virtual-character label on every individual post, story and reply (not just the account bio) so viewers understand at the point of consumption that Mira is AI-generated and non-human. The paid-partnership tag does NOT satisfy this — it discloses payment, not that the persona is synthetic (AI Act Art. 50(4); UCPD Art. 7).

Ensure all AI-generated images and copy carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g., C2PA content credentials or equivalent watermarking) and confirm your generative-AI provider implements compliant marking (AI Act Art. 50(2)).

Clarify whether Mira's replies to fans are automated. If AI-driven, add a persistent 'AI/automated account' indicator and stop replies that reinforce a false human identity or invent real-world routines/dermatologists (AI Act Art. 50(1); GDPR fairness).
Substantiate any product-efficacy claim independently, and clearly flag that any before/after or experiential imagery is AI-generated and not a real user result (UCPD Art. 6).

Given this beauty/skincare content realistically reaches under-18s, do not add any data-collection mechanic (contests, sign-ups, DM capture) without age assurance and, for under-16s, verified parental consent and child-appropriate transparency (GDPR Arts. 8 and 12).

campaign.title: RideLink surge notice
campaign.text: A ride-hailing app applies demand-based multipliers. Before booking, the screen shows: 'High demand — prices are 1.8x normal right now', the full fare estimate, and a 'wait for lower prices' option with a price alert. The multiplier is identical for all users in the zone (no individual profiling) and the promised fare is honoured. Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19' with the range and surge caveat in the same font size.

detected_practices: dynamic surge pricing with disclosed multiplier
pre-booking price transparency (full fare estimate)
'wait for lower prices' price-alert option
'from €19' promotional pricing with range and surge caveat shown in same font size
app-push notification marketing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult app users in EU markets.
