Surge pricing is uniform per zone with no individual profiling, but app usage and push notifications inherently involve personal data (device/account identifiers, location for zone-based pricing, and consent for push messaging), warranting GDPR review. UCPD applies as a consumer-facing campaign — the '€19 from'/surge caveat presentation and 'high demand' framing should be checked for misleading pricing/drip-pricing concerns.
triage.summary: A ride-hailing app uses zone-wide, non-individualised demand-based surge pricing, disclosing the multiplier, full fare estimate, and a 'wait for lower prices' alert before booking. Push marketing advertises 'weekend airport fares from €19' with the price range and surge caveat shown in equal font size. No generative AI or individual profiling is declared.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: App-push marketing is direct marketing delivered to identifiable users via device/account identifiers, constituting processing of personal data that requires a valid lawful basis. Under the ePrivacy regime read with GDPR, unsolicited electronic direct-marketing messages generally require prior consent. The campaign does not state any lawful basis (consent or otherwise) for sending marketing push notifications.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19'
findings.recommendation: Document and rely on a valid lawful basis for push marketing — in practice prior opt-in consent for the marketing push channel (or a defensible soft opt-in/legitimate-interest assessment where legally available). Ensure the app onboarding captures a granular, separate marketing-push consent distinct from transactional notifications.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is the basis for the app-push marketing channel, it must be freely given, specific, unbundled and as easy to withdraw as to give (Art. 7). The campaign gives no indication that push-marketing consent is separated from operational notifications or that withdrawal is straightforward, so the conditions for valid consent cannot be assumed met.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: app, app-push
findings.recommendation: Provide a clearly distinguishable, unbundled opt-in for marketing pushes, in plain language, and an equally easy toggle to withdraw consent in the app settings without dark-pattern friction. Retain records demonstrating consent.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing at any time. Every marketing push must respect and facilitate this opt-out. The campaign describes no unsubscribe/opt-out affordance within or accompanying the marketing pushes.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19'
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, functioning opt-out in every marketing push (e.g., in-message link or reference to a one-tap settings toggle) and suppress marketing to any user who objects, keeping a suppression list.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Zone-based surge pricing relies on the user's location data, which is personal data collected via the app. Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, users be informed of the controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and their rights. The campaign flow (pre-booking screen and push channel) does not evidence that this information is provided at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: The multiplier is identical for all users in the zone (no individual profiling)
findings.recommendation: Ensure a layered privacy notice is accessible at the point location data is collected (and at push opt-in), covering purposes (zone pricing, marketing), legal basis, retention and data-subject rights, with a link from the relevant screens.

verdicts.notes: The campaign does not involve individual profiling, personalised pricing, generative AI, minors, or special-category data, so the higher-risk GDPR provisions (Arts. 4(4), 9, 22) are not engaged. However, it inherently processes personal data: app-push marketing (a direct marketing channel) and location/zone data for surge pricing. The submission is silent on the lawful basis, consent for push messaging, transparency at point of collection, and an opt-out mechanism. These are engaged obligations that appear addressable but are not evidenced as satisfied — hence flagged for attention rather than as clear violations.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: A 'from' entry-price claim is a statement about price/manner of price calculation under Art. 6(1)(d). It is only misleading if the €19 fare is not genuinely available for a meaningful number of the advertised weekend airport journeys, or is achievable only in unrealistic conditions. The campaign already mitigates the drip-pricing risk by showing the price range and surge caveat in the same font size, so this is a substantiation check rather than a likely breach.
findings.evidence_quote: weekend airport fares from €19
findings.recommendation: Keep records substantiating that the €19 fare is actually obtainable on the advertised weekend airport routes for a reasonable proportion of trips, and continue displaying the full range and surge caveat with equal prominence. If €19 is rarely achievable, requalify the claim (e.g. 'fares typically €19–€X').

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Assessed and NOT engaged: Annex I point 7 blacklists FALSE limited-time/availability claims used to force an immediate decision. Here the high-demand pricing is genuine and uniform per zone, the full fare is disclosed pre-booking, the fare is honoured, and the app expressly offers a 'wait for lower prices' option — the opposite of depriving the consumer of time to decide. Flagged only to record that the practice was examined against the false-urgency prohibition and found compliant.
findings.evidence_quote: High demand — prices are 1.8x normal right now
findings.recommendation: No action required. Maintain the truthful, real-time demand disclosure and the 'wait for lower prices' alternative, and avoid layering any artificial countdowns or 'act now' pressure on top of the genuine surge notice.

verdicts.notes: On the UCPD dimension this campaign is well-constructed and does not appear to engage any prohibition. The surge multiplier is disclosed truthfully ("prices are 1.8x normal right now"), the full fare estimate is shown before booking, and the honoured fare plus a "wait for lower prices" option means there is no false urgency, no artificial scarcity and no pressure to decide immediately (Annex I point 7 not engaged). Price transparency addresses the drip-pricing concern under Art. 7, and the "from €19" claim shows the range and surge caveat in equal font size. The only residual UCPD point is an informational one: ensure the advertised "from €19" entry fare is genuinely achievable and representative for the advertised weekend airport routes so the price-advantage claim remains truthful under Art. 6(1)(d).

report.executive_summary: This campaign sends app and push notifications about RideLink's demand-based surge pricing and "weekend airport fares from €19", using uniform zone-based multipliers with no individual profiling. On the advertising/fairness side the campaign is well built: the surge is disclosed truthfully in real time, the full fare estimate is shown before booking, the fare is honoured, and a "wait for lower prices" option removes any false-urgency concern — so there is no clear consumer-protection breach. The main risks are on data protection. Marketing push notifications are direct marketing to identifiable users, and the submission is silent on the lawful basis, consent, opt-out mechanism, and transparency at the point location/zone data is collected. None of these are hard violations, but they are legal obligations that need to be evidenced before this goes live. Note the submission declares "no personalisation/targeting", which is accurate for pricing, but push marketing still triggers ePrivacy/GDPR consent and objection rights. Fix the consent and opt-out plumbing and keep records substantiating the "from €19" claim, and this campaign is in good shape.
recommendations: Obtain and document prior opt-in consent specifically for the marketing-push channel, separate (unbundled) from operational/transactional notifications, and keep records of that consent (GDPR Art. 6, 7 / ePrivacy).

Include a clear, functioning opt-out in every marketing push and honour it via a suppression list, plus an equally easy in-app toggle to withdraw consent without dark-pattern friction (GDPR Art. 21, 7).

Ensure a layered privacy notice is accessible where location/zone data and push consent are collected, covering purposes (zone pricing, marketing), legal basis, retention and data-subject rights (GDPR Art. 13).

Keep evidence substantiating that the '€19' entry fare is genuinely achievable and representative on the advertised weekend airport routes; requalify the claim (e.g. 'fares typically €19–€X') if it is rarely obtainable (UCPD Art. 6).
Maintain the current truthful surge disclosure, equal-prominence price range/caveat, and the 'wait for lower prices' option; do not add artificial countdowns or 'act now' pressure.

campaign.title: Mira.virtual x GlowCosmetics
campaign.text: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line, first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth'), and replies to fan comments about her 'routine'. The account bio states 'virtual personality by StudioNine'; individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication. Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.

detected_practices: AI-generated virtual influencer
influencer endorsement / paid partnership
first-person product testimonial from a non-human persona
implied personal skincare experience ('my texture has never been this smooth')
replies to fans about a fictional 'routine'
missing per-post AI/virtual disclosure (only bio-level disclosure)
implied efficacy / cosmetic health claims
consumers misled into believing influencer is human (asking about her dermatologist)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 18-30 young adults on social platforms, but beauty/skincare content of this type on open social channels is highly likely to reach under-18s, so minor exposure cannot be excluded. Personalisation/targeting was declared as not used, so GDPR is not flagged based on the declaration, though platform-side data processing should be reconsidered if targeting or profiling is later found. Key risks: AI Act Art. 50 transparency for AI-generated/deepfake content, DSA advertising/deceptive-content transparency obligations, and UCPD misleading-practice and disguised-advertising provisions given the human-impersonation and implied efficacy testimonials.
triage.summary: GlowCosmetics uses 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated virtual influencer (2.1M followers), to promote a skincare serum via first-person 'skin-journey' selfies and captions and by replying to fan comments as if human. Posts carry a paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual disclosure, and evidence in the comments shows real consumers believe Mira is a human with genuine skincare results and a dermatologist, raising deception and transparency concerns.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Mira is a 'photorealistic AI-generated influencer' whose selfies and first-person content constitute AI-generated/manipulated image (and likely video) content presenting a synthetic human likeness as if real — the paradigm case of a synthetic influencer / deep fake under Art. 50(4). As deployer of the AI system generating this content, GlowCosmetics/StudioNine must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. The bio note 'virtual personality by StudioNine' does not travel with individual posts, and the evidence that 'some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits' shows the required disclosure is not effective at the point of exposure.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, conspicuous AI-generated/virtual disclosure on every individual post, story and asset featuring Mira (e.g. a persistent on-content label such as 'AI-generated virtual influencer / synthetic image'), not merely in the account bio. Ensure the disclosure is presented at the latest at the moment of first exposure to each piece of content and is understandable to the average follower, including on reshared/embedded content.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The visual assets (and any AI-generated captions) are synthetic image/text outputs of a generative AI system. Under Art. 50(2), providers of the generating AI system must ensure such outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (e.g. watermarking / provenance metadata such as C2PA). Nothing in the campaign indicates machine-readable provenance marking is applied; the only mention of provenance is a human-readable bio note.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated influencer with 2.1M followers, posts a GlowCosmetics campaign: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line
findings.recommendation: Ensure the generative AI provider embeds machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g. C2PA content credentials or equivalent watermark) in all AI-generated Mira images, video and text, and verify this marking survives upload/compression on the social platforms used. Coordinate with StudioNine to confirm the provider meets Art. 50(2) at the point of generation.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of AI interaction (chatbots)
findings.rationale: If the fan-comment replies are generated or delivered by an AI system interacting directly with natural persons, Art. 50(1) requires those persons be informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the circumstances. Here it is plainly not obvious — commenters believe Mira is human and are asking a supposed real person about her dermatologist and skincare routine. The AI interaction is therefore undisclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: replies to fan comments about her 'routine'
findings.recommendation: If replies are AI-generated/automated, clearly disclose the AI nature of the interaction (e.g. an automated 'AI persona' indicator on replies or in-thread notice). If replies are actually written by humans on behalf of a synthetic persona, document this to establish Art. 50(1) does not apply — but note the human-impersonation/deception concern still stands under the transparency and misleading-practice regimes.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Using an AI persona to deliver first-person 'experience' testimonials that consumers cannot distinguish from a real human is a deceptive AI technique that impairs informed decision-making. However, Art. 5(1)(a) requires the deception to materially distort behaviour in a manner causing or likely to cause 'significant harm' — a high threshold that a cosmetics endorsement is unlikely to meet on these facts. Flagged for awareness; the deceptive-endorsement dimension is better addressed under the UCPD (misleading practices) and Art. 50 disclosure obligations above.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Treat this as a transparency issue rather than a prohibited practice: implement the Art. 50 disclosures. Avoid framing AI-generated persuasion in ways that could exploit vulnerable audiences (e.g. minors likely reached by open social beauty content), which would raise the risk profile toward Art. 5.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses 'Mira', a photorealistic AI-generated virtual influencer presented as a real human, to promote skincare. This squarely engages the AI Act's Art. 50 transparency regime. The most serious issue is the absence of any AI/synthetic disclosure on the individual posts and stories (only a bio-level 'virtual personality' note), while the content itself is a photorealistic synthetic likeness and consumers demonstrably believe Mira is human. Art. 50(4) deep fake/synthetic-content disclosure and Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking are both engaged and appear unmet; Art. 50(1) is engaged for the AI-driven fan replies. The Art. 5(1)(a) manipulation prohibition is noted but likely does not reach its 'significant harm' threshold here.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires recipients to identify, clearly and unambiguously, that content is an advertisement and on whose behalf. The paid-partnership label satisfies the 'this is an ad / on whose behalf' element. However, the endorsement is delivered through a non-human synthetic persona presented as a real person, so the disclosure is incomplete as to the true nature of the ad content. The core AI/virtual disclosure gap is governed by AI Act Art. 50(4) and UCPD, but it also weakens the 'clear and unambiguous' ad-identification objective the platform must ensure under Art. 26(1).
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Ensure every post/story bears an in-content, real-time ad label alongside a clear virtual/AI-persona indicator, so recipients can identify both that it is an advertisement and that the endorser is a computer-generated character rather than a human user of the platform.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The dark-patterns concept under Art. 25 expressly covers disguised advertisements and communication design that deceives or manipulates recipients and materially impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. A photorealistic AI persona posting first-person 'skin-journey' testimonials and replying to fans as if human creates a deceptive on-platform experience — evidenced by real consumers believing Mira is a human with genuine results and a dermatologist. While Art. 25 binds the online platform provider directly, the campaign is architected to produce exactly this deception and should be remediated by the advertiser.
findings.evidence_quote: Some commenters clearly believe Mira is human and ask which dermatologist she visits.
findings.recommendation: Redesign the on-platform experience so the account and its interactions cannot deceive recipients into believing Mira is a real human: add persistent per-post/per-story and per-reply AI/virtual labelling, avoid first-person claims of lived physical experience, and configure replies so they cannot be read as a real person's personal skincare account.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Beauty/skincare influencer content on open social channels is highly likely to reach under-18s, so Art. 28's high level of privacy/safety for minors and its ban on profiling-based advertising to minors are potentially in scope for the platform. On the facts as declared, no profiling or targeting is used, so the specific profiling-ad-to-minors prohibition is not triggered by the described conduct; this is flagged for awareness rather than as a likely breach.
findings.evidence_quote: young adults 18-30
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document that no profiling/targeting is applied to this campaign; if any behavioural targeting is later introduced, exclude audiences reasonably certain to be minors and apply age-appropriate design measures for content that predictably reaches under-18s.

verdicts.notes: The DSA obligations here fall mainly on platform providers/VLOPs rather than the advertiser directly, but the campaign's design engages several DSA concepts. Ad identification under Art. 26(1) appears substantially met via the paid-partnership label, though the undisclosed AI/virtual nature (primarily an AI Act Art. 50 / UCPD matter) undermines "clear and unambiguous" identification of the true nature of the endorsement. The human-impersonating persona that leaves real consumers believing Mira is human engages the disguised-advertising/deceptive-design concept behind Art. 25. Minor exposure is plausible, but since no profiling/targeting is declared, the Art. 28 profiling-ad ban is not triggered on the facts as described.

findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Annex I point 23c prohibits, in all circumstances, misrepresenting endorsements to promote a product. Mira presents a genuine, lived first-person testimonial of using the serum ('my texture has never been this smooth') and replies to fans about her 'routine'. As an AI-generated persona incapable of using cosmetics or having a skin journey, this endorsement of personal product experience is inherently false and misrepresented. The evidence that real commenters believe she is human and ask which dermatologist she visits confirms the misrepresentation is operative.
findings.evidence_quote: first-person skin-journey captions ('my texture has never been this smooth')
findings.recommendation: Do not present product experience as a genuine first-person testimonial from a non-human persona. Reframe copy so it cannot read as lived experience (e.g. 'GlowCosmetics serum — a virtual character created by StudioNine'), and remove or restructure fan replies that reinforce a fictional personal 'routine'. Any efficacy statements should come from substantiated brand claims, not a fabricated personal endorsement.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 covers practices that deceive the average consumer about the nature of the product/endorser and the product's main characteristics and results, causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The photorealistic AI persona shown 'wearing' the serum with smooth-skin imagery falsely implies real-world results achieved by a real user, deceiving consumers about the results/benefits of the product and about the nature/authenticity of the endorsement. Consumer confusion is documented ('ask which dermatologist she visits').
findings.evidence_quote: selfies 'wearing' the new serum line
findings.recommendation: Ensure the imagery and claims do not imply real human results attributable to product use. Present the AI-generated visuals honestly (they are not photographs of a person using the product) and substantiate any implied efficacy with genuine evidence rather than synthetic 'before/after' impressions.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 treats as misleading the omission or unclear/untimely provision of material information the average consumer needs. That the influencer is an AI-generated virtual persona rather than a real human user is material to how consumers weigh a first-person skincare testimonial. Disclosing this only in the account bio, while individual posts and stories omit it, provides the information in an unclear and untimely manner — and the recorded confusion shows the average consumer does not receive it at the point of exposure.
findings.evidence_quote: individual posts and stories carry the paid-partnership label but no AI/virtual indication
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent per-post and per-story indication that Mira is a virtual/AI-generated character (not just a bio note), placed so it is seen before or with the content, alongside the existing paid-partnership label. This aligns with the AI Act Art. 50(4) transparency obligation and cures the UCPD omission.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses a photorealistic AI-generated influencer to deliver first-person, experiential product testimonials ("my texture has never been this smooth") and to converse with fans as though she were a human user of the serum. Consumers are demonstrably deceived (asking about "her dermatologist"). While the paid-partnership label satisfies advertorial disclosure (Annex I point 11), the fabricated personal endorsement and the concealment of Mira's non-human nature engage the misleading-practice provisions and, most seriously, the blacklisted prohibition on misrepresenting endorsements. AI-nature transparency itself is primarily an AI Act/DSA matter, but the resulting consumer deception is squarely a UCPD problem.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses "Mira," a photorealistic AI-generated influencer, to promote GlowCosmetics serum through first-person "skin journey" posts and fan replies that read as a real person's lived experience. The core problem is that nothing in the individual posts, stories, or replies tells people Mira is not human — only the account bio does — and real followers are already fooled, asking which dermatologist "she" visits. This triggers the most serious category of violation under EU consumer law: presenting a fake personal endorsement from a persona who cannot actually use the product (a blacklisted practice that is prohibited outright, with no balancing test). On top of that, the campaign breaches the AI Act's transparency rules requiring AI-generated content to be clearly disclosed and machine-readably marked, and it feeds the DSA's deceptive-design concerns. The paid-partnership label is fine as far as it goes, but it does not cure the fact that consumers are being misled about who Mira is and what the serum actually does. This cannot go live as designed. GDPR is not engaged, and the minor-targeting ad ban is not triggered because no profiling is declared.
recommendations: Stop presenting product results as a genuine first-person testimonial from Mira. Rewrite all copy so it cannot read as lived personal experience (e.g. reframe as 'GlowCosmetics serum, featuring Mira — a virtual character by StudioNine'). This addresses the critical blacklisted fake-endorsement violation that has no legal defence.

Add a clear, prominent AI/virtual disclosure to every individual post, story, and reply — not just the bio — visible at the moment of first exposure and on any reshared content. This resolves both the AI Act Art. 50(4) and UCPD misleading-omission problems.

Fix the fan replies: if they are automated/AI-generated, label them as an AI persona; if human-written, document this and still remove content that reinforces a fictional personal 'routine' or implies a real dermatologist visit.
Ensure any implied efficacy (smooth skin, 'wearing' the serum) is backed by genuine substantiated brand evidence, not synthetic imagery that suggests real human results.

Coordinate with StudioNine and the generative AI provider to embed machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA / watermark) in all AI images, video, and text, and verify it survives platform upload/compression.
Keep the existing paid-partnership label and pair it with the AI/virtual indicator on every asset to satisfy DSA ad-identification expectations.
Confirm and document that no profiling/targeting is used; if behavioural targeting is later added, exclude audiences reasonably certain to be minors given beauty content's likely reach to under-18s.

campaign.title: RideLink surge notice
campaign.text: A ride-hailing app applies demand-based multipliers. Before booking, the screen shows: 'High demand — prices are 1.8x normal right now', the full fare estimate, and a 'wait for lower prices' option with a price alert. The multiplier is identical for all users in the zone (no individual profiling) and the promised fare is honoured. Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19' with the range and surge caveat in the same font size.

detected_practices: surge/dynamic pricing (demand-based multiplier)
price transparency disclosure (multiplier and full fare estimate shown pre-booking)
'from' price advertising with stated range and surge caveat
'wait for lower prices' price alert option
app-push notification marketing
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult app users in the EU. No individual profiling declared and the multiplier is zone-uniform; personal data flagged because app-push marketing to logged-in users involves processing of identifiable user data and requires a lawful basis/consent for electronic marketing.
triage.summary: A ride-hailing app runs demand-based surge pricing with pre-booking disclosure of the multiplier and full fare estimate, a zone-uniform (non-individualised) multiplier, and app-push ads advertising 'from €19' weekend airport fares with the range and surge caveat in equal font size. Pricing appears transparent and honoured, but 'from' price advertising and surge framing warrant UCPD review, and app-push messaging to identifiable app users implicates GDPR/ePrivacy consent for marketing communications.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: App-push marketing communications to logged-in, identifiable users constitute processing of personal data for direct marketing, which requires a valid lawful basis. Electronic marketing messages generally require prior consent (Art. 6(1) read with ePrivacy Directive Art. 13); the campaign is silent on whether a lawful basis/consent exists for these pushes.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes announce 'weekend airport fares from €19'
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document a lawful basis for the marketing pushes — typically prior opt-in consent for electronic marketing, or a soft-opt-in/legitimate-interest analysis where applicable. Keep transactional surge notices (shown pre-booking) distinct from promotional pushes, since the latter carry the marketing-consent requirement.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct marketing communication must respect and facilitate the absolute right to object. The promotional airport-fare pushes are direct marketing, but the campaign describes no opt-out mechanism for the marketing messages.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: app, app-push
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, easy-to-use opt-out for marketing pushes (e.g. an in-app toggle and an unsubscribe/settings link referenced in each promotional message), ensure objections are honoured immediately, and maintain a suppression record.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (device/account identifiers) is used to deliver marketing pushes, users must have been informed at collection of the purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and their rights. This is a standard information-obligation touchpoint rather than an evident deficiency in the campaign text.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: app users, adults
findings.recommendation: Verify the app's privacy notice covers use of account/device data for marketing communications, including purpose, legal basis and the right to object, and that it was provided at the point of data collection (registration).

verdicts.notes: The campaign's only GDPR footprint is app-push marketing to identifiable, logged-in app users; the surge-pricing mechanic itself uses a zone-uniform, non-individualised multiplier and explicitly involves no profiling or personalisation, so Arts. 4(4), 22 and 9 are not engaged. Direct marketing pushes to identifiable users require a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1), with ePrivacy consent for electronic marketing) and must facilitate the absolute right to object (Art. 21). The campaign text is silent on consent capture and opt-out, so no breach is evident, but these obligations must be satisfied operationally.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits FALSELY stating limited-time terms to pressure an immediate decision. The multiplier here is described as genuine, identical for all users in the zone, and honoured, and a 'wait for lower prices' option is offered — so the urgency claim is truthful and non-coercive. The blacklist prohibition is therefore not triggered; flagged only so that the '1.8x normal' baseline and surge state must always reflect the real demand condition to stay outside this prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: High demand — prices are 1.8x normal right now
findings.recommendation: Ensure the stated multiplier and the 'normal' reference price are always factually accurate and auditable in real time; never display a surge/urgency state when demand does not actually justify it, and retain logs demonstrating the multiplier was genuine.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: 'From' price advertising risks misleading omission under Art. 7 if the headline entry price obscures that most consumers pay more or that surge applies. As described, the campaign mitigates this by presenting the fare range and the surge caveat in the same font size as the headline, so the material information is given clearly and with equal prominence. The omission risk is therefore addressed as described, but remains the practice's main UCPD-sensitive point.
findings.evidence_quote: weekend airport fares from €19
findings.recommendation: Keep the fare range and surge caveat at equal prominence to the '€19' figure across all creatives and screen sizes, and ensure the €19 entry fare is genuinely available on the advertised weekend routes; monitor availability so the headline price is not effectively unattainable.

verdicts.notes: As described, the campaign is UCPD-compliant. The surge messaging ("1.8x normal right now") is a genuine, zone-uniform, honoured multiplier — not a false urgency/scarcity claim, so Annex I point 7 is not engaged. The "wait for lower prices" alert actively reduces pressure, so there is no aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9). Pre-booking display of the full fare estimate and the equal-font-size disclosure of the range and surge caveat satisfy the transparency expectations of Arts. 6-7; the only residual UCPD touchpoint is the "from €19" headline, which is adequately qualified here but must remain accurate in practice.

report.executive_summary:
This campaign shows a ride-hailing surge-pricing notice in-app plus marketing pushes advertising "weekend airport fares from €19." As described, it is largely compliant. The surge mechanic is well-designed from a fairness perspective: the 1.8x multiplier is uniform across all users in a zone (no profiling), the full fare is shown before booking, the promised price is honoured, and a "wait for lower prices" option removes any high-pressure element — so there is no false-urgency or misleading-omission problem under consumer protection rules, provided the "from €19" headline and the surge caveat stay equally prominent and genuinely available. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. The main open items are procedural, not substantive: because the marketing pushes go to logged-in, identifiable users, you need a documented lawful basis (typically prior opt-in consent for electronic marketing) and an easy opt-out honoured immediately. Nothing in the submission shows a breach, but consent capture, opt-out and privacy-notice coverage must be confirmed operationally before launch. Overall risk is low and the campaign can proceed once the GDPR/ePrivacy housekeeping is verified.</parameter>
<parameter name="recommendations">Confirm and document a lawful basis for the marketing pushes — normally prior opt-in consent for electronic marketing (ePrivacy), or a soft-opt-in/legitimate-interest assessment where it applies. Keep this separate from the transactional pre-booking surge notice, which is not marketing.

campaign.title: VoltRush energy drink stream sponsorships
campaign.text: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code. Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting; no profiling of minors is requested. Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
campaign.target_audience: declared 18+ gaming audience with substantial minor spillover

detected_practices: streaming sponsorship with animated brand overlays
influencer/streamer shout-outs (undisclosed advertising risk)
discount code promotion
interest-based ad targeting ('gaming interest, 18+')
high-caffeine product marketing without warning in creatives
meme-format creatives and use of a streamer popular with young teens
triage.audience_notes: Declared 18+ gaming audience, but brand's own analytics indicate substantial minor spillover (~34% aged 13-17). No profiling of minors is requested, but the actual reach to minors and the appeal of the streamer/creative formats to young teens raise concerns under DSA (advertising to minors, transparency) and UCPD (vulnerable audience, misleading omission of caffeine warning). GDPR engaged via personalised targeting and audience analytics processing.
triage.summary: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams using animated overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, buying interest-based '18+' targeting in EU markets. Despite a declared adult audience, analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and creatives use meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The high-caffeine warning appears on pack but not in the overlays, and the sponsored nature/ad disclosure may be insufficient.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Interest-based ad targeting that segments audiences by 'gaming interest' and age is automated processing to evaluate personal preferences and interests, which meets the GDPR definition of profiling. This characterisation triggers the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection).
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document that the interest-based targeting constitutes profiling and map the underlying data flows (who profiles, on what data, whether the brand acts as controller/joint controller with the platform) before running the campaign.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised/interest-based advertising generally requires either valid consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign relies on the platform's interest and declared-age targeting but does not identify any lawful basis for processing the personal data used to target and reach viewers, nor evidence of a legitimate-interest balancing test or consent capture.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and document the lawful basis for the targeting (typically consent obtained via the platform, or a documented LIA). Obtain contractual assurances/DPA terms from the platform confirming a valid basis exists for the targeting segments the brand purchases, and record joint-controller/processor roles as appropriate.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The brand receives audience analytics derived from viewers' personal data. Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. There is no indication that viewers are informed the brand receives audience/age analytics about them, and the fairness principle is strained where the brand knowingly benefits from data about a large minor audience it is not supposed to be reaching.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Ensure the analytics the brand receives are aggregated/anonymised so no personal data is processed, or, if personal data is involved, ensure a lawful basis and transparent information exist. Assess and mitigate the fairness implications of continuing to rely on analytics that reveal a substantial minor audience.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where a discount code drives viewers to redeem it (e.g. on a website or at checkout, or to sign up), the brand collects personal data and must provide Art. 13 information at the point of collection — identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and rights, including any profiling. The campaign describes no such transparency provision.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: At any redemption/sign-up touchpoint triggered by the discount code, present a layered privacy notice meeting Art. 13 (identity, purposes, legal basis, retention, recipients, data-subject rights, and profiling information) before data is collected.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling connected to direct marketing carries an absolute right to object. The campaign describes no mechanism for recipients to object to the profiling-based advertising or to opt out of the marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+'
findings.recommendation: Provide and clearly signpost an easy way for individuals to object to marketing profiling (e.g. via the platform's ad-preference controls and the brand's own privacy notice), and ensure objections are honoured.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The brand knows from its own analytics that roughly a third of the audience are children aged 13-17. Where consent is the lawful basis for targeting in the context of an information society service, children below the applicable age (16, or 13-15 depending on Member State) cannot give valid consent without parental authorisation. Because the '18+' declared-age targeting is demonstrably failing to exclude minors, any consent-based targeting data almost certainly includes children whose consent is invalid, and no age-verification or parental-consent safeguards are described.
findings.evidence_quote: no profiling of minors is requested... an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on consent-based targeting data that may originate from minors. Strengthen age assurance beyond declared-age targeting, exclude segments/streamers with known heavy minor audiences, and where data of under-16s could be processed, ensure parental consent with reasonable verification efforts — or suppress the campaign on inventory with substantial minor reach.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses interest-based ad targeting ('gaming interest, 18+') and receives audience analytics with viewer age breakdowns — both constitute processing of personal data / profiling under GDPR that require a valid lawful basis, transparency and respect for the right to object. No lawful basis, consent mechanism, transparency notice or opt-out is described. Critically, the brand's own analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, so any consent-based targeting data will include minors who cannot validly consent (Art. 8), and the awareness of substantial minor reach undermines the reliability of the '18+' targeting basis. No special-category data (Art. 9) or solely-automated significant decisions (Art. 22) are evidenced.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using the personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign uses interest/profiling-based targeting ('gaming interest') and the advertiser possesses its own analytics showing that roughly a third of the audience actually reached is 13-17. That documented knowledge undermines reliance on the platform's 'declared-age, 18+' setting: profiled ads are demonstrably reaching a large, identified minor cohort, and the advertiser is aware of it. Combined with creatives and a streamer chosen for appeal to young teens, this presents a real risk that profiling-based advertising is being served to minors contrary to Art. 28.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17.
findings.recommendation: Stop relying on declared-age targeting alone. Either (a) switch the minor-reaching portion of the buy to non-profiled/contextual placement (no behavioural profiling), or (b) require the platform to exclude recipients reasonably certain to be minors and to confirm profiling is disabled for that inventory. Document that the ~34% minor-reach data has been acted upon, and drop or replace streamer/creative choices whose primary appeal is to under-18s where profiling-based delivery cannot be excluded.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, plus meaningful information on the main targeting parameters. Paid streamer shout-outs and animated brand overlays are advertising presented on an online platform; the submission itself flags that 'the sponsored nature/ad disclosure may be insufficient.' Without a clear, real-time ad label and advertiser identification, the transparency obligation is engaged and likely not satisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every sponsored stream segment and overlay carries a clear, real-time advertising label (e.g. persistent 'Ad / Paid partnership with VoltRush' disclosure), identifies VoltRush as the advertiser/payer, and that streamers verbally and on-screen disclose the paid nature of shout-outs. Use the platform's native paid-partnership/ad-disclosure tools so the labelling meets Art. 26(1).

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) bans platform ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories (health, ethnicity, religion, etc.). The targeting described uses only a gaming-interest segment and an age gate; no sensitive attribute is targeted directly or by evident proxy. The high-caffeine warning is product labelling, not health-based targeting. Flagged only to confirm it was assessed and that no special-category targeting must be introduced.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+'
findings.recommendation: Do not enrich the targeting with any special-category signals (e.g. health, fitness-condition or diet inferences) that could be treated as Art. 9 data; keep the segment limited to non-sensitive interest and age parameters.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA through personalised/interest-based ad targeting on a streaming platform with streamer shout-outs and brand overlays. The central DSA concern is Art. 28: the brand buys profiling-based ("gaming interest") advertising and its own analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, meaning profiled ads are in fact being served to a substantial minor audience. Art. 26(1) advertising-transparency (clear ad/sponsorship labelling in real time) is also engaged for the streamer shout-outs and overlays. Art. 26(3) (special-category targeting) is not engaged — only gaming interest is used. Note the platform bears the primary compliance duty for Arts. 26–28/39, but the advertiser's media buy and audience knowledge create shared exposure.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Paid/incentivised streamer promotion and a promotional discount code are commercial communications. Under Art. 7(2) the commercial intent of a practice must be identifiable if not apparent from context. The submission contains no indication that the sponsorship/shout-outs are labelled as advertising (e.g. 'ad'/'sponsored'/'paid partnership'), so the material connection between brand and streamer is undisclosed, constituting hidden commercial intent.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Require clear, prominent and persistent ad disclosure in every sponsored segment: on-stream 'Sponsored by VoltRush / #ad' labels during shout-outs, disclosure in the stream title/description, and verbal disclosure by the streamer. Contractually mandate and monitor these disclosures.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: Where a trader pays for promotion within editorial-style/creator content without making the paid nature clear through identifiable images or sounds, the practice is a blacklisted advertorial prohibited in all circumstances. Streamer shout-outs embedded in the creator's own stream, presented without clear paid-promotion identification, fall within this prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure the paid nature is made unambiguous within the content itself via clearly identifiable persistent visual/audio labelling for the whole sponsored portion, not just platform metadata; document the sponsorship terms to demonstrate compliance.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The high-caffeine warning is material information a consumer needs, especially given a high-caffeine product reaching a large minor cohort. Presenting the product in animated overlays and streamer promotion while omitting the warning provides the marketing message in a way that omits material safety information (Art. 7 misleading omission), and the warning is untimely/absent at the point the promotional decision is prompted.
findings.evidence_quote: The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
findings.recommendation: Include the high-caffeine advisory (e.g. 'High caffeine content — not recommended for children') legibly within the animated overlays and any point-of-promotion creative, matching the on-pack warning.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires assessing practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (by age/credulity) from that group's perspective. The brand's own analytics show a substantial minor audience and the creatives use meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens, foreseeably steering minors toward a high-caffeine product without the safety warning — contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Given known ~34% minor spillover, apply professional-diligence safeguards: adjust media placement to reduce minor reach, avoid streamers/creative formats disproportionately appealing to under-18s, and ensure caffeine warnings and non-appeal-to-minors measures are built into all creatives; document a decision to withdraw or re-target if minor reach cannot be reduced.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 prohibits direct exhortations to children to buy, or to pester adults to buy. The campaign reaches many minors and uses child-appealing formats, but the submitted text contains no verbatim direct exhortation ('buy now', 'ask your parents'). The slogan 'power your grind' and a discount code are not, as quoted, a direct exhortation. Flagged for monitoring in case live shout-out scripts add such phrasing.
findings.evidence_quote: a streamer popular with young teens
findings.recommendation: Prohibit in streamer briefs any direct purchase exhortations or pester-power phrasing; monitor live shout-outs and code-promotion wording to ensure no 'buy it now'-style calls to action are directed at the young-teen audience.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages several UCPD prohibitions. Paid streamer shout-outs and a discount code are commercial communications whose commercial intent must be disclosed; nothing in the submission indicates ad labelling, engaging Art. 7 and the Annex I point 11 advertorial blacklist. The mandatory high-caffeine warning appears on pack but is omitted from the overlays — a misleading omission of material safety information under Art. 7, made more serious because ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17 and the creative formats/streamer are chosen to appeal to young teens, triggering the vulnerable-audience assessment under Art. 5(3). No verbatim direct exhortation to children is present, so Annex I point 28 is flagged as attention rather than a confirmed breach.

report.executive_summary: This campaign sponsors live gaming streams for the VoltRush energy drink using animated overlays, paid streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest-based targeting set to "gaming interest, 18+." The core problem is that your own audience analytics show roughly 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and the creatives and chosen streamer appeal to young teens — so the "18+" setting is demonstrably not working, and you have documented knowledge of a large minor audience. This creates serious, overlapping risks: consumer-protection breaches are likely because the sponsorships are not clearly labelled as ads and the mandatory high-caffeine warning is missing from the creatives (both especially serious given the minor spillover). Under the DSA, serving profiling-based ads to recipients you know with reasonable certainty are minors is prohibited. Under the GDPR, consent-based targeting data that includes under-16s cannot be validly relied upon, and no lawful basis, transparency notice or opt-out is described. The AI Act does not apply. As submitted, the campaign should not run in its current form — it needs disclosure fixes, the caffeine warning added to creatives, and a fundamental change to how the minor-reaching inventory is bought and targeted.
recommendations: Stop relying on declared-age '18+' targeting alone: switch the minor-reaching portion of the buy to non-profiled/contextual placement, or require the platform to confirm profiling is disabled and minors are excluded — because your own 34% minor-reach data shows the current setup is failing (DSA Art. 28, GDPR Art. 8).

Add the high-caffeine advisory (e.g. 'High caffeine content — not recommended for children') legibly to all animated overlays and point-of-promotion creatives, matching the on-pack warning (UCPD Art. 7).

Require clear, persistent, real-time ad disclosure in every sponsored segment — on-screen 'Paid partnership with VoltRush / #ad' labels, stream title/description disclosure, and verbal disclosure by the streamer — and use the platform's native paid-partnership tools (UCPD Art. 7 & Annex I point 11; DSA Art. 26(1)).

Drop or replace streamer and creative choices whose primary appeal is to under-18s where profiling-based delivery cannot be excluded; if minor reach cannot be materially reduced, document a decision to withdraw or re-target the campaign (UCPD Art. 5(3), DSA Art. 28).

Establish and document a lawful basis for the targeting (platform-obtained consent or a documented legitimate-interest assessment), obtain DPA/joint-controller terms from the platform, and ensure the audience analytics you receive are aggregated/anonymised (GDPR Arts. 5, 6).

Provide GDPR-compliant transparency and opt-out: a layered Art. 13 privacy notice at any discount-code redemption/sign-up touchpoint, and a clearly signposted way to object to marketing profiling (GDPR Arts. 13, 21).

Instruct streamers in writing to avoid any direct purchase exhortations or 'ask your parents' pester-power phrasing, and monitor live shout-outs to enforce this (UCPD Annex I point 28); do not enrich targeting with any special-category/health signals (DSA Art. 26(3)).

triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is 18+ gaming, but the brand's own analytics reveal substantial minor spillover (est. 34% aged 13-17). Creative choices (memes, fast cuts, a streamer popular with young teens) and the omission of the caffeine warning from overlays heighten risk of unfair/misleading practices toward minors and questions around ad targeting and profiling under DSA (Art. 26/28 minor-protection and transparency) and GDPR (processing of viewer analytics/interest data, potential incidental minor data).
