triage.summary: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams with animated overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, using platform interest-based targeting declared as 18+. Although no minor profiling is requested, analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17 and creatives use youth-appealing meme formats and a streamer popular with teens, while the high-caffeine warning is omitted from overlays. This raises consumer-protection, ad-transparency/minor-targeting and data-processing concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Interest-based ad targeting on behavioural/interest segments ('gaming interest') is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal preferences and interests, which meets the definition of profiling. The brand also declares use of personalisation/targeting, confirming profiling is in scope.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document that interest-based targeting constitutes profiling, map exactly which data the platform uses to build the 'gaming interest' segment, and confirm the platform (and the brand as advertiser) can demonstrate the profiling is lawful and transparent to the individuals concerned.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling-based/personalised advertising requires a valid lawful basis (consent or a documented, balanced legitimate-interest assessment). The submission describes targeting and receipt of audience analytics but does not identify any lawful basis for the processing of the underlying interest/analytics data, so lawfulness cannot be demonstrated as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and document the lawful basis for the targeting and analytics processing (typically consent for behavioural advertising, or a robust LIA where permissible), and ensure the platform-advertiser controller/joint-controller allocation is defined in a data-processing/joint-controller arrangement.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The brand receives audience analytics (personal data derived from viewers) and thereby has actual knowledge that a substantial share of the audience are minors. Processing personal data — including analytics that reach and profile minors — must be fair and transparent. Continuing interest-based targeting while aware of significant minor exposure, without transparency or mitigation, risks breaching the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Act on the analytics: suppress/mitigate minor exposure, ensure the analytics processing is fair and transparent to data subjects, and record measures taken once minor spillover is known so processing does not become unfair or opaque.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: Where consent is the basis for processing minors' data in the context of information-society services (the streaming/targeting ecosystem), children below the applicable age (13-16 depending on Member State) require verifiable parental consent. Given documented awareness that many reached viewers are 13-17, any consent-based interest processing that captures these minors cannot be presumed valid without parental-consent handling and reasonable verification efforts.
findings.evidence_quote: estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Where processing of minors' data relies on consent, ensure age-gating and verifiable parental-consent mechanisms consistent with the applicable Member State digital-consent age, or exclude under-age data from the targeting/analytics; do not rely on the '18+' declaration alone given contrary analytics.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: If the discount code drives users to a redemption page, sign-up or lead-capture where personal data is collected, Art. 13 information (controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, rights, profiling info) must be provided at the point of collection. This is only weakly engaged on the current facts because no data-collection form is described in the overlay itself.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: If the discount code or any campaign endpoint collects personal data, provide a layered Art. 13 notice at the point of collection, and given the audience, present it in age-appropriate, plain language.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses interest-based ad targeting ("gaming interest, 18+") and receives audience analytics, both of which involve processing of personal data / profiling under GDPR, requiring a valid lawful basis and transparency that are nowhere described. The most acute GDPR concern is that the brand's own analytics establish awareness — with reasonable certainty — that ~34% of the reached audience are minors aged 13-17, which heightens fairness and children's-data obligations even though the age-related profiling ban itself sits under the DSA. No direct data-collection form (sign-up/competition) from children is described, so Art. 8/Art. 13 are engaged only informationally. Recommend documenting lawful basis, transparency, and minor-mitigation measures.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28(2) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients the provider is aware with reasonable certainty are minors. The campaign relies on the platform's interest-based (profiling) ad delivery, and the brand's own audience analytics demonstrate substantial, quantified minor reach (34% aged 13-17). This awareness undermines reliance on the nominal '18+' declared-age setting: where profiling-based ads are in fact delivered to a viewership that is known to include a large minor cohort, the platform's Art. 28 ban is engaged and the campaign heightens that risk. Youth-appealing creatives (meme formats, fast cuts, a streamer popular with young teens) reinforce that minors are foreseeably and knowingly reached.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17.
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on profiling/interest-based delivery for this campaign given documented minor spillover. Coordinate with the platform to move to non-profiled contextual placement (e.g. context of the stream, not behavioural segments), or exclude channels/streamers whose analytics show high 13-17 shares. Retain the analytics as evidence of the mitigation decision, and re-baseline audience composition before scaling.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that each advertisement presented on an online platform be identifiable in a clear, concise, unambiguous manner and in real time as an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it, together with meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. Animated brand overlays and streamer shout-outs woven into live gameplay can blur the line between editorial stream content and paid advertising; without a persistent, clear ad/sponsorship label in the overlay and shout-out, viewers (especially the large teen cohort) may not identify the commercial nature in real time.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every sponsored overlay and shout-out carries a clear, real-time 'Ad'/'Sponsored by VoltRush' label that is legible throughout the placement, and confirm the platform exposes advertiser identity and main targeting parameters in its ad transparency layer. Provide streamers with scripted verbal disclosure of the paid relationship for shout-outs.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA's platform-advertising regime in two ways. First, the profiling-based (interest) ad targeting combined with the brand's own analytics showing ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17 creates a real Art. 28 minor-protection risk despite the nominal "18+" setting: the ban on profiling-based ads to recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors turns on actual awareness, which the analytics arguably create. Second, the sponsored overlays and streamer shout-outs must be clearly and unambiguously identifiable as advertising in real time under Art. 26(1). No evidence of sensitive-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) or dark patterns (Art. 25). Note DSA obligations fall primarily on the platform, but these practices shape the advertiser's compliance exposure.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Paid streamer shout-outs promoting the product and distributing a discount code are commercial communications. If the shout-outs are delivered as the streamer's own enthusiasm without a clear, prominent disclosure of the paid/sponsored connection, the commercial intent is not apparent from context and material information (the paid relationship) is omitted — a misleading omission of hidden commercial intent. This risk is heightened for a young audience less able to recognise embedded advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Require every sponsored stream segment and shout-out to carry a clear, upfront disclosure (e.g. spoken 'This stream is sponsored by VoltRush' plus a persistent on-screen 'Ad/Sponsored' label). Contractually mandate disclosure in the streamer briefs and monitor compliance.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: Sponsored content woven into a streamer's editorial-style broadcast, where the trader has paid for the promotion, is an advertorial that is prohibited in all circumstances if not made clearly identifiable as paid promotion. Animated overlays and shout-outs presented as part of the natural stream content, without a clearly identifiable sponsorship marker, risk falling within this blacklist prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs
findings.recommendation: Ensure the paid nature is unmistakably identifiable within the content itself via clearly identifiable images/sounds and text labels (persistent 'Sponsored by VoltRush' overlay and verbal disclosure), so it can never be mistaken for independent editorial content.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The brand's own analytics reveal a substantial, clearly identifiable minor audience, and the creative choices (fast cuts, meme formats, a streamer popular with young teens) reinforce appeal to that group. Under Art. 5(3) the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group. Continuing to run youth-appealing high-caffeine promotion into a known 34% minor audience, contrary to professional diligence, risks materially distorting the economic behaviour of minors and constitutes an unfair practice.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Treat the analytics as knowledge of substantial minor reach: exclude or heavily rescreen streamers/audiences skewing under-18, tighten creative to avoid youth-appealing meme/fast-cut styles, and apply exclusions or frequency caps once minor spillover is detected. Document a professional-diligence assessment before continuing the campaign.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: For a high-caffeine product marketed to an audience with substantial minor spillover, the caffeine/'not recommended for children' warning is material information a consumer needs to make an informed decision. Presenting the promotion (slogan, discount code) without carrying that warning in the advertising overlays omits material safety information in the channel where the purchasing impulse is created, engaging Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays
findings.recommendation: Include the high-caffeine warning (and any 'not recommended for children/pregnant women' statement) legibly within the advertising overlays themselves, not only on pack, so the material information travels with the promotional message.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: The campaign reaches a large minor audience and uses a discount code, but the submitted text contains no verbatim direct exhortation to children to buy the product or to persuade parents to buy it. The slogan alone is not a direct 'buy now'/'ask your parents' exhortation, so the Annex I point 28 blacklist prohibition is not confirmed on the current text — but it is a live risk if creatives add purchase-prompt phrasing directed at the teen audience.
findings.evidence_quote: VoltRush — power your grind
findings.recommendation: Explicitly prohibit any direct 'buy it now', 'get yours', 'ask your parents' style calls-to-action in creatives or streamer scripts given the known minor audience, and review all shout-out scripts against this rule before broadcast.

verdicts.notes: The VoltRush stream sponsorship engages several UCPD concerns. Paid streamer shout-outs and branded overlays with a discount code create a risk of hidden commercial intent / undisclosed advertorial (Art. 7, Annex I point 11) unless clearly labelled as sponsored. Because the brand's own analytics show ~34% of viewers are 13-17 and creatives (memes, fast cuts, a streamer popular with teens) appeal to minors, the practice must be assessed against the average member of that vulnerable group under Art. 5(3), and omitting the high-caffeine warning from the overlays is a likely misleading omission of material safety information (Art. 7). No verbatim direct exhortation to children is present, so Annex I point 28 is flagged only as attention, not a confirmed blacklist breach.

report.executive_summary: This campaign sponsors live gaming streams for VoltRush, a high-caffeine energy drink, using animated overlays, paid streamer shout-outs and a discount code, delivered via interest-based ("gaming interest, 18+") ad targeting. Although you set an 18+ target, your own audience analytics show that about 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and the creatives (meme formats, fast cuts, a streamer popular with young teens) actively appeal to that group. This documented awareness of substantial minor reach is the core problem: it triggers a serious risk under the DSA's ban on profiling-based ads to people known to be minors, and it means the campaign is assessed against a vulnerable-audience standard under consumer-protection law. On top of that, the streamer shout-outs and overlays risk being unlabelled hidden advertising, and the mandatory high-caffeine warning appears on pack but not in the ad overlays where the purchase impulse is created. On the data side, the interest-based targeting and analytics processing lack a documented lawful basis and transparency, with added obligations because minors are involved. The overall verdict is high risk — the campaign as described should not scale without changing the targeting approach, adding disclosures, and acting on the minor-spillover data.
recommendations: Stop relying on profiling/interest-based delivery for this campaign given your own analytics show ~34% minor viewers. Switch to non-profiled contextual placement and/or exclude streamers and channels whose analytics skew toward 13-17. Retain the analytics as evidence of the mitigation decision and re-check audience composition before scaling.

Act on the minor-spillover data now: apply audience exclusions/frequency caps, and tone down youth-appealing creative (meme formats, fast cuts, teen-favourite streamers). Document a professional-diligence assessment before continuing.

Add clear, real-time advertising disclosures: a persistent 'Sponsored by VoltRush' / 'Ad' label on every overlay, and a scripted spoken sponsorship disclosure in every streamer shout-out. Mandate this contractually in streamer briefs and monitor compliance.

Carry the high-caffeine warning (and any 'not recommended for children/pregnant women' statement) legibly inside the ad overlays themselves, not only on pack, so the safety information travels with the promotional message.

Establish and document a lawful basis for the interest-based targeting and analytics processing (typically consent for behavioural advertising, or a robust legitimate-interest assessment), and define controller/joint-controller responsibilities with the platform.

Do not rely on the '18+' setting to satisfy children's-data obligations given contrary analytics: ensure age-gating/verifiable parental consent where consent is the basis, or exclude under-age data from targeting and analytics entirely.

Explicitly ban direct purchase exhortations aimed at children ('buy it now', 'get yours', 'ask your parents') in all creatives and shout-out scripts, and review scripts before broadcast to avoid an Annex I blacklist breach.

If the discount code or any endpoint collects personal data, provide a layered, age-appropriate privacy notice at the point of collection covering identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention and rights.

campaign.title: VoltRush energy drink stream sponsorships
campaign.text: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code. Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting; no profiling of minors is requested. Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
campaign.target_audience: declared 18+ gaming audience with substantial minor spillover

detected_practices: stream sponsorship with animated brand overlays
streamer shout-outs / influencer endorsement
discount code promotion
interest-based media buying (behavioural targeting)
declared-age (18+) targeting on gaming interest
meme/fast-cut creatives appealing to young audiences
use of a streamer popular with young teens
high-caffeine warning present on pack but omitted from overlay creatives
triage.audience_notes: Declared 18+ gaming audience but brand's own analytics confirm substantial minor spillover (~34% aged 13-17). Product is a high-caffeine energy drink unsuitable for minors; caffeine warning appears on pack but not in overlays. No generative AI declared or apparent, so AI Act not engaged. Behavioural/interest targeting and receipt of audience analytics engage GDPR; the platform-based streaming sponsorship engages DSA (minor protection, targeted advertising rules); consumer-facing claims and warning omissions engage UCPD.
triage.summary: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams using animated overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest-based media buying via declared 18+ targeting. Despite the 18+ declaration, analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and creatives (meme formats, fast cuts, a streamer popular with teens) plus omission of the high-caffeine warning from overlays raise substantial minor-spillover and fair-practices concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Interest-based media buying that segments audiences by 'gaming interest' is behavioural targeting, which meets the GDPR definition of profiling — automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal preferences and interests. This brings the campaign squarely within GDPR's profiling regime.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document that interest-based buying constitutes profiling, and ensure the platform relationship and the brand's own use of segments are covered by a valid GDPR basis and a data-protection assessment before running similar campaigns.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling and personalised/interest-based advertising require a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — generally consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment. The submission describes targeting and receipt of audience analytics but provides no evidence of a lawful basis or a documented LIA, so the processing basis is unverified.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the Art. 6(1) lawful basis for the interest-based targeting and for receiving/using audience analytics; if relying on legitimate interests, complete a balancing test that specifically accounts for the known presence of minors, otherwise obtain consent via the platform.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The brand has actual knowledge that a substantial share of the reached audience are minors (13-17) and processes audience analytics relating to them. Where consent underpins interest-based advertising as an information society service, Art. 8 requires that the child be at least 16 (13 in some Member States) and otherwise parental consent plus reasonable verification. Relying on a 'declared 18+' setting that the brand's own data shows is failing does not amount to a reasonable verification effort.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Given confirmed ~34% minor spillover, treat minors as reached: suppress interest-based/profiled advertising to the under-age segment, apply meaningful age-assurance rather than a self-declared toggle, and do not use analytics derived from minors for targeting. Where children are known to be present, avoid consent-based profiling of them entirely.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle is engaged: the brand states it does not request profiling of minors, yet its own analytics confirm minors form ~34% of the audience and it continues to run interest-based targeting and receive audience data. Processing minors' data in reliance on an 18+ label the controller knows to be inaccurate, without mitigation or child-appropriate transparency, is not fair or transparent processing.
findings.evidence_quote: no profiling of minors is requested
findings.recommendation: Reconcile the stated intent with the observed reality: implement effective exclusion/mitigation for the minor segment, provide clear, child-intelligible privacy information for any data collection touchpoints (e.g. the discount-code flow), and stop relying on a nominal age flag that the data shows is not working.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: If the discount code drives users to a redemption or sign-up flow that collects personal data, Art. 13 requires point-of-collection information (controller identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, rights, and any profiling). This is engaged wherever the campaign captures data, and must be intelligible for the young audience actually reached.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure any discount-code redemption or data-capture point presents a complete, layered Art. 13 notice in clear, plain language appropriate for a young audience, disclosing any profiling and the data subjects' rights.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses interest-based (behavioural) media buying and the brand receives audience analytics, both of which involve processing of personal data and constitute profiling under GDPR. The declared 18+ targeting is demonstrably ineffective — the brand's own analytics confirm ~34% of viewers are 13-17 — so the controller has actual knowledge that minors' data is being processed without a demonstrated lawful basis, verification effort, or child-appropriate transparency. Key gaps concern lawful basis (Art. 6), profiling (Art. 4(4)), children's data (Art. 8), and the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)). Note that whether personalisation crosses into Art. 22 depends on facts not fully described.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 requires online platforms accessible to minors to protect them and prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign is delivered via interest-based/profiling media buying ('gaming interest'), and the brand's own analytics confirm that roughly a third of the reached audience are 13-17. The nominal '18+' declared-age setting is contradicted by the advertiser's documented knowledge of substantial minor reach, so interest-based ad delivery is materially reaching minors. Creatives (meme formats, fast cuts, a streamer 'popular with young teens') reinforce that minors are foreseeably and knowingly in scope. While the platform is the primary duty-holder, the advertiser materially drives the profiling-based buy while aware of the minor spillover.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17.
findings.recommendation: Stop relying on interest/profiling-based media buying for placements with known minor spillover. Either switch these placements to contextual (non-profiled) delivery, or exclude streams/streamers whose analytics show significant under-18 audiences; document age-assurance and require the platform to suppress profiling-based ad presentation where recipients cannot be reasonably certain to be adults. Given the product is a high-caffeine energy drink unsuitable for minors, apply age-appropriate placement controls consistent with Art. 28.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that recipients can identify, clearly, concisely, unambiguously and in real time, that content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters. The sponsorship is delivered as in-stream animated overlays and streamer shout-outs with no indication that the paid/advertising nature and advertiser identity are surfaced to viewers in real time on the platform, nor that targeting-parameter information is made available. As presented, the platform ad-transparency requirements are engaged and not evidently satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure each sponsored placement is clearly labelled as advertising in real time (e.g. persistent 'Ad'/'Sponsored by VoltRush' marking on overlays and in shout-outs), that the advertiser and payer are identified, and that the platform's ad-transparency/targeting-parameter disclosures are populated for the campaign.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA through platform-based advertising (stream sponsorship overlays, streamer shout-outs, interest-based media buying). The most serious concern is Art. 28: the brand's own analytics show ~34% of viewers are 13-17, so profiling/interest-based ad delivery reaches minors despite a declared 18+ setting, undermining the reasonable-certainty threshold behind the profiling-to-minors ban. Ad-transparency obligations (Art. 26(1)) are also engaged and not evidently satisfied by the overlay/shout-out format. The Art. 26(3) sensitive-data ban is not triggered.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The shout-outs and animated brand overlays are paid/incentivised promotion (a sponsorship). The campaign describes no ad or sponsorship disclosure. Under Art. 7(2) a practice is misleading where it fails to identify commercial intent that is not otherwise apparent. Embedded streamer endorsements and overlays can read as native/editorial content, and the commercial connection must be clearly disclosed. This is aggravated because the audience skews heavily to 13-17s who are less able to identify commercial intent.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Require clear, prominent and persistent disclosure that the stream content is a paid sponsorship (e.g. an on-screen 'Ad'/'Sponsored by VoltRush' label plus a verbal disclosure by the streamer at each shout-out). Disclosure must be understandable to the actual, younger-skewing audience.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: If the paid streamer promotion is presented as ordinary streamer/editorial content without making the paid nature clear through clearly identifiable images or sounds, it falls within the Annex I point 11 blacklist (advertorial without disclosure), which is prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer effect. Whether this is a full breach depends on whether current overlays/shout-outs are recognisable as paid promotion.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs
findings.recommendation: Ensure the paid nature is unmistakable within the content itself (persistent 'Sponsored'/'Ad' branding and streamer verbal disclosure), so the promotion cannot be mistaken for independent editorial content.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 prohibits practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort (or are likely to distort) consumer behaviour, and Art. 5(3) assesses practices reaching a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (by age/credulity) from that group's perspective. The brand's own analytics confirm ~34% of viewers are minors, and creatives use meme formats, fast cuts and a streamer popular with young teens to promote a high-caffeine product unsuitable for minors. Continuing to run creatives foreseeably distorting minors' behaviour, despite this knowledge, is contrary to professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Given documented, substantial minor spillover, either suppress the campaign on channels/streamers with a majority-minor following, drop creative devices that disproportionately appeal to children (meme formats, teen-favourite streamers), and/or add robust age-gating. Document the diligence steps taken in response to the 34% analytics figure.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: For a product where a mandatory high-caffeine warning applies, that warning is material information for the consumer's decision. Omitting it from the promotional overlays while it appears only on pack may constitute a misleading omission under Art. 7, particularly where the ad reaches a large minor audience for whom high caffeine is unsuitable and who see the advertising, not the pack.
findings.evidence_quote: carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays
findings.recommendation: Include the high-caffeine warning (or a clear age/suitability advisory) within the sponsorship overlays and creatives, not only on pack, so the material information reaches viewers at the point of exposure to the advertising.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 bans, in all circumstances, direct exhortations to children to buy or to persuade adults to buy. The current copy ('power your grind' + a discount code) is a brand slogan and promotional offer, not a verbatim 'buy now'/'ask your parents' exhortation, so a clear breach is not evidenced. However, the combination of a teen-favourite streamer, discount code and child-appealing creatives creates a real risk that added call-to-action copy could cross into a prohibited direct exhortation.
findings.evidence_quote: a streamer popular with young teens
findings.recommendation: Prohibit any purchase-directed call-to-action aimed at or reaching children (e.g. 'grab yours now', 'get the code') in creatives shown to the minor-heavy audience, and review streamer scripts to avoid direct purchase exhortations to a young audience.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages UCPD on three fronts. Most clearly, the streamer shout-outs and branded overlays with a discount code are paid promotion that appears to carry no ad/sponsorship disclosure, engaging Art. 7 (hidden commercial intent) and, if presented as independent streamer content, the Annex I point 11 blacklist — an especially acute risk since the brand's own analytics show ~34% of viewers are 13-17 and less able to recognise commercial intent. The brand's knowing exposure of a high-caffeine product to a substantial minor audience, via meme/fast-cut creatives and a streamer popular with young teens, engages the Art. 5 professional-diligence standard and the Art. 5(3) vulnerable-group test, compounded by omission of the on-pack high-caffeine warning from the overlays. There is no clear "direct exhortation" wording, so Annex I point 28 is an attention point rather than a confirmed blacklist breach.

report.executive_summary: This campaign sponsors live gaming streams for the VoltRush energy drink using branded overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, bought via "gaming interest, 18+" interest-based targeting. The core problem is that your own audience analytics show roughly 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, so a large minor audience is knowingly being reached despite the nominal 18+ setting. This triggers serious risks under three regimes: the DSA bans profiling-based ads to minors you can reasonably identify (Art. 28); GDPR requires a valid lawful basis and children's-data protections you have not demonstrated (Arts. 6, 8, 5); and the UCPD flags hidden sponsorship (no visible "Ad"/"Sponsored" labels), unfair targeting of a vulnerable young audience with meme-style creatives and a teen-favourite streamer, and the omission of the on-pack high-caffeine warning from the creatives. The AI Act does not apply. As presented, the campaign should not run in its current form — the profiling-based delivery to a known minor audience and the missing disclosures are the most urgent fixes. With contextual (non-profiled) buying, effective age assurance, clear ad labelling and in-overlay warnings, the concept can likely be made compliant.
recommendations: Stop interest/profiling-based media buying on placements with known minor spillover: switch to contextual (non-profiled) delivery and/or exclude streams and streamers whose analytics show significant under-18 audiences (DSA Art. 28 — highest priority).

Replace the self-declared '18+' toggle with meaningful age assurance; do not use analytics derived from minors for targeting, and suppress profiled ad presentation where viewers cannot be reasonably certain to be adults.

Add clear, persistent and real-time advertising disclosure to every placement — an on-screen 'Sponsored by VoltRush'/'Ad' label plus a verbal disclosure by the streamer at each shout-out — understandable to the younger-skewing audience (UCPD Art. 7 / Annex I pt 11; DSA Art. 26(1)).
Include the high-caffeine warning (or a clear age/suitability advisory) within the overlays and creatives, not only on pack, so it reaches viewers at the point of exposure (UCPD Art. 7).

Drop creative devices that disproportionately appeal to children (meme formats, fast cuts, teen-favourite streamers) on any placement with substantial minor reach, and prohibit purchase-directed calls-to-action ('grab yours', 'get the code') in creatives reaching minors (UCPD Art. 5 / Annex I pt 28).

Establish and document the GDPR Art. 6(1) lawful basis for the targeting and for receiving audience analytics; if relying on legitimate interests, complete a balancing test that expressly accounts for the known minor presence (Arts. 4(4), 6).

Ensure any discount-code redemption or data-capture flow carries a complete, layered, plain-language Art. 13 privacy notice appropriate for a young audience, disclosing any profiling and users' rights.

Document the concrete diligence steps taken in response to the 34% minor-audience figure, evidencing that the campaign has been reconciled with its stated 'no profiling of minors' intent (GDPR Art. 5(1)(a)).

campaign.title: GardenPro similar-products digest
campaign.text: A garden-tools retailer emails past purchasers (contact details obtained at sale, opt-out offered at collection and in every message) a quarterly digest of accessories for tools they bought: 'Blades and batteries for your GP-200 trimmer'. Legal basis is documented as legitimate interest with a balancing test on file; unsubscribe is one-click and immediate. One template footer, however, buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email.

detected_practices: email marketing to existing customers
product recommendations based on prior purchases
behavioural personalisation/targeting
legitimate interest legal basis with documented balancing test
one-click unsubscribe (opt-out)
obscured/buried unsubscribe link in one template footer ('preferences' wording below 14 lines of social icons)
triage.summary: A garden-tools retailer sends existing customers a quarterly email digest recommending accessories for tools they previously bought, using personalisation and a documented legitimate-interest basis with one-click unsubscribe. However, one template footer buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and labels it 'preferences' rather than a clear opt-out, raising GDPR (ePrivacy/consent and right-to-object mechanics) and UCPD (potential misleading/obscured withdrawal) concerns.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) gives data subjects an absolute right to object to direct marketing (including profiling for marketing), and controllers must respect and facilitate that opt-out. Where one template hides the unsubscribe link under 14 lines of social icons and relabels it 'preferences' instead of clearly offering to stop email, the objection mechanism is obstructed and not explicitly presented as required, weakening an otherwise-compliant one-click opt-out.
findings.evidence_quote: buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email
findings.recommendation: Standardise every template footer: place a clearly labelled 'Unsubscribe / Stop these emails' link prominently and above decorative content, using unambiguous stop-email wording rather than a generic 'preferences' link that does not obviously terminate the marketing.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information and communications to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible using clear and plain language. Burying the opt-out control and labelling it ambiguously as 'preferences' fails the easily-accessible and clear-language standard for exercising a data-subject right.
findings.evidence_quote: refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email
findings.recommendation: Use clear, plain-language labelling for the opt-out control and ensure it is easily accessible (near the top of the footer, high contrast, single click) consistently across all templates.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Emailing existing customers about accessories for products they previously bought can rely on legitimate interest with a documented balancing test (the 'soft opt-in' rationale), especially where an opt-out was offered at collection and in every message. This appears appropriately grounded; flagged for confirmation that the balancing test expressly accounts for the personalisation/profiling element and that only existing-customer contacts obtained at sale are used.
findings.evidence_quote: Legal basis is documented as legitimate interest with a balancing test on file
findings.recommendation: Retain the documented legitimate-interest balancing test and confirm it explicitly assesses the profiling/personalisation of recommendations; ensure processing stays limited to existing customers with the collection-point opt-out on record.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Generating recommendations from a customer's prior purchases is automated processing to evaluate personal preferences/interests and constitutes profiling under Art. 4(4). This is low-risk profiling (relevant accessories for products actually owned) and does not appear to produce legal or similarly significant effects, so no Art. 22 issue arises, but the right to object under Art. 21 extends to this profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Blades and batteries for your GP-200 trimmer
findings.recommendation: Acknowledge the recommendation logic as profiling in the privacy notice and ensure the Art. 21 opt-out also halts profiling-based personalisation, not just the emails.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is broadly GDPR-conscious: it uses personalisation based on prior purchases (profiling under Art. 4(4)) on a documented legitimate-interest basis with a balancing test, targets existing customers only, and offers a genuine one-click, immediate unsubscribe. The material risk is one email template whose footer buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and mislabels it 'preferences', which undermines the Art. 21 right to object and the Art. 12 requirement for easily accessible communication. Fixing that footer and confirming the balancing test explicitly covers the profiling would bring the campaign into good standing.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: How to stop the marketing is material information the average consumer needs. Placing the opt-out below 14 lines of social icons and relabelling it 'preferences' provides that information in an unclear, ambiguous and non-prominent manner, and can mislead recipients into believing the link only adjusts preferences rather than stopping email. This is an obstruction-of-cancellation style deceptive design captured by UCPD Art. 7 (misleading omission through unclear presentation of material information).
findings.evidence_quote: buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email
findings.recommendation: Redesign the footer template so the unsubscribe control is clearly visible and labelled unambiguously (e.g. 'Unsubscribe' / 'Stop these emails'), placed prominently above or independent of the social-icon block, matching the clear one-click behaviour already used in the other templates.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: UCPD Arts. 8-9 treat 'onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights' as a factor in aggressive practices. A single visually buried opt-out in one template is a minor obstruction and, given the genuine one-click immediate unsubscribe, does not rise to harassment, coercion or undue influence. Flagged only so the footer fix also removes any friction that could compound into an obstruction pattern if repeated.
findings.evidence_quote: buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons
findings.recommendation: Ensure the opt-out remains genuinely one-click and immediate across all templates; avoid adding steps, preference walls or confirm-shaming so the withdrawal mechanism cannot be characterised as a burdensome barrier.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is largely a legitimate existing-customer email program (documented legal basis, opt-out offered at collection and in every message, one-click unsubscribe). The only UCPD concern is one template footer that obscures the opt-out: burying the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and labelling it 'preferences' rather than a clear stop-email option makes material information (how to end the marketing) unclear/ambiguous, engaging Art. 7. This is a fixable deceptive-design issue, not a blacklisted or aggressive practice.

report.executive_summary: This campaign emails past customers a quarterly digest of accessories for tools they already own (e.g. "Blades and batteries for your GP-200 trimmer"). Overall it is a well-run, compliance-conscious program: it targets existing customers only, documents legitimate interest with a balancing test, and offers a genuine one-click, immediate unsubscribe. The AI Act and DSA are not engaged. The single real problem sits in one email template: its footer hides the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and labels it "preferences" instead of clearly offering to stop the emails. This weakens the recipient's right to object (GDPR Art. 21) and the requirement to communicate clearly and accessibly (GDPR Art. 12), and it counts as a misleading omission through unclear design under consumer law (UCPD Art. 7). None of this is a blacklisted or aggressive practice, and none of it stops the campaign from running — it is a fixable footer issue. Fix that one template and confirm the balancing test covers the personalisation, and the campaign is in good standing.
recommendations: Fix the offending template footer: place a clearly labelled 'Unsubscribe / Stop these emails' link prominently, above the social-icon block, and drop the ambiguous 'preferences' wording. This resolves the GDPR Art. 21/12 and UCPD Art. 7 issues in one change.
Standardise all email templates so every footer uses the same clear, high-contrast, one-click unsubscribe wording and placement — no preference walls or extra steps.
Confirm the documented legitimate-interest balancing test explicitly covers the profiling/personalisation of recommendations, not just the emailing itself.
Ensure the opt-out halts the profiling-based personalisation as well as the emails, and describe the recommendation logic as profiling in the privacy notice.
Verify processing stays limited to existing customers whose contact details were obtained at sale, with the collection-point opt-out on record.

However, one template footer buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and mislabels it as 'preferences' rather than a clear stop-email option.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute and must be actively facilitated in every communication. Where one template footer hides the unsubscribe control beneath 14 lines of social icons and relabels it as 'preferences' rather than an unambiguous stop-email option, the objection mechanism is obstructed and made unclear. This does not disable the right but degrades its exercisability, contrary to the obligation to make opt-out easy and effective for recipients.
findings.evidence_quote: buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email
findings.recommendation: Standardise the footer so an unambiguous, prominently placed link labelled clearly as 'Unsubscribe' / 'Stop these emails' appears near the top of the footer (not buried below social icons). findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information and controls provided to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible using clear and plain language. Labelling the opt-out as 'preferences' — implying continued receipt with adjusted settings rather than a clear stop-email action — is not clear and plain, and burying it below 14 lines of icons makes it not easily accessible, so the defective footer fails the transparency standard.
findings.evidence_quote: refers to 'preferences' rather than stopping email
findings.recommendation: Use clear, plain-language wording that states the effect of the action (e.g. 'Unsubscribe from all marketing emails') and place the control where recipients can readily find it, so the choice and its consequence are unambiguous.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Marketing similar products to existing customers whose contact details were obtained at the point of sale, with opt-out offered at collection and in every message, is a recognised legitimate-interest scenario, and a documented balancing test is on file. As described this appears to be an appropriate lawful basis; flagged only to confirm the assessment must remain accurate and current, and that the ePrivacy 'soft opt-in' conditions (own similar products, opt-out at collection and each message) continue to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: Legal basis is documented as legitimate interest with a balancing test on file
findings.recommendation: Keep the legitimate-interest balancing assessment reviewed and dated, and ensure the soft opt-in conditions (existing customer, similar goods, opt-out at every stage) continue to hold; no change to legal basis is required if the buried/mislabelled opt-out defect is fixed.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Recommending accessories based on purchase history is a form of profiling (automated evaluation of personal preferences/behaviour). The objection right under Art. 21 extends to profiling related to direct marketing. Here the profiling is limited, disclosed via the digest concept, and tied to the existing-customer relationship, so risk is low, but it confirms the opt-out must also stop the profiling-based personalisation.
findings.evidence_quote: a quarterly digest of accessories for tools they bought
findings.recommendation: Ensure that when a recipient opts out, the suppression stops not only the emails but also any purchase-history-based profiling used to generate the digest, and reflect this in the privacy information provided at collection.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's core data-processing design is largely GDPR-sound: it relies on a documented legitimate-interest basis with a balancing test on file for marketing similar products to existing customers, contact details were obtained at the point of sale, opt-out was offered at collection, and the primary unsubscribe path is one-click and immediate. The principal GDPR risk is a specific template footer that buries the unsubscribe link below 14 lines of social icons and mislabels it as "preferences" rather than a clear means to stop email — this undermines the facilitation of the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21) and the transparency/plain-language standard (Art. 12). findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a person's momentary emotional/mood state (including 'distressed' or 'low-mood' windows) is inference of data concerning the individual's mental/psychological health. Under GDPR Art. 9, processing of health data — including inferred attributes — is prohibited absent a specific exception such as explicit consent. Here there is no consent and no other Art. 9 exception, so the inference and use of this data is unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring emotional/mental-state attributes for ad targeting. If any emotion-inference is retained, it can only proceed on the basis of the data subject's explicit consent (Art. 9(2)(a)) obtained transparently and freely — which in practice is not viable for covert mood-based targeting. The safest course is to remove mood/emotional-state as a targeting or delivery signal entirely.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Covertly inferring emotional states and exploiting inferred distress to boost ad conversion ('elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed') is neither fair nor transparent — it is exactly the kind of hidden processing and unfair exploitation the principle prohibits. The standard sponsored label does nothing to disclose the mood-based profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Redesign the processing to be fair (do not exploit inferred vulnerability) and transparent (disclose the profiling logic clearly). Absent that, the practice cannot satisfy Art. 5(1)(a) and should be discontinued.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All processing needs a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Behavioural profiling for ad targeting generally requires consent or a defensible legitimate-interest assessment. No consent is obtained and no legitimate interest could survive a balancing test where the intrusive inference of mood is used to exploit distress; the data subjects' interests and fundamental rights clearly override. As described, there is no lawful basis for this processing.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis before any processing. For this type of intrusive emotional profiling, only freely given, specific, informed consent would be plausible, and a legitimate-interest basis would fail the balancing test. Do not run the pilot without one.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data (behavioural signals and the inferred emotional state derived from them) is processed, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis, and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling including meaningful information about the logic involved. Users receive none of this information about the MoodMatch profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy disclosure covering the emotional-state profiling, its purpose (ad delivery timing), the lawful basis, and the profiling logic and consequences, delivered at or before the point of processing.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear plain language. A generic sponsored label conveys nothing about the mood-inference processing, so any transparency obligation is not met in an intelligible, accessible manner.
findings.evidence_quote: the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Ensure the required information about the profiling is communicated clearly and accessibly (e.g., in-context 'why am I seeing this' explanations and the privacy notice), not buried or omitted.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The automated evaluation of personal aspects (emotional state, behaviour, personal preferences) from behavioural data is textbook profiling under Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 22 safeguards, right to object).
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Recognise the operation as profiling and apply the full set of profiling-related GDPR obligations; document a DPIA given the systematic, large-scale, sensitive nature of the processing.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The system makes solely automated decisions, based on profiling, about which ads (including gambling) to serve to users inferred as distressed. Delivering betting ads to vulnerable users on the basis of an automated emotional profile can 'similarly significantly affect' them (financial/psychological harm), potentially bringing it within Art. 22's prohibition, which requires an exception plus safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest — none of which are present.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated targeting of distressed users produces significant effects under Art. 22. If so, it is prohibited unless an exception applies with safeguards; given the exploitation of distress, refrain from the automated betting/'retail therapy' delivery to inferred low-mood users.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Users have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, including profiling related to it, and must be explicitly informed of this right at the latest at first communication. Because users are unaware of the MoodMatch profiling, they cannot meaningfully exercise the Art. 21(2)-(3) right to object.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly and separately inform users of their right to object to direct-marketing profiling and provide an easy, effective opt-out from mood-based ad delivery.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot infers users' momentary emotional/mental state from behavioural signals and uses it to time ad delivery — this is profiling of a health/mental-state-adjacent nature carried out entirely covertly. Multiple GDPR obligations are engaged and, as described, breached: inference of special-category-adjacent data without an Art. 9 exception, absence of any lawful basis or transparency, and automated processing that significantly affects vulnerable users. The complete lack of user notification is the central failing, breaching the fairness/transparency principle and Arts. 12–13, and undermining any possibility of valid consent.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Inferred momentary emotional/mental state (distress, low mood) is data concerning health/mental health, a special category under GDPR Art. 9, which DSA Art. 26(3) incorporates by reference. Presenting advertisements based on profiling that uses such inferred sensitive attributes to decide which ads to deliver is prohibited under Art. 26(3) regardless of any consent. The 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises this prohibited targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease delivering ads based on any profiling that infers emotional or mental-health state. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and the mood-inference model from the ad-delivery pipeline entirely; sensitive-attribute-based targeting cannot be cured by disclosure or consent under the DSA.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Operating the ad-delivery interface to time commercial offers to moments of inferred distress materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, exploiting a manipulated psychological state. The internal note that distressed users convert at elevated rates evidences that the design impairs autonomous decision-making — the harm Art. 25 targets. This is compounded by directing betting ads at vulnerable moments.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Disable emotional-state-triggered ad timing/prioritisation. Ad delivery must not be organised to exploit inferred vulnerability; remove distress-window logic from the interface and prohibit sensitive/high-risk verticals (e.g., gambling) from any behavioural receptivity boosting.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients get, in real time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they are shown the ad and how to change them. A standard 'sponsored' label discloses that content is an ad but conceals the material targeting parameter here — inferred emotional state / low-mood window. Users are affirmatively 'not informed', so the parameter-transparency obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Even setting aside the Art. 26(3) prohibition, disclose per-ad the main targeting parameters and provide controls to change them. Since the operative parameter (inferred mood) is itself unlawful under Art. 26(3), the correct fix is to remove that parameter and disclose only lawful targeting logic.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: The delivery model functions as a recommender/ranking system determining the ads and ordering shown to users. Art. 27 requires the platform to set out in plain language the main parameters of such systems and any options to modify them. Emotional-state inference driving ad prioritisation is an undisclosed main parameter, and no user options to influence it are described.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers ... ads
findings.recommendation: Set out in the terms/settings, in plain language, the main parameters used by the ad recommender and provide options to modify them. Note the emotional-inference parameter must be removed rather than merely disclosed, per Art. 26(3).

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If the platform is (or becomes) designated a Very Large Online Platform (>=45M average monthly EU users), Art. 39 requires a public ad repository disclosing content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. At 28M declared users it is below the VLOP threshold, so this is conditional; but if designated, the emotional-targeting parameters would have to withstand public archival scrutiny, exposing the Art. 26(3)/25 issues.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP status against the 45M threshold. If designated, ensure the ad repository accurately reflects targeting parameters — which, given the current unlawful mood-based logic, is a further reason to remove it before scaling the pilot.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot engages several core DSA advertising and interface provisions. Most seriously, it delivers ads (including betting) based on profiling of inferred emotional/mental-health states — a special category of GDPR Art. 9 data — which DSA Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits for platform advertising regardless of consent. The design also manipulates users' decision-making by exploiting inferred low-mood windows (Art. 25 dark patterns), and fails Art. 26(1) transparency because users are not told about the emotional-state targeting parameters. Art. 27 recommender transparency is engaged and Art. 39 ad-repository duties apply only if the platform qualifies as a VLOP (28M users is below the 45M threshold, so this is conditional).

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that, through undue influence — including the exploitation of a consumer's specific misfortune or emotional state and manipulative timing — significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Deliberately timing ads for impulse-conducive products (comfort food, retail therapy) and, critically, betting/gambling to moments of inferred distress is a textbook exploitation of misfortune and manipulative timing. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is direct evidence that the practice materially distorts economic behaviour and that vulnerability is being exploited rather than merely observed.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease timing or targeting ad delivery to inferred negative/low-mood emotional states. In particular, prohibit any 'receptivity boost' or mood-linked delivery for gambling/betting and other harm-prone categories. If mood inference is retained at all, it must never be used to select delivery timing or audiences for commercial messages exploiting that state.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises the undue-influence mechanism: advertisers pay to have their ads preferentially served when the platform infers the user is emotionally susceptible. This is a systematised exploitation of impaired decision-making capacity, squarely within the Arts. 8-9 factors (timing and exploitation of a consumer's situation), regardless of advertisers not seeing raw mood data.
findings.evidence_quote: advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'receptivity boost' feature entirely, or redefine it so it cannot key delivery to inferred emotional/vulnerability states. Ensure advertiser-facing controls cannot indirectly purchase distress-based targeting.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the consumer needs for an informed transactional decision. Although the sponsored label discloses that the content is an ad, it hides the material fact that delivery is timed to the user's inferred emotional/distressed state. A consumer's assessment of an offer would plausibly differ if they knew it was served precisely because they were inferred to be distressed and more likely to convert. The standard label therefore does not cure the material omission about how and why the ad reached them.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, timely disclosure that ad delivery is influenced by inferred emotional state, and offer users a genuine ability to opt out of mood-based delivery. Better: discontinue mood-based delivery so no such disclosure is needed.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety net: a practice is unfair if it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts (or is likely to) the economic behaviour of the average consumer, assessed from the perspective of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where relevant (Art. 5(3)). Users in inferred momentary distress constitute a group whose decision-making is impaired; deploying AI to detect and monetise that impairment falls short of the standard of professional diligence expected of the trader, independently of and in addition to Arts. 7-9.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Adopt a professional-diligence policy that prohibits monetising inferred vulnerability; subject the MoodMatch pilot to a fairness review and halt distress-targeted delivery pending redesign that respects vulnerable users.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deliberately times betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to reach adults during AI-inferred low-mood/distressed windows, with internal data confirming elevated conversion among distressed users. Under the UCPD this most clearly engages the prohibition on aggressive commercial practices (Arts. 8-9): exploiting a consumer's misfortune/emotional state through undue influence to distort transactional decisions, aggravated by betting/gambling products. The lack of any disclosure of the emotional-profiling mechanism also engages the misleading-omission rule (Art. 7), and the practice fails professional-diligence and vulnerable-consumer standards under the Art. 5 safety net. Adjacent AI Act/GDPR/DSA issues (emotion inference, sensitive data, dark patterns) are covered by other agents but reinforce the unfairness analysis.

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an AI model to secretly infer when your 28M EU users are in a low or distressed mood (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions) and then deliberately serves them comfort-food, betting and "retail therapy" ads at those vulnerable moments, with advertisers able to buy in via a "receptivity boost" toggle. Your own internal review confirms this converts distressed users at elevated rates — which is exactly the evidence regulators will use against you. All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA and UCPD) return "violation likely," several at critical severity. This is not a campaign that can be fixed with a disclaimer, consent box or better labelling: the core mechanic — detecting emotional distress and monetising it — is prohibited outright under the AI Act (Art. 5 manipulation and exploitation of vulnerability), banned as sensitive-data ad targeting under DSA Art. 26(3), unlawful sensitive-data profiling under GDPR Art. 9, and an aggressive/exploitative practice under the UCPD. Targeting betting and impulse-spend products at people you have algorithmically flagged as distressed is the single most damaging element. The verdict is clear: do not launch this pilot in its current form; the mood-inference-to-ad-delivery pipeline must be removed, not merely disclosed.
recommendations: Do not launch MoodMatch. Halt the pilot immediately — the emotional-state inference and its use in ad delivery is a prohibited practice that cannot be cured by consent, disclosure or better labelling.</parameter>
Remove the emotional/mood-state inference model from the ad-delivery pipeline entirely. Stop using inferred mood as an input to ad timing, targeting or ranking.
Delete the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle, or fully redesign it so it can never key delivery to inferred emotional, distress or vulnerability signals.

Absolutely never key gambling/betting or high-risk impulse-spend ('retail therapy') delivery to inferred emotional or financial-distress signals — this is the most legally and reputationally dangerous element.

Preserve and review the internal finding on 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'; treat it as evidence of harm and factor it into your decision to discontinue rather than as a performance metric to optimise.
Run and document a DPIA and a fairness/professional-diligence review before any future mood-adjacent processing; establish a policy that prohibits monetising inferred vulnerability.

If you retain any legitimate behavioural ad targeting, ensure it has a valid GDPR lawful basis, per-ad transparency on the main targeting parameters (DSA Art. 26(1)/27), a clear privacy notice (GDPR Arts. 12-13), and an easy opt-out from direct-marketing profiling (GDPR Art. 21).

Confirm your VLOP status against the 45M EU-user threshold; if designated, ad-repository disclosure obligations (DSA Art. 39) would publicly expose the current targeting logic — a further reason to remove it before scaling.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

mood-based ad targeting during inferred low-mood windows
exploitation of psychological vulnerability / emotional state
targeting of comfort-food, gambling/betting and 'retail therapy' ads at distressed users

advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle
