triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users in the EU; minors explicitly excluded. However, self-declared adult status and behavioural targeting warrant verification, and the practice deliberately targets emotionally distressed adults.
triage.summary: A large social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle. Users are not informed of the mood inference, and internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed, raising serious concerns about exploiting emotional vulnerability. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The AI system infers a transient vulnerability (distress/low-mood, a 'specific social or economic situation' state) and deliberately targets those users with gambling/betting and impulse-spending ('retail therapy') and comfort-food ads precisely when they are least able to resist. This is designed to, and does, materially distort behaviour — the internal review confirms 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Serving betting and impulse-purchase ads to emotionally distressed people is reasonably likely to cause significant financial and psychological harm, meeting the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition threshold. Excluding minors does not cure the violation, since vulnerability here derives from the inferred distress situation, not only age.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue mood/emotion-based ad delivery entirely. Do not use inferred distress or low-mood states to select, boost or time advertising — remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and any pipeline that raises ad exposure during inferred vulnerable states, especially for gambling, high-risk financial or impulse-consumption products.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The mood-inference and emotion-timed delivery operate covertly, beyond users' consciousness — users are not told their emotional state is inferred or that ad delivery is being tuned to their inferred distress. This is a purposefully manipulative AI technique that appreciably impairs the user's ability to make an informed transactional decision, causing decisions (e.g., placing bets, impulse purchases) they would not otherwise take, in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Standard sponsored labelling does not disclose the manipulative timing mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Cease deploying covert AI nudging that exploits inferred emotional states. If any personalisation remains, it must not use hidden emotional-state inference to steer decisions; ensure delivery logic cannot be tuned to psychological vulnerability, and provide meaningful transparency well beyond a generic 'sponsored' label.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot uses an in-house AI system to infer users' momentary emotional/mood state from behavioural signals and deliberately serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, without informing users. This engages two AI Act Article 5 prohibitions: Art. 5(1)(b) (exploiting vulnerability arising from a specific situation to distort behaviour with likely significant harm) and Art. 5(1)(a) (covert/manipulative AI technique distorting decisions). Both are outright prohibited practices, not merely high-risk. Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition) is limited to workplace/education contexts and does not apply here.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's momentary emotional state and specifically identifying 'users inferred as distressed' plausibly produces data concerning mental health/psychological condition. Art. 9 covers inferred attributes revealing health data, whose processing is prohibited absent an exception such as explicit consent. No explicit consent exists here, and the special condition of distress is precisely what the model derives and monetises.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring emotional/mental-state data unless the platform can rely on a valid Art. 9 exception. In practice for advertising this means obtaining freely given, specific, informed explicit consent from each user before inferring emotional/health-adjacent states, or abandoning emotional-state inference altogether.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Emotion-inference profiling and mood-based ad delivery require a valid lawful basis. Given the intrusive nature and the deliberate targeting of distressed users, legitimate interests cannot pass a balancing test, and no consent has been obtained. There is therefore likely no lawful basis for this processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any such processing. Given the sensitivity, this effectively requires prior opt-in consent; conduct a DPIA and legitimate-interests/balancing assessment, which this design is unlikely to pass.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Covertly inferring emotional state and exploiting inferred low-mood windows to boost conversions is neither fair nor transparent. Processing that deliberately leverages users' vulnerability while concealing the mechanism breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Make the mood-inference processing transparent to users and redesign it so it does not unfairly exploit inferred emotional vulnerability; disclose the existence, logic and purpose of the emotional-state profiling.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting behavioural data used to infer mood, the controller must inform users of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling. Users are given only 'standard sponsored labels' and are not informed of the mood inference, so the Art. 13 information duties are not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, layered notice at collection explaining that behavioural signals are used to infer emotional state for ad targeting, the legal basis, retention and the profiling logic, plus data-subject rights.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Even where any information exists, it must be concise, transparent and intelligible. A generic 'sponsored' label does not communicate the emotional-state inference or its purpose, so information provided is neither transparent nor intelligible about this processing.
findings.evidence_quote: the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Communicate the mood-inference processing in clear, plain language accessible to users, distinct from the generic sponsored label.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The automated analysis of behavioural signals to evaluate/predict emotional state and behaviour is textbook profiling under Art. 4(4), which frames the applicability of the profiling-related obligations (Arts. 6, 9, 21, 22).
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Treat MoodMatch expressly as profiling and apply all associated GDPR profiling obligations (lawful basis, special-category rules, information duties, objection rights).

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The ad delivery is decided solely by automated profiling. Systematically steering distressed users toward betting and impulse-purchase ads to exploit vulnerability may 'similarly significantly affect' them (financial and wellbeing harm, especially betting), potentially bringing it within Art. 22's restriction, which then requires an exception and safeguards that are absent here.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... preferentially delivers ... ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the targeting significantly affects users; if so, ensure an Art. 22 exception applies with safeguards (human review, right to contest), or discontinue the solely-automated vulnerability-based targeting.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Users have an absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling. Because users are unaware the mood-based profiling exists, they cannot exercise this right, and no opt-out mechanism for the profiling is described.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easily accessible mechanism to object to marketing profiling (including mood-based targeting) and honour objections absolutely by ceasing the profiling for those users.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot infers users' momentary emotional/mental state from behavioural signals and targets ads accordingly, without informing users. This engages multiple GDPR provisions seriously. Inferring emotional distress/mental state very likely constitutes processing of health-related special-category data (Art. 9) with no valid lawful basis (Art. 6) or explicit consent, and is entirely covert, breaching the fairness/transparency principle and information obligations (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13). The system is automated profiling that plausibly falls under Art. 22, and the right to object to marketing profiling (Art. 21) appears unsupported. Overall this presents a high likelihood of GDPR violation.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using special categories of personal data under GDPR Art. 9. Inferring a user's 'momentary emotional state' / 'low-mood' / 'distressed' condition from behavioural signals produces data revealing mental-health status, a GDPR Art. 9 category. Delivering ads preferentially during inferred low-mood windows is ad targeting based on that inferred sensitive attribute. The ban applies even to inferred/proxy attributes and cannot be cured by consent.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Do not use inferred emotional/mental-health state as an ad-targeting or ad-delivery parameter. Disable the mood-inference layer for advertising and remove the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle; targeting must not rely, directly or by inference, on Art. 9 categories.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits providers of online platforms from designing, organising or operating their online interfaces in a way that manipulates recipients or otherwise materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. Systematically timing betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to inferred moments of psychological vulnerability, with internal review confirming 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed', is manipulative operation of the interface that impairs free and informed decision-making rather than a neutral relevance signal.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Cease operating ad delivery to exploit inferred vulnerability/low-mood windows. Redesign the delivery logic so it does not increase ad exposure or intensity based on inferred negative emotional states, and document that ad timing is not keyed to distress signals.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that, for each ad, recipients can identify in real time — clearly and unambiguously — meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine why the ad is shown to them, and how to change them. A 'standard sponsored label' identifies that content is an ad but does not disclose the mood-inference targeting parameter that actually drives delivery, so the main-parameters transparency obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Even if mood-based targeting is removed as required, ensure per-ad 'why am I seeing this' disclosures accurately describe the real main targeting parameters and offer controls to change them; never leave a material delivery parameter (such as behavioural/receptivity signals) undisclosed.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: With 28M EU users the platform is likely a very large online platform (VLOP). Under DSA Art. 39, VLOPs must maintain a public ad repository including ad content, advertiser, payer, and the targeting parameters and reach. Mood/receptivity-based targeting parameters would have to be disclosed in this public repository and would not withstand that scrutiny, reinforcing that such targeting must not be used.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP status and ensure all ad targeting parameters used in the pilot are accurately reflected in the public ad repository; given repository transparency, remove any mood/receptivity targeting parameters that could not lawfully be published.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot engages multiple DSA obligations and prohibitions. Most seriously, it operates the platform's ad-delivery interface to exploit inferred emotional distress (dark pattern, Art. 25) and targets ads based on profiling that infers a mental-health-related state (special-category data), which is flatly banned for platform advertising under Art. 26(3) regardless of consent. Ad-transparency (Art. 26(1)) is also not satisfied because the mood-based targeting parameter is undisclosed, and as a likely VLOP (28M EU users) the platform must reflect these targeting parameters in its Art. 39 ad repository.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that, by undue influence, significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Relevant factors expressly include timing and the exploitation of specific misfortune. Here the platform deliberately times persuasive ads (including gambling and impulse 'retail therapy' spending) to moments of inferred emotional distress, exploiting a weakened decision-making state. The advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and the internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' show both the intent and the effect of materially distorting economic behaviour — a hallmark of undue influence.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue targeting or timing ad delivery based on inferred negative emotional states. Do not offer any 'receptivity boost' that exploits low-mood windows. If emotion-derived signals are used at all, exclude persuasion-timing on vulnerability and prohibit high-risk verticals (gambling/betting) from any mood-linked delivery.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts (or is likely to distort) economic behaviour, assessed from the perspective of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where relevant (Art. 5(3)). Users inferred to be in a distressed/low-mood state are a clearly identifiable vulnerable group whose behaviour the model is engineered to distort; deliberately optimising ad delivery to that vulnerability is not consistent with the standard of professional diligence expected of a trader. The platform's own conversion data confirms the material distortion.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Adopt a professional-diligence standard that prohibits monetising inferred emotional vulnerability. Conduct a fairness impact review, remove distress-based receptivity optimisation, and document safeguards preventing distorted transactional decisions among vulnerable users.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision, or providing it in an untimely/unclear manner. That the ad selection and timing are driven by an inference about the user's momentary emotional state is material information affecting the consumer's assessment of, and susceptibility to, the ad. A 'standard sponsored label' discloses only that content is an ad, not that it is being served because the user has been algorithmically identified as distressed. Concealing this material fact deprives consumers of the ability to recognise and resist the tailored persuasion.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, timely disclosure where delivery is optimised on inferred emotional state, and give users a meaningful, easily accessible way to opt out of emotion-based ad delivery. Preferably cease the practice entirely rather than relying on disclosure, given the vulnerability exploited.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot infers users' momentary emotional distress and deliberately times comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads to inferred low-mood windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle. Under the UCPD this is a strong candidate for an aggressive commercial practice by undue influence (Arts. 8-9): the platform exploits consumers' misfortune/impaired judgement to distort transactional decisions, evidenced by the platform's own note of "elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed." It also engages the general unfairness prohibition (Art. 5), since distressed users constitute a de facto vulnerable group whose economic behaviour is being materially distorted contrary to professional diligence, and Art. 7 because the material fact that ad delivery is being optimised to emotional vulnerability is concealed (only "standard sponsored labels").

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI model to infer users' momentary emotional state from their behaviour and then deliberately serves betting, comfort-food and impulse-spending ('retail therapy') ads during the windows when users are inferred to be feeling low. Advertisers can amplify this with a 'receptivity boost' toggle, and your own internal review confirms it works — conversions rise among users the system flags as distressed. This is not a borderline case: all four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA, UCPD) independently conclude the pilot likely breaks the law, several at the most serious level. The core problem is that the campaign intentionally monetises emotional vulnerability, which triggers outright prohibitions rather than fixable compliance gaps. Under the EU AI Act this is a banned practice (exploiting vulnerability and covert manipulation); under the DSA it is a banned use of special-category (mental-health) data plus a dark pattern; under GDPR it is unlawful processing of health-adjacent data with no valid basis or consent and no transparency; and under the UCPD it is an aggressive and unfair practice. Excluding minors does not fix any of this, because the harm flows from the inferred distress, not age. The verdict is that MoodMatch cannot proceed in its current form and should be stopped now — the mood-inference-for-advertising mechanism itself must be removed, not merely disclosed.
recommendations: Halt the MoodMatch pilot immediately and stop using inferred emotional/low-mood state to select, time or boost any advertising — this mechanism is prohibited outright under AI Act Art. 5 and DSA Art. 26(3) and cannot be fixed by adding disclosures or consent.
Remove the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and any delivery logic that increases ad exposure or intensity during inferred negative emotional states.
Absolutely bar gambling/betting and impulse-purchase verticals from any mood- or emotion-linked delivery; these carry the highest financial and psychological harm to distressed users.
Do not treat consent as a cure: targeting on inferred mental-health state is banned for platform ads under the DSA regardless of consent, and the AI Act prohibitions apply irrespective of consent.

Stop inferring emotional/mental-state data for advertising unless a valid GDPR Art. 9 basis exists — in practice this means abandoning the inference for ad purposes; document a DPIA showing why the design fails the legitimate-interests balancing test.

If any lawful personalisation is retained, provide genuine transparency well beyond the generic 'sponsored' label (GDPR Arts. 12/13, DSA Art. 26(1)), disclose the real main targeting parameters, and give users an easy, absolute opt-out from marketing profiling (GDPR Art. 21).

Confirm VLOP status (28M EU users) and ensure all targeting parameters are accurately reflected in the DSA Art. 39 public ad repository — any parameter that could not survive public disclosure must not be used.
Escalate to Legal, the DPO and senior management before any relaunch; given regulator focus on emotional manipulation, treat this as a compliance stop-ship, not a marketing optimisation question.

campaign.title: PureFlow water filter trust badges
campaign.text: Product pages and display ads for a water filter show: 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025', a gold laurel badge, ' Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration', and '#1 recommended by dentists'. No such award or institute exists; the badges were designed in-house. The dentist claim traces to a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members. Filtration performance figures themselves match lab reports.

detected_practices: fabricated trust/award badge ('European Water Quality Award 2025')
fake certification claim ('Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration')
non-existent certifying body invented in-house
misleading '#1 recommended by dentists' claim based on unrepresentative 2019 survey of 12 employees' relatives
unsubstantiated endorsement/authority claims
triage.summary: Web and display campaign for the PureFlow water filter displaying fabricated award badges, a fake EU certification from a non-existent institute, and a '#1 recommended by dentists' claim traceable only to a tiny, unrepresentative 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members. While the filtration performance figures are accurate, the trust/authority signals are invented in-house and materially misleading. Targeted at general adult EU consumers with no declared AI or personalisation.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

The DSA obligations in scope (Art. 25 deceptive interface/dark patterns; Art. 26(1) ad transparency; Art. 26(3)/28 profiling-based and minor-targeted ad bans; Art. 27 recommender transparency; Art. 39 VLOP ad repositories) are all addressed to providers of online platforms, not to advertisers/traders creating campaign content. This submission is an advertiser's product pages and display ads by PureFlow, with no platform-provider role, no declared personalisation/targeting, no sensitive-data or minor targeting, and no recommender/VLOP element. The fabricated award badges, fake 'EU Institute of Hydration' certification, and unsubstantiated '#1 recommended by dentists' claim are genuinely deceptive, but under the graph's own RELATED_TO note the DSA applies 'without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers the same conduct for all traders' — these misleading commercial claims fall to the UCPD, not the DSA. No DSA provision is engaged by the facts as described.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: An in-house-designed award emblem and gold laurel presented as an independent quality/award mark is the display of a trust or quality mark without authorisation. Annex I point 7 (recte point 2) prohibits this in all circumstances; because the award does not exist, no authorisation could ever have been obtained. Self-designed 'award' emblems presented as independent are the exact example cited in this provision.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025', a gold laurel badge ... No such award or institute exists; the badges were designed in-house.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated 'European Water Quality Award 2025' badge and gold laurel entirely. Only display trust/quality marks that are issued by a genuine independent body and for which written authorisation exists; retain evidence of that authorisation.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Claiming the product is certified/endorsed by a body — here an invented 'EU Institute of Hydration' that does not exist — is a false claim of approval or endorsement by a body, prohibited in all circumstances under Annex I point 4. The 'EU' framing compounds this by falsely implying official/EU affiliation.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' ... No such award or institute exists
findings.recommendation: Delete the 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' claim and any implied EU/official affiliation. Certification claims may only be used where a real, identifiable body has actually granted certification and its terms are complied with.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Presenting the product as '#1 recommended by dentists' when the only basis is a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members is a misleading action: it deceives the average consumer about the product's endorsement and qualifications and is likely to cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The sample is neither representative nor genuinely professional dental endorsement, making the superlative unsubstantiated.
findings.evidence_quote: '#1 recommended by dentists' ... traces to a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members
findings.recommendation: Remove the '#1 recommended by dentists' claim unless supported by a robust, current, representative and independent survey of practising dentists. If any survey basis is retained, state the actual sample, date and methodology transparently and drop the unsupportable '#1' superlative.

verdicts.notes: The campaign deploys multiple invented trust and authority signals for the PureFlow water filter that engage per-se prohibited (blacklisted) UCPD practices. A self-designed award badge and gold laurel constitute an unauthorised trust/quality mark (Annex I pt 2); the fabricated "EU Institute of Hydration" certification is a false endorsement by a (non-existent) body (Annex I pt 4); the "#1 recommended by dentists" claim rests on an unrepresentative 12-person survey and is a misleading action on the product's qualifications/endorsements (Art. 6). These are clear, blacklisted or highly likely breaches; notably the accurate filtration figures do not cure the deceptive trust signals.

report.executive_summary: Your PureFlow campaign uses three trust signals that are fabricated: a self-designed "European Water Quality Award 2025" gold laurel badge, a "Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration" mark for an institute that does not exist, and a "#1 recommended by dentists" claim based only on a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members. Two of these fall squarely into the EU's blacklist of practices that are banned outright, in all circumstances — displaying a trust/quality mark without authorisation, and falsely claiming certification or endorsement by a body. The dentist claim is a separate misleading action because the "evidence" is neither representative nor a genuine professional endorsement. The fact that your actual filtration performance figures are accurate does NOT fix this — the deceptive badges stand on their own as violations. GDPR, the AI Act and the DSA are not engaged by this campaign; the risk is entirely under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. Because blacklisted practices carry no defence and expose you to enforcement action and penalties across EU markets, the overall risk is critical and the offending elements must be removed before launch.
recommendations: Remove the fabricated 'European Water Quality Award 2025' badge and gold laurel entirely before any publication — this is a per-se banned practice with no available defence.

Delete the 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' claim and any wording that implies official or EU affiliation — falsely claiming endorsement by a (non-existent) body is also outright prohibited.

Remove the '#1 recommended by dentists' claim; do not reinstate it unless backed by a current, representative, independent survey of practising dentists, with the sample size, date and methodology stated transparently and the '#1' superlative dropped if unsupportable.
Only ever display award, quality or certification marks issued by a genuine independent body, and keep written proof of authorisation on file.
Keep the accurate filtration performance figures — these are fine as they match your lab reports — and build the campaign's credibility on substantiated claims rather than invented trust signals.
Have any revised creative reviewed against UCPD Annex I (the blacklist) before relaunch, since the current version would trigger enforcement and penalties across EU markets.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: emotion inference from behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reactions)
AI-driven emotional-state targeting
behavioural retargeting / personalised ad delivery
exploitation of inferred low-mood/vulnerable states
'receptivity boost' advertiser toggle
targeting distressed users with betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads
lack of transparency (users not informed of mood inference)
sponsored labelling of ads
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users across the EU; minors are stated to be excluded from the pilot. Concern centres on adults inferred to be in vulnerable/distressed emotional states being deliberately targeted, which may constitute exploitation of vulnerability regardless of age.
triage.summary: A large social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house AI that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with advertisers able to enable a 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed of the mood inference, and internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed. Minors are excluded, but the practice raises serious concerns about exploiting emotional vulnerability, profiling and transparency.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The AI system infers a transient emotional/economic vulnerability ('distressed', 'low-mood') and deliberately exploits it by timing betting, comfort-food and impulse-spending ('retail therapy') ads to those windows. This fits Art. 5(1)(b): exploiting vulnerabilities arising from a specific situation/state with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences both the distortion effect and the likelihood of significant harm (financial loss from betting/impulse purchases and reinforcement of distress). Because minors are excluded, adult vulnerability grounded in a specific social/economic and emotional situation is the operative basis. This is a prohibited practice.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease the MoodMatch pilot in the EU. Do not use inferred emotional/low-mood states to time or target advertising, and in particular prohibit targeting of gambling/betting or impulse-spend categories against any inferred distress signal. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and disable the low-mood delivery logic entirely.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The system covertly infers momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history and uses it to nudge purchasing decisions without the user's awareness of the mechanism. This is a purposefully manipulative technique operating beyond the user's consciousness, with the objective or effect of impairing informed decision-making and causing users to take decisions (e.g., placing bets, impulse purchases) they would not otherwise have taken, with likely significant harm — engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition. Standard 'sponsored' labels do not cure this because they disclose that an ad is paid, not that mood-based targeting is being applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Discontinue covert emotion-inference-driven ad delivery. If any behavioural personalisation is retained, it must not exploit inferred emotional state, and users must be clearly informed of and able to control the logic used to target them.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: The campaign performs emotion inference, but Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition only in the workplace and education contexts. This is a consumer social-platform advertising context, so 5(1)(f) does not apply directly. Flagged for completeness so it is not overlooked, and because the underlying emotion inference is what triggers the applicable Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) prohibitions.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: No action required under Art. 5(1)(f) as described; ensure MoodMatch is never deployed against employees or students, which would additionally engage this prohibition. Address the practice under Art. 5(1)(a) and (b).

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot uses an AI system to infer users' momentary emotional state and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. This engages the AI Act's Article 5 prohibitions on exploiting vulnerabilities (Art. 5(1)(b)) and on manipulative/subliminal techniques (Art. 5(1)(a)) — both prohibited practices, not merely regulated ones. Internal evidence of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' strengthens the case that the system materially distorts behaviour and is reasonably likely to cause significant (financial/psychological) harm. Art. 5(1)(f) does not apply (this is not a workplace/education context), and Art. 50 transparency duties are not clearly triggered by the described mechanism.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's momentary emotional state — specifically identifying 'low-mood windows' and users 'inferred as distressed' — plausibly amounts to processing of data concerning mental health. Art. 9 expressly captures inferred attributes, so deriving health/emotional-distress signals from behavioural data brings the processing within the special-categories prohibition. No Art. 9 exception (in particular explicit consent) is present: users are not informed at all, so processing of this sensitive inferred data is prohibited as described.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring and processing emotional/distress states unless a specific Art. 9 exception applies. In practice this requires prior, separate, freely given explicit consent for the specific purpose of emotional-state inference and mood-based ad delivery; absent that, the model must not derive or act on distress/low-mood signals. Given the vulnerability-exploitation risk, the safer course is to disable mood-based targeting entirely.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: This is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict personal aspects (emotional state, behaviour, personal preferences) and to differentiate ad delivery accordingly. It squarely meets the Art. 4(4) definition of profiling, which triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, data-subject rights). The profiling here is of an especially intrusive kind because it targets inferred vulnerability.
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads
findings.recommendation: Recognise the mood-inference engine as profiling and apply the full profiling compliance stack: document purposes, complete a DPIA (high-risk profiling of behaviour plus sensitive inference), and implement transparency and objection mechanisms before any processing.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Here the mood-inference profiling is entirely covert — users receive only 'standard sponsored labels' and no indication their emotional state is being inferred and exploited. Covert processing breaches transparency, and deliberately timing betting/retail-therapy/comfort-food ads to inferred low-mood windows (with 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed') breaches the fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, upfront disclosure of the mood-inference profiling and its purpose, and stop exploiting inferred distress as an ad-delivery trigger. Fairness cannot be cured by disclosure alone where the practice deliberately capitalises on emotional vulnerability, so the exploitative timing logic should be removed.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is collected/processed, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes and legal basis, and specifically about automated decision-making including profiling. Users are given no information about the emotional-state inference, its purposes, or the profiling logic, so the Art. 13 information obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice and in-context disclosures to explain the mood-inference profiling: the categories of behavioural data used, the purpose (ad timing/targeting), the legal basis, and meaningful information about the profiling logic and its consequences.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The mood-inference profiling and mood-based ad delivery require a valid Art. 6 legal basis. None is identified. Consent is impossible because users are not informed, and legitimate interests would very likely fail the balancing test given the intrusive inference of emotional state, the exploitation of distress, and the reasonable expectations of 28M users — especially once Art. 9 sensitive-data considerations are engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis before processing. For emotional-state inference this effectively means explicit consent (also required under Art. 9); a legitimate-interest basis is not defensible for exploiting inferred vulnerability. Without a valid basis the processing must not proceed.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Ad-delivery decisions are made solely automatically on the basis of profiling of inferred emotional state. While ad selection may not always 'similarly significantly affect' individuals, deliberately targeting inferred distress with betting and impulse-spend ads (with documented elevated conversion among distressed users) can produce significant effects on vulnerable individuals, potentially bringing the practice within Art. 22 and triggering its safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated mood-based targeting has significant effects on affected individuals; if so, ensure an Art. 22 basis (explicit consent) and implement safeguards (human review, ability to contest, right to obtain intervention). Given betting/impulse categories aimed at distressed users, the recommended course is to exclude such automated vulnerability-based decisions entirely.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot infers users' momentary emotional/distress state from behavioural signals and uses it to time ad delivery, without informing users and with no identified lawful basis. This engages GDPR profiling (Art. 4(4)) and — because inferred distress/low-mood plausibly reveals mental-health data — the Art. 9 prohibition on processing special categories, for which no explicit-consent exception is present. The complete absence of disclosure ("users are not informed") also breaches the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and the Art. 13 information duty, and no valid Art. 6 basis is evident. Overall a likely violation on multiple counts, with the Art. 9 issue most serious.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, and this applies where sensitive attributes are derived by inference. Inferring a user's emotional state / mental-health condition (labelling users as 'distressed') and using that inference to determine which ads are delivered is profiling on inferred health/mental-state data used for ad targeting. The 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises this targeting for advertisers.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease using inferred emotional/mental-state signals as an ad-delivery parameter. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and any pipeline that routes ads based on inferred mood/distress. Advertising selection must not rely, directly or by inference, on emotional or health states regardless of any consent obtained.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that materially distorts or impairs users' ability to make free and informed decisions. Deliberately timing the delivery of impulse/vulnerability-sensitive ads (betting, comfort-food, 'retail therapy') to moments the platform has inferred users are in a low-mood/distressed state exploits a diminished decision-making capacity — the platform's own review confirms this raises conversion. Operating ad delivery to capitalise on inferred distress is manipulative interface design.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Do not condition ad exposure, ordering or intensity on inferred negative emotional states. Disable mood-triggered delivery windows; if any mood signal exists it must not be used to increase exposure to gambling or impulse-purchase advertising. Document that ad delivery does not exploit inferred vulnerability.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify, in real time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they are shown the ad, and how to change them. Here the decisive targeting parameter is the inferred emotional state, yet users receive only a 'standard sponsored label' and are 'not informed' of the mood inference. The mandatory 'main parameters' disclosure is therefore not meaningful or complete.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: For each ad, disclose the meaningful main parameters actually used to select the recipient and provide controls to change them. Given the emotional-inference parameter would itself be unlawful (Art. 26(3)), the correct remedy is to remove that parameter rather than merely disclose it; where lawful parameters remain, ensure they are surfaced in real time.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: A social platform with 28M EU users is likely to meet the VLOP threshold (45M+ average monthly EU users) or be in scope for designation; VLOPs must maintain a public ad repository including targeting parameters and reach under Art. 39. Emotion-based 'receptivity' targeting parameters would have to be recorded and withstand public scrutiny, and unlawful targeting parameters cannot be lawfully archived.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP status against the user threshold. If in scope, ensure all ad targeting parameters are accurately logged for the public ad repository; since emotion/receptivity targeting is not a lawful parameter, it must be discontinued rather than archived. Maintain repository completeness for remaining lawful campaigns.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot presents platform advertisements selected on the basis of an inferred momentary emotional/mental state ("distressed", "low-mood"). Under the DSA this engages the prohibition on profiling-based ad targeting using special-category data by inference (Art. 26(3)), the prohibition on manipulative interface design that distorts free decision-making (Art. 25), and ad-transparency duties (Art. 26(1)); as a large platform (28M EU users) it is also likely a VLOP subject to ad-repository obligations (Art. 39). The core practice — timing commercially sensitive ads (betting, comfort-food, 'retail therapy') to inferred emotional vulnerability without informing users — is a likely violation.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices that, through undue influence, significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken; relevant factors expressly include timing and the exploitation of the consumer's misfortune. MoodMatch deliberately times ads for behaviourally-sensitive products (betting, comfort food, impulse 'retail therapy') to coincide with AI-inferred states of distress/low mood, exploiting a position of psychological weakness the trader itself has detected. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the tactic materially distorts economic behaviour — precisely the impairment the provision targets. The knowledge graph confirms emotion-based AI targeting is governed by UCPD Arts. 8-9.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease serving ads on the basis of inferred negative/low-mood emotional states. Disable the 'receptivity boost' toggle and the low-mood targeting logic entirely, at minimum for behaviourally-sensitive categories (gambling/betting, food, impulse retail). If any mood-adaptive delivery is retained, it must not target detected vulnerability windows and should be independently assessed against Arts. 8-9.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if it is contrary to professional diligence and materially distorts the economic behaviour of the average consumer, and Art. 5(3) requires assessment from the perspective of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group where a practice is likely to distort its behaviour. Users inferred to be in a distressed/low-mood state are, at the moment of exposure, a group of heightened credulity/reduced resistance; systematically targeting them with betting and impulse-spend ads and observing elevated conversion falls below the standard of professional diligence and materially distorts their economic behaviour. This applies even if the aggressive-practice test in Arts. 8-9 were not fully met.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Stop building ad-delivery optimisation around inferred distress, document a professional-diligence review of MoodMatch, and adopt a policy that emotional-state inference is never used to increase the persuasiveness or timing of commercial messages to consumers in vulnerable states.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits misleading omissions — hiding material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, including failing to make the true nature/commercial intent of a practice apparent. While the ads are labelled 'sponsored', the material fact that a user's momentary emotional state is being inferred and used to select and time the ads they see is concealed. A standard sponsored label does not disclose this mood-based selection; consumers cannot appreciate that they are being shown a betting or impulse-spend ad because the platform has inferred they are distressed, which is information that would affect their transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, prominent and timely disclosure that emotional-state inference is used to determine which ads are shown, in the ad-settings/transparency interface and at the point of delivery. Absent such disclosure (and given the vulnerability concern this transparency may not cure the underlying aggressive-practice issue), the mood-inference targeting should not run.

verdicts.notes: The MoodMatch pilot uses AI to infer momentary emotional vulnerability (low mood/distress) and deliberately times the delivery of betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to those inferred low-mood windows, with a measured effect of "elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed". Under the UCPD this is a strong candidate for an aggressive commercial practice by undue influence exploiting misfortune (Arts. 8-9), reinforced by the Art. 5 fairness safety-net and Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer standard. The complete failure to inform users that their mood is inferred and used to select ads also engages Art. 7 (misleading omission of the practice's real nature/commercial intent). Note: minors are excluded and standard sponsored labels are used, so blacklist points 28 and 11 are not engaged.

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI to infer when your users are in a low mood or 'distressed' state (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions) and then deliberately serves them betting, comfort-food and impulse 'retail therapy' ads during those vulnerable moments. All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA and consumer-protection/UCPD) conclude this is a likely serious violation, and several of the breaches are among the most severe in EU law. Under the AI Act, deliberately exploiting inferred emotional vulnerability to distort purchasing behaviour is a prohibited practice — not merely a regulated one — as is the covert, manipulative nature of the system. Inferring emotional/distress states is treated as sensitive mental-health data under GDPR, which you are processing with no user notice, no lawful basis and no explicit consent. The DSA separately bans ad targeting based on such inferred sensitive data and prohibits interface designs that exploit users' decision-making; consumer law treats timing ads to detected distress as an aggressive, misfortune-exploiting practice. The fact that your own internal review found 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is strong evidence of real consumer harm and would be powerful ammunition against you in any enforcement action. Excluding minors and using standard 'sponsored' labels does not fix any of this. The clear verdict: this campaign should not launch in the EU in its current form and the mood-based logic should be switched off.
recommendations: Halt the MoodMatch pilot in the EU immediately. The core mechanic — timing ads to inferred low-mood/distress windows — is a prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5 and cannot be made compliant through disclosure or consent alone.</br>

Disable the emotional-state inference engine and the 'receptivity boost' advertiser toggle entirely; do not use inferred mood/distress as an ad-delivery, ordering or intensity parameter, especially for betting/gambling, food and impulse-retail categories.

Delete or quarantine the internal finding on 'elevated conversion among distressed users' data pipeline and stop optimising delivery around it — but preserve records for your own compliance/DPIA review, as it evidences the harm regulators would target.

Treat any inference of emotional/mental state as GDPR Art. 9 special-category data: it requires prior, separate, explicit consent and cannot rest on legitimate interest. Absent that, stop deriving or acting on these signals.

If you retain any behavioural personalisation, provide clear upfront disclosure (privacy notice + in-context) of what data is used and why, complete a DPIA for high-risk profiling, and implement objection/contest mechanisms and a valid Art. 6 lawful basis.

Under the DSA, ensure ad selection never relies (directly or by inference) on emotional or health states, and surface meaningful 'main parameters' for each ad in real time with controls to change them.

Confirm whether the platform meets the VLOP threshold (45M+ monthly EU users); if designated, all lawful ad targeting parameters must be accurately logged in the public ad repository — unlawful emotion/receptivity parameters must be discontinued, not archived.

Adopt and document a firm policy that emotional-state inference will never be used to increase the timing, persuasiveness or intensity of commercial messages, and never deploy MoodMatch against employees or students (which would additionally engage AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)).
Involve your DPO and legal/compliance function before any relaunch, and consider proactive engagement with the relevant EU regulators given the scale (28M users) and the documented conversion effect.

campaign.title: PureFlow water filter trust badges
campaign.text: Product pages and display ads for a water filter show: 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025', a gold laurel badge, ' Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration', and '#1 recommended by dentists'. fake certification claim ('Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' — non-existent body)
misleading professional endorsement ('#1 recommended by dentists' based on a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members)
gold laurel award imagery implying third-party recognition
unsubstantiated superiority/ranking claim
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult consumers on web and display; no personalisation, targeting, or generative AI declared and none evident. The campaign is consumer-facing (B2C), so UCPD applies. Key concerns: display of trust marks without authorisation, false claims of endorsement by a public/professional body, and misleading claims about approval by a dentist/professional group — several of these map to the UCPD 'blacklist' of always-unfair practices (Annex I). No indicators of personal data processing (GDPR), AI systems (AI Act), or online intermediary/VLOP-specific duties (DSA) beyond ordinary advertising.
triage.summary: Web and display campaign for the PureFlow water filter targeting general adult consumers in the EU. It displays fabricated trust badges, a non-existent EU award and certification body, and a misleading '#1 recommended by dentists' claim traceable to a tiny 2019 survey of employees' family members, though the underlying filtration performance figures match lab reports. The core issues are misleading and unsubstantiated claims and fake quality/certification marks.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: The gold laurel 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025' emblem is a self-designed award/quality mark presented as if it were independent third-party recognition. Displaying a trust or quality mark without the necessary authorisation is prohibited in all circumstances; an invented award emblem is exactly the type of self-designed 'award' emblem this blacklist point targets, and no authorising body even exists.
findings.evidence_quote: a gold laurel badge ... the badges were designed in-house
findings.recommendation: Remove the gold laurel badge and 'European Water Quality Award 2025' emblem entirely. Only display quality/award marks that have been genuinely conferred by an authorised body and for which authorisation to display can be evidenced.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: Claiming a product has been approved, endorsed, certified or authorised by a public or private body when it has not is prohibited in all circumstances. The 'EU Institute of Hydration' is a non-existent body, and the 'EU' framing falsely implies official/public-body endorsement. The 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025' claim likewise falsely asserts endorsement/approval by a body that does not exist.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' ... No such award or institute exists
findings.recommendation: Delete all references to the 'EU Institute of Hydration' certification and the 'European Water Quality Award 2025'. Do not use 'EU' or official-sounding institute names unless a genuine, identifiable body has actually certified the product on stated terms.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: This is a misleading action: it deceives the average consumer about the product's endorsement and superiority. The claim traces to a 2019 survey of just 12 employees' family members — not a representative, independent professional endorsement and not capable of substantiating a '#1' ranking. Such false/unsubstantiated qualification and endorsement claims are likely to cause a transactional decision the consumer would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: '#1 recommended by dentists'
findings.recommendation: Remove the '#1 recommended by dentists' claim. Do not make professional-endorsement or ranking claims unless supported by a robust, independent, representative study; disclose the basis, date and sample if any legitimate claim is retained.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Taken together, the fabricated award, fake certification and misleading endorsement are contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour, engaging the general unfairness safety-net where not fully caught by specific Annex I points.
findings.evidence_quote: Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025
findings.recommendation: Rebuild the trust-signal messaging around verifiable, substantiated claims only (e.g. the accurate lab-verified filtration figures) and drop all invented awards, certifications and endorsements.

verdicts.notes: This B2C web/display campaign for the PureFlow water filter contains multiple always-unfair practices from UCPD Annex I. It displays a self-designed award badge and gold laurel imagery implying independent recognition (Annex I point 2), fabricates a non-existent EU award and certification body implying official/public endorsement (Annex I point 4), and makes a misleading "#1 recommended by dentists" ranking claim resting on a tiny, unrepresentative survey — a misleading action under Art. 6. That the filtration performance figures match lab reports does not cure the badge/endorsement deceptions. Multiple critical, per-se prohibited practices are present.

report.executive_summary: Your PureFlow campaign uses three trust signals — a gold laurel "Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025" badge, a "Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration" mark, and a "#1 recommended by dentists" claim — that are not supported by reality. The award and the certifying institute do not exist, and the badges were designed in-house, while the dentist claim rests on a 2019 survey of just 12 employees' family members. Under EU consumer law (the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive), displaying a trust mark you're not authorised to use and falsely claiming endorsement by a body are outright banned practices — no case-by-case defence is available. The fabricated "EU" institute is especially serious because it implies official/public backing. The fact that your actual filtration performance figures match your lab reports is good, but it does not cure any of these badge and endorsement problems. Overall this is a critical-risk campaign that should not run in its current form; the offending badges and claims must be removed before launch.
recommendations: Immediately remove the gold laurel badge and the 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025' emblem from all web pages and display ads — it is a self-designed award mark, which is prohibited outright (UCPD Annex I).
Delete all references to 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration'; the body does not exist and the 'EU' framing falsely implies official endorsement — also a per-se banned practice.
Remove the '#1 recommended by dentists' claim; a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members cannot substantiate a professional-endorsement or ranking claim.
Only reintroduce awards, certifications or endorsement claims if a genuine, identifiable body has actually conferred them, and keep documentary proof of authorisation to display any mark.
Rebuild your trust messaging around what you can verify — lead with the accurate, lab-verified filtration performance figures rather than invented accolades.
Have marketing/legal sign-off on the revised creative before relaunch, and audit any other products using similar in-house 'award' badges.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The in-house-designed fake award/certification badges ('Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025', 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration', quasi-official gold laurel) are deceptive interface elements that could distort consumers' ability to make free and informed decisions. DSA Art. 25, however, prohibits such deceptive design only in the online interfaces of providers of online platforms; the submission does not indicate PureFlow operates an online platform or VLOP. The graph itself notes Art. 25 applies without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers this same conduct for all traders — so the primary route here is the UCPD (fabricated trust marks / false endorsement), not the DSA. Flagged for awareness only.
findings.evidence_quote: the badges were designed in-house
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether these product pages/ads are served within an online platform interface that PureFlow itself provides. If so, remove the fabricated badges, award and certification, as deceptive interface design would then also engage DSA Art. 25. In all cases, remedy the underlying deception via UCPD compliance (remove unauthorised trust/quality marks and fake endorsements).

verdicts.notes: The DSA's obligations attach to providers of online platforms (ad transparency, recommender transparency, dark-pattern prohibition, minor protection, VLOP ad repositories). This campaign is an advertiser/trader running its own product pages and display ads for a water filter — there is no indication that PureFlow is an online platform provider or VLOP, and the submission declares no personalisation/targeting, no AI, general-adult audience and no reach to minors. Accordingly Arts. 26, 27, 28 and 39 are not engaged. The fabricated trust badges and fake endorsements are deceptive conduct, but as trader-level unfair commercial practices they fall under the UCPD (covered by another agent); DSA Art. 25 governs the same conduct only when it appears in an online platform's own interface design. One info-level flag is recorded to note the conditional Art. 25 exposure.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a quality/trust mark or equivalent award emblem without the necessary authorisation is prohibited in all circumstances. The 'European Water Quality Award 2025' gold laurel badge and other seals were self-designed in-house and presented as independent quality marks, which is exactly the practice this blacklist point captures.

findings.evidence_quote: 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' ... No such award or institute exists
