findings.title: Blacklist: fake reviews and endorsements
findings.rationale: Misrepresenting endorsements to promote a product is prohibited in all circumstances. Presenting a professional endorsement claim ('#1 recommended by dentists') that is derived from a 2019 survey of just 12 employees' family members misrepresents the nature, source and weight of the endorsement to the average consumer.
findings.evidence_quote: '#1 recommended by dentists' ... traces to a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members
findings.recommendation: Remove the '#1 recommended by dentists' claim. Only make professional-endorsement claims that are current, based on a representative and independent sample of the relevant professionals, and substantiated with disclosed methodology.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Independent of the blacklist, these constitute misleading actions: they contain false information about the trader's awards, qualifications and endorsements and are liable to cause the average consumer to make a transactional decision (buying the filter) they would not otherwise take. This provides an alternative/overlapping legal basis reinforcing the blacklist findings.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025' ... '#1 recommended by dentists'
findings.recommendation: Ensure every award, certification and endorsement claim is truthful, verifiable and substantiated before publication; withdraw the fabricated and unsubstantiated claims identified above.

verdicts.notes: The PureFlow campaign displays fabricated trust/quality badges and endorsements presented as genuine. It triggers multiple UCPD Annex I blacklist prohibitions (per se unfair in all circumstances): a self-designed award/quality badge (point 2), a fabricated award and fictitious 'EU Institute of Hydration' certification implying official endorsement (point 4), and a misrepresented 'recommended by dentists' endorsement (point 23c). These are also misleading actions under Art. 6. Note that the actual filtration performance figures match lab reports, so no finding is warranted on the technical product claims.

report.executive_summary: The PureFlow campaign uses trust badges and endorsement claims that are fabricated. The "European Water Quality Award 2025", the gold laurel badge, and the "Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration" seal were all designed in-house — no such award or institute exists — and the "#1 recommended by dentists" claim rests on a 2019 survey of just 12 employees' family members. These are among the most serious advertising violations in the EU: they hit multiple items on the UCPD Annex I "blacklist", which are banned outright in all circumstances regardless of consumer impact. Displaying an unauthorised quality mark (point 2), falsely claiming certification/endorsement by a body (point 4), and misrepresenting a professional endorsement (point 23c) all apply, and the same conduct also amounts to misleading actions under UCPD Art. 6. The good news: your actual filtration performance figures match the lab reports, so those claims are fine. AI Act and GDPR are not engaged, and the DSA only applies here if these pages sit inside an online platform interface you operate — an unlikely but worth-confirming edge case. Bottom line: this campaign cannot run in its current form and must be corrected before publication.
recommendations: Remove immediately: delete the 'Winner — European Water Quality Award 2025' claim, the 'Certified by the EU Institute of Hydration' seal, and the gold laurel badge from all web and display material. These are fabricated trust/quality marks and fake certifications — banned outright under UCPD Annex I points 2 and 4.
Remove the '#1 recommended by dentists' claim. It is based on a 2019 survey of 12 employees' family members and is a misrepresented endorsement prohibited under UCPD Annex I point 23c.
Stop using any EU-style naming, laurels or emblems that imply official or regulatory approval; these amplify the deception and the impression of government endorsement.
Keep the filtration performance figures — they match the lab reports and are substantiated. You may continue to advertise genuine, verifiable product performance.

Going forward, only display awards, certifications and endorsements that come from a real, independent body, for which you hold documented authorisation, and (for professional endorsements) that are current and based on a representative, independent sample with disclosed methodology.

Confirm whether these product pages/ads are served within an online platform interface that PureFlow itself operates. If so, the fabricated badges would additionally engage DSA Art. 25 (dark patterns) — but removing them as recommended above resolves this in any case.

campaign.title: BankEase 'alerts' cross-sell
campaign.text: A banking app's push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'. The bank now sends through the same channel: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps'), insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day. Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts. Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.

detected_practices: push notifications disguised as security/account alerts (misleading channel use)
behavioural targeting based on account events (low-balance, large purchases, salary day)
personalised cross-sell offers (personal loans, insurance, investments)
pre-approved credit offer with urgency framing ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps')
dark pattern: consent for notifications obtained for security purpose then repurposed for marketing
dark pattern: single on/off toggle bundling marketing pushes with fraud/security alerts (no granular control)
exploitation of financial vulnerability (offering loans immediately after low-balance events)
triage.summary: A banking app repurposes a push channel that users enabled for 'security and important account alerts' to deliver behaviourally targeted marketing (loan, insurance and investment cross-sells) triggered by account events, with marketing messages made visually indistinguishable from genuine security alerts. Notification controls bundle marketing with fraud alerts in a single toggle, so users cannot opt out of one without losing the other. This raises misleading/aggressive commercial practice and dark-pattern concerns as well as consent, purpose-limitation and profiling issues.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (permission and account-event data) was obtained under a stated security purpose and is then processed for an unrelated, undisclosed marketing purpose. Repurposing data collected for security to send cross-sell offers is neither fair nor transparent and breaches the incompatibility/purpose-limitation dimension of the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. Making marketing pushes 'visually identical to security alerts' compounds the unfairness by deceiving the data subject about the nature of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Separate marketing from security messaging: obtain a distinct, informed consent for marketing pushes, clearly disclose at collection that account-event data may be used for personalised offers, and visually and functionally distinguish marketing notifications from genuine security/fraud alerts.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Marketing cross-sell messages delivered through a channel consented to only for security/account alerts lack a valid lawful basis. Consent given for security cannot cover marketing; contract necessity does not extend to unsolicited cross-sell; and a legitimate-interest basis is hard to sustain given the deceptive framing and the sensitivity of financial-behaviour profiling. Processing for marketing therefore likely proceeds without any valid Art. 6(1) basis.
findings.evidence_quote: The bank now sends through the same channel: personal-loan offers after low-balance events
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a specific lawful basis for the marketing processing (consent is the safest given the intrusive profiling), and stop sending marketing through the security channel until such basis is in place.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific and as easy to withdraw as to give (Art. 7). Bundling marketing with essential fraud/security alerts under one toggle means users cannot withdraw consent for marketing without losing security protection — withdrawal is not as easy as giving consent and the consent is not specific. The original security-framed permission also cannot serve as specific consent for marketing.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts
findings.recommendation: Provide granular, independent controls so users can disable marketing pushes while keeping fraud/security alerts; ensure marketing consent is separately requested, specific, and withdrawable with a single equivalent action.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: The permission is not a valid consent for marketing: it is not specific (framed only around security), not informed (marketing use undisclosed), and is bundled with a non-marketing purpose. Under the Art. 4(11) definition such bundled, non-specific consent does not qualify as valid consent for the cross-sell processing.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Re-collect consent for marketing with a clearly distinguishable, purpose-specific opt-in that names the marketing purpose and the behavioural triggers used.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and to related profiling, and controllers must facilitate that objection. Here the only way to stop marketing is to disable the toggle, which also switches off fraud alerts — effectively penalising and obstructing exercise of the objection right, so the opt-out is not genuinely facilitated.
findings.evidence_quote: a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts
findings.recommendation: Offer a dedicated, cost-free way to object to direct marketing and marketing-related profiling that stops marketing pushes immediately while leaving security/fraud alerts fully active.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing low-balance events, large purchases and salary timing to trigger tailored financial offers is automated evaluation of the data subject's economic situation and behaviour — profiling within Art. 4(4). This profiling must have a lawful basis, be transparent, and be subject to the objection right, none of which appear satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling operations, ensure a lawful basis and transparency, and honour objections to profiling for marketing purposes.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: A 'pre-approved' credit amount generated automatically from account-behaviour profiling is a decision based on automated processing that can significantly affect the individual (access to and terms of credit). If made solely automatically, Art. 22 restrictions and safeguards (explicit consent/contract basis, information, right to human intervention) apply and do not appear to be met.
findings.evidence_quote: Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the pre-approval is solely automated with significant effect; if so, rely on a valid Art. 22 exception and provide the required safeguards including meaningful information about the logic and a route to human review.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting the permission/data, the controller must inform the data subject of all processing purposes and of profiling, including automated decision-making. The security-only framing omits the marketing and profiling purposes, so the Art. 13 information duties are not met.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Provide, at collection, a complete privacy notice covering the marketing purpose, the behavioural profiling triggers, the legal basis, and the existence of any automated decision-making such as pre-approval.

verdicts.notes: The bank obtained a push-notification permission framed solely for "security and important account alerts" and then repurposes the same channel and underlying account data to deliver behaviourally targeted marketing (loans, insurance, investments) triggered by profiling of customers' economic situation. This engages core GDPR obligations: fairness/transparency and lawful basis (the marketing purpose was neither disclosed nor consented to), invalid bundled consent with an obstructed withdrawal path, an obstructed right to object to direct marketing, profiling, and automated pre-approval decisions. Multiple likely violations are present.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The push permission was obtained for 'security and important account alerts', and marketing messages are made visually identical to genuine security alerts and sent through the same channel. This hides the commercial intent of the communication, which is not apparent from context — a misleading omission / disguised advertising under Art. 7(2). The consumer cannot distinguish a promotional loan/insurance/investment offer from a fraud or account-security notice, distorting their transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently label every marketing push as an advertisement/offer (e.g. distinct visual style, an 'Ad'/'Offer' tag and separate channel), so the commercial nature is immediately apparent. Never present promotional content with the same iconography, styling or channel as security alerts.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Timing loan offers to fire immediately after low-balance events targets consumers precisely when they are in a specific economic situation of financial pressure, using undue influence and exploitation of the consumer's circumstances to push a high-value credit decision ('in 2 taps'). Under Arts. 8-9, timing and exploitation of a consumer's situation are express factors making a practice aggressive where it is likely to impair freedom of choice and prompt a transactional decision the consumer would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps')
findings.recommendation: Do not trigger credit/loan marketing off distress signals such as low-balance, overdraft or missed-payment events. Remove urgency framing ('in 2 taps') that pushes an immediate credit decision, and ensure any credit promotion allows a genuine, unpressured opportunity to consider terms.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Bundling marketing pushes with fraud/security alerts under a single toggle means a consumer cannot decline marketing without sacrificing safety-critical fraud alerts. This is an onerous barrier and a form of undue influence/coercion: the consumer is effectively forced to keep receiving marketing to remain protected, impairing freedom of choice contrary to Arts. 8-9 (a deceptive/obstructive design pattern).
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.

findings.rationale: As a safety-net, Art. 5 (with the vulnerable-group perspective in Art. 5(3)) captures the overall practice: systematically exploiting consumers' financial situations and behavioural triggers via a channel they trusted for security, contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort economic behaviour — particularly for consumers in a fragile financial position around salary/spending events.

findings.recommendation: Adopt a documented professional-diligence standard for a regulated bank: separate transactional/security communications from marketing, avoid event-triggered targeting that leverages financial vulnerability, and obtain specific, informed consent for cross-sell messaging.

verdicts.notes: The campaign delivers behaviourally-targeted marketing (loan, insurance, investment cross-sells) through a push channel the consumer enabled only for "security and important account alerts", with marketing messages made visually indistinguishable from genuine security alerts. This disguises commercial intent (UCPD Art. 7) and, combined with the deliberate timing of loan offers after low-balance events and a single toggle that forces users to keep marketing to retain fraud alerts, engages the aggressive-practice prohibition (Arts. 8-9) and the general fairness/vulnerability safety-net (Art. 5). The financial-distress targeting is a significant aggravating factor. Fixes below are actionable and material to compliance.

report.executive_summary: This campaign sends personalised marketing pushes — pre-approved loans, insurance cross-sells and investment nudges — through the same app-notification channel that customers enabled only for "security and important account alerts," and makes those marketing messages look visually identical to genuine security/fraud alerts. Two independent specialist reviews (GDPR and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive) both flag likely serious violations, so the overall risk is high. The core problems: users never consented to marketing on this channel, the marketing purpose and behavioural profiling were never disclosed, and the single on/off toggle forces customers to lose fraud alerts if they want to stop the ads. The deliberate timing — loan offers fired right after low-balance events — targets people when they are financially stressed, which regulators treat as an aggressive practice and a significant aggravating factor. Disguising ads as security alerts is misleading (hidden commercial intent) and repurposing security data for marketing breaches purpose-limitation, lawful-basis and consent rules. The "pre-approved €3,000" nudge may also trigger automated-decision-making safeguards. As designed, this campaign should not go live; it needs structural fixes to consent, notification controls, labelling and trigger logic before launch.

Split the notification settings into granular controls so customers can turn off marketing pushes while keeping fraud and security alerts fully active; never bundle the two under one toggle.
Clearly and prominently label every marketing push as an offer/ad with a distinct visual style, and never reuse the iconography, styling or channel of genuine security alerts.

Remove financial-distress triggers: do not fire loan or credit offers off low-balance, overdraft or missed-payment events, and drop urgency framing like 'in 2 taps' that pressures an immediate credit decision.

Obtain a fresh, specific, informed marketing consent that names the behavioural triggers (low-balance, large purchases, salary day) and provide a full privacy notice at collection covering the marketing purpose, profiling and any automated decision-making.
Provide an easy, cost-free way to object to direct marketing and marketing-related profiling that takes effect immediately without disabling security alerts.

Assess whether the 'pre-approved €3,000' offer is a solely automated decision with significant effect; if so, add the required safeguards (valid basis, meaningful information about the logic, and a route to human review).
Document a professional-diligence standard separating transactional/security communications from marketing before any relaunch.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (account events, transaction patterns) is processed for marketing under a permission the user granted only for security/account alerts. Using data collected for one stated purpose to deliver disguised marketing is neither transparent nor fair, breaching the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. Making marketing pushes 'visually identical to security alerts' compounds the unfairness by hiding the commercial nature of the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: push permission was requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Separate marketing communications from the security-alert channel entirely, obtain a distinct, purpose-specific consent for marketing pushes, and clearly disclose at collection that the channel/data will be used for personalised commercial offers.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. The permission text refers only to security and account alerts, so it cannot constitute specific, informed consent for personal-loan, insurance and investment marketing delivered through the same channel. Any marketing consent so obtained is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: Enable notifications for security and important account alerts
findings.recommendation: Collect a separate, granular opt-in specifically describing marketing offers (loans, insurance, investments) in plain language, distinct from the security-alert permission.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent is not freely given where users cannot refuse marketing without also losing an unrelated, essential service (fraud/security alerts). Bundling the two into one toggle coerces users into keeping marketing on and makes withdrawal of marketing consent not 'as easy to give as to withdraw' — a detriment prohibited under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide independent toggles: security/fraud alerts must remain available regardless of marketing choices; marketing must be separately switchable off with no impact on essential alerts, and as easy to withdraw as to grant.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The marketing processing and profiling lack a valid legal basis. Consent is invalid (misleading permission, bundled toggle) and legitimate interests would very likely fail the balancing test given the deceptive design, the sensitivity of financial-vulnerability targeting and the users' reasonable expectation that this channel is for security only.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events ('Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps')
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any marketing push: obtain proper specific consent, and run a documented legitimate-interests assessment that accounts for user expectations and the vulnerability-targeting risks (which it would likely not pass as currently designed).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Triggering offers on low-balance events, large purchases and salary day is automated processing of personal data to evaluate and predict the data subject's economic situation and behaviour — profiling under Art. 4(4). This must rest on a lawful basis, be disclosed, and be subject to the marketing objection right.
findings.evidence_quote: insurance cross-sells after large card purchases, and 'investment nudges' on salary day
findings.recommendation: Recognise the event-based targeting as profiling: document it, disclose it in the privacy notice, ensure a valid basis, and allow users to object to profiling for marketing.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing, including profiling for marketing, is absolute — objecting must stop marketing processing. Here the only way to stop marketing also disables fraud alerts, so users cannot exercise an effective, cost-free objection to direct marketing as required by Art. 21(2)-(3).
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Offer a clear, standalone opt-out from marketing pushes and marketing profiling that immediately stops that processing while leaving security/fraud alerts fully operational; present this right explicitly at first contact.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: At the point of collecting the push permission, the controller must inform users of the purposes and legal basis of processing (including marketing and profiling) and of their rights. Presenting the permission only as 'security and important account alerts' omits the marketing/profiling purposes, so the Art. 13 information obligation is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide layered Art. 13 information at permission request disclosing the marketing purpose, the profiling based on account events, the legal basis, and the right to object, before any marketing use.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be concise, transparent and not misleading. Framing a permission that also enables marketing purely as 'security and important account alerts' is misleading rather than transparent, engaging Art. 12's clear-and-plain-language requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: Enable notifications for security and important account alerts
findings.recommendation: Rewrite permission and settings copy in clear, non-misleading language that distinguishes security alerts from marketing communications.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages GDPR seriously. Consent for push notifications was obtained solely for "security and important account alerts" but is now repurposed for personalised marketing (loans, insurance, investments) triggered by account-event profiling — breaching the transparency/fairness principle and rendering the consent neither specific nor freely given. The single on/off toggle unlawfully bundles fraud alerts with marketing, and there is no working right to object to direct marketing that preserves security alerts. Behavioural triggers (low balance, salary day, large purchases) constitute profiling of the data subject's economic situation.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: UCPD Art. 7(2) requires the commercial intent of a practice to be identified where not already apparent from context. Consumers granted the push permission for 'security and important account alerts', so the context signals a non-commercial safety channel. Delivering loan, insurance and investment marketing through the same channel and in a form visually identical to security alerts hides the commercial intent and provides material information (that this is advertising) in an unclear/untimely manner. The average consumer cannot distinguish marketing from a genuine alert and may take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Marketing pushes are visually identical to security alerts.
findings.recommendation: Clearly and prominently label every marketing push as an advertisement/offer (e.g. distinct icon, colour, 'Offer' tag), visually and functionally separate it from security/fraud alerts, and never present commercial content in a form that mimics account-safety notifications.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: UCPD Art. 6 catches practices that deceive the average consumer as to the nature of the communication. Framing the channel as 'security and important account alerts' and then sending commercial offers dressed identically deceives consumers about the nature of the message, lending marketing the false authority and urgency of a security alert and inducing engagement/transactional decisions (e.g. accepting a 'pre-approved' loan) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: requested as 'Enable notifications for security and important account alerts'
findings.recommendation: Do not obtain the notification permission under a 'security/important alerts' framing and then use it for marketing. Seek a separate, clearly described opt-in for promotional messages, and ensure marketing content is never styled to appear as an official account/security alert.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit aggressive practices using undue influence, including exploitation of a specific misfortune and timing designed to impair free choice. Triggering a 'pre-approved' high-value credit offer immediately after a low-balance event targets consumers in financial distress at their most vulnerable moment, exerting undue influence over the decision to take on debt. Combined with the single opt-out toggle that also disables fraud alerts, the design places an onerous barrier on refusing marketing (consumers must sacrifice fraud protection to opt out), which coerces continued exposure. This significantly impairs freedom of choice.
findings.evidence_quote: Running low? Pre-approved €3,000 in 2 taps
findings.recommendation: Stop triggering credit/marketing offers on financial-distress events (low balance, salary day) and separate the notification controls so consumers can disable marketing while keeping security and fraud alerts on, without any detriment or friction.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the fairness safety-net and, via Art. 5(3), requires assessment from the perspective of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group. Consumers experiencing low balances are in a specific economic situation making them more susceptible to credit offers. Deploying event-triggered credit and cross-sell marketing at these moments, through a channel authorised for security alerts, is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of financially vulnerable consumers.
findings.evidence_quote: personal-loan offers after low-balance events
findings.recommendation: Apply professional-diligence safeguards for financial-services marketing: avoid targeting consumers based on distress signals, ensure any credit promotion meets responsible-lending/affordability standards, and route marketing only through a genuine, clearly labelled marketing consent channel.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits persistent and unwanted solicitations via remote media. Because the only way to stop the marketing pushes is to also turn off fraud alerts, consumers who do not want the marketing are effectively unable to refuse it without losing essential safety notifications, so the solicitations continue against their wishes. Depending on frequency and repetition, ongoing event-triggered marketing that consumers cannot practicably opt out of risks amounting to persistent unwanted solicitation.
findings.evidence_quote: Notification settings offer only a single on/off toggle that also disables fraud alerts.
findings.recommendation: Provide a functioning, granular opt-out for marketing notifications that is honoured immediately and does not disable fraud/security alerts, and cease marketing pushes to consumers who have not effectively been able to consent or who opt out.

verdicts.notes: The campaign repurposes a push channel that consumers authorised for "security and important account alerts" to deliver personalised marketing (loans, insurance, investment nudges) that is visually indistinguishable from genuine security alerts. This engages several UCPD prohibitions: hidden commercial intent / misleading omission (Art. 7), misleading action as to the nature of the message (Art. 6), and aggressive practice through exploitation of financial vulnerability and a coercive opt-out that also kills fraud alerts (Arts. 8-9), with the Art. 5 safety-net and vulnerable-consumer standard reinforcing these. Several findings are likely breaches; disguised advertising and the coercive settings design are the most serious.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a banking app's push channel — which customers enabled only for "security and important account alerts" — to send personalised marketing (personal loans, insurance, investment nudges), styled to look identical to genuine security alerts. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, disguising ads as security alerts hides their commercial intent (misleading), and firing "pre-approved" credit offers at people right after a low-balance event exploits financially vulnerable consumers (aggressive practice). The AI Act, DSA were assessed as not applicable. The most damaging issues are the disguised-advertising design and the coercive opt-out that holds fraud protection hostage — both likely breaches with reputational and regulatory consequences. Verdict: high risk; the campaign should not run in its current form and needs structural redesign before launch.

Split the notification controls: fraud and security alerts must always remain on and independent; marketing must have its own separate toggle that customers can switch off immediately with no impact on safety alerts.

Cease triggering credit and cross-sell offers on financial-distress or sensitive events (low balance, salary day, large purchases). Targeting vulnerable moments with 'pre-approved' credit is an aggressive practice and likely breaches responsible-lending expectations.
Obtain a separate, specific, plainly worded opt-in consent for marketing pushes — distinct from the security-alert permission — before sending any promotional content.
Recognise the event-based targeting as profiling: document it, establish and record a valid lawful basis, and provide a working, cost-free right to object to direct marketing and marketing profiling.

Update the permission request and privacy disclosures (GDPR Arts. 12-13) so customers are told at collection about the marketing purpose, the profiling based on account activity, the legal basis, and their right to object — in clear, non-misleading language.
Do not launch in the current form; treat the disguised-advertising design and the bundled fraud-alert toggle as blocking issues requiring redesign and legal sign-off before go-live.
